Decided by AAS, 4–5 September 2026 (spec 0.3c decision register, D06).
  • docs/bellman-calculus/APPX-F-OPERATOR-ALGEBRA.md §F.6: "the graded refinement tower" is renamed the graded realisation tower, and its laws speak of each move of the tower; the convergence net is a settings net. "Refine" now means moving to a finer view of a stage (as in R7 and Appendix B) and is not used for the lifecycle, whose steps are methodize, configure, and calibrate. The wiki entry operator follows.

docs.title: 2026-07-18 — The carrier is exchangeable
docs.text: • docs/bellman-calculus/11-abstract-grammar.md §1: a paragraph added stating that the per-construct encoding — the head, then the keys' values in schema order — is the whole contract a file format must deliver. YAML is the canonical carrier, inherited from the dolo lineage; an alternative carrier is an adapter onto the same tree, changing a model's spelling and never its meaning. The ruling and the precedent survey behind it are recorded in the project road-map.

docs.title: 2026-07-18 — Stage page: abstract-grammar box; the perch state groups renamed
docs.text:
• docs/Bellman-Sym/01-stage.md §1 completed with the normative Abstract grammar: STAGE box, replacing the placeholder. The box fixes the head (!stage, name, optional kind) and the full symbols: block; the equations and dolo_plus sorts are carried opaque (the equations grammar belongs to the Field-equations page). The continuation-states group takes Flat | Branched alternatives, so a fork is read from the block's shape; decorator payloads are terminal atoms, per the no-AST position. The Status paragraph records the two software deviations (the kind: branching requirement; the legacy group names in the loaders).
  • The perch state declaration groups are renamed (decided 18 Jul 2026): arvl_states / dcsn_states / cntn_states, replacing prestate / states / poststates, which parse as permanent aliases. The grouped declaration shape is confirmed — the ruling and its reasons (the abstract syntax tree must carry enough authored context to build the semantic graph deterministically) are recorded in the road-map issue brief. The page's grammar box, group table, and examples carry the new spelling; the loader, translator, schema reference, and example files follow.
  • Smaller corrections on the same page: the summary box now names both aggregation equations — \(G_{\succ}\) (cntn_to_dcsn) and \(G_{\prec}\) (dcsn_to_arvl) — where it previously denied the arrival edge an aggregator; a note records that the feasible set has no declaration of its own beyond the @in domains (open design question, tracked in the road-map); page properties (front matter) added, matching the period and trellis pages.
  • Declarations read unquoted (decided 18 Jul 2026): the language's spelling is w: @in R+; the quoted form (w: "@in R+") remains what today's loaders require — standard YAML reserves @ at the start of an unquoted value — and is what generated files emit. Recorded as a software difference in the stage page's grammar box until the reader accepts the unquoted form.

docs.title: 2026-07-18 — Value symbols are fields; the "perch value objects" section retired
docs.text:
• docs/Bellman-Sym/01-stage.md: the "Perch objects and perch value objects" section removed. It claimed the surface carries two kinds of objects with different identity rules; the calculus says otherwise — every declared symbol is a field typed by perch, role, and domain, and (token, perch) identity holds for all of them (Fields, functions and types and its field catalogue). The section's surviving content — the role and domain of the value groups, the per-perch declaration of the value token, bare V reading at the decision perch, and value fields being defined by backward evaluation equations — is now the "Value fields" subsection §3.1; the shifting section renumbered §5 → §4 with in-page references updated; the namespace callout reduced to one line linking to Periods.
  • docs/Bellman-Sym/appendices/13-perch-tagging-rules.md §4 restated. Value fields are governed by the same tag function as every field: a token declared at several perches is Rule 2's situation, with "unmarked = decision" a naming convention layered on it — replacing the earlier "not governed by these rules" exemption. The tag-function table row updated to match.
  • The shelf index line for the stage page now says "value fields" instead of "perch objects" (and no longer lists branching, which moved to its own page on 17 Jul).

docs.title: 2026-07-17 — Branching gets its own page
docs.text:
• New page docs/Bellman-Sym/05-branching.md ("05 Branching" in the nav, between Methodization and Periods): the stage page's "Branching declarations" section and the field-equations page's branching material (the branch-keyed transition mapping, the branch combination in the policy block, the endogenous-probabilities example) combined into one page — declarations and the coproduct reading, declaration rules, branch transitions and builders, the combining step, value functions on a coproduct, composition within a period, and the worked softmax example. Content moved verbatim; the source pages keep one-sentence pointers, and the periods page's branching links now point here.
  • The shelf renumbered once more: Periods through Appendix D became 06–15 (06-period, 07-trelis, 08-spec-factory (to be renamed 08-bellman-factory by AMD-FAC-002 F12), 09-from-syntax-to-formal-problem-definition, 10-appendix-a-recipes, 11-appendix-b-dolo-translation, 12-equation-parsing-rules, 13-perch-tagging-rules, 14-appendix-c-syntax-to-semantics, 15-appendix-d-node-tag-and-field-indexing), with references, nav, and the shelf index adjusted.

docs.title: 2026-07-17 — Periods and trellises split into two pages; shelf renumbered
docs.text:
• 05-period-and-trelis.md split into docs/Bellman-Sym/05-period.md ("05 Periods") and docs/Bellman-Sym/06-trelis.md ("06 Trellises" — a full section of its own, per AAS). The period page carries the period grammar box, the stage-reference rule, connectors, and branching; the trellis page carries the trellis grammar box, the worked trellis examples, and well-formedness. Content moved verbatim; each page gained its own summary and relationship boxes, and every inbound reference across the docs, wiki, and rules was retargeted to whichever page now owns the material.

docs.title: 2026-07-16 — New theory page: Abstract grammar
docs.text:

The nesting of the authored objects is presented as the language's abstract grammar (its abstract syntax): a constructor grammar bottoming out at the modeller's data — transitions, rewards, shock distributions, parameters — with the builders produced by the Υ evaluation rather than present in the term. Periods and trellises are insert-composition of represented stage objects in Backus's FFP sense, with the FP-versus-FFP licensing of that fold stated precisely; the page closes with what the tree is not (no parse of value-level arithmetic; a shared term graph at run time; many-sorted and fixed-vocabulary where Backus is untyped and open-ended).

docs.title: 2026-06-15 — Operator algebra (Appendix F) + methods catalogue, validated against the applications
docs.text:
• New Appendix F — Operator algebra (docs/bellman-calculus/APPX-F-OPERATOR-ALGEBRA.md): the algebra the operators form — the presented distributive category (cartesian backward / Markov forward), branching by coproducts, the graded refinement tower (mathematize → parameterize → methodize → settingize → horse), and the operator type system (morphisms typed by rank × grade). Hardened against adversarial review by two Matsya models (opus 4.8 and gpt-5.5 pro), which converged on: the carrier is a presented distributive category (not a free SMC); branching needs coproducts; the methodization law is mathematization-preserving with convergence (\(\rho\to\Upsilon\)), not denotation-erasure (this supersedes the §3.4 erasure reading of spec 0.1a); "transpose under the pairing," scoped to the policy-fixed linear fragment, replaces "conjugate."
  • Methods catalogue (Appendix E.5–E.6, catalogues/methods.md, catalogues/method-schemes.md): single source of truth for methods. Methods attach to operators directly — the legacy scheme: classifier is retired (migration table in E.5). Supersedes dolo-plus-spec/reference/method-schemes.md and the methods/operations sections of primitives.md.

docs.title: 2026-06-11 — Forward-builder notation: \(\mathbb{F}_\prec \to \mathbb{F}\), \(\mathbb{F}^{\sigma}_{\succ} \to \mathbb{G}_{\pi}\)
docs.text:
• The decision-edge forward builder is now written \(\mathbb{G}_{\pi}\) — a pushforward under a policy function \(\pi\) — and the arrival-edge forward builder is plain \(\mathbb{F}\) (no subscript). Rationale: the decision-side object exists only once a policy fills the action slot, so the notation should name the policy rather than the perch; with the two builders distinguished by letter, neither needs a \(\prec\)/\(\succ\) subscript. The composite forward stage operator is \(\mathbb{F}^{\pi} = \mathbb{G}_{\pi} \circ \mathbb{F}\) (previously \(\mathbb{F}^{\sigma}\)), and the policy symbol in forward contexts is \(\pi\) throughout (the conjugacy partner is the policy-closed expectation \(\mathbb{E}^{\pi}_{\eta}\)); \(\sigma\) remains in backward-side contexts. Blackboard \(\mathbb{G}\) is distinct from the roman aggregator \(\mathrm{G}\) of the stage tuple.
  • Updated: docs/bellman-calculus/ (02, 03, 04, 05, APPX-B), docs/dolo-plus-spec/reference/symbols-conventions.md, AI/rules/terminology.md (forward-builder row), the wiki (forward_builder page and schema description), and the live specs (semantics 0.0 and 0.1a, rosetta-stone 0.2, forward-builders 0.1m — where the old plain-\(\mathbb{F}\) composite is now \(\mathbb{F}^{\pi}\) to free \(\mathbb{F}\) for the arrival builder). Schema-level symbols F_ad / F_de are unchanged; the math column of the 0.1m mapping table records the correspondence \(\mathbb{F} \leftrightarrow\) F_ad, \(\mathbb{G}_{\pi} \leftrightarrow\) F_de. Historical material (superseded specs, docs/old/, the ModularMDP-era unified sections, past presentation decks) retains the old notation as a record.

The headline structural finding is the mirror image of dolo: HARK's solve_one_period_* functions are natively one backward step (the §6.5 step-count clause holds by construction, no max_iter=1 workaround), but they hard-code their model family's transitions and rewards, so the §6.5 no-re-encoding clause cannot hold without refactoring. docs.title: 2026-04-30 — The multi-period composite renamed from nest to trellis
docs.text:

Both prior names were placeholders without literature precedent; trellis has a precise meaning in coding theory (Forney 1973, "The Viterbi Algorithm") and is used by Bertsekas (DP and Optimal Control Vol I, Ch. 2) for finite-state DP visualisations. Decided jointly by AAS and CDC after a Matsya-led literature search. See AI/working/AAS/30042026/session.md for the full rationale and docs/dolo-plus-spec/reference/definitions.md for the canonical entry.

• spec 0.2a (compiler pipeline architecture): Lean 4-inspired architectural spec for the full dolo-plus compiler pipeline.

    • 8-stage pipeline (Parse → Validate → Υ → Methodize → Calibrate → Ρ → Solve → Analyze) with typed intermediate representations at each stage.
    • Operator registry with attribute-based registration (pluggable methods as Lean-style tactics).
    • Immutable environment threading (scoped extensions pattern).
    • Template-driven Ρ-map code generation.
    • Multi-error validation following Lean's collect-all-errors approach.
    • Composition pipeline design for periods and nests.
    • Pluggable methods as tactics: Lean's tactic framework (registered proof strategies dispatched by name) maps directly to the DDSL operator registry (registered solver methods dispatched by method tag). The @register_method decorator pattern enables extensibility without modifying core pipeline code.
    • Persistent IRs prevent black-box pipelines: Every pipeline stage should produce a serializable, inspectable intermediate representation. This makes debugging, diffing, and testing tractable — you can inspect a methodized stage without running calibration.
    • Immutable environment threading: Following Lean's scoped extensions, each pipeline stage should extend (never mutate) the symbol/method environment. This is especially important for composition, where each stage in a period has its own scope joined by connector renames.
  • Lean 4 ≈ CORE elaboration note: added analogy connecting Lean 4's elaboration pipeline to the φ (SYM → CORE) translation in 08-sym-core-architecture.md, for-engineers.md, and homepage.
    • Elaboration ≈ φ (SYM → CORE): Lean 4's elaboration (surface Syntax → kernel Expr) is the precise analogue of the Bellman-calculus φ map (dolo-plus YAML → normalized typed stage IR). The kernel/elaboration separation principle means CORE should be small and trusted; all complexity lives in the SYM-to-CORE desugaring.
  • AI/matsya.md: added Matsya RAG configuration file to repo.
  • Perch tag propagation (repo-wide):

  • Value object perch tags: V → V[-] and dV → dV[-] in all YAML snippets where decision-perch value objects appeared bare. Value objects that exist at all three perches require explicit [-] tag at the decision perch (unlike controls/states where unmarked = decision by convention). Updated in homepage, symbols-conventions, for-engineers, consumption_savings_iid example doc, ddsl_foundations proposal.

This is a measurability distinction: V[-] asserts "V evaluated at the decision σ-algebra", which differs from V[<] and V[>].

docs.title: Bellman-SYM
docs.text:
Summary

Write a household's consumption problem in .bl, inspect its equations, then separate consumption, discounting, and investment into reusable stages. YAML supplies their connections, numerical choices, and parameter values. This guide covers authoring, assembly, inspection, and the Python interfaces; Bellman calculus develops the mathematical foundations.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Overview: the stage, its perches and fields, and the joining of stages into periods and a trellis, in prose. Used by — Stages: the complete income-and-consumption tutorial. Formal account — Bellman calculus: staged Bellman problems and their mathematical interpretation.

docs.title: 1 Reading order
docs.text:
Begin with the buffer-stock consumption tutorial. The household observes income, consumes from its available resources, and saves without borrowing. A stage is a module of that decision problem with three information sets, its perches: arrival, decision and continuation. The later examples reuse consumption as a separate stage and join it to discounting and investment.

Step Read What to establish Write a stage Stages The household's information, admissible choices, resource transitions, and value equations. Inspect its meaning From syntax to a mathematical problem, then the API The same equations with explicit state arguments and their required assumptions. Reuse and compose Field equations, Periods, and Trellises Separate consumption, discounting, and investment; choose the period boundary and terminal inputs. Choose methods and parameters Methodization and The Bellman factory Numerical choices and economic parameter values for each use of a stage. Keep numerical results Solutions at the perches Where a solver keeps what it computes: one plain dictionary for each stage occurrence, keyed by perch and by field, filled by the stage's compiled kernels. Examine a numerical application the lesson tutorials/models/cons-port/03-solving-the-two-orders.ipynb of the repository The portfolio–consumption model solved in both orders of its stages and the consumption rules and risky shares compared.

The lesson solves with the model's own numerical tool; parsing or constructing a stage solves nothing. A stage occurrence is one use of a stage file at one position of a period. Each stage occurrence can have its own parameter values and numerical settings. Construction and specification prepare stage occurrences; solving additionally requires numerical routines and continuation or terminal data.

For discrete alternatives, read Branching, which uses the separate work-or-retire example. Choosing a continuous portfolio share is not a discrete branch.

For data indexed by a parameter-defined number of cities or shock outcomes, see Indexed data. For an integer state whose values mean, for example, newborn or old, see Category codes; Periods explains how connections preserve those meanings.

docs.title: 2 Files and authoring reference
docs.text:
File Contents Guide .bl Stage declarations, functions, shock laws, and equations. Stages and Field equations. Period and trellis YAML Stage occurrences and compatible field connections. Periods and Trellises. Methods, settings, and calibration YAML Numerical targets and options, and economic parameters. Methodization. Specification-recipe YAML Which sources supply methods, settings and calibration, their precedence, and period-dependent assignments. The Bellman factory.

For individual spellings, use Equation parsing rules, Perch tagging rules, Constraints for bounds and the complementary-slackness clause, Expression forms, Shock distributions, Method types, and Symbol conventions. Operations lists the kinds of operation of which a builder, the operator a block of a stage file defines, is composed, and Refusals the rules under which a stage file, a method target or a model's files are refused. The model directory layout describes the files of a model and where each is kept.

docs.title: 3 Inspection and Python interfaces
docs.text:
Inspection is part of using Bellman-SYM. The API lists every function in three tables, one for each of bellman.stage, bellman.period and bellman.trellis, and every path of the stage object in a fourth, and its pages take the object one level at a time, from the stage to the binding verbs: the mathematical structure a constructed stage retains, its equations, its typed quantities and its numerical attachments. The factories load and specify those stages:

Page Responsibility The factory API The fourteen functions of the Bellman factory and the page that states each. Stage functions Load a stage file into a record, elaborate it, and bind one stage. Recipe functions Read a registry through its recipe: the merge, the slots and the fills. Period functions Append a period, derive the order of its stages from their fields, and make the drawing of the period. The trellis factory Read a trellis file, elaborate and bind every period, and make the drawing of the trellis.

For a new stage occurrence, loading and elaboration come first, then calibration, methodization and configuration, the order the factory uses. Each of the three bindings adds its binding to the stage occurrence it is called on and returns that stage; methodization must precede configuration, since the methods name the settings (Methodization §5). Inspecting the equations and attachments is separate from obtaining numerical policies.

docs.title: 4 Mathematical reference
docs.text:
The Bellman calculus guide explains the mathematical foundations. Within this language guide, Appendix C gives rules R1–R12 for interpreting equations, including the assumptions for representing fields as functions of states. Appendix D explains computation boundaries, collection selection, and implicit policy relations.

Folded abstract-grammar boxes use ASDL, a notation describing syntax-tree structure. Their constructor listings do not prove the economic assumptions needed for an equation's interpretation. The concept wiki defines recurring terms.

docs.title: Stages
docs.text:
#stage#dolo-plus

Summary

Write a household's consumption problem in a .bl file. Declare what the household knows, what it chooses, and which equations determine resources, savings, and value. The example includes income risk and a borrowing constraint. Further examples declare indexed city data and integer states with recorded category meanings.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — The stage: the stage, its perches and its fields in prose, on a buffer-stock model like this page's. Used by — Field equations: consumption as a separate stage file and its first-order equations; Periods: joining stages. Formal account — Appendix C: conditions for interpreting fields as functions of states.

docs.title: 1 Stages and perches
docs.text:
A household begins with nonnegative assets b, earns the gross return R, and observes positive income y. It chooses consumption c from resources w = R*b + y and retains savings a = w-c. Consumption must be strictly positive and savings nonnegative, so the feasible choices satisfy \(0<c\leq w\).

A stage is a module of a Bellman problem with three information sets, called perches. In this example they distinguish income arriving, consumption being chosen, and savings being available for continuation:

Perch What the household knows State used in this example Arrival Beginning assets, before the current income draw. b, beginning assets. Decision Beginning assets and realized income; consumption is chosen here. w, resources available to consume or save. Continuation The consumption choice and the resulting savings. a, savings available for the future.

A state summarizes the information needed for the remaining problem. We assume resources suffice for the consumption decision and savings suffice for continuation value. The household may remember more than these scalar states record; the perch describes its information, whereas the state supplies the arguments of its value function. These sufficiency assumptions are part of the economic model, not consequences of the notation.

docs.title: 2 Declarations and types
docs.text:
A declaration is a name, a colon and a type. The type says what the name may denote: a set of admissible values, called its domain, a role in the decision problem, an information set, or a combination of these. The complete file in §4 declares a parameter, a shock, a control and a value this way:

β : (0,1)
y : ℝ₊₊
c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl
V : ℝ @ !vlu

A type is a list of components joined by @. A component is either a set, written in mathematical notation, or a word with the prefix !. The components are unordered, so c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl and c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊ declare the same type, and a type contains at most one set, one role word and one perch word. The join @ combines descriptions of one quantity; it never multiplies sets. A quantity valued in a product is declared with × inside its set, as x : ℝ × ℝ. The prefix is what marks a vocabulary word, so a bare word is always a name and no word is reserved.

Word What it says !arvl, !dcsn, !cntn The name belongs to the arrival, the decision or the continuation perch. !ctrl The name is a control, chosen at decision. !vlu The name is a value. !shck The name is a shock; written when the shock is declared before its law. !state The name is a state; a restatement, since a name with a set and a perch and no role word is a state. !node Written in a statement's annotation, not after a colon: the statement is a separately inspectable computation (Appendix D).

Parameters carry a set and neither a role nor a perch, as R : ℝ₊₊. States are declared with a set alone; their role is derived. A value carries its role word !vlu, and the control carries !ctrl. A marginal value is no field and has no role word: the derivative of a value is read where a line needs it, by the term D_{a}V[>], the derivative of the continuation value in the continuation coordinate a (Field equations §2).

A field name is local to the stage occurrence that declares it. Another stage may use the same spelling for a different field, and a matching name does not by itself connect the stages. All branches of one stage share its declarations, so separate branch states need separate names. A parameter has different scope: a name declared by two stages in one period denotes one period parameter, with one compatible declaration and one value; the same name in another period denotes another parameter. Fields and Parameters give these distinctions.

The colon binds to the smallest complete object on its left. In (w, c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) the type belongs to c alone, and w is a reference to an earlier declaration. Parentheses make several names one object: (w, c) : S declares two names jointly constrained by the set S, and tuples nest wherever a name may stand, as in ((k, h) : K, y) : !arvl. A tuple of two names and one name valued in a product are different declarations: (w, c) : ℝ × ℝ constrains two names jointly, whereas x : ℝ × ℝ declares one name whose components are selected as x[1] and x[2] (Equation parsing rules).

A law is not a type. A shock's distribution is an object, like the number 0.96, and two shocks with the same distribution are not interchangeable, so the distribution is assigned on its own line with ~, after the shock's set has been declared:

y : ℝ₊₊
y ~ LogNormal(μ_y, σ_y)

The fused form y : ℝ₊₊ ~ LogNormal(…) is not admitted. The distribution declaration makes y a shock; use !shck to declare it before supplying its distribution. A joint distribution takes a tuple subject, (Ψ, θ) ~ N(…). Separate declarations imply conditional independence given the source coordinates unless one names the other as an argument. The stage records this factorization as an assumption. Shock distributions lists the families a shock's distribution may take, LogNormal among them.

Block signatures are typed the same way. In [id=arvl_to_dcsn, (b : ℝ₊, y) : !arvl -> (w : ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn], the word after each parenthesized side names the perch of every coordinate listed on that side, with two exceptions: a shock listed on a side is an argument of the block's equations and belongs to no perch, and a control is at decision wherever it is listed. A backward block's header lists the value fields it reads and writes and the controls at which its lines are read, and no state: a state of the perch at which the block's output stands is a coordinate of that output, which a line reads without listing it, and a listed state is refused under header-coordinate. It lists no marginal value either: a line reads the derivative of a value the header lists by the term D_{a}V[>], and a line of a value builder's block may state the derivative of the value the block writes, D_{m_d}V = 𝑑𝑢(c), with nothing listed for it (Field equations §2). A value field the header lists and no line of the block reads is admitted: it is left out of the block's builder, and the elaboration records it as a diagnostic, the header lists V[>], which no line of the block reads, in place of a refusal. A name's set is declared at its first occurrence, in the preamble or on a side, and its perch is fixed the first time it appears on a perch-named side, by a perch word in its own type, or by its perch mark. A later occurrence may restate the set or the perch, and the restatement must agree with the declaration; it may not change it. A side may omit its perch word only when the perch of every non-shock coordinate on it is already known, as the portfolio application's policy signature (V[>]) -> ς does; a perch is never guessed. Perch tagging rules gives the information-set reading of these rules.

Definitions and binders use the same colon. A named set is defined with :=, as Xa := ℝ₊ or Xa := [0, ā]. A function is defined with typed arguments, 𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(1-ρ)/(1-ρ), whose c is local to the definition and is not the stage's control. Similarly, the binder of a maximization ranges over a feasible set written after a colon, argmax_{c : Γ(w)}(…), with the bare binder argmax_{c} when the control's declared set is its feasible set (Constraints).

These sets describe admissible economic values. A numerical grid used to approximate a continuous domain is supplied separately through the method settings.

The complete file uses the following spellings:

Spelling What the modeller states R : ℝ₊₊ The gross return is a strictly positive parameter. c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl Consumption is a strictly positive decision control. V : ℝ @ !vlu V is a real-valued value field. 𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(1-ρ)/(1-ρ) Utility is a function of positive consumption. a = w - c Savings equal resources less consumption. y ~ LogNormal(μ_y, σ_y) The separately declared income shock has the specified law. :: [id=savings] The equation has the address savings within its block.

Thus : declares a type, @ joins its components, := defines, = states an equation, ~ supplies a shock distribution, and -> separates the two sides of a block signature. @ appears in exactly one other place, the metadata line @stage: buffer_stock that names the stage.

The file declares the discount factor β between zero and one and risk aversion ρ greater than one. For example, ρ = 2 gives utility \(u(c)=-1/c\), finite on positive consumption. This example excludes unit risk aversion, where the displayed formula would divide by zero. The income convention is explicit: conditional on arrival information, log income is normal with mean μ_y and standard deviation σ_y. This conditional distribution is constant given that information, so current income is independent of earlier observations. Positive income ensures positive resources even at zero beginning assets. A zero standard deviation gives deterministic positive income.

docs.title: 2.1 Indexed data
docs.text:
For a household choosing among J cities, the number of cities can remain a parameter when the stage is written. Declare the city set and the data indexed by it:

J : ℤ, >= 1
L_J := {1, …, J}
δ : L_J → ℝ
dist : L_J × L_J → ℝ₊

The collection δ supplies one payoff per city, and dist supplies one distance per ordered pair of cities. If the current city is declared as a state i : L_J and the destination as a control j : L_J @ !ctrl, an equation reads their entries as δ[j] and dist[j][i]. Their use as indices does not determine their economic roles: i records the current location, j is chosen, and J determines the size of the common domain.

Every destination leads to the same successor stage, so the choice is one block and not a branching stage: [id=dcsn_to_cntn, (i_d, j : !ctrl @ L_J) : !dcsn -> (i_n : L_J) : !cntn] { i_n = j } retains the chosen city as the integer continuation state, and the number of cities stays the parameter J.

A numerical key must be integer-valued, including when a parameter determines it. A listed set such as S_θ := {0, θ} ⊂ ℤ is also admitted, with an integer-valued parameter θ; its keys need not be consecutive. By contrast, entries such as payoffs, distances and wages may be real-valued. In q[s] with s : S_θ, the value of s identifies a key; it is not a position in the list supplied at calibration. Positions counted from one select components of a fixed tuple, as in x[1] and x[2] for x : ℝ × ℝ.

Calibration supplies the values of J, δ and dist, checking the integer bounds and the number and domains of their entries. A different J uses the same stage declaration with correspondingly sized data. Symbol conventions §9.2.1 gives the admitted index sets, data order and a calibration example. Each index's declared domain must fit the corresponding table domain: a state ranging over cities and an outside option cannot directly select from a table defined only on cities (Appendix D §5.2).

docs.title: 2.2 Category codes
docs.text:
A household's status can be an integer state whose codes have recorded meanings. Define the set and give each member a category name:

HouseholdStatus := {i : ℤ | i >= 0, i <= 1} :: [!categories household_status, newborn=0, old=1]
n : HouseholdStatus

The expression between braces is a comprehension: it contains the integers satisfying every condition after |, with i local to that definition. The annotation assigns the name newborn to 0 and old to 1. A state declared on HouseholdStatus therefore takes integer values, while the stage retains the correspondence between those values and their meanings. Recording categories does not create a branching stage; the blocks still specify the state transitions and any choices.

Equations use the codes. For example, a transition to old age is written n_next = 1, with n_next also declared on HouseholdStatus; writing n_next = old is refused because the annotation does not declare old as a name usable in equations. Ordinary arithmetic remains available, so 100 - 120*n equals 100 for a newborn household and −20 for an old one. With three or more categories, using an affine formula in the code imposes equal steps in that formula; assigning codes alone supplies no distance between categories.

The marked set must have a nonempty integer range bounded by literal inequalities, with exactly one name per code and one code per name. Use the shared identifier household_status when these meanings are used across stage files; Periods §2 explains how connections check them. The complete annotation rules and the distinction from collection index sets are in Symbol conventions §9.2.2.

docs.title: 3 Builder blocks
docs.text:
A field is a quantity interpreted in its declared information set. A block groups equations between declared inputs and outputs. These two blocks, taken from the complete file in §4, express the household's budget:

[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (b : ℝ₊, y) : !arvl -> (w : ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn] {
    w = R*b + y                  :: [id=resources]
}
[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (w, c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] {
    a = w - c                    :: [id=savings]
}

Read the first signature from left to right: beginning assets and the income shock determine decision resources. Here ℝ₊ means nonnegative real numbers and ℝ₊₊ means strictly positive real numbers. Income and the return parameter are declared elsewhere in the same file. The second signature declares c as a control, a quantity the household chooses at decision, and a as nonnegative continuation savings. Its equation and domains jointly impose the borrowing constraint; the maximization in §4 ranges over these feasible choices.

The words !arvl, !dcsn, and !cntn identify the three information sets, the perches. A shock listed on a signature side is an argument of the transition: listing y on the arrival side does not say that income has already been observed. Similarly, a control retains its decision role when a later block lists it with continuation inputs. Perch tagging rules explains both exceptions.

The identifiers arvl_to_dcsn, resources, and savings supply addresses for inspection and supported numerical methods. Their names do not supply mathematical equations. Renaming resources consistently changes its address but preserves w = R*b + y.

docs.title: 4 A complete stage file
docs.text:
Save this source as buffer_stock.bl. The final three blocks add current utility to continuation value, average over income before it is observed, and choose a feasible consumption maximizer:

@stage: buffer_stock

β : (0,1)
ρ : (1, inf)
R : ℝ₊₊
μ_y : ℝ
σ_y : ℝ₊
y : ℝ₊₊
y ~ LogNormal(μ_y, σ_y)

𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(1-ρ)/(1-ρ)

[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (b : ℝ₊, y) : !arvl -> (w : ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn] {
    w = R*b + y                  :: [id=resources]
}
[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (w, c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] {
    a = w - c                    :: [id=savings]
}
[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu, c) : !cntn -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {
    V = 𝑢(c) + β*V[>]            :: [id=value]
}
[id=dcsn_to_arvl, (V) : !dcsn -> (V[<] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !arvl] {
    V[<] = E_{y}(V)              :: [id=value]
}
[id=policy, (V[>]) : !cntn -> (c) : !dcsn] {
    c = argmax_{c}(𝑢(c) + β*V[>]) :: [id=choice]
}

Here V[>] is the continuation-value input, V is decision value, and V[<] is arrival value. [<] and [>] select the stage's information sets; they do not mean the preceding and following calendar periods. A bare field or [~] uses the decision interpretation when its declaration and equation context establish it, as for V here. An ordinary collection selection such as q[a] has a different meaning from evaluating a function at q(a); see Equation parsing rules.

The continuation input is a function \(W:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\) of savings, supplied by the next period or a terminal boundary. For a given feasible consumption choice, the value equation represents

\[ Q(w,c)=u(c)+\beta W(w-c). \]

The policy block chooses \(\pi(w)\in\arg\max_{0<c\leq w}Q(w,c)\), and decision value is \(v(w)=Q(w,\pi(w))\). Before income is observed, arrival value is \(B(b)=\int v(Rb+y)\,\nu_y(dy)\), where \(\nu_y\) is the specified income distribution. The expectation therefore uses the policy selected after income is observed. Setting \(W=B\) would be an additional stationary-model condition; the stage does not impose it.

Assume \(W\) is finite and continuous on every compact savings interval and select a measurable maximizer. The maximum is attained because utility tends to minus infinity at zero consumption while continuation value is bounded on the feasible savings interval. Concavity of \(W\) makes the consumption maximizer unique. The arrival equation additionally requires \(\int|v(Rb+y)|\,\nu_y(dy)<\infty\); bounded continuous \(W\) is a sufficient case under this lognormal distribution. Appendix C R5–R8 gives the state-representation, integration, and policy conditions.

This documentation example modifies the repository's applications/consumption-savings-iid/declaration/stages/cons_savings_iid/cons_savings_iid.bl: it uses wholly positive income, restricts utility and discount parameters, and states the choice by the maximization alone, as that application's stage file also does, over its declared feasible set Γ(w) = (0, w]; the application writes the interior candidate equation of the endogenous grid in a method block and the derivatives of its values in marginal blocks, which its methods file binds (Methodization §4.1). The displayed source is the example taught here; it does not certify the different application source.

docs.title: 5 Files and next steps
docs.text:
The stage file states the model equations. To solve a finite-horizon problem, supply continuation and terminal values, methods, settings, and calibration. Those outer files use YAML. Field equations separates consumption from income and discounting so that these stage files can be joined in a period.

A block is the authored typed group of equations between declared inputs and outputs, and a builder is the operator that block defines: a transition, a value calculation, or a policy relation. The builder keeps the block's id as its name, and a reader reaches it in the elaborated stage by the pair of perches its block joins, stage.builder["cntn", "dcsn"] for the block cntn_to_dcsn, the policy builder by its own key, stage.builder["policy"], or from a perch, which reaches the builders of the edge that leaves it, the step from that perch to the next: stage.dcsn.builder.bwd is the same builder, which constructs the value at the decision perch, stage.arvl.builder.bwd the builder of dcsn_to_arvl, and stage.dcsn.builder.policy that of policy. The backward builders used in solution form the graph stage.builder.bwd, and the forward ones used in simulation the graph stage.builder.fwd (The builders graphs §§1 to 3). To make one equation separately inspectable, add !node to its annotation; Field equations demonstrates this with savings. Neither a block's name nor a numerical-method choice supplies a missing equation.

For loading, use the factory API, and for inspection the API. The stage retains interpreted equations and definitions in a graph of mathematical operations and their typed connections. With the required assumptions, its field equations can also be inspected as functions of states. Their mathematical relationship is described in Appendix C.

Technical details

.bl inherits its syntax from dynspec, an expression language. Parsing constructs a temporary abstract syntax tree, a structured representation of the written file. Checked interpretation constructs the stage's semgraph, the semantic graph of its equations, and discards that tree and its source spans.

Abstract grammar: FILE

This is a projection of the dynspec host grammar in ASDL, the notation for syntax-tree constructors. * means an ordered list and ? means optional. The omitted declaration alternative and the definitions of the referenced sorts belong to the full grammar; this projection does not redefine them.

file = FILE(item* items)
item = Metadata(identifier key, scalar value)
     | Statement(stmt core, annotation? annot)
     | Block(annotation tag, item* body)

Keys. items preserves source order; key and value give metadata; core is a statement with optional annot; tag is a block header and body its contents. These are ASDL fields, not YAML keys to write in a .bl file. scalar, stmt, and annotation are host sorts.

Head. Stage metadata identifies the stage file; the syntax-tree root remains FILE.

Denotes. Interpretation constructs the declared stage equations and their typed connections, subject to Appendix C.

Status. The three item constructors shown retain their argument order and multiplicity. Scope, type agreement, and complete output definitions are construction checks, not consequences of this grammar box.

docs.title: Field equations
docs.text:
#syntax-rules

Summary

Separate consumption from income and investment so that the same consumption module can be reused. Its equations state the borrowing constraint and the optimal choice. A later variant derives interior candidates from the derivative of the continuation value and explains the additional conditions needed by the endogenous grid method.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Stages: consumption after income is observed, declarations, and information sets. Used by — Methodization: numerical methods for authored computations; Periods: joining consumption, discounting, and investment. Formal account — Appendix C: field and functional interpretation; Appendix D: computation boundaries and indexing.

docs.title: 1 Consumption and savings
docs.text:
The household now enters the consumption stage with observed positive resources m. Resources do not change before its consumption decision, so the decision state is m_d = m. Consumption c leaves savings a = m_d-c, subject to \(0<c\leq m_d\). A field is a quantity interpreted in its declared information set; the signatures place resources at arrival and decision, the control at decision, and savings at continuation.

Save the following complete source as cons.bl:

@stage: cons
ρ : (1, inf)
𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(1-ρ)/(1-ρ)
[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (m : ℝ₊₊) : !arvl -> (m_d : ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn] {
    m_d = m
}
[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m_d, c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] {
    a = m_d - c
}
[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu, c) : !cntn -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {
    V = 𝑢(c) + V[>]
}
[id=dcsn_to_arvl, (V) : !dcsn -> (V[<] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !arvl] {
    V[<] = V
}
[id=policy, (V[>]) : !cntn -> (c) : !dcsn] {
    c = argmax_{c}(𝑢(c) + V[>])
}

V[>] denotes the continuation-value field, which a supplied function \(H:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\) of savings represents. Holding consumption fixed, the backward block denotes the choice value, the objective before a policy is substituted:

\[ Q(m_d,c)=u(c)+H(m_d-c). \]

The policy block selects \(\pi(m_d)\in\arg\max_{0<c\leq m_d}Q(m_d,c)\), giving optimized value \(v(m_d)=Q(m_d,\pi(m_d))\). Because arrival resources already contain the information needed for this decision, arrival value equals \(v(m)\).

Assume \(H\) is finite and continuous on every compact savings interval and select a measurable maximizer. As in Stages, utility's limit at zero consumption gives attainment; concavity of \(H\) makes the maximizer unique. This value-only source includes zero savings and requires no positive continuation derivative. A constant terminal continuation is admissible and leads to consuming all resources.

There is no discount factor in this module. When it is joined to the separate discount stage, \(H\) already includes that stage's discounting. Periods supplies the discount and investment sources and explains their order. The earlier buffer_stock.bl combines income, consumption, and discounting in one stage; adding its discount factor again here would count it twice.

This source is a documentation variant of applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl: it excludes zero consumption and unit risk aversion and uses the constrained maximization as its operative line, the line the block computes with (Constraints §3), in place of the application's candidate line with its complementary-slackness clause, which §3 reads. A numerical solution also requires method choices, settings, and calibration, together with continuation and terminal inputs. The source does not choose those inputs.

docs.title: 2 Equations, definitions, and dependence
docs.text:
The := line defines utility as a function of its explicit argument. By contrast, a = m_d - c relates stage fields. When continuation value is represented as \(H(a)\), substituting the transition gives \(H(m_d-c)\), with consumption still free until the policy block selects it. This substitution uses the state-sufficiency assumptions in Appendix C R5–R7.

An alias is an explicit intermediate definition that can be substituted at its uses. Substitution preserves every declared output, the domains, and every free or bound dependency. The savings equation must continue to determine the output a even if its right side is substituted into a value calculation. The two-output example in Appendix D shows the same rule when a block promises two outputs: substituting one into the other does not delete either output.

The utility definition binds its argument c, a name local to the definition; argmax_{c} binds the control in its objective. A substitution must distinguish these scopes rather than identify variables solely by spelling. An implicit equation supplies a relation between unknowns and cannot be substituted as though it were an explicit alias.

A block identifier supplies an address, not a formula. The labels in §1 are descriptive conventions: typed signatures, economic roles, and equations identify what each block defines. Naming a block policy does not make an arbitrary equation an optimality condition.

A marginal value is the derivative of a value in a state coordinate of its perch. It is no field: a header lists value fields and controls alone, and a line reads the derivative where it needs it by the derivative term D_{a}V[>], the operator D applied to the value field written with its perch mark, the subscript naming a state coordinate of the perch at which the value is read, written without its mark; D_{a}D_{a}V[>] is the second derivative. The term has this one spelling. It denotes a function of the value and no second object, so a block that reads it declares nothing about how the derivative is evaluated: that is a property of the value, fixed by the methods file of the stage that writes it (Methodization §4.1). A derivative line is a line of a value builder's block whose left side is a derivative term of the value the builder writes, D_{m_d}V = 𝑑𝑢(c) in §3. It states the author's assertion that the derivative equals the right side, which holds under the envelope conditions, and it defines no new field. Such a line stands in the stage file, as in §3, or in a marginal block of a block file, which the methods file binds to the value builder with !marginals. The package never computes a derivative: it differentiates no value function, and a derivative that no line states and no representation evaluates is not part of the stage.

docs.title: 3 An implicit policy relation
docs.text:
The endogenous grid method calculates candidate consumption at given savings and then recovers the associated resources. To derive its interior equation from §1, assume \(H\) is differentiable at positive savings with finite strictly positive derivative. Differentiating the choice value with respect to consumption gives \(u'(c)-H'(m_d-c)\), so an interior optimum satisfies

\[ u'(c)=H'(m_d-c),\qquad f(a)=H'(a)^{-1/\rho},\qquad h(a)=a+f(a). \]

Here \(f(a)\) is candidate consumption and \(h(a)\) its resource coordinate. The source below includes zero savings, so also assume a finite strictly positive right derivative \(H'_+(0)\) and use it in \(f(0)\).

For this separate interior example, copy §1's source to cons_interior.bl and change its metadata to @stage: cons_interior. Keep the utility definition and both forward-transition blocks. Replace the three blocks cntn_to_dcsn, dcsn_to_arvl, and policy by the following function definitions and blocks; the argmax policy from §1 is removed, not retained as a second policy:

𝑑𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(-ρ)             :: [id=marg_util]
𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(x : ℝ₊₊) := x^(-1/ρ)        :: [id=inv_marg_util]

[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu, c) : !cntn -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {
    V        = 𝑢(c) + V[>]          :: [id=value]
    D_{m_d}V = 𝑑𝑢(c)                :: [id=marginal]
}
[id=dcsn_to_arvl, (V) : !dcsn -> (V[<] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !arvl] {
    V[<] = V                        :: [id=value]
}
[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {
    c[>]   = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>])      :: [id=InvEuler]
    m_d[>] = a + c[>]                :: [id=endoggrid]
    c      = c[>]                    :: [id=cons_choice]
}

The term D_{a}V[>] reads the derivative of the same continuation function \(H\) supplied through V[>]; how that derivative is evaluated was fixed where \(H\) was built, and this block declares nothing about it. The derivative line D_{m_d}V = 𝑑𝑢(c) states the derivative of the optimized value in cash on hand. Interpreting it so requires an optimal policy and the envelope conditions in Appendix C, R8, applied to consumption in §4.2 of that appendix; the stage lists the reading under marginal-reading and checks it against nothing. The arrival block writes no derivative line: its law between the perches is the identity, so the derivative of V passes through it to V[<]. If discounting is applied in another stage, both continuation value and its derivative must include it once.

At ρ = 2, marginal utility is \(1/c^2\) and its inverse on positive arguments is \(1/\sqrt{x}\). Their composition returns \(c\) for every positive \(c\). A constant continuation has derivative zero and is therefore outside this inverse-marginal example, although it is valid in §1.

The candidate fields c[>] and m_d[>] are represented by \(f(a)\) and \(h(a)\). Through the budget equation, the final line c = c[>] states the feasible relation

\[ \{(m_d,c):c=f(m_d-c),\ 0<c\leq m_d\}. \]

A relation is a set of state–control pairs. This relation defines a policy only where it determines one admissible control per resource state, or a suitable measurable selection is supplied. The equation neither instructs the program to copy an array nor establishes that an arbitrary root is optimal.

Elaboration keeps this division. The two explicit lines form one operation of the policy builder, an Aggregation keyed endoggrid:Aggregation, whose kernel, the map it applies at each saving, is \(G(w, a) = (w^{-1/\rho},\ a + w^{-1/\rho})\), with \(w\) the derivative of the continuation value at \(a\), which the term D_{a}V[>] reads. stage.dcsn.builder.policy['policy.endoggrid:Aggregation'].kernel() answers that map; compile_kernel() refuses it under kernel-form, since the row reads a derivative term, as it refuses a kernel that calls a function defined by D_{c}(𝑢) (Expression forms §3), and the policy builder is realized by a handler (Methodization §4). The last line forms the identification, a Pullback: the policy composed with the resource coordinate and equated to the candidate, \(\pi(h(a)) = f(a)\), which the policy builder's card prints as 𝑐(𝑚_d≻(a)) = 𝑐≻(a), 𝑐 being the card's italic name for the policy. Its output is its own unknown, so it states a relation, which no query solves, and compile_kernel() refuses it. In applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl the first line is the inequality c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) with the clause ⟂ a >= 0; it forms an operation of its own, InvEuler:Aggregation, whose rule is the relation with its clause and whose kernel is its bound \(w^{-1/\rho}\), and the values the clause admits at zero saving give the policy's corner (Constraints §4.3). Neither form differentiates \(H\) or inverts marginal utility: the derivative is read by the term D_{a}V[>] and evaluated as the stage that built \(H\) fixed it, and the inverse is the definition 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣.

For a global optimality interpretation, assume concavity of \(H\) as well as the attainment conditions in §1. At the borrowing boundary \(a=0\), assume the finite right derivative \(H'_+(0)\) exists. Consuming all resources is optimal when

\[ u'(m_d)\geq H'_+(0). \]

The sign follows by differentiating with respect to savings: the derivative is \(-u'(m_d-a)+H'(a)\) and must be nonpositive at the left endpoint. Interior equality alone omits the cases with strict inequality. Thus cons_interior.bl states a candidate relation. A declaration of the full constrained policy writes the Kuhn–Tucker condition in one of its three spellings: the clause ⟂ m_d - c >= 0 on the decision-perch first-order condition, using the forward law a = m_d - c, a multiplier declared in the policy block, or the clause ⟂ a >= 0 on the continuation-marked candidate line written as the inequality c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]), as applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl writes it (Constraints §4). The loading software reads that clause as the corner: at zero saving the candidate takes every value up to the interior value \(f(0)\), and the final line then gives consumption equal to cash on hand at every cash on hand up to \(f(0)\). A declaration may instead restrict the equality to its interior domain and separately state the borrowing-boundary branch, or retain the constrained maximization in §1. If a numerical method adds a boundary segment to the interior candidates, it must report that segment as an extension outside the authored equality. Attaching !egm does not declare the missing branch or establish global optimality; see Appendix C §4.5. The resulting policy must also cover the requested resource domain.

More generally, candidate controls \(U:S\to C\) and coordinates \(K:S\to X\) define pairs \((K(s),U(s))\), where \(S\) is the set that indexes the candidates, \(C\) the control domain, and \(X\) the state domain. They define one control on \(K(S)\) exactly when candidates with equal coordinates have equal controls. Measurability and coverage of the desired state domain are additional conditions. Appendix C R10 and R12 and Appendix D state these conditions without assuming every implicit relation is a function.

Interpolation may approximate candidate pairs on a numerical grid, with its interpolation and extrapolation assumptions stated. It does not add an equation to the model. An authored evaluate(knots, values, x) is a separate optional operation with declared arguments; choosing an endogenous-grid method creates neither that statement nor an automatic upper-envelope computation, which would compare competing candidates.

docs.title: 4 Statements and computation boundaries
docs.text:
In §1's dcsn_to_cntn block, replace the savings equation by:

a = m_d - c    :: [id=savings, !node]

The !node requests a computation boundary, a statement to inspect or realize as a unit. It preserves the budget equation and its output a. The marked statement's result is a function of its own in the constructed stage, one that the statements after it consume and that a numerical method can represent, by interpolation for instance; an unmarked intermediate quantity is substituted into the statements that use it and has no separate existence to which a method could attach. The block itself is authored, while subtraction or maximization inside an equation is a mathematical operation; nesting alone does not make it another authored !node target. Methodization describes which operations and boundaries support numerical methods.

A statement marked !doc contributes documentation and no defining equation. Removing an equation this way can change the model or leave an output undefined. Use the two marks separately: their combined meaning is not specified. An id without either mark supplies an address and changes neither the equation nor its mathematical status.

docs.title: 5 Expectations
docs.text:
The separate consumption module has no shock because resources are already observed. In the income-and-consumption stage, the backward equation V[<] = E_{y}(V) instead integrates decision value over income, conditional on arrival information. The income law is explicitly conditional and constant given earlier information; the expected value must be integrable. Income affects value through resources, so that dependence remains after the transition is substituted.

The scope of the expectation matters. E_{y}(V + y) integrates both terms; E_{y}(V) + y leaves the final shock outside the expectation. When income is unobserved at arrival, the latter cannot define arrival value. Equation parsing rules gives the function, law, and operator spellings; Perch tagging rules gives the information checks.

docs.title: Methodization
docs.text:
#specification#spec_factory

Summary

Methodization attaches a numerical method to an authored computation in a stage. A method type states where the method may stand and which numerical options it reads. We write one on: target per entry in a methods YAML file, then supply numerical settings and economic parameter values separately. Choosing a method adds no equation to the stage file and does not turn candidate controls into an optimal policy. A methods line may name a method block, a block written in a file of its own, whose lines, elaborated with the stage's declarations in scope, become the operations of the builder the line names and satisfy the stage file's declared line only under the condition the stage records (§4.1).

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Stages and Field equations: typed blocks and their equations. Used by — Periods and The Bellman factory: attaching choices to each use of a stage. Formal account — Appendix C: analytic assumptions; Appendix D: computation boundaries and candidate coordinates.

docs.title: 1 A consumption method
docs.text:
The complete cons.bl in Field equations chooses consumption by maximizing current utility plus continuation value over 0 < c ≤ m_d. A numerical method must solve that declared constrained problem, including the zero-savings boundary.

Save the following recognition-only mapping as methodization.yml:

methods:
  - on: argmax

The address argmax identifies the stage's maximization occurrence without adding !node. This entry records the target but attaches no numerical algorithm. Solving requires a registered routine that accepts this constrained objective and its domain; the example does not invent a handler or assert that target recognition supplies one. Settings would then provide the numerical options required by that routine.

docs.title: 1.1 An interior method
docs.text:
The separate cons_interior.bl in Field equations replaces the constrained maximization with an interior candidate relation and adds the derivative line of the decision value. Read the following fragment inside that complete replacement context, which declares the budget transition, domains, utility functions, and continuation values:

[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {
    c[>]   = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>])      :: [id=InvEuler]
    m_d[>] = a + c[>]                 :: [id=endoggrid]
    c      = c[>]                     :: [id=cons_choice]
}

For this interior variant, save the following mapping as cons_interior_methods.yml. It attaches the endogenous grid method, !egm, which calculates candidate consumption at given savings and recovers its cash-on-hand coordinate. The savings at which it does so form its exogenous grid, which the entry names by the setting grid: the grid's kind is the tag on its value, !Cartesian, and the grid's order and bounds in the savings coordinate a stand beside it, written as the names of the settings n_a, a_min and a_max (§3):

methods:
  - on: policy
    method: !egm
    settings: {grid: !Cartesian, orders: {a: n_a}, bounds: {a: [a_min, a_max]}}

Here policy is the interior block's chosen identifier. The equations supply the inverse marginal utility calculation and the implicit condition for consumption. The !egm tag selects a numerical technique for these equations; it supplies no missing condition. Renaming the block requires changing on: to its new address, but leaves the mathematics unchanged. This attachment belongs to cons_interior.bl; the constrained cons.bl writes neither these candidate lines nor the derivative line.

docs.title: 2 Computations and addresses
docs.text:
A block is the authored header and body that define a transition, value calculation, or policy relation. A builder is the operator constructed from that block. A statement marked !node requests a separately addressable computation within the block. The distinction matters when choosing where to attach a method:

Object What it identifies Authored block The header and body written in the stage file, such as the block policy above. Constructed builder The operator constructed from the block. Its wires, the inputs it reads and the outputs it writes, carry functions or measures, not the fields listed in the block header. Declared function A named function declared outside the blocks, such as utility 𝑢. It is not a field. Authored !node statement A computation boundary explicitly requested inside a block. The statement's result becomes a function in its own right, which later statements consume and a method can represent; without the mark the same expression is a subexpression of the statement that uses it, and no method can attach to it. Nested mathematical operation An expectation, derivative, maximization, or other operation inside an equation; nesting alone does not author another !node. Its result is a function of the remaining arguments, obtained exactly through its definition; only the operation's own methods attach to it (a quadrature rule to E, a maximizer to argmax, a root finder to solve), never a representation. Alias address The identity of an explicit intermediate equation, retained for inspection even when substitution removes an intermediate calculation. Numerical representation A grid, interpolant, quadrature rule, or other object a selected method uses to approximate the mathematical calculation.

A declared function or an evaluated field is treated through its exact definition unless a method attached to it supplies a numerical representation. A builder output and the left side of a !node statement are evaluated fields; a declared function such as utility is not a field. The stage file itself never states a representation: the methods file alone chooses one and writes where it stands. An interpolation method attached to either kind of function means that the method stores values on the named grid and uses an interpolant to represent the function between them. This is mathematics supplied by the method and does not change the exact Evaluation, which remains the identity into the declared set of functions. The !node mark determines whether a line's left-side field is evaluated; the attachment determines the representation used for its function.

The outputs of the policy builder and of a backward value builder are stored at the Evaluation that closes the builder, and the methods file names that Evaluation by what it evaluates: policy.evaluate for the policy function, <block-id>.evaluate.value for the value function a backward value builder writes, and <block-id>.evaluate.marginal for the derivative of that value a derivative line states. A representation named on a builder itself or on a derivative line is refused, and the refusal names the address to write (Refusals).

Which methods a target admits follows from what the target is. #functional-semantics

Target Admits Does not admit a declared function an admitted representation or function method treatment as a field an evaluated field: the left side of a !node statement, named by the line's address a representation: an interpolant or a table on the grid the settings name treatment as a declared function an operator occurrence inside an unmarked statement (E, argmax, solve) the operation's own method: quadrature, a maximizer, a root finder a representation, since the occurrence's result is not an authored object a builder a handler for the builder as a whole; !vfi stands on the backward decision builder alone, which it realizes with its maximization; with block:, a method block on the policy builder, under !egm, or a marginal block, whose derivative lines state the derivatives of the value a backward value builder writes, under !marginals (§4.1) a representation, which is written at the builder's Evaluation (the rows below) the Evaluation of a backward value builder, written cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value for the value function it stores and cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.marginal for the derivative of that value its derivative lines state a representation: one method at the Evaluation for the value and its stated derivative, which share it (§4, §4.1) .evaluate.marginal where no derivative line stands at the builder; a solution method, which stands on the builder a derivative line of a value builder, cntn_to_dcsn.envelope the operation's own method on an operator the line holds, such as a quadrature rule on its expectation a representation: the line states a property of the value, whose derivative is represented at cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.marginal the Evaluation of the policy builder, written policy.evaluate, where the policy function is stored a representation of the policy, such as !Linear policy.evaluate.value and policy.evaluate.marginal, since a policy builder writes neither; a solution method the Evaluation of a policy block that writes the grid line (the cash on hand at each saving, m_d[>] = a + c[>]), named by the block id in an entry with no block: !egm, which stores the policy from the pairs the block's lines give at the savings a policy block that writes no grid line the Argmax row of an operative argmax line, one the block computes with rather than marks !doc (Constraints §3), that carries its first-order condition as a property (a line whose id is dotted, optimality.euler) !egm, which inverts the property for the candidate, or a root finder

An author who wants an occurrence's result represented, the expectation of a continuation value held as an interpolant for instance, writes the expectation on its own line and marks the line !node; the result is then an authored function and admits a representation. The converse does not hold: attaching a method to an occurrence, a quadrature rule to an expectation, does not make the occurrence a !node or a separately addressable computation. A methods line without block: names a computation that the stage file created and creates none. A line with block: names a method block, whose lines, elaborated with the stage's declarations in scope, become the method rows of the builder the line names, in the builders graph, and satisfy the declared line only under the condition the stage records (§4.1).

Method attachment resolves an address against a supported computation in the constructed stage. An identifier used for inspection is not by itself evidence that a numerical method can attach there. An unmarked explicit alias can be substituted only with every declared output and free or bound dependency preserved. An implicit equation remains a relation and is not an alias to substitute away.

For example, a policy.InvEuler address identifies the inverse-Euler statement in §1.1. Its identifier alone does not request a separate computation boundary. If that calculation must be separately methodized, author and type the required boundary and use a method supported for it. Appendix D explains this distinction.

Supported implicit equations and operator occurrences can receive methods without an added !node. The following addresses identify different scopes:

Address Target policy The authored policy block. With !egm and no block:, the Evaluation that closes the block, where the block writes the grid line. policy.evaluate The Evaluation of the policy builder, where the policy function is stored: the place of its representation. cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value The Evaluation of the decision value builder, for the value function it stores. cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.marginal The same Evaluation, for the derivative of the value a derivative line of the builder states. policy.cons_choice The consumption example's authored implicit equation. argmax Every argmax occurrence in this stage. policy.choice.argmax The argmax in the retirement example's statement choice within block policy.

An occurrence-specific attachment overrides the stage-wide attachment for that occurrence. Naming an operator this way does not turn its containing statement into an authored node. A !node statement needs its own identifier to be a method target; its automatically assigned positional address is insufficient.

The block-level !egm form requires the grid line, a line whose left side is a decision coordinate under the continuation mark; a policy block that writes no grid line is refused with the requirement named, and a first-order condition written as an operation takes a root finder instead.

Neither a block called policy nor a method called !egm creates an evaluate occurrence or an upper_env target. The address policy.evaluate names the Evaluation every policy builder closes with, not an authored evaluate(…), which keeps its own address <block-id>.<statement-id>.evaluate; evaluate alone names a stage's one authored occurrence and is refused where the stage authors none or several. A stage with discrete choices likewise needs its authored branch-selection equations; see Branching.

docs.title: 3 Method places and options
docs.text:
The expectation of the buffer-stock application, applications/buffer-stock/declaration/stages/buffer_stock/buffer_stock.bl, integrates the shocks \(\psi\) and \(\xi\). The method type of !gauss-hermite admits an expectation operator and gives n_nodes the type "one positive integer per shock". Its methods entry therefore lists the two node-count settings in the order \(\psi\), \(\xi\). These are the two parts of every public method type: admits and options.

The admitted place depends on what the method does. A quadrature or maximization method computes a primitive operator and stands on that operator. A representation method stores a declared function or an evaluated field and stands at that function's definition or at the field's closing Evaluation, whose address the methods file writes (§2). The third placement class is a handler for a whole builder, which stands on the builder. A declared function such as utility is not a field, and a function the stage file does not name has no address at which a method can stand.

An option has a name and a value type. Common types include positive integers, real numbers, positive real numbers, ordered pairs and seeds. n_nodes has one positive-integer entry per shock, in shock order. Methodization checks that required option names are present. Configuration checks the supplied values and joint conditions. An option unknown to the method is refused unless the entry names a handler that owns the option; such a handler-specific option is retained as untyped rather than treated as part of the method's contract.

A representation names two things: the basis, the rule by which a value between the nodes is read, and the grid, the finite set of nodes at which the function's values are stored. The basis is the method, !Linear for piecewise linear interpolation or !pchip for the shape-preserving cubic, and the derivatives the representation evaluates follow from it. The grid is the setting grid, which the method requires: its value is the grid's kind written as a tag, and the grid's fields stand beside it as further settings of the entry. The kind the package defines is !Cartesian, a product of one grid for each coordinate, whose fields are orders, the number of points in each coordinate, and bounds, the interval in each, both required, and, where written, spacing, the name of the spacing in each coordinate, or nodes, the points themselves:

  - on: cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value
    method: !Linear
    settings: {grid: !Cartesian, orders: {m: n_m}, bounds: {m: [m_min, m_max]}}

orders and bounds are records keyed by the actual coordinates being gridded. The keys must name coordinates of the function, but the method may grid only a subset: a !Linear representation of a function of \((m,z_d)\) may, for example, grid \(m\) separately for each income state \(z_d\). An order must be positive, and each bound must be an ordered pair inside its coordinate's declared set. The endogenous grid method names its exogenous grid of savings in the same way, under its own entry, and its coordinates are the states of the continuation perch, orders: {a: n_a} for the savings a (§1.1). A representation at the policy builder's Evaluation, where !egm stands in that builder, writes no grid, and a grid written there is refused, since the knots of its interpolant are the pairs of cash on hand and consumption that the method computes at each saving; nor does a representation of an authored evaluate(knots, values, x) need one, since its first argument holds the knots. !Cartesian is a kind of grid and not a method, and the fields of a grid written without the setting grid are refused, each refusal naming the form to write (Refusals).

Methodization adds no convergence or existence requirement. Defining equations, declared sets and authored constraints remain part of the exact stage, and ordinary type and calibration-definedness checks remain in force.

The listing method_types, which bellman.stage exports, gives the registered method types by their written tags, and Method types prints them in one table with the places each admits and its options. A stage's places() query lists the addresses to which methods may attach and the kind of each place. These are inspection queries: they neither attach a method nor execute one.

docs.title: 4 Writing the methodization file
docs.text:
Every entry requires one on: address. A method tag is optional: an entry containing only on records recognition without attaching a numerical method, and a handler may be given when the operator family determines the method. Separate targets require separate entries. Two entries may name one builder when their methods are of different kinds, a solution method and a marginal block, since each kind has a place of its own: a solution method such as !vfi stands on the builder, and a marginal block under !marginals adds its lines to the builder; a second entry of one kind on one target is refused. A representation entry does not name a builder alone: its target is the builder's Evaluation, such as policy.evaluate beside !egm on policy, or cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value beside !marginals on cntn_to_dcsn. The value and its stated derivative are two addresses of one Evaluation, which holds one representation method: where a methods file writes both, the two entries must name the same method and form one binding, and two different methods there are refused. Do not put a comma-separated list in on: or write a nested schemes: list.

The available entry fields are:

Field Meaning on One supported computation address in the stage. method Optional YAML tag naming the numerical technique, such as !egm. settings Optional mapping of method options to values or references. Referenced setting values are supplied during configuration. The grid of a method that takes one is the setting grid, its kind written as a tag, with the grid's fields beside it (§3). handler Optional identifier of the registered numerical routine used to carry out the computation. block Optional path of a block file, written from the folder of the methods file, whose block the method binds on the builder that on names; only a method whose type takes a block admits it, such as !egm or !marginals (§4.1).

Option names depend on the chosen method. Use the method's documented contract; changing a tag does not establish that another method accepts the same options or solves the same relation.

A handler is a numerical routine, or an adapter calling one, registered for the requested computation. One handler may carry out an entire builder, including internal interpolation or maximization. Alternatively, supported authored boundaries may have separate handlers. The handler's documented capabilities determine which choices it honors. Merely recording an option does not show that a routine uses it, or that two routines agree to a chosen tolerance.

A handler evaluates only the equations of the stage file. A builder's kernels() answers them as one record that refers to no stage. A kernel is the mathematical data an operation uses: a law of motion, a value aggregator, a shock distribution, a correspondence or a policy reference. The record lists each operation of the builder in the order of application, with the plain Python function its kernel compiles to, or its printed relation where its rule is no explicit function, the names of the function's arguments and outputs, and the parameters with the values the calibration binds (A builder §5). A handler builds its numerical operator from such records and from the grids it reads from the settings, and the operator reads no stage. The endogenous-grid handler of the portfolio–consumption application, cons-port:egm, is one call of egm in asva, the numerical toolkit beside the package, asva.egm(stage.dcsn.builder.policy.kernels(), stage.dcsn.builder.bwd.kernels(), savings, evaluation), with the savings grid that the !egm entry names and the evaluation grid that the representation at the decision builder's Evaluation names, each read at the values the settings bind (§3). Each function is made from the source text its kernel holds under python, which reaches array functions through the name np alone; a handler written for another array package executes the same text and then binds np, in the namespace of the function, to that package.

Technical details

Read tagged methods YAML through bellman.stage.sources.load_methods, which preserves method tags and handles YAML's treatment of the key on. Ordinary YAML loading is not a substitute for that loader. Loading a method tag records a choice; it does not verify the numerical algorithm or prove that its assumptions hold.

docs.title: 4.1 A method block and a marginal block
docs.text:
A stage file may state the policy by its maximization alone, as cons.bl of §1 does, and leave the computation to a method block: a block written in a file of its own, the block file, whose header carries the signature of a builder of the stage and whose lines compute that builder's output. A methods line names the block file under block:, by a path from the methods file's own folder, and the builder under on:. The methods file of the consumption stage of the portfolio–consumption application, applications/cons-port/declaration/methods/cons.yml, holds these three entries:

methods:
  - on: policy
    method: !egm
    block: cons_egm.bl
    handler: cons-port:egm
    settings: {grid: !Cartesian, orders: {a: n_a}, bounds: {a: [a_min, a_max]}}
  - on: cntn_to_dcsn
