A recipe names the trellis file and, for each stage, the stage's file and the ordered files from which its parameter values, its numerical settings and its methods are read, every path written from the recipe's own folder; it leaves places, the slots, for values supplied at the call; and it writes the values that differ by period. The calls of this page give back, in turn, the model as written, a dictionary of records read from those files; the same dictionary with a constructed stage at every position and no value in any of them; and that dictionary with every stage bound to its values, its methods and its settings. One call runs the whole route, and nothing on this page solves a model.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Trellises: the three files, the two shapes of a period, the period index and the dictionary a trellis is; Periods: the joins between the stages of a period; Methodization: the methods files a recipe names. Formal account — Periods and the trellis: composition through compatible fields; Appendix G §7: the three binding verbs as maps from stage versions to stage versions. Used by — Factory API: the reference of the fourteen functions named here; Model directory layout: where the files of a registry are kept.

Key terminology Term Meaning Bellman factory The part of the package that takes a model from its files to the specified trellis: load, elaborate, the three bindings, accrete, and the registry and the recipe (wiki). Specification factory The part of the Bellman factory that merges the sources a recipe names: the registry and the recipe read together, the route of §3, whose recipe is spec.yml (wiki). Syntactic trellis The model as written, the dictionary of records that load_trellis and load_recipe return and in which every adjustment is made (wiki). Record The entry of the syntactic trellis at one stage key: the stage's text and origin, its three mappings as data and its provenance. Elaborated trellis The same dictionary with an ElaboratedStage at every key, symbolic when nothing is bound and specified when every stage occurrence carries its three bindings (wiki). Stage occurrence One use of a stage file at one position of one period, an object of its own (Periods §1). Symbolic Said of a stage occurrence, or a trellis, that holds no binding (wiki). Specified Said of a stage occurrence that holds its calibration, its methods and its settings, bound in that order, or of a trellis whose every stage occurrence does (wiki). Binding One of the three mappings once a stage holds it: its calibration, its methods or its settings; the verb that writes it, with its mapping held fixed, is a binding map from stage versions to stage versions (Appendix G §7). Trellis verbs calibrate_trellis, methodize_trellis and configure_trellis, which apply the stage's own verbs to every stage occurrence of a trellis. Accrete To append one period, the one earlier in time, with the inter-period connector that joins it to the period appended before it; the horizon is the number of periods built (Trellises §6; wiki). Registry The folder the recipe stands in, from which every path the recipe writes is read, and nothing else (wiki). Recipe The file spec.yml naming the trellis file, each stage's file and, for each stage and each kind, an ordered source list (wiki). Source A file of assignments of one kind: values to parameters, values to settings, or methods attached to targets; under the registry block, assignments to registry-level names that no stage declares (wiki). Source list The ordered list a recipe names for one stage, one period and one kind, slots included (wiki). Slot A $name in a source list, bound by the keyword of load_recipe of the same name (wiki). Fill The dictionary bound to a slot (wiki). Method choice A methods mapping bound to a methods slot (wiki). Sweep A family of fills, one expression over them (wiki). Join A selected continuation-to-arrival state-field pair between stage occurrences; an authored connector has precedence, and an unclaimed equal-name pair is inferred only when it is the unique compatible choice in a consistent selection (Periods §3).

The listings on this page use the durables model of Dobrescu and Shanker (2026), a household that keeps or adjusts its housing stock over fifty-one ages, written as the registry applications/durables/declaration/ of the repository, the directory that holds a model's files: four stage files (the tenure stage, which chooses between keeping and adjusting; the keeper's and the adjuster's consumption stages; the bequest), three methods files, two calibration files, one settings file, a period template, a trellis file and a recipe, with a second route beside them. The listings are run from the repository root.

docs.title: 1 The two dictionaries and the stage object
docs.text:
The factory works on two dictionaries of one shape and on one stage class, and it introduces nothing else.

The syntactic trellis is the model as written. It is the dictionary {"periods": [...], "inter_connectors": [...]}, whose periods list holds one dictionary per period, {"stages": {key: record}, "connectors": [...]}, and whose inter_connectors list holds the connectors that join adjacent periods. At each stage key stands a record: the stage's source, its text and its origin, together with the three mappings the stage is to be bound with, held as data. The calibration gives a value to each parameter the stage declares, the settings give the numerical options that the methods read, and the methods name the numerical method attached at each target of the stage, a place in the stage's equations that receives a method (Methodization); a binding is one of these mappings once a stage holds it. The record also carries a provenance naming the files each mapping came from. Every adjustment to a model is made in this dictionary before anything is constructed: a fill of parameter values, a value that differs by period, a method choice.

{"periods": [{"stages": {key: record, ...}, "connectors": [...]}, ...],
 "inter_connectors": [...]}

The elaborated trellis is the same dictionary with an ElaboratedStage at every key in place of the record. It is symbolic when no stage occurrence is bound and specified when every stage occurrence carries its three bindings. ElaboratedStage is the only stage object; a syntactic stage is nothing more than its record. A stage occurrence is one use of a stage file at one position of one period, with local fields, methods and settings. A parameter name declared by more than one stage of that period denotes one period parameter, with a reconciled declaration and value (Periods §1); each verb of §2 returns a new version of a stage occurrence and leaves the earlier version unchanged.

periods[0] is the terminal period and periods[h] the period that lies h periods before it; inter_connectors[h] joins the continuation fields that leave periods[h + 1] to the arrival fields of periods[h] (Trellises §1.1). The adjuster's stage occurrence of the terminal period is therefore model["periods"][0]["stages"]["adjuster_cons"], a record in the syntactic trellis and a stage in the elaborated one. A drawing of a period or of the trellis is made from the dictionary when it is asked for and stored nowhere (§7).

docs.title: 2 The calls
docs.text:
The factory has five verbs, each with one meaning. To load is to read files and return a record or the syntactic trellis. To elaborate is to turn a record's source into an ElaboratedStage with its semgraph, the semantic graph that holds its equations: elaborate_trellis makes no binding, and elaborate_stage binds the sources a record supplies unless it is given bind=False (The stage §1). To bind is to calibrate_trellis, methodize_trellis or configure_trellis, the three trellis verbs: each reads the mapping of its kind from the syntactic trellis it is given and returns a new version. To accrete is to append one period. To assemble is to run the whole route, from the files with assemble_trellis or from a syntactic trellis with specify_trellis. Two further calls make drawings, and one counts what a verb changed.

Call Returns What it reads and does bellman.stage.load_stage(path) the record of one stage file: its text and origin under stage, the three mappings empty, the origin and the digest of the text under provenance reads one stage file; elaborates nothing bellman.trellis.load_trellis(file) the syntactic trellis reads one trellis file whose periods list writes each period out, its stages with their three mappings inline or as paths to files, or gives {template: <period file>, repeat: n} for a run of equal periods, and whose inter_connectors holds one connector per adjacent pair or one connector standing for every pair; reads each stage file for its text and digest (Trellises §3) bellman.trellis.load_recipe(directory, recipe, **fills) the syntactic trellis reads the recipe, the trellis file and the stage files at the paths it writes, the period templates and every source file the recipe names, each once; expands each {template, repeat} entry and repeats a single inter-period connector for each adjacent pair; puts each fill in its slot; merges each source list; writes one record per stage and period with its provenance (§3) bellman.stage.elaborate_stage(record, bind=True) an ElaboratedStage, symbolic where the record supplies no source constructs the record's text at its origin, binds the calibration, the methods and the settings the record supplies, in that order, unless given bind=False, and reads no file; given a path string, or a dictionary that is not a record, refuses under record-shape and says to write elaborate_stage(load_stage(path)) bellman.trellis.elaborate_trellis(syntactic, previous=None) the elaborated trellis, symbolic constructs each distinct stage text once and places a full copy at each of its positions; copies a position that already holds a stage; given previous, copies from it every position whose record has the same digest and constructs the others, which is how a changed stage file alone is constructed again (§6); derives the joins and the order of each period (§7); binds nothing bellman.trellis.calibrate_trellis(elaborated, syntactic), bellman.trellis.methodize_trellis(elaborated, syntactic), bellman.trellis.configure_trellis(elaborated, syntactic) a new elaborated trellis each reads its own kind at each key of the syntactic trellis, syntactic["periods"][h]["stages"][key]["calibration"] for calibrate_trellis, and binds the stage occurrence at the same key where the mapping differs from what it holds: for calibration in a value at a name the stage declares, the one value the period supplies standing for a parameter two of its stages declare (The trellis factory §4), for settings in any value, for methods in the digest of the mapping; a stage occurrence whose mapping is unchanged is copied (§6), as is one at a key where the syntactic trellis itself holds a stage object, a period built by hand bellman.trellis.accrete(trellis, period, inter_connector=None) the trellis with the period appended appends a period dictionary at the end of periods, the period earlier in time, and writes the inter-period connector that joins it to the period appended before it at inter_connectors[len(periods) - 2]; the terminal period, appended first, takes no connector; rewrites no existing record; the period may hold records, stage objects or both; when every stage of the period is an ElaboratedStage, derives the period's joins and checks the connector against the fields of the two periods it joins (Trellises §6) bellman.trellis.specify_trellis(syntactic, previous=None, kinds=KINDS) the specified trellis returns the trellis that elaborate_trellis(syntactic, previous) and the trellis verbs of kinds make, kinds naming any of "calibration", "methods" and "settings", the three kinds of KINDS, all three by default, the verbs applied in the order calibrate, methodize, configure whatever order kinds writes; constructs each distinct stage text once, or takes its stage occurrences from previous as elaborate_trellis does, and copies each stage occurrence once, where that route copies it once more for each verb; refuses what that route refuses, a refusal of a binding naming the stage occurrence and the kind in its notes, Stage occurrence: <address> and Binding kind: <kind> bellman.trellis.assemble_trellis(directory, recipe, **fills) the specified trellis is specify_trellis(load_recipe(directory, recipe, **fills)), which returns the trellis that load_recipe, elaborate_trellis, calibrate_trellis, methodize_trellis and configure_trellis make, in that order, copying each stage occurrence once bellman.period.diagram_period(trellis, h) a drawing, of the kind a graph's diagram() returns shows the stages of periods[h] as boxes joined by their joins (§7); stores nothing bellman.trellis.diagram_trellis(trellis, periods=None) a drawing shows the periods of an elaborated trellis, all of them or those whose indices periods lists, each as diagram_period shows it, and every inter-period connector between two of those periods as wires from the continuation fields that leave periods[h + 1] to the arrival fields of periods[h], labeled with its index and its field pairs (§7); stores nothing bellman.trellis.changed_positions(before, after) the list of positions (h, key) the positions whose stage occurrence in after is a new version of the one in before, read from the provenance of the two trellises; its length is the count of what a verb bound, a copy of a binding among them, since it is a new version of its position (§6)

The stage's own verbs are unchanged: stage.calibrate(values or path), stage.methodize(methods or path) and stage.configure(settings or path) each add their binding to the one stage they are called on and return it (The binding verbs), and the trellis verbs apply them once for each distinct stage occurrence and mapping, copying the result to the other positions of that pair (§6).

docs.title: 3 The registry and the recipe
docs.text:
The registry is the folder the recipe stands in, and nothing else: every path the recipe writes is read from it. In a model folder the registry is the subfolder declaration/, which holds every file the language reads (Model directory layout). The durables registry holds the recipe, the trellis file and the period template at its top, with the three files of a second route beside them (§3.6); the calibration and settings files under calibration/ and settings/; under stages/ one folder for each stage, holding its stage file and, where the stage has them, its methods file methods.yml and its note; and under methods/ the block files the methods files name, which hold the endogenous grid lines of the two consumption stages and the derivative lines of the value builders. A file is read whether it is spelled .yml or .yaml, and a calibration, settings or methods file is told apart by its top key, not by its extension.

applications/durables/declaration/
  stages/          tenure/         tenure.bl  methods.yml  tenure.md
                   keeper_cons/    keeper_cons.bl  methods.yml  keeper_cons.md
                   adjuster_cons/  adjuster_cons.bl  methods.yml  adjuster_cons.md
                   bequest/        bequest.bl  methods.yml
  methods/         keeper_cons_egm.bl  adjuster_cons_egm.bl  marginals_<stage>.bl, one for each stage that states a derivative
  calibration/     durables.yml (the parameters the stages declare)  wage_schedule.yml (the schedule and the ages)
  settings/        durables.yml
  period.yml       the three stages of a period before the terminal one and the connector that joins tenure's branches to the decision states of the consumption stages; the order is derived from the fields, not from the list
  trellis.yml      the terminal period written out with the bequest and its connector, then {template: period.yml, repeat: 50};
                   one inter-period connector standing for every adjacent pair
  spec.yml         the recipe
  spec.two-stages.yml  trellis.two-stages.yml  period.two-stages.yml   the route without the tenure stage (§3.6)

docs.title: 3.1 What a recipe is and what it binds
docs.text:
A recipe names every file a model is read from, and it binds nothing itself. At its top, trellis: names the trellis file, whose periods list the stage keys of the model (Trellises §§1, 3). Under stages:, one entry per stage key names the stage's file under stage: and, for each of the three kinds of binding, an ordered source list of the files whose values the stage receives, with slots among them, the entries written $fill and $tenure_method below, for values supplied at the call (§3.3). Every path is written from the recipe's own folder: trellis: trellis.yml, stage: stages/tenure/tenure.bl, and in a source list calibration/durables, a source file named without its extension. trellis: and stage: are both required, so that nothing is read in place of a path the recipe does not write; a recipe without trellis: is refused with the sentence "the recipe names no trellis file; write trellis: trellis.yml, the path from this folder", an entry without stage: with "the entry stages.tenure names no stage file; write stage: stages/tenure/tenure.bl, the path from this folder", both under the rule recipe-shape, and a stage: that names no .bl file is refused as load_stage refuses it (Refusals). A source name written absolute or with .. is refused under recipe-source. The recipe of the durables model, printed from the registry's file with its comment lines left out:

from pathlib import Path

from bellman.refusals import FactoryError
from bellman.stage import load_stage
from bellman.trellis import (assemble_trellis, calibrate_trellis, changed_positions, configure_trellis,
                             elaborate_trellis, load_recipe, methodize_trellis)

registry = "applications/durables/declaration"

def without_comments(path):
    """The text of a YAML file with its comment lines left out."""
    return "".join(line for line in Path(path).read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines(keepends=True)
                   if not line.lstrip().startswith("#"))

print(without_comments(f"{registry}/spec.yml"), end="")

trellis: trellis.yml
stages:
  tenure:        {stage: stages/tenure/tenure.bl,               calibration: {all: [calibration/durables, $fill]}, settings: {all: [settings/durables, $fill]}, methods: {all: [stages/tenure/methods, $tenure_method]}}
  keeper_cons:   {stage: stages/keeper_cons/keeper_cons.bl,     calibration: {all: [calibration/durables, $fill]}, settings: {all: [settings/durables, $fill]}, methods: {all: [stages/keeper_cons/methods, $keeper_method]}}
  adjuster_cons: {stage: stages/adjuster_cons/adjuster_cons.bl, calibration: {all: [calibration/durables, $fill]}, settings: {all: [settings/durables, $fill]}, methods: {all: [stages/adjuster_cons/methods, $adjuster_method]}}
  bequest:       {stage: stages/bequest/bequest.bl,             calibration: {all: [calibration/durables, $fill]}, methods: {all: [stages/bequest/methods]}, periods: [0, 0]}
registry:
  calibration: [calibration/wage_schedule]

What the recipe determines is the three mappings of every stage occurrence. bellman.trellis.load_recipe("applications/durables/declaration", "spec.yml") reads the recipe, the trellis file and the stage files at the paths it writes, the period templates and every source file it names, each once, and writes one record per stage and period, holding the stage's text and digest, the three mappings merged from the lists that apply at that period, and the ordered sources that produced them; it constructs no stage, and it reads a stage file's declarations only to check the names a fill gives. The binding is the work of the trellis verbs, which read those mappings from the records (§4). A recipe cannot stand alone: without the trellis file it names there is no list of periods to write records for, and a stage the recipe names that no period holds, or a stage a period holds that the recipe does not name, is refused under recipe-template-agreement with both files named.

docs.title: 3.2 The source lists and the merge
docs.text:
A source is a file of assignments of one kind: calibration: values to parameters, settings: values to numerical settings, or methods: a list of entries, each attaching a method to the target its on key names. For one stage, one kind and one period, the sources that apply are read in the order the list writes them and merged into one mapping, and where two sources assign the same name the later one stands. The merge is key by key: a mapping is merged into a mapping recursively, so that a later source changes the keys it names and keeps the rest; a methods list is merged entry by entry, matched by on, an entry of !marginals matched only by another of !marginals, since a marginal block and another method may stand on one builder, a later entry changing the keys of the matched entry and keeping its others, an unmatched entry appended, and where an entry of either list carries no on, the later list replacing the earlier whole, since nothing can be matched; any other value, a number, a string or an ordinary list, is replaced by the later one. A source file may name a parent: source it extends, which is read first and merged beneath it in the same way, a chain of at most ten files that may not return to itself; the keys parent, description, version and __comment__ are about the file and assign nothing. Each file is read once per call, and a file whose top key is of another kind than the list it stands in is refused under recipe-source. Recipe functions §2 tabulates the rules.

The durables lists are short, each a file followed by a slot, so the merge is seen best in the provenance a record carries: under provenance["source_lists"], for each kind, the ordered sources that produced its mapping, each file with its path and digest and each slot with its name, whether a fill was bound to it and the fill's names the stage took (§5). A longer list is read the same way: calibration: {all: [calibration/main, calibration/fine, $fill]} gives every value of main, then the values of fine where it assigns a name main also assigns, then the fill's.

docs.title: 3.3 Slots and fills
docs.text:
A slot is a $name in a source list, a place for values supplied at the call. It is bound by the keyword of load_recipe or assemble_trellis that spells the same name without the $: fill= binds $fill, adjuster_method= binds $adjuster_method. The names are the author's and mean nothing by themselves; a slot name is a Python identifier, since a keyword binds it; a keyword that names no slot of the recipe is refused under recipe-slot-unknown with the slots the recipe declares. A slot's position in its list is its precedence, so that $fill written after calibration/durables stands over the file's values, and a slot bound by no keyword contributes nothing. The same slot may stand in the lists of several stages and kinds, as $fill stands in the calibration and the settings lists of all four durables stages, and one fill is then read wherever the slot stands.

A fill is the dictionary bound to a slot, and it takes one of three shapes. A fill keyed by kind, fill={"calibration": {"β": 0.93}, "settings": {"n_a": 500}}, is split, each list taking the part of its kind. A flat fill, fill={"β": 0.93}, is read against the declarations of the stages whose lists name the slot: a name a receiving stage declares as a parameter goes to the calibration lists, a name a receiving stage's settings files or methods files use goes to the settings lists, and a flat fill that names both parameters and settings is refused under fill-mixes-kinds, since one flat mapping cannot say which name is which. A method choice is a methods mapping bound to a methods slot, adjuster_method={"methods": [{"on": "cntn_to_dcsn", "method": "!vfi", ...}]}, merged into the methods list by on, an entry of !marginals matched only by another of !marginals, so that it states the keys in which the chosen method differs from the file's entry and keeps the rest; each durables stage has a methods slot of its own, $tenure_method, $keeper_method and $adjuster_method, because one slot named by the methods lists of two stages would attach one stage's handler, the numerical routine named for a method, to the other. A fill that is no mapping is refused under slot-value-not-a-mapping, and a fill key that no receiving stage declares and no registry block admits (§3.5) under fill-names-nothing, the refusal naming the receiving stages with the names they declare and what may be written (§5).

A fill given to load_recipe produces a fresh syntactic trellis from the registry with the fill in its slot; nothing is constructed. The record's provenance marks the slot's entry bound and lists the fill's names the stage took, and the trellis verbs then bind the stage occurrences whose mapping changed and copy the rest (§5). A sweep is a family of fills, one expression over them, [bellman.trellis.calibrate_trellis(model, bellman.trellis.load_recipe(registry, "spec.yml", fill={"β": beta})) for beta in betas]; an estimation is the same expression inside its criterion function (§6.1).

docs.title: 3.4 Values that differ by period
docs.text:
The sources common to every period stand in a stage's all list. The sources of some periods stand in a range list beside it, keyed by the periods it covers, written "lo-hi" and counted as the trellis counts them, the terminal period being 0 (Trellises §1.1). For a period inside the range, the range list is read after the all list, so that its sources stand over the common ones and over the fill; the ranges of one stage and one kind must not overlap, and a key that is not written lo-hi is refused under recipe-shape. The within-life model of Benhabib, Bisin and Luo (2019), applications/benhabib-2019/, gives its one decision stage a wage profile constant within each of six age brackets of six years, one range list per bracket:

trellis: trellis.yml
stages:
  benhabib_bellman:
    stage: stages/benhabib_bellman/benhabib_bellman.bl
    calibration:
      all:     [calibration/main, $fill]
      "1-6":   [calibration/wage/bracket_6]
      "7-12":  [calibration/wage/bracket_5]
      "13-18": [calibration/wage/bracket_4]
      "19-24": [calibration/wage/bracket_3]
      "25-30": [calibration/wage/bracket_2]
      "31-36": [calibration/wage/bracket_1]
    settings: {all: [settings/default, $fill]}
    methods:  {all: [stages/benhabib_bellman/methods, $bellman_method]}
    periods: [1, 36]
  bequest: {stage: stages/bequest/bequest.bl, calibration: {all: [calibration/main, $fill]}, methods: {all: [stages/bequest/methods]}, periods: [0, 0]}
registry:
  calibration: [calibration/horizon]

At periods[1] to periods[6], ages 60 to 55, the record's calibration holds the wage function of the sixth bracket, read after calibration/main and the fill; at periods[7] it holds the fifth bracket's, and at periods[36], age 25, the first bracket's.

A stage active in some periods only writes periods: [lo, hi] on its entry, the bounds counted the same way, and the stage is then absent from the records of every other period, even where the template lists it. The benhabib template lists both stages in every one of its thirty-seven periods, and the recipe places the bequest in periods[0] alone and the decision stage in periods[1] to periods[36]; a stage restricted to periods that no template holds is refused under recipe-template-agreement. A range list changes what a stage receives at some periods, and periods: changes where the stage occurs; the interval stands in the record's provenance under active.

The bequest is a stage. The file bequest.bl declares its parameters, arrives at the savings, the housing and the income state that the consumption stages continue to, under names of its own, a_bq, h_bq and z_bq, so that no arrival field of the terminal period is declared by two stages, values the wealth left behind, and reads a continuation value V[>] whose value is zero, the boundary data of the terminal period; its methods file, stages/bequest/methods.yml, binds the marginal blocks that state the derivatives of its value, which the consumption stages' method blocks read. There is no separate terminal object of any kind: the bequest stands last in the terminal period, is active there alone through periods: [0, 0], and receives a fill of θ as any stage receives a fill of a parameter it declares.

A value that varies with every period, such as the wage schedule's income level Y and retirement income y_R of the tenure stage, has no key of the recipe and no class: the application writes each period's values into the syntactic trellis before the trellis verbs bind, from the names the registry block carries (§3.5), or calibrates each period with its own values as it accretes.

docs.title: 3.5 The registry block
docs.text:
The recipe's registry block names sources whose assignments no stage declares, here the eight names of calibration/wage_schedule.yml, so that a fill of one of them is not refused. They stand under the trellis's own registry key, {kind: {name: value}}, with their sources under the trellis's provenance, are bound to no stage and are copied unread by elaborate_trellis and the trellis verbs; a fill of such a name changes the registry mapping and nothing else. They are data for the application's own functions. The durables function write_wage_schedule, in applications/durables/code/wage_schedule.py, computes Y and y_R for each age from the schedule's coefficients and writes them into that period's tenure record, appending to the record's source list an entry that names the function, so that a record's provenance names every writer. It runs after every load_recipe, since a fill produces a fresh syntactic trellis, and before the trellis verbs:

import sys

sys.path.insert(0, "applications/durables/code")
from wage_schedule import write_wage_schedule

full = write_wage_schedule(load_recipe(registry, "spec.yml"))
last_age = full["registry"]["calibration"]["last_age"]
for h in (0, 10, 50):
    tenure = full["periods"][h]["stages"]["tenure"]["calibration"]
    print(f"periods[{h}], age {last_age - h}: Y {tenure['Y']:.4f}, y_R {tenure['y_R']}")

periods[10], age 60: Y 0.8986, y_R 0.0
periods[50], age 20: Y 0.3193, y_R 0.0

The tenure stage chooses between keeping and adjusting. It is a branching stage; the full recipe constructs it in each of the fifty-one periods, and the whole trellis then holds one hundred and fifty-four stage occurrences.

docs.title: 3.6 Variants side by side
docs.text:
A second route through the same stages is a second set of the three files beside the first, spec.<name>.yml, trellis.<name>.yml and period.<name>.yml, the name chosen by the author (Trellises §5). The durables registry keeps the route without the tenure stage this way: spec.two-stages.yml names trellis.two-stages.yml under trellis: and the same source files as spec.yml, and that trellis file names period.two-stages.yml under template:. The listings that elaborate on this page read this route, which leaves out the tenure stage, and all but the call of §4 that assembles the fifty-one periods keep its three latest periods, so that each of them runs in under two seconds:

print(without_comments(f"{registry}/trellis.two-stages.yml"), end="")

!trellis
name: durables_two_stages
periods:
  - stages: [keeper_cons, adjuster_cons, bequest]
    connectors:
      - {a_nxt_kp: a_bq, h_nxt_kp: h_bq, z_nxt_kp: z_bq, a_nxt_adj: a_bq, h_nxt_adj: h_bq, z_nxt_adj: z_bq}
  - {template: period.two-stages.yml, repeat: 50}
inter_connectors: []

Its terminal period holds the connector from both consumption stages' continuation fields to the bequest's arrival fields a_bq, h_bq and z_bq, and its fifty other periods repeat the template, which lists the two consumption stages and no connector. Its inter_connectors list is empty, so load_recipe writes the empty connector for each of the fifty adjacent pairs, and the periods are not joined to one another, since this file holds no tenure stage for the consumption stages to continue to.

A variant that changes the values a stage receives and not the route needs no second set of files: it is a further source file, calibration/near_terminal.yml or settings/fine.yml, that a recipe lists after the common one in a source list, or in a range list for some periods, and the merge of §3.2 gives it precedence. A variant supplied at the call is a fill (§3.3).

docs.title: 4 From the recipe to the specified trellis
docs.text:
A trellis is built backward by accretion, one period at a time from the terminal period, and nothing else is imposed on it: bellman.trellis.accrete appends each period with the connector that joins it to the period appended before it, the horizon is the number of periods built, and Trellises §6 shows a trellis built by hand this way from records or from stages already elaborated and bound. Every call of §2 that acts on a trellis is a loop of accretion and adds nothing to it: elaborate_trellis elaborates the periods in order, the three trellis verbs bind stage occurrence by stage occurrence, and assemble_trellis returns in one call the trellis they make. The recipe route is therefore two routes to the same specified trellis.

The first starts from the syntactic trellis, read by load_recipe, adjusts it where the application must, and then elaborates and binds it. The listings keep only the three latest periods of the syntactic trellis, an adjustment made in the dictionary like any other; on all fifty-one periods the same calls construct and bind one hundred and three stage occurrences:

def latest(syntactic, count):
    """The syntactic trellis cut to its `count` latest periods, the terminal period first."""
    return {**syntactic, "periods": syntactic["periods"][:count], "inter_connectors": syntactic["inter_connectors"][:count - 1]}

recipe = "spec.two-stages.yml"
syntactic = load_recipe(registry, recipe)
print(len(syntactic["periods"]), "periods;", len(syntactic["inter_connectors"]), "inter-period connectors, of which",
      sum(1 for connector in syntactic["inter_connectors"] if connector == {}), "empty")
print("periods[0]:", list(syntactic["periods"][0]["stages"]), "  periods[1]:", list(syntactic["periods"][1]["stages"]))

three = latest(syntactic, 3)
elaborated = elaborate_trellis(three)
model = configure_trellis(
    methodize_trellis(
        calibrate_trellis(elaborated, three), three), three)
print(repr(model["periods"][0]["stages"]["adjuster_cons"]))

The second is one call, which returns the trellis the five calls of the first route make, copying each stage occurrence once. On the whole registry it returns the fifty-one periods; its three latest periods equal, stage occurrence by stage occurrence, the trellis the first route built:

model_in_one = assemble_trellis(registry, recipe)
print(len(model_in_one["periods"]), "periods")
print(all(model["periods"][h]["stages"][key] == model_in_one["periods"][h]["stages"][key]

def bound_and_copied(before, after):
    """The count of positions a verb bound and the count it copied."""
    bound = len(changed_positions(before, after))
    return f"bound {bound}, copied {sum(len(period['stages']) for period in after['periods']) - bound}"

docs.title: 6 What a change makes anew
docs.text:
The economist changes Made anew Kept a calibration file, or a fill of parameters by calibrate_trellis: the stage occurrences whose calibration in the syntactic trellis changed in a name they declare, and, in the same period, the stage occurrences that declare a changed name too, since the stages of a period share the parameters they declare under one name the graphs; their methods and settings; every earlier version, and whatever was compiled from it a settings file, or a fill of settings by configure_trellis: the stage occurrences whose settings changed the graphs; their calibration and methods a methods file, or a method choice by methodize_trellis: the stage occurrences whose methods changed, made anew from a fresh elaboration of their record, calibrated with the values they hold, methodized with the new mapping and configured with the settings they hold, since a version holds one methods binding every other stage occurrence a stage file by elaborate_trellis(syntactic, elaborated): the stage occurrences of that file, the digest in the record detecting the change every other stage occurrence, copied from elaborated the period template or the trellis file by load_recipe: the shape of the trellis and the positions the stage occurrences whose record is unchanged

A fill given to load_recipe produces a fresh syntactic trellis from the registry, so values the application wrote into the records period by period are written again by its function after every load_recipe, before the trellis verbs bind; such a function appends to the record's source list an entry naming its file, the names it wrote and its argument, so that a record's provenance names every writer. Only a changed stage file is constructed again: elaborate_trellis given the earlier elaborated trellis as its second argument copies every position whose record kept its digest and constructs the others. As elaborate_trellis constructs each distinct stage text once (§2), a verb binds each distinct input once, except a changed method choice, which methodize_trellis remakes at each position from its record. Where several positions hold versions of one stage file with the same bindings and recorded sources and the syntactic trellis gives them the same mapping, each mapping written with its keys in the same order, since a version prints them in that order, as it gives keeper_cons one calibration at every age, the verb binds the first and places at each of the others a copy that records its own position and parent and equals the version the verb would bind there alone; such a copy is a new version of its position, so changed_positions names it among the positions bound. Every stage occurrence is its own object; two stage occurrences with equal mappings have equal bindings and graphs and are distinct objects. Within a period, stages that declare the same parameter name share the meaning and value of that parameter, while their fields remain local. A verb binds a stage occurrence to the version it is given, never to the version of an earlier fill in a chain, and the earlier trellis is untouched. Binding changes no graph: the semgraphs of a bound version equal those of the symbolic one, and a verb writes to the bindings alone. What a change does to a numerical representation belongs to realization and is not decided here.

docs.title: 6.1 Many draws on many cores
docs.text:
An estimation solves the model once for each draw of its parameters, often on many cores at once. Since binding changes no graph, the specified trellis is built once, by one of the routes of §4, and each draw binds its values to that trellis with calibrate_trellis, as the sweep of §5 does; no stage is constructed, methodized or configured again. A version a verb makes starts with copies of the answers its argument had computed that the graphs determine, among them the table of each stage's wires, so that a drawn trellis holds, without computing them again, the answers the specified trellis holds. On the durables trellis of fifty-one periods and one hundred and fifty-four stage occurrences, measured in one process on an Apple machine, the build takes about 12 s and each draw about 2.5 s, of which 0.4 s is the copying of those answers. Compiling the kernels of a drawn trellis, the functions a solver calls (A piece §2), takes about 2 s where nothing but the build and the draws has been asked of the specified trellis, and 0.7 s once the specified trellis has compiled its own kernels, in 2 s, since a drawn version then carries what they read.

On one node, the trellis is built in a parent process, which asks it once for what every draw asks, by one draw of its own and, where the solver compiles kernels, by compiling them on the specified trellis, then calls gc.freeze() and only then starts its workers by fork, the operating system's call that starts a process as a copy of the running one. Each worker holds the parent's trellis and those answers, and builds nothing. On the durables trellis, a worker started after one draw made its draw in 2.1 s and compiled the kernels of its trellis in 1.8 s, and its own memory, apart from what it shares with the parent, grew from 4 MB just after the fork to about 200 MB. gc.freeze() sets every object that exists when it is called aside from Python's garbage collector, which otherwise traverses the whole trellis at each full collection: it cut the collector's share of the first draw after the build from about 0.65 s to 0.26 s, and the draw from about 2.5 s to 2.1 s, and it keeps a worker's collections from writing to the memory the worker shares with the parent. The listing runs the pattern on the three periods of §4, with two workers and three draws; it asks for fork by name, since not every platform starts a worker that way by default:

import gc
import multiprocessing
import pickle

def draw(beta):
    """One draw of an estimation: the specified trellis bound to the draw's β, as the sweep of §5
    binds it. A solver would read the drawn trellis here."""
    drawn = calibrate_trellis(model, latest(load_recipe(registry, recipe, fill={"calibration": {"β": beta}}), 3))
    return f"β = {beta}: {bound_and_copied(model, drawn)}"

def work(betas):
    """One worker's share of the draws. It builds nothing, since it holds the parent's trellis."""
    for beta in betas:
        results.put(draw(beta))

draw(0.94)                        # the first draw, made once in the parent
gc.collect()
gc.freeze()                       # every object built so far set aside from the garbage collector
fork = multiprocessing.get_context("fork")
results = fork.Queue()
workers = [fork.Process(target=work, args=(betas,)) for betas in ([0.93, 0.95], [0.96])]
for worker in workers:
    worker.start()
print("\n".join(sorted(results.get() for _ in range(3))))
for worker in workers:
    worker.join()

sent = pickle.dumps(model)        # what one rank sends the others under MPI
print("the trellis read back by the standard pickle equals it:", pickle.loads(sent) == model)

β = 0.93: bound 6, copied 1
β = 0.95: bound 6, copied 1
β = 0.96: bound 6, copied 1
the trellis read back by the standard pickle equals it: True

Across nodes, the processes of a job that uses MPI, the message-passing standard of cluster computing, are started separately, one per core, and none is a copy of another. One rank, as such a process is called, builds the trellis and sends it to the others, with mpi4py model = comm.bcast(model if comm.rank == 0 else None, root=0), which writes and reads it with Python's standard pickle, as the last lines of the listing do (The stage §5). The durables trellis pickles to 10.7 MB, written in about 0.17 s and read by each rank in about 0.45 s, against about 12 s to build it. A trellis read in this way keeps none of the answers its stage occurrences had computed, so each rank asks it once for them, as the parent does on one node, and calls gc.freeze() once it holds the trellis.

docs.title: 7 The order of a period from its fields
docs.text:
Field dependencies determine the economic order of the stages within a period; the order of the template's list does not. When a trellis is elaborated, or a period of elaborated stages is accreted, the selected connections determine its joins. Each field belongs to its stage occurrence. An authored connector selects eligible continuation and arrival state fields before automatic matching; where either bare endpoint names several eligible fields, its stage key qualifies it. An unclaimed equal-name pair is selected only where its declared sets are compatible and it is the unique globally consistent choice. A continuation field that no join within the period reads is an output of that period and may be paired with the next period's arrival through the indexed inter-period connector. A complete route also needs the ordered state coordinates, joint forward law and backward value components to agree (Periods §2). The computation order follows from selected joins, and stages that depend on none of each other are computable together.

The connection report shows authored and inferred pairs, candidates left unresolved, compatibility diagnostics and routes whose complete state and value interfaces are established. It names an authored endpoint that names no eligible use or several, and a pair whose compatibility is not established. A malformed connector entry, a continuation use claimed twice by authored entries or a selected cycle is refused. The report and the period drawing read the same selection; neither invents a second joining rule. A selected pair alone does not certify an economically complete route.

The forward order, the backward order and the stages computable together are functions over the joins, and no graph of the period is stored. bellman.period.diagram_period(trellis, h) makes the drawing of periods[h] on request, in the format of a graph's diagram(): one box per stage, labeled by its key, standing in the forward order from left to right; one arrow per selected join, labeled by its field pair; and one unlabeled arrow to a plain label for each continuation field that no stage of the period takes. bellman.trellis.diagram_trellis(trellis, periods=None) shows the periods of an elaborated trellis, all of them or those whose indices periods lists, each as diagram_period shows it inside a frame labeled with h and, where the trellis's registry holds last_age, with the age; the terminal period stands at the right, so that economic time runs from left to right and the backward computation from right to left, as the drawing's title states; and every inter-period connector between two of those periods is shown as wires from the continuation fields that leave periods[h + 1] to the arrival fields of periods[h], each labeled with the connector's index and its field pair. Both calls return a drawing that a notebook displays, built from the dictionary and stored nowhere. The drawing of the three latest periods of the two-stage durables trellis, made by diagram_trellis(model, periods=[0, 1, 2]):

Each frame holds a box for the keeper and a box for the adjuster with their continuation fields shown as outputs of the period, in the terminal frame the six arrows run instead into the bequest's box, labeled a_nxt_kp → a_bq, h_nxt_kp → h_bq, z_nxt_kp → z_bq and likewise for the adjuster, and no wire joins one frame to another, since this trellis file writes no inter-period connector. A trellis of one stage over three periods, whose trellis file writes the connector {a: k} once to stand for every adjacent pair, shows the inter-period connectors:

Each wire runs from the continuation field a of the earlier period to the arrival field k of the later one and is labeled with its index, inter_connectors[1] between periods[2] and periods[1] and inter_connectors[0] between periods[1] and periods[0].

docs.title: From syntax to a mathematical problem
docs.text:
Summary

Read the income-and-consumption stage as a problem with explicit state arguments. The budget equation determines where continuation value is evaluated; the policy chooses consumption after income is observed; the arrival equation averages over income. The same reading applies when consumption is separated from discounting and investment.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Stages: the complete buffer_stock.bl; Field equations: the reusable consumption source. Formal account — Appendix C: rules R1–R12; Appendix D: computation boundaries and indexing; Bellman calculus: mathematical foundations. Used by — Semantics and Methodization: the constructed stage read in words, and the selection of numerical methods for its equations.

docs.title: 1 State the consumption context
docs.text:
Use the complete buffer_stock.bl in Stages. Its fields are quantities interpreted in declared information sets, called perches. We use the following state and control notation:

Quantity Information and domain \(b\) Beginning assets, observed at arrival, in \([0,\infty)\). \(y\) Current income, drawn after arrival and observed before consumption, in \((0,\infty)\). \(w=Rb+y\) Decision resources in \((0,\infty)\), with gross return \(R>0\). \(c\) Consumption chosen at decision, with \(0<c\leq w\). \(a=w-c\) Savings available for continuation, in \([0,\infty)\). \(W\) Supplied continuation-value function on \([0,\infty)\).

Utility is \(u(c)=c^{1-\rho}/(1-\rho)\) for \(\rho>1\) and \(c>0\), and \(0<\beta<1\) is the discount factor. Under the example's explicit law, log income has mean \(\mu_y\) and standard deviation \(\sigma_y\geq0\), with a conditional distribution constant given arrival information. Write \(\nu_y\) for this positive income law.

Assume resources contain the information needed for the consumption problem and savings contain the information needed for continuation value. This does not say the household forgets its earlier observations. A representative is a function of the declared state describing a field; the state must suffice for that representation and for the required conditional laws. Choose representatives on every feasible state where the equations or alternative controls evaluate them. Agreement almost surely under one state distribution does not fix their values at all those states (Appendix C R5–R6).

docs.title: 2 Make the state arguments explicit
docs.text:
The following backward block is an excerpt from the complete buffer_stock.bl, with its budget transition and utility definition retained:

[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu, c) : !cntn -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {
    V = 𝑢(c) + β*V[>]            :: [id=value]
}

V[>] denotes the continuation-value field, which the function \(W\) represents; holding a feasible consumption choice fixed, the field's value is \(W(a)\). Substitution of the savings transition gives the choice value, the objective with the control still an argument:

\[ Q(w,c)=u(c)+\beta W(w-c),\qquad w>0,\quad 0<c\leq w. \]

This is the reading of the value equation before a policy is evaluated. The control remains a decision choice even when the signature lists it alongside continuation inputs. The stage's information marks are not calendar-time subscripts.

Substitution must retain every declared output and every free or bound dependency. In particular, savings must still be determined by a = w-c even when w-c is also substituted into \(W\). The local utility argument and the control bound by argmax_{c} have distinct scopes. Appendix D gives a generic two-output example of this preservation rule. Marking the savings equation !node records a computation boundary without changing its budget relation; !doc instead removes its defining equation.

docs.title: 3 Choose consumption and average over income
docs.text:
The policy equation in buffer_stock.bl is c = argmax_{c}(𝑢(c) + β*V[>]). Its feasible set comes from positive consumption, nonnegative savings, and the budget equation. A policy is a measurable choice of consumption for each resource state. An optimal selection \(\pi\) and its decision-value function \(v\) satisfy

\[ \pi(w)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{0<c\leq w}Q(w,c),\qquad v(w)=Q(w,\pi(w)). \]

For attainment, assume \(W\) is finite and continuous on every compact savings interval. It is then bounded on \([0,w]\), while utility tends to minus infinity as consumption tends to zero. The maximization excludes a sufficiently small interval near zero and attains its maximum on the remaining compact interval. Select a measurable maximizer; if \(W\) is concave, strict concavity of utility makes the maximizer unique. These are mathematical conditions, not conclusions of parsing argmax.

The arrival equation V[<] = E_{y}(V) averages the decision value after that policy has been selected. Substituting the resource transition gives

\[ B(b)=\int v(Rb+y)\,\nu_y(dy),\qquad b\geq0, \]

where \(B\) is arrival value. Require \(\int|v(Rb+y)|\,\nu_y(dy)<\infty\). Bounded continuous \(W\) is one sufficient case under the stated lognormal law, which has the required negative income moment. Appendix C R7–R8 gives the integration and policy conditions.

The order matters: consumption responds to realized income inside the expectation. Maximizing before income were observed would describe a different decision problem. The supplied \(W\) comes from an adjoining period or terminal boundary; the equation does not silently set \(W=B\). Stationary closure would be an additional model assumption.

docs.title: 4 Reuse the consumption module
docs.text:
The separate cons.bl in Field equations begins with observed resources \(m>0\), sets decision resources \(m_d=m\), and uses the same savings equation. Let \(H:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\) be its supplied continuation function. Because its value equation contains no beta, the choice value is

\[ Q_H(m_d,c)=u(c)+H(m_d-c),\qquad 0<c\leq m_d. \]

Apply the continuity, attainment, and measurable-selection conditions above to \(H\). Arrival resources are already observed, so the module evaluates its policy without taking another income expectation. When the adjoining discount and investment stages supply \(H=\beta P_v\), where \(P_v\) is investment value given next-period resource value \(v\), discounting appears exactly once. Periods derives the composed problem and states the additional conditions on \(P_v\).

The separate cons_interior.bl uses the endogenous grid method's candidate relation, described in Field equations. Its equation c = c[>] becomes a relation through savings, not an assignment or a guarantee of global optimality. Its inverse-marginal formula requires a finite strictly positive continuation derivative agreeing with the supplied value function. The first-order boundary criterion uses the finite right derivative at zero. To declare the full constrained policy, write the Kuhn–Tucker condition in one of its three spellings, the clause ⟂ m_d - c >= 0 on the decision-perch first-order condition using the forward law a = m_d - c, a multiplier declared in the policy block, or the clause ⟂ a >= 0 on the continuation-marked candidate line written as an inequality, which the loading software reads as the corner (Constraints §4); or restrict the equality to the interior and declare the boundary branch separately, or retain constrained maximization. A numerical boundary extension is not a solution of the unrestricted interior equality. Candidate coordinates must determine a measurable policy on the required domain. Those additional conditions do not belong to the value-only constrained source used above.

docs.title: 5 Inspect equations and then solve
docs.text:
A stage is inspected through the queries of the constructed object: its fields, its definitions table, its graphs, whose boxes open from whole builders down to their single operations, the conditions its construction states, and the card that denote() prints for any piece or definition (API). A builder's card prints each of its operations with its rule written at a point, the state arguments explicit (A builder §1), so the functions of §§2 and 3 are read from the constructed stage itself. On buffer_stock.bl:

Card Rule printed Function of §§2 and 3 The decision builder, stage.dcsn.builder.bwd.denote() 𝑉(w) = 𝑢(𝑐(w)) + β · 𝑉≻(𝑔≻(w, 𝑐(w))) \(v(w)=Q(w,\pi(w))\) The policy builder, stage.dcsn.builder.policy.denote() 𝑐(w) ∈ argmax_{c ∈ ℝ₊₊} [𝑢(c) + β · 𝑉≻(𝑔≻(w, c))] the maximization of §3 The arrival builder, stage.arvl.builder.bwd.denote() 𝑉≺(b) = E_{y}[𝑉(𝑔≺(b, y))] \(B(b)\)

Here 𝑉≻ is the continuation value \(W\). The two laws of motion are 𝑔≻(w, c), the savings \(w-c\), and 𝑔≺(b, y), the resources \(Rb+y\). The decision builder's card writes the law at the policy out where a rule reads it, 𝑉≻(𝑔≻(w, 𝑐(w))), the continuation value at the savings the policy leaves. The analytic conditions the construction assumes, such as the integrability of the arrival expectation, are what stage.obligations() returns (The stage §5); the factory API states the calls that construct a stage.

Construction retains interpreted equations and definitions after discarding the temporary syntax tree. Inspection therefore needs neither a second source-string model nor an inferred policy formula based on block names.

Selecting methods, settings, and parameters prepares numerical calculation. Solving also requires the adjoining stages and terminal data; neither inspecting equations nor recognizing a numerical target supplies those results. The lesson tutorials/models/cons-port/03-solving-the-two-orders.ipynb of the repository solves the portfolio–consumption model numerically, separately from the source-to-function derivation here.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
Summary

A constraint on a choice is written in one of three places, according to what it is. A fixed bound is part of the control's declared set. A bound that depends on the state is a feasibility correspondence, a set-valued function defined at the top of the file and named in the maximization statement of the policy block. A constraint that binds at some states and not at others is written with the Kuhn–Tucker condition in one of three spellings, which denote one relation between the state and the choice under the hypotheses of §2: the complementary-slackness clause ⟂ after the first-order condition, a multiplier declared in the policy block, or the clause after the candidate line of the endogenous grid method. The candidate line written without a clause states the policy only at the states its candidates reach and nothing at the states where the constraint binds.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Field equations §3: the consumption stage and its inverse Euler line, the running example of this page. Formal account — Appendix C R10, §4.5 and §4.6: the reading of the clause and of the declared multiplier, and the theorem that the three spellings denote one relation and, under concavity, one policy. Used by — Methodization §6: how a method such as the endogenous grid method reads a constraint. See also — A builder §§1 and 2: the policy builder, its operations and its printed card; Refusals: the rules under which the loading software refuses a writing.

docs.title: 1 Three kinds of constraint and where each is written
docs.text:
An economic model constrains a choice in three ways, and the language, Bellman-SYM, gives each its own place.

A fixed bound does not depend on the state. A portfolio share lies in \([0,1]\); investment is nonnegative; a labor supply lies in \([0,1]\). Such a bound is the control's declared set, written in the signature of the block where the control is introduced, for example ς : [0,1] @ !ctrl or i : ℝ₊ @ !ctrl. Nothing further is written, because the set is the constraint. Declarations, roles such as !ctrl and annotations :: [id=…] are read as in Stages §2, Symbol conventions and Equation parsing rules §1; [>] marks a field at the continuation perch, the information set at which the quantities after the decision are known (Stages §1).

A state-dependent bound is a feasibility correspondence, a function from states to sets, which the notation of the Bellman calculus writes \(\Gamma\). It is defined at the top of the file by a function definition whose body is a set rather than a formula, and it is named in the binder of the maximization statement of the policy block, the block of a stage that states how the control is chosen; the maximization statement names the control as a maximizer of its objective over its feasible set, and §4 states, for each spelling, whether it forms an operation. A statement marked !doc is a declaration: it forms no operation, and no method is attached to it. A correspondence is not written as the type of a control: controls keep plain declared sets, and the loading software reads the feasible set from the maximization statement.

In the maximization statement the binder introduces a bound variable, local to the statement, that ranges over the feasible set: argmax_{cp : Γ(w, h)} binds cp to \(\Gamma(w,h)\), the feasible set at the state \((w, h)\) of §5.2, with the same colon that types a declaration. When the bound is fixed the bare binder suffices, argmax_{i}(…), because the control's declared set is its feasible set.

A feasible set for a pair of jointly chosen quantities may be a product:

Γ(z : ℝ₊) := [0, z] × ℝ₊

The first component lies between zero and z, while the second is nonnegative. To couple components by a budget identity, write a set comprehension, which gives a domain and conditions on its members:

Γ(z : ℝ₊) := {q : ℝ₊ × ℝ₊ × ℝ₊ | q[1] + q[2] = z}

Here q is one nonnegative triple, and its first two components must sum to z; its third component remains nonnegative. For z = 3, (1, 2, 0) is feasible, whereas (1, 1, 0) violates the equality and (1, 2, -1) violates nonnegativity. Comma-separated conditions must all hold, so an equality may be combined with inequalities. The policy's maximization statement retains this complete feasible set for the joint choice; Appendix C R7 states the separate requirements for a maximizer and its numerical selection.

An occasionally binding constraint holds with equality at some states and with slack at others: the borrowing limit that binds at low wealth, the irreversibility of investment that binds when capital is abundant, the collateral limit that binds when house prices fall. Its first-order condition is the Kuhn–Tucker condition of §2, which the language writes in one of three spellings (§4).

A fixed bound on a parameter is written in its declaration as a comma-separated condition after the set, β : ℝ₊₊, < 1 for a discount factor, read as the set of values of the declared name that satisfy the condition; several conditions are separated by commas, as in x : ℝ, >= 0, <= 1.

Abstract grammar: CorrDef 

stmt  += CorrDef(identifier name, coordinate* params, setexpr body)
params has at least one entry, each a typed argument; body is an interval, a finite set, a product of sets or a set comprehension, in the arguments. A comprehension may restrict its member by equalities and inequalities. A set comprehension is admitted in one other place, after := in the definition of a named set, which has no arguments, as in H := {i : ℤ | i >= 0, i <= 1} (Symbol conventions §9.2); marked !categories, such a set is bounded by inequalities alone, and an equality condition is refused under category-codes.

Keys. name is the correspondence's name, applied in a binder (§1); params are its typed arguments; body is the set it assigns to each argument value (§1).

Head. A function-definition line, name(arg : set, …) := body, whose body is a set rather than a formula.

Denotes. The feasibility correspondence \(\Gamma\) of Stages and perches §1, a function from decision states to sets of admissible controls.

Status. The loading software parses the definition and reads the feasible set from the binder of the maximization statement into the declared set of functions for the policy, which the policy card prints beside the policy's type as 𝑐(m_d) ∈ Γ(m_d) (§4).

Abstract grammar: In 

subscript = Var(identifier name)
          | In(identifier var, expr set)
var is the bound variable; set is a named set or an applied correspondence.

Keys. var is the name bound by the operator (§1); set is the set it ranges over (§1).

Head. Inside the operator's subscript braces, argmax_{var : set}; the bare form argmax_{var} is Var.

Denotes. The maximization of Appendix C R7 over the set the binder names, with the variable local to the statement.

Status. The loading software parses both forms and records the binder with the operator occurrence. A maximization statement marked !doc is printed on the policy card under the heading Declared with the policy substituted for the control, 𝑐(m_d) ∈ argmax_{cp ∈ Γ(m_d)} [𝑢(cp) + 𝑉≻(𝑔≻(m_d, cp))], and forms no operation; written without the mark, it forms the Argmax operation that outputs the policy, and the card prints the same statement as that operation's rule (§4.1).

docs.title: 2 The Kuhn–Tucker condition
docs.text:
The running example is the consumption stage of Field equations §3. At cash on hand \(m_d > 0\) the household chooses consumption \(c > 0\) and saves \(a = m_d - c\), subject to the borrowing limit \(a \ge 0\), to maximize \(u(c) + V_\succ(a)\), where \(u\) is utility and \(V_\succ\) is the continuation value, the function the field V[>] denotes; the period's other stage, disc, applies the discount factor, so \(V_\succ\) is already discounted and no \(\beta\) appears (Appendix C §4.2). The page writes \(u'\) for marginal utility, 𝑑𝑢 in the file, \((u')^{-1}\) for its inverse, 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣, and \(V_\succ'\) for the marginal value of saving, the derivative of the continuation value, which the derivative term D_{a}V[>] denotes and a card prints as D_{a}𝑉≻. Throughout, \(u'\) is a strictly decreasing bijection of \(\mathbb R_{++}\), and \(V_\succ\) is differentiable on \(X_a = \mathbb R_+\), from the right at zero, with derivative \(V_\succ'\) valued in \(\mathbb R_{++}\).

With a multiplier \(\mu\) on the borrowing limit, the Kuhn–Tucker condition of Karush (1939) and Kuhn and Tucker (1951) for this problem is

\[ u'(c) - V_\succ'(m_d - c) = \mu, \qquad \mu \ge 0, \qquad m_d - c \ge 0, \qquad \mu\,(m_d - c) = 0 . \]

The last three parts are complementary slackness: the multiplier and the slack \(m_d - c\) of the bound are nonnegative and their product is zero, so the Euler equation holds with equality where the household saves, and marginal utility may exceed the marginal value of saving where it saves nothing. The states at which the bound binds form the constrained region. The residual \(r = u'(c) - V_\succ'(m_d - c)\), the left side of the Euler equation less its right side, equals the multiplier, so the condition is

\[ r \ge 0, \qquad m_d - c \ge 0, \qquad r\,(m_d - c) = 0 , \]

written \(0 \le r \perp m_d - c \ge 0\) in the complementarity-problem literature (§6). This is the form the language writes. Under the concavity hypotheses of Appendix C §4.5 the condition has one solution at each \(m_d\), and that solution is the maximizer.

For an upper bound \(z \le b\) the slack is \(b - z\), and the residual is nonpositive, zero wherever the bound is slack. For two bounds on one quantity, \(lb \le z \le ub\) with \(lb < ub\), each bound has a multiplier, \(\mu_{lo}\) and \(\mu_{hi}\), at most one of them positive, and the residual is \(\mu_{lo} - \mu_{hi}\): nonnegative where the lower bound binds, zero where neither binds, and nonpositive where the upper bound binds.

docs.title: 3 The complementary-slackness clause
docs.text:
A statement of a block may have a clause after its equality or inequality:

    lhs = rhs ⟂ bound >= 0

The clause pairs the residual, the left side less the right side, with the slack of the bound, as in §2: on a lower bound >= the residual is nonnegative, the bound holds and their product is zero, so the equation holds wherever the bound is slack; on an upper bound <= the residual is nonpositive instead. The author orients the equation so that its residual has the sign its bound requires, as the examples of §5 do. After an inequality statement the residual takes the sign of that inequality, and the clause adds the bound and the zero product (§4.3). The sign is read from the relation as written, so a clause with one bound writes the bounded quantity first: a >= 0 on a continuation-marked candidate line, or m_d - c >= 0 on a decision-perch condition whose forward law is a = m_d - c. The reversed one-bound spelling ⟂ 0 <= a is refused under readable-form. The glyph is ⟂ (U+27C2); ⊥ (U+22A5) is not admitted. The rules under which the loading software refuses a writing are listed in Refusals.

A clause names one bounded quantity. On a statement it may have two bounds, written as an ascending chain of weak inequalities, from the lower bound through the bounded quantity to the upper bound:

    lhs = rhs ⟂ lb <= x <= ub

The two-bound clause states the condition of §2 for two bounds. The worker's saving stage of the pension application writes one on the pension deposit \(c_p\), which lies between zero and earnings \(w_d\), in the method block of its policy builder, applications/pension-retirement/declaration/methods/worker_saving_foc.bl, whose two lines are the first-order conditions of the stage's maximization:

    𝑑𝑢(c) = β*(1 + 𝑑𝜒(c_p))*D_{y_p}V[>] ⟂ 0 <= c_p <= w_d

Its residual is the stationarity condition in the deposit less that in consumption. In a system of several conditions each clause is written so that its residual is the multiplier of its own bound, the other multipliers being eliminated by combining the first-order conditions; the loading software holds the statements as written and checks no such arrangement (Appendix C R10).

The clause is written on the first-order condition (§4.1), on the declaration of a multiplier (§4.2), or on the candidate line of the endogenous grid method (§4.3). Where the maximization statement is marked !doc and the control enters the first-order condition only through the law of motion, as in §5.1 and §5.3, the condition names no output of the block, and a block that states the control by that condition alone is refused under the rule output-defined; attached as the property of the maximization statement written without !doc, the first spelling of §4.1, the same condition is accepted.

Technical details

Where the left side of a statement is an expression rather than a name, as it is in the examples of §5.1 and §5.2, its unknowns are the outputs of the policy block that its two sides mention and that no other operative statement of the block defines by name, an operative statement being one the block computes with, so any line that is neither marked !doc nor attached to another line as its property by a dotted id (§4.1; Appendix C R10). Where the maximization statement is marked !doc it is not operative, so the control it names on its left side stays an unknown of the operative statements below it; in the first spelling (§4.1) it is written without !doc and is itself the operation that outputs the control. Several such statements of one block that share an unknown state one system, whose unknowns are taken in the order of the block's header.

Abstract grammar: Slack 

stmt  += Slack(stmt core, cond bound)
cond   = Rel(expr left, relop op, expr right)
relop  = Lt | Le | Eq | Ge | Gt
The statement core is an equality or an inequality; on an inequality the residual takes the sign of its relation. The relation bound is written with >= for a lower bound or <= for an upper bound (≥ and ≤ are the same spellings); left is the bounded quantity and right the bound, an expression in the stage's declared quantities, and a left that is a number or inf alone is refused. A clause with two bounds is the Between of the next box.

Keys. core is the equality or inequality whose residual the clause constrains (§3); bound is the relation the constrained quantity satisfies throughout (§3).

Head. The glyph ⟂ between the statement and its bound, on one statement line, before any annotation.

Denotes. The Kuhn–Tucker condition of §2 for the residual of core and the slack of bound, with the residual's sign taken from the relation of core; stated with its concavity hypotheses in Appendix C §4.5.

Status. The loading software parses the clause and keeps it with its statement. It reads the clause by the product of the residual and the slack: where the slack is positive the residual is zero, and where the slack is zero the residual has the sign the clause states; a chain has three such cases, one at each bound and one between them. This reading admits at each state exactly the values the condition of §2 admits, and nothing is solved. The card prints the clause in the rule of the operation its statement forms, read at the point, the state at which the rule holds: on a first-order condition, each function at the coordinates of its own perch and each continuation state replaced by the law of motion at the decision state and the policy, under the Argmax operation when the condition is its property and under an Aggregation of its own when the condition is an operative line (§4.1); on the candidate line, at the saving (§4.3). The statements of one system share one rule, their conjunction.

Abstract grammar: Between 

cond  += Between(expr lower, relop lo, expr middle, relop hi, expr upper)
lo and hi are both <= (or ≤), so the chain ascends from the lower bound through the bounded quantity to the upper bound. A descending, strict or mixed chain, a chain after an inequality statement and a chain on the declaration of a multiplier are refused.

Keys. lower and upper are the two bounds (§3); middle is the bounded quantity (§3); lo and hi are the two relation signs as written (§3).

Head. Two relation signs after the glyph ⟂, ⟂ lb <= x <= ub, on one statement line, before any annotation.

Denotes. With \(r\) the residual of the statement, the bounds \(lb \le x \le ub\) together with \(r\,(x - lb) \le 0\) and \(r\,(ub - x) \ge 0\): the residual is nonnegative where the lower bound binds, zero where neither binds and nonpositive where the upper bound binds, and with \(lb < ub\) it is the difference of the two bounds' multipliers (§2).

Status. The loading software parses the chain, keeps both relation signs, and prints the chain read at the point. On the card of the pension application's worker stage the chain on the deposit is printed after the clause of the first condition, whose bound prints as y_f ≥ 0: y_f is the name that the card's Where line gives to the financial saving in the law of motion. The refusals above are made under readable-form, and on a declaration under multiplier-declaration.

docs.title: 4 Three spellings of one condition
docs.text:
The endogenous grid method (Carroll 2006, §2.2) inverts the interior Euler equation on a grid of the continuation state, the state after the decision is taken (Stages and perches §1). In the running example the continuation state is the saving \(a\), with declared set Xa, and the law of motion \(g_\succ\), the map from the decision state and the control to the continuation state, is \(a = m_d - c\). Inverting the interior Euler equation \(u'(c) = V_\succ'(a)\) at each saving gives the candidate at each saving, which the field c[>] denotes, \(c_\succ(a) = (u')^{-1}(V_\succ'(a))\) (Carroll's equation 17), and the budget gives the cash on hand at each saving, which m_d[>] denotes, \(m_{d\succ}(a) = a + c_\succ(a)\) (his equation 18), written in the file by the grid line m_d[>] = a + c[>]; a card prints them 𝑐≻ and 𝑚_d≻. Where the candidate line has no clause, both are functions of the saving alone (Appendix C R8); with the clause of §4.3 they are correspondences of the saving alone, 𝑐≻ : Xa ⇉ ℝ₊₊ and 𝑚_d≻ : Xa ⇉ Xm, the double arrow marking a correspondence, each taking several values at zero saving; with the multiplier of §4.2 they are functions of the saving and the multiplier. Write \(\bar m = (u')^{-1}(V_\succ'(0))\) for the interior value at zero saving. The image \(m_{d\succ}(X_a)\) is the set of cash on hand that some saving reaches; under the hypotheses of Appendix C §4.5 it is \([\bar m, \infty)\).

The policy block's lines are read into the policy builder, the operator the block denotes, whose printed card lists its operations under the heading Operations, one entry each: the entry's number and its key: the id of the line it realizes followed by its kind, as in InvEuler:Aggregation, or the kind alone, as in Pullback and Evaluation, for an operation that no line of the block forms; the functions it reads after in: and those it writes after out:; and its rule after rule:, with a note at the right margin, on …, naming the set on which the rule holds. Under the heading Source the card gives the lines of the file its operations come from (A piece §1). An operation of a policy builder is of one of five kinds, each a row of Operations: a Pullback composes a function with a map, such as a continuation function with the law of motion; an Aggregation applies a pointwise map, or holds the relation its line writes, with the unknown on both sides where the line puts it there; an Expectation integrates over a shock; an Argmax maximizes an objective over the feasible set; and the Evaluation is the identity into the declared set of functions for the policy, the place at which a numerical method stores its representation of the policy. The three spellings share the header of the policy block and its maximization statement, which the second and the third mark !doc, as below, a declaration of what their operations are meant to reach that the operations neither confirm nor check, and which the first writes without the mark, as the operation itself (§4.1):

[id=policy, (V[>] : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {
    c      = argmax_{cp : Γ(m_d)}(𝑢(cp) + V[>])   :: [id=optimality, !doc]
    …
}

A stage file may instead write the maximization alone and leave the candidate lines to a method block, a block in a file of its own that the methods file binds to the policy builder (Methodization §4.1). A method block writes the second or the third spelling. It holds no maximization line, since the stage file's maximization stays the policy block's declared line, so the first spelling, a property of that line, has no line to attach to there; the first spelling belongs to a stage file that writes the maximization as an operation and attaches to it the first-order condition, which reads the derivative term D_{a}V[>]. The block file cons_egm.bl of the portfolio–consumption demonstration writes the third spelling, c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) ⟂ a >= 0.

docs.title: 4.1 The clause on the first-order condition
docs.text:
c      = argmax_{cp : Γ(m_d)}(𝑢(cp) + V[>])   :: [id=optimality]
    𝑑𝑢(c) = D_{a}V[>] ⟂ m_d - c >= 0          :: [id=optimality.euler]

The first line is the maximization statement without the mark !doc: it is the operation that outputs the policy, and a method is attached to it. The second line is attached to the first as its property by the dotted id optimality.euler: it forms no operation, and the loading software neither checks it against the objective nor derives anything from it. Its bound writes the decision-perch expression \(m_d-c\) supplied by the law of motion \(a = g_\succ(m_d, c) = m_d - c\), so the property states the Kuhn–Tucker condition of §2 at every cash on hand \(m_d\). No candidate and no cash on hand at each saving is written, so a method attached to the Argmax operation solves the condition at each \(m_d\), by a root finder in \(c\) or by the endogenous grid method, which inverts the property for the candidate, as the lines of §4.3 do in the file, and forms the cash on hand by the law of motion.
