The operations are those of the maximization: a Pullback of the continuation value along the law of motion, an Aggregation that forms the objective, the Argmax over the feasible set with the policy as its output, and the Evaluation. The property prints under the Argmax entry, labeled by its id and read at the point, and no Declared section is printed, since no line is marked !doc. A block may instead keep the maximization statement marked !doc and write the first-order condition with its clause as an operative line of its own, 𝑑𝑢(c) = D_{a}V[>] ⟂ m_d - c >= 0 :: [id=euler], as the pension application's worker stage writes its two conditions using its own forward laws. The condition then forms a Pullback of the derivative D_{a}𝑉≻ along the law of motion and an Aggregation whose rule is the relation with the policy on both sides, 𝑑𝑢(𝑐(m_d)) = D_{a}𝑉≻(𝑔≻(m_d, 𝑐(m_d))) ⟂ 𝑔≻(m_d, 𝑐(m_d)) ≥ 0 on Xm, and a root finder is attached to that line.

docs.title: 4.2 The declared multiplier
docs.text:
μ[>]   : ℝ₊ ⟂ a >= 0             :: [id=slackness]
    c[>]   = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>] + μ[>]) :: [id=InvEuler]
    m_d[>] = a + c[>]                :: [id=endoggrid]
    c      = c[>]                    :: [id=cons_choice]

The first line declares a multiplier: a field μ at the continuation perch with the declared set \(\mathbb R_+\), joined by its clause to the bound a >= 0. It is a declaration inside the block's body and defines no equation. The second line is the inverse Euler equation with the multiplier added, \(c = (u')^{-1}(V_\succ'(a) + \mu)\). For the functions the block defines at the continuation perch, the candidate and the cash on hand, the declaration adds the coordinate \(\mu\) beside \(a\) and restricts the pair to the admitted pairs, those at which complementary slackness holds:

\[ A_{\succ,\mathrm{policy}} = \{(a, \mu) \in X_a \times \mathbb R_+ \mid a \ge 0,\ \mu\, a = 0\} , \]

where \(X_a\) is the declared set Xa of the saving; the half-line \(a = 0\) is thus declared by the file, not inferred. On this set the candidate and the cash on hand are functions of the saving and the multiplier, \(c_\succ(a, \mu) = (u')^{-1}(V_\succ'(a) + \mu)\) and \(m_{d\succ}(a, \mu) = a + c_\succ(a, \mu)\), while \(V_\succ\) and its derivative \(V_\succ'\) remain functions of \(a\) alone and the multiplier is an input or output of no block. The identification equates the policy at the cash on hand of each admitted pair with the candidate there, \(c(m_{d\succ}(a, \mu)) = c_\succ(a, \mu)\) on the image \(m_{d\succ}(A_{\succ,\mathrm{policy}})\). On the half-line \(\mu = 0\) that image is the image \(m_{d\succ}(X_a)\) of §4. On the half-line \(a = 0\) the candidate \((u')^{-1}(V_\succ'(0) + \mu)\) decreases from \(\bar m\) toward zero as \(\mu\) grows, because \(u'\) is a strictly decreasing bijection of \(\mathbb R_{++}\) (§2), so the image there is \((0, \bar m]\), the constrained region. Technical details

The card states the set of admitted pairs once, under the heading Where, as A≻,policy; its coordinates have no perch marks, because on a card μ≻ names the measure of the continuation state.

The bound is held as written, even where the declared set of the continuation state already implies it: the loading software compares no bound with a declared set, and on a state declared on \(\mathbb R\) the bound is the only place the constraint enters the set of admitted pairs; §5.2 writes such a bound. Because a bound may not name a control, a constraint on a control, such as the cap on the pension deposit in §3, is written with the clause on the first-order condition.

Abstract grammar: Complementary 

typer += Complementary(typer d, cond bound)
d declares one coordinate with the continuation mark [>] and one set; bound is one relation, a Rel written with the bounded quantity first, and a Between is refused here. The item is Declare(Complementary(d, bound), annot), so Declare keeps its two ASDL fields. The bound may name continuation states, other multipliers of the block, parameters, numbers and inf. A multiplier with a mark other than [>], a bound naming a control, a decision or arrival state or a candidate such as c[>], a second declaration of one name, a block header that lists the multiplier's name, and a declaration without its clause are refused.

Keys. d is the declaration of the multiplier, its name, its perch and its set (§4.2); bound is the constraint whose multiplier it is (§4.2).

Head. A declaration in the body of a policy block followed by the glyph ⟂ and one relation, μ[>] : ℝ₊ ⟂ a >= 0, before any annotation.

Denotes. For the functions its block defines at the continuation perch, the coordinate \(\mu\) beside the continuation states, the pair restricted to the admitted pairs \(\{(a, \mu) \mid \text{bound},\ \mu\, s = 0\}\), where \(s\) is the slack of the bound, \(x - b\) for x >= b and \(b - x\) for x <= b. The declaration forms no operation and no wire, a wire being an input or output of an operation on the card. That this spelling and the clause of §3 denote one relation is a theorem of Appendix C §4.5.

Status. The loading software parses the declaration, gives its name the role of a multiplier at the continuation perch, adds it to the coordinates of the functions its block defines there, forms the set of admitted pairs from the bound as written, with one bound and one product for each declaration where a block declares several (§4.5), and the identification, a Pullback, states the grid relation on the image of that set. The grid line is checked against the law of motion as in §4.3. The refusals above are made under multiplier-declaration, and that of a declaration without its clause under syntax.

docs.title: 4.3 The clause on the candidate line
docs.text:
c[>]   <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) ⟂ a >= 0       :: [id=InvEuler]
    m_d[>] = a + c[>]                :: [id=endoggrid]
    c      = c[>]                    :: [id=cons_choice]

The first line, the candidate line, is the inverse Euler statement of Field equations §3 with <= in place of = and the clause of §3 after it. An inequality statement defines its left side as a correspondence, and the clause takes the sign of its residual from the inequality (§3). A value \(x\) is admitted at the saving \(a\) when

\[ x - (u')^{-1}\bigl(V_\succ'(a)\bigr) \le 0, \qquad a \ge 0, \qquad \bigl(x - (u')^{-1}(V_\succ'(a))\bigr)\, a = 0 . \]

A product is zero exactly when one of its factors is zero. Where the bound is slack, \(a > 0\), the residual is therefore zero and one value is admitted, \((u')^{-1}(V_\succ'(a))\); where it binds, \(a = 0\), every \(x\) with \(0 < x \le \bar m\) is admitted, the lower end open because consumption is declared positive. The card writes the set admitted at \(a\) as 𝑐≻(a), so that 𝑐≻(0) is the segment \((0, \bar m]\). The second line gives each admitted value its cash on hand, \(a + x\). The third line, the identification, is a Pullback, the pullback of the policy along the cash on hand at each saving equated to the candidate; its rule is the grid relation 𝑐(𝑚_d≻(a)) = 𝑐≻(a) on 𝑚_d≻(Xa), the candidate and the cash on hand taking their values together, so that it states \(c(a + x) = x\) at every saving \(a\) and every value \(x\) admitted there:

\[ c(m_d) = m_d \quad \text{for } 0 < m_d \le \bar m, \qquad c\bigl(a + (u')^{-1}(V_\succ'(a))\bigr) = (u')^{-1}(V_\succ'(a)) \quad \text{for } a \ge 0 . \]

The first part is the corner, the pairs at which the household consumes all its cash on hand, and the second is the interior policy on the image \(m_{d\succ}(X_a)\); the two share the pair \((\bar m, \bar m)\). The corner is Carroll's segment from the origin to the first grid point (2006, §4.2.2, equation 29). The card writes each rule at the saving; three answers beside it show the correspondences. The card of the first entry, cons.dcsn.builder.policy["InvEuler:Aggregation"].denote(), gives its output as 𝑐≻ : Xa ⇉ ℝ₊₊, and the card of the second gives 𝑚_d≻ : Xa ⇉ Xm. The query signature(), which answers an operation's inputs and outputs with their sets, gives as the output of the identification the set of policies \(f\) with \(f(a + x) = x\) for every saving \(a\) and every value \(x\) admitted there, the relation over the pairs each saving admits. The loading software checks the second line, the grid line, against the law of motion: it solves \(a = m_d - c\) for the decision coordinate, \(m_d = a + c\), puts the candidate in place of the control, and compares the result with the line. A line that does not agree, such as m_d[>] = a + 2*c[>], is refused under the rule grid-line-consistency, and the refusal names the line as written and the law solved for the coordinate.

Without the clause the candidate line is read as the equality selection, \(c_\succ(a) = (u')^{-1}(V_\succ'(a))\) at every saving, the part of the relation of §2 with \(\mu = 0\), and is no spelling of the Kuhn–Tucker condition. The identification then states the policy on the image \(m_{d\succ}(X_a)\); below it, where the constraint binds, it states nothing.

Abstract grammar: Inequality 

stmt  += Inequality(expr lhs, relop op, expr rhs)
The relation op is <= or >= for a bound (< and > are also admitted); lhs names the quantity defined and rhs is the bound the definition admits.

Keys. lhs is the quantity the statement defines as a correspondence (§4.3); op and rhs state the relation its values satisfy (§4.3).

Head. The relation sign between two expressions on a statement line, where an equation would have =.

Denotes. The set-valued relation \(\{\,\text{lhs} : \text{lhs} \le \text{rhs}\,\}\) at each state, a correspondence. Written as the inverse Euler line without a clause, it is read as the equality selection, the interior candidate \((u')^{-1}(V_\succ'(a))\) at every saving, and is no spelling of the Kuhn–Tucker condition (§4.3). With a clause of one bound after it, the residual takes the sign of the relation and the clause adds the bound and the zero product: the Kuhn–Tucker condition of §2, one value at each saving where the bound is slack and, where it binds, the segment of values up to the interior value at zero saving, \(\bar m\) (§4.3).

Status. The loading software parses the statement, keeps the relation, and forms from it one Aggregation of the policy builder, whose output is the candidate at each saving and whose rule is the relation as written, read at the saving, 𝑐≻(a) ≤ 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}𝑉≻(a)). With a clause of one bound the rule holds the clause as well, 𝑐≻(a) ≤ 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}𝑉≻(a)) ⟂ a ≥ 0, the operation's record holds the values the clause admits at each saving, and the card of that operation prints its output as the correspondence 𝑐≻ : Xa ⇉ ℝ₊₊; a clause with two bounds after the inequality is refused under readable-form. The identification, a Pullback, states the grid relation 𝑐(𝑚_d≻(a)) = 𝑐≻(a) on 𝑚_d≻(Xa): with the clause it holds at every value admitted at each saving, the corner among them; without it the candidate is the interior value at every saving, and the relation states nothing below the image of the grid. No inverse of the cash on hand at each saving is formed.

docs.title: 4.4 One relation
docs.text: Under the hypotheses of §2 and the law of motion \(a = m_d - c\), the three spellings denote one relation between cash on hand and consumption: the pairs that satisfy the clause on the first-order condition, the pairs the declared multiplier reaches on its two half-lines, and the pairs of the grid relation of §4.3, corner included, are one set. The identity of the first spelling with the second uses only that 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣 is the inverse of \(u'\); that of the third with them also uses the monotonicity of \(u'\), through which \(x \le \bar m\) holds exactly when \(u'(x) \ge V_\succ'(0)\). For the first spelling, whose operation is the maximization and whose first-order condition is its property (§4.1), the pairs are those of the property; that the maximizer is among them, and is the only one, holds under the concavity hypotheses of Appendix C §4.5 and not otherwise. Appendix C §4.5 proves the identity and, under concavity hypotheses stated there, that the relation is the graph of one policy and that this policy maximizes the objective over the feasible set; the loading software checks none of these hypotheses. The spellings differ in what a method reads: the first states the condition at every decision state, for a method attached to the Argmax operation to solve; the second and the third state the candidate and the cash on hand at every saving, which the endogenous grid method, attached at the Evaluation, evaluates at the savings of its grid, joins with the pairs of the corner and interpolates as one function of cash on hand, without forming the inverse of the cash on hand at each saving (Appendix C §4.6).

docs.title: 4.5 A bound on both sides
docs.text:
Take a saving bounded on both sides, \(0 \le a \le \bar a\), with ā : ℝ₊₊ a declared parameter. In the first spelling the chain is written on the first-order condition, 𝑑𝑢(c) = D_{a}V[>] ⟂ 0 <= m_d - c <= ā, using the forward law \(a=m_d-c\). In the second each bound has its own multiplier, since a declaration's clause has one bound, and the two enter the inverse Euler line with the signs of §2:

    μ_lo[>] : ℝ₊ ⟂ a >= 0                    :: [id=slack_lo]
    μ_hi[>] : ℝ₊ ⟂ a <= ā                    :: [id=slack_hi]
    c[>]   = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>] + μ_lo[>] - μ_hi[>])  :: [id=InvEuler]

In the third the correct writing is the equation with the chain and the interior value on the left, 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) = c[>] ⟂ 0 <= a <= ā, whose residual is nonnegative at zero saving and nonpositive at the cap. The loading software refuses it under signature-complete, since a field is defined only by a line with its name on the left, so a bound on both sides is written in the first or the second spelling. A chain after the inequality, c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) ⟂ 0 <= a <= ā, is refused under readable-form, because a chain has a sign rule after an equation alone.

Warning

The line c[>] = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) ⟂ 0 <= a <= ā is accepted but states the wrong constraint. Its residual, the candidate less the interior value, has the opposite sign to the Euler residual (Appendix C §4.5), so the chain places consumption above the interior value at zero saving and below it at the cap. The loading software checks no sign.

docs.title: 5 Examples
docs.text: Each example shows the transition block and the policy block; the declarations of parameters and shocks and the backward blocks of a complete stage file are omitted.

docs.title: 5.1 Irreversible investment
docs.text:
A firm with capital \(k\) and depreciation rate \(\delta\) chooses investment \(i \ge 0\), and its capital next period is \(k' = (1-\delta)k + i\). Investment cannot be undone, so the constraint binds when the firm would rather disinvest. The Kuhn–Tucker condition is

\[ 1 - \beta\, W'(k') \ge 0, \qquad i \ge 0, \qquad \bigl(1 - \beta\, W'(k')\bigr)\, i = 0 , \]

where \(W\) is the continuation value of capital and \(\beta\) the discount factor: the firm invests until the discounted marginal value of capital equals its unit cost, unless that value is below the cost, in which case it invests nothing. The bound is fixed, so the control's declared set is the nonnegative reals, and the clause is written on the first-order condition with the unit cost on the left, which makes the residual nonnegative at the bound.

[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (k_d : ℝ₊₊, i : ℝ₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn -> (k_n : ℝ₊₊) : !cntn] {
    k_n = (1 - δ)*k_d + i
}

[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (i : ℝ₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {
    i = argmax_{i}(-i + β*V[>])     :: [id=optimality, !doc]
    1 = β*D_{k_n}V[>] ⟂ i >= 0      :: [id=investment]
}

In the fragment k_d is \(k\), k_n is \(k'\), V[>] is \(W\) and the derivative term D_{k_n}V[>] is \(W'\). The first statement, marked !doc, declares the control to be a maximizer over its declared set and forms no operation. Investment enters the first-order condition only through the transition, so the condition names no output of the block, and the loading software refuses the block under output-defined (§3). In the first spelling of §4.1 the maximization statement is written without !doc and the condition is attached to it as its property, :: [id=optimality.investment]; the block is then accepted, the maximization forming the Argmax operation that outputs investment and the condition printing under it.

docs.title: 5.2 A collateral constraint
docs.text:
A household with a house of size \(h\) and price \(p\) consumes \(c\) out of cash on hand \(w\) and may borrow against the house: end-of-period net assets \(a = w - c\) may be negative down to a fraction \(\theta\) of the house's value. The feasible set of consumption depends on the state, so it is a correspondence,

\[ \Gamma(w, h) = \bigl(0,\; w + \theta p h\bigr] , \]

and the Euler equation has the collateral limit as its bound. The house is held fixed within this stage, \(h' = h\).

Γ(x : ℝ₊₊, h : ℝ₊) := (0, x + θ*p*h]        :: [id=feasible]

[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (w : ℝ₊₊, h : ℝ₊, c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ, h_n : ℝ₊) : !cntn] {
    a   = w - c
    h_n = h
}

[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {
    c = argmax_{cp : Γ(w, h)}(𝑢(cp) + β*V[>])   :: [id=optimality, !doc]
    𝑑𝑢(c) = β*D_{a}V[>] ⟂ w - c >= -θ*p*h       :: [id=euler]
}

In the fragment h_n is \(h'\), and 𝑢 and 𝑑𝑢 are utility and marginal utility, defined as in Field equations §3. The Euler clause writes w - c for a and h for h_n, as the forward block defines them. At states where the limit has slack the Euler equation holds with equality. Where it binds, the household borrows the full \(\theta p h\), consumption is \(w + \theta p h\), and marginal utility exceeds the discounted marginal value of assets by the multiplier on the collateral constraint. The bound is an expression in declared quantities; a constant limit w - c >= 0 is the special case \(\theta = 0\).

docs.title: 5.3 A portfolio share with two bounds
docs.text:
A household allocates a share \(\varsigma \in [0,1]\) of its savings \(s\) to a risky asset with gross return \(\Psi\), the rest earning the safe gross return \(R\), and receives income \(\eta\); next period's resources are \(m' = s\,(\varsigma\Psi + (1-\varsigma)R) + \eta\). Both bounds are fixed, so the control's declared set states them, and with \(W\) the continuation value of resources the first-order condition, divided by the positive savings \(s\), holds with equality only in the interior:

\[ \mathbb{E}\bigl[W'(m')\,(\Psi - R)\bigr] \begin{cases} \le 0 & \text{if } \varsigma = 0, \\ = 0 & \text{if } 0 < \varsigma < 1, \\ \ge 0 & \text{if } \varsigma = 1 . \end{cases} \]

The two-bound clause of §3 states this condition exactly. Written with zero on the left and the expectation on the right,

    0 = E_{Ψ,η}(D_{m}V[>]*(Ψ - R)) ⟂ 0 <= ς <= 1

the statement has the residual \(-\mathbb E\bigl[W'(m')\,(\Psi - R)\bigr]\), which is nonnegative where the share is zero, zero in the interior and nonpositive where the share is one, as the display requires; written the other way round, it would have the opposite sign at each bound. The share enters the condition only through the transition, so a block that states the share by this line alone is refused under output-defined (§3). The block therefore writes the interior first-order condition with solve_{ς}, which names its unknown, and the declared set [0,1] states the two bounds; the maximization statement, marked !doc, declares the share to be a maximizer over that set and forms no operation:

[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (s : ℝ₊₊, ς : [0,1] @ !ctrl, Ψ, η) : !dcsn -> (m : ℝ₊₊) : !cntn] {
    m = s*(ς*Ψ + (1-ς)*R) + η
}

[id=policy, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (ς : [0,1] @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {
    ς = argmax_{ς}(E_{Ψ,η}(V[>]))              :: [id=optimality, !doc]
    ς = solve_{ς}(E_{Ψ,η}(D_{m}V[>]*(Ψ - R)))   :: [id=foc]
}

In the fragment s is the savings allocated, m is \(m'\), the derivative term D_{m}V[>] is \(W'\), and E_{Ψ,η} is the expectation \(\mathbb{E}\) over the declared distribution of the shocks, under which \(W'(m')\,(\Psi - R)\) is assumed integrable. The solve_{ς} statement determines the share as a root of the residual in its argument (Appendix C R8) and states nothing at a corner. A method that solves the first-order condition must check both corners before accepting an interior root; the declared set is what tells it where the corners are. In the first spelling of §4.1 the two-bound line above is instead attached as its property to the maximization statement written without !doc, :: [id=optimality.foc], and the block is accepted, the condition with both corners printing under the Argmax operation.

docs.title: 6 Notation in the literature
docs.text:
The Kuhn–Tucker conditions with complementary slackness are stated in the standard texts on constrained optimization: Nocedal and Wright (2006, Theorem 12.1), whose condition (12.34e) is named the complementarity condition, and Boyd and Vandenberghe (2004, §5.5.2–5.5.3). The perpendicular sign for a pair of inequalities with a zero product is the notation of the complementarity-problem literature: Ferris and Pang (1997, §2.1) write the problem as \(0 \le x \perp F(x) \ge 0\) and explain the sign as adding the equation \(x^{\mathsf T} F(x) = 0\) to the stated inequalities; Cottle, Pang and Stone (1992) treat the linear problem in the form of the three conditions, and Facchinei and Pang (2003) the general theory. In economics, Brumm and Grill (2014, §2.1) write the borrowing constraint of their equilibrium conditions as \(0 \le b - \underline{b} \perp \mu \ge 0\) with the sign denoting orthogonality.

The notation entered computational economics through the complementarity formulation of equilibrium (Mathiesen 1985), the GAMS and PATH software (Rutherford 1995; Dirkse and Ferris 1995), and the toolkits for models with occasionally binding constraints. Dynare up to version 6 attaches the bound to an equation with the mcp tag; from version 7 it writes the bound after the equation separated by ⟂ (U+27C2, or _|_), with the residual positive at a lower bound, zero between the bounds, and negative at an upper bound, the convention of §3 (Dynare Team 2026, §4.12). Dolo writes an arbitrage equation as rhs-lhs ⟂ lb <= x <= ub and states the same sign at a binding lower bound (EconForge 2024).

In dynamic programming the same condition is usually written without the sign. Ljungqvist and Sargent (2018, §17.5 and §18.5.2) write the Euler equation of a household with a borrowing constraint as an inequality that holds with equality when savings are positive; Christiano and Fisher (2000) and Guerrieri and Iacoviello (2015) state the Kuhn–Tucker conditions of the investment constraint in equilibrium models, and Swarbrick (2021, §2) reviews the solution methods; Maliar, Maliar and Winant (2021, §4.1) rewrite the Kuhn–Tucker conditions of the constrained consumption problem as a single equation for solution by a neural network. Carroll (2006, §2.2) inverts the first-order condition on an exogenous grid of end-of-period assets, his equations 17 and 18 being the candidate and the cash on hand at each saving of §4, and handles the borrowing constraint by the segment from the origin to the first grid point (§4.2.2, equations 28 and 29); Hintermaier and Koeniger (2010) extend the method to occasionally binding constraints among endogenous variables. Dobrescu and Shanker (2024) define the inverse Euler problem on the observables, the post-decision states joined with the Kuhn–Tucker multipliers (§2.1, Definition 1; an observable is not a quantity the agent observes), pair the first-order condition with complementary slackness (§3, conditions (3) and (4)), index the pieces of the exogenous grid by the set of binding constraints (§4.1, equation (5)), give the invertibility results in §4.2 (Claim 4.1, Theorem 4.1 and Claim 4.2), and lay a piece out in any variables in one-to-one correspondence with its observables (§4.3); the one-dimensional case is the declared multiplier of §4.2. Their later paper (Dobrescu and Shanker 2026, p. 10) appends the constrained region, written as consumption values, to the endogenous grid, which is the corner of §4.3.

docs.title: Solutions at the perches
docs.text:
Summary

A stage holds its model and no numerical solution. A solver keeps what it computes in plain dictionaries, one for each stage occurrence: keyed by perch as the stage file marks it, arvl, dcsn or cntn, then by the name the file gives each field, each entry a NumPy array on the grid the settings define for that perch. A trellis's solutions are one such dictionary for each period and stage.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Parameters and settings and A piece §2: the parameters, settings and kernels a stage answers; Trellises: the periods of a model and their index. See also — API: every path and verb of the stage object; the lesson tutorials/topics/kernels.ipynb of the repository, which computes the example of §2.

docs.title: 1 One dictionary for each stage occurrence
docs.text: The package constructs and binds a stage; it computes and stores no value function. A solver keeps its results in one dictionary for each stage occurrence, a stage file elaborated at one position of a period. Its keys are the perches as the stage file marks them: arvl for arrival, dcsn for decision, cntn for continuation. Under each perch is a dictionary keyed by the name the file gives each field there, such as m, m_d, c, a and V, holding NumPy arrays. A solver that stores the derivative of the value keeps it under dV: the keys V and dV of a perch hold the value and its derivative in the perch's coordinate, the function that the derivative term D_{a}V[>] reads at the continuation. The grid of a perch stands under the name of its coordinate, m_d at the decision of the consumption stage and a at its continuation, and every other array of the perch holds one entry for each grid point. The grid is the one the settings define: at the decision of the consumption stage, n_m points from m_min to m_max.

docs.title: 2 An example on the consumption stage
docs.text:
The lesson tutorials/topics/kernels.ipynb calibrates the consumption stage applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl at \(\rho = 6\), takes at the continuation ten levels of savings and the value of consuming all of them, and computes with the stage's kernels one step of the decision builder at the consumption rule \(c(\mathrm m_d) = \mathrm m_d/2\). It keeps the results in this form:

solution = {
    "cntn": {"a": a, "V": v, "dV": dv},
    "dcsn": {"m_d": m_d, "c": m_d / 2, "V": V, "dV": dV},
}

a holds the savings levels and v and dv the continuation value and its derivative at them; m_d holds the levels of resources, c the consumption the rule gives, and V and dV the value and its derivative at the decision. The value comes from the decision builder's two compiled kernels, the law of motion \(g\) and the aggregator \(G\), with \(\rho\) passed at the call; the aggregator returns the value alone. The derivative is what the stated derivative line D_{m_d}V = 𝑑𝑢(c) of the decision builder gives, marginal utility \(c^{-\rho}\) at the rule, with \(\rho\) the one entry of values:

g = cons.dcsn.builder.bwd["Pullback"].compile_kernel()
G = cons.dcsn.builder.bwd["Aggregation"].compile_kernel()
values = cons.dcsn.builder.bwd["Aggregation"].kernel().parameter_values
V = G(np.interp(g(m_d, m_d / 2), a, v), m_d, m_d / 2, *values)
dV = (m_d / 2) ** -values[0]

The lesson's ten points are its own, checkable by hand; a solver takes its grids from the settings.

docs.title: 3 A trellis
docs.text: A trellis holds its periods in a list indexed by h, the number of periods before the last. Its solutions are held in the same way, one dictionary of perches for each period and stage, solutions[h]["cons"], which a backward solver fills in the order \(h = 0, 1, 2, \dots\). A stage's continuation arrays are the arrival arrays of the stage its continuation fields join, in the same period or, through the inter-period connector, in solutions[h - 1].

docs.title: 4 What the stage supplies
docs.text: The stage supplies the numbers and the functions. stage.par["ρ"] answers a parameter and its value, and stage.settings["n_m"] a setting and the places that read it. A builder's kernels compute the arrays of one perch from those of the next: compile_kernel() answers one kernel as a plain function, and a builder's kernels() answers all of them in the order they are applied, with the parameters' values, in a record that refers to no stage (A builder §5). A solver needs the records, the grids and the dictionaries, not the stage.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Summary

The public names of bellman.stage, bellman.period and bellman.trellis, one table each, and every path and verb of the way in to the stage object: the functions that read, elaborate and bind stage files and trellises, find the joins and the order of the stages of a period and draw periods, the table of method types, and the pieces of the stage object reached from the stage by name, each with what it answers, the type of its answer, one answer the package prints and where the package defines it. The attributes of the records these paths answer, such as a parameter's value or a kernel's origins, and the class ElaboratedStage, the module semgraph and the four refusal classes have no row. The tables are written from the package by the documentation's own script, so they list what the installed package answers. The pages below this index take the stage object one level at a time.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Stage tutorial: the stage file whose object these paths reach. Used by — The factory API and The stage: the pages of the two groups below. See also — Operations and Methods: the kinds of operation and the method types a listing names.

Key terminology Term What it names Stage One self-contained decision problem, written as one stage file, a .bl file; in Python, the object elaborate_stage returns for that file. Perch One of the three information sets of a stage: arrival arvl, decision dcsn and continuation cntn. Field A named quantity at a perch, with a declared set: a state, a control, a shock or a value. Block A group of equations of a stage file between declared inputs and outputs (Stage tutorial §3). Initial diagram The blocks of one direction of a stage on the fields they read and write, one graph backward and one forward. Builder The operator one block denotes: on value functions backward, on finite measures forward. Builders graph The builders of one direction: stage.builder.bwd, the backward builders a solution applies, and stage.builder.fwd, the forward builders a simulation applies. Piece A component of a stage reached by its name from the component that holds it: a builder, a block, a sub-builder, an operation or a line. Operation One primitive operator inside a builder, such as a pullback or an aggregation (A piece §1). Line One equation of a block, read by its id; a line marked !doc states what the control is, is not computed and has no box (The initial diagrams §3). Grain How far a graph's boxes are opened: one box per block, or one box per primitive operator. Wire A typed connection of a graph, carrying one object: a field in an initial diagram, a function or a measure in a builders graph. Coordinate A control a block lists among its inputs: its lines are written in it, and no wire carries it (The initial diagrams §3). Kernel The pointwise object one operation applies: a law of motion 𝑔, a value aggregator 𝐺 or a declared distribution (A piece §2). Denotation The mathematical object a piece denotes under the declarations of its file and the calibration of its version: a set, a map between sets, a measure, a relation or an operator; denote() states it, and the package computes none. Builder at a policy A backward builder or a push-forward stated at the policy function: one operator for each policy, all with the same inputs and outputs (A builder §1).

docs.title: 1 The way in
docs.text:
Every piece of a stage is reached from the piece that contains it, and each answers for itself, a verb meaning the same at every level that answers it. A builder is identified by the ordered pair of perches it joins and read by that pair as a key of stage.builder: stage.builder["cntn", "dcsn"] is the backward builder from continuation to decision, and the policy builder is read by its own key, stage.builder["policy"]. Each perch reaches the builders of the edge that leaves it, stage.dcsn.builder.bwd, a path defined as that one pair, and the pages below write a builder by its perch path (The builders graphs §§1 and 2). Every other piece is read by its name as a key, stage.dcsn.builder.bwd["pullback"]; one parameter, one setting and one bound method by the name their file writes, stage.par["ρ"], stage.settings["n_a"] and stage.methods["policy"]; and the value alone of a parameter or a setting by the same name as an attribute, stage.par.ρ and stage.settings.n_a. A graph, a builder and a sub-builder open to a finer grain by an attribute, primitives or sub_builders. The verbs are view() for the stage's printed view, list() for the pieces inside, denote() for the piece's printed record, signature() for its inputs and outputs, diagram() for its drawing, kernel() and compile_kernel() for the rule an operation applies, kernels() for the kernels of every operation of a builder or a sub-builder, as one record that refers to no stage, and methods for the methods bound within it. The stage answers no signature() or diagram(); stage.initial answers list() and methods alone, and stage.builder these two and view(); a perch answers no verb, and the builders of a perch, stage.dcsn.builder, answer list() alone; only the stage, stage.builder, stage.par and stage.settings answer view(); an operation answers no diagram(); a block answers no kernels(), which the builder of the same name answers; and a line marked !doc answers denote() and methods alone.

The pages take the two groups of the API in turn.

Group Pages Bellman factory API The factory API, Stage functions, Recipe functions, Period functions, The trellis factory: the functions that read files, elaborate and bind trellises and draw periods. The stage object The stage, The initial diagrams, The builders graphs, A builder, A piece, Parameters and settings, Methods and places, The definitions table, The binding verbs: one page per level of the object.

Beside the drawing that diagram() answers, a stage or a trellis is read interactively in Google's Model Explorer through the functions explore and write_model_explorer, which stand in bellman.stage and in bellman.trellis and are no verbs of a piece: The view in Model Explorer.

docs.title: 2 Every path, in four tables
docs.text:
One row per public function and per public constant of bellman.stage, bellman.period and bellman.trellis, in one table per namespace, then one row per path and verb of the way in, each written from what the package answers; a class or a module that a namespace exports, such as the class ElaboratedStage, has no row. Every table has five columns:

  • path is what you type: a function with the parameters a call must give; the stage itself, stage, the object elaborate_stage returns; or an attribute or verb of an object reached from stage, at the path that reaches the object. A reading by a key is written with the name the package gives the key, stage.par[name], and a reading by an attribute, by which a parameter or a setting answers its value under its own name, with that name in angle brackets, stage.par.<name>.
  • what it answers is the first sentence of the docstring the package gives the function, the attribute or the verb. An attribute or a reading by a key with no docstring of its own takes the first sentence of the docstring of the class of its answer, where that class is the package's own and the answer is no frozen copy, the immutable copy a stage holds of an object of DisCoPy, the library the package builds its graphs with; otherwise it takes the sentence of the docstring of the class holding it that names the attribute or writes a key. The row of the stage itself takes the first sentence of the docstring of its class. A constant, such as the method table or a perch word, takes the first sentence of the docstring of its class where the package defines that class, and otherwise that of the comment above the line that assigns it.
  • type is the class of the answer: for a frozen copy, the class of the object it copies, BellmanHypergraph, Builder or Box; otherwise the answer's class, or, where that class's name begins with an underscore, the first class it inherits from whose name does not, such as Mapping for the method table.
  • example is the call, where the path takes an argument or a key, and the answer as the package prints it, on one line: the first line it prints, each run of white space written as one space and a function's memory address left out, cut to its first 75 characters where it runs past 76. The mark … stands for what the cell leaves out, the rest of a cut line or the later lines of an answer that prints several. Where the package refuses the path, the type is a dash and the example names the object that refuses it, with the refusal's class and message.
  • defined in is the module, by its path in the package, and the name of the function, the class, the attribute or the verb that the row describes.

The row of the stage itself and every row of an object reached from it, the rows of §2.4, are printed on the specified version of the stage file applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl, calibrated by applications/cons-port/reference/legacy/syntax/calibration.yaml, methodized by applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.yml and configured by applications/cons-port/reference/legacy/syntax/settings.yaml; the example of calibrate is applied to the symbolic stage, that of methodize to the calibrated version and that of configure to the methodized one. An object has the attributes and verbs of its class, so the rows of one object name what every object of its kind answers, and each kind has its rows at the paths named here: those of a graph stand at stage.initial.backward, stage.builder.bwd and stage.builder.fwd; those of a builder at stage.builder["cntn", "dcsn"], except state_choice_measure(), the forward decision builder's joint measure of state and choice, at stage.builder["dcsn", "cntn"]; those of an operation at stage.builder["cntn", "dcsn"]["pullback"]; those of a line with a box at stage.initial.backward["cntn_to_dcsn"]["value"], the line read from its block by its id; and those of a line marked !doc at stage.initial.backward["policy", "optimality"]. The mapping stage.builder has one row for each pair it reads on cons.bl, and the builders of a perch have their rows at each of the three perches, stage.arvl.builder, stage.dcsn.builder and stage.cntn.builder, since each perch answers or refuses its paths for reasons of its own. A block shares its class with a builder, so only its reading by a key has a row, at stage.initial.backward["cntn_to_dcsn"]. The functions of bellman.stage are printed on cons.bl: in their calls, text is the text of the file, record the record load_stage reads from it, and stage the symbolic stage elaborate_stage(record), not the specified version of §2.4. The functions of bellman.period and bellman.trellis are printed on the trellis file applications/cons-port/declaration/trellis.cons-port.yml, where in a call syntactic is the trellis the file writes, elaborated its elaborated trellis and periods that trellis's periods, or on the durables registry applications/durables/declaration with the recipe spec.two-stages.yml. The functions of a period are printed on periods[0], and inter_period_joins on the file's inter-period mapping, mapping, with periods[1], the period appended later and so earlier in time, and periods[0]. The functions of the view in Model Explorer are printed in bellman.stage on the symbolic stage of cons.bl and in bellman.trellis on elaborated; explore and write_model_explorer each write their two files into a folder model-explorer inside a temporary folder, which is removed afterwards, and answer their paths relative to the temporary folder. A trellis is a plain Python dictionary, whose printed form is Python's own.
