docs.title: 5 Reading a card
docs.text:
These conventions are read across every card and every printed signature, and written on none of them.

  • x ↦ e binds the point, and an operator acting pointwise writes its image as x ↦ ….
  • ↦ maps a point to its image in a Defines line and in a rule; the file's := and its ids stand only in the lines of Source, as the author wrote them.
  • The policy is a free name: there is one operator for each policy, and that policy indexes the pullback, the aggregation or the conditional distribution in which it occurs. A decision builder's card names it under At, never as a parameter or as an input wire.
  • An evaluation is the identity on a function, or on a set of feasible policies, into its declared carrier.
  • Under Operations the pieces stand in the order of application, each after every piece that writes a wire it reads, and ∘ applies its right factor first.
  • A card's Conditions section carries no status word: the words required, assumed and established, and the evidence of a condition the declarations settle, stand on obligations() (§3).
  • A set written {f ∈ … | ∀ a ∈ Xa, x ∈ 𝑐≻(a): …}, as the identification's signature() prints it (A builder §2), is the set of the functions that satisfy the rule at every admitted pair, possibly empty, with no selection made.
  • A push-forward's rule gives the image measure at a set B, μ≻(B) = μ({m_d ∈ Xm | 𝑔≻(m_d, 𝑐(m_d)) ∈ B}), the measure of the points the law of motion at the policy sends into B; and λ⊗P is the extension of a measure λ by the declared distribution P of a shock, whose rule integrates P against λ.
  • A mark at the right margin of a line is the region note on … of a rule, the set on which the rule holds, or the address at which a method is bound; undeclared in a type is a set the file does not declare; and ⇉ marks a correspondence.
  • Method names the numerical method bound within the piece, which is part of what the piece denotes on the version asked; a block, a line and a piece read through stage.declared print none, and their methods answers the methods bound within them.

docs.title: 6 Types and defining expressions
docs.text:
A wire's type is derived from the declarations when it is asked for and stored nowhere. The continuation input of the decision builder goes through seven steps from the file to the printed type:

  1. The file declares V[>] : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu.
  2. The declaration introduces a field, a named quantity at the continuation perch with the declared value set [-inf, inf).
  3. The builders graph has a wire for that input, whose Sort keeps the wire's identity and its field classification.
  4. The wire's mathematical type is derived from the declared sets of its ordered coordinates and its declared value set; where a control is among the coordinates, its feasibility correspondence also restricts the domain of the arguments. Here the type is the set of measurable functions from the savings set Xa, declared ℝ₊, to [-inf, inf).
  5. The query answers a structured carrier expression, which denotes that set of functions.
  6. The set itself is the carrier, and no object of the package is that set.
  7. The printed type, Xa → [−∞, ∞), is the printed form of the carrier expression.

The wire stage.dcsn.builder.bwd.signature().inputs[0] answers the derived type through .mathematical_type, a WireType with two attributes: .sort, the representation, the field classification where there is one, the ordered identities of the coordinates, the domain of the arguments and the result set; and .carrier, the structured carrier expression. The wire's .identity names the continuation input; neither the type nor the carrier identifies that particular input. A wire of an initial diagram is typed by the field it carries, printed {V≻}, and a wire of the forward graph by the finite measures on the states of its perch.

An operation's record answers its typed defining expression, stage.dcsn.builder.bwd["Pullback"].denote().expression, the composition with the stage's law of motion, whose .bindings and .body are expression objects and not fragments of the printed card; denote().kernel.denoted[0] answers the .mathematical_type and the .expression of the law of motion itself. The definitions of a utility or an aggregator answer the same queries where their data determine them, and a component the package cannot resolve names the mathematical data it lacks rather than being assumed real-valued. Denoted.type and Denoted.rule are the printed forms of the carrier and of the defining expression, each computed from the object beside it, mathematical_type and expression, so that the card, the structured answer and the encoding present one object and never two readings of it. A set marked !categories (Symbol conventions §9.3) denotes a second object, its category map, and its card, stage.definitions.denote(identity), holds a second Denoted, whose expression is the set's CategoryCodes record, Definition.categories (The definitions table §2), and whose rule is the map as bellman.typing.category_codes.describe writes it, 0 ↦ newborn, 1 ↦ old (categories household_status), or (categories local to HouseholdStatus) where the marker names no identifier. Every answer of denote() whose definitions include the set holds both objects. A declaration of one real shock by N, LogNormal, Uniform, TruncatedNormal or TypeIExtremeValue likewise denotes a second object, its measure at the written arguments under the symbol P_y (Shock distributions §1); the answers of denote() of the other records that read the declaration list it by its law alone, the measure standing on the declaration's own card, and the cards of the expectations and distribution extensions that read it print the law as written alone; the forward builder's card also names the measure P_y that its extension rule reads, as before.

A printed carrier, a function belonging to the set it denotes and a numerical representation of that function are three different objects. Methodization leaves the carriers unchanged, and a declared carrier says where an object must lie: it proves no measurability, finiteness or feasibility, and no numerical method's correctness. The restricted domains of the defining expressions state those requirements.

A wire that is the output of a joint choice answers two more attributes. Wire.controls names the declared controls of the policy, in the order the block writes them, and is empty on every other wire. Wire.component(name) answers the set-valued type of one of them, the set of functions of the decision state that agree, coordinate by coordinate, with some member of the joint set; it creates no wire, selects no policy, and raises KeyError for a name that is no control of the wire. A wire holds the carrier its query derived and no reference to its stage, which is how a card or an encoding is written away from the version it came from.

On a branching stage the continuation state space is the disjoint union of the branches' state spaces, \(\mathsf X_\succ = \bigsqcup_j \mathsf X_{\succ,j}\), one set for each label, named by the fields its branch writes. A function on it is the tuple \((Q_j)_j\) of functions, one on each branch's set, and a finite measure on it the tuple of measures, \(\operatorname{Meas}(\bigsqcup_j \mathsf X_{\succ,j}) \cong \prod_j \operatorname{Meas}(\mathsf X_{\succ,j})\), writing \(\operatorname{Meas}(\mathsf X)\) for the finite measures on \(\mathsf X\). Each branch value is therefore typed on its own branch's set, V_w[>] of the retirement choice on the set of a_w, and the forward builder writes one measure for each branch.

docs.title: Parameters and settings
docs.text:
Summary

stage.par answers the parameters of a stage and stage.settings the settings bound to it, each a read-only mapping read by the name the file writes, stage.par["ρ"] and stage.settings["n_a"]. A parameter is part of the economic problem; a setting is a numerical choice of the method that computes it. Every listing is printed by the package from applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl, calibrated and configured by applications/cons-port/reference/legacy/syntax/calibration.yaml and settings.yaml, and methodized by applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.yml, whose methods fill the settings table's last three columns: the place at which each setting is read, the method that reads it and, where the setting is a field of that method's grid, the grid's kind.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — The stage: the object stage below; The binding verbs: calibrate and configure, which bind the values these tables read. Used by — Methods and places: the methods that read the settings. See also — API §2.4: every path of the stage object in one table; Methodization: the settings file a method reads.

Parameters are the declared constants of the model, such as the risk aversion ρ, each declared in the stage file on a set and given a value by calibration; change one and the economic problem changes. Settings are the numerical choices of the methods, such as a grid size or a tolerance, given by configuration; none of them is an assertion of the model. The two tables are queries: each reads the one place the stage holds what it answers, and neither keeps a copy.

from bellman.stage import elaborate_stage, load_stage

stage = elaborate_stage(load_stage("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl"))
calibrated = stage.calibrate("applications/cons-port/reference/legacy/syntax/calibration.yaml")
specified = (calibrated.methodize("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.yml")
             .configure("applications/cons-port/reference/legacy/syntax/settings.yaml"))

docs.title: 1 The parameters
docs.text:
stage.par answers one row per declared parameter, with the set it is declared on, its bound value or the word unbound, and the description the file gives. stage.par["ρ"] answers the record of one parameter, keyed by its name as the file declares it, which prints on one line; its value is the number the calibration binds. list() answers the table the mapping prints, and view() the same table as text.

print(stage.par)
print(stage.par["ρ"])
print()
print(calibrated.par)
print(calibrated.par["ρ"])
print(calibrated.par["ρ"].value)

name  set       value    describes
ρ     [1, inf)  unbound
ρ : [1, inf), unbound

name  set       value  describes
ρ     [1, inf)  6.0
ρ = 6.0 : [1, inf)
6.0

The record is read from the parameter's declaration in the definitions table and the value in the version's bindings. The key is the name the file declares, and no other spelling is a key:

try:
    stage.par["rho"]
except KeyError as refusal:
    print(refusal)

"stage 'cons': 'rho' is no parameter of the stage; a parameter is read by the name the file declares, and the parameters are ρ"

docs.title: 2 The settings
docs.text:
stage.settings answers one row for each method that reads a setting, with the setting's name, its configured value, the place it is read at, the method that reads it and, where the setting is a field of that method's grid, the grid's kind; a setting that no method reads has one row with the last three empty. A method that takes a grid names it by the setting grid, whose value is the grid's kind written as a tag, grid: !Cartesian, with the grid's fields beside it (Methodization §3); the kind is no setting, and the column grid gives it on the row of each setting that one of the fields names. Here the representation at the decision builder's Evaluation reads n_m, m_min and m_max as its grid of resources, and the endogenous grid method on the policy builder reads n_a, a_min and a_max as its exogenous grid of savings. One settings file may serve every stage of an application, so a stage can be bound settings that no method bound to it reads, here among others n_k, n_θ_nodes and n_Ψ_nodes, the grid and quadrature sizes of the application's portfolio stage. stage.settings["n_m"] answers the record of one setting, and its value is the configured value.

print(specified.settings)
print(specified.settings["n_m"])
print(specified.settings["n_m"].value)

name           value    read at                  by       grid
grid_spacing   expmult
n_m            8000     cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation  !Linear  !Cartesian
m_min          0.01     cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation  !Linear  !Cartesian
m_max          2000.0   cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation  !Linear  !Cartesian
n_a            800      policy                   !egm     !Cartesian
a_min          1e-10    policy                   !egm     !Cartesian
a_max          100.0    policy                   !egm     !Cartesian
n_k            800
k_min          1e-10
k_max          1000.0
n_θ_nodes      7
n_Ψ_nodes      7
n_joint_nodes  49
n_sim          10000
sim_seed       42
tol_vfi        1e-08
max_iter       1000
n_m = 8000, read at cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation by !Linear for its grid !Cartesian
8000

A setting has no declaration in the definitions table, so the table is read from the settings the version binds and the bound methods that name them. A version that no configuration has bound holds no setting, and a key it does not hold is refused with the reason:

print(len(stage.settings))
try:
    stage.settings["n_a"]
except KeyError as refusal:
    print(refusal)

0
"stage 'cons': 'n_a' is no setting of this version, which binds no settings; configure(stage, source) binds them"

docs.title: 3 One value by its name
docs.text:
Each table also answers one value alone, read by its name as an attribute: calibrated.par.ρ answers the number calibrated.par["ρ"].value holds and specified.settings.n_a the configured value of n_a, except that a parameter or a setting whose name is one of the table's own attributes, such as list, view or values, is read by its key alone.

print(calibrated.par.ρ)
print(specified.settings.n_a)

6.0
800

docs.title: Methods and places
docs.text:
Summary

stage.places() answers the places of a stage at which a methods file may bind a method, and methods, at every level, answers the methods bound within the piece it is asked of, read by the target the method is bound at or by the target as the methods file writes it, stage.methods["policy"]. Choosing a method changes no equation and runs no computation. Every listing is printed by the package from applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl and its methods file methods.yml.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — The stage: the object stage below; The binding verbs: methodize, which binds the methods. Used by — Parameters and settings: the settings the bound methods read. See also — Methods: every method type and the places it may be bound at; Methodization: the methods file; API §2.4: every path of the stage object in one table.

A method names a numerical technique for one piece of a stage, such as the endogenous grid method for the policy, and a handler names the routine that carries it out. The methods file binds each at a target, an address in the stage: a block, a line, an operator of a line or of the whole stage, or a definition. Binding a method records the choice on the version; nothing in the package executes it.

from bellman.stage import elaborate_stage, load_stage

stage = elaborate_stage(load_stage("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl"))
specified = (stage.calibrate("applications/cons-port/reference/legacy/syntax/calibration.yaml")
             .methodize("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.yml")
             .configure("applications/cons-port/reference/legacy/syntax/settings.yaml"))

docs.title: 1 The places
docs.text:
stage.places() answers one row per place at which a method may be bound, its address as a methods file writes it in the first column and its kind in the second: a builder, by the id of its block; a statement, by the line's address <block>.<line>; an operator of one line, <block>.<line>.<operator>, or of every line of the stage that holds it, by the operator's name alone; and a definition, by its name. A line marked !node is a place of the kind node, and the consumption stage has no such line. After the lines of the policy builder and of each backward value builder stand the addresses of the Evaluation that closes it, of the kind operator evaluate, where a representation of what the builder writes is bound: policy.evaluate for the policy function, and for a backward value builder cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value for the value function, with cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.marginal for the derivative of it that a derivative line states, where one stands (Methodization §2). A representation is bound at these addresses and at no builder. The kinds are read from the objects of the stage, whatever method is later bound there.

print(stage.places())

address                         kind
arvl_to_dcsn                    builder
dcsn_to_cntn                    builder
cntn_to_dcsn                    builder
cntn_to_dcsn.value              statement
cntn_to_dcsn.marginal           statement
cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value     operator evaluate
cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.marginal  operator evaluate
dcsn_to_arvl                    builder
dcsn_to_arvl.value              statement
dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.value     operator evaluate
policy                          builder
policy.optimality               statement
policy.optimality.argmax        operator argmax
policy.InvEuler                 statement
policy.InvEuler.D               operator D
policy.grid                     statement
policy.identification           statement
policy.evaluate                 operator evaluate
argmax                          operator argmax
D                               operator D
𝑢                               definition
𝑑𝑢                              definition
Γ                               definition
𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣                           definition

A target that names no place is refused when the methods file is bound, as is an unknown method and a known method at a place it does not admit: a quadrature rule, for instance, belongs to an expectation and not to the policy builder. Methods states the places each method type admits. Choosing a method adds no condition of convergence or of existence, and runs nothing.

docs.title: 2 The methods of a version
docs.text:
specified.methods answers every method the version binds, one line each: the target the method is bound at and the method, or handler only where the entry names a handler and no method. Before methodization it is empty and prints none, as a stage elaborated afresh from the same file shows; the binding verbs bind the stage they are called on, so stage and specified above name one stage.

print(elaborate_stage(load_stage("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl")).methods)
print(specified.methods)

none
policy                    !egm   block ../../methods/cons_egm.bl
cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation   !Linear
arvl_to_dcsn              !deterministic
dcsn_to_cntn              handler only

The methods file methods.yml writes six entries:

from pathlib import Path

print(Path("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.yml").read_text(encoding="utf-8"), end="")

stage: cons

methods:
  - on: policy
    method: !egm
    block: ../../methods/cons_egm.bl
    handler: cons-port:egm
    settings:
      grid: !Cartesian
      orders:
        a: n_a
      bounds:
        a: [a_min, a_max]

  - on: cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value
    method: !Linear
    settings:
      grid: !Cartesian
      orders:
        m_d: n_m
      bounds:
        m_d: [m_min, m_max]
    handler: cons-port:_make_interp

  - on: cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.marginal
    method: !Linear
    settings:
      grid: !Cartesian
      orders:
        m_d: n_m
      bounds:
        m_d: [m_min, m_max]
    handler: cons-port:_make_interp

  - on: dcsn_to_arvl

  - on: arvl_to_dcsn
    method: !deterministic

  - on: dcsn_to_cntn
    handler: cons-port:transition_fwd

The version binds four methods, the four lines specified.methods prints above. A solution method is kept on the builder its entry names: the entry on: policy of !egm, which names the block file the method opens the builder with and its exogenous grid of savings, is kept at policy. A representation is kept at the Evaluation that closes the builder, where the builder's output is represented, and the methods file writes that place (Methodization §2): the two !Linear entries, written at the decision builder's Evaluation for the value, cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value, and for its stated derivative, cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.marginal, are one method kept at cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation. Each entry names the grid of resources on which the representation stores its values by the setting grid, whose value is the grid's kind, the tag !Cartesian, with the grid's order and bounds beside it (Methodization §3). The entry on: dcsn_to_arvl, which names no method, handler or setting, is checked against the places and binds nothing.

The mapping's entries give each target's method and handler, the registered routine that carries the method out. An entry may name a method, a handler or both, and None marks the one it omits:

for name, method in specified.methods.items():
    print(f"{name:<32} {method.tag!r:<16} {method.handler!r}")

policy                           'egm'            'cons-port:egm'
cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation          'Linear'         'cons-port:_make_interp'
arvl_to_dcsn                     'deterministic'  None
dcsn_to_cntn                     None             'cons-port:transition_fwd'

One method is read by the target it is bound at, or by the target as the methods file writes it: specified.methods["policy"] answers the one method bound within the policy block, and specified.methods["cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value"] the representation bound at the decision builder's Evaluation. The answer is the method's record, with its tag, its handler and the settings it names. The record prints the kind of a grid as the methods file writes it, 'grid': '!Cartesian', and its settings hold it as load_methods of bellman.stage.sources holds a tag written alone, {'__yaml_tag__': 'Cartesian', 'value': ''}.

print(repr(specified.methods["policy"]))
print(repr(specified.methods["cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value"]))

Method(tag='egm', handler='cons-port:egm', settings={'bounds': {'a': ('a_min', 'a_max')}, 'grid': '!Cartesian', 'orders': {'a': 'n_a'}}, block='../../methods/cons_egm.bl')
Method(tag='Linear', handler='cons-port:_make_interp', settings={'bounds': {'m_d': ('m_min', 'm_max')}, 'grid': '!Cartesian', 'orders': {'m_d': 'n_m'}}, block=None)

A target within which no method is bound, or within which two different methods are bound, is refused with a KeyError that names the methods bound there.

docs.title: 3 Methods at every level
docs.text:
Every piece answers methods, the methods bound at it or inside it, read from the one store stage.bindings.methods; no piece keeps a copy. A graph answers the methods bound within it, and stage.builder those bound within both builders graphs; a builder answers those bound at it or inside it, and an operation or a line the method bound at it.

print(specified.builder.bwd.methods)
print()
print(specified.dcsn.builder.bwd.methods)
print()
print(specified.dcsn.builder.bwd["evaluation"].methods)

policy                    !egm   block ../../methods/cons_egm.bl
cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation   !Linear

cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation   !Linear

cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation   !Linear

docs.title: The definitions table
docs.text:
Summary

stage.definitions is the read-only table of everything a stage file declares, each name once, and of every line its blocks write, in file order. A record is read by its identity as a key, list() answers the table grouped by kind and denote(identity) the card of one record. Every listing is printed by the package from applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — The stage: the object stage below; Stage tutorial: the declarations as the file writes them. Used by — A piece: the kernels an operation reads from this table. Formal account — Fields, functions and types: the sets and functions a record denotes. See also — API §2.4: every path of the stage object in one table.

The graphs of a stage refer to its definitions by identity, a key of the form <stage>:<kind>:<name>, cons:parameter:ρ, whose middle segment names the kind of the record; a line's record is keyed by the line's address instead, cntn_to_dcsn.value. Two kinds are made by the construction from the blocks: a record of kind g is a law of motion, the map a forward block applies to the state, and a record of kind G is a value aggregator, the pointwise function a backward block applies to the continuation value.

from bellman.stage import elaborate_stage, load_stage

stage = elaborate_stage(load_stage("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl"))

docs.title: 1 The table
docs.text:
stage.definitions is a read-only mapping from each identity to its record, in file order. list() answers the records grouped by kind, each with the set, the map or the relation it denotes, so that the table says what the model is.

print(repr(stage.definitions))
print(stage.definitions.list())

Definitions('cons', 21 records)
BELLMAN-SYM / STAGE cons / DEFINITIONS                          [RECORDS = 21]
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

SETS 2 ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  cons:set:Xm   Xm  = ℝ₊₊
  cons:set:Xa   Xa  = ℝ₊

PARAMETERS 1 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  cons:parameter:ρ   ρ  ∈ [1, ∞)

FUNCTIONS 3 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  cons:function:𝑢       𝑢  : ℝ₊₊ → ℝ,  c ↦ c^(1 − ρ)/(1 − ρ)
                        conditions ¬(1 − ρ = 0)
  cons:function:𝑑𝑢      𝑑𝑢  : ℝ₊₊ → ℝ₊₊,  c ↦ c^(−ρ)
  cons:function:𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣   𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣  : ℝ₊₊ → ℝ₊₊,  x ↦ x^(−1/ρ)

CORRESPONDENCES 1 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  cons:correspondence:Γ   Γ  : ℝ₊₊ ⇉ ℝ₊₊,  x ↦ (0, x]

LAWS OF MOTION 2 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  cons:g:arvl_to_dcsn   𝑔≺  : Xm → Xm,  m ↦ m
  cons:g:dcsn_to_cntn   𝑔≻  : {m_d, c ∈ Xm × ℝ₊₊ | c ∈ Γ(m_d)} → Xa,
                              (m_d, c) ↦ m_d − c

VALUE AGGREGATORS 3 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  cons:G:cntn_to_dcsn   𝐺≻  : {V≻, m_d, c ∈ [−∞, ∞) × Xm × ℝ₊₊ | c ∈ Γ(m_d)}
                                → [−∞, ∞),
                              (V≻, m_d, c) ↦ 𝑢(c) + V≻
                        conditions 𝑉(m_d) ∈ [−∞, ∞)
  cons:G:dcsn_to_arvl   𝐺≺  : [−∞, ∞) × Xm → ℝ,  (V, m) ↦ V
                        conditions 𝑉≺(m) ∈ ℝ
  cons:G:policy         𝐺_InvEuler≻   : ℝ₊₊ × Xa → ℝ₊₊,
                                        (D_{a}𝑉≻, a) ↦ 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}𝑉≻)
                        𝐺_endoggrid≻  : ℝ₊₊ × Xa → Xm,  (c≻, a) ↦ a + c≻
                        conditions 𝑚_d≻(a) ∈ Xm

BLOCK LINES 9 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  arvl_to_dcsn.1          m_d = m
  dcsn_to_cntn.1          a = m_d - c
  cntn_to_dcsn.value      V        = 𝑢(c) + V[>]          :: [id=value]
                          conditions 𝑉(m_d) ∈ [−∞, ∞)
  cntn_to_dcsn.marginal   D_{m_d}V = 𝑑𝑢(c)                :: [id=marginal]
                          conditions 𝑉(m_d) ∈ [−∞, ∞)
  dcsn_to_arvl.value      V[<] = V                        :: [id=value]
                          conditions 𝑉≺(m) ∈ ℝ
  policy.optimality       c      = argmax_{cp : Γ(m_d)}(𝑢(cp) + V[>])
                            :: [id=optimality, !doc]
  policy.InvEuler         c[>]   <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) ⟂ a >= 0
                            :: [id=InvEuler]
  policy.endoggrid        m_d[>] = a + c[>]                :: [id=endoggrid]
                          conditions 𝑚_d≻(a) ∈ Xm
  policy.cons_choice      c      = c[>]                    :: [id=cons_choice]

The answer of list() also reads as a mapping from each kind to the identities of its records:

for kind, identities in stage.definitions.list().items():
    print(f"{kind:<14} {', '.join(identities)}")

function       cons:function:𝑢, cons:function:𝑑𝑢, cons:function:𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣

G              cons:G:cntn_to_dcsn, cons:G:dcsn_to_arvl, cons:G:policy

docs.title: 2 One record
docs.text:
A record is read by its identity as a key and has eight attributes, which are attributes and not fields, a field being an economic quantity of the model: identity; kind, one of set, parameter, distribution, function, function_alias, correspondence, g, G, line and multiplier; coordinates, the record's named coordinates, each with its declared set where the file declares one; equations, which for a law of motion or an aggregator holds the addresses of the block's lines and no copy of their algebra; tags, the entries of a line's annotation; address, where the file writes the record, the block for a law of motion or an aggregator; ordinal, the position of a line among the items of its block's body, counted from 1 with the branches of a branching block counted in turn, which outside a branch is the n of an unnamed line's address <block>.<n> and is the number a refusal names a line by, and None on a record of any other kind; and categories, on a set marked !categories (Symbol conventions §9.2), its category map as one frozen CategoryCodes record of the identifier written after the marker, or None, and the pairs of a code and its category's name in increasing code order, CategoryCodes(identifier='household_status', codes=((0, 'newborn'), (1, 'old'))) for the set HouseholdStatus of that section, and None on every other record.

record = stage.definitions["cons:G:cntn_to_dcsn"]
for attribute in ("identity", "kind", "equations", "tags", "address", "ordinal"):
    print(f"{attribute:<12} {getattr(record, attribute)!r}")
print(f"{'coordinates':<12} {[name for name, _ in record.coordinates]!r}")

identity     'cons:G:cntn_to_dcsn'
kind         'G'
equations    ('cntn_to_dcsn.value',)
tags         ()
address      'cntn_to_dcsn'
ordinal      None
coordinates  ['V', 'c']

docs.title: 3 The card of a record
docs.text:
stage.definitions.denote(identity) answers the card of one record: the function or set it defines, the conditions on its values, the lines of the file it comes from and the records of the declared names it refers to. The card is asked of the table, since a record does not hold the stage it belongs to. The card of a set marked !categories prints the set's category map, the second object the set denotes (A piece §6), on the row under the set, 0 ↦ newborn, 1 ↦ old (categories household_status), and list() prints the same row. The card of a distribution declared by N, LogNormal, Uniform, TruncatedNormal or TypeIExtremeValue prints in the same way the second object the declaration denotes, its measure at the written arguments (Shock distributions §1), on the row under the law: y ~ N(0, 1) is followed by P_y = measure on ℝ given by B ↦ …, and list() prints the same row. The row stands on the declaration's own card alone: the card of another record that reads the declaration lists it by its law.

docs.title: The binding verbs
docs.text:
Summary

stage.calibrate(source), stage.methodize(source) and stage.configure(source) each add one binding to the stage they are called on and return that stage: the values of the parameters, the methods of its pieces, or the settings those methods read. Nothing is copied, a later binding of a target replaces the earlier one, and no verb solves anything. Every listing is printed by the package from applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl, calibrated and configured by applications/cons-port/reference/legacy/syntax/calibration.yaml and settings.yaml, and methodized by applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.yml; the listing of §2 is calibrated instead at the mapping {"ρ": 2.0}.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — The stage: the symbolic stage the verbs bind. Used by — Parameters and settings and Methods and places: the tables that read the bindings. See also — The trellis factory: the same three verbs applied to every stage of a trellis; API §2.4: every path of the stage object in one table.

Each verb takes one source: the path of a YAML file or a mapping of the same content. calibrate binds a value to every declared parameter; methodize binds the methods a methods file names to their targets; configure binds the settings those methods read. The recommended order is calibration, methodization and configuration: the parameter values complete the economic problem before the numerical choices are made, and the settings are read against the methods that name them.

from bellman.stage import elaborate_stage, load_stage

stage = elaborate_stage(load_stage("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl"))

docs.title: 1 The three verbs in order
docs.text:
The short form of a version names what it binds: symbolic, calibrated, methodized and specified are the four stopping points of the recommended order.

print(repr(stage))
backward = stage.initial.backward.graph
calibrated = stage.calibrate("applications/cons-port/reference/legacy/syntax/calibration.yaml")
print(repr(stage))
methodized = stage.methodize("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.yml")
print(repr(stage))
specified = stage.configure("applications/cons-port/reference/legacy/syntax/settings.yaml")
print(repr(stage))

ElaboratedStage('cons', symbolic)
ElaboratedStage('cons', calibrated)
ElaboratedStage('cons', methodized)
ElaboratedStage('cons', specified)

Each verb adds its binding to the stage it is called on and returns that stage, so calibrated, methodized and specified are three names of stage, and nothing is copied. A later binding replaces the earlier one of its target: a second calibration replaces the values of the parameters, a method bound again at a target replaces the method of its kind there, and a setting given again replaces its value. A binding that is refused leaves the stage as it was. The initial diagrams and the declared builders, stage.declared, are those the stage file states, the same objects before and after every binding; a method block that methodize binds changes the operative builders stage.builder and the definitions table stage.definitions, which gains the block's definitions and lines, and nothing else (Methods and places):

print(specified is stage)
print(stage.initial.backward.graph is backward)

True
True

A record may hold the three sources itself, as mappings, and then one call binds them: elaborate_stage(record) binds every source the record supplies in the order above, on the stage it constructs, and copies that stage once, at the end, and a record whose sources are empty, such as the one load_stage returns, gives the symbolic stage (The stage §1). The verbs remain the route for a version already made, such as stage here, and for a binding made after elaboration. A methods file is read into a mapping by load_methods of bellman.stage.sources, which keeps each method's tag:

from bellman.stage.sources import load_calibration, load_methods, load_settings

record = load_stage("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl")
record["calibration"] = load_calibration("applications/cons-port/reference/legacy/syntax/calibration.yaml")
record["methods"] = load_methods("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.yml")
record["settings"] = load_settings("applications/cons-port/reference/legacy/syntax/settings.yaml")
in_one_call = elaborate_stage(record)
print(repr(in_one_call), in_one_call.bindings == specified.bindings)

ElaboratedStage('cons', specified) True

docs.title: 2 Calibration
docs.text:
calibrate requires a value for every declared parameter, in the set the file declares it on; a name the stage does not declare is not bound. A parameter declared on the functions from a finite integer or label set, δ : L_J → ℝ, takes a sequence with one entry per member in the members' order, nested for a product of index sets, or a mapping keyed by those integers or labels. The entries may be real-valued; the integer keys identify the entries and are not their values. The version holds the sequence, and a wrong count, a key the set does not hold or an entry outside the entries' set is refused naming the declaration and the key.

Calibration then decides every condition of the stage that involves parameters and numbers alone: a condition that holds becomes established, with the values as its evidence, and a condition that fails refuses the calibration. So stage.calibrate({"ρ": 1.0}) is refused, since the utility c^(1-ρ)/(1-ρ) divides by 1 - ρ, while at ρ = 2.0 that condition is established, as the listing below shows; a condition that involves a field, a control, a function the file does not declare or an expression calibration cannot evaluate stays as the construction left it, and is never turned into a claim of proof. A source may be a mapping as well as a file:

at_rho_2 = stage.calibrate({"ρ": 2.0})
print(repr(at_rho_2), at_rho_2.par["ρ"])
print(at_rho_2.obligations())

ElaboratedStage('cons', calibrated) ρ = 2.0 : [1, inf)
arithmetic-definedness      ¬(1 − ρ = 0)   [established]
finite-real-arithmetic      The operands of Add at policy.endoggrid must be finite real numbers.
finite-real-arithmetic      The operands of Add at policy.optimality must be finite real numbers.
aggregation-admissibility   V(m_d) ∈ [−∞, ∞)
marginal-reading            The right side of cntn_to_dcsn.marginal equals the derivative of V in m_d under the envelope conditions.
aggregation-admissibility   V≺(m) ∈ ℝ
finite-real-arithmetic      The operands of Add at policy must be finite real numbers.
aggregation-admissibility   m_d≻(a) ∈ Xm
range-compatibility         m_d − c(m_d) ∈ Xa   [established]

docs.title: 3 Methodization and configuration
docs.text:
methodize binds each entry of a methods file at the place its target names: a method must admit the kind of place it is bound at, and an unknown method, a target that names no place and a method at a place it does not admit are each refused. configure requires a value for every setting the bound methods name, and is refused on a version with no methods bound, since a setting is read against the method that names it. Methodization may also precede calibration:

other_order = (stage.methodize("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.yml")
               .configure("applications/cons-port/reference/legacy/syntax/settings.yaml")
               .calibrate("applications/cons-port/reference/legacy/syntax/calibration.yaml"))
print(repr(other_order), other_order.bindings.methods == specified.bindings.methods)

ElaboratedStage('cons', specified) True

No method changes a graph, and nothing in the package executes a method: a method records how a piece is to be computed, and the routine that computes it is supplied outside the package. Methods and places reads the bound methods, and Parameters and settings the bound values.

docs.title: The view in Model Explorer
docs.text:
Summary

explore(stage) opens the four graphs of a stage version in Model Explorer, Google's viewer of large graphs, which runs in the browser: its two initial diagrams, the fields of the stage file in the boxes of their perches, related by its blocks, and its two builders graphs. In a builders graph each builder is a box that opens to its sub-builders and its primitive operators, each operator a box that names its kind above its symbol, every wire is an edge whose two ends hold its perch and its type, and a selected operation shows the rows of its card, its kernel and the method bound to it, each on its own line. The package writes the view as two files and serves the graph file to the viewer; a trellis is viewed in the same way, with a box for each period and for each stage occurrence inside it, a stage occurrence being one use of a stage file in a period (The Bellman factory §1), and the fill of a box names its level, from a period to a sub-builder. The view writes no mathematics of its own: an operator's symbol is the one the drawing prints, with each law of motion named as the operator's card names it and without the arguments of a law or an aggregator written out at a policy, (·, 𝑐) and (·, ·, 𝑐); every port's label is one the drawing prints; and the drawing that diagram() answers remains the figure of a page or a lesson. The examples are from applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl where no other file is named.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — The builders graphs: the two graphs and their grains, which the view draws as boxes inside boxes; A builder: the operations of a builder and their cards, which the side panel shows row by row. See also — Methods and places: the methods whose tags the boxes of §4.2 carry; The trellis factory: the trellises that §5 views.

Key terminology Term What it names Model Explorer Google's viewer of large graphs, the Python package ai-edge-model-explorer: a server on the reader's machine and a page in the browser. Layer A box of the view that is drawn closed and opens with a click to show what it holds: a builder or a sub-builder, and in a trellis a period or a stage occurrence. Node A box of the view that opens to nothing: a primitive operator, or one of the two nodes that hold a graph's own inputs and outputs. Port One input or one output of a node, the end of one wire. Side panel The pane at the right of the page, which lists the attributes of the node or the layer selected and the ports of a node. Overlay A set of lines in one color that the reader turns on and off: each line joins the two nodes of an edge of the graph (§4.1).

docs.title: 1 What a user writes
docs.text:
The view is written by two functions that stand in bellman.stage and in bellman.trellis, explore and write_model_explorer, defined in the module bellman.factory.model_explorer of the Bellman factory, and by no verb of the stage:

from bellman.stage import elaborate_stage, explore, load_stage, write_model_explorer

stage = elaborate_stage(load_stage("applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl"))
paths, address = explore(stage)

explore(stage) writes the two files of §2 into the folder model-explorer/ beside the stage file, starts the viewer's server unless a server already answers at port 8080, and opens the page in the default browser with the layers of the builders open; port 8080 is a network port of the machine, not a port of a node. It prints the address and a reminder of the one setting of §6, and answers the paths of the two files and the address. The call that starts the server, the first explore of a notebook's kernel or of a script where no other process serves the port, also prints the viewer's own start-up lines, among them a second address and "Press Ctrl+C to stop.", which the reader may ignore. folder= names another folder for the files and port= another port; open_browser=False writes the files alone and answers the address None. explore(trellis) does the same for a trellis, the dictionary that elaborate_trellis returns, opens the layers of its periods and locates the page on the first period after the terminal one (§5).

write_model_explorer(stage, folder) writes the two files alone and answers their paths, the graph file first. serve, which answers the address of a page on the viewer's server that shows a graph file and opens no browser, is imported from the module:

from bellman.factory.model_explorer import serve

graph, overlays = write_model_explorer(stage, "model-explorer")
address = serve(graph, port=8080, layers=("cntn_to_dcsn", "policy"))

The page opens on the graph that graph_id= names, one of the four of §3.1, or, where none is named, on the backward builders graph backward, and on the file's first graph where it holds none, with the layers that layers names open, and fitted to the whole graph unless located= names a layer, located="periods[1]", which the page then selects and fits to its window. serve starts a server only where none answers on the port. A server that another Python process started, the kernel of another notebook for instance, serves the page as well, since the address names the graph file by its path on the machine; a port at which something other than the viewer answers is refused in one sentence. The server runs in a background thread of the process that started it and stops when that process ends. One server serves any number of pages at once, and each page stays independent of the others.

to_model_explorer and perch_overlays, functions of bellman.factory.model_explorer, answer for a stage or a trellis the same graphs and overlays as the viewer's own Python objects, without writing a file.

The viewer is installed with the package's extra explore, from the root of the repository:

pip install -e "packages/bellman[explore]"

Without it, a function of the module that needs the viewer raises an ImportError whose one sentence names the extra and the commands that install it.

docs.title: 2 The two files
docs.text:
The two files are named by the view's label: the stage's name, followed by a word for each binding the version holds, calibrated, methodized and configured, with a hyphen in place of each space; a trellis is labeled trellis. The symbolic version of cons writes two files:

  • cons.graph.json, the four graphs of §3.1, backward initial diagram, forward initial diagram, backward and forward, which the viewer opens as a model file;
  • cons.edge-overlays.json, the three perch overlays of §4.1, each holding every edge of the four graphs whose wire stands at its perch, which a reader loads through the viewer's panel of edge overlays.

cons methodized alone writes cons-methodized.graph.json and cons-methodized.edge-overlays.json, and the specified version, calibrated, methodized and configured, writes cons-calibrated-methodized-configured.graph.json and the file of overlays beside it. The viewer shows the label with its spaces, cons methodized, at the top of the page. The files are JSON in ASCII alone: every other character is written as its JSON escape, so that 𝑉≻ stands in a file as \ud835\udc49\u227b, which the viewer reads back as 𝑉≻. The viewer's server reads a file in the system's default encoding, which on some machines is not UTF-8, and a file in ASCII is read alike under any code page.

docs.title: 3.1 The graphs and their layers
docs.text:
The viewer shows one graph at a time, chosen at the top of the page, where four are listed: backward initial diagram and forward initial diagram, the two initial diagrams, the fields of the stage file at their perches, related by the blocks that read and write them; then backward, the builders a solution applies, on value functions, the policy builder among them, and forward, the builders a simulation applies, on measures (The builders graphs §3). explore(stage) opens the page on backward. The viewer lays out each graph itself, a builders graph from top to bottom and an initial diagram from left to right.

In an initial diagram the fields are the nodes and the blocks relate them, as the field diagram of the calculus is drawn (Fields, functions and types §2). Each perch that holds a field of the diagram is a layer named by the perch's word, arvl, dcsn or cntn, and the layers stand in the order the direction reads the perches, so that the forward diagram reads arrival, decision, continuation from left to right and the backward one continuation, decision, arrival. Each field is a node inside the layer of its perch, named by the field's identity, cons:dcsn:m_d, labeled as the drawing labels the field, V≻, m_d, a≻, and filled white; the fields of one perch stand one under another. A shock, which belongs to no perch, stands outside the layers. Each block is a node outside the layers, named and labeled by its id and filled white, with an edge from each field it reads and an edge into each field it writes, so that it stands between the perches it joins; the diagram opens no further layer, since a block's lines stand in its attributes (§3.3). The diagram has no nodes Inputs and Outputs: a field no block writes is one the diagram takes, and a field no block reads one it gives. The backward initial diagram of cons holds V≻ in the layer cntn, V and c in dcsn and V≺ in arvl, related by the three blocks cntn_to_dcsn, dcsn_to_arvl and policy, and the forward one m≺, m_d and a≻, one in each layer, related by arvl_to_dcsn and dcsn_to_cntn.

Each builder is a layer named by the id of its block: cntn_to_dcsn, dcsn_to_arvl and policy in the backward graph of cons. A builder's layer opens to its sub-builders, each a layer named by its builder and its key, such as cntn_to_dcsn/risk_ce in the savings stage applications/smooth-ambiguity-savings/declaration/stages/sa_savings/sa_savings.bl, and to its primitive operators, the finest boxes the construction makes (The builders graphs §4). These are the three grains a reader reaches from the stage, and the view shows no other. An operator formed by a line that is no sub-builder, such as the aggregation of the policy builder's candidate line, stands directly in its builder's layer.

Each primitive operator is a node. Its id is its whole name, cntn_to_dcsn:Aggregation, the key that reads it at the primitive grain, and its label is two lines. The first is the kind of its operator, as the attribute kind writes it (§3.3), followed, where the operator is stated at a policy (Operations §3), by at and the policies it is stated at, separated by commas: Pullback at 𝑐 in cons, and Pullback at 𝑐, ℎ_choice in the durables model's adjuster stage applications/durables/declaration/stages/adjuster_cons/adjuster_cons.bl, whose policy chooses consumption and housing together. The second is the symbol the drawing shows for the operator, without the arguments of a law or an aggregator written out at a policy, the (·, 𝑐) of the drawing's 𝑉≻ ∘ 𝑔(·, 𝑐) and the (·, ·, 𝑐) of its 𝐺(·, ·, 𝑐), which the operator's rules state in full (§3.3). The pullback of the decision builder is labeled Pullback at 𝑐 over 𝑉≻ ∘ 𝑔≻ and its aggregation Aggregation at 𝑐 over 𝐺; the candidate line and the identification of the policy builder are labeled Aggregation over 𝐺 · InvEuler and Pullback over 𝑐 ∘ 𝑚_d≻; and an evaluation names the outputs it produces, as the drawing does, so that the evaluation of the decision builder is labeled Evaluation over 𝑉(m_d). An evaluation with three or more outputs names the first two and counts the others, ending its label with and 1 more where it has three, and its rule rows and its output ports name them all (§3.2 and §3.3). A law of motion is named as the operator's card names it, so that the operators that read one law name it alike: the pullback of cntn_to_dcsn and the push-forward of dcsn_to_cntn both name 𝑔≻, the law from the decision perch to the continuation perch, 𝑉≻ ∘ 𝑔≻ and 𝑔≻∗μ, and the pullback of dcsn_to_arvl and the push-forward of arvl_to_dcsn both name 𝑔≺, the law from the arrival perch to the decision perch, 𝑉 ∘ 𝑔≺ and 𝑔≺∗μ, where the drawing that diagram() answers writes the letter 𝑔 for both laws. Where a method is bound within the operator, the second line ends with its tag (§4.2). Inputs, Outputs and the fields and blocks of an initial diagram, which apply no operator, have labels of one line.

The view takes its colors from the project's site, and they tell apart the levels a reader opens and what each builder gives: navy for borders and labels, white and three pale blues for the fills, ultramarine for a builder's outputs, and orange for a refusal (§3.5). A node is white with a navy border and a navy label, and its border turns ultramarine under the pointer. The node of an operator that writes a wire read outside its builder's layer, by another builder, by Outputs or, in a trellis, by a join (§5), has an ultramarine border instead, which turns navy under the pointer, so that what each builder gives is seen at a glance: in the view of cons, the three evaluations of the backward graph and the two push-forwards of the forward graph. Each layer has a navy border and a navy label, and its fill names its level, one shade darker at each level a reader opens: in a trellis a period is white and a stage occurrence stands on the lightest of the three blues (§5), a builder stands on the second and a sub-builder on the third, the darkest. The perch layers of an initial diagram stand on the lightest blue, the shade of the stage they divide. The viewer draws no dashed border, by which the drawing marks an evaluation and a policy insertion; the first line of a label names the kind of every operator, and a kind has no color. The drawing that diagram() answers keeps its own colors.

Two further nodes, Inputs and Outputs, white with a navy border, stand in no layer and hold the graph's own inputs and outputs. The backward graph of cons takes the continuation value, 𝑉≻(a), from Inputs, and gives the arrival value and the policy, 𝑉≺(m) and 𝑐(m_d), to Outputs.

docs.title: 3.2 Wires and ports
docs.text:
Every wire of a builders graph is an edge from the node that writes it to each node that reads it; in an initial diagram a field is a node (§3.1), and an edge joins it to each block that writes or reads it. The ports of a node stand in the order of the wires its operator reads and writes, and the id of a port is the identity of its wire, such as cons:function:cntn:V, the same at both ends of an edge. The two ends of a wire hold the same attributes, and an attribute that would hold nothing is not written:

  • label, the wire's label as the drawing prints it, such as 𝑉≻(a) or μ≺;
  • perch, the perch the wire stands at, arvl, dcsn or cntn; a wire at no perch, such as the result of an aggregation, has none;
  • role, the role of the object the wire carries, such as value, control, state or measure;
  • type, the wire's type as a builder's signature() prints it, such as Xm → [−∞, ∞) or finite measure on Xm; on a field wire of an initial diagram, set instead, the field's declared set as the fields table prints it, [-inf, inf), where the header declares one.

The side panel lists the ports of a selected node, each with these attributes, and under an input also namespace, which the viewer adds. An input is headed by the wire's label followed, in parentheses, by the label of the node that writes the wire, whose two lines the panel prints on one: on cntn_to_dcsn:Aggregation, 𝑉≻(𝑔(m_d, 𝑐(m_d))) (Pullback at 𝑐 𝑉≻ ∘ 𝑔≻). An output is headed by the label of the node that reads it, printed in the same way, or by output where several nodes read it, and its attribute label names the wire: the one output of Inputs is read by Pullback at 𝑐 𝑉≻ ∘ 𝑔≻ and by Aggregation 𝐺 · InvEuler, whose line reads the derivative term D_{a}V[>], so it is headed output and lists label 𝑉≻(a).

A parameter and the policy a builder is stated at are no wires: they stand in the rows of an operation's card, as the stage holds them, and each parameter stands with its declared set in the attributes of the layer of every builder whose operations read it (§3.3).

The edges that cross the border of a layer are the wires its operators read and write. A wire of a builder's signature that none of its operators reads is therefore no edge of its layer, and the whole signature stands in the attributes of the layer (§3.3).

docs.title: 3.3 The side panel
docs.text:
Selecting a primitive operator lists its attributes in the side panel, each on one line and in this order: the kind of the operator, the rules of the Rule section of its card, one attribute to a rule and numbered only where there are several, the lines of its kernel, the method bound within it where one is (§4.2), and the numbers of the lines of the stage file it realizes (A builder §1). A value wider than the panel is cut with an ellipsis, and a control at the end of its row expands it to the whole value. A rule that the card breaks over several lines stands on one line, and the region a rule holds on, which the card sets at the right margin or on a line of its own, follows the rule after two spaces, as one attribute: 𝑐(𝑚_d≻(a)) = 𝑐≻(a) on 𝑚_d≻(Xa) on policy.cons_choice:Pullback. On cntn_to_dcsn:Aggregation of cons:

Attribute What it holds On cntn_to_dcsn:Aggregation kind the kind of the operator (Operations) Aggregation rule, or rule 1, rule 2, … the rules of the card's Rule section rule: 𝑉(m_d) = 𝑢(𝑐(m_d)) + 𝑉≻(𝑔≻(m_d, 𝑐(m_d))) kernel, or kernel 1, kernel 2, … the lines its kernel() prints (A piece §2) kernel 1: 𝐺 of cntn_to_dcsn: 𝐺(V≻, m_d, c) = 𝑢(c) + V≻kernel 2: outputs (V); unused m_d; V reads V≻, c lines the stage file and the numbers of the lines the card's Source section quotes, a run of consecutive lines by its first and its last, house_choice.bl 18–19, 22; the address the operator is born at is the first segment of its id, and the text of the lines is not repeated, since the rules state it cons.bl 22

An evaluation, whose kernel is the identity, lists under rule only the rows that type its outputs, 𝑉 : Xm → [−∞, ∞) on cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation, and none of the rules of the operation before it, which that operation lists. The stated derivative of the value, D_{m_d}𝑉(m_d) = 𝑑𝑢(𝑐(m_d)), stands at cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation with its source line cntn_to_dcsn.marginal and the obligation marginal-reading, beside the method bound there, and adds no edge. An operation that quotes no line of the stage file, such as the evaluation of dcsn_to_arvl, has no lines. The rows of the card's Where section, the local abbreviations its rules write, stand on the layer of the operation's builder, and those of its Conditions are not shown. Where a method is bound within the operator, the panel also lists method, handler, option and setting, the last two numbered in the same way (§4.2).

Selecting a layer lists inputs and outputs, the two sides of its builder's signature as signature() prints them, each on one line. On policy they are 𝑉≻ : Xa → [−∞, ∞) and 𝑐(m_d) : 𝒫({c ∈ (Xm → ℝ₊₊) | c(m_d) ∈ Γ(m_d)}). The layer of a builder, and not of a sub-builder, also lists what the builder's operations share, each on one line and numbered only where there are several. On the layer policy of cons:

Attribute What it holds On policy where, or where 1, where 2, … the rows of the Where section of the builder's card, the local abbreviations the rules of its operations write, each once, such as the law of motion at a branch in applications/housing-frictions/declaration/stages/house_choice/house_choice.bl, 𝑔_keep≻ : ℝ₊₊ × ℝ₊₊ → ℝ₊₊ × ℝ₊₊, 𝑔_keep≻(m_f, m_h) = 𝑔≻(m_f, m_h, keep) none feasible set, or feasible set 1, … on the layer of the policy builder, the definition of each feasible set its policy names, as the stage's definitions hold it Γ(x : ℝ₊₊) := (0, x] parameter, or parameter 1, … each parameter the builder's operations read, directly or through a function such as 𝑢, in the order the file declares them, as stage.par prints it: its declared set, and on a calibrated version its value (Parameters and settings §1) ρ : [1, inf), unbound; on the calibrated cons, ρ = 6.0 : [1, inf) setting, or setting 1, … every setting the version binds, as stage.settings prints it, whether or not a method names it (Parameters and settings §2) none; on the configured cons, seventeen, from grid_spacing = 'expmult' to max_iter = 1000

The settings are the version's, so every builder's layer of a configured version lists all of them. A sub-builder's layer lists its signature alone. Selecting Inputs or Outputs of a builders graph lists the graph's own signature as signature() prints it, under inputs or outputs, the wires as one object, which on the Inputs of the backward graph of cons is the one wire 𝑉≻ : Xa → [−∞, ∞); their ports give the wires one by one. An initial diagram has neither node and lists its signature on no layer: the fields it takes and gives are the nodes no block writes and no block reads (§3.1), and the signature's line for a field, V≻ : {V≻}, restates the field's label.

Selecting a block of an initial diagram lists kind, which is block; header, the block's header as the file writes it after the id; statement, or statement 1, statement 2, …, each line of the block as the card's Source section quotes it, with its line number; and lines, the file and the numbers of the header's line and the quoted lines. On cntn_to_dcsn of cons the header is (V[>] : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu, c) : !cntn -> (V : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu) : !dcsn, the statements 22 V = 𝑢(c) + V[>] :: [id=value] and 23 D_{m_d}V = 𝑑𝑢(c) :: [id=marginal], and the lines cons.bl 21–23. A block carries no method; the method bound within a line stands on the operator the line forms, in the builders graph.

Selecting a field of an initial diagram lists kind, which is field; perch, the perch the field belongs to, or, for a shock, which belongs to none, edge, the pair of perches of the transition that draws it as the fields table prints it, ∼→≻; role, where the field has one; set, its declared set as the fields table prints it, where a header declares one; and lines, the file and the line of the header that first lists the field, the order in which the fields table lists them (The stage §5). On V≻ of cons the rows are field, cntn, value, [-inf, inf) and cons.bl 21; on c, which the header of the forward block dcsn_to_cntn lists at line 17, among the inputs the block is read at, before the policy writes it at line 30, lines is cons.bl 17. The ports of a field's node carry its label, perch, role and set, as every port does (§3.2).

docs.title: 3.4 The search box
docs.text: The search box at the top left of the page takes a regular expression and finds every node and layer whose label, or one of whose attributes, matches it; an attribute is read as key=value, and the id of a node counts among its attributes. kind=Aggregation finds the aggregations, and method=!egm every operator and every layer that lists !egm as its method. Expressions separated by spaces must all match.

docs.title: 3.5 A refused graph
docs.text: Where the construction refused a direction, its graph is one node with an orange border, forward:refused or backward:refused, labeled with the direction and the rule the refusal names, with the refusal's whole text in its attribute refusal; the other graph is drawn as usual, and an initial diagram the construction refused is one node in the same way, backward initial diagram:refused. The forward graph of the retiree stage applications/cagetti-denardi-2006/declaration/stages/retiree_death/retiree_death.bl is the one node forward builders graph refused (not-constructed), since the distribution of its shock y_n is written with a family whose set of results is not declared.

docs.title: 4.1 The perches
docs.text: The three perch overlays, arrival, decision and continuation, stand in the second file of §2, cons.edge-overlays.json, and the view opens without them. The viewer draws an overlay edge as a straight line from the border of one node to the border of the other, not along the edge of the graph, and neither an overlay nor its edges has a setting that makes it follow that edge; the perch of every wire stands on its ports (§3.2). A reader who wants the overlays opens the panel of edge overlays from the toolbar above the graph and loads the file with its button Upload. Each overlay is drawn in the color the project's site gives its perch, navy for arrival, a dark orange for decision and ultramarine for continuation, while a node it touches is selected, and paints every edge whose wire stands at its perch, with no label. The viewer also outlines the nodes a selected node reads from in green and those it writes to in orange, with the edges between them in the same colors; these colors are the viewer's own, which the two files do not set, and an edge they draw carries no label. Bellman Workbench, the editor that draws the same graph beside the stage file, marks the selected box and the wires that enter or leave it in a bright blue and outlines no other box, and its legend lists the color of each perch while its overlays are on (Bellman Workbench §2).

docs.title: 4.2 The methods
docs.text:
A method bound within a primitive operator is shown on the operator's node by one mark: the second line of its label ends with · and the method's tag, written with its ! as the methods file writes it. On cons methodized by applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/methods.yml, cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation is labeled Evaluation over 𝑉(m_d) · !Linear and policy:Evaluation Evaluation over 𝑐(m_d) · !egm, the method of the entry on: policy, which is kept on the policy builder (Methods and places §2), being marked on the Evaluation that closes that builder, and no other node carries a tag. The ! tells a tag apart from the id of a statement, which a symbol may write after the same ·, 𝐺 · InvEuler. No color stands for a method: the method is named by its tag, by which the search box finds it, method=!egm (§3.4), and the operation it realizes is stated in Method types. A version within which no method is bound, such as the symbolic cons, shows no mark.

The side panel of such a node lists the method: method, its tag; handler, the routine the methods file names for it (handler); option, the rows of the card's Options section; and, on a configured version, setting, each setting those options name, as the version's settings print it (Parameters and settings §2); the options and the settings are numbered where there are several, option 1, option 2. On the specified cons, calibrated by applications/cons-port/reference/legacy/syntax/calibration.yaml, methodized as above and configured by applications/cons-port/reference/legacy/syntax/settings.yaml, cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation lists, among its attributes, method !Linear, handler cons-port:_make_interp, option 1 grid = !Cartesian, the kind of its grid, option 2 orders = {'m_d': 8000} and setting 1 n_m = 8000, read at cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation by !Linear for its grid !Cartesian. A method bound at a builder, and at none of its operators, stands in the attributes of the builder's layer, and no label carries its tag: in the forward graph of the methodized cons, the layer arvl_to_dcsn lists method !deterministic. Such a method lists no setting of its own, since the builder's layer lists every setting of a configured version (§3.3). The legend of Bellman Workbench lists each method bound in the graph it shows with its place, an operator's id or a layer's name, !egm policy:Evaluation in the backward graph and !deterministic arvl_to_dcsn in the forward graph (Bellman Workbench §2).

docs.title: 5 A trellis
docs.text:
explore(trellis) and write_model_explorer(trellis, folder) take the dictionary that elaborate_trellis returns, or a version the trellis verbs bound (The trellis factory §§3 and 4), and write one collection of two graphs, the backward and the forward trellis and no initial diagram, labeled trellis: the files are trellis.graph.json and trellis.edge-overlays.json, which explore(trellis) writes into model-explorer/ in the working directory unless folder= names another. Where the construction refused one direction of a stage occurrence, the trellis's graph of that direction is one node labeled as in §3.5, whose attribute refusal opens with the occurrence's address. explore(trellis) opens the backward graph with its periods open and located on periods[1], the first period after the terminal one: the page selects that period's layer, lists its attributes, and fits the window to it, and the other periods stand beside it, a scroll away. A trellis of one period is fitted to the window whole.

Each period is a layer periods[h], white with a navy border, h being its index in the dictionary and periods[0] the terminal period; its attribute age shows the age where the trellis's registry gives last_age, as the drawing of diagram_trellis writes it, and the index stands in the layer's name and in no attribute. Each stage occurrence is a layer inside its period, named by its key, periods[0]/cons, whose attribute stage shows the stage's name and bindings; it holds that occurrence's builders exactly as the view of the stage does. Every node id and port id is the id in the stage's own view, prefixed by its occurrence, periods[0]/cons/cntn_to_dcsn:Aggregation, so that two occurrences of one stage are told apart. The viewer lays out the periods side by side and the stages of a period next to one another, each graph in the direction its wires pass, and the builders of an occurrence from top to bottom. In the forward graph economic time runs from left to right, with the terminal period at the right and the stages of a period in their forward order, as in the drawing of diagram_trellis; the backward graph, laid out in the direction its value functions pass, from the terminal period back, stands the other way round.

A join, which connects a continuation field of one stage occurrence to an arrival field of another (The Bellman factory §7), is drawn at the grain of the wires, from the node that writes a wire of one occurrence to each node that reads the joined wire of the other: forward, from the continuation measure of one occurrence to the arrival measure of the next; backward, from the arrival value of the later occurrence to the continuation value of the earlier one. The reading port holds the attribute join, the text the drawing writes on the wire: a for a field joined by its name, m_next → m where a connector renames it, and inter_connectors[0] a → k for a join between periods; in the backward graph it also holds paired by, the rule that paired the wire with the one that supplies it, one wire per role or equal name, the two rules below in their order, so that a pairing by equal names, the view's own convention, is never silent. A joined wire that no operator of its occurrence reads is a port of a node Inputs inside the occurrence's layer, so that its join is drawn. The policy of each occurrence, which no join reads, ends at a node Outputs inside the occurrence's layer, periods[0]/cons/GraphOutputs, so that no edge of a policy crosses the periods.

A trellis has no Inputs and no Outputs of its own. A wire that no join supplies enters the graph at a boundary node, and a wire that no join reads leaves it at one: a node at the graph's root, outside every layer, that holds the wire's one port and is joined by the wire's edge to the operator that reads or writes it. Its attribute kind names its role, start where the wire enters and end where it leaves, and its label, which its attribute label repeats, is a word for that role followed by the wire's own label: in the forward graph, starting data where the arrival measure of the first occurrence in time enters and terminal where the measure of the last one leaves; in the backward graph, terminal condition where the terminal value enters and result where the value of the first stage in time leaves. Its id is its kind followed by the id of the wire's port. In the trellis applications/cons-port/declaration/trellis.port-cons.yml, six periods of three stages, the forward graph begins at starting data μ≺, the node start:periods[5]/port/port:measure:arvl, and ends at terminal μ≻; the backward graph takes the continuation value of periods[0]/disc, the last stage of the terminal period, at terminal condition 𝑉≻(a), and gives the arrival value of periods[5]/port, the first stage in time, at result 𝑉≺(k).

Each edge of a join carries, under its attribute route, the record of the route that establishes it: the connection from one branch of the source occurrence into the destination occurrence, as connection_report answers it (The trellis factory §9). The record holds branch, the label of the source's branch, or null for a stage without branches; source and destination, the addresses of the two occurrences, periods[5]/port; source_fields and destination_fields, the continuation fields of the source and the arrival fields of the destination, in the route's order; pairs, one entry for each field joined, in the route's order, with source_field, destination_field, origin, authored for a pair a connector writes and inferred for one joined by equal names, and address, the entry that writes an authored pair, periods[5].connectors[0], or the period of an inferred one; status, certified or uncertified; and law, the joint measure the source's branch writes, port:measure:cntn. Every value is read from the route and none is computed by the view, so that the edge and the report agree; an edge that no route establishes, inside an occurrence or at a boundary node, has no attributes. Unlike the attributes of a node, those of an edge are not shown by the viewer's page, which reads no attribute of an edge; Bellman Workbench reads them.

The backward graph pairs the value wires a join carries by what the stage files state and nothing else. Where one value wire stands on each side of a join, the two are paired whatever their names; where several stand on either side, the wires of the same name are paired. Where a wire is then left with no counterpart, or with two, the backward graph is refused: it is one node whose attribute refusal counts the joins that leave a wire unpaired and states these two rules, and whose attributes join 1, join 2, … name each such join on a row of its own. The forward graph is drawn. The backward graphs of the pension, durables and housing models are not refused on this ground, since their joins carry value wires alone, which these two rules pair. A reader loads these three trellises through their registries and recipes, load_recipe("applications/pension-retirement/declaration", "spec.yml"), load_recipe("applications/durables/declaration", "spec.yml") and load_recipe("applications/housing-frictions/declaration", "spec.yml") (Recipe functions §2), and gives explore the dictionary that elaborate_trellis returns for each. load_trellis refuses their files trellis.yml under the rule trellis-file-shape, since the periods of those files name each stage by its key alone and the recipe supplies its source and mappings (The trellis factory §1).

Building the view of a trellis takes a few seconds for the eighteen stage occurrences of trellis.port-cons.yml and tens of seconds for a hundred occurrences, since the graphs of each occurrence are built when first asked for.

A view of part of a trellis is asked for by the periods and the stage keys it holds, to_model_explorer(trellis, periods=range(0, 2), stages=["cons"]), the periods selected as diagram_trellis selects them: the view holds the occurrences of those periods whose keys are given, every period or every key where one of the two is not given, and the joins between them as above. A join that leaves the occurrences held is no edge between them: the wire it carries enters or leaves the graph at a boundary node of kind outside, one for each occurrence outside the view that such joins reach, labeled with that occurrence's address, which its attribute target repeats, periods[1]/disc, and named by its kind, the id of the wire's port and that address, outside:periods[1]/cons/cons:measure:cntn:periods[1]/disc; the wire's port names the join in join and those occurrences in outside, so that nothing is lost without a mark. An index the trellis does not hold, a key no period selected holds and a selection of no occurrence are refused under trellis-file-shape, each in one sentence.

unpaired_joins(trellis) answers the rows join 1, join 2, … of the refusing backward node as records, one UnpairedJoin for each join that leaves a wire unpaired, in the order of the rows: its label, the addresses of the two occurrences, the address in the trellis of the connector that makes it, inter_connectors[0] or periods[0].connectors[0], empty for a join by equal names, and each wire it leaves unpaired as an UnpairedWire, with its occurrence, its name as the stage file writes it, the stage file and the line of the header that first lists it. It takes periods and stages as to_model_explorer does, and answers no join where the graph is drawn.

docs.title: 6 The viewer's settings
docs.text:
The viewer's default text renderer cannot draw the mathematical letters of the labels on the canvas, and draws other characters in their place. The setting "Use SVG text renderer", among the advanced settings behind the gear icon at the top right of the page, draws every label exactly. The side panel draws every attribute exactly with either renderer. The browser keeps the setting in its local storage for the page's host and port, which is why every view is served from one port, 8080 unless port= names another: the setting is turned on once for that port, and a view served from another port needs it turned on again.

The view is an interactive reading of the stage and changes nothing in it. The drawing that diagram() answers (A builder §1) remains the recorded figure of a page and of a lesson, since a view opens only while a Python process serves it.

docs.title: Equation parsing rules
docs.text:
Summary

A .bl file contains declarations, function definitions, shock laws, and typed equation blocks. This reference explains their written forms and distinguishes parsing from the checks needed to construct a mathematical stage. Timing and information restrictions belong to Perch tagging rules.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Stages: complete contexts for introductory fragments; Field equations: a consumption stage. Formal account — Appendix C: the interpretation of equations; Appendix D: nodes and collection selection. See also — Symbol conventions: notation; Operations: the kinds of the operations a builder holds, Argmax among them.

docs.title: 1 Statements and blocks
docs.text:
Equations are written directly inside braces, as in this complete transition fragment:

@stage: arithmetic

[id=transform, (a : ℝ) : !dcsn -> (y : ℝ, q : ℝ) : !cntn] {
    y = 2 + a    :: [id=shift]
    q = 4*y      :: [id=scale]
}

Each equation has a left and right expression separated by =. The optional :: [...] annotation gives an identifier, a documentation string, or a supported mark. A block's header supplies its identifier and the typed sides of its inputs and outputs. Newlines separate statements; parentheses group subexpressions. Use the braced block itself, without YAML quotes or a YAML | indicator.

Abstract grammar: Equation and annotation

This projection uses ASDL constructor notation. It shows the equation alternative and the annotation structure; other statement alternatives are omitted rather than redefined.

stmt = Equation(expr lhs, expr rhs)
annotation = Annotation(entry* entries)
entry = Tag(string tag)
      | KeyValue(identifier key, scalar value)
      | Typer(typer t)

Keys. lhs and rhs are expressions; entries preserves annotation order; tag is text; key and value record a named scalar; t is type material. expr, scalar, and typer are defined by the full grammar. * permits a list; it does not establish uniqueness or scope.

Head. = separates equation expressions; :: introduces the statement annotation.

Denotes. An equation imposes equality in its declared context. Its explicit or implicit reading depends on its dependencies and unknowns, as Field equations explains.

Status. Construction checks declarations, operator scope, domain agreement, and output definitions. A parsed equation is not evidence that those checks or its mathematical assumptions hold.

For example, substituting an undeclared name missing for a still has the grammatical shape of an equation.
