docs.title: Appendix D — Nodes and field indexing
docs.text:
Summary

A statement's equations determine its mathematical meaning; !node marks a statement as an authored node, a computation that can be named and addressed separately. Perch marks identify fields in their information context, while other bracket selections require a declared collection or family. This appendix explains how these distinctions preserve composition in both the field diagram and the functional diagram that Appendix C reads.

Relationship with other documents

Formal account — Fields, functions and types: field and functional diagrams; Operators and builders: operations within a block. Builds on — Appendix C: the declared context, substitution, and the conditions for interpreting equations as functions or relations; Perch tagging rules: the information sets of fields. Used by — Methodization: numerical methods address the computations identified here.

docs.title: 1 What the marks describe
docs.text:
The rules concern a .bl stage file. A typing context collects the declared domains, roles, perches, the typed arguments of the declared functions, and shock laws. A perch is an information set, and a field is a random variable measurable at its declared perch. Representing that field by a function of the declared state requires the sufficiency assumptions of Appendix C §1.2 and R5.

Three pieces of syntax answer different questions:

  • A block's header, with its typed inputs and outputs, states which quantities it relates. Its equations determine the relation or operator.
  • An annotation such as :: [id=shift, !node] names a statement and marks it as an authored node: a computation to inspect or realize as a unit within the block.
  • A perch mark such as [>] identifies a field at continuation. It does not supply a state space, a representative function, or a numerical grid.

For example, this transition fragment has one real input and two real outputs. The intermediate result y is also a declared output:

[id=transform, (a : ℝ) : !dcsn -> (y : ℝ, q : ℝ) : !cntn] {
    y = 2 + a    :: [id=shift, !node]
    q = 4*y      :: [id=scale]
}

The header identifies a decision-to-continuation transition. Renaming transform or shift does not change that transition. The !node on the first line keeps that line as a unit of its own; the addition and multiplication are mathematical operations whether that mark is present or absent.

The statement mark is !node, written inside the annotation after ::. Methods remain in a separate methods file, and neither a block identifier nor a method name selects the block's mathematical formula.

docs.title: 2 What an equation determines
docs.text:
An explicit definition such as y = 2 + a gives a function when its arguments, domains, and dependencies are established. In §1, with \(a\in\mathbb R\), its representative is \(\mathrm g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\), \(\mathrm g(a)=2+a\). The field equation and the function equation are related as Appendix C specifies; they are not the same kind of object.

An implicit equation instead states a relation. For example, suppose the stage declares \(a=w-c\) and the continuation candidate \(c_\succ=\mathrm f(a)\). The policy equation c = c[>] then gives $$ {(w,c):c=\mathrm f(w-c),\ (w,c)\text{ is feasible}}. $$ It defines a policy only where a unique solution, or a specified selection from its solutions, meets the required measurability conditions. Adding !node makes the relation separately addressable; it proves neither existence nor uniqueness and does not make a root an optimizer (Appendix C R8 and R10).

An alias is an explicit definition of an intermediate quantity that can be substituted at its uses. Substitution must preserve local binding, domains, shock dependence, and any retained control arguments. An implicit condition cannot be used as an assignment before its unknowns are determined. An equation defining a block output must continue to determine that output even if its expression is also substituted elsewhere.

A statement marked !doc is documentation and contributes no defining equation. Consequently, adding !doc can remove a condition from the mathematical problem; it is not equivalent to adding or removing !node. An identifier alone changes neither kind of statement.

docs.title: 3 Authored nodes and operator occurrences inside equations
docs.text:
There are three levels of detail within the diagrams of a stage:

  1. A block is represented as a unit with its declared inputs and outputs.
  2. A statement marked !node specifies a unit within that block.
  3. The mathematical operations inside each equation remain available at finer detail, including their arguments and local binding.

A computational statement is an authored node exactly when it carries !node. An operator occurrence is a particular use of an operation within an expression. An expectation, argmax, solve, upper_env, or an authored evaluate remains an operator occurrence even when its statement is unmarked. It does not thereby make that statement an authored node.

For example, this arrival-value fragment contains two expectations and no authored nodes:

[id=dcsn_to_arvl, (V) : !dcsn -> (V[<] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !arvl] {
    V[<]      = E_{y}(V)          :: [id=value]
    D_{b}V[<] = E_{y}(R*D_{w}V)   :: [id=marginal]
}

The surrounding stage supplies the transition w = R*b + y from the arrival state b to the decision state w, the law of y, the return parameter R, and the decision value field. The second line is a derivative line: it states the derivative of the arrival value in b, with the factor R that the transition contributes. Both integrations belong to the mathematical interpretation, subject to Appendix C R7. A numerical method can address them without adding !node to either line.

Arithmetic and the applications of declared functions also remain, within the equations that a block or a statement marked !node carries. Being mathematically represented does not make every operation a separately supported method target: a method target is a computation or output representation for which the methods interface defines an address and an admissible numerical attachment (§6).

These three levels occur within both the field diagram and the functional diagram, and replace neither. Both sides of an implicit equation and the rule relating the two diagrams must remain available; a printed formula or a method attachment cannot replace those mathematical objects.

docs.title: 4 Composition and substitution
docs.text:
In §1, let \(\mathrm g(a)=2+a\) and \(\mathrm h(y)=4y\), both maps from \(\mathbb R\) to \(\mathbb R\). The second output is $$ \mathrm q(a)=\mathrm h(\mathrm g(a))=4(2+a). $$ The whole transition has type \(\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\) and is $$ \mathrm F(a)=\bigl(\mathrm g(a),\mathrm h(\mathrm g(a))\bigr). $$ Substituting 2 + a for y in the second equation preserves \(\mathrm F\). Deleting the first output would not: the block promises both y and q. Keeping shift as a node records the intermediate computation while the composite function remains \(\mathrm F\).

Composition requires matching types. For general maps \(\mathrm g:A\to B\) and \(\mathrm h:B\to C\), the composite \(\mathrm h\circ\mathrm g:A\to C\) is defined because the output of \(\mathrm g\) is an admissible input to \(\mathrm h\). If the second operation also needs a shock or another state argument, that argument must be retained; a node does not supply it.

A node also does not hide dependencies. If y depends on a shock, substitution must retain that dependence. An expectation integrates over that shock only when its stated binding and law require it; other free arguments remain free. The formal arguments of functions and operator-bound variables keep their own scope. A perch mark binds no variable; a statement identifier binds no mathematical argument (Appendix C R2, R4, R5, and R11).

Denotation means the mathematical object represented by an expression or diagram. For the same typed equations, adding or removing !node preserves their mathematical denotation while changing the recorded nodes: the marked statement's result becomes a function that later statements consume and a method may represent exactly or by an approximation. An operation occurring inside an unmarked statement also returns a function of the remaining arguments, but that function is not an authored object: it is obtained exactly through its definition and admits only the operation's own methods, never a representation (Appendix C R7, the result of an occurrence). #functional-semantics The diagrams therefore need not be identical. Likewise, equality of mathematical functions does not guarantee identical floating-point results after different numerical methods are attached.

Technical details

The substitution argument concerns equal denotations on the required domain, with local binding preserved. Almost-sure equality under one state law alone does not justify substituting representatives at states reached under a different policy or initial law. The distinction and the required representative choices are stated in Appendix C R5.

docs.title: 5 Field marks, collection selection, and function arguments
5.1 Perch marks
docs.text:
V[<], V, and V[>] identify the arrival, decision, and continuation value fields. V[~] is an explicit spelling of the decision field V. For other names, the complete declarations and headers establish the native perch. A non-native marked occurrence, such as c[>], needs a definition or supplied interpretation at that perch; it is not automatically equal to the decision control c.

The state at a perch can have several coordinates. A field marked [>] may therefore be represented by a function of a vector, not necessarily one scalar asset. Its arguments follow from the declared state and the equations, under the sufficiency assumptions of Appendix C. The mark alone establishes no factorization through a particular coordinate.

docs.title: 5.2 Collection and family selection
docs.text:
Brackets other than the perch marks require an appropriate collection or family. For a tuple, positions start at one: (y, q)[1] selects y. A named selector must resolve to a declared key or to a selector with a compatible domain. For example, the retirement choice uses

V = (V_w[>] - δ, V_r[>])[d]    :: [id=choice_value]

Here the surrounding declaration gives d the ordered labels {work, retire}. work selects the first expression and retire the second. Each expression must have the required value type. The tuple of alternative values is distinct from the labeled union of successor state spaces (Appendix C R3 and §4.7).

An indexed collection may have a parameter-defined number of entries. With an integer parameter J, L_J := {1, …, J} and δ : L_J → ℝ, a name j : L_J selects the entry δ[j]; dist : L_J × L_J → ℝ₊ is selected as dist[j][i] when both names have suitable declared domains. The selector can be a state, a control or a parameter. Its declaration must establish membership in the index set; declaring it only on ℕ does not do so. Symbol conventions §9.2.1 states the admitted index sets and how calibration associates keys with entries.

For a product-valued field, q[>][1] first identifies the continuation field and then selects its first component. Put the perch mark before component selectors. An integer literal in brackets selects a component by position; it is not an inter-period time shift.

A name in brackets does not declare an information set

The spellings q[a] and q[y] do not by themselves declare that q is a function of the state a or the intermediate value y. They require an established indexed object and the appropriate selection rule. They neither bind the bracketed name in an equation's right side nor provide missing domains or measurability assumptions. A state can select an entry when its declared domain supplies suitable keys, as above. To apply a declared function to a state, use parentheses, 𝑞(a) (§5.3).

docs.title: 5.3 Explicit function arguments
docs.text:
Use a declared function when the intended mathematical map and its arguments should be explicit:

𝑔(a : ℝ) := 2 + a
𝑞(y : ℝ) := 4*y

The second declaration defines a function on \(\mathbb R\); its formal argument y is local to that function. In a field equation, 𝑞(y) applies the function to the field y, while 𝑞(𝑔(a)) writes the composition directly. Neither application changes the field's declared perch.

Suppose \(q_A:A\to Q\) is a function on a state space \(A\), with value set \(Q\), and \(g:A\to Y\) is an intermediate map. Representing \(q_A\) using only that intermediate value requires \(q_Y:g(A)\to Q\) with \(q_A=q_Y\circ g\). Such a function exists exactly when \(g(a_1)=g(a_2)\) implies \(q_A(a_1)=q_A(a_2)\). To construct it, set \(q_Y(g(a))=q_A(a)\); the condition makes the result independent of the chosen \(a\). Conversely, the composition forces equal \(g\) values to give equal \(q_A\) values. Measurability of \(q_Y\) remains a separate requirement. A bracket spelling cannot establish that equation. Appendix C R10 uses the same condition when candidate parameters represent a policy.

docs.title: 6 Addresses and numerical methods
docs.text:
An address identifies a declared block, statement, or operation for inspection or method attachment. The address says where to attach; the typed equations say what computation is being approximated. In the examples above:

  • transform addresses the whole transition, and transform.shift addresses the statement marked !node.
  • dcsn_to_arvl.value.E_y addresses the expectation in the named value equation. The statement's id=value identifies that occurrence; it does not make the statement a node.
  • A stage-wide E_y address applies to the occurrences of expectation over y covered by that methods interface. A statement-qualified address distinguishes the integration in the value line from the one in the derivative line when they need different attachments.

Use explicit statement identifiers for stable addresses. A line number is not a method address: inserting documentation must not redirect an attachment. Renaming identifiers consistently in the stage and its methods file preserves the equations and the intended attachments. Identifiers must be unambiguous in their enclosing scope.

An address used for inspection is not necessarily a valid method target. An unmarked scalar alias can remain identifiable without defining a separate numerical task. An authored node, a supported operator occurrence, and a declared output representation are different possible targets. Attaching a method requires both a supported target and a method suitable for its mathematical operation.

The address <block-id>.<statement-id>.<operator> must identify the intended occurrence. If a statement contains two indistinguishable occurrences under that address, the attachment is ambiguous; it must not silently choose the first. A stage-wide attachment, where supported, is an explicit choice to govern the corresponding group.

Methods and their settings are written separately from the stage. A quadrature rule approximates an integral; a root finder approximates a solution of the stated relation. Neither supplies a missing shock law, constraint, or optimality condition. A numerical grid is part of a chosen representation, whereas the field's domain belongs to the model: the methods file names the grid by the setting grid, whose value is the grid's kind written as a tag, grid: !Cartesian, with the grid's fields, orders and bounds, beside it, and the method by its basis, such as !Linear (see Methodization §3).

The name evaluate. An authored evaluate(knots, values, x) denotes evaluation of a stated representation, with coordinates first and values second. The numerical interpolation and extrapolation must be specified as Appendix C R7 requires. It is an operation inside its line, with declared arguments, and a method attaches to it at its own address, <block-id>.<statement-id>.evaluate, where a representation needs no grid, since the first argument holds the knots; evaluate alone names the one authored occurrence of a stage and is refused where the stage authors none or several. A methods file also writes evaluate after a block id for the Evaluation that closes the builder, the place of a declared output representation, and says what that Evaluation evaluates: <block-id>.evaluate for the policy function of the policy builder, <block-id>.evaluate.value for the value function of a backward value builder, and <block-id>.evaluate.marginal for the derivative of that value a derivative line states. That address names an operation every such builder closes with; it does not assert that an evaluate expression was written in the stage, and it creates none. A form that names what its builder does not write, policy.evaluate.value or .evaluate.marginal where no derivative line stands, is refused, and so is a representation named on the builder itself or on a derivative line. See Methodization for the attachment syntax.

docs.title: 7 Policy relations and numerical decomposition
docs.text:
The policy block of the consumption stage cons of Appendix C §4.2, written in the interior form with its candidate line an equation, provides an example in which an unmarked statement is a relation rather than an alias:

[id=policy, (V[>] : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {
    c[>]   = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>])    :: [id=InvEuler]
    m_d[>] = a + c[>]             :: [id=endoggrid]
    c      = c[>]                 :: [id=cons_choice]
}

The surrounding cons stage declares the transition \(a=m_d-c\) and the inverse marginal-utility function. Its continuation value, and so the derivative D_{a}V[>] that the candidate line reads, is already discounted; no discount factor should be inserted into this fragment. Appendix C §4.2 derives its functions and §4.5 states sufficient conditions and a constrained extension; the file applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl writes the candidate line as the inequality c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) ⟂ a >= 0, whose clause states the borrowing constraint (Appendix C §4.5).

The first two lines define the candidate and its decision coordinate. The third identifies the decision control with the candidate. Read at the decision perch, it determines the control implicitly through the transition; rewritten at the continuation perch, through the coordinate map of the second line, it states the policy at the cash on hand of each saving, the relation the construction states (Appendix C R5 and §4.3). It remains a relation even though it has no !node mark and contains no written solve operator: the policy builder, the operator the policy block denotes, holds it as an operation whose output is its own unknown. A method may address it as a solution, and the methods interface records a solve place for it; that recognition does not turn it into an authored solve expression or erase either side of the equation.

The endogenous grid method approximates this relation by computing candidate pairs and representing the resulting policy, which the pairs determine under Appendix C R10's consistency, single-valuedness, coverage, and measurability conditions. When the final line is omitted, no line states the policy and the block is refused under the rule output-defined (Appendix C R1 and §4.6); an implementation does not invent a missing final equation or a method target from the names of the lines.

Choosing a numerical method does not add evaluate, upper_env, or !node statements to the model. If a method internally interpolates or compares candidate values, those computations realize the stated problem. An authored upper_env is instead a mathematical operation in its own right, with the selection and attainment requirements of Appendix C R12. A method's internal steps may be displayed for inspection, but must remain distinguishable from the authored equations and their nodes.

docs.title: 8 Compositional meaning
docs.text:
The compositionality requirement is that the meaning of an expression is determined by the meanings of its parts. For a language with names, those meanings retain their declared context, free arguments, and local binding. An operator's interpretation can then combine them without guessing what a statement identifier was intended to mean. This is the denotational discipline described by Hutton (2023, §3), applied here to the field equations and typed operations of Appendix C.

It permits substitution of equal mathematical meanings within a valid context. It does not equate every diagram recording those meanings: an annotated diagram also records authored addresses and nodes. Removing a !node mark can preserve the represented mathematical function or relation while changing the diagram available for method attachment.

Technical details

A syntactic sort is a category of expressions. For an ordinary many-sorted signature, which lists constructors together with their input and output sorts, the freely generated terms form an initial algebra. Initial means that there is a unique map preserving those constructors into each specified algebra of the same signature (Goguen, Thatcher, Wagner, and Wright 1977, §2, Proposition 2.1). The target must already specify the mathematical sets and operations. The theorem does not choose missing interpretations, solve implicit equations, or prove their analytic assumptions. Binding and substitution require a representation that accounts for contexts; a many-sorted list of constructor arities alone is not a proof that those binding rules are respected (Lamiaux and Ahrens 2024, §1.1.1).

The formal implementation must preserve these distinctions when it constructs the two diagrams. This appendix specifies their mathematical meaning and authored nodes; it does not prescribe parser constructors, storage records, or an execution order for a numerical solver.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Goguen, J. A., Thatcher, J. W., Wagner, E. G., and Wright, J. B. (1977). Initial Algebra Semantics and Continuous Algebras. Journal of the ACM 24(1), 68–95. §2, especially Proposition 2.1.
  • Hutton, G. (2023). Programming language semantics: It's easy as 1,2,3. Journal of Functional Programming 33, e9. §3, pp. 3–4.
  • Lamiaux, T., and Ahrens, B. (2024). An Introduction to Different Approaches to Initial Semantics. §1.1.1, on syntax with binding and substitution.

docs.title: Expression forms
docs.text:
Summary

An expression in a line of a stage file is built from names, numbers and arithmetic, and from nine named forms: the expectation E_{θ}(…), the maximization argmax_{c}(…), the implicit solution solve_{c}(…), the derivative D_{c}(𝑢) of a declared function and D_{a}V[>] of a value, the inverse Inv(𝑓), and the real functions exp, log, max and min. A shock's law is written on a line of its own, after ~. The table gives each form as a stage file writes it, what it computes, the object of the Bellman calculus it realizes where the calculus defines one, and the entry of the package that defines it. A block file, which a methods file names, holds two forms of block, the method block and the marginal block (§4).

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Field equations: the lines in which these forms stand; Constraints: the inequalities and the ⟂ clause a line may carry. Formal account — Operators: the operations the forms denote; Equation parsing rules §§4–5: the variable a form binds and the reading of a law. See also — Shock distributions: the families a law names; Symbol conventions: declarations, domains and type words.

docs.title: 1 Reading the table
docs.text:
Each row is one form. written gives the first occurrence of the form that the package finds in the stage files under applications/, printed back as normalized .bl text by to_source of syntax/source.py, so that E_{Ψ,θ} in port.bl shows as E_{Ψ, θ}, with the file, or says that no stage file writes it; the arithmetic row gives the six signs of the grammar, and the laws row the call of each family as the module docstring of distributions/families.py spells it. meaning gives, for an operator written with a subscript, the words the package attaches to it in OPERATOR_MEANINGS of typing/line_unknowns.py, followed for D by its defining expression; for a named function of the definitions table, its defining expression; and for the arithmetic, the names the grammar gives its six operations, add, sub, neg, mul, div and pow. denotes links to the section of Appendix E.3 that defines the object the form realizes, and shows a dash where E.3 defines no such object, as for a real function applied at each point, such as exp. The laws row also shows a dash: each family has its own row, with its own link to E.3, on the laws page. read from names the module under packages/bellman/bellman/, its table and the key: BOUND_OPERATORS for the four heads written with a subscript in braces, and PRIMITIVE_DEFINITIONS["definitions"] for the named functions, each of which it defines exactly.

A subscript in braces names the variable the form binds: the shock an expectation integrates, the control a maximization chooses, or the unknowns a solution solves for. The subscript of a derivative instead names an argument of a function the file has already defined, as in 𝑑𝑢 := D_{c}(𝑢), or, where the operator is applied to a value field written with its perch mark, a state coordinate of the perch at which the value is read, written without its mark: D_{a}V[>] is the derivative term, the derivative of the continuation value in the continuation coordinate a, and D_{a}D_{a}V[>] its second derivative. The term has this one spelling; D_{a}(V[>]) is not admitted. A subscript that names no state coordinate of that perch, or a discrete coordinate, is refused with the perch's coordinates named, and a derivative term of a value the block neither reads nor writes is refused as an undeclared name is (Refusals). A derivative term may stand on the right side of any line, where it reads a derivative, and on the left side of a line of a value builder's block, where it states the derivative of the value the builder writes, D_{m_d}V = 𝑑𝑢(c) (Field equations §2). The term applies an operator to a function the graph already holds; the package reads it and differentiates nothing.

A law names a shock, or a tuple of shocks, on the left of ~ and a family applied to its arguments on the right. Shock distributions lists the families and the meaning of their arguments; Equation parsing rules §4 states how separate laws and a joint law are read.

A braced form with any other head, such as max_{c}(…), is refused under the rule not-constructed of Refusals. A call of a name that neither the stage file nor the table defines, such as sqrt(x), has no definition and denotes nothing; define the function in the stage file instead, 𝑟(x : ℝ₊) := x^(1/2).

docs.title: 2 Arithmetic
docs.text:
Between the named forms stand numbers, the names of fields, parameters and functions, and the arithmetic of the grammar, syntax/grammars/stage.lark:

Written Reading a + b, a - b, -a Sum, difference and negation. A leading minus negates the product that follows it: -a*b is -(a*b). a*b, a/b Product and quotient. A product is always written with *. a^b, a**b Power. The exponent is a single term, a name, a number, a call or an expression in parentheses: c^(1-ρ). ∞, inf Infinity; both spellings are one constant. (a, b) A tuple, a finite family of values. x[1], (V_young[>], W_old[>])[s] Selection from a family, by position counted from one or by the label a coordinate takes. 𝑢(c) A function the stage file defines, applied to as many arguments as it declares.

A power binds more tightly than a product or a quotient, and these more tightly than a sum or a difference; parentheses group. A line relates two expressions by = or by one of the inequalities <=, >=, <, >, ≤ and ≥, and may carry a complementary-slackness clause after ⟂.

docs.title: 3 Forms that compile
docs.text:
A kernel is the function an operation of a stage applies: the law of motion 𝑔 that a pullback or a push-forward applies, and the value aggregator 𝐺 that an aggregation applies. compile_kernel() answers the kernel of such an operation as a plain Python function, made from the source text that kernel().python holds. It answers one where the row writes its output as a function of its inputs, or states a relation with an explicit side whose function it compiles; a pullback or an aggregation whose row states a relation with no explicit side, such as the identification c = c[>], is refused under the rule kernel-target of Refusals, and a row that reads a derivative term, c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) ⟂ a >= 0 in cons.bl, is refused under the rule kernel-form, naming the term, as a kernel that calls a function defined by D_{c}(𝑢) is (below). The function takes the kernel's arguments and then the parameters the kernel reads, and computes on numbers or on NumPy arrays. The values the calibration gives those parameters stand in kernel().parameter_values, None on a version not yet calibrated, and are passed at each call, so that a new calibration needs no new compilation. The text holds numbers and infinity, the kernel's arguments, the parameters, the arithmetic of §2, and the functions the stage file defines in closed form, such as 𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(1-ρ)/(1-ρ), written as functions inside the one function. An expectation over a label shock, a shock whose law gives each label of a finite set its probability, compiles to the sum of the values weighted by those probabilities.

The named functions exp, log, max, min and Inv, and a function the stage file defines by a derivative or an inverse, such as 𝑑𝑢 := D_{c}(𝑢), have no compile rule: their definitions state what they denote, and a kernel that calls one is not compiled, under the rule kernel-form of Refusals. The same function written in closed form, 𝑑𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(-ρ), compiles. The other operations, among them an expectation that stands as an operation of its own, whatever the law of its shock, and a maximization, have no compiled kernel: compile_kernel() refuses them under the rule kernel-target.

docs.title: 4 The blocks of a block file
docs.text:
A block file is a file of blocks that a methods file names under block: (Methodization §4.1). It opens with a line naming its stage, @methods: cons, or with the stage's mark, @stage: cons, either of which the package accepts; it may define functions in closed form, 𝑑𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(-ρ), whose kernels compile as a stage file's do (§3), and holds blocks of two forms, each written as a block of a stage file is (Stages):

Written Reading [id=egm, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] { … } A method block: its header carries the signature of a builder of the stage, here the policy builder, in terms of the values it reads and the controls at which its lines are read, and its lines compute that builder's output; a line may read the derivative of a value the header lists by the term D_{a}V[>], and the header lists nothing for it. A methods entry with block: and a method whose type takes a block, !egm here, binds it on the builder that on names; its lines become the builder's operations, and the stage file's line stays the builder's declared line. [id=dcsn_marginal, (c) : !cntn -> (V) : !dcsn] { … } A marginal block: its header is the value builder's header restricted to what its lines read, and its lines are derivative lines, each stating a derivative of the value the builder writes as the author asserts it, D_{m}V = 𝑑𝑢(c) here. A methods entry with !marginals and block: on a backward value builder records its lines at that builder's closing Evaluation as stated derivatives of the value, beside the representation bound there; the builder gains no wire and no box, and its signature is unchanged (Methodization §4.1).

A block is matched to the builder its entry names by the perches it joins and the outputs it writes. Its header is checked against the builder's own: a method block's outputs are the builder's and its inputs are among the builder's inputs; a marginal block's inputs are among the builder's inputs and the controls at which its lines are read, and the values whose derivatives its lines state are among the builder's outputs. A header that does not match is refused under block-header-mismatch, and a function that neither the stage file nor the block file defines under block-name-undefined (Refusals). The demonstration's block file is applications/cons-port/declaration/methods/cons_egm.bl.

docs.title: Shock distributions
docs.text:
Summary

A line such as y ~ LogNormal(μ_y, σ_y) declares the probability distribution of a shock, of a tuple of shocks jointly, or of each component of a collection of shocks, by one of eleven families. This page lists the families, with the arguments each takes and what they mean, links each to the object of the Bellman calculus a declaration denotes, and names the table of the package the row is read from. A declared distribution is what an expectation integrates against and what a forward builder extends a measure by.

Relationship with other documents

Formal account — Appendix E.3 Operators §4: the conditional distribution of a shock, a probability kernel, and the two operators that read it. Builds on — Stage tutorial §2: where a distribution is declared in a stage file. See also — Operations: the Expectation and DistributionExtension rows that read a declared distribution; Refusals: the smallest example of each rule a declaration can be refused under.

docs.title: 1 Reading a declaration
docs.text:
A declaration writes the shock on the left of ~ and a call of a family on the right. The shock's set is declared on its own line, y : ℝ₊₊, and the declaration gives the distribution of the shock over that set: the set says which values the shock can take, and the distribution how probability is spread over them.

A tuple subject declares one joint distribution of its shocks, (y, z) ~ N((μ_y, μ_z), ((σ_y^2, r), (r, σ_z^2))). An argument may name a parameter; a state or a control at the source perch of the shock's edge, where an edge is the step from one perch to the next that one forward builder makes; or another shock, called a parent of the declaration. The declaration is then the distribution of the shock conditional on those arguments, a probability kernel: a distribution for each value the arguments take. Ψ ~ LogNormal(ν, σ_Ψ) in sa_savings.bl is conditional on the shock ν, and y_n ~ MarkovChain(P_y, y_grid, y_wa) in worker_ageing.bl on last period's ability y_wa.

A shock is drawn on the edge of one forward builder: the builder whose block lists the shock among its inputs, or else the edge of a shock declared with it or of a shock whose declaration reads it. The declarations drawn on one edge form one joint distribution, the product of their conditional distributions, each given its parents and the states and controls it reads. Two declarations that do not name one another are therefore conditionally independent given those states and controls; stage.obligations() lists that product as the assumption joint-distribution-factorization. On the card a builder prints (Operations §1), the distribution of ψ prints as P_ψ: an expectation integrates against it, E_{ψ}[…], and a distribution extension extends a measure by it, μ≺⊗P_ψ.

A declaration of one real shock by N, LogNormal, Uniform, TruncatedNormal, TruncatedLogNormal or TypeIExtremeValue, the scalar families whose definition the package's table of definitions holds (the column definition of §2), denotes two objects: the law as written, the family applied to the written arguments, and the measure at those arguments, the family's definition with the written arguments in place of its variables. The card that stage.definitions.denote prints for the declaration gives the second on the row under the first, so that y ~ Uniform(a_y, b_y) has the row P_y = measure on ℝ given by B ↦ ∫_{x ∈ {x ∈ ℝ | x ∈ B ∧ a_y ≤ x ∧ x ≤ b_y}} [1/(b_y − a_y)] Lebesgue(dx): the probability of a set B is the length of the part of B in [a_y, b_y], divided by b_y − a_y. A Mixture, a declaration of a tuple subject and a declaration by any other family denote the law as written alone.

A shock may be declared on the functions from a finite index set to the reals, ε : I_J → ℝ with I_J := {0, …, J} (Symbols and conventions), so that ε has one real component ε[i] for each member i of I_J. A call of LogNormal, Uniform, TruncatedNormal, TruncatedLogNormal or TypeIExtremeValue with real arguments is then the law of each component, and the declaration denotes the finite product of that law over the index set, printed ⊗_{i ∈ I_J} TypeIExtremeValue(0, 1) for ε ~ TypeIExtremeValue(0, 1); its measure, the second object, is the product of the scalar measures. The product of probability measures P_i on ℝ, one for each i in I_J, is the probability measure on the functions e from I_J to ℝ that gives the set of the functions with e(i) in B_i for every i the probability P_0(B_0) · P_1(B_1) · … · P_J(B_J). The components are therefore independent draws of one law, not copies of one draw, conditionally on the arguments the law reads, such as a parent shock η in ε ~ TypeIExtremeValue(η, 1), and the sentence of joint-distribution-factorization states it: the components of ε are independent, each with the law TypeIExtremeValue(0, 1), or conditionally independent given η for the law with the parent. N on such a shock is the joint normal law of its components, written ε ~ N(μ_ε, Σ_ε) with a mean μ_ε : I_J → ℝ and a covariance matrix Σ_ε : I_J × I_J → ℝ; it is not a product, and it denotes the law as written alone, as a Mixture on such a shock does.

The second argument

N(μ, v) takes the variance, not the standard deviation: sa_savings.bl writes ν ~ N(κ_1, σ_ν^2). LogNormal(μ, σ) takes the mean and the standard deviation of the logarithm of the draw, so μ is not the mean of the draw: buffer_stock.bl writes ψ ~ LogNormal(-(σ_ψ^2)/2, σ_ψ), whose mean is one. TruncatedNormal(μ, σ, l, u) takes the mean and the standard deviation of the normal law before the truncation to [l, u], so that σ is a standard deviation, not a variance as in N, and neither μ nor σ is the mean or the standard deviation of the draw. TruncatedLogNormal(μ, σ, l, u) takes the mean and the standard deviation of the logarithm, as LogNormal does, and its two endpoints in the draw's own units, so that TruncatedLogNormal(μ, σ, 0, inf) is LogNormal(μ, σ) and a bound stated as k standard deviations of the logarithm is written exp(μ + k·σ). TypeIExtremeValue(μ, s) takes a location and a scale, and the mean of the draw is μ + γs, γ ≈ 0.5772 being Euler's constant. A numerical routine written in another convention needs its arguments converted.

docs.title: 2 The families
docs.text:
The table has one row for each family of the package's table of families, FAMILY_ARGUMENTS in distributions/families.py, in that table's order. The column law names the family, and written gives its calls as the module docstring of distributions/families.py spells them. arguments gives how many arguments the family takes and what they are, and meaning gives the distribution a declaration gives, in the words of the same docstring. definition gives, for the seven families the package's table of definitions defines, N for one shock, LogNormal, Uniform, TruncatedNormal, TruncatedLogNormal, TypeIExtremeValue and Mixture, the defining expression, the measure as a function of the arguments; the other rows hold a dash. denotes links to the section of Appendix E.3 that defines the conditional distribution of a shock and the expectation that integrates against it. read from names the module, the table and the key of the family's arguments and, for the six families the table of definitions defines, of its definition.

docs.title: 3 Conditions and refusals
docs.text:
A call of a family with a number of arguments the family does not take is refused under readable-form. An argument outside its family's domain is refused under distribution-domain: a negative variance, a negative standard deviation of the logarithm, weights outside the unit interval or not summing to one, a probability of Bernoulli outside [0, 1], and a mean or a covariance matrix that does not have the subject's dimension or a covariance matrix that is not symmetric positive semidefinite. A zero variance and a zero standard deviation of the logarithm lie in the domain: N(μ, 0) is a point mass at μ, and LogNormal(μ, 0) a point mass at exp(μ). A component of a Mixture written as a number is a point mass at that number, as the 0 of ξ ~ Mixture((p_zero, 0), (1 - p_zero, LogNormal(μ_ξ, σ_ξ))) in buffer_stock.bl.

The arguments of Uniform, TruncatedNormal, TruncatedLogNormal and TypeIExtremeValue are real numbers, and the same rule refuses each of the following:

  • endpoints that are not in order, Uniform(1, 0), Uniform(1, 1) or TruncatedNormal(0, 1, 2, 2);
  • a standard deviation or a scale that is not positive, TruncatedNormal(0, 0, -1, 1), TruncatedLogNormal(0, 0, 0, inf) or TypeIExtremeValue(0, 0);
  • a negative lower endpoint of a truncated lognormal, TruncatedLogNormal(0, 1, -1, 1), since the draw is positive: TruncatedLogNormal(0, 1, 0, inf) is LogNormal(0, 1) itself, and TruncatedLogNormal(0, 1, 0.5, 2) the lognormal law conditional on [0.5, 2];
  • an infinite argument other than an endpoint of a truncation: Uniform(0, inf) is refused, whereas TruncatedNormal(0, 1, 0, inf) is the normal law truncated to the nonnegative half-line and TruncatedNormal(0, 1, -inf, inf) the normal law itself;
  • an argument whose names all have values and whose arithmetic has no number, 0/0, or is not a number, inf - inf;
  • a tuple written as an argument, Uniform((0, 1), 2), and an argument that reads a parameter declared on a collection, μ : I_J → ℝ, or on a product set, b : ℝ × ℝ;
  • a tuple subject, (y, z) ~ Uniform(0, 1), since each of the three is the law of one real subject or of each component of a collection.

Every component of a Mixture that is a call of N, LogNormal or one of the four families is checked as a declaration of that family would be, and a refusal names the component: Mixture((0.5, 0), (0.5, N(0, -1))) is refused for the negative variance of its N component. A refusal under distribution-domain names the declaration's line of the file.

Where an argument names a parameter, the condition is decided when the calibration gives the number, and a calibration whose values break it is refused under distribution-domain. In the meantime three conditions stand among stage.obligations(): the condition on weights as distribution-weights-are-a-probability-vector, the condition on the covariance matrix of a tuple subject as covariance-positive-semidefinite, and the condition on the parameters of Uniform, TruncatedNormal, TruncatedLogNormal and TypeIExtremeValue, of a declaration or of a component of a mixture, as distribution-parameters-in-domain. The sentence of distribution-parameters-in-domain states the family's condition in the written terms, the parameters of the Uniform declaration two_nodes:distribution:y of y lie in the family's domain: a < b, with a = a_y and b = b_y, both finite. An argument that is a call, Uniform(exp(1), 3), or any other term outside the arithmetic of numbers and parameters the package evaluates, or that reads a state, a control or a parent shock, TypeIExtremeValue(0, z), keeps its condition as the obligation distribution-parameters-in-domain, which no calibration decides.

Every declaration also records the condition law-support: the distribution gives probability only to values in the shock's declared set. The package decides it at calibration where it knows the law's support and reads the bounds of the declared set: a truncated lognormal's support is [l, u], open at a lower endpoint 0 and at an upper endpoint inf, and calibrate establishes the condition when that interval lies within the declared set and refuses the calibration when it does not. For every other family the condition stays required and unchecked, so a normal distribution declared for a shock in ℝ₊₊ is not refused; a strictly positive shock takes a family whose draws are positive, such as LogNormal, or a mixture of such families with positive numbers. The numerical routine that provides a distribution to a solver is no condition of the stage: a solver reads one where a methods file names it and chooses its own otherwise.

The distribution of a shock whose labels select the branches of a block gives one probability to each label, written Categorical((p₁, …, pₙ)) in the order of the labels or Bernoulli(p) on two; any other is refused under branch-law. An expectation that needs a conditional distribution the declarations do not give, a posterior among them, is refused under conditional-not-declared.

A call of a family outside the table is not refused when the file is read: the declaration is kept as the file writes it, as the author's own distribution. The backward builders graph is constructed, but the forward builders graph is not: stage.builder.fwd holds a refusal under not-constructed, since a forward builder extends a measure only by the families of the table.

docs.title: Method types
docs.text:
Summary

A method type is a numerical method that a methods file can attach to a place of a stage, such as !egm or !gauss-hermite. The table lists every method type the package defines, one row each: the line a methods file writes, the places at which the method may be bound, the settings it reads, the object of the Bellman calculus it realizes, and the line of the package that defines it. The table is printed from the package's method table, and a methods file that names a method type absent from it is refused.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Methodization: how a methods file attaches a method to a place of a stage and supplies its settings. Formal account — Methods: a numerical method as distinct from the operation it approximates; Operators: the operations the methods realize. See also — Expression forms: the forms a stage file writes, among them the operators E, argmax and solve at which a method may be bound; Refusals: the rules method-attachment and method-option-value.

docs.title: 1 Reading the table
docs.text:
Each row is one method type. written is the line of an entry of a methods file that names it, the tag after method:.

bound at lists the kinds of place the method type admits, in the words of the method table:

  • builder, a whole builder, named by the id of its block, such as policy or cntn_to_dcsn;
  • node, a line marked !node, and statement, any other line with an id, both named <block id>.<line id>;
  • definition, a function the stage file defines, named as the file writes it, such as 𝑢;
  • operator and a head, one occurrence of that operator in a line, named by <block id>.<line id>.<head>; the operator's stage-wide name, such as E_Ψ_θ, names every occurrence of it in the stage at once, and one entry then binds them all; the heads evaluate and upper_env name places a methods file reaches by their addresses and have no row on Expression forms, although applications/retirement-choice/declaration/stages/worker_cons/worker_cons.bl writes upper_env(w[>], c[>], v[>]) as a call. The operator evaluate also names the Evaluation that closes the policy builder or a backward value builder, where a representation of what the builder writes is bound: policy.evaluate for the policy function, and <block id>.evaluate.value and <block id>.evaluate.marginal for the value function a backward builder writes and the derivative of it that a derivative line states (Methodization §2).

options lists the settings the method reads, each with the kind of value it takes. An entry gives them under settings:; it must give every setting marked required, and it may give the others, save that a representation at the policy builder's Evaluation where !egm stands writes no grid and one at an authored evaluate(knots, values, x) needs none (Methodization §3). A method that takes a grid names it by the setting grid, whose value is the grid's kind written as a tag, such as grid: !Cartesian; the cell then lists, beside each kind of grid, the fields that kind admits as further settings of the entry, orders and bounds for !Cartesian among them. The grid of a representation, !Linear or !pchip, lies in the coordinates of the represented function, and the exogenous grid of savings of !egm in the states of the continuation perch (Methodization §3).

takes a block says whether an entry of the method may name a block file under block:, whose block the method binds on the builder on: names (Methodization §4.1). derivatives it evaluates says, for a representation method, which derivatives of the represented function the representation evaluates: a block of a later stage that reads the derivative of the value by the term D_{a}V[>] is served by the representation alone where no derivative line states that derivative, and the stage that reads it checks nothing against this column (Trellises §2.1). The column is information about the representation; a derivative line, in the stage file or bound with !marginals, whose values the representation at the builder's Evaluation stores, is the other way the derivative of a value is evaluated, and the methods file names that representation <block id>.evaluate.marginal or <block id>.evaluate.value (Methodization §4.1). condition names the condition under which the method's construction reaches the stage file's declared line, with its sentence; stage.obligations() lists it under that name, and nothing checks it.

denotes links to the section of Appendix E.3 that defines the object the method realizes. That object is the one E.3 defines for the first operator in the row's bound at cell, so a method bound at two operators links only the section of the first of them. A method bound at no operator, such as !deterministic, !histogram or !identity, is bound on a whole builder; the method table names no operator for it, so its row links no section and shows a dash; E.3 defines the backward builders in §2 and the forward builders in §3. A method realizes its object through its handler, the routine that carries the method out, and an adapter, which converts the stage's objects into the routine's representation and converts its results back.

defined in links to the line of packages/bellman/bellman/stage/method_table.py in the repository econ-ark/bellman that defines the method type's row of METHOD_TYPES; the module's docstring names this page in return. read from names the module under packages/bellman/bellman/, the table and the key.
