A methods file that names a tag absent from the table is refused, and so is an entry that places a method at a kind of place its row does not admit, omits a required setting, or writes a setting the row does not name without naming a handler that reads it; each refusal is under the rule method-attachment of Refusals, except that !Cartesian written as a method, the fields of a grid written without the setting grid, and a grid written at the policy builder's Evaluation under !egm are refused under grid-kind-as-method, grid-without-kind and grid-under-egm. Configuration checks the values of the settings, and a value of the wrong kind is refused under the rule method-option-value.

Grids and the model's sets

The settings orders and bounds describe a numerical grid: the number of points and the interval, coordinate by coordinate, at which a function is computed and between which it is interpolated. A representation and !egm write them beside the setting grid, which names the grid's kind; !vfi, !histogram and !root-find write them alone. Changing them changes the approximation and leaves the model as it was. A finite set of alternatives the household chooses from is part of the model and is declared in the stage file.

docs.title: Model directory layout
docs.text:
Summary

Each model of the repository has a folder of its own under applications/, and every such folder keeps the files the language reads in one subfolder, declaration/: the recipe, the trellis and period files, the calibration and settings files, and one folder for each stage, holding the stage file, its methods file and its note. Beside declaration/ stand the folder's first page, README.md, its economics.md, and its code, tests, papers and results. This page states the layout, the rules it follows and the variants of a model it admits. The package's functions that read these files require no layout, since they read the paths a recipe or a trellis file writes; the layout is the convention of the repository's model folders, which Bellman Workbench reads and a test of the repository checks.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Trellises §§1, 5: the trellis file, the period file and the recipe, and the paths a recipe writes; Methodization: the methods, settings and calibration files. Used by — The Bellman factory §3 and Recipe functions: the registry a recipe is read from; Bellman Workbench: the folder it opens and the folder its form new trellis writes.

Key terminology Term Meaning Model folder The folder of one model under applications/, laid out as this page states. Stage key The name under which a period lists a stage, chosen by the author. A model's recipe normally uses the name of the stage's folder, which the stage file and the note share; an equation variant or a second use of a stage lists the folder under another key (§§2.3, 3). Registry The folder a recipe stands in, from which every path the recipe writes is read; in a model folder, its declaration/ (wiki). Recipe The file spec.yml that names the trellis file, each stage's file and, for each stage, the ordered files from which its parameter values, its settings and its methods are read (wiki). Source A file of assignments of one kind, parameter values, settings or methods, which a recipe names by its path without the extension, as calibration/durables (wiki). Variant A second version of a model, written beside the first in the same folder (§3).

docs.title: 1 The layout
docs.text:
The durables model of Dobrescu and Shanker (2026), in which a household keeps or adjusts its housing stock over fifty-one ages, shows the layout:

applications/durables/
├── README.md                   the first page: the model in one sentence, a drawing where the folder holds one and the command that opens it
├── economics.md                the economics in full
├── declaration/                every file the language reads
│   ├── spec.yml                the recipe: trellis: trellis.yml and, for each stage, its stage file and its sources
│   ├── spec.two-stages.yml     a second recipe: trellis: trellis.two-stages.yml, with the same stage files
│   ├── trellis.yml             the periods, counted backward from the terminal one
│   ├── trellis.two-stages.yml
│   ├── period.yml              the template of one period, which the trellis file repeats
│   ├── period.two-stages.yml
│   ├── stages/
│   │   ├── tenure/             tenure.bl  methods.yml  tenure.md
│   │   ├── keeper_cons/        keeper_cons.bl  methods.yml  keeper_cons.md
│   │   ├── adjuster_cons/      adjuster_cons.bl  methods.yml  adjuster_cons.md
│   │   └── bequest/            bequest.bl  methods.yml
│   ├── methods/                the block files the methods files name: keeper_cons_egm.bl  adjuster_cons_egm.bl  marginals_tenure.bl …
│   ├── calibration/            durables.yml  wage_schedule.yml
│   └── settings/               durables.yml
├── code/                       wage_schedule.py, which writes each period's income into the trellis
├── results/                    what the code writes; git ignores it
└── tests/                      test_durables_ast.py

declaration/ holds every file the language reads: the recipe, the trellis and period files, the folders calibration/ and settings/, under stages/ one folder for each stage, holding its stage file, written in .bl, its methods file and its note, and under methods/ the block files a methods file names under block:, the method blocks and the marginal blocks of the stages. Beside declaration/ stand README.md, economics.md, code/ for the folder's programs, tests/ for its tests, results/ for what its programs write, paper/ for the descriptions of its stages that Bellman Workbench's button paper writes for a paper's model section (§4), and reference/ for the papers it keeps, as PDF files, such as applications/benhabib-2019/reference/benhabib-bisin-luo-2019.pdf; the durables folder keeps none. A folder holds only the parts its model has: applications/portfolio-choice/, whose stage files the portfolio–consumption application assembles, holds its stage folders, a README.md and its tests, and no recipe.

The portfolio–consumption application, applications/cons-port/, holds its stages under declaration/stages/, its methods files and the block files they name under declaration/methods/, and two recipes, one for each order of its period, each with its trellis file. Beside them stand its trellis files of records, declaration/trellis.<name>.yml, each of which writes every stage of a period as a record naming the stage file and the calibration, settings and methods files the stage is bound from, all of the folder's own declaration/, and is read with no recipe (Trellises §3). Beside declaration/ it keeps code/ for its numerical tool, tests/, notebooks/ for its notebook and its earlier reference notebook, and reference/legacy/ for its fixed numerical reference, with the reference's recorded sources in the earlier YAML form.

The form new trellis of Bellman Workbench writes a new model folder in this layout (Bellman Workbench §6), with two more files at the folder's top, beside its README.md: the record of the form's answers, answers.yml, and a .gitignore. The repository's test packages/bellman/tests/test_layout.py fails on a folder under applications/ that git tracks and that departs from the layout, so it fails on a tracked folder that holds those two files at its top.

docs.title: 2.1 What you write where
docs.text:
Every file the language reads stands under declaration/, and the only other files there are the notes of the stages, each in its stage's folder. A stage file holds the mathematics of one stage, its declarations, its typed blocks and its equations; the YAML files hold the rest: the periods and the trellis that compose the stages, the numerical methods and the settings they read, the parameter values, and the recipe that names them all. What the folder holds for its readers and for its programs, the README, the economics, the code, the tests and the papers, stands beside declaration/.

The division between the stage file and the YAML files follows the economics. A finite set of choices belongs in the stage's domain definitions, and the grid sizes and tolerances that approximate a continuous domain belong in the settings. Keeping the files apart does not settle which is which, so decide for each number whether it changes the household's problem or only the numerical calculation.

declaration/ is the model's registry, the folder a recipe stands in and from which every path the recipe writes is read. load_recipe of bellman.trellis is therefore given declaration/ and the name of the recipe; run from the repository root, it reads the durables model:

from bellman.trellis import load_recipe

syntactic = load_recipe("applications/durables/declaration", "spec.yml")
print(len(syntactic["periods"]), "periods, from", syntactic["provenance"]["trellis"]["path"])
tenure = syntactic["periods"][0]["stages"]["tenure"]
print(f"{'stage':12}{tenure['stage']['origin']}")
for kind in ("calibration", "settings", "methods"):
    for source in tenure["provenance"]["source_lists"][kind]:
        if "path" in source:
            print(f"{kind:12}{source['path']}")

51 periods, from applications/durables/declaration/trellis.yml
stage       applications/durables/declaration/stages/tenure/tenure.bl
calibration applications/durables/declaration/calibration/durables.yml
settings    applications/durables/declaration/settings/durables.yml
methods     applications/durables/declaration/stages/tenure/methods.yml

The call returns the syntactic trellis, the model as written, with one record for each stage and period. The record of the tenure stage in the terminal period, periods[0], names the stage file and the three files the stage is bound from, each read at the path the recipe writes. Bellman Workbench reads the same folder: it opens on a model folder, binds the open stage file through the recipe declaration/spec.yml where the folder holds one, and shows the folder's files in its tree (Bellman Workbench §1).

docs.title: 2.2 What a recipe names
docs.text: A recipe writes the path of every file it reads, from its own folder, and the package finds no file by a name or a suffix (Trellises §5). In the durables recipe, trellis: trellis.yml names the trellis file, and the entry of the stage key tenure names its stage file, stage: stages/tenure/tenure.bl, and lists its sources, each named by its path without the extension: calibration/durables, settings/durables and the stage's methods file, stages/tenure/methods. A trellis file names the period file it repeats, template: period.yml, from its own folder in the same way. A recipe without trellis:, or an entry without stage:, is refused with a sentence that says what to write, stage: stages/tenure/tenure.bl for the entry tenure (Refusals). A recipe and a trellis file that disagree on the stage keys are refused under the rule recipe-template-agreement, so that a mismatched pair does not load. A suffix in a file's name, the two-stages of spec.two-stages.yml, is for the reader alone: the links between a recipe, its trellis file and its period file are the lines these files write.

docs.title: 2.3 One folder for each stage
docs.text: The files of a stage stand together in one folder, declaration/stages/<stage>/: the stage file <stage>.bl and the note <stage>.md, the page that explains the stage, which share the folder's name, and the methods file methods.yml. A method belongs to the operators of one stage, so a stage reused in another model is copied with its methods as one folder. Calibration and settings sources may be reused by stages, so they stand in declaration/calibration/ and declaration/settings/. Sharing a source file does not identify all its names across the model: two stages in one period that declare one parameter name share that period parameter, while their field names remain local and the same parameter name in another period denotes another parameter. The recipe names the two files of a stage's folder that the language reads, stage: stages/tenure/tenure.bl and the methods source stages/tenure/methods, and it normally lists the stage under the folder's name as its stage key, as the durables recipe lists tenure; an equation variant or a second use of the stage lists the folder under another key (§3). A stage's folder holds the files the stage has: the bequest of the durables model, which is bound from no methods file and has no note, holds its stage file alone.

docs.title: 2.4 Variants side by side
docs.text: A variant of a model stands beside the files it varies, in the same declaration/, and not in a folder of its own, and every link between its files is written in them. §3 sets out the three kinds.

docs.title: 2.5 The first page of a folder
docs.text: README.md is the page a visitor reads first. It states the model in one sentence, shows a drawing of the model where the folder holds one, gives the command that opens the folder in Bellman Workbench, bellman-workbench applications/durables, and names the folder the code writes into. economics.md, where a folder has one, holds the economics in full: the model's equations, its calibration with its sources, and what the stage files cannot state. A folder without economics.md, such as applications/portfolio-choice/, explains its model in its README.md and in the notes of its stages.

docs.title: 2.6 Where generated files stand
docs.text: The recordings of a model's stage files, the parsed term (<stage>.bl.ast.json) and the encoding of the elaborated stage (<stage>.bl.stage.json) of each, stand with the package's tests, in packages/bellman/tests/snapshot/corpus/<model>/, and not in the model folder. The test packages/bellman/tests/sym/test_corpus.py parses and elaborates every stage file under applications/ and compares the results with these recordings, and PYTHONPATH=. python tests/snapshot/record.py --corpus, run from packages/bellman/, writes them again. The model's code writes into results/, which git ignores, as it ignores model-explorer/, where Bellman Workbench writes the views it exports. The generated files a folder tracks are records kept on purpose: the portfolio–consumption application keeps its fixed numerical reference, reference/legacy/port_cons_h5.npz with its manifest, and reference/legacy/preflight.json, the record that identifies the notebook and the helper from which the reference was computed; the record of the comparison with that reference that its acceptance test writes, code/tests/evidence/reference-comparison.json and .txt; and the figures its earlier reference notebook drew, the PNG files under notebooks/port-cons/figures/, beside which stage_lifecycle.svg is a drawing and not a generated file.

docs.title: 3 Variants
docs.text:
A variant is a second version of a model that shares most of its files with the first. It is written beside the first, in declaration/, in one of three ways, according to what it changes.

  • A variant of the route, which changes the stages a period holds or how the periods are joined, is a second set of the three files: a recipe spec.<name>.yml, which names its trellis file under trellis:; the trellis file trellis.<name>.yml, which names its period file under template:; and the period file period.<name>.yml, the name between the dots being the author's choice. The durables folder keeps its route without the tenure stage in this way: spec.two-stages.yml names trellis.two-stages.yml, which names period.two-stages.yml, and the recipe names the same stage files and sources as spec.yml, without those of the tenure stage, so that load_recipe("applications/durables/declaration", "spec.two-stages.yml") reads the second route (Trellises §5; The Bellman factory §3.6). Since the suffix links nothing, a recipe may name a trellis file of another suffix where that is the intent.
  • A variant of the values, which changes the numbers a stage receives and not the route, needs no second set of files. It is a further source file, such as calibration/near_terminal.yml or settings/fine.yml, which a recipe lists after the common one in a stage's list of sources, or in the list of sources of a range of periods, so that its values stand over the common ones (The Bellman factory §§3.2, 3.4). A variant supplied when the recipe is read is a fill, a mapping given by keyword to a slot, a place written $name in a list of sources (The Bellman factory §3.3).
  • A variant of an equation is another stage folder beside the first, holding the changed stage file, which a second recipe names under the same stage key in place of the first, as tenure: {stage: stages/tenure_flat/tenure_flat.bl, …} names the stage file of a folder stages/tenure_flat/.

Distinct uses of one stage file need distinct stage keys, each with its own bindings, also when the two uses stand in one period.

docs.title: 4 What each file contains
docs.text:
File Contents declaration/stages/<stage>/<stage>.bl The stage file: the declarations, typed blocks and equations of one stage. declaration/stages/<stage>/methods.yml The stage's methods: the targets that receive numerical methods, and the method chosen at each (Methodization). declaration/methods/<name>.bl A block file: the method blocks and the marginal blocks that a methods entry names under block:, by a path from the methods file's folder (Methodization §4.1). It stands beside the methods files that name it; a stage's own methods file, which stands in the stage's folder, names it by the path ../../methods/<name>.bl, as the stages of the retirement-choice application do. declaration/methods/ is the one folder outside a stage's folder that holds a .bl file. declaration/stages/<stage>/<stage>.md The stage's note, which explains the stage file. declaration/calibration/<name>.yml Economic parameter values, under the top key calibration. declaration/settings/<name>.yml Numerical setting values, under the top key settings. declaration/period.yml The period file: the stage keys of one period and the connectors within it. declaration/trellis.yml The trellis file: the periods of the model, each written out or given by a period file repeated, and the inter-period connectors. declaration/spec.yml The recipe: the path of the trellis file and of each stage's file, from this folder; for each stage and each kind, the ordered sources and slots; the registry block. README.md The folder's first page (§2.5). economics.md The economics in full (§2.5). code/ The model's programs: code that writes values into the syntactic trellis, supplies boundary data or calls numerical routines. tests/ The model's tests, such as the structural test that parses each stage file and compares its terms with terms written by hand. reference/ The papers the model rests on, as PDF files. results/ What the model's programs write (§2.6). paper/ For each stage, the two files Bellman Workbench's button paper writes once and never rewrites: <stage>.md, the printed card of each of the stage's builders (A builder), the link to the drawing and a footnote with the SHA-256 digest of the stage file and of each file the stage is bound from; and <stage>.svg, the drawing of the graph of the stage's backward builders. An author converts the Markdown to LaTeX with Pandoc.

A file is read whether it is spelled .yml or .yaml, and a calibration, settings or methods file is told apart by its top key, not by its name or its extension. A connector selects a continuation state field of one stage occurrence and an arrival state field of another without changing either local name; an inter-period connector does so between consecutive periods. A bare endpoint must identify one eligible field at its side of the connection; a stage key qualifies an ambiguous endpoint (Periods §2). The recipe chooses the sources of each binding; it contains no stage equation and determines the sequence of periods only through the trellis file it names.

docs.title: 5 Paths in a model's documents
docs.text: The documents of a model folder, its README.md, its economics.md, its stage notes and the docstrings of its code, write a path in one of two ways. A path that says where a file of the folder stands is written from the model folder, declaration/stages/tenure/tenure.bl or declaration/calibration/durables.yml, whichever document writes it. A path quoted as a recipe or a trellis file writes it is kept as that file writes it, from the file's own folder, and is introduced as that file's line: the recipe's stage: stages/tenure/tenure.bl, or its methods source stages/tenure/methods.

docs.title: 6 Paths and the readers
docs.text:
The functions that read files interpret their path arguments differently:

Reader Path supplied bellman.stage.load_stage(path) A .bl file, read into a record. bellman.trellis.load_trellis(file) A trellis file of records; the stage files and the mapping files it names are read from its folder. bellman.trellis.load_recipe(directory, recipe) A registry, in a model folder its declaration/, and the name of its recipe, spec.yml or a variant's spec.<name>.yml; the trellis file and the stage files are the paths the recipe writes, read from that folder. bellman.trellis.assemble_trellis(directory, recipe) The same two arguments; the specified trellis in one call.

load_recipe returns the syntactic trellis, and assemble_trellis elaborates and binds it in one call. load_trellis reads a trellis file whose periods write their stages as records, each naming its stage file and its three mappings inline or as paths, and needs no recipe. An application can also build the trellis dictionary itself, one period at a time with bellman.trellis.accrete. The trellis factory states these calls.

A record that elaborate_trellis of bellman.trellis reads holds a stage mapping with text and origin, as load_stage writes it, and mapping-valued calibration, settings and methods; a path string in place of the mapping is refused. Precedence is settled in the syntactic trellis before elaboration; the elaborator and the verbs merge no file and no default. The factory API gives the complete record. Moving a file requires updating the recipe, the trellis file or the application code that names it.

docs.title: 7 Stage files in the earlier YAML form
docs.text: load_stage of bellman.stage reads a stage file written in .bl and refuses any other file under the rule readable-file of Refusals. A stage written in the earlier YAML format is therefore rewritten in .bl, since changing its extension translates none of its declarations, type words, equations or shock laws. YAML remains the format of the recipe, the trellis and period files, and the calibration, settings and methods files. The earlier YAML stages of the portfolio–consumption application are kept, as recorded sources of its fixed reference, under applications/cons-port/reference/legacy/syntax/.

docs.title: 8 Related references
docs.text:
• Trellises states the trellis file, the period file and the paths a recipe writes.
  • Methodization describes the methods file and the settings and calibration files beside it.
  • Stage functions specifies loading, elaborating and binding one stage.
  • Period functions specifies accretion and the order of a period.
  • Recipe functions specifies the recipe, its merge and its slots.
  • The trellis factory specifies the trellis file and the calls on a trellis.
  • Bellman Workbench opens a model folder and writes a new one in this layout.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
Summary

A builder of a stage is composed of primitive operators, and its card lists them under its operations, one row each, with what the row reads, what it writes and its rule. Every row of a card is of one of eight kinds. This page says which lines of a stage file form a row of each kind and in which builder it stands, and lists the operations of the package's table of definitions, the eight kinds and the one relation that is no kind, each with its defining expression, the operator of the Bellman calculus it denotes and the entry of the table that defines it.

Relationship with other documents

Formal account — Appendix E.3 Operators §4: the operator each kind realizes, with its domain and codomain. Builds on — The builders graphs and A builder: the builders, their cards and the names of their rows, printed from the package. See also — Shock distributions: what an expectation integrates against and a distribution extension extends a measure by; Methodization §3: where a method may be bound.

Key terminology Term What it names Builder The operator one block of a stage file denotes: backward on value functions, forward on finite measures of the states, such as their probability distribution. A builder is reached by the pair of perches it joins, stage.builder["cntn", "dcsn"], or from the perch its edge leaves, stage.dcsn.builder.bwd or stage.arvl.builder.fwd; the policy builder is stage.dcsn.builder.policy. Card What a builder, or one of the operators in it, prints: its inputs and outputs, its operations and the lines of the stage file they come from. print(stage.dcsn.builder.bwd) prints the card of the decision builder. Row One primitive operator of a builder, listed on the card under its operations with a number, a name, what it reads (in), what it writes (out) and its rule. Grain How far the boxes of a graph, the operators it holds, are opened: stage.builder.bwd holds one box per builder, and at the primitive grain, stage.builder.bwd.primitives, one box per primitive operator; see semgraph. Kind Which of the eight primitive operators a row is, named in the row's name after the builder or the line: Pullback in cntn_to_dcsn:Pullback. Rule The equation or relation a row states, printed under the row, read at a point of the row's domain. Edge The step from one perch to the next that one forward builder carries. Law of motion The map 𝑔 that a forward block's lines define, from the states of one perch, with the control and the shock where the block reads them, to the states of the next. Value aggregator 𝐺 The map a backward line applies pointwise to the functions it reads, its right side read as a function of them; see aggregation. Policy The function the policy builder writes, 𝑐 of the decision state. A builder stated at the policy reads it as a fixed function, which the builder's card names under At. Declared carrier The set of functions in which the stage declares an output to lie: from the states of its perch to the set its block's header declares for it, and for a policy only the functions whose values are feasible.

docs.title: 1 Reading a row
docs.text:
A card lists the rows of a builder in the order in which they apply, each after every row whose output it reads. A row has a number, a name, what it reads, what it writes and its rule. The name is the builder, or the address of the line the row realizes, followed by the kind: cntn_to_dcsn:Pullback, policy.InvEuler:Aggregation, policy:Evaluation; the builder's own card leaves out the builder, InvEuler:Aggregation, Evaluation. Where one builder or one line holds several rows of one kind, a number, a label or the shocks the row concerns tell them apart, value:Expectation:1, arvl_to_dcsn:DistributionExtension:ψ. An input written as a number in brackets, (1), is the output of the row with that number. The API page on a builder, linked in the box above, prints the cards of cons.bl, the consumption stage of the portfolio application, and says how each entry of a card's Operations is read.

Five kinds stand in the backward builders, which act on functions, and three in the forward builders, which act on finite measures. Each builder is named below by the pair of perches it joins, as the title of its card prints it, cntn → dcsn for the decision builder, which stage.builder["cntn", "dcsn"] reads (The builders graphs §1); the policy builder is named by its own key, policy. The lines of a stage file form the rows of each kind as follows.

  • Pullback: the lines of a backward block that read functions of the later perch at the states of an earlier perch form one row that composes those functions with the law of motion of the forward block on the same edge, a = m_d - c in cons.bl. Such a row stands in cntn → dcsn, along 𝑔≻ read at the policy, and in dcsn → arvl, along 𝑔≺; in policy one stands along 𝑔≻ where an objective or residuals that the builder constructs read such a function, as the solve_{…}(…) line of port.bl does, and the identification line of §4 forms another, along the coordinate map 𝑚_d≻. Where the forward block branches, as in ret_choice.bl, one such row stands for each branch, Pullback:work and Pullback:retire, along the law of motion read at that branch's label, 𝑔_work≻(a_d) = 𝑔≻(a_d, work). A policy line written at the continuation perch, its left side marked [>], such as c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) ⟂ a >= 0 in cons.bl, reads the function at the continuation states and forms none.
  • Aggregation: the lines of a backward block that write its values together form one in the block's builder, dcsn → arvl or cntn → dcsn, each right side read as the value aggregator 𝐺 and printed as one equation of the row's rule, as V = 𝑢(c) + V[>] alone forms the Aggregation of cntn → dcsn in cons.bl. A derivative line of the same block, D_{m_d}V = 𝑑𝑢(c), forms no part of it: it states the derivative of the value the builder writes and stands at the builder's Evaluation. In a policy block, or in a method block that opens the policy builder, adjacent explicit lines written at the continuation perch together form one, as c[>] = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(β*D_{a}V[>]) and m[>] = a + c[>] of the method block of buffer_stock_egm.bl, which the buffer-stock methods file binds on policy, form g_cntn_to_dcsn:Aggregation, and a line stating a relation, a solve_{…}(…) line and the objective of an argmax_{…}(…) line not marked !doc each form one, in policy (§4). In both kinds of block, a line that takes the expectation of an expression other than one function it reads forms one more for that expression: in port.bl, the row of the derivative line of cntn → dcsn, which the package's card names marginal:Aggregation:1, and foc:Aggregation:1 of policy; a line marked !node forms its own in its sub-builder and joins no other.
  • Expectation: an occurrence E_{θ}(·) in a line of a backward block forms one, one row per occurrence on the builder's card, value:Expectation:1; at the primitive grain of the whole graph, stage.builder.bwd.primitives, the expectations of a block's several lines stand as one box named by the block, cntn_to_dcsn:Expectation in port.bl, which is the name the table below shows. In policy, the objective of an argmax_{…}(…) line forms one where it holds an expectation, as in ez_savings.bl.
  • Argmax: an argmax_{…}(…) line of a policy block that is not marked !doc forms one, in policy, as d = argmax_{d}(V_w[>] - δ, V_r[>]) in ret_choice.bl.
  • Evaluation: no line forms one. It is the closing row of every backward builder, the policy builder among them, and of every sub-builder, the operator a line marked !node denotes, and it places each output in its declared carrier. On the card of policy of cons.bl its rule is the declared carrier with its feasibility, 𝑐 : Xm → ℝ₊₊, 𝑐(m_d) ∈ Γ(m_d), since the relation that defines the function it carries is printed at the row that forms it, cons_choice:Pullback; the row's own card, stage.dcsn.builder.policy["Evaluation"], prints that relation under Rule, 𝑐(𝑚_d≻(a)) = 𝑐≻(a) on 𝑚_d≻(Xa).
  • DistributionExtension: a ~ line declaring the distribution of a shock forms one, one row per declaration, in the forward builder whose block lists the shock among its inputs.
  • PolicyInsertion: no line forms one, and no card shows one (§3).
  • Pushforward: the lines of a forward block, which define its law of motion, a = m_d - c in cons.bl, form one. It is the closing row of every forward builder, arvl → dcsn and dcsn → cntn, the latter along the law of motion read at the policy (§3).

docs.title: 2 The kinds and the relation
docs.text:
The table has one row for each operation that the package's table of definitions, PRIMITIVE_DEFINITIONS, defines, in that table's order: the eight kinds, and the relation that the rows of §4 read, which is no kind. The column operation names it, and kind of a row says whether a row of a card can be of it. written gives the first row of it on the stage files under applications/, read with cons.bl and port.bl of the portfolio application first: the lines of the file that the row realizes, one line or the lines of a block, then the row's name, the file and the builder that holds it, written as the key of stage.builder that reads it; where no stage file forms such a row, the cell says so. reads and writes gives what that row reads and writes, its in and out lines as its card prints them. rule gives that row's rule as the row's own card prints it, stated for the row's own functions, and §§1, 3 and 4 quote those of cons.bl; definition gives the operation's defining expression in the table of definitions, as the package prints it. denotes links to the section of Appendix E.3 that defines the operator the operation realizes. read from names the module, the table and the key of the definition, which states the defining map and its conditions exactly; primitive_definition in the same module returns the definition by its key.

docs.title: 3 Rows at the policy
docs.text:
The backward decision builder and the forward decision builder are each stated at the policy: the law of motion, the value aggregator and any conditional distribution of a shock read the policy as a fixed function, and none of them takes the policy builder's output as an input. The law of motion read at the policy, the map m_d ↦ 𝑔≻(m_d, 𝑐(m_d)), which a card writes out where a rule reads it and names nowhere, holds the insertion of the policy: a Pushforward along it is the insertion followed by the push-forward along 𝑔≻, and a Pullback along it the pullback along 𝑔≻ followed by the insertion, as Appendix E.3 §4 states. That is why no card shows a PolicyInsertion row, while the table of definitions keeps the insertion as a kind.

On the cards of cons.bl, the Pullback of cntn → dcsn has the rule (𝑉≻ ∘ 𝑔≻(·, 𝑐))(m_d) = 𝑉≻(𝑔≻(m_d, 𝑐(m_d))) and its Aggregation the rule 𝑉(m_d) = 𝑢(𝑐(m_d)) + 𝑉≻(𝑔≻(m_d, 𝑐(m_d))), and the closing Pushforward of dcsn → cntn has the rule μ≻(B) = μ({m_d ∈ Xm | 𝑔≻(m_d, 𝑐(m_d)) ∈ B}). Each reads the policy 𝑐 as a fixed function.

docs.title: 4 Lines that state their output implicitly
docs.text: In a policy block, a line may state its output only implicitly. Appendix C R8 and R10 state how such a line is read. In cons.bl the line m_d[>] = a + c[>] defines the coordinate map 𝑚_d≻, the cash on hand at each saving, and the identification line c = c[>] forms a Pullback whose rule equates the policy read along the coordinate map with the candidate policy 𝑐≻ at each saving, the grid relation 𝑐(𝑚_d≻(a)) = 𝑐≻(a) on 𝑚_d≻(Xa); a line stating a relation, c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) ⟂ a >= 0, forms an Aggregation whose rule is that relation, 𝑐≻(a) ≤ 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}𝑉≻(a)) ⟂ a ≥ 0 on the card of policy; and a solve_{…}(…) line forms an Aggregation whose rule is its system of residuals. The identification row, the row of a solve_{…}(…) line and the row of a relation line that holds its output on both sides each denote the set of the functions that satisfy their rule at every point the row admits, which may be empty or hold several functions, and read the one relation definition of the same table, which is the definition of no kind; stage.dcsn.builder.policy["cons_choice:Pullback"].signature() prints that set. A relation line one of whose sides is the output's name alone and the other an explicit function of the row's inputs, as c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) ⟂ a >= 0 in cons.bl, is read by the definition of its kind, the relation with its clause standing as its rule. Its output is a correspondence, a map that gives each point a set of values, which a card writes with ⇉: the clause admits at each positive saving the one value 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}𝑉≻(a)) and at zero saving every value up to it (Appendix C, R10), so stage.dcsn.builder.policy["InvEuler:Aggregation"].signature() prints 𝑐≻ : Xa ⇉ ℝ₊₊. Its kernel() answers the map of the explicit side, 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}𝑉≻), and compile_kernel() refuses it under kernel-form, since the row reads a derivative term. No row selects a member of a set: a selection is the numerical method's.

docs.title: 5 Lines that form no row
docs.text: Two kinds of line form no row. A line marked !doc states what the construction is meant to reach and prints under Declared, and a line attached to another by a dotted id is a property of that line: it forms no row, the row of that line holds it, and that row's own card lists the property line under Source. Methodization §3 states at which rows and builders a method may be bound, and stage.places() lists them for one stage.

docs.title: Refusals
docs.text:
Summary

A stage file the package cannot read is refused, and so is a method target that names no place of a stage and a compilation the stage does not support. Every refusal says four things: where it is, what stands there, why it cannot be read, and what to write instead. This page lists every rule the package refuses under, each with the smallest example that breaks it and the refusal that example provokes. Every listing below is printed from the package, so what you read here is what your own session prints.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Stage tutorial: the file whose rules these are, written line by line. Used by — The stage: the object a file becomes once it passes them.

A refusal of the file is raised when the file is read: elaboration returns a stage or refuses the file. A refusal is held rather than raised only where the construction builds no graph for a form the file writes: the stage then holds a refusal under not-constructed in place of that graph, as it does for the forward builders graph where a shock's distribution names a family outside the table of Shock distributions. A method target is refused when methodize binds it, a setting's value when configure reads it, and a compilation when compile_kernel() is asked for it. Each refusal carries the rule it names as a field, so an editor or a script reads the rule rather than the sentence.

docs.title: 1 The four parts
docs.text:
Take the consumption stage and write ] where a side of a block's header closes with ). The parser stops at that character, and the refusal reads:

from bellman.refusal_examples import EXAMPLES
from bellman.refusal_catalogue import refusal_of

print(refusal_of(EXAMPLES["syntax"]))

cons.bl:16:40: the file writes `]` here, and the language admits `)` or `,` at this place
    [id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m_d, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊] : !dcsn -> (a : Xa) : !cntn] {
                                           ^
a side of a block header: a side is parenthesized in general; a single coordinate may stand bare (V : !dcsn -> …) (rule syntax)

Where is the file, the line and the column, which leads every refusal, as an editor and a compiler both print it. What is the line of the file with a mark under the column. Why is what the file writes there and the forms the language admits at that place, in the spellings you write them in. What to write is the sentence the grammar keeps for that place, given where the position falls — here inside the side of a block header.

A word the vocabulary does not hold is refused in the same four parts, at the word itself:

from bellman.refusal_examples import Example
from bellman.refusal_catalogue import refusal_of

print(refusal_of(Example(
    rule="syntax", address=None, words=(),
    text="@stage: t\n[id=b, (x : ℝ) : !contrl -> (y : ℝ) : !dcsn] {\n    y = x\n}\n")))

t.bl:2:18: the file writes `!contrl` here, which is no word-type of the language
    [id=b, (x : ℝ) : !contrl -> (y : ℝ) : !dcsn] {
                     ^
the word-types are !arvl, !cntn, !ctrl, !dcsn, !shck, !state, !vlu (rule syntax)

docs.title: 2 The three vocabularies of rules
docs.text:
The package refuses under three closed vocabularies. The rules of graph construction are claims about the authored file: that it names itself once, that every name it writes is declared where it is used, that a forward block's header lists every field its lines read and a backward block's the value fields its lines read, with the controls at which they are read. The rules of the identity table are the rules by which the string written after on: in a methods file is read: which places a target may name and how each is spelled. The rules of the Bellman factory are claims about a model's files and the dictionaries made from them: the recipe, its source files and its fills, the trellis file, the records, the joins of a period, and a file given by its path to load_stage or to a binding verb, which is read as one YAML mapping with each key written once; each refusal names the file or the address, what stands there, why it is refused and what to write.

A representation method, such as !Linear, is attached to the Evaluation of a builder, and the methods file writes that place: <block-id>.evaluate for the policy builder, whose Evaluation stores the policy function, and <block-id>.evaluate.value or <block-id>.evaluate.marginal for a backward value builder, whose Evaluation stores the value function and the derivative of it that a derivative line states (Methodization §2). The identity table refuses a representation named on a builder (representation-on-builder), one named on a derivative line (representation-on-derivative-line), and evaluate alone in a stage that authors no evaluate occurrence (rule (g)); each refusal names the address to write.

A representation names its basis as the method, such as !Linear, and its grid by the setting grid, whose value is the grid's kind written as a tag, grid: !Cartesian, with the grid's fields orders and bounds beside it; the endogenous grid method names its exogenous grid of savings in the same way (Methodization §3). The identity table refuses these forms under three rules: a kind of grid written as a method (grid-kind-as-method), the fields of a grid written without the setting grid that names its kind (grid-without-kind), and a grid written at the Evaluation of the policy builder where !egm stores the pairs that are the knots of the interpolant (grid-under-egm); each refusal names the form to write or the reason.

A rule is written once, in the package, and a refusal names it. The three vocabularies are:

from bellman.refusals import FACTORY_RULES, RULES, TARGET_RULES

for vocabulary, rules in (("graph construction", RULES), ("the identity table", TARGET_RULES),
                          ("the Bellman factory", FACTORY_RULES)):
    print(vocabulary)
    print("\n".join("  " + rule for rule in rules))

The table gives each rule of graph construction: written, the rule's name as a refusal closes with it, (rule X), or ; rule X) after the address the refusal names; claim, what the rule requires of a stage file, in the words of the package; denotes, a dash, since a rule is a claim about the file and not an object of the Bellman calculus; and read from, the module under packages/bellman/bellman/, its table and the key.

rule written claim denotes read from syntax (rule syntax) The file is written in the forms the grammar admits, and every !-marked word is one of the vocabulary. It is the first rule a file meets: the refusal is raised where the parser or the lowering stops, and names the forms admitted at that place. — refusals.py, RULES, "syntax" marginal-role-retired (rule marginal-role-retired) The roles !mrgnvl and !sndmrgnvl are retired from the language: a backward header lists value fields and controls, and a derivative of a value is the term D_{x}V (AMD-MB-001 §4.1). — refusals.py, RULES, "marginal-role-retired" stage-name (rule stage-name) The file names itself once: exactly one @stage line, with a name. — refusals.py, RULES, "stage-name" declared-once (rule declared-once) Each name, block id, statement id, and law is written once. — refusals.py, RULES, "declared-once" defined-once (rule defined-once) Within one block, an operative equation defines each name-sided left side once, and a derivative line states each derivative term, D_{m}V, once. A documentary line (!doc) defines and states none. — refusals.py, RULES, "defined-once" one-name-one-meaning (rule one-name-one-meaning) A name is a field, a function, a named space, a shock, or a parameter — one of them — and is not the name of a numerical operator. — refusals.py, RULES, "one-name-one-meaning" parameter-or-field (rule parameter-or-field) A top-level scalar declaration is a parameter; only a shock is both declared at the top level and listed on the side of a block. — refusals.py, RULES, "parameter-or-field" field-perch (rule field-perch) Every listed field has one perch, fixed by its side's perch word, its mark, or its role, and the three must agree. — refusals.py, RULES, "field-perch" name-in-scope (rule name-in-scope) Every name a statement or a definition body mentions is declared where the statement stands, and every set a typing names, n_m : Foo, is a named set the stage defines or a set of the language. — refusals.py, RULES, "name-in-scope" family-selection (rule family-selection) A selection takes a coordinate of a declared family by a key the family admits. — refusals.py, RULES, "family-selection" well-typed (rule well-typed) Every operation of a line, a function body or a declared set reads values of the kinds it takes: arithmetic, an ordered comparison and the bounds of an interval read numbers, and a label is no number; a function is applied to as many arguments as it declares, each of the kind it declares; Inv inverts one function; the two sides of a line are of one kind, and its left side names one field for each result of its right side. — refusals.py, RULES, "well-typed" divisor-nonzero (rule divisor-nonzero) A divisor the file writes as a number is not zero: a division by a written zero is defined at no point (the definedness conditions of the fold). — refusals.py, RULES, "divisor-nonzero" shock-observed (rule shock-observed) A statement's perch has observed every shock the statement's right side depends on; otherwise the statement asks for an expectation. — refusals.py, RULES, "shock-observed" shock-reintroduced (rule shock-reintroduced) A backward function does not read a shock again beside a term whose expectation has integrated it. — refusals.py, RULES, "shock-reintroduced" forward-composite (rule forward-composite) The fields a statement's right side mentions are at the left side's perch, before it, or forward of it along the stage's transitions. — refusals.py, RULES, "forward-composite" one-builder-per-output (rule one-builder-per-output) One block writes a field between two perches: a second block that joins the same perches and writes a field the first writes is refused naming both blocks. — refusals.py, RULES, "one-builder-per-output" candidate-coordinate (rule candidate-coordinate) A candidate line of a policy block, x[>] = …, names a control at the candidate points, c[>], a state of the decision perch, the grid line m[>] = a + c[>], or the value candidate an upper envelope of the block compares; any other name is refused with the coordinates in scope. — refusals.py, RULES, "candidate-coordinate" candidate-read (rule candidate-read) A candidate a policy block writes is read by a later line of the block or is the grid line, whose points are the knots of the policy; a candidate nothing reads is refused naming the line. — refusals.py, RULES, "candidate-read" transition-without-expectation (rule transition-without-expectation) A transition block's statements define the state transition g and contain no expectation: the forward builder is the push-forward of a measure through g, and integration over a shock belongs to a value block (Operators and builders, §"Forward operators"). — refusals.py, RULES, "transition-without-expectation" one-implicit-statement (rule one-implicit-statement) A block has at most one implicit statement for each output field. — refusals.py, RULES, "one-implicit-statement" definition-order (rule definition-order) The function definitions have a dependency order, and each applies a defined function. — refusals.py, RULES, "definition-order" derivative-one-name (rule derivative-one-name) A derivative names one formal argument, not several arguments at once. — refusals.py, RULES, "derivative-one-name" derivative-scalar-coordinate (rule derivative-scalar-coordinate) The one formal argument a derivative names is scalar, not product-valued. — refusals.py, RULES, "derivative-scalar-coordinate" derivative-coordinate (rule derivative-coordinate) A derivative of a value field, D_{a}V[>], names a state coordinate of the perch at which the field is read, and not a discrete one (AMD-MB-001 §4.2); for the value of a branch, D_{a_w}V_w[>], a state the branch writes. — refusals.py, RULES, "derivative-coordinate" stage-boundary (rule stage-boundary) Every field is produced and consumed: a block writes it or the stage receives it, and a block reads it or the stage delivers it. — refusals.py, RULES, "stage-boundary" output-defined (rule output-defined) Every required block output has an equation. — refusals.py, RULES, "output-defined" grid-line-consistency (rule grid-line-consistency) A grid line, a line that writes a decision state under the continuation mark (m_d[>] = a + c[>]), agrees with the law of motion solved for that state at the candidates: its right side and the law of motion so solved reduce to one expression, every function read as an opaque symbol. — refusals.py, RULES, "grid-line-consistency" identity-collision (rule identity-collision) No authored name collides with the spelling of an identity: a name containing the colon that separates its segments, or a name equal to one of the words a reader tests for in the last segment — result, declared, merged. — refusals.py, RULES, "identity-collision" readable-form (rule readable-form) The item is a form the construction rules read. — refusals.py, RULES, "readable-form" typing-entry-unattached (rule typing-entry-unattached) A typing entry or a handler binding, policy.method : !egm, is written in a methods file, which the union attaches to its stage and the semantics reads; a stage elaborated alone carries none. — refusals.py, RULES, "typing-entry-unattached" declared-twice (rule declared-twice) Over the files of a stage, a component is typed once, whether by an absolute or a relative spelling of its path, a name is defined once, or identically in each file, and a line id names one line of a block; the union of the stage file and its additions refuses a second entry, definition or line naming both positions. — refusals.py, RULES, "declared-twice" label-not-in-parent (rule label-not-in-parent) A nested block of an addition merges with the branch of the same label under its parent, and a path inside a block names a line or an operator of that block: a label the parent lacks, and a first segment that names another block, are refused. — refusals.py, RULES, "label-not-in-parent" type-conflict (rule type-conflict) The field names determine a signature: a coordinate an addition restates keeps the stage's typing, and a different type on it, or a different perch word on its side, is refused. — refusals.py, RULES, "type-conflict" metadata-mismatch (rule metadata-mismatch) An addition names the stage it adds to, @methods: <stage>, with the name the stage file gives itself, and a metadata line of another key agrees with the stage file's line of that key. — refusals.py, RULES, "metadata-mismatch" multiplier-declaration (rule multiplier-declaration) A multiplier is declared inside the block whose continuation grid it extends, once, marked [>], with one declared set and one bound after ⟂ that names continuation states, multipliers of the block, parameters, numbers or inf. — refusals.py, RULES, "multiplier-declaration" set-mismatch (rule set-mismatch) A field produced on one declared set and consumed on another is declared with sets whose inclusion holds; otherwise the stage declares the inclusion through the control's feasible set. — refusals.py, RULES, "set-mismatch" category-codes (rule category-codes) A set marked !categories is a nonempty range of integers written as a comprehension over ℤ or ℕ, whose annotation gives each member one category name and each name one member. The marker is written only on a top-level named set, and a field declared on a set with category codes names that set at every site that names a set. — refusals.py, RULES, "category-codes" value-input-role (rule value-input-role) A statement of a backward block reads values or marginal values, not both: its kernel acts on one role and its output has that role. — refusals.py, RULES, "value-input-role" signature-complete (rule signature-complete) A forward block's header lists every field its lines read that no earlier line of the block defines. A backward block's header lists the value fields its lines read and the controls at which they are read, but no state; a state of its output perch is a coordinate. A value field a backward header lists and no line of the block reads is admitted: it is left out of the block's builder and recorded as a diagnostic, unread-input, in place of a refusal. — refusals.py, RULES, "signature-complete" header-coordinate (rule header-coordinate) A backward block's header lists the value fields it reads and writes and the controls at which its lines are read, and no state: a state of the perch at which its output stands is a coordinate of the output function, and a state of its input perch is reached through the law of motion. — refusals.py, RULES, "header-coordinate" input-perch-state (rule input-perch-state) A backward line reads a state of its input or a later perch only through the law of motion. A direct read is refused, including in a relation or a condition after ⟂. A read under the expectation over the edge's shock and continuation-state indexing on a policy candidate line are admitted. — refusals.py, RULES, "input-perch-state" kernel-form (rule kernel-form) A kernel that compile_kernel writes as a Python function is retained arithmetic and calls to closed-form functions; a symbolic derivative has no compile rule. The function takes the values of the parameters it reads as arguments, so a symbolic version compiles too and answers no values, parameter_values None. — refusals.py, RULES, "kernel-form" method-option-value (rule method-option-value) Every configured method option has the type its public method row names. — refusals.py, RULES, "method-option-value" kernel-target (rule kernel-target) kernel and compile read a primitive operator box, and compile one whose kernel is g or G. — refusals.py, RULES, "kernel-target" distribution-dependency (rule distribution-dependency) The distribution declarations read one another without a cycle, and a declaration does not read its own subject. — refusals.py, RULES, "distribution-dependency" distribution-edge (rule distribution-edge) The shocks of connected declarations are drawn on the edge of one forward builder. — refusals.py, RULES, "distribution-edge" distribution-domain (rule distribution-domain) A declaration's family parameters lie in the family's domain: matched dimensions, a symmetric positive semidefinite covariance, nonnegative variances and deviations, finite endpoints in order, positive scales, and real arguments that have a number. — refusals.py, RULES, "distribution-domain" conditional-not-declared (rule conditional-not-declared) The conditional distribution an expectation needs is a declared conditional, a product of them, or a marginal or conditional of a joint normal declaration whose conditioning block is positive definite. — refusals.py, RULES, "conditional-not-declared" branch-form (rule branch-form) A branching block holds one labeled nested block per label and nothing else, at least two, in the forward block from the decision perch to the continuation perch, whose own output side is empty; a nested block has an empty input side and writes continuation fields. — refusals.py, RULES, "branch-form" branch-labels (rule branch-labels) The nested blocks carry the labels of the block's label coordinate, a control or a shock with its law, whose set is a finite set of at least two labels, each once and in the set's order. — refusals.py, RULES, "branch-labels" branch-tuple-mismatch (rule branch-tuple-mismatch) The value line selects by one tuple indexed by the label coordinate, one entry per label, and the policy maximizes over the same tuple in the same order; a branch a shock selects is read under the expectation over the shock alone. — refusals.py, RULES, "branch-tuple-mismatch" branch-value-position (rule branch-value-position) A continuation value stands at one position of the selection tuples, the position of the branch on whose fields it is a function. — refusals.py, RULES, "branch-value-position" branch-law (rule branch-law) The law of a label shock gives one probability to each label in the order of the labels, Categorical((p₁, …, pₙ)) or Bernoulli(p) over two. — refusals.py, RULES, "branch-law" not-constructed (rule not-constructed) The item is a form of the language the construction does not read (NotConstructed). — refusals.py, RULES, "not-constructed" block-header-mismatch (rule block-header-mismatch) A method block's header matches the builder the methods file opens with it: the block joins the builder's perches, writes the builder's outputs, and reads the builder's inputs or inputs its header declares with a set and a role (specification 0.6 §4.1). — refusals.py, RULES, "block-header-mismatch" block-name-undefined (rule block-name-undefined) A line of a method block calls a function the stage file or the block file defines, or a primitive function of the language (specification 0.6 §4.1). — refusals.py, RULES, "block-name-undefined"

docs.title: 3 The catalogue
docs.text:
Every rule with the four parts of its refusal, provoked from the smallest example the package keeps for it. The example of each rule is the text the refusal test provokes, so a rule that changes is read here and in the test at once.

from bellman.refusal_catalogue import catalogue

print(catalogue())

syntax  (graph construction)
  where  cons.bl, line 16, column 40
  what
    [id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m_d, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊] : !dcsn -> (a : Xa) : !cntn] {
                                           ^
  why    the file writes `]` here, and the language admits `)` or `,` at this place
  write  a side of a block header: a side is parenthesized in general; a single coordinate may stand bare (V : !dcsn -> …)

marginal-role-retired  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 2, column 91
  what
    [id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊) : !cntn -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu, dV : ℝ₊₊ @ !mrgnvl) : !dcsn] {
                                                                                              ^
  why    the file writes `!mrgnvl` here, a role retired from the language: a backward header lists value fields and controls alone, and a derivative of a value is written as the term `D_{x}V`, with `x` a state coordinate of the value's perch, such as `D_{m}V` or `D_{a}V[>]` (AMD-MB-001 §4.1)
  write  remove the field from the header; write the line that defined it as a derivative line, `D_{m}V = …`, and read the derivative as the term `D_{a}V[>]`

stage-name  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 2, column 1 (address '2')
  what
    @stage: two
    ^
  why    2 '@stage' lines name the stage: 'one' at t.bl:1:1 (term address '1'), 'two' at t.bl:2:1 (term address '2'); a stage file has exactly one, so delete all but the line that names it

declared-once  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 5, column 5 (address 'b.3')
  what
        y = u + z :: [!node]
        ^
  why    an authored node requires a nonempty explicit id; write an id before the mark, `:: [id=<name>, !node]`

defined-once  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 4, column 5 (address 'b.second')
  what
        W = 2*V[>] :: [id=second, !node]
        ^
  why    block 'b' already defines W at t.bl:3:5 (term address 'b.first'), and this operative equation defines it again; an operative left side is defined once within a block
  write  Remove one definition, give one result another name, or mark a line that only documents the model `!doc`.

one-name-one-meaning  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 3, column 1 (address 'b')
  what
    [id=b, (x : ℝ) : !dcsn -> (y : ℝ) : !dcsn] {
    ^
  why    'y' is a field, first listed here, and a function, defined at t.bl:2:1 (term address '2'); a name has one meaning in a stage

parameter-or-field  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 2, column 1 (address '2')
  what
    c : ℝ₊ @ !ctrl
    ^
  why    the top-level declaration of 'c' carries the role word for 'control', but no block header lists 'c': a role belongs to a field, and a field is a name a block reads or writes, while a top-level declaration that no header lists is a parameter, a number calibration binds. List 'c' on a side of the block that uses it, or drop the role word and leave it a parameter

field-perch  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 2, column 1 (address 'b')
  what
    [id=b, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn -> (W : ℝ) : !dcsn] {
    ^
  why    the mark on V[>] places the field at the cntn perch, but the input side of block 'b' is marked `: !dcsn`; a mark agrees with its side's perch word (D06)

name-in-scope  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 3, column 5 (address 'b.1')
  what
        y = q
        ^
  why    the line mentions q, which the stage does not declare: it is no field of the stage, no line of block 'b' above it defines it, and it is no parameter, shock, named space, or function. Declare it, or write one of the names in scope here: x, y

family-selection  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 3, column 5 (address 'b.1')
  what
        y = (a, b)[q]
        ^
  why    the selection (a, b)[q] selects by 'q', which the stage does not declare; a key requires a finite set of 2 members

well-typed  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 4, column 5 (address 'b.1')
  what
        w = 𝑓 + 1
        ^
  why    `𝑓` is a function, and `𝑓 + 1` reads it as a number; arithmetic, an ordered comparison and the bounds of an interval read numbers. Apply the function to its arguments, `𝑓(…)`

divisor-nonzero  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 3, column 5 (address 'b.1')
  what
        y = x/0
        ^
  why    `x/0` divides by zero, which is defined at no point; a divisor the file writes as a number is not zero. Write a divisor other than zero

shock-observed  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 31, column 5 (address 'dcsn_to_arvl.value')
  what
        V[<] = V                 :: [id=value]
        ^
  why    the line is read at the arvl perch and mentions V, a field at the dcsn perch; the edge from the arvl perch to the dcsn perch draws the shock y, so the value of V is not known at the arvl perch. Write the expectation over it, `E_{y}(…)`

shock-reintroduced  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 17, column 5 (address 'cntn_to_dcsn.value')
  what
        V = E_{y,z}(V[>]) + y :: [id=value]
        ^
  why    the line reads the shock y beside a term in which cntn_to_dcsn.value:Expectation:1 has already integrated y, and no other value input of that combination still depends on y; a backward function does not depend again on a shock after its expectation (AMD-SG-008 §4, rule shock-reintroduced); move the read of y inside that expectation, or integrate the combination after it

forward-composite  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 35, column 5 (address 'policy.g_cntn_to_dcsn')
  what
        w[>] = w                        :: [id=g_cntn_to_dcsn]
        ^
  why    the line is read at the cntn perch and mentions w, a field at the dcsn perch, which comes before it: a stage runs arrival, decision, continuation, so a line at the cntn perch is a function of the cntn state, and the file defines the cntn state from the dcsn state, not the dcsn state from the cntn state. Write the cntn-perch field the law of motion defines, or state the equation at the dcsn perch

one-builder-per-output  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 22, column 1 (address 'egm')
  what
    [id=egm, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {
    ^
  why    block 'egm' writes c at the dcsn perch from the cntn perch, which block 'policy' already writes; one builder writes a field between two perches (rule one-builder-per-output). Write the lines of the two blocks in one block, or make block 'egm' write another field
  write  Write the lines of the two blocks in one block, or make the second block write another field.

candidate-coordinate  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 19, column 5 (address 'policy.grid')
  what
        w[>] = a + c[>]        :: [id=grid]
        ^
  why    the line writes w[>], a candidate of 'w', which is no control and no state of the dcsn perch, and no upper envelope of block 'policy' compares it; a candidate line of a solution method names a control at the candidate points, a state of the decision perch, which is the grid line, or the value candidate an upper envelope reads (rule candidate-coordinate). The controls are c and the states of the dcsn perch are m
  write  Name a control at the candidate points, `c[>]`, or a state of the decision perch, the grid line `m[>] = a + c[>]`.

candidate-read  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 18, column 5 (address 'policy.InvEuler')
  what
        c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{a}V[>]) ⟂ a >= 0    :: [id=InvEuler]
        ^
  why    the line writes the candidate c[>], which no later line of block 'policy' reads; a candidate is read by a later line of the block, as an identification `c = c[>]` reads it, or is the grid line, a state of the decision perch at the candidates, whose points are the knots at which the policy is stored (rule candidate-read). Read the candidate on a later line, or remove the line
  write  Read the candidate on a later line of the block, or remove the line.

transition-without-expectation  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 5, column 5 (address 'step.1')
  what
        y = x + E_{z}(z)
        ^
  why    the transition block 'step' integrates over a shock in statement 'step.1'; a forward builder is the push-forward of a measure through the law of motion 𝑔 and takes no expectation; write the integration in a backward block

one-implicit-statement  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 8, column 5 (address 'policy.first')
  what
        c + 0 = c[>]   :: [id=first]
        ^
  why    2 statements of builder 'policy' (policy.first, policy.second) state a relation in 1 unknowns (c); a system of implicit statements is constructed where its statements are exactly as many as its unknowns. Write as many equations as there are unknowns, or name the unknowns a statement determines by the solve_{…} spelling, `c = solve_{c}(…)`

definition-order  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 2, column 1 (address '2')
  what
    𝑓(x : ℝ) := 𝑔(x)
    ^
  why    the function definitions form a cycle: 𝑓 (t.bl:2:1 (term address '2')) references 𝑔 (t.bl:3:1 (term address '3')) references 𝑓 (t.bl:2:1 (term address '2')). No dependency order exists, so no definition can be expanded; break the cycle

derivative-one-name  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 3, column 1 (address '3')
  what
    df := D_{x,y}(f)
    ^
  why    the derivative D_{x, y}(f) names 2 formal arguments (x, y); a derivative names exactly one formal argument
  write  Write one derivative for one named formal argument, such as `D_{x}(f)`.

derivative-scalar-coordinate  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 3, column 1 (address '3')
  what
    df := D_{x}(f)
    ^
  why    the derivative D_{x}(f) names the formal argument 'x' of function 'f', which is product-valued; a derivative names one scalar formal argument
  write  Declare scalar formal arguments and write one derivative with respect to one of them.

derivative-coordinate  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 7, column 5 (address 'policy.InvEuler')
  what
        c = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(D_{q}V[>]) :: [id=InvEuler]
        ^
  why    the derivative D_{q}V[>] names 'q', which is no state coordinate of the cntn perch, at which V[>] is read; a derivative of a value is taken in a state coordinate of the perch at which the value is read, written without its mark, and the coordinates of the cntn perch are a
  write  Name a state coordinate of the perch at which the value is read, `D_{a}V[>]`.

stage-boundary  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 24, column 1 (address 'dcsn_to_cntn')
  what
    [id=dcsn_to_cntn, (w, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊, z : ℝ) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊) : !cntn] {
    ^
  why    no block writes the field 'z' at the dcsn perch, and the stage does not receive it: the stage receives the continuation values and the arrival state, and a field at the dcsn perch in this position is neither. Write it as the output of a block, or list it where the stage receives it

output-defined  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 16, column 1 (address 'dcsn_to_cntn')
  what
    [id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m_d, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn -> (a : Xa) : !cntn] {
    ^
  why    block 'dcsn_to_cntn' declares output 'cons:cntn:a', but its body supplies no defining equation

grid-line-consistency  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 19, column 5 (address 'policy.grid')
  what
        m[>] = a + 2*c[>]      :: [id=grid]
        ^
  why    the grid line m[>] = a + 2*c[>] disagrees with the law of motion of block 'dcsn_to_cntn': with its line a = m - c solved for m at the candidate c[>], the law of motion gives m[>] = a + c[>], and a + 2*c[>] does not reduce to a + c[>] by algebraic simplification; write the grid line as the law of motion solved for m, m[>] = a + c[>]

identity-collision  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 2, column 1 (address 'b')
  what
    [id=b, (x : ℝ) : !dcsn -> (result : ℝ) : !dcsn] {
    ^
  why    the field 'result' is one of the reserved words result, declared, merged, by which a reader knows an occurrence's result wire, a declared wire and a merged box from the last segment of an identity; write another name for the field

readable-form  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 2, column 1 (address '2')
  what
    ρ : ℝ := 2
    ^
  why    the declaration of ρ carries a value; a stage file declares what a name is, not what it equals: calibration supplies the value, and the stage reads it through `.calibration`

typing-entry-unattached  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 2, column 1 (address '2')
  what
    policy.method : !egm
    ^
  why    the entry of `policy.method` types a component of an operator or binds its handler; a typing entry or a handler binding is written in a methods file, which the union attaches to its stage and the semantics reads, and a stage elaborated alone carries none
  write  Write the entry in a methods file, `@methods: t`, which the union attaches to the stage; a stage file carries the model alone.

declared-twice  (graph construction)
  where  m.bl, line 2, column 29 (address 'policy.policy.method')
  what
    [id=policy, method : !egm | policy.method : !vfi] {
                                ^
  why    the component `method` of block 'policy' is written twice with different content: `method : !egm` at m.bl:2:13 (term address 'policy.method') and `policy.method : !vfi` here; a component holds one entry over the files of a stage, so keep one of the two
  write  Keep one entry on the component, `method : !egm` or `policy.method : !vfi`; the two name one component of the block, by the relative and by the absolute spelling of its path.

label-not-in-parent  (graph construction)
  where  m.bl, line 3, column 5 (address 'dcsn_to_cntn.rent')
  what
        [label=rent, () -> (a_x : ℝ₊) : !cntn] {
        ^
  why    the nested block `label=rent` has no branch of that label in block 'dcsn_to_cntn', whose header stands at t.bl:5:1 (term address 'dcsn_to_cntn'); a nested block of an addition merges with the branch of the same label under its parent, and the union adds no branch
  write  Write the nested block under a label the stage's block holds, `work` or `retire`; a branch is added in the stage file, whose header declares the label set.

type-conflict  (graph construction)
  where  m.bl, line 2, column 26 (address 'cntn_to_dcsn.out.V')
  what
    [id=cntn_to_dcsn, () -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {
                             ^
  why    the coordinate 'V' on the output side of block 'cntn_to_dcsn' is typed `[-inf, inf) @ !vlu` at t.bl:20:62 (term address 'cntn_to_dcsn.out.V') and `ℝ @ !vlu` here; the field names determine the signature and the stage's typing is kept, so write the coordinate without a type or with the stage's
  write  Restate the coordinate without a type, `() -> (V) : !dcsn`, or with the stage's, `() -> (V : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu) : !dcsn`.

metadata-mismatch  (graph construction)
  where  m.bl, line 1, column 1 (address '1')
  what
    @methods: port
    ^
  why    the addition names the stage 'port', and the stage file names itself 'cons' at t.bl:1:1 (term address '1'); an addition's first line is `@methods: <stage>` with the name of the stage file it adds to
  write  Name the stage the addition adds to on its first line, `@methods: cons`.

multiplier-declaration  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 18, column 5 (address 'policy.slackness')
  what
        μ[>]   : ℝ₊ ⟂ c >= 0             :: [id=slackness]
        ^
  why    the bound of the multiplier 'μ' names 'c', written c, a control; the bound of a declared multiplier names continuation states, multipliers of block 'policy', parameters, numbers or `inf` (AMD-SG-035 D11). Write the bound on a continuation state, or state the condition on a line of the block with its own clause

set-mismatch  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 2, column 1 (address 'a')
  what
    [id=a, (x : ℝ) : !arvl -> (y : ℝ) : !dcsn] { y = x }
    ^
  why    the field y is produced by 'a' on ℝ and consumed by 'b' on ℝ₊₊, and ℝ does not lie in ℝ₊₊; declare matching sets, or state the control's feasible set in the declarative maximisation statement (D18, D19)

category-codes  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 3, column 1 (address 't.bl:3')
  what
    HouseholdStatus := {i : ℤ | i >= 0, i <= 1} :: [!categories household_status, newborn=0, old=2]
    ^
  why    the set HouseholdStatus is marked `!categories`, and its definition and its annotation give no category map. The entry `old=2` gives a code outside HouseholdStatus, the integers from 0 to 1; give each category a code from 0 to 1. The set HouseholdStatus holds the integers from 0 to 1, and the member 1 has no category; give each member one category

value-input-role  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 5, column 51
  what
    [id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu, dV[>] : ℝ₊₊ @ !mrgnvl) : !cntn -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {
                                                      ^
  why    the file writes `!mrgnvl` here, a role retired from the language: a backward header lists value fields and controls alone, and a derivative of a value is written as the term `D_{x}V`, with `x` a state coordinate of the value's perch, such as `D_{m}V` or `D_{a}V[>]` (AMD-MB-001 §4.1)
  write  remove the field from the header; write the line that defined it as a derivative line, `D_{m}V = …`, and read the derivative as the term `D_{a}V[>]`

signature-complete  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 6, column 5 (address 'd.1')
  what
        w = x + y
        ^
  why    the line reads x, which the header of block 'd' does not list and no earlier line of the block defines; a forward block's header lists every field its lines read (AMD-SG-007 §5, rule signature-complete). List it in the header, `(y, x) : !dcsn -> (w : ℝ) : !dcsn`, or define it on an earlier line of the block. The correction writes a perch word on each field of a side where the side's one word no longer holds for every field; the perch of a control is unchanged by either spelling, being the decision perch wherever a header lists it (AMD-SG-017 §2)

header-coordinate  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 5, column 1 (address 'cntn_to_dcsn')
  what
    [id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu, x_d : !dcsn) -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {
    ^
  why    the header of block 'cntn_to_dcsn' lists x_d on its input side, and the block is a backward block, whose header lists the value fields it reads and writes and the controls at which its lines are read, and no state (rule header-coordinate). x_d is a state of the dcsn perch, the perch at which the block's output stands, so it is a coordinate of the output function and no input of the block. Remove the listing, `(V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn`; a line of the block may still mention a state of the dcsn perch, which is a coordinate of what it defines
  write  Remove the state from the header; a line of the block may mention a state of the perch at which its output stands, as a coordinate of what it defines.

input-perch-state  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 9, column 5 (address 'cntn_to_dcsn.1')
  what
        V = a + V[>]
        ^
  why    the line is read at the dcsn perch and mentions a, a state of the cntn perch, the perch block 'cntn_to_dcsn' reads its inputs at; a backward block reaches a state of its input perch, or of a later perch, through the law of motion alone, and read directly the state would stand free in a rule that holds on the dcsn state (rule input-perch-state). The forward block 'dcsn_to_cntn' defines it at t.bl:6:5 (term address 'dcsn_to_cntn.1'), `a = x_d`. Write `x_d` in its place
  write  Write the forward block's expression for the state in its place, or read the state under the expectation over the shock drawn on the edge.

kernel-form  (graph construction)
  where  address 'cntn_to_dcsn.marginal'
  why    stage 'cons_savings_iid': the kernel of 'marginal:Derivative:1' (cons_savings_iid:G:cntn_to_dcsn) contains the call 𝑑𝑢(c) of 𝑑𝑢 := D_{c}(𝑢) (cons_savings_iid:function:𝑑𝑢), which is not a closed-form function; no compile rule evaluates it: compile evaluates retained arithmetic and calls to closed-form named functions and selects no numerical method (AMD-SG-007 §3.1, rule kernel-form); define that function in closed form, or read the kernel with kernel(stage, box)

method-option-value  (graph construction)
  where  address 'cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation'
  why    stage 'cons', place cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation, method !Linear, option 'orders': {'m_d': -5} does not give positive integers; configure requires the option value to have its declared type; write positive integer orders at actual coordinates

kernel-target  (graph construction)
  where  address 'cntn_to_dcsn'
  why    stage 'cons': compile evaluates the explicit numerical kernels g and G, and 'cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation' is a Evaluation box whose kernel, identity at m_d; no policy is inserted, has no callable representation (AMD-SG-007 §3.1, rule kernel-target); inspect it with kernel(stage, box), or compile a pullback, push-forward or aggregation box

distribution-dependency  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 4, column 1 (address '4')
  what
    y ~ N(z, 1)
    ^
  why    the distribution declarations form a cycle: t:distribution:y (at 4) reads z, t:distribution:z (at 5) reads y; the joint distribution of an edge is the product of declared conditional distributions in a dependency order, which a cycle does not have (AMD-SG-009 §§2–3, rule distribution-dependency); remove one of the shock arguments, or write the dependent shocks as one joint declaration

distribution-edge  (graph construction)
