  where  t.bl, line 3, column 1 (address '3')
  what
    y ~ N(0, 1)
    ^
  why    the shock y is listed by the forward builders 'arvl_to_dcsn' and 'dcsn_to_cntn'; a shock is drawn on one edge, the edge of the one forward builder whose signature lists it (AMD-SG-009 §2, rule distribution-edge); list it on one forward builder

distribution-domain  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 4, column 1 (address 't.bl:4')
  what
    (y, z) ~ N((0, 0), ((1, 2), (2, 1)))
    ^
  why    the covariance ((1, 2), (2, 1)) of the normal declaration t:distribution:y_z is not positive semidefinite: its smallest eigenvalue is -1.0 (AMD-SG-009 §4, rule distribution-domain); write a symmetric positive semidefinite covariance matrix

conditional-not-declared  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 17, column 5 (address 'cntn_to_dcsn.value')
  what
        V = E_{z}(E_{y}(V[>])) :: [id=value]
        ^
  why    the expectation cntn_to_dcsn.value:Expectation:2 needs the distribution of y given z from the normal declaration two_nodes:distribution:y_z, whose conditioning covariance Σ_CC = 0 = 0.0 is singular (smallest eigenvalue 0.0); the normal conditional requires Σ_CC positive definite, and no pseudoinverse is taken (AMD-SG-009 §4, rule conditional-not-declared); condition on shocks whose covariance block is positive definite, or integrate them jointly

branch-form  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 5, column 1 (address 'dcsn_to_cntn')
  what
    [id=dcsn_to_cntn, (a_d, d : !ctrl @ {work, retire}) : !dcsn -> ()] {
    ^
  why    block 'dcsn_to_cntn' holds one nested block; a branching block holds at least two, one for each label of its label coordinate; write a nested block for each missing label

branch-labels  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 9, column 5 (address 'dcsn_to_cntn.stop')
  what
        [label=stop, () -> (a_r : ℝ₊) : !cntn] {
        ^
  why    the label 'stop' is not a member of {work, retire}, the set of the label coordinate 'd'; write one nested block for each member, in the set's order

branch-tuple-mismatch  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 14, column 5 (address 'cntn_to_dcsn.choice_value')
  what
        V = (V_w[>], V_r[>])[d]                :: [id=choice_value]
        ^
  why    the value line selects from (V_w[>], V_r[>]) by 'd', and the policy line policy.choice maximizes over (V_r[>], V_w[>]); write the policy's maximand as the value line's tuple, in its order

branch-value-position  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 14, column 5 (address 'cntn_to_dcsn.choice_value')
  what
        V = (V_w[>], V_w[>])[d]                :: [id=choice_value]
        ^
  why    V_w[>] is read at the position of 'work' and at the position of 'retire'; a branch value stands at one position in every tuple, the position of its branch; write each branch value at its own branch's position alone

branch-law  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 7, column 1 (address 'dcsn_to_cntn')
  what
    [id=dcsn_to_cntn, (a_d, s) : !dcsn -> ()] {
    ^
  why    the shock 's' selects the branches of block 'dcsn_to_cntn' and has no distribution; the branches are weighted by the distribution of the shock, so write `s ~ Categorical((p_young, p_old))`, one probability for each label in the order {young, old}

not-constructed  (graph construction)
  where  t.bl, line 5, column 1 (address 'dcsn_to_cntn')
  what
    [id=dcsn_to_cntn, (a_d, c : !ctrl @ [0,1], d : !ctrl @ {work, retire}) : !dcsn -> ()] {
    ^
  why    block 'dcsn_to_cntn' lists the controls 'c', 'd' beside its branches; this version of the package constructs a branching block whose branches state equations alone and whose label coordinate is its one control, or a shock over a finite set in a stage that chooses nothing (docs/Bellman-Sym/05-branching.md)

block-header-mismatch  (graph construction)
  where  address 'egm'
  why    stage 'cons': the block 'egm' of egm.bl has the signature (V[>], dV[>]) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn, and the builder 'policy' it opens has the signature (V[>]) : !cntn -> (c) : !dcsn; a method block joins the builder's perches, writes the builder's outputs, and reads the builder's inputs and no other field; a derivative of a value it lists is written as a term of its lines, `D_{a}V[>]` (specification 0.6 §4.1; AMD-MB-001 §5.1); write the builder's outputs on the block's output side and its inputs on the input side
  write  List the builder's inputs alone, write a derivative of a value as the term `D_{a}V[>]` in the lines, and write the builder's outputs on the block's output side.

block-name-undefined  (graph construction)
  where  address 'egm.InvEuler'
  why    stage 'cons': the line egm.InvEuler of egm.bl calls '𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣', which neither the stage file nor the block file defines; a method block reads the stage's definitions and the block file's own (specification 0.6 §4.1); define 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣 in the block file, or call a function the stage file defines
  write  Define the function in the block file, `𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣 := Inv(𝑑𝑢)`, or call a function the stage file defines.

(a) a builder box by its block id; `<block-id>_builder` for a transition block  (the identity table)
  where  stage 'cons', target 'nowhere'
  why    'nowhere' in stage 'cons' names no builder of the stage and no operator a statement of it records. The places of stage 'cons' are — builders: arvl_to_dcsn, dcsn_to_cntn, cntn_to_dcsn, dcsn_to_arvl, policy; named lines: cntn_to_dcsn.value, cntn_to_dcsn.marginal, dcsn_to_arvl.value, policy.optimality; Evaluations of the builders: cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value, cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.marginal, dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.value, policy.evaluate; operators: argmax (policy.optimality.argmax); `evaluate` alone: not a target here, since the stage authors no `evaluate` occurrence.

(b), (c) a node box or a line by `<block-id>.<statement-id>`, a line of a branch by `<block-id>.<label>.<statement-id>`  (the identity table)
  where  stage 'cons', target 'cntn_to_dcsn.absent'
  why    'cntn_to_dcsn.absent' in stage 'cons' names no line of block 'cntn_to_dcsn': no line carries the id 'absent'; the block's named lines are cntn_to_dcsn.value, cntn_to_dcsn.marginal. The places of stage 'cons' are — builders: arvl_to_dcsn, dcsn_to_cntn, cntn_to_dcsn, dcsn_to_arvl, policy; named lines: cntn_to_dcsn.value, cntn_to_dcsn.marginal, dcsn_to_arvl.value, policy.optimality; Evaluations of the builders: cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value, cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.marginal, dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.value, policy.evaluate; operators: argmax (policy.optimality.argmax); `evaluate` alone: not a target here, since the stage authors no `evaluate` occurrence.

(c.ii) a positional address `<block-id>.<n>` is not a target; the line needs an id  (the identity table)
  where  stage 'cons', target 'cntn_to_dcsn.1'
  why    'cntn_to_dcsn.1' in stage 'cons' is a positional address; line 1 of block 'cntn_to_dcsn' is `V = 𝑢(c) + V[>]`, named 'cntn_to_dcsn.value' — name it by its id. The places of stage 'cons' are — builders: arvl_to_dcsn, dcsn_to_cntn, cntn_to_dcsn, dcsn_to_arvl, policy; named lines: cntn_to_dcsn.value, cntn_to_dcsn.marginal, dcsn_to_arvl.value, policy.optimality; Evaluations of the builders: cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value, cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.marginal, dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.value, policy.evaluate; operators: argmax (policy.optimality.argmax); `evaluate` alone: not a target here, since the stage authors no `evaluate` occurrence.

(d) every occurrence of an operator by its stage-wide name  (the identity table)
  where  stage 'cons', target 'E'
  why    'E' in stage 'cons' names the expectation over the shocks; no statement of the stage records an occurrence of 'E', and an operator is a target only where a statement records it — none is derived from a method name. The places of stage 'cons' are — builders: arvl_to_dcsn, dcsn_to_cntn, cntn_to_dcsn, dcsn_to_arvl, policy; named lines: cntn_to_dcsn.value, cntn_to_dcsn.marginal, dcsn_to_arvl.value, policy.optimality; Evaluations of the builders: cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value, cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.marginal, dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.value, policy.evaluate; operators: argmax (policy.optimality.argmax); `evaluate` alone: not a target here, since the stage authors no `evaluate` occurrence.

(e) every occurrence of an operator in one line by `<block-id>.<statement-id>.<operator>`  (the identity table)
  where  stage 'cons', target 'cntn_to_dcsn.value.E'
  why    'cntn_to_dcsn.value.E' in stage 'cons' names an operator in `V = 𝑢(c) + V[>]`, the output statement cntn_to_dcsn.value, which carries no operator occurrence; a method attaches to an operator occurrence, to the builder, to a node box, to an output statement with no operator occurrence (the representation of the field it defines, written at the builder's Evaluation, `on: cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value`), to one occurrence of a named line that carries it, by `<block-id>.<statement-id>.<operator>`, or to the Evaluation of a builder, written `<block-id>.evaluate` for the policy builder and `<block-id>.evaluate.value` or `<block-id>.evaluate.marginal` for a backward value builder. The places of stage 'cons' are — builders: arvl_to_dcsn, dcsn_to_cntn, cntn_to_dcsn, dcsn_to_arvl, policy; named lines: cntn_to_dcsn.value, cntn_to_dcsn.marginal, dcsn_to_arvl.value, policy.optimality; Evaluations of the builders: cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value, cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.marginal, dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.value, policy.evaluate; operators: argmax (policy.optimality.argmax); `evaluate` alone: not a target here, since the stage authors no `evaluate` occurrence.

(g) `evaluate` alone: the one authored occurrence; two or more are named by their addresses, and a stage that authors none is refused naming `<block-id>.evaluate.value`  (the identity table)
  where  stage 'cons', target 'evaluate'
  why    'evaluate' in stage 'cons' names no place, since the stage authors no `evaluate` occurrence, and the value the builder 'cntn_to_dcsn' writes is represented at its Evaluation, `on: cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value`. The places of stage 'cons' are — builders: arvl_to_dcsn, dcsn_to_cntn, cntn_to_dcsn, dcsn_to_arvl, policy; named lines: cntn_to_dcsn.value, cntn_to_dcsn.marginal, dcsn_to_arvl.value, policy.optimality; Evaluations of the builders: cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value, cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.marginal, dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.value, policy.evaluate; operators: argmax (policy.optimality.argmax); `evaluate` alone: not a target here, since the stage authors no `evaluate` occurrence.

(h) one target per entry; a comma-separated entry is split by L02  (the identity table)
  where  stage 'cons', target 'policy, cntn_to_dcsn'
  why    'policy, cntn_to_dcsn' in stage 'cons' lists several targets separated by commas, and an entry names one target (spec 0.3c §4.3: a comma-containing string is not an operator identifier); the migration L02 splits such an entry, and each part resolves on its own. The places of stage 'cons' are — builders: arvl_to_dcsn, dcsn_to_cntn, cntn_to_dcsn, dcsn_to_arvl, policy; named lines: cntn_to_dcsn.value, cntn_to_dcsn.marginal, dcsn_to_arvl.value, policy.optimality; Evaluations of the builders: cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value, cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.marginal, dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.value, policy.evaluate; operators: argmax (policy.optimality.argmax); `evaluate` alone: not a target here, since the stage authors no `evaluate` occurrence.

(i) the Evaluation of a builder by `<block-id>.evaluate`, `<block-id>.evaluate.value` or `<block-id>.evaluate.marginal`  (the identity table)
  where  stage 'cons', target 'policy.evaluate.value'
  why    'policy.evaluate.value' in stage 'cons' names a value at the Evaluation of the policy builder 'policy', which writes the policy and neither a value nor its derivative; its Evaluation is written `on: policy.evaluate`. The places of stage 'cons' are — builders: arvl_to_dcsn, dcsn_to_cntn, cntn_to_dcsn, dcsn_to_arvl, policy; named lines: cntn_to_dcsn.value, cntn_to_dcsn.marginal, dcsn_to_arvl.value, policy.optimality; Evaluations of the builders: cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value, cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.marginal, dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.value, policy.evaluate; operators: argmax (policy.optimality.argmax); `evaluate` alone: not a target here, since the stage authors no `evaluate` occurrence.

a target has one, two, or three dot-separated parts, or four where the second is a branch label  (the identity table)
  where  stage 'cons', target 'a.b.c.d'
  why    'a.b.c.d' in stage 'cons' is not the form of a target: a block id, `<block-id>.<statement-id>`, `<block-id>.<statement-id>.<operator>`, a line of a branch, `<block-id>.<label>.<statement-id>`, with its operator after it, the Evaluation of a builder, `<block-id>.evaluate`, `<block-id>.evaluate.value` or `<block-id>.evaluate.marginal`, or a stage-wide operator name. The places of stage 'cons' are — builders: arvl_to_dcsn, dcsn_to_cntn, cntn_to_dcsn, dcsn_to_arvl, policy; named lines: cntn_to_dcsn.value, cntn_to_dcsn.marginal, dcsn_to_arvl.value, policy.optimality; Evaluations of the builders: cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value, cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.marginal, dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.value, policy.evaluate; operators: argmax (policy.optimality.argmax); `evaluate` alone: not a target here, since the stage authors no `evaluate` occurrence.

a target reaches one place; two is a construction defect  (the identity table)
  where  stage 'two_places', target 'arvl_to_dcsn_builder'
  why    'arvl_to_dcsn_builder' in stage 'two_places' reaches 2 places, which is a construction defect: the builder box 'arvl_to_dcsn_builder' and the builder box 'arvl_to_dcsn' under the suffix `_builder`. The places of stage 'two_places' are — builders: arvl_to_dcsn, arvl_to_dcsn_builder; named lines: none; Evaluations of the builders: none; operators: none; `evaluate` alone: not a target here, since the stage authors no `evaluate` occurrence.

target-not-found  (the identity table)
  where  stage 'cons', target 'cntn_to_dcsn:Substitution:V'
  why    stage 'cons': 'cntn_to_dcsn:Substitution:V' names no box of the version's views and no record of its definitions table; a printed view, a kernel and a compiled kernel read an actual box or definition (AMD-SG-007 §2, rule target-not-found); write a box name that stage.builder.bwd.primitives.list() or stage.builder.fwd.primitives.list() shows, or an identity of stage.definitions

target-ambiguous  (the identity table)
  where  stage 'cons', target 'cntn_to_dcsn'
  why    stage 'cons': 'cntn_to_dcsn' names 2 different targets — the box cntn_to_dcsn in the initial diagram, backward at the grain builder, builder cntn_to_dcsn | the box cntn_to_dcsn in the builders graph, backward at the grain builder, builder cntn_to_dcsn; one name selects one target only when the boxes it names are equal (AMD-SG-007 §2, rule target-ambiguous); pass the box itself from the view and grain you mean

target-version  (the identity table)
  where  stage 'cons', target 'cntn_to_dcsn:Pullback'
  why    stage 'cons': the box 'cntn_to_dcsn:Pullback' passed is no box of a graph of this version; a query reads the boxes of the version it is asked of, and versions share no object (AMD-SG-007 §2, rule target-version); ask the version whose view holds the box, or pass a box of this version's view

method-attachment  (the identity table)
  where  stage 'cons', target 'cntn_to_dcsn.value'
  why    Method target 'cntn_to_dcsn.value' in stage 'cons': !egm does not admit target kind statement; method-attachment admits builder, operator argmax; !egm is written on the policy builder by its block id, `on: policy`, with `block:` naming a method block, or with no block where the policy block writes the grid line, or on a maximization that carries its first-order condition as a property; write an on: target of one of these kinds

representation-on-builder  (the identity table)
  where  stage 'cons', target 'policy'
  why    Method target 'policy' in stage 'cons': !Linear is a representation, attached to the Evaluation of a builder and not to the builder; write `on: policy.evaluate`

representation-on-derivative-line  (the identity table)
  where  stage 'cons', target 'cntn_to_dcsn.marginal'
  why    Method target 'cntn_to_dcsn.marginal' in stage 'cons': !Linear is a representation, and cntn_to_dcsn.marginal is a derivative line, which states a derivative of the value the builder writes; write `on: cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.marginal`, the Evaluation of the builder 'cntn_to_dcsn', at which the stated derivative is represented

grid-kind-as-method  (the identity table)
  where  stage 'cons', target 'cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value'
  why    Method target 'cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value' in stage 'cons': !Cartesian is a kind of grid and not a method; write the basis as the method, `method: !Linear` for piecewise linear interpolation or `method: !pchip` for shape-preserving cubic interpolation, and the grid as its setting, `grid: !Cartesian` under `settings` with `orders` and `bounds` beside it

grid-without-kind  (the identity table)
  where  stage 'cons', target 'cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value'
  why    Method target 'cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value' in stage 'cons': !Linear writes `orders` and `bounds` without the setting `grid`; a grid is written by its kind, the tag on the value of `grid`, with its fields beside it: write `grid: !Cartesian` in the entry's settings beside `orders` and `bounds`

grid-under-egm  (the identity table)
  where  stage 't', target 'policy.evaluate'
  why    Method target 'policy.evaluate' in stage 't': !Linear at the Evaluation of the policy builder interpolates the policy between the pairs of the decision state and the control that !egm computes at the points of its exogenous grid and stores there, which are its knots, so the entry writes no grid; remove `grid`, `orders` and `bounds` from its settings, the exogenous grid standing in the settings of the !egm entry

recipe-shape  (the Bellman factory)
  where  registry/spec.yml, address 'stages'
  what
{'registry': {}}
  why    the recipe has no top-level `stages` mapping
  write  stages: {<stage key>: {stage: <path>.bl, calibration: {all: [...]}, settings: {all: [...]}, methods: {all: [...]}}}

recipe-source  (the Bellman factory)
  where  registry/spec.yml, address 'stages.two_nodes.calibration.all'
  what
calibration/absent
  why    the registry holds no source file 'calibration/absent'; tried registry/calibration/absent.yml, registry/calibration/absent.yaml, registry/calibration/absent
  write  the name of a file under the registry, without its extension

recipe-slot-unknown  (the Bellman factory)
  where  registry/spec.yml, address 'fil'
  what
fil
  why    the keyword 'fil' names no slot of the recipe; its slots are $fill, $method_switch
  write  one of $fill, $method_switch, or a new `$` name in a source list of the recipe

recipe-template-agreement  (the Bellman factory)
  where  registry/spec.yml, address 'other'
  what
other
  why    the recipe names the stage 'other', which no period of registry/trellis.yml holds
  write  'other' in a period template of registry/trellis.yml, or no entry for it in the recipe

slot-value-not-a-mapping  (the Bellman factory)
  where  registry/spec.yml, address 'fill'
  what
'β: 0.9'
  why    slot 'fill' is given a str, not a mapping
  write  fill={'calibration': {...}, 'settings': {...}} or a flat mapping of names to values

fill-names-nothing  (the Bellman factory)
  where  registry/spec.yml, address 'fill'
  what
beta
  why    slot 'fill', key 'beta': no stage that receives this slot declares 'beta' as a parameter (two_nodes declares β, R) or as a setting (two_nodes declares n_k), and no registry block admits it; a fill key names a parameter or a setting of a stage that receives it (AMD-FAC-002 §5)
  write  one of the declared names R, n_k, β

fill-mixes-kinds  (the Bellman factory)
  where  registry/spec.yml, address 'fill'
  what
β, n_k
  why    slot 'fill' names the parameters β and the settings n_k in one flat mapping
  write  fill={'calibration': {...}, 'settings': {...}}, each name under its kind

trellis-file-shape  (the Bellman factory)
  where  registry/broken.yml, address 'periods'
  what
{'stages': []}
  why    the trellis file has no list `periods`
  write  periods: [{template: period.yml, repeat: 51}] or the periods written out

record-shape  (the Bellman factory)
  where  address 'record'
  what
['stage']
  why    missing fields ['calibration', 'methods', 'settings']; unknown fields []
  write  a record with stage, calibration, settings and methods, and optionally label, provenance and additions

period-join-cycle  (the Bellman factory)
  where  address 'periods[0]'
  what
disc continues to 'a' and port arrives at 'k'; port continues to 'm_next' and disc arrives at 'a'
  why    the joins of the period form a cycle: disc continues to 'a' and port arrives at 'k'; port continues to 'm_next' and disc arrives at 'a'; the stages of a period are ordered by their field dependencies, so no stage may take a field it produces through the others
  write  remove or redirect an authored connector so that the stage dependencies have no cycle; qualify an endpoint with its stage key where its bare name is ambiguous

connector-names-no-field  (the Bellman factory)
  where  address 'periods[0].connectors[0]'
  what
{'from': 'cons', 'to': 'port', 'fields': {'a': 'k'}, 'label': 'x'}
  why    the connector is written in the keyed form and has the key 'label' beside from, to and fields
  write  {<continuation field>: <arrival field>}, or within a period {from: <stage key>, to: <stage key>, fields: {<continuation field>: <arrival field>}}

period-parameter-agreement  (the Bellman factory)
  where  registry/trellis.yml, address 'periods[0]'
  what
R : ℝ₊₊ in two_nodes; R : (-inf, 0) in other
  why    the stages two_nodes (registry/stages/two_nodes/two_nodes.bl) and other (registry/stages/other/other.bl) of the period declare the parameter 'R' with the sets ℝ₊₊ and (-inf, 0), which have no nonempty intersection; a parameter name names one parameter of the period, shared by the stages that declare it, so their declared sets agree (AMD-COMP-001 §2.3)
  write  one set for 'R' in every stage of the period, or sets the package reads whose intersection is not empty, or distinct names for distinct parameters

readable-file  (the Bellman factory)
  where  cons.txt
  what
cons.txt
  why    load_stage reads a stage file, and cons.txt is no .bl file
  write  the path of a stage file, `<name>.bl`

The example of recipe-shape above is a recipe with no stages mapping. A recipe names every file it reads by its path from its own folder, the trellis file under trellis: and each stage's file under stage: in the stage's entry, and nothing is read in place of a path it does not write. The same rule therefore refuses the example registry's recipe without its trellis: line, and without the stage: line of its one entry, although trellis.yml and stages/two_nodes/two_nodes.bl stand in the registry:

from bellman.refusal_examples import EXAMPLES
from bellman.refusal_catalogue import refusal_of

for name in ("recipe-names-no-trellis-file", "entry-names-no-stage-file"):
    print(refusal_of(EXAMPLES[name]))

registry/spec.yml: address 'trellis': the recipe names no trellis file; write `trellis: trellis.yml`, the path from this folder (rule recipe-shape)
registry/spec.yml: address 'stages.two_nodes': the entry `stages.two_nodes` names no stage file; write `stage: stages/two_nodes/two_nodes.bl`, the path from this folder (rule recipe-shape)

docs.title: Symbol conventions
docs.text:
Summary

Bellman-SYM distinguishes a field, its domain, and a function representing that field in state coordinates. Perch marks identify arrival, decision, and continuation information within a stage. Names such as V and policy are conventions; their declarations and equations determine their roles, and the derivative of a value is read by the term D_{a}V[>], not named by a field. The last section lists the punctuation, the reserved sets and the type words with which a stage file declares its objects.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Stages: a complete stage file; Perch tagging rules: typing and information. Used by — Field equations, Periods, and Trellises. Formal account — Appendix C for mathematical interpretation; Appendix D for nodes and indexing. See also — Expression forms: the operators and functions a line of a stage file writes.

docs.title: 1 Reading a stage equation
docs.text:
The discounting stage multiplies the continuation value by the discount factor. This is its complete source:

@stage: disc

Xa := ℝ₊
β : (0,1)

[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (a : Xa) : !arvl -> (a_d : Xa) : !dcsn] {
    a_d = a
}

[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (a_d) : !dcsn -> (a[>] : Xa) : !cntn] {
    a[>] = a_d
}

[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (V : ℝ @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {
    V = β*V[>]                      :: [id=value]
}

[id=dcsn_to_arvl, (V) : !dcsn -> (V[<] : ℝ @ !vlu) : !arvl] {
    V[<] = V                        :: [id=value]
}

Here a, a_d, and a[>] are assets at three information contexts. The transition equations state that their values agree in this stage. The stage writes no derivative line: its two backward lines are a scaling and an identity of the value, whose state passes unchanged, so the derivative of the value passes through them, and a stage before this one that reads D_{a}V[>] of its continuation receives the derivative of the discounted value. No letters of a name establish a derivative; the derivative of a value is read by the term D_{a}V[>], which applies the operator D to the declared value in the named coordinate (§4).

The block identifier cntn_to_dcsn provides an address. Renaming it changes references such as a methods target, but does not change multiplication by β. In a model with a separate discounting stage, do not insert a second discount factor into the beta-free consumption equations.

docs.title: 2 Fields, functions, and spaces
docs.text:
A field is a named quantity at one perch: a state, a control, a shock, or a value. Once shocks are declared, fields may be interpreted as random variables on the underlying probability space. A state function represents such a quantity using explicit state arguments. A domain describes the values an object may take; it is distinct from the space of functions on a state domain.

Mathematical notation Object \(\mathsf X_\prec\), \(\mathsf X\), \(\mathsf X_\succ\) Arrival, decision, and continuation state domains. \(\mathrm x_\prec\), \(\mathrm x\), \(\mathrm x_\succ\) State fields taking values in those domains. \(\mathrm V_\prec\), \(\mathrm V\), \(\mathrm V_\succ\) Value fields. \(v_\prec\), \(v\), \(v_\succ\) Functions of state coordinates representing the value fields under the stated assumptions. \(g_\prec\), \(g_\succ\) Laws of motion, from arrival to decision and from decision to continuation. \(\pi\) A policy, meaning a measurable choice as a function of decision information. \(\mu\) A probability distribution. \(\mathbb T_\pi\) The backward value operator at a fixed policy. \(\mathbb M_\pi\) The forward distribution operator at that policy.

Sans-serif capitals denote spaces, italic letters denote functions, and roman letters denote the fields those functions represent, the same letter for both. These typography conventions help the reader; they do not type a source identifier. The source V[>] is a value field because of its declaration. A name such as V_fn has no reserved function meaning.

For example, if the continuation state field is \(x_\succ\) and a value field is measurable with respect to that state, an appropriate measurable factorization gives \(\mathrm V_\succ=v_\succ(x_\succ)\). The factorization requires the measurable-space assumptions stated in Appendix C. It does not follow from choosing a font, and it need not specify a unique extension away from the states represented by \(x_\succ\).

The notation \(L^2(\Omega,\mathcal F)\) denotes square-integrable fields on a probability space with information \(\mathcal F\). Use it only when square integrability is assumed. A declaration allowing extended values does not automatically put a field in \(L^2\).

docs.title: 3 Perches and information
docs.text:
A perch is one of the three information contexts within a stage:

Context Mathematical subscript .bl reference Type word Arrival \(\prec\) V[<] !arvl Decision \(\sim\), usually omitted V or V[~] !dcsn Continuation \(\succ\) V[>] !cntn

When nested information is assumed, the information structure can be written \(\mathcal F_\prec\subseteq\mathcal F_\sim\subseteq\mathcal F_\succ\). Stage marks alone do not establish this assumption. These inclusions need not be strict: an identity transition can reveal no additional information. Nor must a list of current state coordinates alone generate all past information. State sufficiency is an assumption used when passing to functions of those coordinates.

Information marks distinguish field references within the stage. They are not dates, and a perch is not an operator endpoint. In particular, a shock listed as a transition argument need not be observed before that transition. A decision control written beside continuation values is still a decision control. The rules for the sides of a block's header respect these role exceptions.

The diagram below records information order and the usual directions of transition and value calculations; its circles denote information contexts:

arrival information  ── state transition ──>  decision information
        ^                                            |
        | arrival value calculation                  | state transition
        |                                            v
        +                                  continuation information
                        <── backward value calculation ──

A stage can use pre-decision shocks, post-decision shocks, both, or neither. In a deterministic stage the law can be degenerate, but determinism does not require the arrival transition to be the identity. The equations decide the transition.

docs.title: 4 Operators and derivatives
docs.text:
The policy is written as a subscript: \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\) and \(\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\). Superscripts can then denote iteration, such as \(\mathbb T_\pi^n\). When a stage index is needed it comes first, for example \(\mathbb T_{k,\succ,\pi}\). Omit an index only when its referent is unambiguous.

In the usual two-transition stage, backward composition is \(\mathbb T_\pi=\mathbb T_\prec\circ\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\), while forward composition is \(\mathbb M_\pi=\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\circ\mathbb M_\prec\). These equations specify order on compatible domains; the backward operator additionally depends on the declared reward and discounting. It must not be identified with a probability transition merely because both use the same state transition.

Technical details

For a transition-only calculation, let \((X,\mathcal X)\) and \((Y,\mathcal Y)\) be measurable state spaces. A probability kernel \(P\) assigns a probability measure \(P(x,\cdot)\) on \(Y\) to each \(x\in X\), with \(x\mapsto P(x,A)\) measurable for every \(A\in\mathcal Y\). For bounded measurable \(f:Y\to\mathbb R\), define \((Kf)(x)=\int f(y)P(x,dy)\), a bounded measurable function on \(X\). For a probability measure \(\mu\) on \(X\), define the probability measure on \(Y\) by \((M\mu)(A)=\int P(x,A)\mu(dx)\) for \(A\in\mathcal Y\). Integration then gives \(\int f\,d(M\mu)=\int Kf\,d\mu\). This identity concerns transition and expectation. Adding a reward, discount, or maximization requires the corresponding additional operations; a rewarded Bellman operator need not satisfy this identity.

A derivative expression applies the operator D to a function the file holds: to a declared function, D_{c}(𝑢), where the subscript names one of its formal arguments, or to a value field written with its perch mark, D_{a}V[>], where the subscript names a state coordinate of the perch at which the value is read, written without its mark. The second form is the derivative term; it denotes the derivative of the value in that coordinate, a function of the value and no second object, and it has this one spelling. A name such as 𝑑𝑢 can be defined by a derivative expression or by a closed form, and a stage file may define dV = D_{a}V[>] and read the name. The package differentiates nothing: a kernel that calls a function defined by D_{c}(𝑢) or reads a derivative term has no compiled form, and the derivative of a value is evaluated as the stage that built the value fixed it (Methodization §4.1). A line whose left side is a derivative term of the value its builder writes, D_{m_d}V = 𝑑𝑢(c), is the author's assertion that the derivative equals the right side, which holds under the envelope conditions; the stage lists the reading and checks it against nothing.

Expectation and maximization subscripts bind their integration and choice variables. The derivative subscript selects a declared formal argument of the function, or a state coordinate of the perch at which a value is read; it does not create a new local stage variable. An ordinary underscore is part of a name. Thus E_{θ}(V[>]) specifies integration over a shock, while μ_θ is simply a chosen parameter name. The operation forms are listed in Expression forms.

docs.title: 5 Equations and nodes
docs.text:
A block is an authored typed header and body. Its identifier provides an address, and its header and statements declare the fields and equations. A builder is the operator a block denotes. Within a block, !node marks a line as an authored node, a computation kept as a unit of its own that a method can address; in a backward block it forms a sub-builder of the block's builder. An expectation nested inside an equation remains a mathematical operation whether or not its containing statement is marked.

Conventional labels such as value, marginal, InvEuler, and cons_choice can make a file readable. They do not select mathematical rules. Likewise, calling a block policy does not insert optimization. Method attachment can address supported implicit equations or operator occurrences without !node; Methodization distinguishes those targets from arbitrary alias addresses.

An unmarked explicit intermediate equation may be substituted while preserving all outputs and dependencies. An implicit equation instead defines a relation. For candidate state coordinates \(H(s)\) and controls \(U(s)\) indexed by \(s\), the pairs \((H(s),U(s))\) define one control on the image of \(H\) exactly when equal coordinates imply equal controls. Measurability, coverage of the intended state domain, and optimality remain separate conditions. Appendix D applies this distinction to the endogenous grid method.

docs.title: 6 Branches and collections
docs.text:
For a finite nonempty set of alternatives, a branch can have its own state coordinates and continuation value. A branch state can be described as a pair \((j,x_j)\), where \(j\) labels an alternative and \(x_j\) belongs to its state domain. When the domains differ, retaining the label is necessary to interpret the coordinates. When every alternative shares a domain \(X\), these pairs belong to the product of the alternative set and \(X\).

A tuple of continuation values and selection by the declared choice can express this distinction in .bl. Ordinary selection such as q[d] selects a collection entry; it does not declare a function over d. The complete retirement example in Branching supplies the domains, values, selection equation, and finite maximization. Finite maximization attains a value when the feasible set is nonempty and each candidate value is defined; ties still need a choice rule.

Stochastic alternatives use a declared joint or conditional law and an expectation instead. A list of marginal laws does not specify independence. Neither the spelling of a branch label nor a method tag decides whether the model maximizes or averages.

docs.title: 7 Stage and period indices
docs.text:
A stage occurrence is one use of a stage file under a particular key in a period. Reusing the same .bl source requires distinct occurrence keys; it does not identify the resulting stages or their bindings.

Notation or key Meaning periods[h] The period h periods before terminal. periods[0] The terminal period. inter_connectors[h] Field renaming joining period h+1 to period h. syntactic["periods"][h]["stages"][stage_name] The record of that occurrence and period: its merged parameter, setting, and method mappings. [<], [~], [>] Information contexts within one stage, independently of h.

Terminal continuation values are separate boundary data for period zero. A connector renames corresponding fields between occurrences; matching names alone does not prove matching domains or information roles. The per-stage mathematical graph and the syntactic trellis, a dictionary of stage records, serve different purposes; the order of a period's stages is computed from the fields they join. Periods and Trellises give their composition rules.

docs.title: 8 Parameters, settings, and interpretation
docs.text:
A parameter defines the economic problem; a setting controls a numerical calculation. A finite menu of housing sizes is a mathematical domain, so changing its endpoints or number of available sizes changes the problem. A grid approximating a continuous housing domain is a numerical choice. A simulation grid need not equal the solution grid.

The meaning map \(\Upsilon\) interprets declarations and equations. The representation map Ρ denotes their numerical realization after the required choices and bindings. Lowercase \(\rho\) remains available for an economic parameter, such as risk aversion. These names do not assert that interpretation or approximation is invertible, or that different numerical choices commute.

Elaboration keeps the fields, with the interpreted equation bodies and definitions, in the two initial diagrams, and derives from them, under explicit assumptions, the two builders graphs, on functions and on measures. The temporary syntax tree and source spans are discarded; a second independently editable function model is not required. See From source to a formal problem.

docs.title: 9.1 Punctuation
docs.text:
The examples are lines of the stage files under applications/portfolio-choice/: disc.bl, whose source §1 shows, cons.bl and noport.bl.

Spelling Use Example : Declare a type: a domain, a role or an information context. β : (0,1) @ Join the components of a type; their order does not matter. c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊ := Define a named set, which may be written as a comprehension (§9.2), or a function. Xa := ℝ₊; Xa := [0, ā]; 𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := c^(1-ρ)/(1-ρ) = State an equation inside a block, explicit or implicit. V = β*V[>] ~ Give a shock its law, on a line of its own. θ ~ LogNormal(μ_θ, σ_θ) -> Separate the input side of a block's header from its output side. (a : Xa) : !arvl -> (a_d : Xa) : !dcsn :: [id=…] Give a line an id, by which a methods file and the stage object name it. :: [id=value] @stage: name Name the stage, once in the file. @stage: disc

The argument c of 𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) is local to the definition and declares no control, and a name such as 𝑑𝑢 differentiates nothing: the body of its definition defines the function. An equation is not an assignment or a policy function by its form alone: c = c[>] in the policy block of cons.bl is an implicit relation between the policy and the candidate c[>], which the line m_d[>] = a + c[>] places at the cash on hand of each saving (Appendix D §7).

docs.title: 9.2 Domains
docs.text:
A domain is the set of values a field or a parameter may take. These set names are reserved by the grammar and need no definition line:

Spelling Set ℝ All real numbers. ℝ₊, also R+ or R_{+} Nonnegative real numbers, zero included. ℝ₊₊, also R++ or R_{++} Strictly positive real numbers. ℤ Integers. ℕ Natural numbers; state a sharper lower bound where it matters. ℝ_{-∞} Real numbers with negative infinity adjoined, written with the ASCII hyphen. ℝ_{+∞} Real numbers with positive infinity adjoined. ℝ_{±∞}, also ℝ̄ Real numbers with both infinities adjoined.

A bare R, N or Z is an ordinary name and not one of these sets; R may be the gross return on assets. Define any other named set before using it, Xa := ℝ₊. A named set may also be an interval, Xa := [0, ā], Xa := (0, ā] or Xa := [0, ā), whose endpoints may name parameters; a field typed a : Xa then has the same declared set as a : [0, ā]. The open-open form is the exception: after :=, (0, ā) is read as a pair of values, not as a set, so an open interval is written after the typing colon where it is used, a : (0, ā). An interval writes its endpoints with the usual brackets, (a,b), (a,b], [a,b) and [a,b], and an endpoint may be infinite, ρ : [1, inf); a finite set lists its labels, R_type := {r1, r2, r3, r4, r5} or, inline, d : !ctrl @ {work, retire}; a product uses ×, x : ℝ × ℝ; and a condition after a comma narrows a declared set, ρ : ℝ₊, > 1.

Adjoining infinity lets a value reach an endpoint; it does not make every operation on such values defined. An expectation needs integrability or an extended-value convention, and infinity minus infinity is undefined. Appendix C states the assumptions used for value equations.

docs.title: 9.2.1 Finite indexed data
docs.text:
A finite set of integer keys lists them, {0, 1}, or names the set its members lie in when a member names a parameter, S_θ := {0, θ} ⊂ ℤ, with θ integer-valued. An integer range whose bounds may name parameters, L_J := {1, …, J}, with … or ... between the commas, holds every integer from the first bound to the second, including both bounds. The bounds and the listed members must be integers; their conditions are retained until calibration if they depend on parameters. A value such as 3.0 is integer-valued and identifies the same key as 3, without rounding another integer to it. Separately listed keys must be distinct. A bare {a, b} continues to list two labels.

A collection is declared with one entry per key, δ : L_J → ℝ, or per ordered pair, dist : L_J × L_J → ℝ₊. The admitted index sets are integer ranges, listed integer keys, finite label sets, and products of these sets. Selection uses a name declared on the corresponding index set: δ[j] selects the entry at j : L_J, and dist[j][i] the entry at the pair of keys. An integer literal in brackets denotes a position, so use a declared key name to select from an indexed collection. Numerical keys must be integer-valued; the entries they identify, such as wages, distances and shock outcomes, may be real-valued. Separate indices of a finite shock distribution may identify equal numerical outcomes.

Calibration supplies a sequence in index order or a mapping from keys to entries. Integer ranges are ordered from the lower bound to the upper bound; listed sets retain the order in which their members are written. For example, declare:

θ : ℤ, >= 1
S_θ := {0, θ} ⊂ ℤ
q : S_θ → ℝ₊

The calibration fragment below sets θ to 5 and supplies 10.25 at key 0 and 20.75 at key 5:

θ: 5
q: [10.25, 20.75]

Writing q: {5: 20.75, 0: 10.25} gives the same association. If s : S_θ takes the value 5, q[s] selects 20.75; 5 is the key, not the fifth position. Calibration checks the integer keys, their distinctness, the data shape and the entries' declared domains. A matrix uses this order on each axis. Copying a collection between stages also requires matching key order (Periods §2).

Technical details

Compiled numerical selection uses signed 64-bit integers, with arithmetic checks that require each operand and intermediate result to fit that range. Constant integer expressions are evaluated exactly before the function is written. A power in an index bound or listed member requires a nonnegative integer exponent, which may depend on parameters, and parameter-dependent division is compiled only when the denominator is 1. For another division, supply the integer result as a separately declared parameter; the mathematical set remains available for inspection when compile_kernel() refuses the expression under kernel-form. A compiled integer calculation that overflows is refused rather than identifying another key.

docs.title: 9.2.2 Category codes
docs.text:
A named set may also be a comprehension, H := {i : ℤ | i >= 0, i <= 1}, which binds the name i to the set after the colon and holds the members that satisfy every condition after the bar. Mark such a set with !categories to assign meanings to its integer members, called category codes:

HouseholdStatus := {i : ℤ | i >= 0, i <= 1} :: [!categories household_status, newborn=0, old=1]
n : HouseholdStatus

A marked comprehension must range over ℤ or ℕ, and every condition must compare its bound name with an integer literal by a strict or weak inequality, with the name on either side. The conditions must give a nonempty range bounded below and above. Parameter bounds and equality conditions are refused on a marked set, although equality remains available in ordinary unmarked comprehensions. A marked range over ℕ must have a lower bound of at least 1, since the language does not decide whether 0 is a natural number. The annotation supplies exactly one category name for each member, with no repeated name or code (§9.3).

Here the code 0 stands for a newborn household and 1 for an old one. The category map records these associations between codes and categories. Arithmetic on the field has its usual numerical meaning: 100 - 120*n is 100 for a newborn household and −20 for an old one. With three or more categories, a formula affine in the code gives equal steps between the values at successive codes; that is an assumption of the formula the author writes. Assigning codes supplies no distance between categories or meaning to interpolation between them. The word category here denotes a value of a categorical variable, as in a statistical value label. Appendix C §2.1 gives the mathematical interpretation.

A category name is not a name usable in stage equations. The transition to old age is written with the code, n_next = 1; n_next = old is refused under name-in-scope. The category map remains part of the set's displayed definition, denotation and exported stage, so the meanings can be inspected alongside equations using the codes. Unmarked comprehensions keep their ordinary set meaning.

The identifier household_status asserts shared category meanings across stage files. Two sets using it identify a category by that identifier and the category's name; a different identifier denotes different categories. Without an identifier, categories are local to the named set in its stage text and shared by occurrences of that text. Periods §2 states when fields using these meanings can be connected.

Important

A comprehension marked !categories is admitted as a field domain, but is not an admitted index set for a collection. Thus n : HouseholdStatus is admitted, while payment : HouseholdStatus → ℝ is refused under readable-form. Use the index-set forms in §9.2.1 for indexed data.

Technical details

A stage constructed by make_stage from a syntax tree has no stage text. A marked set without an explicit category identifier therefore has no established category identity for connections in such a stage; supply the identifier when constructing it this way.

docs.title: 9.3 Type words and statement marks
docs.text:
A type word is a word after ! that gives a field its role or its information context; the ! sets it apart from a name the author chooses.

Word Meaning !state A state field. !ctrl A control, chosen with the information of the decision perch. !shck A shock, whose law and timing are declared separately. !vlu A value field. !arvl, !dcsn, !cntn The arrival, decision and continuation perches of §3.

Removing a word can change the problem: without !ctrl, c is no longer chosen. A parameter needs no word; β : (0,1) declares one. A type restated elsewhere in the file must agree with the first statement, and a word written on a side of a block's header follows the rules for roles: a shock listed as an argument is not thereby observed on that side, and a control listed beside continuation values remains a decision control (Perch tagging rules §2).

Two marks go in a line's annotation, :: [id=value, !node], and a third in the annotation of a named set, :: [!categories household_status, newborn=0, old=1]:

Mark Effect !node Keep the line as a computation of its own, an authored node that a method can address, without changing its equation. !doc Exclude the line from the equations that define the model; it documents them. !categories Give each member of a named integer comprehension a category name (§9.2.2). Write the marker, optionally followed by one shared identifier, and one name=code entry per member.

No mark is a role of a field, and !node and !doc together have no specified meaning. A failed check of the category marker, its entries or its set, the marker on any other item, and a field declared on a set with category codes at one site and on another set at another are refused under category-codes.

Technical details

A category name begins with a letter and continues with letters, digits and _. Its code is decimal digits with an optional sign, read as an integer, so 0, -0 and 00 are one code. An id= entry supplies the declaration's address, and a double-quoted description may accompany the category entries.

Inside the brackets a double-quoted entry keeps its quotes and is read as a description, so ["!categories"] marks nothing, while :: "!categories", written without brackets, is the marker without codes and is refused. Single quotes are characters of the entry, so 'old=1' is the key 'old with the value 1', which a marked annotation refuses, and a single-quoted marker, ['!categories'], marks nothing.

docs.title: 9.4 Brackets
docs.text:
Written Reading V[<], V or V[~], V[>] The field at the arrival, decision or continuation perch (§3). x[1], q[a] Selection from a family, by position counted from one, by a label or by a key declared on the collection's index set; a position is a whole number. L_J := {1, …, J} The integers from the first bound to the second, each bound integer-valued and allowed to depend on parameters. S_θ := {0, θ} ⊂ ℤ A finite set of integer keys in authored order, with integer membership and distinctness checked at calibration when they depend on parameters. δ : L_J → ℝ One parameter whose value is a collection with one entry, in ℝ, per member of L_J. (x, y) An ordered tuple. (x, y) : S Two fields constrained together by the set S. x : ℝ × ℝ One field whose values lie in a product set. 𝑞(x) A declared function applied to an argument.

In a type, (a,b) is an open interval; in an expression it is a tuple. Brackets never declare a function's domain: a function is defined with typed arguments. Equation parsing rules §3 gives the rules for functions and families.
