docs.title: Asva
docs.text:
Summary

Asva is the numerical toolkit beside bellman. It builds two numerical steps of backward builders from functions the reader writes: the endogenous grid step, which it also builds from the records of a stage's kernels, and the step that evaluates functions known on a grid of decision states at the points of an arrival grid, through the transition from arrival to decision. It also replaces missing and infinite entries of value and policy arrays, and its runner repeats a computation over the variants of a model, saves solutions, computes moments of simulated data and estimates parameters, in one process or in several. Its functions take arrays, functions, dictionaries and those records, and import nothing of bellman: the structure of a model, its stages, periods, trellis and inter-period connectors, is defined in bellman, and asva holds none of it.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — The Bellman factory: the recipe and the specified trellis, the runner's tests holding the fills of a recipe's slots; A builder §5: the record of a builder's kernels, from which egm builds the endogenous grid step. Used by — Numerical steps, The runner, Parameter sweeps, Saving solutions, Estimation and The cross-entropy method: the reference pages of the package. See also — Handler: the routine a methods file names for a method.

Key terminology Term Meaning Perch One of the three information sets within a stage: arrival, when the stage begins; decision, when the choice is made; continuation, after the choice (wiki). Handler The routine a methods file names for a method, written package:function, such as asva:make_egm_1d (wiki). Record of a builder's kernels What a builder's kernels() answers: for each of the builder's operations, in the order they apply, its printed kernel and the wires it reads and writes, and, where its kernel is an explicit function, its compiled function with the names of its arguments and outputs, or, for a row that states a relation its output satisfies, such as the identification of a policy block, its printed relation; the parameters' names and values; and the declared sets; with no reference to the stage (A builder §5). Endogenous grid method The method that computes the optimal choice at each point of a grid of the continuation state by inverting the Euler equation, and then the decision state at which that choice is made (Carroll 2006). Upper envelope Where the continuation value is not concave, the Euler equation has several solutions at some decision states; the upper envelope keeps, at each such state, the solution with the highest value. Registry and recipe A registry is the folder that holds a model's stage files and the files of their calibration, settings and methods; a recipe, a file such as spec.yml, lists for each stage the files from which its calibration, settings and methods are read (wiki). Slot and fill A slot is a $name in a recipe's list of files; a fill is the dictionary bound to it by the keyword of the same name (wiki). Test One variant of a model in a run: the fills of a recipe's slots, with a label, held as a TestSpec (The runner). Simulated method of moments Estimation that chooses the parameter values whose simulated moments come closest to the moments of the data (Estimation). Cross-entropy method A minimization method that draws candidate parameter values from a distribution and refits the distribution to the best of them (The cross-entropy method). MPI The Message Passing Interface, the standard for running one program as several processes that exchange data; Python uses it through the package mpi4py.

docs.title: 1 Installing and importing
docs.text: From the root of the repository, pip install -e packages/asva installs the package into the active environment. Each module is imported by its name, for instance from asva.egm_1d import make_egm_1d or from asva.run.sweep import sweep. The functions of asva.run.mpi use the package mpi4py when it is installed and run in one process when it is not; pip install -e "packages/asva[mpi]" installs asva together with mpi4py.

docs.title: 2 The modules
docs.text: Module Holds Page asva.egm_1d make_egm_1d and make_egm, the endogenous grid step on a grid of one dimension and of K dimensions; egm, the one-dimensional step built from the records of a stage's kernels Numerical steps §2, §3, §6 asva.compose_interp make_compose_interp, the step that evaluates functions known on a grid of decision states at the points of an arrival grid Numerical steps §4 asva.numerics clamp_value, clamp_policy and clamp_scalar Numerical steps §5 asva.simulate the forward simulator §4 asva.run.types, asva.run.make_test TestSpec, SimSpec, RunSpec and make_test The runner asva.run.sweep, asva.run.metrics, asva.run.mpi param_grid, sweep and SweepResult; the tables; the functions of MPI Parameter sweeps asva.run.io save_solution and load_solution Saving solutions asva.run.moments, asva.run.estimate the moment functions; the criterion, estimate and diagnostics Estimation, The cross-entropy method

docs.title: 3 Asva and bellman
docs.text:
A methods file may name an asva function as the handler of a method. The retirement-choice application attaches the endogenous grid method to the consumption stages of its retiree and its worker with entries such as the worker's, which names the method block of worker_cons_egm.bl and the exogenous grid of savings by the setting grid, its kind the tag !Cartesian with the grid's order and bounds beside it (Methodization §3):

  - on: policy
    method: !egm
    block: ../../methods/worker_cons_egm.bl
    handler: asva:make_egm_1d
    settings:
      grid: !Cartesian
      orders:
        b: n_a
      bounds:
        b: [a_min, a_max]

bellman keeps the method on the policy builder, policy, whose operations the method block writes (the method type !egm), and records the handler's name with it; it neither imports the function nor calls it. The reader's own code builds the step and applies it: from the specified stage it computes the arrays and the functions that make_egm_1d or another asva function takes, or it passes the records of the stage's kernels to egm (Numerical steps §6).

A test of the runner holds fills keyed by slot name, and these are the keyword arguments of load_recipe and assemble_trellis of bellman.trellis, so that one test selects one variant of the model that a registry's recipe describes (The runner §2).

docs.title: 4 Simulation
docs.text: This release of asva does not simulate. The module asva.simulate is installed with the package, and its two functions that simulate a population of agents, simulate over the periods and simulate_period over the stages of one period, raise an error when they are called. The simulated panels that an estimation needs are therefore computed by the reader's own code (Estimation §1).

docs.title: References
docs.text: • Carroll, C. D. (2006). "The method of endogenous gridpoints for solving dynamic stochastic optimization problems." Economics Letters 91(3), 312–320.

docs.title: Numerical steps
docs.text:
Summary

make_egm_1d builds the step of the endogenous grid method on a one-dimensional grid of the continuation state from four functions of numbers that the reader writes, and make_egm builds the same step on a grid of K dimensions. make_compose_interp builds the step that evaluates arrays known on a grid of decision states at the decision states \(g(x)\) of the points \(x\) of an arrival grid, with the transition \(g\) and the interpolation supplied by the reader. The three functions of asva.numerics replace missing and infinite entries of value and policy arrays. egm builds the one-dimensional step from the records of a stage's kernels, the two grids supplied by the caller, and passes the parameter values at each call. make_egm_1d, make_egm, make_compose_interp and egm each return a function, and none of the functions on this page reads a stage.

Relationship with other documents

Formal account — Operators and builders: the backward builders whose numerical steps these functions compute. Builds on — Perch: the arrival, decision and continuation perches that the names of the arguments refer to. See also — Constraints §4: the inverse Euler statement of a stage file, which the endogenous grid method reads.

docs.title: 1 The names of the arguments
docs.text: The suffix of an argument's name gives the perch at which its quantity stands: _arvl the arrival perch, _dcsn the decision perch and _cntn the continuation perch (perch). v is a value, dv a marginal value, ddv the second derivative of the value, c a control and x the state coordinate of a grid; the suffix _i marks the entry at one grid point. The suffix _hat marks a result of the endogenous grid step before an upper envelope: where the continuation value is not concave, the Euler equation has several solutions at some decision states, and the upper envelope keeps, at each such state, the solution with the highest value. fixed_state is a state held constant during the step, such as the housing stock of a household that keeps its house, and is 0.0 when there is none.

docs.title: 2 The one-dimensional step
docs.text:
The endogenous grid method (Carroll 2006) computes, at each point of a grid of the continuation state, the control from the marginal continuation value there, and then the decision state from which that control leads to the point. make_egm_1d builds this step from four functions:

make_egm_1d(fn_inv_euler, fn_bellman_rhs, fn_cntn_to_dcsn, fn_concavity)

The four arguments are functions of numbers compiled with numba.njit, the decorator of the Numba package that compiles a Python function to machine code. Each holds the model's parameters as constants: Numba reads their values when it compiles the function, at the step's first call, so a model with other parameter values needs its own four functions and its own step.

Argument Called at grid point i as Returns fn_inv_euler fn_inv_euler(dv_cntn_i, fixed_state) the control, from the marginal continuation value: the inverse Euler equation fn_bellman_rhs fn_bellman_rhs(c_i, v_cntn_i, fixed_state) the value at the decision perch fn_cntn_to_dcsn fn_cntn_to_dcsn(c_i, x_cntn_i, fixed_state) the decision state from which the control leads to the continuation state x_cntn_i: the point of the endogenous grid fn_concavity fn_concavity(c_i, ddv_cntn_i, fixed_state) a number that an upper-envelope step reads, such as the derivative of the continuation state with respect to the decision state

The call returns the step, a function that Numba compiles at its first call:

egm_step(dv_cntn, ddv_cntn, v_cntn, x_cntn, fixed_state)

Its first four arguments are one-dimensional arrays of one length: the marginal continuation value, its derivative and the continuation value at the points of the continuation grid x_cntn, and the grid itself. At each point the step calls the four functions in the order of the table, and it returns four arrays of the same length: the controls c_hat, the values v_hat, the endogenous grid x_dcsn_hat and the results of fn_concavity, del_a. The grid is an argument of the step, so one step computes on grids of every length without being compiled again. A function that Numba has not compiled is refused at the step's first call, with Numba's TypingError.

The example is one step of a consumption–savings problem at the decision perch: cash on hand \(m\), consumption \(c\) and savings \(a = m - c\), the utility \(u(c) = c^{1-\rho}/(1-\rho)\) with \(\rho = 2\), and the continuation value \(V_\succ(a) = -1/(1+a)\) on a grid of savings. The first-order condition \(u'(c) = V_\succ'(a)\) gives \(c = V_\succ'(a)^{-1/\rho} = 1 + a\); the point of the endogenous grid is \(m = a + c = 1 + 2a\); the value is \(u(c) + V_\succ(a) = -2/(1 + a)\); and the derivative of savings with respect to cash on hand, \(u''(c)/(u''(c) + V_\succ''(a))\), is one half at every point. The listing passes \(V_\succ'\), \(V_\succ''\) and \(V_\succ\) at the savings grid as the step's arguments dv_cntn, ddv_cntn and v_cntn, and names the endogenous grid, which is in cash on hand, m_hat.

import numpy as np
from numba import njit
from asva.egm_1d import make_egm_1d

ρ = 2.0

@njit
def inv_euler(dv_cntn, fixed_state):
    return dv_cntn ** (-1.0 / ρ)

@njit
def bellman_rhs(c, v_cntn, fixed_state):
    return c ** (1.0 - ρ) / (1.0 - ρ) + v_cntn

@njit
def cntn_to_dcsn(c, a, fixed_state):
    return a + c

@njit
def savings_slope(c, ddv_cntn, fixed_state):
    ddu = -ρ * c ** (-ρ - 1.0)
    return ddu / (ddu + ddv_cntn)

egm_step = make_egm_1d(inv_euler, bellman_rhs, cntn_to_dcsn, savings_slope)

a = np.array([0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0])
c_hat, v_hat, m_hat, del_a = egm_step((1 + a) ** -2, -2 * (1 + a) ** -3, -1 / (1 + a), a, 0.0)
print(c_hat, m_hat, v_hat.round(4), del_a)

[1.  1.5 2.  3. ] [1. 2. 3. 5.] [-2.     -1.3333 -1.     -0.6667] [0.5 0.5 0.5 0.5]

docs.title: 3 The step on K dimensions
docs.text:
make_egm(fn_inv_euler, fn_bellman_rhs, fn_cntn_to_dcsn, fn_concavity, params, n_dims, n_controls)

make_egm builds the same step on a grid of K = n_dims dimensions with n_controls controls. params is an array of the model's parameters, held by the step and passed to each function at every point. The four functions, compiled with numba.njit, also receive the grid point, since a coordinate of the grid may enter the utility, and they return what the table states:

Argument Called at grid point i as Returns fn_inv_euler fn_inv_euler(dv_cntn_i, x_cntn_i, fixed_state, params) the controls, an array of length n_controls fn_bellman_rhs fn_bellman_rhs(c_i, v_cntn_i, x_cntn_i, fixed_state, params) the value at the decision perch, a number fn_cntn_to_dcsn fn_cntn_to_dcsn(c_i, x_cntn_i, fixed_state, params) the point of the endogenous grid, an array of length K fn_concavity fn_concavity(c_i, ddv_cntn_i, x_cntn_i, fixed_state, params) the numbers an upper-envelope step reads, an array of length K

dv_cntn_i is the gradient of the continuation value at the point and ddv_cntn_i the diagonal of its matrix of second derivatives. The step is called as the one-dimensional step is, egm_step(dv_cntn, ddv_cntn, v_cntn, x_cntn, fixed_state), with arrays of these shapes for N grid points:

Array Shape dv_cntn, ddv_cntn, x_cntn (N, K) v_cntn (N,) the returned controls c_hat (N, n_controls) the returned values v_hat (N,) the returned x_dcsn_hat and del_a (N, K)

A coordinate that the decision leaves unchanged, such as the housing stock of a household that keeps its house, is returned unchanged by fn_cntn_to_dcsn, and fn_concavity may return 0.0 for it. The step constructs no grid: where the decision acts on fewer states than the continuation state holds, the grid lies on a set of lower dimension within the continuation states, and the reader constructs it before the call.

docs.title: 4 Composing with the arrival transition
docs.text:
make_compose_interp(g_transition, interp_fn)

g_transition(x_arvl, params) returns the decision states \(g(x)\) of an array of arrival states \(x\), params being an array of the model's parameters. interp_fn(xp, y_1, …, y_k, x) interpolates k arrays given at the points xp at the points x, both sorted in increasing order, and returns the k results as a tuple. The call returns the function

compose(x_dcsn_src, y_1, ..., y_k, x_arvl, params)

which computes the targets g_transition(x_arvl, params) and returns interp_fn(x_dcsn_src, y_1, …, y_k, targets): the arrays y_1 to y_k, given at the decision states x_dcsn_src, evaluated at the decision states \(g(x)\) of the points \(x\) of the arrival grid. For a transition \(g\) without a shock this is the pullback of each decision-perch function \(f\) along the transition, the composition \(f \circ g\), which is what the backward builder from the decision perch to the arrival perch computes. The step computes no expectation: with a shock in the transition, the reader integrates over it. The first argument is the grid of decision states, the last two are the arrival grid and the parameter array, and every argument between them is an array to interpolate. compose is a Python function, and the two functions given to make_compose_interp, g_transition and interp_fn, may be Python functions or functions compiled by Numba. Asva supplies no interpolation function; linear interpolation by numpy.interp is one the reader may pass.

The example continues §2. The arrival state is the assets \(k\) held before an income \(y\), so that cash on hand is \(m = Rk + y\), here with \(R = 1\) and \(y = 1\):

from asva.compose_interp import make_compose_interp

def arrival_to_decision(k, params):
    R, y = params
    return R * k + y

def interp_two(xp, y1, y2, x):
    return np.interp(x, xp, y1), np.interp(x, xp, y2)

compose = make_compose_interp(arrival_to_decision, interp_two)
k = np.array([0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0])
c_arvl, v_arvl = compose(m_hat, c_hat, v_hat, k, np.array([1.0, 1.0]))
print(c_arvl, v_arvl.round(4))

[1.   1.25 1.5  2.  ] [-2.     -1.6667 -1.3333 -1.    ]

Consumption, \((m + 1)/2\), is linear in cash on hand, so its interpolated values are exact. The value, \(-4/(m + 1)\), is not, and linear interpolation gives −1.6667 at \(m = 1.5\), where the value is −1.6.

docs.title: 5 Clamping values and policies
docs.text:
Function Returns clamp_value(arr, nan_val=-1e10) a copy of arr with every entry that is NaN or infinite, of either sign, replaced by nan_val, so that a state whose value is missing is never chosen clamp_policy(arr, min_val, max_val) a copy of arr with NaN replaced by min_val, the entries below min_val by min_val, and the entries above max_val, infinity included, by max_val clamp_scalar(val, min_val, max_val, nan_replacement) one number: nan_replacement for NaN, max_val for infinity, min_val for minus infinity, and otherwise val clipped to the interval from min_val to max_val

The three are compiled with numba.njit, so compiled functions may call them; the first two take one-dimensional arrays of floating-point numbers and leave them unchanged.

from asva.numerics import clamp_value, clamp_policy

print(clamp_value(np.array([1.0, np.nan, np.inf, -np.inf])))
print(clamp_policy(np.array([np.nan, -1.0, 0.5, 2.0, np.inf]), 0.0, 1.0))

[ 1.e+00 -1.e+10 -1.e+10 -1.e+10]
[0.  0.  0.5 1.  1. ]

docs.title: 6 The step from the records of a stage's kernels
docs.text:
egm builds the one-dimensional step of §2 from the records that the package bellman answers for a consumption stage, with no stage in hand:

step = egm(policy, decision, savings, evaluation)

policy and decision are the records stage.dcsn.builder.policy.kernels() and stage.dcsn.builder.bwd.kernels() (A builder §5): for each piece of the builder, its compiled function with the names of its arguments and outputs, and the parameters' names and bound values. egm reads from policy the inverse Euler equation and the endogenous grid, and from decision the law of motion and the aggregation, and refuses any other record. savings is the grid of the continuation state and evaluation the grid of the decision state, both read by the caller from the stage's methods and settings: the exogenous grid of savings that the stage's !egm entry names by its setting grid and the grid that the representation at the decision builder's Evaluation names the same way, each given by its kind, !Cartesian, and the order and bounds written beside it, with the values the stage's settings bind (Methodization §3). The step returned, step(value, marginal), takes the continuation value and its derivative as functions of the continuation state and returns the arrays of one endogenous grid step, EndogenousGridStep: the control, the continuation state, the value and the marginal value on the evaluation grid, and the endogenous grid with its control and value on the savings grid. The three functions the step applies are compiled once for their text, and the parameter values are passed at each call, so a new calibration needs no compilation. The lesson tutorials/topics/kernels.ipynb of the repository shows the records the step is built from.

docs.title: References
docs.text: • Carroll, C. D. (2006). "The method of endogenous gridpoints for solving dynamic stochastic optimization problems." Economics Letters 91(3), 312–320.

docs.title: The runner
docs.text:
Summary

The runner, asva.run, is used from Python. The variants of a model in a run are its tests: a test is a TestSpec, which holds a bundle, the dictionary from the names of a recipe's slots to the fills bound to them, and a label; make_test turns a list of bundles into tests. The slots of a test are the keyword arguments of load_recipe and assemble_trellis of bellman.trellis, so a test selects one variant of the model a recipe describes. RunSpec records a run for the reader's script. The reader's own function turns a test into a result, and the other modules of the runner repeat that function over the tests, tabulate, save and estimate.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Recipe functions: slots, fills, load_recipe and assemble_trellis. Used by — Parameter sweeps: the tests as the points of a sweep. See also — Asva §2: the modules of the package.

docs.title: 1 The modules of the runner
docs.text: Module Holds Page asva.run.types TestSpec, SimSpec and RunSpec §2, §4 asva.run.make_test make_test §2 asva.run.sweep param_grid, sweep and SweepResult §3; Parameter sweeps asva.run.metrics format_table, write_table and write_results_table Parameter sweeps §3 asva.run.mpi get_comm, rank_size, is_root, scatter_items, gather_results, bcast_item and mpi_map Parameter sweeps §4 asva.run.io save_solution and load_solution Saving solutions asva.run.moments make_moment_fn, compute_moments_from_panels, compute_moments_from_dataframe, load_data_moments and moment_names Estimation §2, §3 asva.run.estimate make_criterion, estimate, diagnostics, load_estimation_spec and EstimationResult Estimation §4, §5; The cross-entropy method

docs.title: 2 Tests
docs.text:
TestSpec(slots={}, label="") is a record that cannot be changed once it is made. slots maps the name of a slot, written without its $, to the fill bound to it, and label names the test in tables. make_test(slot_bundles) returns a tuple with one test for each bundle of the list, each with an empty label; an empty list gives one test with no slots, which is the model as its recipe writes it.

The durables registry, the folder applications/durables/declaration/ (Model directory layout), holds a recipe, spec.two-stages.yml, for the model without its tenure stage, the stage at which the household chooses whether to keep or adjust its housing; it names the slot $fill in the calibration list of every stage and in the settings lists of the two consumption stages (The Bellman factory §3). Run from the root of the repository, two tests that differ in the discount factor β give two syntactic trellises, the model as written with its fills in place:

from bellman.trellis import load_recipe
from asva.run.make_test import make_test

registry = "applications/durables/declaration"
recipe = "spec.two-stages.yml"

tests = make_test([{"fill": {"β": 0.93}}, {"fill": {"β": 0.95}}])
for test in tests:
    syntactic = load_recipe(registry, recipe, **test.slots)
    print(test.slots, syntactic["periods"][0]["stages"]["adjuster_cons"]["calibration"]["β"])

{'fill': {'β': 0.93}} 0.93
{'fill': {'β': 0.95}} 0.95

assemble_trellis(registry, recipe, **test.slots) of bellman.trellis takes the same keywords and goes on to elaborate and bind: it returns the specified trellis of the test's model, every stage of every period with its calibration, methods and settings bound, which the reader's own code solves. A slot that no test binds contributes nothing, so the tests of a run name only the slots they change (Recipe functions §2.3).

docs.title: 3 Tests over several axes
docs.text:
param_grid(**axes), from asva.run.sweep, returns the Cartesian product of named lists of values as a list of dictionaries, the last axis varying fastest. A test set over several axes writes each dictionary of the product into a bundle:

from asva.run.sweep import param_grid
from asva.run.types import TestSpec

points = param_grid(β=[0.93, 0.945], n_a=[300, 500])
tests = tuple(
    TestSpec(
        slots={"fill": {"calibration": {"β": p["β"]}, "settings": {"n_a": p["n_a"]}}},
        label=f"β={p['β']}, n_a={p['n_a']}",
    )
    for p in points
)
print([test.label for test in tests])

['β=0.93, n_a=300', 'β=0.93, n_a=500', 'β=0.945, n_a=300', 'β=0.945, n_a=500']

A fill keyed by kind, {"calibration": …, "settings": …}, is split between the calibration and the settings lists of the recipe, whereas a flat fill that names a parameter and a setting together is refused by load_recipe (Recipe functions §2.3). A test with an empty label is named in tables by its slots: a flat fill as fill.β=0.93, and a fill keyed by kind by its kinds alone, fill.calibration=…,fill.settings=…, which is why the tests above are given labels.

docs.title: 4 The record of a run
docs.text:
RunSpec is the record of one run that the reader's script builds and reads. It cannot be changed once it is made, every field is required, and no function of asva reads it. SimSpec(n_sim, seed, plots) is the record of a simulation: the number of simulated agents, the seed of the draws and whether plots are drawn.

Field Holds name the run's name base_spec the path of the model's specification, such as a registry output_dir the folder the run writes to, such as the model folder's results/ run_tag a label for the run's files, or None test_set the tests, a tuple of TestSpec sweep_runs the repetitions of each test in a sweep warmup whether a sweep calls each test once before its repetitions sim a SimSpec, or None mode the kind of run as a word, "single", "compare" or "sweep", which the script reads to decide what to run extra_args the model's own options, by name verbose, trace, mpi, gpu, skip_egm_plots, csv_export switches, each True or False, that the script reads 
from pathlib import Path
from asva.run.types import RunSpec

run = RunSpec(
    name="durables", base_spec=Path(registry), output_dir=Path("applications/durables/results"), run_tag=None,
    test_set=tests, sweep_runs=3, warmup=True, sim=None, mode="sweep", extra_args={},
    verbose=False, trace=False, mpi=False, gpu=False, skip_egm_plots=False, csv_export=False,
)
print(run.mode, len(run.test_set))

sweep 4

With a trial function that assembles and solves the model of one test, sweep(trial, run.test_set, metric_fns, n_reps=run.sweep_runs, warmup=run.warmup) runs the tests of the record (Parameter sweeps §1).

docs.title: Parameter sweeps
docs.text:
Summary

sweep(solve_fn, points, metric_fns) calls the reader's function at every point of a list, repeats each call, keeps at each point the repetition that is best by the first metric, and returns one SweepResult per point. The points are dictionaries from param_grid or tests from The runner. write_results_table writes the results of a sweep over tests as a Markdown or LaTeX table, and format_table and write_table format any list of dictionaries. Given an MPI communicator, the object through which the processes of a program run under MPI exchange data, sweep divides the points among the processes and collects the results on the first of them.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — The runner: tests and param_grid. Used by — The cross-entropy method §3: the functions of MPI that §4 states.

docs.title: 1 Running a sweep
docs.text:
sweep(solve_fn, points, metric_fns, n_reps=3, warmup=True, best="min", on_error="raise", verbose=True, comm=None)
Argument Default Meaning solve_fn the reader's function of one point, returning any result points the list of points, dictionaries or tests metric_fns a dictionary of named functions, each from a result to a number; the first is the primary metric n_reps 3 the number of repetitions at each point warmup True whether solve_fn is called once at each point before the repetitions, its result discarded, so that the time of compilation and of reading files falls outside them best "min" "min" keeps the repetition with the lowest primary metric, "max" the one with the highest on_error "raise" "raise" stops at the first exception; "skip" issues a warning and continues verbose True whether each point and each repetition are printed, by the process of rank 0 (§4) comm None an MPI communicator, which divides the points among processes (§4)

At each point sweep makes the warm-up call when warmup is true and then n_reps calls, evaluating every metric function on each result, and it keeps the metrics and the result of the repetition whose primary metric is best. It returns a list of SweepResult(point, metrics, result), one for each point in the order of the points: metrics are the best repetition's metrics, not averages over the repetitions, and result is that repetition's result. With on_error="skip", a failed call gives NaN for every metric, and a point at which every repetition failed has NaN metrics and the result None.

The example computes the mean of a lognormal income shock, \(E[e^{\sigma\varepsilon}] = e^{\sigma^2/2}\) with \(\varepsilon\) standard normal and \(\sigma = 0.5\), by Gauss–Hermite quadrature with two, four and six nodes, and records the time of each computation and its error:

import time
import numpy as np
from asva.run.sweep import param_grid, sweep

σ = 0.5

def solve(point):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    nodes, weights = np.polynomial.hermite.hermgauss(point["n_nodes"])
    mean = (weights * np.exp(σ * np.sqrt(2.0) * nodes)).sum() / np.sqrt(np.pi)
    return {"seconds": time.perf_counter() - start, "mean": mean}

metric_fns = {
    "seconds": lambda r: r["seconds"],
    "error": lambda r: abs(r["mean"] - np.exp(σ ** 2 / 2)),
}
results = sweep(solve, param_grid(n_nodes=[2, 4, 6]), metric_fns, verbose=False)
for r in results:
    print(r.point, f"error {r.metrics['error']:.1e}")

{'n_nodes': 2} error 5.5e-03
{'n_nodes': 4} error 2.5e-06
{'n_nodes': 6} error 3.9e-10

The primary metric is the time, so each point keeps the fastest of its three repetitions; the error is the same in every repetition.

docs.title: 2 Sweeping over tests
docs.text:
A sweep over the tests of The runner passes each test to the reader's function, which reads its slots. The function of a model assembles the test's model with assemble_trellis(registry, recipe, **test.slots) of bellman.trellis and solves it with the reader's own code; here the slot quadrature holds the number of nodes of the example of §1, and each test has its label:

from asva.run.types import TestSpec

tests = [TestSpec(slots={"quadrature": {"n_nodes": n}}, label=f"{n} nodes") for n in (2, 4, 6)]
results = sweep(
    lambda test: solve(test.slots["quadrature"]),
    tests,
    {"error": metric_fns["error"]},
    verbose=False,
)
print([(r.point.label, f"{r.metrics['error']:.1e}") for r in results])

[('2 nodes', '5.5e-03'), ('4 nodes', '2.5e-06'), ('6 nodes', '3.9e-10')]

docs.title: 3 Tables
docs.text:
format_table(rows, columns, fmt="markdown", float_fmt=".4f", caption=None) returns a table of a list of dictionaries as text: in Markdown, or, with fmt="latex", as a LaTeX table environment with the rules of the booktabs package and the caption when one is given. A floating-point number is formatted by float_fmt and any other value by str, and a column that a row lacks is left empty in that row. write_table(path, rows, columns, fmt="markdown", **kwargs) writes the same table to a file and creates the folders its path names; its further keywords, float_fmt and caption, are those of format_table. The results of sweep are not dictionaries, so a sweep over dictionaries is tabulated from {**r.point, **r.metrics}:

from asva.run.metrics import format_table

rows = [{**r.point, **r.metrics} for r in sweep(solve, param_grid(n_nodes=[2, 4, 6]), metric_fns, verbose=False)]
print(format_table(rows, ["n_nodes", "error"], float_fmt=".1e"))
print(format_table(rows, ["n_nodes", "error"], fmt="latex", float_fmt=".1e", caption="Quadrature error"))

| n_nodes | error   |
|---------|---------|
|       2 | 5.5e-03 |
|       4 | 2.5e-06 |
|       6 | 3.9e-10 |
\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\toprule
n\_nodes & error \\
\midrule
2 & 5.5e-03 \\
4 & 2.5e-06 \\
6 & 3.9e-10 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Quadrature error}
\end{table}

write_results_table(results, path, fmt="markdown", float_fmt=".4f", display_max_label=200) writes the results of a sweep over tests. Its first column holds each test's label, or, when the label is empty, the label derived from the test's slots (The runner §3), cut to display_max_label characters; the other columns hold the metrics in alphabetical order. A result whose point is not a test is refused with TypeError.

from asva.run.metrics import write_results_table

write_results_table(results, "tables/quadrature.md", float_fmt=".1e")
print(open("tables/quadrature.md").read())

| label   | error   |
|---------|---------|
| 2 nodes | 5.5e-03 |

docs.title: 4 Processes
docs.text:
The functions of asva.run.mpi use the package mpi4py when it is installed. The processes of a program run under MPI are numbered from 0, the number of a process being its rank. A communicator is the object through which a group of processes exchange data; get_comm() returns the communicator of all the processes of the program, MPI.COMM_WORLD, or None when mpi4py is not installed; every function below takes comm=None to mean one process.

Function Returns get_comm() MPI.COMM_WORLD, or None without mpi4py rank_size(comm=None) the pair (rank of this process, number of processes); (0, 1) without a communicator is_root(comm=None) whether this process has rank 0; True without a communicator scatter_items(items, comm=None) the slice of a list that this process takes: contiguous slices in the order of the ranks, the first processes taking one item more when the division is not exact gather_results(local_results, comm=None) on rank 0, the lists of all the processes joined in the order of the ranks; an empty list on the others bcast_item(item, comm=None, root=0) the item of the process of rank root, on every process mpi_map(fn, items, comm=None) [fn(x) for x in items], each process computing its slice, collected on rank 0

Given comm, sweep gives each process its slice of the points by scatter_items and collects the results by gather_results: rank 0 receives every result in the order of the points, and the other processes receive an empty list. The same script therefore runs in one process or in several:

from asva.run.mpi import get_comm, is_root

comm = get_comm()
results = sweep(solve, param_grid(n_nodes=[2, 4, 6]), metric_fns, verbose=False, comm=comm)
if is_root(comm):
    print(len(results))

3

Saved as sweep_script.py, it runs in four processes under the command mpirun -n 4 python -m mpi4py sweep_script.py, and in one process under python sweep_script.py.

docs.title: Saving solutions
docs.text:
Summary

save_solution writes a solution, a structure of dictionaries and lists whose leaves are arrays, numbers and strings, to a folder: the arrays to a compressed NumPy archive, and the rest of the structure with the reader's metadata to a JSON file. load_solution reads the folder back and returns the structure and the metadata. Neither file is a Python pickle, the format in which Python stores its own objects and which only Python reads, so the folder can also be read without asva, by any program that reads the two formats.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — The runner: the module asva.run.io among the modules of the runner. See also — The cross-entropy method §5: the checkpoints of an estimation, which are written separately.

docs.title: 1 Writing a solution
docs.text:
save_solution(path, solution, metadata=None)

path is a folder, solution any structure of the reader's, for instance a list holding, for each period of a trellis, a dictionary of the arrays that the reader's solver computed, and metadata a dictionary of the reader's own, such as the method and the grid sizes. save_solution creates the folder with any missing parent, writes two files into it, replacing files of the same names, and returns the folder as a pathlib.Path:

File Holds solutions.npz every array of the solution, compressed, under its dotted path: the array at solution["periods"][0]["c"] under the key periods.0.c metadata.json skeleton, the structure with each array replaced by a reference to its key and every other leaf in place; user_metadata, the dictionary given as metadata; array_keys, the keys of the archive in alphabetical order

A NumPy number among the leaves is written as a Python number.

docs.title: 2 Reading it back
docs.text:
load_solution(path) returns the pair (solution, metadata): the structure with its arrays read from the archive, and the dictionary given as metadata when the solution was written. A structure of dictionaries with string keys and of lists is read back as it was written. Three differences follow from the JSON format. A dictionary key is read back as a string, so a dictionary keyed by the integers 0, 1, … is read back keyed by "0", "1", …; a solution with string keys avoids the difference. A tuple is read back as a list. An array inside a tuple is not placed in the archive, since only dictionaries and lists are searched for arrays; it is written into the JSON file as a list of numbers.

import numpy as np
from asva.run.io import save_solution, load_solution

solution = {
    "periods": [{"c": np.array([0.5, 0.75, 1.0]), "note": "terminal"}],
    "solve_seconds": 1.25,
}
folder = save_solution("results/run_001", solution, metadata={"method": "EGM", "n_a": 3})
print(sorted(p.name for p in folder.iterdir()))

back, metadata = load_solution(folder)
print(back["periods"][0]["c"], back["periods"][0]["note"], back["solve_seconds"], metadata)

['metadata.json', 'solutions.npz']
[0.5  0.75 1.  ] terminal 1.25 {'method': 'EGM', 'n_a': 3}

docs.title: Estimation
docs.text:
Summary

Estimation by the simulated method of moments chooses the parameter values whose simulated moments come closest to the moments of the data. The reader writes a trial function, from a dictionary of parameter values to simulated panels; make_moment_fn turns a moment specification into a function from panels to named moments; make_criterion composes the two with the data moments into a loss; estimate minimizes the loss by the cross-entropy method; and diagnostics tabulates the fit.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Parameter sweeps §4: the functions of MPI with which an estimation divides its work among processes. Used by — The cross-entropy method: the steps and options of the minimization that estimate runs.

The parts compose as follows, the loss being minimized over θ by estimate:

θ  →  trial(θ): panels  →  moment_fn(panels): simulated moments  →  loss against the data moments

docs.title: 1 The trial function
docs.text: The trial function is the reader's. It takes a dictionary of parameter values, such as {"β": 0.95, "ρ": 2.0}, solves and simulates the model at those values with the reader's own code, and returns the panels: a dictionary from variable names to arrays of shape (T, N), with the T periods in rows and the N simulated agents in columns. A missing observation is NaN, and a discrete choice is a number, such as 0 or 1, and not a string. The trial function draws its shocks from one fixed seed at every call, so that every candidate θ is evaluated on the same shocks and the loss is a deterministic function of θ; estimate passes it no seed.

docs.title: 2 The moment specification
docs.text:
A moment specification is a dictionary, usually read from YAML, with three keys:

  • setup holds t0, the age of the first row (0 by default), and age_groups, which maps a group's name to a pair of ages [first, last]: the group takes the rows of the ages from first up to, but not including, last. Without age_groups, one group named all takes every row. derived_variables maps the name of a new variable to an expression in the panel's variables, computed before the moments; an expression may hold numbers, names, +, -, *, / and the functions np.log, np.maximum, np.minimum and np.abs, and nothing else is evaluated.
  • identification names the moments computed in every group: mean, sd (the standard deviation, with the number of observations as divisor), corrs (pairs of variables), autocorrs (the correlation of a variable between each row of the group and the row after it), branch_fractions (for a variable with integer values, the share of the group's observations equal to each value the variable takes in the panel) and conditional (the mean, standard deviation or correlation among the observations at which a discrete variable takes a given value).
  • targets lists moments under keys of the reader's choosing: {key, stat, var} with stat one of mean, sd and autocorr, {key, stat: fraction, var, value}, or {key, stat: corr, vars: [x, y]}.

A moment's key names the statistic, the variables and the group:

Moment Key mean of c in group 1 mean_c__age1 standard deviation of c sd_c__age1 correlation of c and a corr_c_a__age1 autocorrelation of a autocorr_a__age1 share of the value 1 of d branch_frac_d_1__age1 mean of c where d is 1 cond_d_1_mean_c__age1 the target with key avg_log_c avg_log_c__age1

A statistic computed from fewer than ten observations that are not NaN is NaN. make_moment_fn(spec) returns the function from panels to moments, and compute_moments_from_panels(panels, spec) computes them in one call:

import numpy as np
import yaml
from asva.run.moments import make_moment_fn

spec = yaml.safe_load("""
setup:
  t0: 20
  age_groups:
    1: [20, 25]
    2: [25, 30]
  derived_variables:
    log_c: np.log(np.maximum(c, 1e-10))
identification:
  mean: [c, a]
  sd: [c]
  corrs:
    - [c, a]
  autocorrs: [a]
  branch_fractions: [d]
  conditional:
    d:
      1: {mean: [c]}
targets:
  - {key: avg_log_c, stat: mean, var: log_c}
""")

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
panels = {
    "c": rng.uniform(0.5, 1.5, (10, 200)),
    "a": rng.uniform(0.0, 2.0, (10, 200)),
    "d": (rng.uniform(size=(10, 200)) > 0.7).astype(float),
}
moments = make_moment_fn(spec)(panels)
print(len(moments))
print([key for key in moments if key.endswith("__age1")])

18
['mean_c__age1', 'mean_a__age1', 'sd_c__age1', 'corr_c_a__age1', 'autocorr_a__age1', 'branch_frac_d_0__age1', 'branch_frac_d_1__age1', 'cond_d_1_mean_c__age1', 'avg_log_c__age1']

Each of the two groups gives nine moments: eight of identification, of which branch_fractions gives two since d takes the values 0 and 1, and the target.

moment_names(spec) lists the keys a specification gives on a synthetic panel of ten rows. It agrees with the keys of a real panel when every group lies within the first ten rows and the only variables of branch_fractions are discrete and z_idx, to which it gives the values 0 and 1; otherwise the keys of a real panel are list(moment_fn(panels)).

docs.title: 3 The data moments
docs.text:
The data moments are a dictionary with the same keys, from one of three sources:

  • Self-generated. The moment function applied to panels simulated at known values, moment_fn(trial(theta_true)). An estimation on them tests whether the method recovers theta_true.
  • A table of moments. load_data_moments(path, spec) reads a CSV file whose first column names the group and whose other columns are moments: the entry of the column mean_c in the row of group 5 becomes mean_c__age5, and an empty entry is left out. spec["column_map"], when present, maps a column's name to a key written with {age} in the place of the group, such as {"av_c": "mean_c__age{age}"}.
  • Microdata. With data_source: microdata in the specification, load_data_moments(path, spec) reads a table in long form, one row per agent and period, from a CSV file or a Parquet file (a compressed table format that pandas reads). The period stands in the column that setup.time_var names (t by default) and the agent in the column that setup.id_var names (_idx by default); compute_moments_from_dataframe turns the table into panels and applies the specification.

load_data_moments also accepts a dictionary of moments, of which it keeps the numbers that are not NaN.

docs.title: 4 The criterion
docs.text:
make_criterion(trial_fn, moment_fn, data_moments, weights=None) returns the loss as a function of a dictionary of parameter values. It orders the moments by their keys in alphabetical order and leaves out the data moments that are NaN. At each call it runs the trial function and the moment function, and returns

\[ \sum_i w_i\,(s_i - d_i)^2 \;+\; 10^6 \times n_{\text{missing}}, \]

where \(d_i\) is a data moment, \(s_i\) the simulated moment of the same key, the sum runs over the moments the simulation gives, and \(n_{\text{missing}}\) counts the moments that are missing from the simulation or NaN in it. Without weights, \(w_i = 1/d_i^2\) where \(|d_i| \ge 1\), a squared relative deviation, and \(w_i = 1\) otherwise, a squared absolute deviation, so that correlations and shares, which lie below one in absolute value, are not magnified. When it is given, weights is an array of the weights in the order of the moments. An exception in the trial or the moment function gives the loss \(10^{10}\), and the first three exceptions are printed with their tracebacks, the lists of the calls at which they were raised. After each call the criterion holds the simulated moments that are not NaN in its attribute last_sim_moments, which is None after an exception.

docs.title: 5 Estimating
docs.text:
estimate(criterion, param_spec, method="cross-entropy", method_options=None, comm=None, verbose=True, resume_state=None, checkpoint_fn=None, progress_fn=None)

estimate minimizes the criterion over the box that param_spec gives, a dictionary from each free parameter's name to {"bounds": [low, high]}. method accepts the cross-entropy method alone, written "cross-entropy", "ce" or "cross_entropy", and another value is refused with ValueError; The cross-entropy method states its steps, the options of method_options, and the use of comm, resume_state, checkpoint_fn and progress_fn. The result is an EstimationResult:

Field Holds theta the best parameter values found objective the loss at theta converged whether the stopping rule was met before the iterations ran out n_iter the number of iterations, those of a resumed estimation included history for each iteration, the mean means and the covariance cov of the sampling distribution, the best loss so far best_loss, and the mean loss elite_mean_loss of the iteration's best candidates, the elite sim_moments the simulated moments of the last candidate the criterion evaluated on the first process (rank 0, Parameter sweeps §4), which in general is not theta

To read the fit at theta, the reader evaluates the criterion there and places its moments in the result before calling diagnostics, as the example of §6 does.

diagnostics(result, data_moments, moment_names=None, weights=None) returns a dictionary with three entries. fit_table holds one row for each data moment with its data value, simulated value, residual, contribution and share of the total contribution in percent; total_loss is the result's objective; and worst_moments holds the five largest contributions. A contribution is the squared residual, multiplied by the moment's weight when weights is given, and \(10^6\) for a moment the simulation lacks; the criterion's default weights are not applied. moment_names gives names to display, as a dictionary by key or as a list in the keys' alphabetical order.

load_estimation_spec(path) reads a YAML file with an estimation block, which holds free, method, method_options and optionally theta_true, and a moments block, which is the moment specification. It returns a dictionary with the keys free, moment_spec, data_moments, method and method_options, and theta_true when the file gives it. With data_source: precomputed, which is the default, it reads the data moments from the CSV file that data_file names (moments.csv by default) in the folder of the YAML file, keeping the rows whose first entry is a number and not applying column_map; with another source its data moments are an empty dictionary.

docs.title: 6 A complete example
docs.text:
The model of the example is an outcome y equal to a mean μ plus σ times a standard normal shock, simulated for 500 agents over 20 periods, and the data moments are self-generated at μ = 1 and σ = 0.5:

from asva.run.estimate import make_criterion, estimate, diagnostics

def trial(theta):
    shocks = np.random.default_rng(42).standard_normal((20, 500))
    return {"y": theta["mu"] + theta["sigma"] * shocks}

moment_fn = make_moment_fn({"identification": {"mean": ["y"], "sd": ["y"]}})
data_moments = moment_fn(trial({"mu": 1.0, "sigma": 0.5}))

criterion = make_criterion(trial, moment_fn, data_moments)
result = estimate(
    criterion,
    {"mu": {"bounds": [0.0, 2.0]}, "sigma": {"bounds": [0.1, 1.0]}},
    method_options={"n_samples": 40, "n_elite": 8, "max_iter": 30, "tol": 1e-6, "sampling_seed": 0},
    verbose=False,
)
print({name: round(value, 2) for name, value in result.theta.items()}, result.converged)

criterion(result.theta)
result.sim_moments = dict(criterion.last_sim_moments)
for row in diagnostics(result, data_moments)["fit_table"]:
    print(row["moment"], round(row["data"], 3), round(row["simulated"], 3))

{'mu': 1.0, 'sigma': 0.5} True
mean_y__ageall 0.995 0.996
sd_y__ageall 0.503 0.503

Run under MPI with comm=get_comm() from asva.run.mpi, the same script evaluates the candidates of each iteration on several processes (The cross-entropy method §3).

docs.title: The cross-entropy method
docs.text:
Summary

estimate minimizes a criterion by the cross-entropy method of Kroese, Porotsky and Rubinstein (2006). At each iteration it draws candidate parameter values, evaluates the criterion at each, keeps the best of them, the elite, and refits the sampling distribution to the elite; it stops when the mean loss of the elite changes by less than a tolerance. This page states the steps, the options, the division of the work among MPI processes, what happens when a step fails, and the checkpoints from which an estimation resumes.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Estimation: the criterion that the method minimizes and the result it returns. See also — Parameter sweeps §4: the functions of MPI.

docs.title: 1 The steps
docs.text:
The free parameters are ordered by name, and every draw comes from one random generator, numpy.random.default_rng(sampling_seed), so that one seed gives one sequence of candidates. Before the first iteration the best values are the midpoints of the bounds with the loss \(10^{10}\), a placeholder that is never evaluated. Each iteration then makes six steps:

  1. Draw. At the first iteration, n_samples candidates are drawn independently and uniformly within the bounds. At later iterations they are drawn from the multivariate normal distribution with the current mean and covariance; a draw outside the bounds is drawn again, up to a thousand times, and then clipped to the bounds. A share noise_fraction of the candidates is drawn uniformly instead.
  2. Evaluate. The criterion is evaluated at every candidate.
  3. Select. The n_elite candidates with the lowest losses form the elite.
  4. Record the best. An elite candidate whose loss is below the best loss so far becomes the best.
  5. Refit. The new mean and covariance are the weighted mean and covariance of the elite, the weight of candidate i proportional to \(\exp(-(L_i - \min_j L_j))\) for the losses \(L\), with \(10^{-12}\) times the identity added to the covariance. With alpha_smooth below one, from the second iteration the mean and the covariance are alpha_smooth times the new ones plus 1 − alpha_smooth times the previous ones.
  6. Stop or continue. From the second iteration, the estimation has converged when the mean loss of the elite differs from that of the previous iteration by less than tol. It stops then, after max_iter iterations, or after max_iter_this_run iterations of the present call.

The weights make the refit depend on the scale of the losses: a candidate whose loss exceeds the elite's lowest by ten has about \(4.5 \times 10^{-5}\) times the weight of the best. The result's theta and objective are the best candidate and its loss (Estimation §5).

docs.title: 2 The options
docs.text:
The options are the entries of method_options, in Python or under estimation.method_options of the YAML file that load_estimation_spec reads:

Option Default Meaning n_samples 48 the number of candidates drawn at each iteration n_elite 10 the size of the elite, at least 1 and at most n_samples max_iter 50 the largest number of iterations tol 0.01 the change in the elite's mean loss below which the estimation has converged sampling_seed 0 the seed of the draws noise_fraction 0.0 the share of the candidates drawn uniformly after the first iteration alpha_smooth 1.0 the weight of the new mean and covariance against the previous ones max_iter_this_run max_iter the largest number of iterations of one call checkpoint_dir None a folder in which the state is written after every iteration (§5) 
estimation:
  free:
    beta: {bounds: [0.88, 0.99]}
    rho: {bounds: [1.0, 5.0]}
  method: cross-entropy
  method_options:
    n_samples: 48
    n_elite: 10
    max_iter: 50
    tol: 1.0e-3
    sampling_seed: 42

The number of candidates sets how widely an iteration explores the box: ten to twenty candidates for each free parameter is a common choice. The elite's size sets how many candidates the refit averages: a small elite follows the few best candidates, and a large one moves the distribution slowly; five to twenty percent of the candidates is a common choice. The tolerance is in the units of the loss, and a smaller one continues the iterations until the elite's losses agree more closely.

The example minimizes a criterion whose minimum is known, at \(x = 0.3\) and \(y = -0.2\):

from asva.run.estimate import estimate

def criterion(theta):
    return (theta["x"] - 0.3) ** 2 + (theta["y"] + 0.2) ** 2

free = {"x": {"bounds": [-1.0, 1.0]}, "y": {"bounds": [-1.0, 1.0]}}
options = {"n_samples": 30, "n_elite": 6, "max_iter": 40, "tol": 1e-8, "sampling_seed": 0}

result = estimate(criterion, free, method_options=options, verbose=False)
print({name: round(value, 3) for name, value in result.theta.items()}, result.converged)

{'x': 0.3, 'y': -0.2} True

With verbose=True, the first process, of rank 0 (Parameter sweeps §4), prints one line for each iteration, with the best loss, the elite's mean loss and the best values, and between iterations a line on the memory the process uses.

docs.title: 3 Processes
docs.text: With comm=get_comm() from asva.run.mpi, the process of rank 0 draws the candidates and sends them to every process; mpi_map gives each process a contiguous slice of the candidates and collects the losses on rank 0 in the order of the candidates; rank 0 selects the elite, refits the distribution and sends the new state, and whether the stopping rule was met, to every process before the next draw. With n_samples equal to the number of processes, each process evaluates one candidate at each iteration; with more candidates some processes evaluate several in turn, and with fewer some are idle. Only rank 0 prints and writes checkpoints. A script that calls estimate(..., comm=get_comm()), saved as estimate_script.py, runs in 48 processes under the command mpirun -n 48 python -m mpi4py estimate_script.py.

docs.title: 4 Failures
docs.text: Failure What happens the criterion raises an exception at a candidate the candidate's loss is \(10^{10}\), and the first three exceptions are printed with their tracebacks, the lists of the calls at which they were raised a draw stays outside the bounds after a thousand attempts it is clipped to the bounds the elite's weights sum to zero, or to a number that is not finite the weights are equal the elite's covariance is singular adding \(10^{-12}\) times the identity, as step 5 does, makes it positive definite a process stops the estimation stops; no other process evaluates that process's candidates

docs.title: 5 Checkpoints and resuming
docs.text:
With checkpoint_dir, rank 0 writes the state after every iteration to the file state.pkl in that folder: a dictionary stored in the pickle format, Python's own format for storing objects, with the keys means, cov, best_theta, best_loss, it (the iteration just completed, counted from zero), history, elite_mean_loss_prev and rng_state, the state of the random generator. The file is written under another name and then renamed, so that an interrupted write leaves the previous state in place. estimate(..., resume_state=state), with state the dictionary read from that file, continues at the next iteration with the same generator state, so that an estimation run in several calls draws the same candidates as one run in a single call. max_iter_this_run lets a long estimation run as a sequence of shorter calls in this way:

import pickle

options = {**options, "max_iter": 6, "max_iter_this_run": 3, "checkpoint_dir": "checkpoints"}
first = estimate(criterion, free, method_options=options, verbose=False)
with open("checkpoints/state.pkl", "rb") as f:
    state = pickle.load(f)
second = estimate(criterion, free, method_options=options, verbose=False, resume_state=state)

in_one_call = estimate(criterion, free, method_options={**options, "max_iter_this_run": 6, "checkpoint_dir": None}, verbose=False)
print(first.n_iter, state["it"], second.n_iter, second.theta == in_one_call.theta)

3 2 6 True

The first call stops after three iterations, and its last state records the iteration 2, counted from zero; the second call continues to the sixth iteration, and its best values equal those of one call of six iterations.

checkpoint_fn, a function of the state dictionary, takes the place of the file that checkpoint_dir writes, and progress_fn(it, info), called after every iteration with info holding best_theta, best_loss and elite_mean_loss, takes the place of the line that verbose prints.

docs.title: References
docs.text: • Kroese, D. P., Porotsky, S. and Rubinstein, R. Y. (2006). "The cross-entropy method for continuous multi-extremal optimization." Methodology and Computing in Applied Probability 8(3), 383–407.

docs.title: Bellman calculus
docs.text:
Summary

The Bellman calculus describes staged recursive decision problems through their states, information, equations and composed operators. These pages explain the mathematical interpretation, with one buffer-stock running example and explicitly unfinished chapters on composition.

Relationship with other documents

Used by — Bellman-SYM documents the .bl stage source and supporting YAML whose meaning these pages state; Bellman-SYM's Appendix C states the interpretation rules and their assumptions. See also — Concept wiki provides linked definitions.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
A recursive dynamic program specifies sequential choices, current rewards and continuation values. The calculus records which information is available at each stage and how its operations compose. It distinguishes random fields from representing functions, mathematical interpretation from numerical approximation, and fixed-policy evaluation from optimization.

The intended reader is an economist interpreting or constructing a model. The exposition uses mathematical prose and selected derivations; unfinished sections remain labeled. A typed graph does not by itself prove integrability, optimal selection or numerical convergence. The source rules and Python interfaces belong to Bellman-SYM, while these pages discuss their mathematical meaning.

docs.title: 2. Reading order
docs.text:
Start with Introduction and the buffer-stock example, then read stages, fields and operators. The branching notes contain further example outlines; they are not additional fully developed running examples.

Page Subject Introduction Source, mathematical interpretation and numerical computation. Illustrative example The buffer-stock Bellman equation and staged factorization. Stages and perches Information, sufficient states, conditional laws and stage operators. Fields, functions and types Random quantities, value domains, representative functions and binding. Operators and builders Unfinished notes on transition expectation, evaluation, selection and implicit relations. Methods The signature of an operator with its method and grid components, composition over the field component, the grid as a retract, the handler, the two erasures and the two levels of a stage. Stage composition Unfinished notes on compatible joins within periods. Periods and the trellis Unfinished notes on occurrence-specific composition and boundary data. Branching Unfinished notes on labeled choices and exogenous selection. Semi-conjugacy Unfinished notes on conditional relations between operator forms. Abstract grammar Mathematical composition notation and its distinction from concrete source grammar. Ingredients Symbol and terminology reference.

docs.title: 3. Appendices and catalogues
docs.text: Reference Subject Appendix A — Semantics Source interpretation, retained equations and numerical attachments. Appendix B — Initial-algebra semantics Ground/free terms, specified interpretations and exact refinement. Appendix C — The stage term Typed builder symbols and compatible stage compositions. Appendix D — Kinds and sorts Declared type order, interpreted inclusion and local classification conventions. Appendix F — Operator algebra Composition, transition pairing, branching and numerical obligations. Appendix G — Functional programming Primitive objects, typed expressions, stages, calibration and methodization functors, and numerical realization. Catalogue index Field, function, operator and parameter/settings inventories. Fields Field declarations, value domains and representatives. Functions Typed functions and their mathematical roles. Operators Operations and their input/output types. Parameters and settings Economic model inputs and numerical choices.

docs.title: Introduction to Bellman calculus
docs.text:
Summary

The Bellman calculus describes a recursive decision problem as a composition of operations with declared inputs and outputs. It separates the economic equations, their mathematical interpretation and the numerical procedures used to approximate their solution.

Relationship with other documents

Used by — Bellman-SYM introduces the authored source; Bellman-SYM's Appendix C specifies how source constructs are interpreted. See also — Illustrative example develops the buffer-stock model.

The Bellman calculus is a mathematical account of staged recursive dynamic programs, sequential decision problems specified by states, feasible actions, rewards, transitions and continuation values. The modeler writes stage equations in .bl, with supporting YAML for composition and numerical choices. Their semantics states what those expressions mean. Numerical methods approximate the resulting operations under separate assumptions.

Recursive dynamic programs

A fixed-policy operator \(\mathbb T_\pi\) evaluates a specified policy \(\pi\); an optimizing Bellman operator \(\mathbb T\) takes the supremum over feasible actions. Finite-horizon problems use backward recursion from a terminal value. In a stationary infinite-horizon problem, a value can be characterized by a fixed point under suitable existence and optimality conditions. A type signature alone does not establish those conditions; see Periods and the trellis.

A stage organizes a local decision around its available information, transitions, rewards and controls. Stages compose into periods, and periods compose across time into a trellis, the declared sequence of period occurrences and their inter-period connections. A stage can be examined separately once its continuation input and other required inputs have been supplied. Replacing it in a larger model requires compatible boundaries and may change values elsewhere in that model.

docs.title: 1. Modularity
docs.text:
Dynamic programming studies operators on value functions; their composition makes the dependence between local problems explicit.1 Consider two fixed-policy operators

\[ \mathbb T_{A,\pi}:\mathsf V_0\to\mathsf V_1, \qquad \mathbb T_{B,\pi}:\mathsf V_1\to\mathsf V_2. \]

Here each \(\mathsf V_i\) is a specified class of functions on the corresponding state space, and \(\pi\) collects the relevant fixed policies. With primitives and other free inputs held fixed, define \(v_A=\mathbb T_{A,\pi}v\) and \(v_B=\mathbb T_{B,\pi}v_A\). The second operation receives the first operation's result as its continuation input. More generally, \(K\) operators with matching types \(\mathbb T_{k,\pi}:\mathsf V_{k-1}\to\mathsf V_k\) compose as

\[ \mathbb T_\pi=\mathbb T_{K,\pi}\circ\mathbb T_{K-1,\pi}\circ\cdots\circ\mathbb T_{1,\pi}, \qquad v_k=\mathbb T_{k,\pi}v_{k-1},\quad k=1,\ldots,K. \]

This is an order of backward calculation: the rightmost operator acts first. Each output must lie in the next operator's domain, including its regularity and integrability requirements. Once the common parameters and policies are fixed, the displayed chain connects the operators through the value functions \(v_k\).

Combining functions through explicit composition follows the functional-programming approach illustrated by Backus.2 Referential transparency means that an expression can be replaced by another with the same denotation in the same context.3 It does not mean an operator is independent of its arguments or that changing it preserves the result.

Functional programming gives the full account of objects, functions, application, combining forms and definitions, then explains represented functions and the connection to typed economic operations. It defines calibration and methodization on those objects and works through the distinction between a stage, its mathematical target and its numerical realization.

For example, changing an interpolation method produces a different numerical approximation to a specified mathematical operation. A compatible input/output representation permits substitution in the calculation, but the approximation error can affect every subsequent value in backward order. Inserting or removing a type-compatible operator likewise defines a composition; it need not preserve the economic problem. Exact replacement requires equality of the relevant operations, as qualified in Initial-algebra semantics.

Modularity has four intended uses:

  • Write the economic equations once. Their definitions can be used in exposition and numerical construction.
  • Compare numerical choices. Alternative approximations can be attached to a declared operation and assessed for accuracy.
  • Inspect what is computed. An explicit interpretation connects equations to mathematical objects; implementation correctness still requires verification.
  • Communicate at different levels of detail. A stage operator can be examined as a whole or through its defined constituent operations.

In an applied model, separately maintained equations and solver routines can disagree about timing, shock placement or feasible choices. Declared domains, information and dependencies help identify such disagreements. This is a reason to record the relation between the model and its computation, not a claim that other mathematical notation or programming styles cannot express it.

The calculus therefore names the operations and the inputs on which they depend. It also distinguishes the Υ (Upsilon) interpretation, which assigns mathematical meaning, from the Ρ (Rho) numerical construction, which uses selected methods, calibration and settings to obtain executable computations. An interpretation of the equations does not itself certify a numerical procedure's accuracy or convergence.

docs.title: 2. Mathematical interpretation
docs.text:
A denotational semantics assigns mathematical meanings to expressions, with a compound expression interpreted from its constituents and the relevant input environment.4 The environment assigns values to free inputs, such as a continuation function. In the specified construction, arithmetic in .bl equations is parsed; the temporary abstract syntax tree, a record of the source's grammatical structure, and the recorded source locations are used during interpretation. Retained stage equations, local definitions and typed diagrams record the interpreted structure. This is the specified construction rather than a statement that every runtime component already implements it.

YAML declarations of periods and the trellis retain the outer model organization, and each occurrence has fresh stage objects. A connector identifies compatible boundary quantities by declared renaming; a nonidentity economic transformation requires an authored equation. No single stored graph of the entire trellis is required by these statements.

Several related calculations may be derived from a model. Under a fixed feasible policy \(\pi\), the backward transition expectation \(P_\pi\) and forward distribution operator \(\mathbb M_\pi\) satisfy the restricted expectation–measure pairing described in Operators and builders §3. A reward-bearing or optimizing Bellman operator \(\mathbb T\) does not have that linear-distribution pairing in general. Relations between alternative value representations require their own conditions; see Semi-conjugacy.

A typed diagram records which operations can compose. It does not by itself establish that states are sufficient, integrals finite, maximizing policies measurable, fixed points unique or numerical approximations convergent. Those properties can be stated mathematically and checked under explicit hypotheses. They do not depend on whether source code gives every intermediate operation a name.

docs.title: 3. Source and numerical construction
docs.text:
The source and mathematical components have distinct roles:

  • Stage source. Bellman-SYM defines .bl declarations and equations, including local functions and arithmetic expressions.
  • Model composition. Supporting YAML describes periods, the trellis, connectors, calibration, method assignments and settings. The current forms are documented with the source language.
  • Mathematical interpretation. The calculus describes fields, functions and composed operators. The stage term distinguishes this mathematical structure from concrete syntax.
  • Numerical construction. Methodization attaches supported numerical procedures to declared equations. A handler is the implementation of such a procedure; its requirements include the mathematical and representation assumptions it needs. Bellman-SYM's Python API documents construction and use from Python.

Parsing, interpretation, method assignment, calibration and numerical execution must agree for a computed result to approximate the declared problem. These notes describe the mathematical relations, while the source documentation states the authoring and API rules. Comparisons with alternative solver formulations remain conditional on the correspondence and approximation results established for them.

The following chapters introduce the buffer-stock Bellman equation, stages and perches, fields and functions, operators and builders, and the composition of stages into periods and trellises. The branching and semi-conjugacy chapters retain their unfinished example outlines.

These are background results under their stated hypotheses, not a claim that every model below satisfies them. ↩

  2. Backus, J. (1978). Can programming be liberated from the von Neumann style? A functional style and its algebra of programs. Communications of the ACM 21(8), 613–641, §5.2, pp. 616–617. ↩

  3. Stoy, J. E. (1977). Denotational Semantics: The Scott-Strachey Approach to Programming Language Theory. MIT Press, §1.1, pp. 5–7. ↩
