docs.title: Abstract grammar
docs.text:
This page describes mathematical composition terms for stages, periods and trellises. #syntax #ffp

Summary

A composition term records which stage and connector operations are combined. This mathematical notation is distinct from the concrete .bl grammar, its temporary parser tree and the retained structures of a constructed stage. The period and trellis calculations below illustrate the distinction.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Stage composition and Periods and the trellis define the compatible compositions. Formal account — Initial-algebra semantics treats specified terms and interpretations; The stage term gives the stage-level signature. Used by — Stages, Field equations, Period Syntax, Trellis Syntax and Methodization state the authoring rules; Bellman-SYM's Appendix C states the interpretation rules.

docs.title: 1 Two grammars
docs.text:
The concrete grammar specifies which source strings are well formed. The abstract grammar describes the structure of their expressions after punctuation is removed. Schmidt distinguishes the derivation tree from the string that abbreviates it.1 For the current language, .bl stage declarations and arithmetic equations are parsed, while supporting YAML records model composition and bindings. The mathematical composition notation used here is a separate description of the resulting operations.

The syntax pages use ASDL, the Zephyr Abstract Syntax Description Language, to describe constructor positions and their types.2 An ASDL field is a named position in a constructor, distinct from an economic field. The symbols ? and * denote an optional position and a list. These notations describe syntax structure; they do not make every mathematical diagram on this page a concrete parser constructor. An operator's method and grid components, written as typing entries of the operator's name, are described in Methods §2.

The following is schematic mathematical composition notation, not the .bl abstract grammar or a loader schema. It suppresses documentation names and binding records to show the composition operands:

model_term = TRELLIS(period* periods, connector* inter_connectors)
period     = PERIOD(stage_occurrence* stages, connector* connectors)
connector  = CONNECTOR(pair* pairs)
pair       = (identifier source, identifier target)

Here a stage occurrence supplies an already specified stage operation with its required inputs. Stage declarations, function bodies, arithmetic, local binders and branches have their own source structures; they are not terminal atoms in the concrete grammar. The current forms are recorded on Bellman-SYM's pages on stages and field equations. The stage term gives a mathematical inventory, not a competing STAGE parser production.

A connector records compatible field identifications. An empty explicit rename list gives an identity connection only when the source rules already determine matching boundaries; it cannot supply missing compatibility. The compositions below are restricted to chains with those identifications specified. General branching and the economic order of stages are not determined by the order of entries in an ASDL list. Periods and the trellis §§3–6 supplies the boundary conditions.

A source format can be changed without changing meaning only when its translation preserves the declared terms, binding and interpretation. A new file format is not automatically equivalent because it can store similar lists. Three objects therefore remain distinct: the source string, a mathematical term describing composition, and its interpretation in a specified algebra of operations.

docs.title: 2 Expressions are objects
docs.text:
Backus's FFP systems use objects to represent functions systematically. Functional forms are represented by sequences whose first element identifies the form and whose remaining elements give its parameters.3 The representation and evaluation functions are part of the description of the system.4 This provides a comparison with headed composition records; it does not prescribe the parser or runtime representation of Bellman-SYM.

Functional programming §§1–5 supplies the underlying definitions, the algebra of combining forms and the distinction between an FP object and an object in a category. The examples below apply that account to model composition.

Note

Backus's representation function \(\rho\) and meaning function \(\mu\) are his notation. This page uses \(\Upsilon\) for the interpretation of its mathematical terms. Backus's \(\rho\) is distinct from this project's numerical-construction map Ρ and from a utility-curvature parameter.

Consider the existing two-stage consumption–portfolio composition schematically. The current period authoring example of Bellman-SYM includes a separate discount stage; here its placement is left within the specified stage operations. Once their compatible boundaries and fixed policies have been supplied, a coarse object representation is

\[ P\equiv\langle\mathrm{PERIOD},\langle s_{\mathrm{cons}},s_{\mathrm{port}}\rangle,\langle C\rangle\rangle, \qquad C\equiv\langle\mathrm{CONNECTOR},\langle\langle a,k\rangle\rangle\rangle. \]

The symbols \(s_{\mathrm{cons}}\) and \(s_{\mathrm{port}}\) represent stage occurrences, and \(\langle a,k\rangle\) identifies outgoing assets with incoming capital. The sequence is a mathematical encoding of these operands, not the actual YAML mapping. Its interpretation is

\[ \Upsilon(P)=\Upsilon(s_{\mathrm{cons}})\circ\varkappa^*\circ\Upsilon(s_{\mathrm{port}}) =\mathbb T_{[\mathrm{cons}],\pi}\circ\varkappa^*\circ\mathbb T_{[\mathrm{port}],\pi}. \]

The map \(\varkappa\) identifies the compatible boundary states, and its pullback acts on functions by \((\varkappa^*v)(x)=v(\varkappa(x))\). It implements the declared renaming, not a new economic transformation. Consumption precedes portfolio choice in economic time; the portfolio operator is applied first in backward calculation. Field dependencies and declared joins establish this order, not YAML list position.

This composition resembles Backus's insert, which applies a binary function repeatedly across a sequence.6 To use insert on representations of functions, one must specify an operation that constructs a representation of their composite. Backus's FFP allows forms represented by objects; it does not by itself define the calculus's composition rules. Here those rules are the displayed equations on compatible domains.

For a finite horizon of \(H\ge2\) periods, numbered here in forward economic order, write

\[ N\equiv\langle\mathrm{TRELLIS},\langle P_0,\ldots,P_{H-1}\rangle, \langle\chi_0,\ldots,\chi_{H-2}\rangle\rangle, \qquad \Upsilon(N)=\Upsilon(P_0)\circ\chi_0^*\circ\Upsilon(P_1)\circ\cdots\circ\chi_{H-2}^*\circ\Upsilon(P_{H-1}). \]

This numbering differs from the application's backward-from-terminal index described in §1 of Bellman-SYM's Trellis Syntax page.

Each \(\chi_i^*\) is the pullback of the compatible inter-period identification. For one period, there are no inter-period connectors. With terminal function \(v_T\) in the last operator's domain, backward evaluation is

\[ \Upsilon(N)(v_T)=\Upsilon(P_0)\Bigl(\chi_0^*\bigl(\Upsilon(P_1)(\cdots\Upsilon(P_{H-1})(v_T)\cdots)\bigr)\Bigr). \]

Every intermediate output must belong to the next input domain. Free parameters and policies are held fixed in these displays; an optimizing interpretation requires its separately defined operators. The calculation resembles evaluating a represented compound form from its constituent meanings, but Backus's metacomposition rule does not supply the economic identities or assumptions.5

Backus's inner-product example combines summation, pairwise multiplication and transposition.7 The comparison is structural:

Role Backus's inner product Mathematical model composition Constituent functions \(+\), \(\times\), \(\mathrm{Trans}\) Stage operators and connector pullbacks Combining forms \(/{+}\), \(\alpha\times\), \(\circ\) Compatible composition at period and trellis levels Whole expression \(\mathrm{IP}\equiv(/{+})\circ(\alpha\times)\circ\mathrm{Trans}\) \(P\) or \(N\) as defined above Application \(\mathrm{IP}:\langle x,y\rangle\) \(\Upsilon(N)(v_T)\)

Here \(/{+}\) sums a sequence, \(\alpha\times\) multiplies corresponding entries and \(\mathrm{Trans}\) transposes a pair of lists. Backus wrote this example in FP; representation of functions by objects is the additional FFP construction. The table is an analogy between compositions, not an identity of languages.

docs.title: 3 The model term
docs.text:
The mathematical nesting can be displayed as a tree. This schematic suppresses the internal equation structures:

TRELLIS
├─ PERIOD P₀
│   ├─ stage occurrence s_cons
│   │   ├─ transitions and reward
│   │   ├─ conditional shock laws
│   │   └─ definitions, parameters and domains
│   ├─ stage occurrence s_port
│   └─ CONNECTOR
│       └─ field pair (a, k)
├─ inter-period connector χ₀
├─ PERIOD P₁
└─ …

The stage entries have internal structure. The tree suppresses it for the composition calculation; it is not a claim that arithmetic or local definitions are unparsed. Backus distinguishes primitive functions, defined functions and functional forms.8 This classification offers a comparison with supplied operations, local definitions and ways of combining operations. Parameters, field names and domains are other inputs, not automatically members of that function classification.

The displayed tree suppresses builder symbols. At this coarse level, \(\Upsilon\) assigns each stage occurrence its specified backward operation and composes those operations through the connectors. In the finer signature of The stage term, builders are themselves symbols. The uniqueness statement in Initial-algebra semantics §§1–2 applies only after the signature, target operations and assignments to free inputs have been supplied. It does not infer missing economic equations from a stage header.

The encoding resembles FFP representations. A head and its operands describe a represented compound operation. The term remains distinct from its mathematical meaning and from whichever software structures retain interpreted equations.

docs.title: 4 Source and retained structures
docs.text:
Arithmetic such as R*k + y is parsed into expression structure. Local function types and binders remain available to interpretation; substitution must respect scope. The source may author evaluation, optimization and implicit relations. Their meaning and applicable conditions come from the declared expression and the interpretation rules of Bellman-SYM's Appendix C, not an inference that all branches expose the same method operations.

In the specified construction, parser trees and source locations are temporary. The stage retains interpreted equations, definitions and typed diagrams. Periods and the trellis retain their outer records, with fresh objects for distinct occurrences; reuse of a module does not imply one shared mutable stage object or a retained whole-trellis syntax graph. These statements describe the construction specified for the language, not completion of every runtime component.

The mathematical signatures used here are many-sorted: their symbols have declared input and output types. Their vocabulary is the specified signature under discussion. Adding a form requires extending that signature and its interpretation; defining a local function within the admitted language is a different act. Neither statement proves all the identities an extension might need.

Branching also requires its own interpretation. A finite choice compares complete feasible branch values; an exogenous branch uses the declared conditional probabilities. Evaluating all feasible branch values and then maximizing is generally different from evaluating a single branch selected by a pre-existing predicate. Ties and measurable policy selection retain the qualifications in Branching.

docs.title: 5 The typing entries of a methods file
docs.text:
A methods file adds to a stage file the numerical choices of its operators without changing the model: a typing entry types one component of an operator by the path of that component, policy.method : !egm(tol=tol_v) for the method and policy.grid : !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a)) for the grid, the discretized domain on which the operator's function is represented; a handler binding, policy.handler : "cons-port:egm", names the program that realizes the operator. An entry stands inside a block's header, in the groups that | opens after the block's own entries, or at file level with the full path. A typing entry assigns the method or the grid component of one operator's signature, so that the operator is realized by that method on that grid while the model's equations are unchanged, and a handler binding names the program that realizes it (the handler); this section records the constructors the entries parse to, in the house dialect of the ASDL notation, with the grammar that owns each line: (core) for a form that dyno's own files could carry, (stage) for a form that belongs to the typing layer of Bellman-SYM.

Abstract grammar: the typing entries

The host constructors keep their profiles; the lines below are added as alternatives of existing sorts (+=) or as new sorts. Declaration is the host's, reused: a typing entry is a Declaration whose subject is a Path and whose one classifier is the Method or the Grid.

entry      += Tagged(word tag)                               -- (core)  a tag with keyword arguments
word        = Word(identifier name, keyword* arguments)       -- (core)  a name with its keyword arguments
keyword     = Keyword(identifier key, argument value)         -- (core)
argument    = Name(identifier name)                           -- (core)  the name of a setting
            | Literal(number value)                           -- (core)
            | Quoted(string text)                             -- (core)
            | Values(argument* items)                         -- (core)  a tuple of values
            | Nested(word word)                               -- (core)  a word with arguments of its own
subject    += Path(segment* segments)                         -- (stage) the path of a component
segment     = Segment(identifier name, selector* selectors)   -- (stage) a name with its selectors
selector   += Term(expr at)                                   -- (stage) a term as a selector
typer      += Handler(subject subject, string program)        -- (stage) the handler binding
classifier += Method(word m)                                  -- (stage) the method component
classifier += Grid(grid g)                                    -- (stage) the grid component
grid        = Cartesian(factor* factors)                      -- (stage) one factor per coordinate
factor      = Spaced(identifier coordinate, argument lower, argument upper,
                     argument count, word? spacing)           -- (stage) bounds, a count, a spacing word
            | Listed(identifier coordinate, identifier nodes) -- (stage) a node set, or the operator whose nodes the coordinate takes
            | Feasible(identifier coordinate, identifier set, argument count)   -- (stage) a control's feasible set with a count

The requirements the notation cannot state are part of well-formedness instead: a path has at least one segment and its last segment names the component, method, grid or handler; a word's arguments are keyed once each; a grid has at least one factor and names no coordinate twice, and the order of its factors carries no meaning; a bound or a count of a factor is the name of a declared setting or a number; a spacing is a word, with or without arguments.

Keys. segments are the names from the block to the component, each with the selectors that name the object an Evaluation stores (evaluate[V], evaluate[D_{k}V[<]]); m is the method word with its keyword arguments, read by the catalogue of methods; g is the grid; program is the handler's name as the quoted string writes it. These are ASDL fields, not keys to write in a file.

Head. Inside a header, an entry is one entry of the block's annotation, whatever group it is written in; at file level it is a declaration whose subject is a dotted path. The ! marks a word, the dot joins the segments of a path, = joins a keyword to its value, and a quoted string names a handler.

Denotes. The method and the grid are the classifier components of the operator's signature, read by the numerical semantics and by nothing in the exact semantics; the handler is a binding beside the term. Methods gives the account.

Status. The grammar parses these entries and lowers them to the constructors above. A grid's kind is Cartesian; a sparse kind is reserved. Which words are admitted at which operator, which keywords each reads, and whether a factor's name is a node set or an expectation operator are judged when the entries bind, not by this grammar box.

docs.title: Appendix A — Semantics
docs.text:
Summary

This appendix relates authored equations to their mathematical interpretation and numerical use. The buffer-stock decision equation illustrates binding, continuation arguments and the separate assumptions needed for optimization and approximation.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Illustrative example supplies the economic model. Used by — Bellman-SYM's Appendix C specifies binding and interpretation rules; Stages and Methodization give the .bl source and the authoring rules for methods. See also — Initial-algebra semantics distinguishes exact interpretation from numerical approximation.

Denotational semantics assigns mathematical values to expressions. A compound expression is interpreted from its constituents under an assignment of its free inputs, such as a continuation function.1 The elaboration is the construction of interpreted equations and composed operations from the authored source. It provides a record that can be inspected before numerical methods are applied. Its mathematical meaning is distinct from the particular data structure used to represent it.

docs.title: 1. The decision equation
docs.text:
For resources \(m>0\), the buffer-stock decision operator on a continuation function \(\mathrm v_\succ\) is

\[ (\mathbb T_\succ\mathrm v_\succ)(m) =\sup_{0<c\le m}\bigl\{\mathrm u(c)+\beta\,\mathrm v_\succ(m-c)\bigr\}, \]

where \(c\) is consumption, \(\mathrm u\) utility, \(\beta\) the discount factor and \(m-c\) assets after consumption. The continuation input and utility must have domains for which this objective is defined. A fixed feasible policy \(\pi\) instead gives \((\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\mathrm v_\succ)(m)=\mathrm u(\pi(m))+\beta\,\mathrm v_\succ(m-\pi(m))\). Attainment and a measurable maximizing policy require additional assumptions. The arrival income expectation is the separate operator \(P_\prec\); it equals \(\mathbb T_\prec\) here because the arrival aggregator is the identity.

Bellman-SYM's Stages page writes the transition and value calculation in .bl. The integration and optimization subscripts bind their own local variables, while a continuation field is represented by a function evaluated at the state produced by the declared transition. For representation up to almost-sure equality, the field must have a version measurable with respect to the information generated by the state, under suitable measurable-domain assumptions. A version agrees with the field almost surely. Available information alone is not a proof of state sufficiency. Bellman-SYM's Appendix C, §§1.2–1.3 and rules R4–R8, states these distinctions. It also separates an equation defining a choice value from one selecting a policy.

docs.title: 2. The interpreted equations
docs.text:
In the specified construction, arithmetic expressions and local binders are parsed into a temporary abstract syntax tree, which records grammatical structure. Interpretation constructs retained equation graphs, definitions and typed diagrams from those terms. Later substitution and inspection use those retained structures; the temporary parser tree and source locations are not the mathematical representation of a stage occurrence. Fresh occurrences remain separate, even when their common stage source is parsed once.

The decision expression contains composition with the asset transition, utility, discounting and optimization. Its continuation function has a declared state domain and the regularity required by the operation. An implicit equation records a relation in its designated unknown; it defines a function only after existence and uniqueness, or an admissible selection, has been supplied. A first-order condition alone does not establish a constrained optimum.

An authored equation or occurrence can supply a numerical target when that target is supported. A physical line of source does not automatically create an independently methodizable operation, and an implicit relation does not automatically insert an inversion method. Fields, functions and types states the mathematical rules, and Bellman-SYM's rules for methodization state the authoring rules, separately.

docs.title: 3. Meaning and computation
docs.text:
Syntax records expressions and their binding structure; semantics specifies their mathematical interpretation. Parsing an equation does not establish integrability, a sufficient state or existence of a maximizing policy. These conditions can be stated mathematically even when source text has no separate name for each operation. An explicit interpretation helps compare them with the declared problem and numerical procedure.

Changing independent and identically distributed income to a first-order autoregressive process changes the shock law and generally the state information needed for prediction. It is a change in the economic model. Changing a quadrature rule for a fixed conditional law is a numerical choice. Likewise, replacing value iteration by a policy-based calculation requires a proved relation between the mathematical operators as well as a valid numerical method.

Stoy distinguishes a program's denotation from different ways of computing it.1 This does not imply that arbitrary numerical approximations are exact or equivalent. For Coleman–Reffett time iteration, Sargent and Stachurski describe a value–policy correspondence in volume 2, §8.3.4, pp. 290–292.2 Here it is used only on specified classes preserved by the respective operators, with a verified bijection and operator identity. The marginal-utility inverse requires finite integrals at zero, and a distance defined through corresponding value functions must be finite on the chosen class. Convergence in that distance does not automatically imply ordinary uniform policy convergence. Semi-conjugacy retains the unfinished derivation and these qualifications.

docs.title: 4. Numerical attachment
docs.text:
A handler implements a numerical procedure for a supported declared target, such as expectation or an implicit relation. Its assumptions and representation requirements remain explicit: a root finder needs an appropriate equation and admissible domain; a candidate-envelope comparison needs a specified candidate family. A method name does not prove accuracy, optimality or convergence.

The remaining comparison with solver libraries must identify the mathematical operation, the authored target and the actual numerical procedure. Exact interpretation and refinement are treated in Initial-algebra semantics; numerical error and stability require the additional conditions summarized in Operator algebra §6.

  1. Stoy, J. E. (1977). Denotational Semantics: The Scott-Strachey Approach to Programming Language Theory. MIT Press, §2.2, p. 11. ↩↩

  2. Sargent, T. J. and Stachurski, J. (2026). Dynamic Programming, volume 2, authors' May 2026 edition, §8.3.4, Lemma 8.3.11 and Proposition 8.3.12, pp. 290–291, and §8.3.4.2, p. 292. The conditional scope used here is stated in §3. ↩

docs.title: Appendix B — Initial-algebra semantics
docs.text:
Summary

A signature lists the mathematical operations and their input and output sorts. Once their interpretation and any free inputs are fixed, the term algebra determines the interpretation of composite expressions. Exact refinement preserves the interpretation under stated assignments; numerical approximation requires additional assumptions.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Fields, functions and types gives the field and function distinctions. See also — Operators and builders supplies the stage operators used below. Used by — Bellman-SYM's Appendix C specifies binding and substitution.

We use the many-sorted algebra account of Goguen, Thatcher, Wagner, and Wright (1977, hereafter ADJ), §2. The results concern a specified mathematical signature and interpretation; they do not prescribe a stored software representation.

docs.title: 1. Signature and term algebra
docs.text:
A many-sorted signature \(\Sigma = \langle S, \Omega \rangle\) declares a set \(S\) of sorts and a family \(\Omega\) of operator symbols, each with an arity (a string of input sorts) and an output sort, and nothing else: no carriers, no functions (ADJ 1977, §2; signature). A \(\Sigma\)-algebra \(A\) supplies a carrier set \(A_s\) for each sort and an actual operation per symbol of matching rank. A homomorphism \(h : A \to A'\) is a sort-indexed family of maps commuting with every operation.

The coarse stage signature contains perch-indexed value-function sorts \(\mathsf V_p\), distribution sorts \(\mathsf M_p\), and typed backward and forward builder symbols. The model supplies state spaces, feasible actions, shock laws, transitions and local payoff functions. These data determine the operations under the conditions in Stages and perches. A diagram records a finite expression using those operations; the signature also specifies their ranks and cannot be inferred from unlabeled arrows alone.

The ground terms over \(\Sigma\) form the term algebra \(T_\Sigma\), whose operations construct terms. Ground terms contain no free inputs. For a sort-indexed family of free input names \(X\), use the free algebra \(T_\Sigma(X)\). An environment \(e_s:X_s\to A_s\) assigns a value to every free input of sort \(s\). The environment and the target operations together determine evaluation. A finite acyclic term graph can represent such an expression with shared subterms (§6); this is mathematical notation, not a claim that the parser's abstract syntax tree is retained.

docs.title: 2. Initiality
docs.text:
Definition (ADJ 1977, p. 68). An algebra \(S\) is initial in a class \(\mathbf{C}\) of algebras iff for every \(A \in \mathbf{C}\) there exists a unique homomorphism \(h_A : S \to A\).

Theorem (ADJ 1977, §2, Proposition 2.1, p. 71). The term algebra \(T_\Sigma\) is initial in the category of all \(\Sigma\)-algebras. Any two initial algebras over \(\Sigma\) are canonically isomorphic (ADJ Prop. 1.1), so one may speak of the initial algebra.

Thus a fixed target algebra determines a unique interpretation of ground terms. For terms with free inputs, ADJ Propositions 2.3 and 2.6 (pp. 72, 75) give the unique homomorphism \(h_{A,e}:T_\Sigma(X)\to A\) extending the environment \(e\). Neither the target operations nor the environment is chosen by initiality.

docs.title: 3. Value and measure interpretations
docs.text:
A target for the combined stage signature must interpret every declared sort and symbol. Its value-function part uses chosen spaces \(\mathsf V_p\) on the perch state spaces; its measure part uses \(\mathsf M_p\). We may discuss these parts separately by restricting to their respective subsignatures. Reversing arrows alone does not turn a value algebra into a measure algebra of the same rank signature.

Write \(\mathcal V\) for the target algebra of the value-operation subsignature and \(\Pi_\Gamma\) for its feasible measurable policies. For the value interpretation, let \(\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)\) be the feasible state–action pairs and \(\mathsf Q_\Gamma\) the choice-value functions on those pairs. With an integrable payoff at every required pair, the pointwise objective is

\[ (B_\succ\mathrm v_\succ)(x,a) =\int \mathrm G_\succ\bigl(\mathrm v_\succ(\mathrm g_\succ(x,a,\eta)),x,a,\eta\bigr)\,\mu_\eta(d\eta). \]

Here \(\mathrm G_\succ\) acts on a scalar value, state, action and shock, and \(\mu_\eta\) is the conditional shock law, displayed without state arguments only when those arguments are unnecessary. A trajectory conditional expectation agrees almost surely with this pointwise expression only under the state-representation and conditional-law conditions of Stages and perches §2. It does not define counterfactual action values by itself. A statement may apply a further map outside the integral; the two-map form of Stages and perches §2.3a adds one fine symbol, and the factorization below applies to it unchanged.

On a domain admitting the specified measurable maximizing selection, the optimizing builder is

\[ \mathbb T_\succ =\operatorname{evaluate}\circ \langle B_\succ,\operatorname{argmax}\circ B_\succ\rangle. \]

The fixed-policy builder instead satisfies \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}v=\operatorname{evaluate}(B_\succ v,\pi)\). Evaluation means \(\operatorname{evaluate}(Q,\pi)(x)=Q(x,\pi(x))\). Arrival evaluation is the policy-free aggregator \(\mathbb T_\prec=B_\prec\). Domains must be chosen so all operations are defined and closed under these compositions; initiality supplies no selection or integrability theorem.

The measure interpretation uses transition pushforwards \(\mathbb M_\prec\) and \(\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\). Write \(P_\prec\) and \(P_{\succ,\pi}\) for the corresponding undiscounted Markov expectations and \(\langle\mu,f\rangle=\int f\,d\mu\). For bounded measurable \(f\), or when both sides are absolutely integrable, their pairing is

\[ \langle\mathbb M_\prec\mu,f\rangle=\langle\mu,P_\prec f\rangle, \qquad \langle\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\mu,f\rangle=\langle\mu,P_{\succ,\pi}f\rangle. \]

These identities extend to composites of the paired transition operators, with order reversed. Reward-bearing evaluation, nonlinear aggregation and optimizing selection are not the probability-transition expectations. No carrier isomorphism is asserted.

The valuation \(\Upsilon\) is the unique interpretation homomorphism after these target choices and any free-input environment have been supplied. A term is syntax; its image is its mathematical meaning. Additional equations may restrict admissible targets, but an equation imposed on a quotient syntax also requires its interpretation to satisfy that equation.

docs.title: 4. Exact refinement
docs.text:
Let \(\Sigma\) be the coarse signature with optimizing builder \(\mathbb T_\succ\) and arrival builder \(\mathbb T_\prec\), and \(\Sigma'\) a finer signature containing the operations used to define them. A derived signature morphism \(\delta:\Sigma\to\Sigma'\) assigns each coarse symbol a fine term of the same input and output ranks. The sorts are held fixed here, and the term's formal inputs are explicit. Composition and pairing below abbreviate substitution into ordinary many-sorted terms. For the stage builders, the assignment is

\[ \delta(\mathbb T_\succ)=\operatorname{evaluate}\circ\langle B_\succ,\operatorname{argmax}\circ B_\succ\rangle, \qquad \delta(\mathbb T_\prec)=B_\prec. \]

The fine operations may further express pullback along the law of motion, local aggregation and shock integration, with the domains and selection conditions of §3. A numerical envelope routine is not automatically one of these exact operations.

Any \(\Sigma'\)-algebra \(A'\) becomes a \(\Sigma\)-algebra \(A'|_\delta\) (the reduct) by letting each coarse symbol act as its assigned composite. In particular the fine term algebra \(T_{\Sigma'}\) becomes a \(\Sigma\)-algebra \(T_{\Sigma'}|_\delta\), and initiality of \(T_\Sigma\) yields a unique homomorphism

\[ \mathrm{tr}_\delta : T_\Sigma \to T_{\Sigma'}|_\delta, \]

the term translation: the map that expands every occurrence of every builder symbol into its assigned sub-term. Uniqueness is the coherence claim of Fields, functions and types §5: a homomorphism uses the same interpretation for repeated occurrences of a symbol. Occurrence-specific data must therefore be supplied as inputs or distinguished in the signature.

Factorization theorem. For every \(\Sigma'\)-algebra \(A'\), the unique \(\Sigma\)-homomorphism \(T_\Sigma \to A'|_\delta\) factors through the fine term algebra:

\[ h_{A'|_\delta} \;=\; \bigl(h_{A'}\bigr)\big|_\delta \circ\, \mathrm{tr}_\delta . \]

Proof. Both sides are \(\Sigma\)-homomorphisms from \(T_\Sigma\) to \(A'|_\delta\); the left by definition, the right as a composite of \(\mathrm{tr}_\delta\) with the \(\delta\)-reduct of the fine valuation \(h_{A'} : T_{\Sigma'} \to A'\), reducts preserving homomorphy. Initiality of \(T_\Sigma\) admits only one such map. \(\square\)

For free-input terms, the same argument uses \(T_\Sigma(X)\) and the same input assignment on both sides: translation leaves the free generators fixed, and uniqueness is the free-algebra extension property. Applied to an exact target algebra, the theorem says that a coarse term and its assigned fine translation have equal meanings. It does not say that an approximate numerical routine equals either meaning.

The additional proof obligations. If a coarse theory imposes equations, the assigned fine terms must satisfy those equations for translation to descend to the quotient theory. Monotonicity and contraction are order and metric properties, not plain signature equations; they require the corresponding structures and separate proofs. A definitionally expanded builder satisfies its defining equality by construction, but an independently proposed formula must be checked against it.

A hierarchical mathematical expression can retain a builder name together with its assigned expansion. Compatible derived translations compose, giving a chain \(\Sigma^0\to\Sigma^1\to\cdots\to\Sigma^k\). This describes exact expression refinement. It does not assert that every period or trellis is stored as a nested syntax graph; the source and retained representations are described in The stage term.

docs.title: 5. Method assignment at different levels
docs.text:
A handler is a numerical routine assigned to a mathematical operation. Methods may evaluate an individual operation, such as an expectation by quadrature, a whole builder, or a composite expression. The following cut specifies the level of assignment in the hierarchy of §4.

Definition (cut). Let \(t\) be a finite hierarchical tree term over the chain \(\Sigma^0 \to \cdots \to \Sigma^k\), its boxes partially ordered by containment. A cut \(C\) is a set of boxes of \(t\) that contains no two boxes nested inside one another and covers \(t\): every maximal path from the outermost box to a fine leaf meets exactly one element of \(C\).

Induced signature and method algebra. For a fixed finite hierarchical tree, a cut \(C\) supplies the operation boundaries at which methods are assigned. Use distinct typed symbols when identically named boxes have different data or interpretations. Unfolding the boxes above the cut produces a term \(t_C\) over this signature. Once carrier representations, routines and any free inputs are assigned, the term has a unique evaluation. A compatible refinement of the cut has the exact factorization of §4 when its operations agree with the original assignments. This statement does not require a general lattice claim for arbitrary shared graphs. The finest cut contains the fine leaves and the coarsest contains the outermost box. A shared subterm reached from two boxes of the cut must be treated consistently, either by unraveling or by an explicit ownership convention; the representation choice remains open. #ambiguity

Admissibility (per-box agreement). An atomic handler \(\widehat{b}\) for a box \(b \in C\), with interior term \(\delta(b)\) over the next-finer signature, is exactly admissible iff its denotation equals the valuation of the interior,

\[ \llbracket\, \widehat{b}\, \rrbracket \;=\; h_{\mathcal{V}}\bigl(\delta(b)\bigr), \]

Here \(h_{\mathcal V}(\delta(b))\) denotes the induced operation for every admissible assignment of its formal inputs, with other parameters fixed; the equality is between operations, not just one evaluated output. This equality is the commuting-square condition: evaluating the whole box and evaluating its assigned interior give the same result. It is an assumption to verify for an independently supplied handler. If every box satisfies it, composition and the factorization theorem give equality of the resulting exact composite interpretations. Retaining names can make this agreement easier to state, but equalities can also be stated directly between expressions; naming is not a mathematical necessity.

For an approximate handler, state an error or convergence claim in specified spaces and observables, together with the required stability assumptions. Initiality neither chooses that claim nor proves it. A method may use a fixed tolerance, a sequence of grids, or another approximation family; no one numerical criterion is imposed by the term algebra.

docs.title: 6. Shared term representations
docs.text: Initiality above concerns tree terms. A finite acyclic term graph represents a tree by unraveling: duplicate each shared subterm at its uses. With pure deterministic operations, the same environment and the same input arguments, evaluating equal subterms once or repeatedly gives equal values. Under those hypotheses, sharing changes representation without changing denotation. Sharing a sampled outcome and independently resampling are different stochastic operations; the deterministic argument does not equate them. The mathematical graph notation does not identify the retained equation graph with the temporary parsed abstract syntax tree.

docs.title: 7. Binders
docs.text: The first-order mathematical signature can treat \(\operatorname{argmax}:\mathsf Q_\Gamma\to\Pi_\Gamma\) as an operation on functions, on the restricted domain admitting its stated selection. Its function input then already contains the argument dependence. This is distinct from the concrete source syntax, where expectation, maximization and solve expressions have local variables. Parsing records their binders and bodies; interpretation resolves scope and capture-avoiding substitution. Free inputs still require an environment. Bellman-SYM's Appendix C, §2.5 and rule R2, specifies these requirements. First-order initiality for the mathematical operation signature is not a claim that source binding disappears.

docs.title: 8. The adequacy obligation
docs.text:
Initiality determines the meaning of composite terms once primitive meanings and free inputs have been fixed. It does not certify a backend. For an exact implementation, verify agreement at the chosen operation boundaries and then use the factorization result. For an approximate method, identify the reference numerical operation, its relation to the mathematical operator, and whether the package computes that reference.

Convergence requires method-specific approximation and stability results in declared spaces. Optimization may also require selection assumptions; value convergence alone need not imply policy convergence. The defining identities of Stages and perches provide mathematical checks, but a finite collection of numerical tests is not a proof of those identities on their full domains. No general adequacy or convergence theorem follows from the architecture.

docs.title: Appendix C — The stage term
docs.text:
Summary

This appendix records the typed builder symbols and their stage compositions. The mathematical term specifies which operations compose; the model supplies their interpretation. The term notation is distinct from the concrete stage grammar and its temporary parsed syntax tree.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Stages and perches supplies the stage data and operator definitions. Formal account — Initial-algebra semantics states the conditional interpretation and refinement results. Used by — Stages describes .bl authoring; Period Syntax and The factory API describe the application representation of periods and trellises.

docs.title: 1. The stage signature
docs.text:
A many-sorted signature \(\Sigma=(S,\Omega)\) consists of sort names \(S\) and operator symbols \(\Omega\). Each symbol has a rank, its ordered input sorts and output sort, written \(\mathrm{op}:s_1\times\cdots\times s_n\to s\). The signature declares names and ranks; an algebra assigns a carrier set to each sort and a function of the specified rank to each operator. A declared subsort requires compatible carrier inclusion, but inclusion in one interpretation does not establish a declared subsort relation. Kinds and sorts distinguishes these notions.

The stage tuple of Stages and perches §1 supplies mathematical data for the interpretation: state spaces, feasible actions, shock laws, transitions and local payoff maps. It is not the list of sort names. Writing \(\mathsf L\) for the scalar value domain, \(\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)\) for feasible state–action pairs, and \(\mathsf Z_\eta,\mathsf Z_\zeta\) for post- and pre-decision shock spaces, the pointwise aggregators have types

\[ \mathrm G_\succ:\mathsf L\times\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)\times\mathsf Z_\eta\to\mathsf L, \qquad \mathrm G_\prec:\mathsf L\times\mathsf X_\prec\times\mathsf Z_\zeta\to\mathsf L. \]

Here \(\mathsf X_\prec\) is the arrival state space. These maps act on scalar continuation values. Pullback along the law of motion and shock integration define the function-valued aggregators \(B_\succ,B_\prec\) on stated domains. Policy evaluation at a supplied policy and optimization are then distinct operations. Neither a type declaration nor a numerical routine proves integrability, existence of a maximizing policy, or convergence.

docs.title: 2. Perch indices and builder symbols
docs.text:
The three perch indices and two directed edges form the stage's indexing path:

\[ \prec\;\xrightarrow{e_\prec}\;\sim\;\xrightarrow{e_\succ}\;\succ. \]

The indices stand for arrival, decision and continuation information sets. State spaces are assigned to these indices; the indices are not themselves state spaces. The path generates a free category of paths once identities and composition are included. This is a different construction from a many-sorted term algebra, and neither says the bare graph is initial in an unspecified category.

The coarse stage signature uses value-function and distribution sort names:

\[ S=\{\mathsf V_p:p\in\{\prec,\sim,\succ\}\} \cup\{\mathsf M_p:p\in\{\prec,\sim,\succ\}\}. \]

An interpretation assigns chosen value-function spaces on each state space and spaces of probability measures on the corresponding state spaces, with the closure and integrability conditions needed by its operations. A random value field has a representative in the value-function space only under the state-generated measurability conditions in Fields, functions and types; it is not that function itself.

Operator symbol Rank Interpretation \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\) \(\mathsf V_\succ\to\mathsf V_\sim\) decision evaluation under a fixed feasible measurable policy \(\pi\) \(\mathbb T_\succ\) \(\mathsf V_\succ\to\mathsf V_\sim\) optimizing decision evaluation on its stated domain \(\mathbb T_\prec\) \(\mathsf V_\sim\to\mathsf V_\prec\) arrival evaluation \(\mathbb M_\prec\) \(\mathsf M_\prec\to\mathsf M_\sim\) arrival transition pushforward \(\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\) \(\mathsf M_\sim\to\mathsf M_\succ\) decision transition pushforward under \(\pi\)

The policy-indexed rows have one symbol for each supplied policy. A finer signature can instead include a policy sort and policy as an explicit argument. In this coarse signature the pairing and function application are not additional symbols. They remain available when defining its target interpretation; mathematical properties can be stated without adding an authored name for every expression.

docs.title: 3. Coarse and fine signatures
docs.text:
State, action and shock sorts are omitted from this coarse signature because none of its displayed ranks uses them. That is a choice of abstraction, not a ban on unused sorts in a signature or a claim that state domains lack types. The underlying state, action and shock spaces enter the target operations. A finer signature can include them when it displays pullback along the law of motion, scalar aggregation, or selection explicitly; Operators and builders gives those types.

The mathematical signature is not a replacement for the concrete stage grammar. Stage equations are authored in .bl; arithmetic, binders and equation bodies are parsed. In the specified construction, interpretation maps the temporary abstract syntax tree into equations, definitions and typed graph connections. Scope and substitution use the declared context. The syntax tree and its source spans are not retained as the stage's mathematical representation. Distinct stage occurrences have fresh objects and bindings even if their common module text is parsed once.

Periods, trellises, connectors, methods, settings, calibration and specification recipes remain YAML. A mathematical composition expression does not assert a new stored whole-trellis graph. Bellman-SYM's factory API and its Period Syntax page describe the application representation.

docs.title: 4. Stage compositions
docs.text:
For a supplied policy, the backward and forward compositions are

\[ \mathbb T_\pi=\mathbb T_\prec\circ\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}, \qquad \mathbb M_\pi=\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\circ\mathbb M_\prec. \]

The optimizing stage operator is \(\mathbb T=\mathbb T_\prec\circ\mathbb T_\succ\). These are distinguished compositions, not the only possible terms over the signature. Their common perch indexing does not make the reward-bearing backward operators probability-transposes. If \(P_\prec\) and \(P_{\succ,\pi}\) denote undiscounted transition expectations, their composite \(P_\pi=P_\prec\circ P_{\succ,\pi}\) satisfies

\[ \langle\mathbb M_\pi\mu,f\rangle=\langle\mu,P_\pi f\rangle, \qquad \langle\mu,f\rangle:=\int f\,d\mu, \]

for bounded measurable \(f\), or whenever the evaluations are absolutely integrable. Stages and perches defines these expectations. Rewards, discounting and selection require their own interpretation.

A ground term has a unique evaluation once the signature's target operations are fixed. A term with free continuation or distribution inputs also requires their assignment; Initial-algebra semantics §2 states the free-algebra result. The relation between this term account and a complete categorical presentation of the indexing path remains to be developed. #todo

docs.title: Appendix D — Kinds, sorts, and types
docs.text:
Summary

We distinguish declared sorts from the sets that interpret them, and kinds from greatest sorts. The field classification uses information context, role, and value domain, with shocks treated separately. The propositions state which conclusions follow from these declarations and which require additional conventions or nonempty examples. The grid of a numerical method is a sort of its own and no subsort of a state space.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Fields, functions and types distinguishes random fields, value domains, and representing functions. Used by — Bellman-SYM's Appendix C states the current typing context and information rules. See also — Stage term describes the mathematical signature; Methods §5 states the grid as the discretized domain, with a representation as a retract on it.

docs.title: 1 Setup
docs.text:
A many-sorted signature \(\Sigma=\langle S,\Omega\rangle\) lists sorts and operations with specified input and output sorts. We fix an interpretation assigning each sort \(s\) a carrier \(A_s\), the set interpreting it. A declared sort name, its carrier, and an element of that carrier are different objects.

The subset construction below is a local mathematical account of field classifications. It does not assert that every proposed type-theoretic extension is already part of the source language. Current .bl declaration rules are owned by §§1–2 of Bellman-SYM's Appendix C.

docs.title: 2 Definitions
docs.text:
D1 (Signature). The sort set \(S\) specifies categories of inputs and outputs. For a finite sequence \(w=(s_1,\ldots,s_n)\) and output sort \(s\), \(\Omega_{w,s}\) is the set of operation symbols with those input sorts and that output sort. Its number of arguments is \(n\). We call the input–output specification its type or rank; terminology concerning “rank” differs between sources (Goguen, Thatcher, Wagner and Wright 1977, §2).

D2 (Carrier). An interpretation gives sets \(A_s\) and, for each symbol \(o\in\Omega_{w,s}\), an operation \(o_A:A_{s_1}\times\cdots\times A_{s_n}\to A_s\). These are the carriers and operations of a \(\Sigma\)-algebra. A function's own domain and codomain are not erased when it occurs inside another operation.

D3 (Kind). A kind groups sorts in a connected component of the declared subsort order. Connected means that sorts can be joined by a finite sequence of comparisons, allowing either direction. A component need not have a greatest sort: an order with \(a\leq b\) and \(a\leq c\), with \(b,c\) incomparable, has no greatest element. If a membership presentation supplies a carrier \(K\) for the whole kind, that is distinct from declaring a greatest sort with carrier \(K\). Below we explicitly supply such ambient carriers and, where useful, a named greatest sort.

D4 (Membership). Within an ambient kind carrier \(K\), a sort may be interpreted by a predicate whose satisfying elements form \(A_s\subseteq K\). The judgment \(t:s\) asserts that the interpreted term belongs to \(A_s\). An expression can have an ambient kind before membership in a more restrictive sort has been established.

D5 (Subsort). A declared subsort relation \(s\leq s'\) requires compatible carrier inclusion,

\[ s\leq s'\quad\Longrightarrow\quad A_s\subseteq A_{s'}. \]

Carrier inclusion in one interpretation does not establish the converse declaration. In particular, two incomparable sort names can have equal carriers. Multiple inheritance permits a sort to be below several incomparable sorts. For the local classifier construction below we explicitly declare the inclusion relations induced by domain inclusion and intersection; these declarations are additional to the one-way requirement (Martí-Oliet and Meseguer 1996, §2.1, Definition 2.2).

D6 (Classifier). A classifier is a total function \(c:K\to I\) on a specified domain \(K\). Its fibers \(c^{-1}(i)=\{x\in K:c(x)=i\}\) are disjoint and exhaustive. We may introduce sorts interpreted by these fibers; the function itself is not a sort. For value-domain classification, let \(D_f\) be the domain recorded for field declaration \(f\) and define the subset

\[ \mathrm{Dom}[D]=\{f:D_f\subseteq D\}. \]

This is a domain refinement rather than an exact-domain fiber. In this appendix classifier elements are field declarations with their metadata, not realized numbers. A declaration's value domain \(D_f\) is distinct from the carrier of the sort of such declarations and from a space of random variables.

D7 (Intersection sort). We explicitly close the local collection of classifier subsets under intersections, identifying extensionally equal subsets. In this local inclusion order the meet is the intersection,

\[ A_{s\wedge s'}=A_s\cap A_{s'}. \]

It is the greatest lower bound because every subset contained in both components is contained in their intersection. An arbitrary order-sorted signature need not already contain a sort denoting every such intersection. A combined field sort intersects one perch sort, one role sort, and one domain refinement where those classifiers are defined.

docs.title: 3 Field classification
docs.text:
Step 1 — the ambient declarations. Let \(F\) be the set of declared random-quantity names with their metadata, including shocks. Let \(F_{\mathrm{loc}}\subseteq F\) be the declarations assigned a native perch. Shock declarations are classified by their transition and law separately; they need not belong to \(F_{\mathrm{loc}}\). We explicitly use Field as an ambient kind and a greatest local declaration sort with carrier \(F\). This greatest-sort convention does not follow merely from connectedness in D3.

Step 2 — the classifiers. The perch classifier is total on \(F_{\mathrm{loc}}\):

\[ \mathrm{perch}:F_{\mathrm{loc}}\to\{\prec,\sim,\succ\}. \]

Role is total on \(F\), with values state, control, value, and shock. The domain assignment records each declaration's value set \(D_f\). A shock can be measurable at a later information set without being a state coordinate there. A decision control remains a decision control when listed as an available argument at a later perch. §2.2 of Bellman-SYM's Appendix C gives these exceptions.

Step 3 — the component sorts. The perch fibers are ArrivalField, DecisionField, and ContinuationField, subsets of \(F_{\mathrm{loc}}\). The role fibers in \(F\) are StateField, ControlField, ValueField, and ShockField. Domain refinements include \(\mathrm{Dom}[\mathbb R]\), \(\mathrm{Dom}[\mathbb R_+]\), and \(\mathrm{Dom}[\mathbb R_{++}]\). The Sort of a value lists under derivatives the coordinates of its stated derivatives; the derivative of a value is read by the derivative term D_{a}V[>], which is distinct from a function name and is no field.

Step 4 — domain order. Since \(\mathbb R_{++}\subseteq\mathbb R_+\subseteq\mathbb R\), the domain-refinement subsets satisfy the corresponding non-strict inclusions by D6. We declare those relations in this local system. Strictness additionally requires declarations distinguishing the subsets (P3).

Step 5 — combined field sorts. For a classified declaration,

\[ \mathsf{Field}[p,r,D] :=\mathrm{PerchField}[p]\cap\mathrm{RoleField}[r]\cap\mathrm{Dom}[D]. \]

This is a local intersection sort under D7, not an assertion that three arbitrary classifiers are probabilistically independent or that every combination is inhabited.

Step 6 — other mathematical objects. We distinguish the following families by declaration. Their mathematical encodings do not by themselves prove that they are separate connected components of a subsort order.

Family Mathematical objects Required types Field declarations names, roles, value domains, and information metadata the classifier subsets above Interpreted fields measurable random variables random variables valued in \(D_f\) with the required information Transition measurable state-transition maps \(g_\prec:\mathsf X_\prec\times\mathsf Z_\zeta\to\mathsf X_\sim\) and \(g_\succ:\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)\times\mathsf Z_\eta\to\mathsf X_\succ\) Kernel pointwise reward/continuation aggregators \(G_\succ(v,x,a,\eta)\) and \(G_\prec(v,x_\prec,\zeta)\) with the domains in Stages and perches; an outer map \(G^{\mathrm{out}}_\succ(w,x,a)\) written outside the shock integral has the same sort without the shock argument (§2.3a there) Value representing value functions specified function spaces \(\mathsf V_p\) on \(\mathsf X_p\) Policy measurable feasible action functions \(\Pi_\Gamma=\{\pi:\mathsf X_\sim\to\mathsf A:\pi\text{ measurable},\ \pi(x)\in\Gamma(x)\}\) Dist probability measures \(\mathsf M_p\) on \(\mathsf X_p\) Grid the discretized domain of a function an operator stores or evaluates the finite subsets \(G \subset \mathsf X\) of the domain of that function, each with its inclusion \(\iota : G \to \mathsf X\); one such subset is the grid component of the operator's signature (Methods §5)

Here \(\Gamma(x)\) is the feasible action set and \(\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)\) its set of feasible state–action pairs. The declared field \(V[>]\) has a continuation representing function under the state-generated measurability and measurable-domain assumptions in Fields, functions and types. No separate V_fn source declaration is required. A law over population states is distinct from the law of an individual shock. Forward propagation uses the operators \(\mathbb M_\prec\) and \(\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\), under a specified policy.

The grid is a sort of its own. The grid component of an operator's signature is typed by the family Grid: the carrier of the sort is the set of finite subsets of the domain of the function the operator stores or evaluates, each with its inclusion, and one grid is an element of that carrier. The inclusion is a map in one interpretation and establishes no declared subsort relation between the grid and the state sort (D5). A function stored at the points of a grid is not thereby a member of the value sort \(\mathsf V_p\): it becomes one through the interpolant that extends it, the section of Methods §5. A discrete domain the model declares, such as a finite set of housing sizes, is a value domain \(D_f\) of a field and no grid.

Internal functions remain typed. A utility function, a local function definition, and an intermediate expression retain their parameter and result types when substituted. A bound parameter may be renamed consistently, but its type and scope remain. No separate named sort for “reward function” is required to make \(\mathrm u:\mathbb R_{++}\to\mathbb R\) a typed function. The pointwise-kernel description does not settle the unfinished representation of Epstein–Zin certainty equivalents. #todo

docs.title: 4 Propositions
docs.text:
P1 (Partitions on the stated domains). The perch classifier partitions \(F_{\mathrm{loc}}\), while the role classifier partitions \(F\).

For a total single-valued function \(c:K\to I\), each \(f\in K\) has one image \(i\), so it belongs to one fiber. If it belonged to fibers \(i\) and \(j\), single-valuedness would give \(i=j\). The fibers are therefore disjoint and exhaustive on \(K\). Apply this argument to the two stated classifier domains. It makes no perch assignment for a shock outside \(F_{\mathrm{loc}}\). ∎

P2 (No inhabited common subsort of disjoint fibers). Let \(i\ne j\) be values of one classifier. By P1, its two fiber carriers have empty intersection. If \(s\) is a declared subsort of both, D5 gives

\[ A_s\subseteq A_{\mathrm{Sort}_c[i]}\cap A_{\mathrm{Sort}_c[j]}=\varnothing. \]

Thus \(A_s=\varnothing\). The conclusion uses only the declared-order-to-inclusion implication. ∎

Corollary. An inhabited field-declaration sort cannot be below both ArrivalField and DecisionField. Per-perch value-field sorts are instead \(\mathrm{ValueField}\cap\mathrm{PerchField}[p]\), each below the cross-perch role sort ValueField. These declaration subsets are not the value-function spaces \(\mathsf V_p\).

P3 (Domain refinement inclusions). If \(D\subseteq D'\), then \(D_f\subseteq D\) implies \(D_f\subseteq D'\). By D6,

\[ \mathrm{Dom}[D]\subseteq\mathrm{Dom}[D']. \]

These give the declared non-strict domain chain in Step 4. For strictness, one additionally needs a declaration \(f\in\mathrm{Dom}[D']\setminus\mathrm{Dom}[D]\). For example, an assets declaration with \(D_f=\mathbb R_+\) distinguishes \(\mathrm{Dom}[\mathbb R_+]\) from \(\mathrm{Dom}[\mathbb R_{++}]\) because \(0\in D_f\). A declaration with \(D_f=\mathbb R\) distinguishes the next inclusion because it admits negative values. Without such declarations, the corresponding classifier subsets can be equal. P2 excludes inhabited inclusions between distinct fibers of one partition; it does not prohibit further separately declared refinements. ∎

P4 (Combined constraints). Fix a declaration \(f\in F_{\mathrm{loc}}\) with perch \(p\), role \(r\), and declared domain \(D_f\). By the definitions, the combined subset is

\[ \mathsf{Field}[p,r,D] =\{g\in F_{\mathrm{loc}}:\mathrm{perch}(g)=p,\ \mathrm{role}(g)=r,\ D_g\subseteq D\}. \]

It is an intersection sort by D7. Within this family for fixed \(p,r\), the choice \(D=D_f\) gives the least subset containing \(f\): every \(D\) that admits \(f\) satisfies \(D_f\subseteq D\), so P3 gives the required inclusion. It is inhabited by \(f\). A general combined sort is inhabited exactly when some declared field satisfies all three constraints; independence of the classifiers is unnecessary. ∎

P5 (Arrival is a subsort under the local greatest-sort convention). ArrivalField is the fiber \(\mathrm{perch}^{-1}(\prec)\subseteq F_{\mathrm{loc}}\subseteq F\). Step 1 and the local inclusion declarations make it a subsort of the ambient Field sort. It is proper if a declaration outside that fiber exists, as the decision resource field \(m\) does in the buffer-stock example. Without such a witness the inclusion need not be strict. The separate use of Field as an ambient kind is a presentation convention, not a consequence that every connected component has a top. ∎

P6 (A field and its representative are distinct objects). Let \(V_\succ\) be a random field with value domain \(\mathsf L\) at continuation information. It belongs to an appropriate space of measurable random variables, not to \(\mathsf L\) itself; \(V_\succ(\omega)\) is an element of \(\mathsf L\). Its representing function is a map \(\mathrm v_\succ:\mathsf X_\succ\to\mathsf L\).

When \(V_\succ\) is measurable with respect to \(\sigma(X_\succ)\) and the value space has the required measurable structure, the representation is

\[ V_\succ=\mathrm v_\succ(X_\succ)\quad\text{almost surely}. \]

This is the state-representation rule of Bellman-SYM's Appendix C, §1.2. It does not imply square integrability, nor does it determine values of the representative on states outside the relevant state law. Pointwise representative choices are required for counterfactual evaluation. The field/function distinction applies to policy controls as well; the derivative of a value is a function determined by the value's function and is no field. It supplies no converse inference about subsort declarations merely from how the objects are encoded. ∎

P7 (Distribution objects are separately declared). In this local signature we assign probability laws to the family Dist and declare no subsort relations connecting it to any other family. Its sorts therefore share no connected component with a sort in another family. Treating all distribution sorts as one component would additionally require declared connections among those sorts. This follows from the chosen declarations, not from a claim that measures cannot be represented as functions or that unlike-looking carriers cannot be included in one another.

Its forward operators are \(\mathbb M_\prec:\mathsf M_\prec\to\mathsf M_\sim\) and \(\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}:\mathsf M_\sim\to\mathsf M_\succ\). Their pairing is with the undiscounted transition expectations \(P_\prec\) and \(P_{\succ,\pi}\) defined in Stages and perches §2.7, not with reward-bearing Bellman evaluation. ∎

docs.title: 5 Buffer-stock example
docs.text:
Declaration or object Family Classification or type Interpretation \(k\) Field \(\mathrm{ArrivalField}\cap\mathrm{StateField}\cap\mathrm{Dom}[\mathbb R_+]\) random arrival assets \(m\) Field \(\mathrm{DecisionField}\cap\mathrm{StateField}\cap\mathrm{Dom}[\mathbb R_{++}]\) random resources \(c\) Field \(\mathrm{DecisionField}\cap\mathrm{ControlField}\cap\mathrm{Dom}[\mathbb R_{++}]\) consumption, additionally constrained by \(c\leq m\) \(a\) Field \(\mathrm{ContinuationField}\cap\mathrm{StateField}\cap\mathrm{Dom}[\mathbb R_+]\) random assets after consumption \(y\) Field \(\mathrm{ShockField}\cap\mathrm{Dom}[\mathsf Z_\zeta]\) income supplied on the arrival-to-decision transition \(V[>]\) Field \(\mathrm{ContinuationField}\cap\mathrm{ValueField}\cap\mathrm{Dom}[\mathsf L]\) continuation random field \(\mathrm v_\succ\) Value \(\mathsf V_\succ\) specified measurable representative \(g_\succ\) Transition \(\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)\times\mathsf Z_\eta\to\mathsf X_\succ\) \(g_\succ(m,c)=m-c\) for a trivial post-decision shock \(G_\succ\) Kernel \(\mathsf L\times\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)\times\mathsf Z_\eta\to\mathsf L\) \(G_\succ(v,m,c,\eta)=\mathrm u(c)+\beta v\) where defined \(G^{\mathrm{out}}_\succ\) Kernel \(\mathsf L\times\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)\to\mathsf L\) the identity \(G^{\mathrm{out}}_\succ(w,m,c)=w\) in the buffer-stock example \(G_\prec\) Kernel \(\mathsf L\times\mathsf X_\prec\times\mathsf Z_\zeta\to\mathsf L\) identity \(G_\prec(v,k,\zeta)=v\) \(\mathrm u\) typed function \(\mathbb R_{++}\to\mathbb R\) utility function

Here \(0<\beta<1\) is the discount factor. The constraints and integrability conditions of the buffer-stock example remain additional to these type declarations. Declaring utility inside an aggregator does not remove its function type. The value field and its representative are related by P6; their evaluation is not an equality between a sort carrier and the value domain.

docs.title: 6 Remarks and open questions
docs.text:
• A field's value domain, its space of random variables, and its representative-function space must remain distinct. Fields, functions and types now uses this distinction throughout.
  • Local functions retain typed parameters and results after substitution. Operators retain their domain/codomain types whether or not an operator-valued sort is introduced.
  • A transition and a probability kernel are distinct objects: a measurable transition with its shock law induces a kernel. Rewards, conditional laws, and policy selection additionally determine Bellman evaluation.
  • Domain refinement uses \(D_f\subseteq D\), not \(D_f=D\). The exact-domain fibers form a different partition and do not provide the same inclusion order.
  • A discrete state domain is model data; a numerical grid approximating a continuous domain is the grid component of an operator's signature, a sort of its own (§3, Step 6). An encoding or embedding does not by itself establish a declared subsort relation.
  • Whether to add a greatest Function sort encompassing value and policy functions is a further design choice. Connectedness alone cannot provide it. The general source-level treatment of all such intersection and kind constructions remains a design question; this appendix states the local conventions needed for its propositions.

docs.title: 7 Sources
docs.text:
• Goguen, J. A., Thatcher, J. W., Wagner, E. G., and Wright, J. B. (1977). Initial algebra semantics and continuous algebras. Journal of the ACM 24(1), 68–95, §2, pp. 69–75. Signatures, carriers, and their interpretations.
  • Martí-Oliet, N., and Meseguer, J. (1996). Inclusions and subtypes I: First-order case. Journal of Logic and Computation 6(3), 409–438, §2.1, Definition 2.2, p. 413. Declared subsort order requires compatible carrier inclusion.
  • Meseguer, J. (1998). Membership algebra as a logical framework for equational specification. WADT 1997, LNCS 1376, 18–61. Background for distinguishing ambient kinds from membership in sorts.

docs.title: Appendix F — Operator algebra
docs.text:
Summary

Operator composition combines transition, reward, selection and evaluation operations with compatible types. The transition operators have a distribution/function pairing; optimizing operations require additional assumptions. This appendix distinguishes exact algebraic identities from numerical convergence claims.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Operators and builders defines the stage operators. Formal account — Initial-algebra semantics proves exact refinement for specified interpretations. Used by — Methodization attaches the methods, settings and calibration whose obligations §6 states; Bellman-SYM's Appendix C and Appendix D state the reading of the authored equations and their boundaries. See also — The stage term distinguishes mathematical composition from concrete source and storage.

“Operator algebra” here concerns composition of the Bellman calculus's operations, not a functional-analytic algebra of bounded operators. We state which additional structures each interpretation uses.

docs.title: 1. Signatures and operator types
docs.text:
A stage has a mathematical many-sorted signature, together with model data and an interpretation. Its sorts name domains of values, functions or distributions, while operation symbols have ranks \(\omega:s_1\times\cdots\times s_n\to s\). In a categorical presentation, objects represent these types and a morphism is a typed operation between them. A signature alone does not supply categorical products or coproducts.

At perch \(p\), write \(\mathsf V_p\) for a chosen value-function space on state space \(\mathsf X_p\), and \(\mathsf M_p\) for probability measures on that state space. Let \(\mathsf L\) be the scalar value domain, \(\Gamma(x)\) the feasible actions, \(\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)=\{(x,a):a\in\Gamma(x)\}\), and \(\mathsf Q_\Gamma\) a chosen space of measurable choice-value functions on those pairs. The spaces must satisfy the closure and integrability requirements of the displayed operations.

Operators have domain and codomain types. A first-order signature can treat them solely as operation symbols, without declaring an additional carrier of operator-valued data. This is a choice of signature, not a claim that functions can never be elements of a function space. Kinds and sorts states the local typing conventions.

docs.title: 2. Composition and builders
docs.text:
A categorical presentation must declare its generators, their types, the allowed composition operations and equations. For deterministic functions, product domains support pairing and copying of common inputs. A disjoint union represents labeled alternatives; its injections put each alternative into that union. These descriptions do not prove that every Bellman graph supports all the stated operations and identities.

Composition \(g\circ f\) requires compatible intermediate types. In the deterministic interpretation, a tensor \(f\otimes g\) acts on paired inputs. In a stochastic interpretation a tensor typically specifies independent joint transitions; this is not automatically a categorical product. Builder symbols can be primitive in a coarse signature and derived compositions in a finer one.

For a continuation field \(V_\succ\) with decision-measurable state \(X\) and feasible action \(A\), the trajectory payoff field is

\[ Q=\mathbb E[\mathrm G_\succ(V_\succ,X,A,\eta)\mid\mathcal F_\sim]. \]

Here \(\mathcal F_\sim\) is decision information and \(\eta\) the post-decision shock. The integrability actually required is that of the displayed local payoff. To compare every feasible action, specify instead the pointwise objective

\[ (B_\succ\mathrm v_\succ)(x,a) =\int\mathrm G_\succ\bigl(\mathrm v_\succ(\mathrm g_\succ(x,a,\eta)),x,a,\eta\bigr)\,\mu_\eta(d\eta), \]

with absolute integrability on every required pair. The map \(\mathrm g_\succ\) is the decision-to-continuation transition, \(\mathrm G_\succ\) the scalar payoff aggregator, and \(\mu_\eta\) its conditional shock law, with state/action arguments suppressed only when unnecessary. State representation and conditional-law assumptions relate this function to the trajectory identity almost surely; that identity does not determine counterfactual action values. A map written outside the integral, \(B_\succ=\mathrm G^{\mathrm{out}}_\succ(\int\cdots)\), is the two-map form of Stages and perches §2.3a; the display is its case with the outer map the identity.

Let \(\Pi_\Gamma\) be feasible measurable policies. On a domain admitting a specified measurable maximizing selection,

\[ \operatorname{argmax}:\mathsf Q_\Gamma\to\Pi_\Gamma, \qquad \operatorname{evaluate}:\mathsf Q_\Gamma\times\Pi_\Gamma\to\mathsf V_\sim, \qquad \operatorname{evaluate}(Q,\pi)(x)=Q(x,\pi(x)). \]

Then optimizing evaluation and its derived maximum satisfy

\[ \mathbb T_\succ=\operatorname{evaluate}\circ\langle B_\succ,\operatorname{argmax}\circ B_\succ\rangle, \qquad \max=\operatorname{evaluate}\circ\langle\mathrm{id}_{\mathsf Q_\Gamma},\operatorname{argmax}\rangle. \]

Without attainment the supremum value need not have this selected-policy representation. Direct search and first-order inversion approximate the same optimum only under their feasibility, sufficiency, selection and domain-coverage assumptions; at ties they need not select the same policy. Fixed-policy evaluation is \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}v=\operatorname{evaluate}(B_\succ v,\pi)\).

For the arrival transition \(\mathrm g_\prec\), pre-decision shock \(\zeta\), law \(\mu_\zeta\), and local aggregator \(\mathrm G_\prec\), arrival evaluation is

\[ \mathbb T_\prec=B_\prec:\mathsf V_\sim\to\mathsf V_\prec, \qquad (B_\prec v)(x_\prec)=\int\mathrm G_\prec\bigl(v(\mathrm g_\prec(x_\prec,\zeta)),x_\prec,\zeta\bigr)\,\mu_\zeta(d\zeta). \]

The optimizing stage operator is \(\mathbb T=\mathbb T_\prec\circ\mathbb T_\succ\), and its fixed-policy counterpart is \(\mathbb T_\pi=\mathbb T_\prec\circ\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\).

A joint implicit system may specify several outputs with a product codomain. It defines a selected function only where existence and a specified measurable selection are established; roots need separate optimality conditions. A nested builder may appear inside another mathematical expression. These facts do not supply either a generic solver theorem or a new source grammar.

docs.title: 3. Interpretation and copying
docs.text:
An algebra supplies carriers and operations of the declared ranks. For ground terms its interpretation extends uniquely to composite terms; free-input terms also require an environment. For a category presented by generators and equations, an interpretation must additionally respect those equations and whichever categorical structures are required. The many-sorted initial-algebra theorem alone does not establish those further properties. Initial-algebra semantics gives the precise term-level statement.

Interpretation Objects and operations Conditions Value recursion value functions, local aggregation and selection/evaluation pointwise domains, integrability and specified selection where required Probability propagation state distributions and transition kernels under a supplied policy measurable transitions and conditional laws

Copying is available in the Markov category of probability kernels: a state can be duplicated by the diagonal map. What fails for a general stochastic transition is preservation of that copying. Duplicating one random draw produces the same outcome twice, while two independent draws need not agree. Deterministic transitions preserve the diagonal. Fritz (2020), §10, Definition 10.1 and Remark 10.2, describes this distinction; it does not prove that every operation in a particular Bellman diagram preserves copying.

DisCoPy supplies typed graph representations and composition operations. Any claimed universal property or equation-preserving interpretation still needs its own mathematical argument. The field and functional graphs represent the same authored equations under the assumptions of Bellman-SYM's Appendix C; they are not independently authored model sources.

docs.title: 4. Transition pairing
docs.text:
Write \(P_\prec\) and \(P_{\succ,\pi}\) for undiscounted transition expectations and \(\mathbb M_\prec,\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\) for their forward probability propagation. With \(\langle\mu,f\rangle=\int f\,d\mu\),

\[ \langle\mathbb M_\prec\mu,f\rangle=\langle\mu,P_\prec f\rangle, \qquad \langle\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\mu,f\rangle=\langle\mu,P_{\succ,\pi}f\rangle. \]

These identities hold for bounded measurable \(f\) and extend to absolutely integrable evaluations. They compose with reversed order. Constant-discount expected utility instead gives \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}f=\bar r_\pi+\beta P_{\succ,\pi}f\), where \(\bar r_\pi\) is expected reward and \(0<\beta<1\) is the constant discount factor. An arrival reward or nonlinear aggregator also remains outside the transition pairing. Neither optimization nor a generic reward-bearing backward graph is the transpose of probability propagation.

docs.title: 5. Branching
docs.text:
A disjoint union \(\mathsf X_\succ=\bigsqcup_{j\in J}\mathsf X_{\succ,j}\) can represent labeled continuation alternatives, with \(J\) a finite label set. Two economic mechanisms determine how the label is obtained.

  • Agent choice: the policy chooses an alternative, possibly together with continuous controls. Branch values may be compared by a maximum when an optimum and a measurable maximizing selection exist. For a deterministic branch choice \(\pi_J(x)\), routing uses \(\mathbf1\{j=\pi_J(x)\}\). The maximizing decision is nonlinear in branch values; propagation under the resulting fixed policy is linear in the source measure.
  • Exogenous selection: a conditional law \(p(j\mid x)\) assigns branch probabilities. The backward expectation is a weighted sum of branch continuation values; the forward distribution is split using the same law. Finite mixtures need no action-feasibility coproduct condition. A persistent label is retained in the state when it affects future laws or payoffs; independence and persistence are model assumptions, not numerical methods.

For exhaustive mutually exclusive alternatives, the component output measures satisfy mass conservation:

\[ \sum_{j\in J}\mu_{\succ,j}(\mathsf X_{\succ,j})=\mu_\sim(\mathsf X_\sim). \]

An optimizing policy must specify its choice on ties, or supply an admissible randomized rule. Ties can occupy a positive-measure region even when states have an atomless law. A fixed tie-breaking rule makes the selected policy definite but does not by itself guarantee convergence of approximate policies. Exogenous routing is supplied by the model's conditional law; fixed-policy simulation can use an externally supplied policy.

Nonempty feasible sets, attainment and measurable selection are separate assumptions. Empty feasible sets may be assigned value \(-\infty\) in an extended-real convention, but have no feasible policy; this is not automatically the interpretation of a categorical initial object. Branching develops the economic cases.

Scope. Stationary distributions and tail behavior of iterated random transitions require invariant-measure and asymptotic analysis. They do not follow from the finite branching representation alone. A stationary distribution is a fixed point of probability propagation; one may introduce an operator that returns such a fixed point under additional assumptions.

docs.title: 6. Model interpretation and numerical realization
docs.text:
We distinguish the authored equations, a calibrated mathematical operator, a reference numerical approximation, and the package routine that computes it. These are different assignments, not automatically a chain of categorical functors:

\[ \text{equations and model parameters} \longrightarrow\text{mathematical operator} \longrightarrow\text{reference approximation} \longrightarrow\text{package computation}. \]

Calibration fixes parameter values in the model. Method assignment specifies a numerical procedure; settings choose its resolution or tolerances. A reference approximation is the numerical map defined by that procedure and its settings, independently of one implementation. A handler is the package routine intended to compute it. Equations and stages are authored in .bl; methods, settings and calibration remain YAML, as Bellman-SYM's rules for methodization describe.

docs.title: 6.1 Conditions on realization
docs.text:
• L1 — Types. A numerical representation must state its own input and output domains and any maps between grid and exact objects. Equal mathematical ranks do not make different numerical representations identical.
