docs.title: Appendix E — Catalogues
docs.text:
Summary

These catalogues summarize the calculus's fields, functions, operators, parameters and numerical choices. The method types that a methods file can name are listed with the language, each with the operation of these catalogues it realizes.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Fields, functions and types and Operators and builders define the mathematical objects. Formal account — Kinds and sorts states the classification conventions. Used by — Method types and Expression forms: the language's catalogues, whose rows link to the operations of Operators; Methodization and The Bellman factory: the current numerical attachment forms and the binding of occurrences.

The type catalogues describe the objects and function spaces used in the mathematical interpretation Υ. Methods describes the numerical procedures of the construction Ρ. These maps distinguish meaning from numerical computation.

Part Catalogue What it lists E.1 Fields Declared quantities, value domains and information contexts. E.2 Functions Representing functions, transitions, aggregators and policies with their domains. E.3 Operators Mathematical operations and their input/output types. E.4 Parameters and settings Economic inputs and numerical choices, classified by their mathematical role.

Related language references

Bellman-SYM's Methodization page, listed under Used by above, explains how to attach numerical choices to a declared stage.

These calculus catalogues supply mathematical explanations rather than superseding the source grammar.

docs.title: 1. Catalogue entries
docs.text:
Entry Meaning Reference Operator A mathematical operation with declared input and output types, called its rank. Operators Method A numerical procedure for a supported mathematical target. Methods Settings Numerical inputs required by the selected procedure. Parameters and settings Handler The implementation of a numerical procedure, including its input/output requirements. Handler

A method may require its own representation and equation inputs. Initial-algebra semantics states conditions for exact interpretation and refinement; Operator algebra §6 explains why numerical accuracy and stability require additional assumptions. No ordering between method tags and operator symbols is inferred merely from these inventory categories.

docs.title: 2. Types and equation inputs
docs.text:
Compatible types allow composition. Distinct operations can have the same rank without the same meaning. An approximate method can change the values received by subsequent operations even when its declared boundaries agree. Numerical representation compatibility and approximation error must therefore be checked separately.

The model supplies its equations. Stage equations and local definitions are authored in .bl. Method entries select supported targets and supply numerical choices; they do not invent omitted economic relations or make an implicit equation optimal. The current source rules of Bellman-SYM's Methodization page determine permitted target and reference forms. A method's tag binds no equation.

The method's documented settings specify the numerical inputs it accepts. A handler must interpret those settings as intended by its package. A grid that defines a discrete economic state or action space is model data; a grid approximating a continuous domain is numerical data. The same integer or real value can have either role depending on what it changes.

docs.title: 3. Authoring
docs.text:
Stage source is .bl. Supporting YAML describes method assignments, settings, calibration and specification recipes. Bellman-SYM's Methodization page gives the current syntax and distinguishes a declared target from an available method attachment, and its page on the Bellman factory explains how bindings are resolved for occurrences.

Before using a method, establish that the target exists, the handler supports the required operation and its assumptions hold for the model. The comparison with other toolkits, the coverage map of the Rosetta stone, which is being rebuilt, is a separate inventory, not a default handler-selection rule.

docs.title: 4. Related documents
docs.text:
• Fields, functions and types §5 — exact refinement and numerical methods.
  • Operators and builders — the defined operations and their compositions.
  • Kinds and sorts — declared type relations and interpreted carriers.
  • Bellman calculus — chapter reading order.

docs.title: Appendix E.1 — Field types
docs.text:
Summary

A field is a named random variable with a declared value domain, role, and information context. This catalogue lists the domains and fields in the buffer-stock example. The value domain is distinct from a space of random variables and from a representing function's domain.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Fields, functions and types states the field-to-function representation conditions. Formal account — Kinds and sorts distinguishes classifier declarations from their interpretations. Used by — Bellman-SYM's Appendix C gives the .bl rules that declare these fields. See also — Function types lists the representing functions.

A field at perch \(p\) is a random variable measurable with respect to the information set \(\mathcal F_p\). A declaration specifies its value domain, the set in which its realized values lie, and its role. The source declares types with a colon and combines type components with @; §2 of Bellman-SYM's Appendix C gives the .bl rules. Shock declarations require their transition timing and law, rather than an inferred native perch.

docs.title: 1. Value domains and state spaces
docs.text:
Domain Realized elements Meaning \(\mathsf X_\prec,\mathsf X_\sim,\mathsf X_\succ\) arrival, decision, continuation states spaces of declared state vectors \(\mathsf A\) actions action domain, with feasible actions \(a\in\Gamma(x)\) at decision state \(x\) \(\mathsf Z_\zeta,\mathsf Z_\eta\) shock realizations pre- and post-decision shock spaces with specified conditional laws \(\mathsf L\) values a stated value domain, such as \(\mathbb R\) or extended reals where all operations are defined

These are domains for realized coordinates and vectors. The field itself belongs to a space of measurable random variables. A real value domain does not imply finite expectation or finite second moment; expectations and derivatives require their separate assumptions. Unbounded utility does not by itself require infinite values or determine a suitable value-function space.

docs.title: 2. Buffer-stock fields
docs.text:
Here \(k\) is arrival assets, \(y\) is income, \(m\) is resources, \(c\) is consumption, and \(a\) is assets after consumption.

Field Perch or transition Role Value domain \(k\) arrival state \(\mathbb R_+\) \(y\) arrival to decision shock \(\mathsf Z_\zeta\subseteq\mathbb R_{++}\) \(m\) decision state \(\mathbb R_{++}\) \(c\) decision control \(\mathbb R_{++}\), with \(c\leq m\) \(a\) continuation state \(\mathbb R_+\) \(V_\succ\) continuation value \(\mathsf L\)

The derivative of a value is no field and has no role. It is read by the derivative term D_{a}V[>], the derivative operator applied to the declared continuation value in the continuation coordinate a, and a derivative line of the builder that writes a value states what that derivative equals. The derivative operator D_{x} and a chosen function name such as 𝑑𝑢 are different objects, and neither the term nor a derivative line proves differentiability or positivity.

A perch's state space uses its declared state coordinates, not all fields known there. With no joint restriction it is their product; the buffer-stock example has one state coordinate at each perch. If the continuation field is measurable with respect to \(\sigma(X_\succ)\), the information generated by the continuation state, it has a measurable representative \(V_\succ=\mathrm v_\succ(X_\succ)\) almost surely. Its realization is a value, and \(\mathrm v_\succ\) is the function listed in Function types. Local utility functions and intermediate definitions also retain their argument and result types.

docs.title: Appendix E.2 — Function types
docs.text:
Summary

Functions have argument and result domains, including functions defined locally inside an equation. This catalogue lists the value functions, transitions, aggregators, and policies associated with a stage. Operators acting on those functions also have domain and codomain types.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Fields, functions and types distinguishes fields from their representatives. Used by — Bellman-SYM's Appendix C and Appendix D state the representation and substitution rules for these functions. See also — Field types lists value domains and information contexts. See also — Operators lists operations on these function spaces.

A function type specifies a domain and codomain. We write \(\operatorname{Meas}(A,B)\) for measurable maps from \(A\) to \(B\). A representing function is distinct from the field obtained by evaluating it at a random state. Representation up to almost-sure equality requires a version of the field measurable with respect to the information generated by the state, together with suitable measurable value domains. A version is a random variable agreeing with the field almost surely. Sufficiency for the model's conditional laws and payoffs is a separate requirement; see Bellman-SYM's Appendix C, §1.2 and rule R5.

docs.title: 1. Functions of a stage
docs.text:
For perch \(p\in\{\prec,\sim,\succ\}\), let \(\mathsf X_p\) be its state space and \(\mathsf L\) the value domain. The action domain is \(\mathsf A\), feasible actions are \(\Gamma(x)\), and \(\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)=\{(x,a):a\in\Gamma(x)\}\) is the feasible state–action domain. Shock spaces are \(\mathsf Z_\zeta\) before choice and \(\mathsf Z_\eta\) after choice.

Function Domain and codomain Interpretation \(\mathrm v_\prec,\mathrm v,\mathrm v_\succ\) \(\mathsf X_p\to\mathsf L\), in a specified function space \(\mathsf V_p\) supplied or derived value representatives \(\partial_j\mathrm v_p\) \(\mathsf X_p\to\mathbb R\) where defined derivative with respect to state coordinate \(j\), when the function is differentiable \(\mathrm g_\prec\) \(\mathsf X_\prec\times\mathsf Z_\zeta\to\mathsf X_\sim\) arrival-to-decision transition \(\mathrm g_\succ\) \(\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)\times\mathsf Z_\eta\to\mathsf X_\succ\) decision-to-continuation transition \(\mathrm G_\succ\) \(\mathsf L\times\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)\times\mathsf Z_\eta\to\mathsf L\) pointwise decision reward/continuation aggregator, where defined \(\mathrm G_\prec\) \(\mathsf L\times\mathsf X_\prec\times\mathsf Z_\zeta\to\mathsf L\) pointwise arrival aggregator, identity in the buffer-stock example \(\pi\) \(\mathsf X_\sim\to\mathsf A\) measurable feasible policy, \(\pi(x)\in\Gamma(x)\) \(Q_f\) \(\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)\to\mathsf L\) choice value for a specified continuation function \(f\) \(\mathrm u\) \(\mathbb R_{++}\to\mathbb R\) in the consumption example typed utility function, including when defined locally

Measurability, integrability, and closure under the required operators restrict the listed function spaces. A derivative line states the author's assertion about the derivative of the value its builder writes; it is not a differentiability theorem. A policy derived from a solution relation requires existence and a specified measurable selection; optimality is an additional condition.

docs.title: 2. Local functions and distribution pairing
docs.text:
A declared function retains its typed parameters and result domain when substituted into another expression. Its local parameter names are distinct from stage fields with the same spelling. The derivative operator on a declared function, D_{c}(𝑢), the derivative term on a value field, D_{a}V[>], and the function name 𝑑𝑢 therefore remain distinct. Bellman-SYM's Appendix D, §§4–5, gives the substitution rules.

Probability measures \(\mu_p\in\mathsf M_p\) are separately defined objects on \(\mathsf X_p\). Their pairing with an integrable function is \(\langle\mu_p,f\rangle=\int f\,\mathrm d\mu_p\). The forward transition on measures pairs with the undiscounted transition expectation on functions, as defined in Stages and perches §2.7. This does not identify a measure with a value function or make the reward-bearing Bellman operator its transpose.

docs.title: Appendix E.3 — Operators
docs.text:
Summary

This catalogue lists mathematical operations and their input and output types. It distinguishes transition expectation, reward-bearing evaluation and optimizing selection, and records the conditions needed for each operation. §4 names the eight operations a builder is composed of by the kinds under which the package prints them.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Functions describes the model functions used by these operators. Used by — Operations and Shock distributions, the reference catalogues of the language, whose rows link to what they denote here; Field equations and Methodization give the block and method-target forms, and Bellman-SYM's Appendix D defines the supported method targets that §8 names. Formal account — Operator algebra qualifies composition, copying and numerical approximation. See also — Methods discusses numerical procedures.

An operator maps objects in a declared domain to a declared codomain. Its rank lists its input and output sorts. In a first-order signature, operators can be operation symbols without an additional carrier of operator-valued data; they are nevertheless typed. Whether a builder is primitive or a named composite depends on the chosen signature.

At perch \(p\), \(\mathsf X_p\) is the state space, \(\mathsf V_p\) a chosen value-function space, and \(\mathsf M_p\) the probability measures on \(\mathsf X_p\). Let \(\mathsf L\) be the scalar value domain, \(\Gamma(x)\) the feasible actions, \(\mathsf Q_\Gamma\) the choice-value functions on \(\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)=\{(x,a):a\in\Gamma(x)\}\), and \(\Pi_\Gamma\) the feasible measurable policies. Domains below are restricted so the operations are defined, integrable when required, and closed under the stated compositions.

docs.title: 1. Structural operations
docs.text:
These operations describe composition of inputs and alternatives. They do not alone prove that a software graph has a categorical universal property. Here \(s,t\) denote types, \(I\) the one-point type, \(\otimes\) a product in the deterministic interpretation, and \(\bigsqcup\) a labeled disjoint union.

Operation Rank Role \(\Delta_s\) \(s\to s\otimes s\) duplicate an input; duplicating one draw differs from independent resampling \(!_s\) \(s\to I\) discard an input; probability propagation to a one-point space retains total mass \(\sigma_{s,t}\) \(s\otimes t\to t\otimes s\) reorder paired coordinates \(\iota_j\) \(\mathsf X_j\to\bigsqcup_k\mathsf X_k\) identify an alternative by its label \([f_j]_j\) \(\bigsqcup_j\mathsf X_j\to\mathsf Y\) apply the corresponding \(f_j\) to a labeled input \(\operatorname{codiag}\) \(\bigsqcup_j\mathsf X\to\mathsf X\) discard a label when all alternatives share the same state space Connector compatible boundary types identify or rename fields between stages Inter-period connector compatible boundary types identify or rename fields between periods

A nonidentity state transformation must be authored explicitly; a connector renaming does not define it. Copying is available in the probability-kernel interpretation, but a general stochastic map need not preserve it. Operator algebra §§2–3 gives the distinction.

docs.title: 2. Backward builders
docs.text:
Operator Rank Meaning \(\mathbb T_\succ\) \(\mathsf V_\succ\to\mathsf V_\sim\) optimize the pointwise choice value over feasible actions \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\) \(\mathsf V_\succ\to\mathsf V_\sim\) evaluate that choice value under a supplied policy \(\mathbb T_\prec\) \(\mathsf V_\sim\to\mathsf V_\prec\) arrival aggregation and pre-decision shock integration \(\mathbb T=\mathbb T_\prec\circ\mathbb T_\succ\) \(\mathsf V_\succ\to\mathsf V_\prec\) optimizing stage evaluation \(\mathbb T_\pi=\mathbb T_\prec\circ\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\) \(\mathsf V_\succ\to\mathsf V_\prec\) fixed-policy stage evaluation

These are mathematical names, not prescribed YAML stage keys. Stage equations are .bl; current block and method-target forms belong to Bellman-SYM's pages on field equations and methodization.

docs.title: 3. Forward builders and transition expectations
docs.text:
Forward operator Rank Induced by \(\mathbb M_\prec\) \(\mathsf M_\prec\to\mathsf M_\sim\) arrival transition and conditional shock law \(\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\) \(\mathsf M_\sim\to\mathsf M_\succ\) decision transition, conditional shock law and policy \(\mathbb M_\pi=\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\circ\mathbb M_\prec\) \(\mathsf M_\prec\to\mathsf M_\succ\) composed stage transition

The corresponding undiscounted expectations \(P_\prec\), \(P_{\succ,\pi}\) and \(P_\pi=P_\prec\circ P_{\succ,\pi}\) act in the reverse direction on test functions. With \(\langle\mu,f\rangle=\int f\,d\mu\),

\[ \langle\mathbb M_\prec\mu,f\rangle=\langle\mu,P_\prec f\rangle, \qquad \langle\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\mu,f\rangle=\langle\mu,P_{\succ,\pi}f\rangle. \]

The equalities hold for bounded measurable test functions, or absolutely integrable evaluations. Reward-bearing \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\) is not \(P_{\succ,\pi}\): with constant discount \(\beta\) and expected reward \(\bar r_\pi\), it equals \(\bar r_\pi+\beta P_{\succ,\pi}\). General arrival aggregation and optimization also remain outside this pairing.

docs.title: 4. Constituent operations
docs.text:
The induced aggregator \(B_\succ\) maps a continuation function to its choice-value function. It composes pullback along the law of motion, pointwise aggregation by the value aggregator and shock integration on every required feasible pair. The optimizing decision builder then takes two further steps, which the table keeps apart: \(\operatorname{argmax}\) answers the set of maximizing policies and chooses none of them, and a selection chooses one member of that set.

For \(Q\in\mathsf Q_\Gamma\) the maximizing set is

\[ \operatorname{argmax}Q=\bigl\{\pi\in\Pi_\Gamma : Q(x,\pi(x))\ge Q(x,a)\ \text{for every } x\in\mathsf X_\sim \text{ and every } a\in\Gamma(x)\bigr\}, \]

the feasible measurable policies that attain the maximum of \(Q(x,\cdot)\) over \(\Gamma(x)\) at every state. It is empty when that maximum is not attained at some state, and also when no measurable policy attains it at every state. A selection is a partial map \(s:\mathsf Q_\Gamma\rightharpoonup\Pi_\Gamma\) with \(s(Q)\in\operatorname{argmax}Q\) for every \(Q\) in its domain \(\operatorname{dom}s\), which is therefore contained in \(\{Q:\operatorname{argmax}Q\neq\varnothing\}\). The maximizing set supplies no selection; a composite that needs one policy names its selection.

Every member \(\pi\) of \(\operatorname{argmax}Q\) gives \(Q(x,\pi(x))=\max_{a\in\Gamma(x)}Q(x,a)\) at every state, so a composite of the form below takes the same value whichever selection it names. The optimizing decision builder, \((\mathbb T_\succ v)(x)=\sup_{a\in\Gamma(x)}(B_\succ v)(x,a)\) where that supremum lies in \(\mathsf L\), is an explicit selection from the maximizing set followed by the insertion of the selected policy into the choice-value function:

\[ \mathbb T_\succ=\iota^{*}\circ\langle B_\succ,s\circ B_\succ\rangle\ \text{on}\ \{v\in\mathsf V_\succ:B_\succ v\in\operatorname{dom}s\}, \qquad \mathbb T_\prec=B_\prec, \]

that is, \((\mathbb T_\succ v)(x)=(B_\succ v)\bigl(x,s(B_\succ v)(x)\bigr)=\max_{a\in\Gamma(x)}(B_\succ v)(x,a)\). Where the supremum is not attained, or is attained by no measurable policy, the optimizing value has no representation of this form.

Domains and assumptions. \(\Pi_\Gamma\) holds the measurable maps \(\pi\) from \(\mathsf X_\sim\) to the action space with \(\pi(x)\in\Gamma(x)\) at every state, and \(\mathsf Q_\Gamma\) holds functions on \(\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)\) measurable for the σ-algebra that the product σ-algebra induces on it. Then \(x\mapsto(x,\pi(x))\) is measurable for every \(\pi\in\Pi_\Gamma\), so \(\iota^{*}(Q,\pi)\) is a measurable function, and \(\mathsf V_\sim\) is chosen to contain these functions. The maximizing set is nonempty, for example, when the action space is finite, \(\Gamma(x)\) is nonempty at every state, and for each action the states at which it is feasible form a measurable set on which \(Q(\cdot,a)\) is measurable (Sargent and Stachurski 2026, Dynamic Programming, vol. 2, Lemma 7.1.1), or when the state and action spaces are metric spaces with their Borel σ-algebras, the action space is separable, \(\Gamma\) is nonempty, compact-valued and continuous, and \(Q\) is continuous on \(\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)\) (ibid., Lemma 7.1.2 and Theorem A.3.3). These conditions are sufficient and are not part of the definitions: the factorization states what \(\mathbb T_\succ\) is on the domain of the named selection, and asserts nothing about which continuation functions lie in that domain.

In the display, \(\iota^{*}\) inserts a policy into a choice-value function, as the table defines. The first column of the table names the kind of each operation, the name under which the package lists it among the operations of a builder; the last column links to the reference row that states which lines of a stage form an operation of that kind. \(B_\succ\) has no kind: a builder lists it as the operations it is composed of.

Kind Operation Domain and codomain Meaning Reference Pullback \(K_g\) functions on the output space of \(g\) → functions on its input space pullback along \(g\), \(K_gf=f\circ g\) realized by Aggregation pointwise \(G\) tuples of functions on a common domain → functions on that domain apply the aggregator at each point, \((f_1,\dots,f_k)\mapsto\bigl(z\mapsto G(f_1(z),\dots,f_k(z),z)\bigr)\); where the aggregated equation holds its own output on both sides, as a relation or a residual system, the operation is the implicit solution of §7 realized by Expectation \(\mathbb E_z\) integrable functions of retained arguments \(h\) and shock \(z\) → functions of the retained arguments \((\mathbb E_zf)(h)=\int f(h,z)\,\mu(dz\mid h)\), integration against the conditional distribution \(\mu\) of the shock realized by — \(B_\succ\) \(\mathsf V_\succ\to\mathsf Q_\Gamma\) construct choice values on all feasible state–action pairs; composed of the three operations above — Argmax \(\operatorname{argmax}\) \(\mathsf Q_\Gamma\to\mathcal P(\Pi_\Gamma)\) the maximizing set: every feasible measurable policy that attains the maximum at every state; possibly empty; chooses no member, a selection from it being a numerical method's realized by — \(s\) \(\mathsf Q_\Gamma\rightharpoonup\Pi_\Gamma\) a named selection, \(s(Q)\in\operatorname{argmax}Q\), defined only where the maximizing set is nonempty — PolicyInsertion \(\iota^{*}\), with \(\iota_\pi(x)=(x,\pi(x))\) \(\mathsf Q_\Gamma\times\Pi_\Gamma\to\mathsf V_\sim\); on measures, for each \(\pi\in\Pi_\Gamma\), finite measures on \(\mathsf X_\sim\) → finite measures on \(\operatorname{Gr}(\Gamma)\) insert the policy: \(\iota^{*}(Q,\pi)=Q\circ\iota_\pi\), the choice value \(Q(x,\pi(x))\) at the policy; on measures \(\lambda\mapsto(\iota_\pi)_\#\lambda\), and \(\langle(\iota_\pi)_\#\lambda,Q\rangle=\langle\lambda,\iota^{*}(Q,\pi)\rangle\) for bounded measurable \(Q\) realized by Evaluation \(f\mapsto f\) the derived carrier of an object, the set its construction places it in → its declared carrier, the set the stage declares it to lie in the identity into the declared carrier: a function is carried as the same function and a set of policies as the same set; defined where the object lies in the declared carrier, and an inclusion where the derived carrier does; selects nothing realized by Pushforward \(g_\#\) finite measures on the domain of \(g\) → finite measures on its codomain the image measure, \((g_\#\lambda)(B)=\lambda(g^{-1}(B))\) realized by DistributionExtension \(\lambda\mapsto\lambda\otimes\mu\) finite measures on retained arguments \(H\) → finite measures on \(H\times\mathsf Z\) extend a measure by the conditional distribution of the shock, \((\lambda\otimes\mu)(B)=\int\mu(\{z:(h,z)\in B\}\mid h)\,\lambda(dh)\); followed by \(g_\#\) it gives the Markov propagation of a transition with a shock realized by

An operation whose result is a set, the maximizing set here or the solution set of §7, keeps that set until a selection is named. Placing a builder's result in the declared space of its output selects nothing: a function is carried as the same function, and a set of policies as the same set.

At a policy \(\pi\), a law of motion \(g_\succ\) on the feasible pairs is read at the policy, \(g_{\succ,\pi}=g_\succ\circ\iota_\pi\), a shock coordinate carried unchanged. Then \(K_{g_{\succ,\pi}}=K_{\iota_\pi}\circ K_{g_\succ}\) and \((g_{\succ,\pi})_\#=(g_\succ)_\#\circ(\iota_\pi)_\#\), where \(K_{\iota_\pi}Q=\iota^{*}(Q,\pi)\): a builder at a policy composes the insertion of the policy with the pullback or the push-forward along \(g_\succ\).

The conditional distribution \(\mu\) of a shock with values in \(\mathsf Z\), given retained arguments with values in \(H\), is a probability kernel: \(\mu(\cdot\mid h)\) is a probability measure on \(\mathsf Z\) for each \(h\in H\), and \(h\mapsto\mu(B\mid h)\) is measurable for each measurable \(B\subseteq\mathsf Z\). A distribution that reads no retained argument is constant in \(h\). The expectation integrates against it, the distribution extension extends a measure by it, and the shock discretization of §7 approximates it.

The value of a function at a point and a numerical interpolation of that function are different descriptions: a numerical routine may interpolate internally, and representing a function on a grid adds no operation to this catalogue.

For an invertible transformation \(\varphi\) on the relevant value domain, a certainty equivalent may take the form \(R_z^\varphi=\varphi^{-1}\circ\mathbb E_z\circ\varphi\) when the integrals and inverse are defined. It reduces to expectation for \(\varphi=\mathrm{id}\). This formula does not make every recursive preference a single local integrand; that extension remains unfinished. #todo

A vector shock can be integrated sequentially with its conditional laws, under the conditions for iterated integration. Replacing those laws by independent marginals requires independence; the tower property does not supply it. Intermediate numerical integrations do not introduce new information perches by themselves.

docs.title: 5. Named composites
docs.text:
A named expression can remain a derived operation or be treated as a primitive symbol in a coarser signature. Exact agreement with its expansion is the condition in Initial-algebra semantics §4.

Composite Rank Meaning \(\max=\iota^{*}\circ\langle\mathrm{id},s\rangle\) \(\operatorname{dom}s\to\mathsf V_\sim\) an explicit selection from the maximizing set followed by the insertion of the selected policy: \((\max Q)(x)=Q(x,s(Q)(x))=\max_{a\in\Gamma(x)}Q(x,a)\), the same for every selection \(s\) whose domain holds \(Q\) (§4) \(W=\mathbb E_\eta\circ K_{g_2}\) continuation functions → post-decision functions \(Wf(a)=\int f(g_2(a,\eta))\,\mu_\eta(d\eta)\) \(\max_J\) \(\mathsf L^J\to\mathsf L\) for finite nonempty \(J\) largest branch value \(\mathbb E_J\) \(\mathsf L^J\to\mathsf L\) for a fixed finite probability vector weighted branch value

The post-decision value function is \(\mathfrak w=Wf\). Its derivative \(\mathfrak w'\) is the marginal value function where differentiability holds; in the language it is the derivative operator applied to the value field, the term D_{a}V[>], and is no field of its own. Additive expected utility with constant discount separates the choice value into reward plus \(\beta Wf\) after the appropriate post-decision transition. A general nonlinear aggregator need not have that separation. Operators and builders §10 fixes the timing convention.

docs.title: 6. Branch values and envelopes
docs.text:
For finite alternatives, a vector of branch values is the input to the maximum or weighted expectation. A single labeled value in a disjoint union is not that vector. Agent choice determines a policy; exogenous selection uses a declared conditional law. A persistent regime remains in the state where it affects future laws or payoffs. These economic choices are not interchangeable numerical methods.

Operation Domain and codomain Role Envelope selection specified candidate-value/control representation → selected representation compare candidates at common states under the declared criterion

Envelope selection belongs to a numerical method and is not an operation a stage states: the comparison of candidates at common states is internal to the method. No envelope routine automatically resolves missing candidates, policy ties or convergence; Methods discusses the numerical distinctions.

docs.title: 7. Implicit and auxiliary operations
docs.text:
Operation Domain and codomain Conditions Implicit solution a relation in unknown functions and given functions, such as a residual system \(r(z,u(z))=0\) → the set of tuples of measurable functions that satisfy it at every point of its stated domain the set may be empty or hold several members; a composite that needs one member names a selection from it, as §4 does for the maximizing set; that a member maximizes an objective is a separate statement Differentiation differentiable functions → derivative functions coordinate and differentiation domain specified Gradient differentiable scalar functions → vector-valued derivatives one partial derivative per coordinate Shock discretization specified law/kernel → finite approximation approximation of that fixed law; source attachment remains method-specific #ambiguity Linear solution compatible \((A,b)\) → selected solution of \(Ax=b\) uniqueness or a specified solution rule

Derivatives and names

A derivative operation and a name given to a function are distinct. Differentiation of a declared function in one of its formal coordinates yields a function, and the derivative term on a value field, D_{a}V[>], yields the derivative of that value; naming a function defines nothing further, and no field stands for a derivative. Functions describes their types.

Iterated transitions

Stationary distributions are fixed points of probability propagation; tail behavior is an asymptotic property. They require further assumptions and analysis beyond a one-step transition or finite branch operation. This catalogue does not prohibit defining a solver operator for them.

docs.title: 8. Authored computation boundaries
docs.text: Stage equations and definitions are authored in .bl. Block identifiers are addresses, not reserved formula names such as InvEuler or MarginalBellman. A marked !node retains an authored computation boundary; operation occurrences and dependencies can remain inside an unmarked equation. An implicit statement remains a relation until its selection conditions are met. The supported method targets are defined by Bellman-SYM's Appendix D, rather than inferred from this mathematical inventory.

docs.title: 9. Related documents
docs.text:

  • Methods — numerical procedures and their requirements.

docs.title: Appendix E.4 — Parameters and settings
docs.text:
Summary

Parameters help define the economic model; settings control its numerical approximation. Their role depends on what they change, not on whether their values are real numbers, integers, arrays or flags.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Fields, Functions and Operators describe the mathematical inputs and operations. Used by — Method types: the method types a methods file names, with the settings each reads; Methodization and The Bellman factory: the source and binding rules that supply parameter values and settings; Bellman-SYM's Appendix C: the specified construction.

A parameter is an input on which the mathematical problem depends. A setting controls the numerical representation or algorithm used for that problem. The interpretation Υ and numerical construction Ρ distinguish these roles; they are maps, not stages in the economic model. Inputs may be scalar or structured, according to the declared problem.

Role What the value determines Source Parameter A reward, transition, conditional law, constraint or economic domain. Typed declarations in .bl, with values supplied through calibration bindings. Setting A numerical grid, quadrature size, stopping tolerance or other method input. Supporting settings/methods YAML, in the forms Bellman-SYM's Methodization page gives.

A constant has a declared type and admissible value domain. That type may include a real interval, integers, vectors, matrices or a finite set of symbols. A domain does not by itself determine a unique source type name or a declared subsort relation; Kinds and sorts distinguishes those choices. A parameter supplied to an occurrence is held fixed in that occurrence's equations, even when other occurrences use different values.

Supporting YAML supplies calibration, methods and settings through occurrence bindings. The stage equations themselves are .bl. The specified construction of Bellman-SYM's Appendix C retains interpreted equations and definitions; a completed numerical solution additionally needs admissible inputs and supported methods.

Classifying an input

Ask whether the input changes the declared economic problem or how that fixed problem is approximated. Finer discretization does not automatically remove every setting's effect: convergence requires a suitable method and refinement sequence. An economic parameter may also be irrelevant to a particular outcome, so sensitivity alone is not the classification test.

A grid defining discrete economic choices is part of the model. A grid approximating a continuous domain is numerical data. Bounds and sizes have the corresponding role; a file named settings does not change their mathematical meaning. The current source rules determine how to declare the economic domain and supply numerical grids.

docs.title: 1. Value domains
docs.text:
The following domains illustrate the existing parameter/setting distinction. Their types do not certify any particular handler option or source key.

Domain Example Role depends on Real interval Discount \(\beta\in(0,1)\), gross return \(R\in\mathbb R_{++}\), persistence coefficient \(\rho_\zeta\) in its declared admissible set. These are economic parameters when they define preferences, returns or the income law. Stationarity may impose additional restrictions. Integer Grid size \(n_m\), quadrature-node count, iteration limit. Numerical approximation and iteration choices are settings; a count defining the economic domain is model data. Vector or array Wage-profile coefficients, a shock mean vector. Parameters when they determine the economic equations or law; numerical arrays can instead be settings. Matrix Shock covariance or income transition matrix. Parameters when they define the model law; numerical approximations of a fixed law have a separate approximation role. Finite admissible set A method choice, a jump-handling flag, or an initialization choice. Settings when they select numerical behavior; model data when they select an economic regime or constraint.

A numerical grid can be supplied as points or specified through a construction using sizes and bounds, according to the method's supported representation. A mathematical state or action space is a domain, and a function or distribution is a mathematical object; none is reduced to a scalar constant merely because it appears in a data file. Fields and Functions describe their types.

The same Boolean domain can have two roles. A flag changing an algorithm's jump handling is a setting; a flag adding a tax schedule to the budget changes the economic problem. These are conceptual examples, not new reserved YAML keys.

Horizon and estimation bounds

An economic finite horizon changes the decision problem; a numerical truncation of an infinite-horizon problem is an approximation choice. How to record the horizon in source remains open in this inventory; that question is separate from its mathematical role. A parameter's admissible domain, such as \(\beta\in(0,1)\), is also distinct from a narrower search interval chosen for an estimation procedure. The latter is an estimation setting, subject to the model's admissible domain.

A method's documented settings describe the inputs and domains it accepts. A handler, the implementation of that procedure, must map those inputs to the package arguments it supports. A method type records the options it admits and the kind of value each takes; recording an option does not show that a handler reads it.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The examples below include individual stages and applications that compose several stages into periods. A stage is one decision episode, with its arrival state, shocks, transitions, constraints and preferences. An application specifies one or more stage occurrences, each a stage file placed at one position of a period, and the connectors that join them by identifying or renaming the quantities one stage passes to the next.

Each stage is structured around three perches — information sets at which the agent's state is observed:

  • Arrival — the agent enters with the states of the arrival perch (e.g., beginning-of-period assets before shocks resolve).
  • Decision — shocks have resolved; the agent observes states and chooses controls.
  • Continuation — the decision has been made; the states of the continuation perch (e.g., end-of-period savings) carry forward.

Current stages are authored in .bl stage files. Application files place those stages in periods and supply their calibration, settings and methods. Several pages in this directory record the earlier dolo-plus YAML design; they remain as historical examples and do not state the current source format.

The table therefore distinguishes three kinds of source page:

  • Stage describes one current .bl stage file.
  • Application describes a composition of stage occurrences.
  • Historical YAML preserves an earlier source design for reference.

The formal MDP pages state selected examples as Markov decision processes (MDPs) in mathematical notation. They are not generated round trips from the historical YAML pages. See also the Concept wiki for one-page definitions of stages, perches and builders.

docs.title: Formal MDP Document: Consumption-Saving with Medical Shocks
1. Rosetta Stone
docs.text:
HARK variable DDSL concept Mathematical notation kLvl Prestate (arrival perch) \(k \in \mathbb{R}_+\) pLvlPrev Prestate (arrival perch) \(p^- \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) PermShk Permanent income shock \(\Psi \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) TranShk Transitory income shock \(\xi \in \mathbb{R}_+\) pLvl Post-income-shock state \(p \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) yLvl Labor income realization \(y \in \mathbb{R}_+\) wLvl Wealth from assets \(w \in \mathbb{R}_+\) mLvl Market resources (decision perch) \(m \in \mathbb{R}_+\) MedCost Medical cost shock \(\mu \in \mathbb{R}_+\) MedShk Medical utility shock \(\zeta \in \mathbb{R}_+\) Care Medical care decision \(\mathbb{1}_{\text{care}} \in \{0,1\}\) MedLvl Realized medical expenditure \(\tilde{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}_+\) bLvl Bank balances post-medical \(b \in \mathbb{R}_+\) cLvl Consumption (control) \(c \in \mathbb{R}_+\) aLvl End-of-period assets (continuation perch) \(a \in \mathbb{R}_+\) live Survival indicator \(\mathbb{1}_{\text{live}} \in \{0,1\}\)

Timing Convention: The model features a four-perch structure within each period: 1. Arrival perch: Agent begins with state \((k, p^-)\) 2. Post-income perch: After permanent income growth/shocks, state becomes \((m, p)\) 3. Decision perch: After medical shock realization, agent chooses care and consumption 4. Continuation perch: End-of-period state \((a, p)\) transitions to next period's \((k', p'^-)\)

docs.title: 2.1 State Spaces
docs.text:
The agent's economic state evolves through multiple perches within each period:

Arrival State: At the beginning of period \(t\), the agent possesses: - Capital holdings \(k_t \in \mathbb{R}_+ \coloneqq [0, \infty)\) - Previous permanent income level \(p_t^- \in \mathbb{R}_{++} \coloneqq (0, \infty)\)

Post-Income State: After income realization but before decisions: - Market resources \(m_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) - Current permanent income \(p_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\)

Decision State: After observing medical shocks: - Market resources \(m_t\) - Permanent income \(p_t\) - Medical cost \(\mu_t\) - Medical utility shock \(\zeta_t\)

Continuation State: After all within-period decisions: - End-of-period assets \(a_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) - Current permanent income \(p_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\)

docs.title: 2.2 Action Spaces
docs.text:
The agent makes two sequential decisions each period:

Medical Care Decision: \(\mathbb{1}_{\text{care},t} \in \{0, 1\}\) — binary choice of whether to purchase medical care at cost \(\mu_t\).

Consumption Decision: \(c_t \in [0, b_t]\) where \(b_t\) denotes bank balances after medical expenditure.

docs.title: 2.3 Shock Distributions
docs.text:
Income Shocks: The joint distribution of permanent and transitory income shocks is denoted \(F_{\Psi, \xi}\), with support \(\mathbb{R}_{++} \times \mathbb{R}_+\). Each period, the agent draws: $\((\Psi_t, \xi_t) \sim F_{\Psi, \xi}\)$

Medical Shocks: The joint distribution of medical costs and utility penalties is denoted \(G_{\mu, \zeta}\), with support \(\mathbb{R}_+ \times \mathbb{R}_+\). Each period, independently of income shocks: $\((\mu_t, \zeta_t) \sim G_{\mu, \zeta}\)$

Survival Shock: At the end of each period, the agent survives with probability \(\pi \in (0, 1]\): $\(\mathbb{1}_{\text{live},t} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi)\)$

Initial Conditions: At model initialization (period \(t=0\)), the agent draws: - Permanent income: \(p_0^- \sim F_{p,0}\) - Normalized capital: \(\kappa_0 \sim F_{\kappa,0}\) - De-normalized capital: \(k_0 = p_0^- \cdot \kappa_0\)

docs.title: 2.4 Transition Dynamics
docs.text:
The within-period dynamics proceed sequentially through four distinct phases:

Phase 1 — Income Realization: Beginning with arrival state \((k_t, p_t^-)\), the agent experiences income shocks and realizes:

  1. Expected permanent income before shock: \(\bar{p}_t = \mathbb{E}[p_t | p_t^-]\) (deterministic growth function)
  2. Permanent income realization: \(p_t = \bar{p}_t \cdot \Psi_t\)
  3. Labor income: \(y_t = \xi_t \cdot p_t\)
  4. Wealth from assets: \(w_t = R \cdot k_t\) where \(R > 0\) is the gross risk-free return
  5. Market resources: \(m_t = w_t + y_t\)

Phase 2 — Medical Shock and Care Decision: After observing medical shock \((\mu_t, \zeta_t)\), the agent evaluates:

  1. Bank balances if care purchased: \(b_{\text{care}} = m_t - \mu_t\)
  2. Value if care purchased: \(V^{\text{mid}}(b_{\text{care}}, p_t)\)
  3. Value if no care: \(V^{\text{mid}}(m_t, p_t) - \zeta_t\)
  4. Optimal care decision: $\(\mathbb{1}_{\text{care},t} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } V^{\text{mid}}(m_t - \mu_t, p_t) > V^{\text{mid}}(m_t, p_t) - \zeta_t \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\)$
  5. Realized medical expenditure: \(\tilde{\mu}_t = \mathbb{1}_{\text{care},t} \cdot \mu_t\)
  6. Bank balances post-medical: \(b_t = m_t - \tilde{\mu}_t\)

Phase 3 — Consumption Decision: Given bank balances \(b_t\) and permanent income \(p_t\), the agent consumes: $\(c_t = c^*(b_t, p_t)\)$ where \(c^*: \mathbb{R}_+ \times \mathbb{R}_{++} \to \mathbb{R}_+\) is the optimal consumption policy function.

Phase 4 — Asset Accumulation and Survival: 1. End-of-period assets: \(a_t = b_t - c_t\) 2. Survival realization: \(\mathbb{1}_{\text{live},t} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi)\)

Twist (Between-Period Transition): For surviving agents (\(\mathbb{1}_{\text{live},t} = 1\)), the continuation state \((a_t, p_t)\) becomes next period's arrival state: $\(k_{t+1} = a_t, \quad p_{t+1}^- = p_t\)$

Non-survivors exit the model (absorbing state).

docs.title: 2.5 Preferences
docs.text:
The agent has additively separable utility over consumption with medical utility shocks. The period utility function is: $\(u(c_t, \mathbb{1}_{\text{care},t}, \zeta_t) = u(c_t) - (1 - \mathbb{1}_{\text{care},t}) \cdot \zeta_t\)$

The specific functional form of \(u(\cdot)\) is not specified in the YAML but is typically CRRA: $\(u(c) = \frac{c^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}\)$ for relative risk aversion \(\rho > 0\), with \(u(c) = \log(c)\) when \(\rho = 1\).

docs.title: 3. Bellman Equation
docs.text: The agent's problem decomposes into a sequence of value functions corresponding to different information sets within the period.

docs.title: 3.1 Arrival Value Function
docs.text:
At the beginning of the period, before observing any within-period shocks, the agent's arrival value is: $\(V^{\text{arr}}(k, p^-) = \mathbb{E}_{\Psi, \xi, \mu, \zeta}\left[ V^{\text{dec}}(m, p, \mu, \zeta) \mid k, p^- \right]\)$

where the expectation is taken over: - Income shocks \((\Psi, \xi)\) - Medical shocks \((\mu, \zeta)\)

and market resources and permanent income are determined by: - \(\bar{p} = \mathbb{E}[p | p^-]\) - \(p = \bar{p} \cdot \Psi\) - \(y = \xi \cdot p\) - \(w = R \cdot k\) - \(m = w + y\)

Information Set at Arrival: \(\mathcal{I}^{\text{arr}}_t = \{k_t, p_t^-\}\)

docs.title: 3.2 Decision Value Function
docs.text:
After observing market resources \(m\), permanent income \(p\), and medical shocks \((\mu, \zeta)\), the agent solves: $\(V^{\text{dec}}(m, p, \mu, \zeta) = \max_{\mathbb{1}_{\text{care}} \in \{0,1\}} \left\{ V^{\text{mid}}(m - \mathbb{1}_{\text{care}} \cdot \mu, p) - (1 - \mathbb{1}_{\text{care}}) \cdot \zeta \right\}\)$

This can be written explicitly as: $\(V^{\text{dec}}(m, p, \mu, \zeta) = \max\left\{ V^{\text{mid}}(m - \mu, p), \; V^{\text{mid}}(m, p) - \zeta \right\}\)$

The optimal medical care policy is: $\(\mathbb{1}_{\text{care}}^*(m, p, \mu, \zeta) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } V^{\text{mid}}(m - \mu, p) \geq V^{\text{mid}}(m, p) - \zeta \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\)$

Equivalently, care is purchased if and only if: $\(\zeta \geq V^{\text{mid}}(m, p) - V^{\text{mid}}(m - \mu, p)\)$

That is, care is purchased when the utility loss from the medical shock exceeds the value loss from paying the medical cost.

Information Set at Decision: \(\mathcal{I}^{\text{dec}}_t = \{m_t, p_t, \mu_t, \zeta_t\}\)

docs.title: 3.3 Mid-Period Value Function
docs.text:
After making the medical care decision, the agent has bank balances \(b\) and must choose consumption: $\(V^{\text{mid}}(b, p) = \max_{c \in [0, b]} \left\{ u(c) + \beta \pi \cdot V^{\text{cont}}(b - c, p) \right\}\)$

where \(\beta \in (0, 1)\) is the time discount factor and \(\pi\) is the survival probability.

Information Set at Mid-Period: \(\mathcal{I}^{\text{mid}}_t = \{b_t, p_t\}\) (medical shocks and care decision already resolved)

docs.title: 3.4 Continuation Value Function
docs.text:
At the end of the period, with assets \(a\) and permanent income \(p\), the continuation value (for survivors) is: $\(V^{\text{cont}}(a, p) = V^{\text{arr}}(k', p'^-) \Big|_{k' = a, \, p'^- = p}\)$

This reflects the transition from continuation perch to next period's arrival perch via the twist mapping.

Information Set at Continuation: \(\mathcal{I}^{\text{cont}}_t = \{a_t, p_t\}\)

docs.title: 3.5 Complete Bellman System
docs.text:
The complete recursive problem can be written as a system:

\[\begin{aligned} V^{\text{arr}}(k, p^-) &= \mathbb{E}_{\Psi, \xi, \mu, \zeta}\left[ V^{\text{dec}}(R k + \xi \bar{p} \Psi, \bar{p} \Psi, \mu, \zeta) \right] \\[0.5em] V^{\text{dec}}(m, p, \mu, \zeta) &= \max\left\{ V^{\text{mid}}(m - \mu, p), \; V^{\text{mid}}(m, p) - \zeta \right\} \\[0.5em] V^{\text{mid}}(b, p) &= \max_{c \in [0, b]} \left\{ u(c) + \beta \pi \cdot V^{\text{arr}}(b - c, p) \right\} \\[0.5em] \end{aligned}\]

where \(\bar{p} = \mathbb{E}[p | p^-]\) and we've substituted the twist mapping in the final line.

docs.title: 4.1 Consumption Euler Equation
docs.text:
For the consumption decision at the mid-period perch, the first-order condition with respect to \(c\) is: $\(u'(c) = \beta \pi \cdot \frac{\partial V^{\text{arr}}}{\partial k}(a, p)\)$

where \(a = b - c\) denotes end-of-period assets.

By the envelope theorem applied to \(V^{\text{arr}}(k, p^-)\): $\(\frac{\partial V^{\text{arr}}}{\partial k}(k, p^-) = R \cdot \mathbb{E}_{\Psi, \xi, \mu, \zeta}\left[ \frac{\partial V^{\text{dec}}}{\partial m}(m, p, \mu, \zeta) \mid k, p^- \right]\)$

And by the envelope theorem applied to \(V^{\text{dec}}\): $\(\frac{\partial V^{\text{dec}}}{\partial m}(m, p, \mu, \zeta) = \frac{\partial V^{\text{mid}}}{\partial b}(b, p)\)$

where \(b = m - \mathbb{1}_{\text{care}} \cdot \mu\) is bank balances after the optimal medical care decision.

Finally, applying the envelope theorem to \(V^{\text{mid}}\): $\(\frac{\partial V^{\text{mid}}}{\partial b}(b, p) = u'(c)\)$

where $c = c^*(

docs.title: Formal MDP Specification: Consumption-Saving with General Income Process
1. Rosetta Stone
docs.text:
HARK variable DDSL concept Mathematical notation kLvl Arrival state (capital) \(k_t\) pLvlPrev Arrival state (permanent income) \(p_{t-1}\) PermShk Permanent income shock \(\psi_t\) TranShk Transitory income shock \(\xi_t\) pLvl Decision state (current permanent income) \(p_t\) yLvl Labor income realization \(y_t\) bLvl Bank balances (capital income) \(b_t\) mLvl Market resources (decision state) \(m_t\) cLvl Control variable (consumption) \(c_t\) aLvl Continuation state (assets) \(a_t\) live Survival indicator \(\mathbb{1}_{\text{survive}}\) Rfree Risk-free return factor \(R\) LivPrb Survival probability \(\pi\) pLvlNextFunc Permanent income growth function \(\mathbb{G}(\cdot)\) IncShkDstn Joint shock distribution \(F_{\psi,\xi}\)

Timing convention: The subscript \(t\) denotes the period. Variables with "Prev" suffix or subscript \(t-1\) represent the value from the previous period that arrives at the beginning of period \(t\).

docs.title: 2.1 State Spaces
docs.text:
The model features a consumption-saving problem with income uncertainty. The state space evolves through three perches within each period:

Arrival Perch (pre-shock): At the beginning of period \(t\), the agent arrives with: - Capital holdings \(k_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\), which are the assets carried forward from period \(t-1\) - Permanent income level from the previous period \(p_{t-1} \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\)

Decision Perch (post-shock, pre-decision): After observing income shocks \((\psi_t, \xi_t)\), the agent observes: - Updated permanent income level \(p_t = \mathbb{G}(p_{t-1}) \cdot \psi_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) - Market resources \(m_t = R k_t + \xi_t p_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\)

Continuation Perch (post-decision): After choosing consumption \(c_t\), the agent reaches: - End-of-period assets \(a_t = m_t - c_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) - Current permanent income level \(p_t\) (carried forward) - Survival status determined by mortality shock

docs.title: 2.2 Action Space
docs.text: At the decision perch, the agent chooses consumption \(c_t \in [0, m_t]\), subject to the liquidity constraint that consumption cannot exceed available market resources.

docs.title: 2.3 Shock Distributions
docs.text:
Income shocks: The pair \((\psi_t, \xi_t)\) is drawn from a joint distribution \(F_{\psi,\xi}\) at the beginning of each period, where: - \(\psi_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) is the permanent income shock - \(\xi_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) is the transitory income shock

Mortality shock: At the end of each period, the agent survives with probability \(\pi \in [0,1]\). If the agent dies, they are replaced by a newborn with initial state drawn from the initialization distribution.

Initial distribution: Newborn agents draw: - Initial permanent income \(p_0 \sim F_{p,\text{init}}\) - Initial normalized capital holdings \(\kappa_0 \sim F_{\kappa,\text{init}}\), with \(k_0 = p_0 \kappa_0\)

docs.title: 2.4 Permanent Income Process
docs.text:
The permanent income component evolves according to a general function \(\mathbb{G}: \mathbb{R}_{++} \to \mathbb{R}_{++}\) that captures deterministic growth, mean reversion, or other dynamics:

\[p_t = \mathbb{G}(p_{t-1}) \cdot \psi_t\]

This specification nests several common processes: - Constant growth: \(\mathbb{G}(p) = \Gamma \cdot p\) yields \(p_t = \Gamma \psi_t p_{t-1}\) - Mean reversion: \(\mathbb{G}(p) = \bar{p}^\alpha p^{1-\alpha}\) yields partial adjustment toward \(\bar{p}\) - General nonlinear dynamics: Any smooth function of past permanent income

docs.title: 2.5 Transition Equations
docs.text:
The within-period dynamics proceed sequentially:

  1. Income realization: Draw shocks \((\psi_t, \xi_t) \sim F_{\psi,\xi}\)

  2. Permanent income update: $\(p_t = \mathbb{G}(p_{t-1}) \cdot \psi_t\)$

  3. Labor income: $\(y_t = \xi_t p_t\)$

  4. Bank balances: $\(b_t = R k_t\)$

  5. Market resources: $\(m_t = b_t + y_t = R k_t + \xi_t p_t\)$

  6. Consumption decision: $\(c_t = \mathfrak{c}(m_t, p_t)\)$ where \(\mathfrak{c}\) is the policy function to be solved for.

  7. Asset accumulation: $\(a_t = m_t - c_t\)$

  8. Survival: Draw \(\mathbb{1}_{\text{survive}} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi)\)

  9. State transition: $\(k_{t+1} = \begin{cases} a_t & \text{if survive} \\ p_t \kappa_0' & \text{if die, where } \kappa_0' \sim F_{\kappa,\text{init}} \end{cases}\)$ $\(p_t^{\text{next}} = \begin{cases} p_t & \text{if survive} \\ p_0' & \text{if die, where } p_0' \sim F_{p,\text{init}} \end{cases}\)$

docs.title: 3. Bellman Equation
docs.text: The agent's problem admits a recursive formulation decomposed into three value functions corresponding to the three perches.

docs.title: 3.1 Arrival Value (Pre-Shock Expectation)
docs.text:
At the arrival perch, before observing income shocks, the agent's value function is:

\[V^A(k_t, p_{t-1}) = \mathbb{E}_{\psi_t, \xi_t} \left[ V^D(m_t, p_t) \mid k_t, p_{t-1} \right]\]

where the expectation is taken over the joint shock distribution \(F_{\psi,\xi}\), and the decision state variables are determined by: $\(p_t = \mathbb{G}(p_{t-1}) \cdot \psi_t, \quad m_t = R k_t + \xi_t p_t\)$

Information set at arrival perch: \(\mathcal{I}_t^A = \{k_t, p_{t-1}\}\)

docs.title: 3.2 Decision Value (Post-Shock Optimization)
docs.text:
At the decision perch, after observing shocks and computing market resources, the agent solves:

\[V^D(m_t, p_t) = \max_{c_t \in [0, m_t]} \left\{ u(c_t) + \beta V^C(a_t, p_t) \right\}\]

subject to: $\(a_t = m_t - c_t\)$

where: - \(u(\cdot)\) is the per-period utility function (typically \(u(c) = \frac{c^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}\) for CRRA preferences) - \(\beta \in (0,1)\) is the time discount factor - \(V^C\) is the continuation value function

Information set at decision perch: \(\mathcal{I}_t^D = \{m_t, p_t, k_t, p_{t-1}\}\) (though the optimization problem depends only on \((m_t, p_t)\) due to Markovian structure)

docs.title: 3.3 Continuation Value (Post-Decision)
docs.text:
At the continuation perch, after choosing consumption but before mortality is resolved, the continuation value is:

\[V^C(a_t, p_t) = \pi \cdot V^A(a_t, p_t) + (1-\pi) \cdot V^{\text{newborn}}\]

where: - \(\pi\) is the survival probability - \(V^A(a_t, p_t)\) is the arrival value for next period with state \((k_{t+1}, p_t^{\text{next}}) = (a_t, p_t)\) - \(V^{\text{newborn}} \coloneqq \mathbb{E}_{p_0, \kappa_0} [V^A(p_0 \kappa_0, p_0)]\) is the value of a newborn agent drawing from initial distributions

Information set at continuation perch: \(\mathcal{I}_t^C = \{a_t, p_t\}\) plus the history, but future uncertainty remains.

docs.title: 3.4 Complete Bellman System
docs.text:
Combining the three perches, the complete recursive problem is:

\[\begin{aligned} V^A(k, p_{-1}) &= \int \int V^D(Rk + \xi p, p) \, dF_{\psi,\xi}(\psi, \xi) \\ &\quad \text{where } p = \mathbb{G}(p_{-1}) \psi \\[1em] V^D(m, p) &= \max_{c \in [0,m]} \left\{ u(c) + \beta V^C(m-c, p) \right\} \\[1em] V^C(a, p) &= \pi V^A(a, p) + (1-\pi) \mathbb{E}_{p_0, \kappa_0}[V^A(p_0 \kappa_0, p_0)] \end{aligned}\]

The policy function \(\mathfrak{c}(m,p)\) is characterized by the argmax in the decision value function.

docs.title: 4.1 Euler Equation
docs.text:
The first-order condition for the consumption choice yields the standard Euler equation. Taking the derivative with respect to \(c_t\) in the decision value function:

\[u'(c_t) = \beta \frac{\partial V^C}{\partial a_t}(a_t, p_t)\]

Using the envelope theorem on the continuation value:

\[\frac{\partial V^C}{\partial a}(a,p) = \pi \frac{\partial V^A}{\partial k}(a, p)\]

And applying the envelope theorem to the arrival value:

\[\frac{\partial V^A}{\partial k}(k, p_{-1}) = \mathbb{E}_{\psi,\xi} \left[ \frac{\partial V^D}{\partial m}(m, p) \cdot R \mid k, p_{-1} \right]\]

Since \(\frac{\partial V^D}{\partial m}(m,p) = u'(c)\) by the envelope theorem at the decision stage, we obtain:

\[u'(c_t) = \beta \pi R \mathbb{E}_t \left[ u'(c_{t+1}) \right]\]

where the expectation \(\mathbb{E}_t[\cdot]\) is taken over the period \(t+1\) shocks \((\psi_{t+1}, \xi_{t+1})\) conditional on the end-of-period state \((a_t, p_t)\).

docs.title: 4.2 CRRA Specification
docs.text:
For constant relative risk aversion (CRRA) utility \(u(c) = \frac{c^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}\), we have \(u'(c) = c^{-\rho}\), and the Euler equation becomes:

\[c_t^{-\rho} = \beta \pi R \mathbb{E}_t \left[ c_{t+1}^{-\rho} \right]\]

docs.title: 4.3 Endogenous Grid Method Representation
docs.text:
The model is particularly amenable to the Endogenous Grid Method (EGM). Define the marginal value of end-of-period assets:

\[\mathfrak{v}(a, p) \coloneqq \frac{\partial V^C}{\partial a}(a,p) = \pi \mathbb{E}_{\psi,\xi} \left[ u'(\mathfrak{c}(Ra + \xi p', p')) \cdot R \mid p \right]\]

where \(p' = \mathbb{G}(p) \psi\).

Given a current iterate of the consumption function \(\mathfrak{c}\), the EGM approach:

  1. Specifies exogenous grid: Choose grid points \(\{a^j\}\) for end-of-period assets

  2. Computes marginal value: For each \((a^j, p^i)\): $\(\mathfrak{v}(a^j, p^i) = \pi R \mathbb{E}_{\psi,\xi} \left[ u'(\mathfrak{c}(Ra^j + \xi p', p')) \right]\)$ where \(p' = \mathbb{G}(p^i) \psi\)

  3. Inverts FOC: Use \(u'(c) = \beta \mathfrak{v}(a,p)\) to find: $\(c^j_i = (u')^{-1}(\beta \mathfrak{v}(a^j, p^i))\)$

  4. Constructs endogenous grid: Compute market resources: $\(m^j_i = a^j + c^j_i\)$

  5. Interpolates: The consumption function is the interpolation of \((m^j_i, c^j_i)\) for each \(p^i\)

This method is efficient because it avoids root-finding in the optimization step.

docs.title: 4.4 Envelope Conditions
docs.text:
The envelope conditions with respect to the state variables are:

\[\frac{\partial V^A}{\partial k}(k, p_{-1}) = R \mathbb{E}_{\psi,\xi} \left[ u'(c) \mid k, p_{-1} \right]\] \[\frac{\partial V^A}{\partial p_{-1}}(k, p_{-1}) = \mathbb{E}_{\psi,\xi} \left[ u'(c) \cdot \left(\xi \psi \mathbb{G}'(p_{-1}) + \frac{\partial \mathfrak{c}}{\partial p}(m,p) \cdot \psi \mathbb{G}'(p_{-1})\right) \mid k, p_{-1} \right]\]

These conditions are used in computing the distribution dynamics and welfare analysis.

docs.title: Formal MDP Document: Consumption-Saving Model with Permanent and Transitory Income Shocks
1. Rosetta Stone
docs.text: HARK variable DDSL concept Mathematical notation kNrm Prestate/Arrival perch \(k_t\) pLvlPrev Prestate/Arrival perch \(P_{t-1}\) PermShk Shock realization \(\Psi_t\) TranShk Shock realization \(\theta_t\) yNrm Post-shock intermediate \(y_t\) pLvl Post-shock state \(P_t\) G Growth factor realization \(G_t\) bNrm Post-shock intermediate \(b_t\) mNrm Decision perch state \(m_t\) cNrm Control/Action \(c_t\) aNrm Continuation perch state \(a_t\) live Survival indicator \(\mathbb{1}_{\text{survive}}\) cFunc Policy function \(c(m_t, P_t)\) Rfree Risk-free return \(R\) PermGroFac Expected growth factor \(\Gamma\) LivPrb Survival probability \(\mathcal{L}\)

docs.title: 2.1 Overview
docs.text:
We consider an infinite-horizon consumption-saving problem for a household facing idiosyncratic income risk. The household receives labor income subject to both permanent shocks and transitory shocks, and can save in a risk-free asset yielding gross return \(R > 0\). The household faces mortality risk with survival probability \(\mathcal{L} \in (0,1]\) each period.

All individual-level variables are normalized by the household's permanent income level \(P_t\), which follows a stochastic growth process. This normalization ensures stationarity of the problem despite permanent income shocks.

docs.title: 2.2 Timing and Information Structure
docs.text:
The model follows a four-perch structure within each period \(t\):

  1. Arrival Perch: The agent enters period \(t\) with normalized assets \(k_t\) (capital carried forward from period \(t-1\), normalized by \(P_{t-1}\)) and previous permanent income \(P_{t-1}\).

  2. Decision Perch: After observing current income shocks \((\Psi_t, \theta_t)\), permanent income updates to \(P_t = P_{t-1} \cdot \Gamma \cdot \Psi_t\), and the agent computes normalized market resources \(m_t\) (bank balances plus current income). The agent chooses consumption \(c_t\) given information set \(\mathcal{F}_t = \{k_t, P_{t-1}, \Psi_t, \theta_t\}\).

  3. Continuation Perch: After consumption, the agent holds normalized end-of-period assets \(a_t = m_t - c_t\). Survival is then determined.

  4. Twist/Transition: Surviving agents carry forward \(a_t\) as next period's \(k_{t+1}\), and \(P_t\) becomes \(P_{t}\) (the "previous" permanent income for period \(t+1\)). Non-survivors exit the model.

docs.title: 2.3 State Space
docs.text:
Arrival State Space: The prestate is \(\mathcal{S}_{\text{arr}} = \mathbb{R}_+ \times \mathbb{R}_{++}\), with elements \((k_t, P_{t-1})\) where: - \(k_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) denotes normalized assets (beginning-of-period capital) - \(P_{t-1} \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) denotes the permanent income level from the previous period

Decision State Space: After shocks realize, the decision state is \((m_t, P_t) \in \mathbb{R}_+ \times \mathbb{R}_{++}\) where: - \(m_t \coloneqq b_t + y_t\) represents normalized market resources - \(P_t\) is the updated permanent income level

Continuation State Space: After consumption choice, the continuation state is \((a_t, P_t) \in \mathbb{R}_+ \times \mathbb{R}_{++}\) where: - \(a_t \coloneqq m_t - c_t\) represents normalized end-of-period assets

docs.title: 2.4 Action Space
docs.text: At the decision perch, the agent chooses normalized consumption \(c_t \in [0, m_t]\). The budget constraint requires \(c_t \leq m_t\), ensuring non-negative assets.

docs.title: 2.5 Shock Structure
docs.text:
Income Shocks: Each period, the household draws a shock pair \((\Psi_t, \theta_t)\) from a joint distribution: $\((\Psi_t, \theta_t) \sim F_{\text{inc}}\)$

where: - \(\Psi_t \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\) is a permanent income shock with \(\mathbb{E}[\Psi_t] = 1\) - \(\theta_t \in \mathbb{R}_+\) is a transitory income shock with \(\mathbb{E}[\theta_t] = 1\)

The permanent shock multiplies the permanent income level, creating a unit root component, while the transitory shock affects only current income.

Survival Shock: At the end of each period, the agent survives with probability \(\mathcal{L}\): $\(\mathbb{1}_{\text{survive}} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\mathcal{L})\)$

Non-survivors exit the model (die without bequest motive in the baseline specification).

docs.title: 2.6 Transition Dynamics
docs.text:
The dynamics unfold sequentially within each period:

  1. Income shock realization: $\((\Psi_t, \theta_t) \sim F_{\text{inc}}\)$

  2. Normalized transitory income: $\(y_t \coloneqq \theta_t\)$

  3. Permanent income growth: $\(G_t \coloneqq \Gamma \cdot \Psi_t\)$ $\(P_t \coloneqq P_{t-1} \cdot G_t\)$

  4. Normalized bank balances (return on assets, adjusted for permanent income growth): $\(b_t \coloneqq \frac{R \cdot k_t}{G_t}\)$

This captures that the gross return \(R \cdot k_t\) (in period \(t-1\) permanent income units) must be renormalized by \(G_t\) to express in period \(t\) permanent income units.

  1. Normalized market resources: $\(m_t \coloneqq b_t + y_t = \frac{R \cdot k_t}{G_t} + \theta_t\)$

  2. Consumption decision: $\(c_t = c(m_t, P_t)\)$

  3. End-of-period assets: $\(a_t \coloneqq m_t - c_t\)$

  4. Survival determination: $\(\mathbb{1}_{\text{survive}} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\mathcal{L})\)$

  5. Twist to next period (for survivors): $\(k_{t+1} \coloneqq a_t, \quad P_{t} \to P_{t} \text{ (as } P_{t-1} \text{ for next period)}\)$

docs.title: 2.7 Initial Distribution
docs.text:
At model "birth" (the agent's entry into the economy), the initial state is drawn from: $\(P_{-1} \sim F_{P,\text{init}}, \quad k_0 \sim F_{k,\text{init}}\)$

where \(F_{P,\text{init}}\) is the initial permanent income distribution and \(F_{k,\text{init}}\) is the initial normalized capital distribution.

docs.title: 3. Bellman Equation
docs.text:
The household's problem is to maximize expected discounted utility over consumption, accounting for survival risk. We adopt the standard CRRA utility specification (though not explicitly given in the YAML, this is the HARK default):

\[u(C) = \frac{C^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}\]

where \(C\) denotes consumption in levels and \(\rho > 1\) is the coefficient of relative risk aversion.

Given normalization by permanent income, we have \(C_t = c_t \cdot P_t\), so: $\(u(C_t) = \frac{(c_t \cdot P_t)^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho} = \frac{c_t^{1-\rho} \cdot P_t^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}\)$

docs.title: 3.1 Continuation Value (Post-Decision)
docs.text:
At the continuation perch, after consuming \(c_t\) and observing end-of-period assets \(a_t\), the agent faces survival uncertainty. Let \(\mathfrak{v}(a_t, P_t)\) denote the continuation value:

\[\mathfrak{v}(a_t, P_t) \coloneqq \mathcal{L} \cdot \mathbb{E}_t[\mathfrak{w}(a_t, P_t)]\]

where \(\mathfrak{w}(a_t, P_t)\) is the arrival value for the next period (since \(k_{t+1} = a_t\) and the permanent income \(P_t\) is carried forward). The expectation is trivial here since no additional uncertainty realizes between the continuation perch and next period's arrival.

Thus: $\(\mathfrak{v}(a_t, P_t) = \mathcal{L} \cdot \mathfrak{w}(a_t, P_t)\)$

Non-survivors receive zero continuation utility.

docs.title: 3.2 Decision Value (Post-Shock, Pre-Consumption)
docs.text:
At the decision perch, the agent observes market resources \(m_t\) and current permanent income \(P_t\). The information set is \(\mathcal{F}_t = \{m_t, P_t\}\) (equivalently, \(\{k_t, P_{t-1}, \Psi_t, \theta_t\}\)). The agent chooses \(c_t\) to maximize:

\[v(m_t, P_t) \coloneqq \max_{c_t \in [0, m_t]} \left\{ \frac{(c_t \cdot P_t)^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho} + \beta \cdot \mathfrak{v}(m_t - c_t, P_t) \right\}\]

where \(\beta \in (0,1)\) is the time discount factor. Substituting the continuation value:

\[v(m_t, P_t) = \max_{c_t \in [0, m_t]} \left\{ \frac{(c_t \cdot P_t)^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho} + \beta \mathcal{L} \cdot \mathfrak{w}(m_t - c_t, P_t) \right\}\]

docs.title: 3.3 Arrival Value (Pre-Shock)
docs.text:
At the arrival perch, the agent holds normalized assets \(k_t\) and previous permanent income \(P_{t-1}\), but has not yet observed current period shocks. The arrival value is:

\[\mathfrak{w}(k_t, P_{t-1}) \coloneqq \mathbb{E}\left[v(m_t, P_t) \mid k_t, P_{t-1}\right]\]

Expanding the expectation over the shock distribution:

\[\mathfrak{w}(k_t, P_{t-1}) = \int \int v\left(\frac{R k_t}{\Gamma \Psi} + \theta, P_{t-1} \Gamma \Psi\right) dF_{\text{inc}}(\Psi, \theta)\]

This is the expected decision value, averaging over all possible realizations of permanent and transitory shocks.

docs.title: 3.4 Recursive Bellman System
docs.text:
Combining the three perches, the full Bellman system is:

Arrival Value: $\(\mathfrak{w}(k_t, P_{t-1}) = \mathbb{E}_{\Psi_t, \theta_t}\left[v\left(\frac{R k_t}{\Gamma \Psi_t} + \theta_t, P_{t-1} \Gamma \Psi_t\right)\right]\)$

Decision Value: $\(v(m_t, P_t) = \max_{0 \leq c_t \leq m_t} \left\{ \frac{(c_t P_t)^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho} + \beta \mathcal{L} \cdot \mathfrak{w}(m_t - c_t, P_t) \right\}\)$

Continuation Value: $\(\mathfrak{v}(a_t, P_t) = \mathcal{L} \cdot \mathfrak{w}(a_t, P_t)\)$

The solution to this system is a policy function \(c^*(m_t, P_t)\) (or, exploiting homogeneity, \(c^*(m_t)\) in normalized terms).

docs.title: 3.5 Homogeneity and Normalization
docs.text:
A key property: with CRRA utility, the value function and policy functions are homogeneous of degree \(1-\rho\) in permanent income. This allows us to work entirely in normalized variables. Define normalized value functions:

\[\tilde{v}(m_t) \coloneqq P_t^{\rho-1} \cdot v(m_t, P_t)$$ $$\tilde{\mathfrak{w}}(k_t) \coloneqq P_{t-1}^{\rho-1} \cdot \mathfrak{w}(k_t, P_{t-1})\]

Then the Bellman equations simplify to:

Normalized Arrival Value: $\(\tilde{\mathfrak{w}}(k_t) = \mathbb{E}_{\Psi_t, \theta_t}\left[(\Gamma \Psi_t)^{1-\rho} \cdot \tilde{v}\left(\frac{R k_t}{\Gamma \Psi_t} + \theta_t\right)\right]\)$

Normalized Decision Value: $\(\tilde{v}(m_t) = \max_{0 \leq c_t \leq m_t} \left\{ \frac{c_t^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho} + \beta \mathcal{L} \cdot \tilde{\mathfrak{w}}(m_t - c_t) \right\}\)$

The optimal consumption function \(c^*(m_t)\) depends only on normalized market resources, not on the permanent income level.

docs.title: 4.1 Euler Equation
docs.text:
The first-order condition for the consumption choice at the decision perch is:

\[u'(C_t) = \beta \mathcal{L} \cdot \mathbb{E}_t\left[\frac{\partial \mathfrak{w}(a_t, P_t)}{\partial a_t}\right]\]

In levels, with \(C_t = c_t P_t\) and \(u'(C_t) = C_t^{-\rho} = (c_t P_t)^{-\rho}\):

\[(c_t P_t)^{-\rho} = \beta \mathcal{L} \cdot \mathbb{E}_t\left[\frac{\partial \mathfrak{w}(a_t, P_t)}{\partial a_t}\right]\]

docs.title: 2.1 Overview
docs.text:
The ConsKinkedR model describes an infinitely-lived agent facing idiosyncratic income risk who accumulates a risk-free asset to smooth consumption over time. The key friction is a kinked interest rate schedule: the agent faces interest factor \(R^{\text{save}}\) when saving (\(k_t \geq 0\)) but pays a higher interest factor \(R^{\text{boro}} > R^{\text{save}}\) when borrowing (\(k_t < 0\)). This asymmetry captures realistic credit market imperfections such as credit card interest rates exceeding savings account returns.

The agent receives labor income subject to both permanent shocks \(\psi_t\) (affecting the income level permanently) and transitory shocks \(\theta_t\) (affecting only current income). Permanent income follows a geometric random walk with trend growth \(\Gamma\). The agent optimizes consumption to maximize expected discounted lifetime utility, subject to this kinked budget constraint and the risk of mortality.

docs.title: 2.2 State Space
docs.text:
Arrival (Prestate) Variables: - \(k_t \in \mathbb{R}\): normalized capital holdings at the beginning of period \(t\), measured relative to permanent income \(p_{t-1}\) from the previous period - \(p_{t-1} \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\): permanent income level from period \(t-1\)

The arrival state space is \(\mathcal{K} \times \mathcal{P} \coloneqq \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}_{++}\).

Decision (Post-Shock) Variables: After observing shocks \((\psi_t, \theta_t)\), the agent computes: - \(G_t \coloneqq \Gamma \psi_t\): realized permanent income growth factor - \(p_t \coloneqq p_{t-1} G_t\): updated permanent income level - \(R_t \coloneqq R^{\text{save}} + (R^{\text{boro}} - R^{\text{save}}) \mathbb{1}_{k_t < 0}\): realized interest factor - \(b_t \coloneqq \frac{R_t k_t}{G_t}\): normalized bank balances (capital plus interest, re-normalized by new permanent income) - \(y_t \coloneqq \theta_t\): normalized labor income - \(m_t \coloneqq b_t + y_t\): normalized market resources (total resources available for consumption)

Continuation (Post-Decision) Variables: - \(a_t \coloneqq m_t - c_t \in \mathbb{R}\): normalized end-of-period assets

docs.title: 2.3 Action Space
docs.text: The agent chooses normalized consumption \(c_t \in [0, m_t]\), implicitly determining end-of-period assets \(a_t = m_t - c_t\).

docs.title: 2.4 Shock Distributions
docs.text:
Income Shocks: Joint distribution of permanent and transitory shocks: $\((\psi_t, \theta_t) \sim F_{\text{inc}} \quad \text{with support on } \mathbb{R}_{++}^2\)$

Typically specified with \(\mathbb{E}[\psi_t] = 1\) (so \(\Gamma\) captures expected growth) and \(\mathbb{E}[\theta_t] = 1\) (so the transitory shock is mean-preserving).

Survival Shock: $\(\ell_{t+1} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\Lambda)\)$ where \(\Lambda \in [0,1]\) is the survival probability (LivPrb).

Initial Distributions: - \(p_0 \sim F_{p,0}\): initial permanent income distribution - \(k_0 \sim F_{k,0}\): initial normalized capital distribution

docs.title: 2.5 State Transitions
docs.text:
The dynamics unfold in the following sequence:

  1. Arrival: Agent enters period with \((k_t, p_{t-1})\)
  2. Income realization: Draw \((\psi_t, \theta_t) \sim F_{\text{inc}}\)
  3. Income update: Compute \(G_t = \Gamma \psi_t\) and \(p_t = p_{t-1} G_t\)
  4. Interest rate determination: Set \(R_t = R^{\text{save}}\) if \(k_t \geq 0\), else \(R_t = R^{\text{boro}}\)
  5. Resource calculation: $\(b_t = \frac{R_t k_t}{G_t}, \quad y_t = \theta_t, \quad m_t = b_t + y_t\)$
  6. Consumption choice: Agent chooses \(c_t \in [0, m_t]\) optimally
  7. Asset accumulation: \(a_t = m_t - c_t\)
  8. Survival: Draw \(\ell_{t+1} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\Lambda)\)
  9. Twist (if alive): Set \(k_{t+1} = a_t\) and \(p_t\) carries forward as \(p_t\)

The state transition for survivors is: $\(k_{t+1} = a_t = m_t - c_t = \frac{R_t k_t}{G_t} + \theta_t - c_t\)$

docs.title: 3. Bellman Equation
docs.text: The agent's optimization problem decomposes into three value functions corresponding to the ADC (Arrival-Decision-Continuation) framework.

docs.title: 3.1 Arrival Value Function
docs.text:
At the arrival perch, before observing current income shocks, the agent's expected value is: $\(V^{\text{arr}}(k_t, p_{t-1}) = \mathbb{E}_{\psi_t, \theta_t}\left[V^{\text{dec}}(k_t, p_{t-1}; \psi_t, \theta_t)\right]\)$

Information set: \(\mathcal{F}_t^{\text{arr}} = \{k_t, p_{t-1}\}\)

docs.title: 3.2 Decision Value Function
docs.text:
At the decision perch, after observing shocks \((\psi_t, \theta_t)\), the agent solves: $\(V^{\text{dec}}(k_t, p_{t-1}; \psi_t, \theta_t) = \max_{c_t \in [0, m_t]} \left\{u(c_t p_t) + \beta \Lambda V^{\text{cont}}(a_t, p_t)\right\}\)$

where: - \(G_t = \Gamma \psi_t\) - \(p_t = p_{t-1} G_t\) - \(R_t = R^{\text{save}} + (R^{\text{boro}} - R^{\text{save}}) \mathbb{1}_{k_t < 0}\) - \(b_t = R_t k_t / G_t\) - \(m_t = b_t + \theta_t\) - \(a_t = m_t - c_t\) - \(u(\cdot)\) is the period utility function (typically CRRA: \(u(C) = \frac{C^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}\)) - \(\beta\) is the time discount factor - \(\Lambda\) is the survival probability

Information set: \(\mathcal{F}_t^{\text{dec}} = \{k_t, p_{t-1}, \psi_t, \theta_t\} = \{m_t, p_t, R_t\}\)

Equivalently, working with normalized consumption \(c_t\) (consumption divided by \(p_t\)): $\(V^{\text{dec}}(m_t, p_t) = \max_{c_t \in [0, m_t]} \left\{p_t^{1-\rho} u(c_t) + \beta \Lambda V^{\text{cont}}(m_t - c_t, p_t)\right\}\)$

docs.title: 3.3 Continuation Value Function
docs.text:
At the continuation perch, after the consumption decision but before next period's arrival: $\(V^{\text{cont}}(a_t, p_t) = V^{\text{arr}}(k_{t+1}, p_t)\)$

where the twist mapping gives \(k_{t+1} = a_t\) and \(p_t\) becomes next period's \(p_{t-1}\).

Information set: \(\mathcal{F}_t^{\text{cont}} = \{a_t, p_t\}\)

docs.title: 3.4 Recursive Formulation
docs.text:
Combining the perches, the full Bellman equation is: $\(V^{\text{arr}}(k_t, p_{t-1}) = \mathbb{E}_{\psi_t, \theta_t}\left[\max_{c_t \in [0, m_t]} \left\{p_t^{1-\rho} u(c_t) + \beta \Lambda V^{\text{arr}}(m_t - c_t, p_t)\right\}\right]\)$

subject to the state evolution equations specified above.

The kinked interest rate creates a non-convexity in the budget constraint: the effective return on savings differs depending on whether \(k_t \gtrless 0\). This kink propagates through the policy function, potentially creating a region of rapid adjustment near \(k_t = 0\).

docs.title: 4.1 Euler Equation
docs.text:
The first-order condition for consumption at the decision perch yields: $\(u'(c_t p_t) p_t = \beta \Lambda \frac{\partial V^{\text{cont}}(a_t, p_t)}{\partial a_t}\)$

By the envelope theorem at the continuation perch: $\(\frac{\partial V^{\text{cont}}(a_t, p_t)}{\partial a_t} = \frac{\partial V^{\text{arr}}(k_{t+1}, p_t)}{\partial k_{t+1}} = \mathbb{E}_{\psi_{t+1}, \theta_{t+1}}\left[\frac{\partial V^{\text{dec}}}{\partial m_{t+1}} \cdot \frac{\partial m_{t+1}}{\partial k_{t+1}}\right]\)$

Since \(m_{t+1} = \frac{R_{t+1} k_{t+1}}{G_{t+1}} + \theta_{t+1}\) where \(G_{t+1} = \Gamma \psi_{t+1}\) and \(R_{t+1}\) depends on the sign of \(k_{t+1} = a_t\): $\(\frac{\partial m_{t+1}}{\partial k_{t+1}} = \frac{R_{t+1}}{G_{t+1}} \quad \text{for } k_{t+1} \neq 0\)$

At \(k_{t+1} = 0\), there is a kink in the marginal return: - Right derivative: \(\frac{R^{\text{save}}}{\Gamma \psi_{t+1}}\) - Left derivative: \(\frac{R^{\text{boro}}}{\Gamma \psi_{t+1}}\)

The Euler equation becomes: $\(u'(c_t p_t) = \beta \Lambda \mathbb{E}_{\psi_{t+1}, \theta_{t+1}}\left[u'(c_{t+1} p_{t+1}) \cdot \frac{R_{t+1}}{\Gamma \psi_{t+1}}\right]\)$

where \(R_{t+1} = R^{\text{save}} \mathbb{1}_{a_t \geq 0} + R^{\text{boro}} \mathbb{1}_{a_t < 0}\).

docs.title: 4.2 Normalized Euler Equation
docs.text:
Working with normalized consumption \(c_t \coloneqq C_t / p_t\) and assuming CRRA utility \(u(C) = \frac{C^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}\): $\(c_t^{-\rho} = \beta \Lambda \mathbb{E}_{\psi_{t+1}, \theta_{t+1}}\left[\left(\frac{R_{t+1}}{\Gamma \psi_{t+1}}\right) \psi_{t+1}^{-\rho} c_{t+1}^{-\rho}\right]\)$

Simplifying: $\(c_t^{-\rho} = \beta \Lambda R_{t+1} \Gamma^{-1} \mathbb{E}_{\psi_{t+1}, \theta_{t+1}}\left[\psi_{t+1}^{-\rho} c_{t+1}^{-\rho}\right]\)$

docs.title: 4.3 Envelope Condition
docs.text:
The envelope theorem at the decision perch gives: $\(\frac{\partial V^{\text{dec}}}{\partial m_t} = u'(c_t p_t) p_t = p_t^{1-\rho} c_t^{-\rho}\)$

This marginal value of resources is used in the backward iteration of the solution algorithm.

docs.title: 4.4 Endogenous Gridpoint Method (EGM) Representation
docs.text:
The model is well-suited for the Endogenous Gridpoint Method (Carroll, 2006), which inverts the Euler equation:

  1. Construct a grid over end-of-period assets: \(\{a^{(j)}\}_{j=1}^{N_a}\)
