docs.title: Retirement choice
docs.text:
Summary

A worker chooses at the start of each period whether to work or to retire, and then how much to consume; retirement is permanent. The model of Iskhakov, Jørgensen, Rust and Schjerning (2017) is written as three stage files: the choice between working and retiring, the consumption of a worker and the consumption of a retiree. The derivatives of the values and the steps of the endogenous grid method stand in block files, which the stages' methods files bind. A period file joins the three stages, and a trellis file joins the periods. Every file on this page is quoted from the application folder applications/retirement-choice/, and every result is printed from the package.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Branching: the rules of the choice stage, whose file this page quotes again. See also — Periods, Trellis syntax and Methodization: the connectors within a period and between periods, and how a methods file attaches a numerical method.

docs.title: 1 The model
docs.text:
An agent lives from date 0 to date \(T\). She holds assets \(a \ge 0\), which earn the gross return \(R\), consumes \(c > 0\) with utility \(\log c\), and discounts the future by \(\beta\). In a period of work she earns the wage \(y\) and bears the utility cost \(\delta\) of working. She may retire, and retirement is permanent: a retiree never returns to work. There is no income risk and no taste shock, so every quantity is deterministic given the state.

Iskhakov, Jørgensen, Rust and Schjerning (2017) solve this model with the endogenous grid method for discrete-continuous choice, which computes consumption by inverting the Euler equation on a grid of savings, and Dobrescu and Shanker make it the first application of their fast upper envelope scan (FUES), whose code's retirement example supplies the calibration and settings of §7. The option to retire later makes the worker's continuation value non-concave: it is the upper envelope of concave values, one for each future sequence of work and retirement. The Euler equation then has several solutions at some levels of wealth, and a method that inverts it must select among the candidate solutions by their value.

In the stage files the choice made at the start of a period governs that period: the wage enters that period's cash on hand, and the cost \(\delta\) is charged in that period's choice. In the two papers the choice made at a date governs the next date's wage. The two recursions describe the same model when the papers' cost of work equals \(\beta\delta\); the application's economics.md sets out the comparison.

docs.title: 2 Bellman equation
docs.text:
Write \(\mathcal W_t(a)\) for the value of a worker who begins date \(t\) with assets \(a\), before she chooses whether to work; \(Q_t(a)\) for the value of working at date \(t\) before the cost of work is charged; and \(\mathcal U_t(a)\) for the value of a retiree who begins date \(t\) with assets \(a\). The stage files state

\[ \mathcal W_t(a) = \max\bigl\{ Q_t(a) - \delta,\; \mathcal U_t(a) \bigr\}, \] \[ Q_t(a) = \max_{0 < c \le Ra + y} \bigl\{ \log c + \beta\, \mathcal W_{t+1}(Ra + y - c) \bigr\}, \qquad \mathcal U_t(a) = \max_{0 < c \le Ra} \bigl\{ \log c + \beta\, \mathcal U_{t+1}(Ra - c) \bigr\}. \]

A worker's savings \(Ra + y - c\) are the assets with which she begins the next date, when she chooses again; a retiree's savings \(Ra - c\) are the assets with which she begins the next date as a retiree. After the last date \(T\), \(\mathcal W_{T+1}\) and \(\mathcal U_{T+1}\) are the terminal value, which §5 describes.

docs.title: 3 The stages of one period
docs.text:
A stage is one step of the recursion, written as one file with three perches, the information sets at arrival, at the decision and at continuation (Stage tutorial). One period of this model has three stages, and none of them has a shock:

Stage Arrival Decision Continuation ret_choice assets a a_d = a; the control d chooses a label in {work, retire} a_w = a_d on the work branch, a_r = a_d on the retire branch worker_cons assets a_w cash on hand w = R*a_w + y; consumption c is chosen savings b = w - c retiree_cons assets a_ret cash on hand w_ret = R*a_ret; consumption c is chosen savings b_ret = w_ret - c

docs.title: 3.1 The choice between work and retirement
docs.text:
The choice stage is applications/retirement-choice/declaration/stages/ret_choice/ret_choice.bl:

@stage: ret_choice

δ : ℝ₊₊          :: ["utility cost of working, charged in the period whose wage it earns"]

[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (a : ℝ₊) : !arvl -> (a_d : ℝ₊) : !dcsn] {
    a_d = a                                   :: [id=assets]
}

[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (a_d, d : !ctrl @ {work, retire}) : !dcsn -> ()] {
    [label=work,   () -> (a_w : ℝ₊) : !cntn] { a_w = a_d }
    [label=retire, () -> (a_r : ℝ₊) : !cntn] { a_r = a_d }
}

[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V_w[>] : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu, V_r[>] : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu, d) : !cntn -> (V : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {
    V = (V_w[>] - δ, V_r[>])[d]                   :: [id=choice_value]
}

[id=dcsn_to_arvl, (V) : !dcsn -> (V[<] : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu) : !arvl] {
    V[<] = V                                  :: [id=value]
}

[id=policy, (V_w[>], V_r[>]) : !cntn -> (d : {work, retire} @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {
    d = argmax_{d}(V_w[>] - δ, V_r[>])        :: [id=choice]
}

Its derivative line stands in the block file applications/retirement-choice/declaration/methods/marginals_ret_choice.bl, as the marginal block of the decision builder, a block of derivative lines that the stage's methods file binds with !marginals (§6):

@methods: ret_choice
# The derivative of the value of the discrete choice in assets, stated by the
# marginal block of the decision value builder: the derivative of the branch
# value the choice d selects; the cost of work, a constant, contributes nothing.

[id=dcsn_marginal, (V_w[>], V_r[>], d) : !cntn -> (V) : !dcsn] {
    D_{a_d}V = (D_{a_w}V_w[>], D_{a_r}V_r[>])[d]  :: [id=marginal]
}

The forward block dcsn_to_cntn holds one nested block for each label of the control d, and each writes its own branch's field: a_w on the work branch and a_r on the retire branch. A branch is one alternative of the choice, with its own continuation (branch). The value statement V = … selects, by the tuple indexed by d, the worker's value less the cost of work or the retiree's value; the derivative line D_{a_d}V = … of the marginal block selects the derivative in assets of the chosen branch's value, in the same order; and the policy statement d = argmax_{d}(…) chooses a label whose entry of the same tuple is largest. Branching reads this file line by line. The package's queries kind, branches and combination answer, for this stage:

kind(stage)          branching
branches(stage)      work: a_w
                     retire: a_r
combination(stage)   choice

The stage is branching, its branch work writes a_w and its branch retire writes a_r, and the branches combine by the choice of a label.

docs.title: 3.2 The worker's consumption
docs.text:
The worker's stage is applications/retirement-choice/declaration/stages/worker_cons/worker_cons.bl:

@stage: worker_cons

Xa := ℝ₊

β : (0,1)        :: ["discount factor"]
R : ℝ₊₊          :: ["gross return on assets"]
y : ℝ₊₊          :: ["wage paid in a period of work"]

𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := log(c)                :: [id=util]
𝑑𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := 1/c                  :: [id=marg_util]
𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(x : ℝ₊₊) := 1/x               :: [id=inv_marg_util]
Γ(x : ℝ₊₊) := (0, x]                :: [id=feasible]

[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (a_w : Xa) : !arvl -> (w : ℝ₊₊) : !dcsn] {
    w = R*a_w + y                   :: [id=cash_on_hand]
}

[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (w, c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn -> (b : Xa) : !cntn] {
    b = w - c                       :: [id=savings]
}

[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu, c) : !cntn -> (V : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {
    V = 𝑢(c) + β*V[>]               :: [id=value]
}

[id=dcsn_to_arvl, (V) : !dcsn -> (V[<] : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu) : !arvl] {
    V[<] = V                        :: [id=value]
}

[id=policy, (V[>] : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {
    c = argmax_{c : Γ(w)}(𝑢(c) + β*V[>])        :: [id=optimality]
}

The derivative lines of its two values stand in the marginal blocks of applications/retirement-choice/declaration/methods/marginals_worker_cons.bl:

@methods: worker_cons
# The derivatives of the worker's two values, each stated by the marginal
# block of the value builder that writes the value. The decision value's line
# is the envelope condition; the arrival value's line keeps the factor R of the
# law w = R*a_w + y, which is not the identity.

[id=dcsn_marginal, (c) : !cntn -> (V) : !dcsn] {
    D_{w}V = 𝑑𝑢(c)                  :: [id=marginal]
}

[id=arvl_marginal, (V) : !dcsn -> (V[<]) : !arvl] {
    D_{a_w}V[<] = R*D_{w}V          :: [id=marginal]
}

and the steps of the endogenous grid method in the method block of applications/retirement-choice/declaration/methods/worker_cons_egm.bl, a block whose lines compute the output of the builder it opens, here the policy builder (§6):

@methods: worker_cons
# The endogenous grid method as the method block of the worker's policy
# builder, whose stage file states the maximization alone. The candidate line
# reads the derivative of the continuation value by the term D_{b}V[>]; the
# worker's continuation value need not be concave, so the block selects among
# the candidates by their values with an upper envelope.

[id=egm, (V[>] : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {
    c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(β*D_{b}V[>])                 :: [id=InvEuler]
    w[>] = b + c[>]                            :: [id=endoggrid]
    v[>] = 𝑢(c[>]) + β*V[>]                    :: [id=cand_value]
    c    = upper_env(w[>], c[>], v[>])          :: [id=envelope]
}

Cash on hand is w = R*a_w + y, and consumption lies in Γ(w) = (0, w]. The value statement adds the discounted continuation value to the utility of consumption, and the policy block states the maximization, which also declares the feasible set of consumption. The derivative line D_{w}V = 𝑑𝑢(c) of the first marginal block states the derivative of the value in cash on hand, 1/c, and the second marginal block's line multiplies it by R, the factor of the law w = R*a_w + y, to state the derivative of the arrival value in assets. The method block writes the steps of the endogenous grid method as equations. The inverse Euler inequality c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(β*D_{b}V[>]), which reads the derivative of the continuation value in savings, gives the candidate consumption at each level of savings. It carries no complementary-slackness clause ⟂ b >= 0, which would pair the Euler equation with the borrowing limit, so it is read as the equation c[>] = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(β*D_{b}V[>]): at every level of savings the candidate is the interior value, at which the Euler equation holds with equality (Constraints §4.3). The endogenous grid is w[>] = b + c[>], the value of each candidate is v[>], and the upper envelope upper_env(w[>], c[>], v[>]) keeps, at each level of cash on hand, the candidate of largest value. The worker needs the upper envelope because her continuation value is not concave.

docs.title: 3.3 The retiree's consumption
docs.text:
The retiree's stage is applications/retirement-choice/declaration/stages/retiree_cons/retiree_cons.bl:

@stage: retiree_cons

Xa := ℝ₊

β : (0,1)        :: ["discount factor"]
R : ℝ₊₊          :: ["gross return on assets"]

𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := log(c)                :: [id=util]
𝑑𝑢(c : ℝ₊₊) := 1/c                  :: [id=marg_util]
𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(x : ℝ₊₊) := 1/x               :: [id=inv_marg_util]
Γ(x : ℝ₊) := (0, x]                 :: [id=feasible, "empty at zero resources"]

[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (a_ret : Xa) : !arvl -> (w_ret : Xa) : !dcsn] {
    w_ret = R*a_ret                 :: [id=cash_on_hand]
}

[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (w_ret, c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn -> (b_ret : Xa) : !cntn] {
    b_ret = w_ret - c               :: [id=savings]
}

[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu, c) : !cntn -> (V : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {
    V = 𝑢(c) + β*V[>]               :: [id=value]
}

[id=dcsn_to_arvl, (V) : !dcsn -> (V[<] : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu) : !arvl] {
    V[<] = V                        :: [id=value]
}

[id=policy, (V[>] : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn] {
    c = argmax_{c : Γ(w_ret)}(𝑢(c) + β*V[>])     :: [id=optimality]
}

Its derivative lines stand in the marginal blocks of applications/retirement-choice/declaration/methods/marginals_retiree_cons.bl:

@methods: retiree_cons
# The derivatives of the retiree's two values, each stated by the marginal
# block of the value builder that writes the value. The decision value's line
# is the envelope condition; the arrival value's line keeps the factor R of the
# law w_ret = R*a_ret, which is not the identity.

[id=dcsn_marginal, (c) : !cntn -> (V) : !dcsn] {
    D_{w_ret}V = 𝑑𝑢(c)              :: [id=marginal]
}

[id=arvl_marginal, (V) : !dcsn -> (V[<]) : !arvl] {
    D_{a_ret}V[<] = R*D_{w_ret}V    :: [id=marginal]
}

and the steps of the endogenous grid method in the method block of applications/retirement-choice/declaration/methods/retiree_cons_egm.bl:

@methods: retiree_cons
# The endogenous grid method as the method block of the retiree's policy
# builder, whose stage file states the maximization alone. The candidate line
# reads the derivative of the continuation value by the term D_{b_ret}V[>].

[id=egm, (V[>] : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu) : !cntn -> (c : ℝ₊₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn, "method = egm! will look for policy[>] and x[>] grid and invert it. Important here that the grids contain all constrained sections"] {
    c[>]     <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(β*D_{b_ret}V[>])                :: [id=InvEuler, "Implies a correspondence: where equality holds, c[>] takes on a single value, where inequality holds, it is multiple values"]
    w_ret[>] = b_ret + c[>]                          :: [id=endoggrid]
    c        = c[>]                                  :: [id=cons_choice]
}

Cash on hand is w_ret = R*a_ret, with no wage. The method block writes the inverse Euler inequality and the endogenous grid as the worker's does, and then the identification c = c[>], which equates the policy at the cash on hand of each level of savings with the candidate there. The package forms from the policy block the policy builder, the operator whose output is the policy. Once the methods file binds the method block, the builder's operations are the lines of that block, and stage.dcsn.builder.policy.denote() prints its card, a statement of its operations, with the maximization of the stage file under Declared. The card gives the identification as the operation cons_choice:Pullback, the policy composed with the cash on hand at each level of savings, with the rule 𝑐(𝑤_ret≻(b_ret)) = 𝑐≻(b_ret) on 𝑤_ret≻(Xa), the set of cash on hand that the candidates reach. The inverse Euler inequality carries no clause, so the policy is stated on that set and not below it, where the borrowing limit binds (Constraints §4.3). The retiree's continuation value is concave, so the block needs no upper envelope. At zero assets the feasible set (0, w_ret] is empty, as the description of Γ in the file records.

docs.title: 4 The period
docs.text:
A period is the stages of one date, joined by connectors (Periods). The period file is applications/retirement-choice/declaration/period.yml:

!period
name: retirement_period

# One period of the retirement model: the choice between work and retirement,
# then consumption on the branch that choice selects. The order of the stages
# is derived from their fields, not from this list. The work branch joins the
# worker's arrival assets by name (a_w); the retire branch connects to the
# retiree's arrival assets. The terminal period, which adds the bequest, is
# written out in trellis.yml, since its connector names the bequest's arrival
# field and a connector to a stage absent from a period is refused.
stages:
  - ret_choice
  - worker_cons
  - retiree_cons
connectors:
  - {a_r: a_ret}

A connector connects a continuation field of one stage to an arrival field of another (Periods §2). The work branch's a_w has one compatible reading occurrence, the worker's arrival field, so the package infers that connection. The connector {a_r: a_ret} selects the retire branch's continuation and the retiree's arrival assets without changing either local name. These two endpoints are unique, so no stage prefix is needed. The package derives the order of the stages from the selected connections; the order of the list in the file carries no meaning:

period_joins(period)["joins"]
  ret_choice:a_r → retiree_cons:a_ret
  ret_choice:a_w → worker_cons:a_w
period_joins(period)["outputs"]
  retiree_cons:b_ret
  worker_cons:b
computable_together(period)
  1  ret_choice
  2  retiree_cons, worker_cons

computable_together lists the stages in layers, each layer computable once the layers before it are: in forward time the choice stage comes first and the two consumption stages follow it, and value is computed backward, from the two consumption stages to the choice. The savings b and b_ret are the fields that leave the period. In the figure, workers begin the period at a, the choice stage's arrival assets, and retirees of the date before begin it at a_ret, the retiree stage's arrival assets, which also receive the workers who retire.

retirement_period stage perch field a ≺ aret ≺ ret_choice worker_cons retiree_cons b ≻ bret ≻ work retire

docs.title: 5 The trellis
docs.text:
A trellis is the sequence of periods, indexed backward from the last date: periods[0] is the terminal period, and periods[h+1] is the period one date before periods[h] (Trellis syntax). The trellis file is applications/retirement-choice/declaration/trellis.yml:

!trellis
name: retirement_lifecycle
# periods[h] is the date T - h: periods[0] is the terminal period. The model
# has twenty dates, the horizon of the FUES retirement example whose
# calibration and settings this registry holds (economics.md, "Calibration and
# settings"); the working paper's tables use fifty, which is `repeat: 49`.
# The terminal period is written out, since its connector names the bequest,
# which no other period holds: it adds the bequest, the terminal value as a
# stage, and the connector from both consumption stages to its
# arrival field a_bq, a name of its own, since the savings left after the last
# date begin no further date. The nineteen earlier periods repeat the template.
periods:
  - stages: [ret_choice, worker_cons, retiree_cons, bequest]
    connectors:
      - {a_r: a_ret}
      - {b: a_bq, b_ret: a_bq}
  - {template: period.yml, repeat: 19}
# One mapping stands for every adjacent pair and holds both routes
# (docs/Bellman-Sym/07-trellis.md §2): the worker's savings go to the next
# period's choice stage, the retiree's to the next period's retiree stage, so
# no route returns a retiree to work. In periods[0] the name a is ret_choice's
# alone and a_ret retiree_cons's alone, so the mapping reaches the bequest
# nowhere.
inter_connectors:
  - {b: a, b_ret: a_ret}

The file writes the terminal period out, with the bequest stage, and repeats the period of §4 for the 19 dates before it, so that the package reads a trellis of 20 periods. Its one inter-period mapping stands for every pair of adjacent periods.

The mapping {b: a, b_ret: a_ret} joins each period to the one before it in the list, which is the next date: a worker's savings become the assets with which she begins the next date at the choice stage, and a retiree's savings the assets with which she begins it at the retiree stage. Between two adjacent periods the package makes these joins:

inter_period_joins(mapping, periods[h + 1], periods[h])
  worker_cons:b → ret_choice:a
  retiree_cons:b_ret → retiree_cons:a_ret

Nothing sends a retiree to the choice stage, which is what makes retirement permanent; the stage files themselves do not say so. The retiree's arrival assets a_ret have two sources: within the period, the workers who retire at that date, through the connector {a_r: a_ret}; across the pair, the retirees of the date before. The distribution of assets at a_ret is the sum of the two incoming distributions (Trellis syntax §2).

The terminal period adds the bequest stage, applications/retirement-choice/declaration/stages/bequest/bequest.bl, the terminal value written as a stage:

@stage: bequest

# The terminal value of the retirement model, written as a stage. The papers
# consume all resources at the last date, so the savings left after the
# terminal period have no value (economics.md, "The terminal continuation
# value"). V[>] is the terminal boundary data, zero, supplied at
# realization. The arrival field is a_bq and not a
# or a_ret, the names at which ret_choice and retiree_cons of the terminal
# period arrive: the savings left after the last date begin no further date.

[id=arvl_to_dcsn, (a_bq : ℝ₊) : !arvl -> (x : ℝ₊) : !dcsn] {
    x = a_bq                                           :: [id=wealth]
}

[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu) -> (V : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {
    V = V[>]                                           :: [id=value]
}

[id=dcsn_to_arvl, (V) : !dcsn -> (V[<] : [-inf, inf) @ !vlu) : !arvl] {
    V[<] = V                                           :: [id=value]
}

Its derivative line stands in the marginal block of applications/retirement-choice/declaration/methods/marginals_bequest.bl, which the bequest's methods file binds (§6):

@methods: bequest
# The derivative of the terminal value in wealth, stated in closed form by the
# marginal block of the decision value builder: the savings left after the
# last date have no value, so the derivative is zero.

[id=dcsn_marginal, () -> (V) : !dcsn] {
    D_{x}V = 0                                         :: [id=marginal_wealth]
}

Its arrival field a_bq receives the savings of both consumption stages of the terminal period, through the connector {b: a_bq, b_ret: a_bq}. Its value is the continuation value V[>], boundary data equal to zero, since the papers' agent consumes all her resources at the last date, and the derivative line D_{x}V = 0 of its marginal block states that the derivative of its value in wealth is zero. The state-field connections are:

period_joins(periods[0])["joins"]
  ret_choice:a_r → retiree_cons:a_ret
  ret_choice:a_w → worker_cons:a_w
  retiree_cons:b_ret → bequest:a_bq
  worker_cons:b → bequest:a_bq

The join check compares value fields alone. The terminal stage states the derivative of its value in wealth, zero, by its marginal block, and the law of its arrival block, x = a_bq, is the identity, so the stated derivative passes through to the arrival value, which both consumption stages of the terminal period read by the terms D_{b}V[>] and D_{b_ret}V[>]. The inverse marginal utility 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣 of both consumption stages is declared on ℝ₊₊, which excludes zero, so in the terminal period the inverse Euler line reads the terminal derivative outside the declared domain of 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣. Changing the terminal treatment or the consumption declarations requires an economic decision, not a different connector spelling. The nonterminal connections preserve the route that keeps a retiree retired.

docs.title: 6 Methods
docs.text:
A methods file attaches a numerical method to a named place of a stage: a block, a line or an operator (Methodization). The choice stage's methods file is applications/retirement-choice/declaration/stages/ret_choice/methods.yml:

stage: ret_choice

methods:
  # The discrete choice is the larger of the two branch values. The handler is
  # the routine of the FUES retirement example that compares them.
  - on: policy
    method: !max
    handler: fues-retirement:dcsn_mover

  # The derivative of the choice value in assets, the derivative of the branch
  # value the choice selects, is stated by the marginal block of
  # marginals_ret_choice.bl on the decision value builder.
  - on: cntn_to_dcsn
    method: !marginals
    block: ../../methods/marginals_ret_choice.bl

The worker's is applications/retirement-choice/declaration/stages/worker_cons/methods.yml:

stage: worker_cons

methods:
  # The endogenous grid method opens the policy builder with the method block
  # of worker_cons_egm.bl, which writes the grid line w[>] = b + c[>]; the
  # stage file states the maximization alone. The candidates the block
  # computes at each level of savings are selected by the upper envelope
  # below, since the worker's continuation value need not be concave. The
  # setting grid names the exogenous grid of savings b by its kind,
  # !Cartesian, with its order and bounds beside it, the asset grid of the
  # settings file.
  - on: policy
    method: !egm
    block: ../../methods/worker_cons_egm.bl
    handler: asva:make_egm_1d
    settings:
      grid: !Cartesian
      orders:
        b: n_a
      bounds:
        b: [a_min, a_max]

  # The derivatives of the decision value and the arrival value are stated by
  # the two marginal blocks of marginals_worker_cons.bl, one for each value
  # builder.
  - on: cntn_to_dcsn
    method: !marginals
    block: ../../methods/marginals_worker_cons.bl

  - on: dcsn_to_arvl
    method: !marginals
    block: ../../methods/marginals_worker_cons.bl

  # The upper envelope over the candidates that satisfy the first-order
  # condition; m_bar is the jump-detection threshold of the scan.
  - on: upper_env
    method: !FUES
    handler: dcsmm:EGM_UE
    settings:
      m_bar: m_bar

  # The arrival value and its stated derivative in assets are tabulated on the
  # asset grid at the arrival builder's Evaluation, dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.value
  # and dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.marginal, and read by linear interpolation, the
  # basis !Linear; the setting grid names the asset grid by its kind,
  # !Cartesian, with its order and bounds beside it.
  - on: dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.value
    method: !Linear
    handler: dcsmm:interp_as_2
    settings:
      grid: !Cartesian
      orders:
        a_w: n_a
      bounds:
        a_w: [a_min, a_max]

  - on: dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.marginal
    method: !Linear
    handler: dcsmm:interp_as_2
    settings:
      grid: !Cartesian
      orders:
        a_w: n_a
      bounds:
        a_w: [a_min, a_max]

The retiree's is applications/retirement-choice/declaration/stages/retiree_cons/methods.yml:

stage: retiree_cons

methods:
  # The endogenous grid method opens the policy builder with the method block
  # of retiree_cons_egm.bl, whose implicit statement c = c[>] gives the
  # policy; the stage file states the maximization alone. The retiree's
  # continuation value is concave, so no envelope operation is needed. The
  # setting grid names the exogenous grid of savings b_ret by its kind,
  # !Cartesian, with its order and bounds beside it, the asset grid of the
  # settings file.
  - on: policy
    method: !egm
    block: ../../methods/retiree_cons_egm.bl
    handler: asva:make_egm_1d
    settings:
      grid: !Cartesian
      orders:
        b_ret: n_a_ret
      bounds:
        b_ret: [a_ret_min, a_ret_max]

  # The derivatives of the decision value and the arrival value are stated by
  # the two marginal blocks of marginals_retiree_cons.bl, one for each value
  # builder.
  - on: cntn_to_dcsn
    method: !marginals
    block: ../../methods/marginals_retiree_cons.bl

  - on: dcsn_to_arvl
    method: !marginals
    block: ../../methods/marginals_retiree_cons.bl

  # The arrival value and its stated derivative in assets are tabulated on the
  # asset grid at the arrival builder's Evaluation, dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.value
  # and dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.marginal, and read by linear interpolation, the
  # basis !Linear; the setting grid names the asset grid by its kind,
  # !Cartesian, with its order and bounds beside it.
  - on: dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.value
    method: !Linear
    handler: dcsmm:interp_as_3
    settings:
      grid: !Cartesian
      orders:
        a_ret: n_a_ret
      bounds:
        a_ret: [a_ret_min, a_ret_max]

  - on: dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.marginal
    method: !Linear
    handler: dcsmm:interp_as_3
    settings:
      grid: !Cartesian
      orders:
        a_ret: n_a_ret
      bounds:
        a_ret: [a_ret_min, a_ret_max]

The bequest's is applications/retirement-choice/declaration/stages/bequest/methods.yml:

stage: bequest

methods:
  # The derivative of the terminal value in wealth, zero, is stated by the
  # marginal block of marginals_bequest.bl on the decision value builder.
  - on: cntn_to_dcsn
    method: !marginals
    block: ../../methods/marginals_bequest.bl

Binding each file to its stage with methodize gives:

ret_choice    binds
worker_cons   binds
retiree_cons  binds
bequest       binds

The four files bind. The worker's endogenous grid entry opens the policy builder with the method block of worker_cons_egm.bl, whose four lines become the builder's operations, and the upper envelope over the candidates is the method !FUES on the block's line envelope, as the comment in the file records. The retiree's entry opens its policy builder with the method block of retiree_cons_egm.bl, which holds the identification c = c[>]. Each endogenous grid entry names its exogenous grid of savings, b for the worker and b_ret for the retiree, by the setting grid, whose value is the grid's kind, the tag !Cartesian, with the grid's order and bounds beside it. Each !marginals entry records the lines of a marginal block at the Evaluation of the value builder it names, as stated derivatives of the value, and adds no operation; the entries on dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.value and dcsn_to_arvl.evaluate.marginal represent the arrival value and its stated derivative by the basis !Linear on the asset grid that their setting grid names in the same way, one method at the arrival builder's Evaluation. The worker's stage prints its methods, str(stage.methods), as

policy.envelope           !FUES
policy                    !egm   block ../../methods/worker_cons_egm.bl
cntn_to_dcsn:Evaluation   !marginals   block ../../methods/marginals_worker_cons.bl
dcsn_to_arvl:Evaluation   !marginals   block ../../methods/marginals_worker_cons.bl
dcsn_to_arvl:Evaluation   !Linear

docs.title: 7 Calibration and settings
docs.text:
The calibration is applications/retirement-choice/declaration/calibration/retirement.yml:

# The benchmark calibration of the FUES retirement example, which reports the
# interest rate r = 0.02, so that the gross return is R = 1 + r.
calibration:
  β: 0.96
  R: 1.02
  y: 20
  δ: 1

and the settings are applications/retirement-choice/declaration/settings/retirement.yml:

# Numerical choices, not model content: the asset grids the methods tabulate on
# and the jump-detection threshold of the upper envelope scan. The FUES
# retirement example uses 3,000 points on assets between 1e-10 and 500 for both
# consumption stages, and a threshold of 1.01.
settings:
  n_a: 3000
  a_min: 1.0e-10
  a_max: 500
  n_a_ret: 3000
  a_ret_min: 1.0e-10
  a_ret_max: 500
  m_bar: 1.01

The calibration is the benchmark of the FUES retirement example. The settings are numerical choices and no part of the model: the asset grids on which the methods tabulate the arrival values, which serve also as the exogenous grids of savings of the endogenous grid entries, and the jump-detection threshold of the upper envelope scan. The number of dates is not a setting; it is the number of periods the trellis holds.

The recipe, applications/retirement-choice/declaration/spec.yml, names the trellis file and, for each stage, its stage file and the calibration, settings and methods files it reads, each by its path from the recipe's folder, and load_recipe reads it with the trellis file (The Bellman factory):

# The recipe of the retirement model: the trellis file and each stage's file,
# by their paths from this folder, and for each stage and each kind the
# ordered sources; `$fill` and the three methods slots are bound by keyword of
# `load_recipe`. Each stage has its own methods slot, `$ret_choice_method`,
# `$worker_method` and `$retiree_method`, so that a method choice reaches one
# stage. The bequest declares no parameter or setting; its one methods file
# binds the marginal block of its derivative, and it is active in the
# terminal period alone, `periods: [0, 0]`.
trellis: trellis.yml
stages:
  ret_choice:   {stage: stages/ret_choice/ret_choice.bl,     calibration: {all: [calibration/retirement, $fill]}, settings: {all: [settings/retirement, $fill]}, methods: {all: [stages/ret_choice/methods, $ret_choice_method]}}
  worker_cons:  {stage: stages/worker_cons/worker_cons.bl,   calibration: {all: [calibration/retirement, $fill]}, settings: {all: [settings/retirement, $fill]}, methods: {all: [stages/worker_cons/methods, $worker_method]}}
  retiree_cons: {stage: stages/retiree_cons/retiree_cons.bl, calibration: {all: [calibration/retirement, $fill]}, settings: {all: [settings/retirement, $fill]}, methods: {all: [stages/retiree_cons/methods, $retiree_method]}}
  bequest:      {stage: stages/bequest/bequest.bl,           methods: {all: [stages/bequest/methods]}, periods: [0, 0]}

docs.title: 8 References
docs.text:
• Dobrescu, L. I., and Shanker, A. "A fast upper envelope scan method for discrete-continuous dynamic programming." Working paper, SSRN No. 4181302.
  • Iskhakov, F., Jørgensen, T. H., Rust, J., and Schjerning, B. (2017). "The endogenous grid method for discrete-continuous dynamic choice models with (or without) taste shocks." Quantitative Economics 8(2), 317–365.

docs.title: Smooth-ambiguity savings
docs.text:
Summary

The household chooses consumption under uncertainty about the mean of its log return. Risk aversion, ambiguity aversion and the elasticity of intertemporal substitution are separate parameters. Two nested certainty equivalents—the sure continuation values the household regards as equivalent to the uncertain ones—distinguish return risk from uncertainty about its mean.

Relationship with other documents

The separation of the three curvatures follows Ju and Miao (2012). The uncertain normal mean of the log return and the lognormal return given that mean adapt the ambiguous-mean example of Backus, Ferrière and Zin (2015). The stage file is applications/smooth-ambiguity-savings/declaration/stages/sa_savings/sa_savings.bl; the rules it relies on are in Appendix C, R7.

docs.title: 1 The model
docs.text:
The household begins its decision with resources \(m_d > 0\) and chooses consumption \(c\) in the open interval \((0, m_d)\). Savings \(m_d - c\) earn a gross return \(\Psi\), so the continuation state is \(a = (m_d - c)\,\Psi\). The log return is normal with an uncertain mean \( u\):

\[ u \sim N(\kappa_1, \sigma_ u^2), \qquad \log \Psi \mid u \sim N( u, \sigma_\Psi^2). \]

Both shocks are drawn after the decision. Uncertainty is resolved within the period, and there is no learning about \( u\) across periods.

docs.title: 2 Bellman equation
docs.text:
With \( eta \in (0, 1)\) the discount factor, \(1/ ho\) the elasticity of intertemporal substitution, \(\gamma\) relative risk aversion and \(\eta\) ambiguity aversion,

\[ V(m_d) = \sup_{0 < c < m_d} \Bigl( (1- eta)\, c^{1- ho} + eta\, \mathrm{AMB}(m_d, c)^{1- ho} \Bigr)^{ rac{1}{1- ho}}, \] \[ \mathrm{CE}(m_d, c, u) = \Bigl( \mathbb E igl[ V_\succ(a)^{1-\gamma} \mid u igr] \Bigr)^{ rac{1}{1-\gamma}}, \qquad \mathrm{AMB}(m_d, c) = \Bigl( \mathbb E_ u igl[ \mathrm{CE}(m_d, c, u)^{1-\eta} igr] \Bigr)^{ rac{1}{1-\eta}} . \]

The inner certainty equivalent CE evaluates return risk conditional on its mean; the outer one AMB evaluates uncertainty about the mean. When \(\eta = \gamma\) the two powers cancel and the recursion is Epstein–Zin under the predictive distribution of the return. When \(\eta > \gamma\) the household dislikes uncertainty about the mean more than risk.

docs.title: 3 The stage file
docs.text:
The stage file is applications/smooth-ambiguity-savings/declaration/stages/sa_savings/sa_savings.bl:

@stage: sa_savings

β : (0,1) :: ["discount factor"]
ρ : (1,inf) :: ["1/ρ is the elasticity of intertemporal substitution"]
γ : (1,inf) :: ["relative risk aversion"]
η : (1,inf), > γ :: ["ambiguity aversion"]
κ_1 : ℝ
σ_ν : ℝ₊
σ_Ψ : ℝ₊

ν : ℝ
ν ~ N(κ_1, σ_ν^2)
Ψ : ℝ₊₊
Ψ ~ LogNormal(ν, σ_Ψ)

Γ(x : ℝ₊₊) := {c : ℝ₊₊ | c < x}

[id=dcsn_to_cntn, (m_d : ℝ₊₊, c : !ctrl @ ℝ₊₊, Ψ) : !dcsn -> (a : ℝ₊₊) : !cntn] {
    a = (m_d - c)*Ψ :: [id=savings]
}

[id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>] : ℝ₊₊ @ !vlu, c) : !cntn -> (V : ℝ₊₊ @ !vlu) : !dcsn] {
    CE = E_{Ψ}(V[>]^(1-γ))^(1/(1-γ)) :: [id=risk_ce, !node]
    AMB = E_{ν}(CE^(1-η))^(1/(1-η)) :: [id=ambiguity_ce, !node]
    V = ((1-β)*c^(1-ρ) + β*AMB^(1-ρ))^(1/(1-ρ)) :: [id=value]
}

[id=policy, (V[>]) : !cntn -> c] {
    c = argmax_{c : Γ(m_d)}(((1-β)*c^(1-ρ) + β*E_{ν}(E_{Ψ}(V[>]^(1-γ))^((1-η)/(1-γ)))^((1-ρ)/(1-η)))^(1/(1-ρ))) :: [id=objective]
}

N(κ_1, σ_ν^2) is written with its variance and LogNormal(ν, σ_Ψ) with the standard deviation of the logarithm. The declaration of η adds the condition > γ: ambiguity aversion exceeds risk aversion, the case \(\eta > \gamma\) of §2. The feasible set {c : ℝ₊₊ | c < x} is open at both ends: at \(c = m_d\) the continuation state is zero and its negative powers are undefined. Each group of equations between braces is a block, and its header, the bracketed list before the braces, names its inputs and outputs. The header of the forward block dcsn_to_cntn names only the shock the law of motion reads, Ψ; the mean ν is drawn on the same edge because the declaration of Ψ names it.

docs.title: 4 What elaboration constructs
docs.text:
Elaboration, elaborate_stage(load_stage(path)) for the file at path, with both functions imported from bellman.stage, constructs the stage object from the stage file. The block cntn_to_dcsn denotes the backward builder that constructs the value at the decision perch, the information set at which the household chooses, reached as stage.dcsn.builder.bwd. The builder is stated at a policy \(c\), a consumption function of \(m_d\) with values in the feasible set, and \(c\) is not an argument of the functions below. Each builder and each of its operations answers denote() with its card, a printed statement of what it denotes; the builder's card, stage.dcsn.builder.bwd.denote(), names the policy under the heading At.

The two !node statements define two sub-builders, named groups of operations within that builder. The first composes \(V_\succ\) with the law of motion at the policy, raises it to \(1-\gamma\), integrates \(\Psi\) under its declared distribution given \(\nu\) and takes the root, so CE is a function of \((m_d, \nu)\). The second raises CE to \(1-\eta\), integrates \(\nu\) under its own distribution and takes the root, so AMB is a function of \(m_d\). The last aggregation applies the aggregator of the first equation of §2 at the policy. The last operation of each sub-builder and of the builder is an evaluation, the identity map from the function computed into the set of functions its card prints: 𝐶𝐸 : ℝ₊₊ × ℝ → ℝ₊₊, 𝐴𝑀𝐵 : ℝ₊₊ → ℝ₊₊ and, for \(V\), the set the file declares, the functions from \(\mathbb R_{++}\) to \(\mathbb R_{++}\). stage.dcsn.builder.bwd.list() prints the builder's operations in the order of application, each a primitive operator, a step the construction does not divide further, with the name of each sub-builder above its operations:

    risk_ce          sub-builder  → 𝐶𝐸(m_d, ν)
 1    Pullback       primitive
 2    Aggregation:1  primitive
 3    Expectation:1  primitive
 4    Aggregation    primitive
 5    Evaluation     primitive    → 𝐶𝐸
    ambiguity_ce     sub-builder  → 𝐴𝑀𝐵(m_d)
 6    Aggregation:1  primitive
 7    Expectation:1  primitive
 8    Aggregation    primitive
 9    Evaluation     primitive    → 𝐴𝑀𝐵
10  Aggregation      primitive    → 𝑉
11  Evaluation       primitive    → 𝑉

The card of an operation names under Source the lines of the file it comes from, and for an expectation these include the line that declares the distribution it integrates. The card of the expectation over \(\Psi\), stage.dcsn.builder.bwd.primitives["risk_ce:Expectation:1"].denote(), prints its rule and its sources as:

Rule
  risk_ce:Expectation:1(m_d, ν) = E_{Ψ}[risk_ce:Aggregation:1(m_d, Ψ)]
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Source  sa_savings.bl
  14  Ψ ~ LogNormal(ν, σ_Ψ)
  27  CE = E_{Ψ}(V[>]^(1-γ))^(1/(1-γ))  :: [id=risk_ce, !node]

The card of the expectation over \(\nu\), ambiguity_ce:Expectation:1, cites line 12, ν ~ N(κ_1, σ_ν^2), and integrates at each \(m_d\).

The forward builder from the decision perch, stage.dcsn.builder.fwd, extends the measure on the decision state \(m_d\) first by the distribution of \(\nu\) and then by the distribution of \(\Psi\) given the same \(\nu\), and pushes the measure on \((m_d, \nu, \Psi)\) forward through the law of motion at the policy, \((m_d, \nu, \Psi) \mapsto (m_d - c(m_d))\,\Psi\), to a measure on \(a\), in which \(\nu\) no longer appears.

Writing the expectations in the reverse order, \(\nu\) inside and \(\Psi\) outside, would need the distribution of \(\nu\) given \(\Psi\), which the file does not declare; the elaboration refuses the file under the rule conditional-not-declared.

docs.title: 5 Closed-form checks
docs.text:
With continuation value \(v(a) = a\) and \(s = m_d - c\), the lognormal moments give

\[ \mathrm{CE} = s\, e^{ u + (1-\gamma)\sigma_\Psi^2/2}, \qquad \mathrm{AMB} = s\, e^{\kappa_1 + (1-\eta)\sigma_ u^2/2 + (1-\gamma)\sigma_\Psi^2/2}. \]

Under the predictive distribution of the return the Epstein–Zin certainty equivalent is \(s\, e^{\kappa_1 + (1-\gamma)(\sigma_ u^2 + \sigma_\Psi^2)/2}\), so the ratio of AMB to it is \(e^{(\gamma-\eta)\sigma_ u^2/2}\). The ratio is one when \(\eta = \gamma\) or \(\sigma_ u = 0\), and below one when \(\eta > \gamma\) and \(\sigma_ u > 0\). At \( eta = 0.96\), \( ho = 2\), \(\gamma = 5\), \(\eta = 8\), \(\kappa_1 = 0.02\), \(\sigma_ u = 0.05\) and \(\sigma_\Psi = 0.15\) it is approximately 0.996257. The package's tests compare these values with the compiled kernels of the builder's pullback and aggregations, the plain Python functions that compile_kernel() makes from each operation's pointwise map, given the two expectations as analytic inputs. Those tests do not compute an integral, optimize the policy or solve the Bellman equation.

docs.title: 6 References
docs.text:
• Backus, D., A. Ferrière and S. Zin (2015). "Risk and ambiguity in models of business cycles." Journal of Monetary Economics. doi:10.1016/j.jmoneco.2014.12.005. The nested certainty equivalents are equation (19) of the August 2014 author draft, and the ambiguous-mean example follows it on pp. 17–18 of that draft; the draft's random mean \(s_2\) is \( u\) here, and its variance parameters \(\kappa_2\) and \( u\) are \(\sigma_\Psi^2\) and \(\sigma_ u^2\).
  • Ju, N. and J. Miao (2012). "Ambiguity, learning, and asset returns." Econometrica. doi:10.3982/ECTA7618.

docs.title: Unemployment Branching Portfolio-Consumption
docs.text:
Source reconcile (2026-05-23)

This prose describes a cons-port-based branching sketch aligned with the port-with-shocks stage library. The canonical branching registry was applications/unemployment-branching/registry/ (dolo-plus multi-stage layout), which is no longer in the repository; no stage file of this model stands under applications/.

A branching variant of the port-with-shocks example in which employment status is realized first, portfolio choice is branch-specific, and both branches fan in to a shared consumption stage.

Note

This example uses branch_control: nature, so the branching stage is a weighted-sum builder rather than a discrete choice. It also uses allowed fan-in at the arrival perch: both portfolio branches produce the common cash-on-hand quantity m, which is then consumed by the shared cons_stage.

docs.title: Stage graph
docs.text:
employment_status -> worker_port      -> cons_stage
employment_status -> unemployed_port  -> cons_stage

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
The agent enters the period with investable assets k. With probability p_e the employed branch is realized and the agent solves worker_port, choosing risky share ς before the joint shocks (Ψ_w, θ_w) realize. With probability 1-p_e the unemployed branch is realized and the agent solves unemployed_port, choosing risky share ς before a single placeholder return shock Ψ_u realizes. In both branches the continuation quantity is cash-on-hand m, so the period then fans in to a common cons_stage where the agent chooses c and carries assets a = m - c forward.

The unemployed branch is intentionally simple: it removes labour income and replaces the worker branch's richer post-decision shock structure with a single return shock whose first two moments are matched to the worker branch as a first-pass approximation.

In the syntax-semantic reading, each stage is interpreted as implicit transition maps \(\mathrm{g}_{\prec\sim}\) and \(\mathrm{g}_{\sim\succ}\) together with backward builders on the perch value objects \(\mathrm{v}_{\prec}\), \(\mathrm{v}\), and \(\mathrm{v}_{\succ}\). The formal MDP page uses that notation explicitly.

docs.title: Stage library
docs.text:
Stage Role Mapping employment_status exogenous branching stage k -> {k_w, k_u} worker_port employed portfolio choice k_w -> m unemployed_port unemployed portfolio choice k_u -> m cons_stage common consumption stage m -> a

The source YAMLs were in the folder unemployment_branching_doloplus/stages/ of the earlier dolo-plus design; the folder is no longer in the repository.

Method attachments are stage-local, matching the current docs/Bellman-Sym direction that methodization/configuration/calibration attach to stage objects rather than to a separate period-level branching artifact.

docs.title: Period
docs.text:
name: unemployment_port_period

stages:
  - employment_status: !stage
  - worker_port: !stage
  - unemployed_port: !stage
  - cons_stage: !stage

No intra-period connector is needed here. worker_port and unemployed_port both expose the same continuation field m, which matches the arrival field of cons_stage, so the fan-in is an identity composition on a common arrival space. The inter-period connector is the usual rename {a: k}, i.e. \(\tau : a \mapsto k\) in the formal notation.

docs.text:

├── stages/
│   ├── employment_status.yaml

│   ├── worker_port_methods.yml

docs.title: Formal problem
docs.text: See Formal MDP for the problem-level perch-value Bellman factorization and the stage decomposition.

docs.title: Matsya Prompt: Unemployment Branching Variant Of The cons-port Model
docs.text:
Start from the existing cons-port example in explore/cons-port/port-cons and the canonical stage YAMLs in packages/dolo/examples/models/doloplus/port-with-shocks/library/.

I want a branching unemployment variant of that model with the following within-period graph:

employment_status  -> worker_port      -> cons_stage
employment_status  -> unemployed_port  -> cons_stage

Interpret this as an exogenous employment-status branch, not an agent choice:

  • employment_status should be a kind: branching stage with branch_control: nature.
  • The branch labels should be worker and unemployed.
  • The branch sends the agent into a worker-specific portfolio stage or an unemployed-specific portfolio stage.

docs.title: Economic Intent
docs.text:
• Begin from the standard port_stage -> cons_stage logic.
  • The worker_port branch is the employed version of the portfolio stage.
  • The unemployed_port branch has no labour income.
  • There is also a difference in the perceived portfolio return distribution across employment states.
  • For now, keep that unemployment-side difference simple: use a single placeholder return shock for unemployed_port, calibrated so its mean and variance match the worker branch's portfolio-risk object as a first-pass approximation.
  • After the branch-specific portfolio stage, both paths should feed a common consumption stage cons_stage that takes cash-on-hand m and outputs end-of-period assets a.

docs.title: What I Need
docs.text:
Please produce the following:

  1. A clean problem-level MDP writeup in standard dynamic-programming language.
  2. A stage-by-stage decomposition for:
  3. employment_status
  4. worker_port
  5. unemployed_port
  6. cons_stage
  7. Strict dolo-plus YAML for those stages.
  8. If the shared downstream cons_stage creates a fan-in / recombination issue under the current branching spec, then:
  9. explain the issue clearly,
  10. keep the stage YAMLs branch-safe with disjoint poststate names where needed,
  11. and add the lightest valid period-level wiring needed to make the recombination explicit, using connectors for intra-period renames and inter_connectors for inter-period renames where appropriate.
  12. Minimal calibration / settings / methodization scaffolding only if needed to make the example coherent. Prefer stage-local methodization files if that is more consistent with the current dev-specs.

docs.title: Syntax And Spec Constraints
docs.text:
• Use strict dolo-plus stage YAML, not generic YAML and not plain legacy dolo YAML.
  • Use the canonical top-level groups under symbols::
  • spaces
  • prestate
  • states
  • poststates
  • controls
  • exogenous
  • values
  • values_marginal when needed
  • parameters
  • Use the canonical equation blocks:
  • arvl_to_dcsn_transition
  • dcsn_to_cntn_transition
  • cntn_to_dcsn_builder
  • dcsn_to_arvl_builder
  • Use perch tags canonically:
  • arrival: [<]
  • decision: unmarked
  • continuation: [>]
  • Keep branch poststates disjoint on the branching stage.
  • Prefer a common cons_stage if that can be represented cleanly; otherwise, make the recombination explicit rather than silently relying on ambiguous implicit fan-in.
  • Use canonical repo terminology:
  • dolo-plus
  • stage
  • period
  • connector
  • branch_control
  • Bellman operator

docs.title: Output Format
docs.text:
Please answer in this order:

  1. Assumptions you are making
  2. Problem-level Bellman / MDP
  3. Stage decomposition
  4. Stage YAMLs
  5. Period wiring / recombination
  6. Open issues / ambiguities

Be concrete and repo-compatible. Do not hand-wave the recombination step.

docs.title: Formal MDP: Unemployment Branching Portfolio-Consumption
docs.text: Source: the folder of stage files unemployment_branching_doloplus/ of the earlier dolo-plus YAML design; the folder is no longer in the repository.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
An agent enters the period with investable assets \(k \in \mathbb{R}_{++}\). Employment status is then realized exogenously:

  • with probability \(p_e\), the agent is employed and enters the worker_port stage,
  • with probability \(1-p_e\), the agent is unemployed and enters the unemployed_port stage.

In the employed branch, the agent chooses a risky portfolio share \(\varsigma \in [0,1]\) before the joint shocks \((\Psi_w, \theta_w)\) are realized. Cash-on-hand is

\[ m = k\bigl(\varsigma \Psi_w + (1-\varsigma)R\bigr) + \theta_w. \]

In the unemployed branch, the agent chooses a risky portfolio share \(\varsigma \in [0,1]\) before a single placeholder return shock \(\Psi_u\) is realized. There is no labor-income shock in this branch, so cash-on-hand is

\[ m = k\bigl(\varsigma \Psi_u + (1-\varsigma)R\bigr). \]

After either branch, the period fans in to a common consumption stage. The agent chooses consumption \(c \in (0,m]\), end-of-period assets are

\[ a = m - c, \]

and the next period is reached via the inter-period connector

\[ \tau : a \mapsto k. \]

That is, the current continuation field a is renamed to the next-period arrival field k; this is a wiring map, not a new economic transition equation.

Preferences are CRRA:

\[ u(c) = \frac{c^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho}, \]

with discount factor \(\beta \in (0,1)\) and risk-aversion parameter \(\rho > 0\).

docs.title: Perch-Value Bellman Factorization
docs.text:
Let \(\mathrm{v}_{\prec}^{+}(k)\) denote the next-period arrival value function. Under the inter-period connector \(\tau : a \mapsto k\), the continuation value entering the current consumption stage is

\[ \mathrm{v}_{\succ}(a) \coloneqq (\tau^{*}\mathrm{v}_{\prec}^{+})(a) = \mathrm{v}_{\prec}^{+}(\tau(a)). \]

This is the canonical pullback rule from the syntax-semantic composition pages: the predecessor stage consumes a continuation value \(\mathrm{v}_{\succ}\), while the successor period provides the arrival value \(\mathrm{v}_{\prec}^{+}\).

Let \(\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{cons}}\), \(\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{worker}}\), and \(\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{unemployed}}\) denote the decision-perch values of the three non-trivial stages. Then:

\[ \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{cons}}(m) = \max_{0 < c \le m} \left\{ \frac{c^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho} + \beta \mathrm{v}_{\succ}(a) \right\}, \qquad a = m-c. \] \[ \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{worker}}(k) = \max_{\varsigma \in [0,1]} \mathbb{E}_{\Psi_w,\theta_w}\left[\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{cons}}\!\left(k(\varsigma \Psi_w + (1-\varsigma)R) + \theta_w\right)\right]. \] \[ \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{unemployed}}(k) = \max_{\varsigma \in [0,1]} \mathbb{E}_{\Psi_u}\left[\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{cons}}\!\left(k(\varsigma \Psi_u + (1-\varsigma)R)\right)\right]. \] \[ \mathrm{v}(k) = p_e\, \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{worker}}(k) + (1-p_e)\, \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{unemployed}}(k). \]

docs.title: Employment status
docs.text:
This is a nature-controlled branching stage with arrival state \(x_{\prec} = \{k\}\), decision state \(x = \{k\}\), and branch-keyed continuation states

\[ x_{\succ,\mathrm{worker}} = \{k_w\}, \qquad x_{\succ,\mathrm{unemployed}} = \{k_u\}. \]

In the syntax-semantic reading, the equality blocks implicitly define

\[ \mathrm{g}_{\prec\sim}^{\mathrm{empl}}(k_{\prec}) = k_{\prec}, \qquad \mathrm{g}_{\sim\succ,\mathrm{worker}}^{\mathrm{empl}}(k) = k, \qquad \mathrm{g}_{\sim\succ,\mathrm{unemployed}}^{\mathrm{empl}}(k) = k. \]

Equivalently, in SYM surface syntax,

\[ k = k[<], \qquad k_w[>] = k, \qquad k_u[>] = k. \]

The branch-specific continuation-value family is \(\left(\mathrm{v}_{\succ,\mathrm{worker}}, \mathrm{v}_{\succ,\mathrm{unemployed}}\right)\), so the backward builder is the probability-weighted aggregation

In YAML surface syntax, this is the branch family declared by values.V[>] = {worker: V_worker, unemployed: V_unemployed}, so the builder reads as V = p_e*V[>][worker] + (1-p_e)*V[>][unemployed].

\[ \mathrm{v}(k) = p_e\, \mathrm{v}_{\succ,\mathrm{worker}}(k) + (1-p_e)\, \mathrm{v}_{\succ,\mathrm{unemployed}}(k), \qquad \mathrm{v}_{\prec}(k) = \mathrm{v}(k). \]

docs.title: Worker portfolio
docs.text:
This stage has arrival state \(\{k_w\}\), control \(\varsigma\), post-decision shocks \((\Psi_w,\theta_w)\), and continuation state \(\{m\}\).

Its transition equalities define the implicit maps

\[ \mathrm{g}_{\prec\sim}^{\mathrm{worker}}(k_w) = k_w, \] \[ \mathrm{g}_{\sim\succ}^{\mathrm{worker}}(k_d,\varsigma,\Psi_w,\theta_w) = k_d(\varsigma \Psi_w + (1-\varsigma)R) + \theta_w. \]

Equivalently, the SYM equations are \(k_d = k_w\) and \(m = k_d(\varsigma \Psi_w + (1-\varsigma)R) + \theta_w\).

Because the shocks are realized after the portfolio decision, the expectation sits inside cntn_to_dcsn_builder, not in dcsn_to_arvl_builder. The backward recursion is

\[ \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{worker}}(k_d) = \max_{\varsigma \in [0,1]} \mathbb{E}_{\Psi_w,\theta_w}\left[ \mathrm{v}_{\succ}\!\left(\mathrm{g}_{\sim\succ}^{\mathrm{worker}}(k_d,\varsigma,\Psi_w,\theta_w)\right) \right], \qquad \mathrm{v}_{\prec,\mathrm{worker}}(k_w) = \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{worker}}(k_w). \]

docs.title: Unemployed portfolio
docs.text:
This stage has arrival state \(\{k_u\}\), control \(\varsigma\), shock \(\Psi_u\), and continuation state \(\{m\}\).

Its transition equalities define

\[ \mathrm{g}_{\prec\sim}^{\mathrm{unemployed}}(k_u) = k_u, \] \[ \mathrm{g}_{\sim\succ}^{\mathrm{unemployed}}(k_d,\varsigma,\Psi_u) = k_d(\varsigma \Psi_u + (1-\varsigma)R). \]

Equivalently, the SYM equations are \(k_d = k_u\) and \(m = k_d(\varsigma \Psi_u + (1-\varsigma)R)\).

Its backward recursion is

\[ \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{unemployed}}(k_d) = \max_{\varsigma \in [0,1]} \mathbb{E}_{\Psi_u}\left[ \mathrm{v}_{\succ}\!\left(\mathrm{g}_{\sim\succ}^{\mathrm{unemployed}}(k_d,\varsigma,\Psi_u)\right) \right], \qquad \mathrm{v}_{\prec,\mathrm{unemployed}}(k_u) = \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{unemployed}}(k_u). \]

docs.title: Consumption
docs.text:
This stage has arrival state \(\{m\}\), control \(c\), and continuation state \(\{a\}\).

Its transition equalities define

\[ \mathrm{g}_{\prec\sim}^{\mathrm{cons}}(m) = m, \qquad \mathrm{g}_{\sim\succ}^{\mathrm{cons}}(m_d,c) = m_d - c. \]

Equivalently, the SYM equations are \(m_d = m\) and \(a = m_d - c\).

Its backward builder is

\[ \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{cons}}(m_d) = \max_{0 < c \le m_d} \left\{ \frac{c^{1-\rho}}{1-\rho} + \beta \mathrm{v}_{\succ}(a) \right\}, \qquad \mathrm{v}_{\prec,\mathrm{cons}}(m) = \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{cons}}(m). \]

The EGM representation uses the marginal continuation value \(\partial_a \mathrm{v}_{\succ}(a)\) and the inverse map associated with \(\mathrm{g}_{\sim\succ}^{\mathrm{cons}}\):

\[ c(a) = \left(\beta\,\partial_a \mathrm{v}_{\succ}(a)\right)^{-1/\rho}, \]

and

\[ \left(\mathrm{g}_{\sim\succ}^{\mathrm{cons}}\right)^{-1}(a,c) = a + c. \]

docs.title: Composition and Wiring
docs.text:
The period wiring is

employment_status -> worker_port      -> cons_stage
employment_status -> unemployed_port  -> cons_stage

The branching stage fans out via the disjoint continuation fields k_w and k_u. The two portfolio stages then fan in to the shared arrival field m of cons_stage. In the syntax-semantic composition rules, this is an identity composition on a common arrival space: both upstream stages expose the same continuation field m, so no intra-period connector is needed.

The inter-period connector is the standard rename

{a: k}

so the next period starts again from investable assets k. This inter-period connector induces the pullback \(\mathrm{v}_{\succ} = \tau^{*}\mathrm{v}_{\prec}^{+}\) used in the Bellman factorization above.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text: Symbol Value Description \(\beta\) 0.96 discount factor \(\rho\) 2.0 CRRA risk aversion \(R\) 1.02 gross risk-free return \(p_e\) 0.95 employment probability \(\mu_{\Psi_w}\) 0.04 worker risky-return log-mean \(\sigma_{\Psi_w}\) 0.15 worker risky-return log-std \(\mu_{\theta_w}\) 0.0 worker labor-income log-mean \(\sigma_{\theta_w}\) 0.10 worker labor-income log-std \(\rho_{\zeta_w}\) 0.0 worker shock-correlation placeholder \(\mu_{\Psi_u}\) 0.04 unemployed risky-return log-mean \(\sigma_{\Psi_u}\) 0.15 unemployed risky-return log-std

docs.title: Matsya
docs.text:
Summary

Matsya is the service of Project Bellman that helps an economist state a dynamic model in Bellman-SYM, the project's language for staged Bellman problems. This page says in one paragraph what Matsya does and for whom, and then maps its documentation: four groups of pages, read in order, from what Matsya is, through how it is used and the exact forms looked up while using it, to how it is built.

Relationship with other documents

Continued by — Matsya in three parts, the user guide's first page, which defines the words that every later page uses. Explained for developers in — the Matsya developer guide, which describes the program, the configuration and the parts of Matsya that training revises. See also — For an assistant using Matsya, the same map for an assistant that runs Matsya's commands for a user, with the files the client keeps on the user's machine.

docs.title: 1 What Matsya does and for whom
docs.text: Matsya reads a description of a dynamic economic model, written in prose and displayed equations as a paper's model section is written, or the text of a paper, and writes the model's declaration in Bellman-SYM: its stage files and, at the level the user names, the files that join the stages into periods and the periods in time, with the methods and values that Bellman Workbench loads. It restates the model in prose before it writes, checks the files with the program that reads the language, reads the checked files back into prose and compares that prose with its restatement, so that what it returns either says what the source says or reports where it does not; where the source leaves something necessary unsaid, it ends its work with a question instead of supplying an answer. It also answers questions about a model, about its declaration, about the language and about the literature on dynamic programming, and it quotes and cites the passages on which each answer rests. Matsya is for an economist who has a model and wants its declaration, whether the economist types Matsya's commands or has a language model running on the same machine, such as Claude Code, run them; the developer guide is for those who build and train Matsya itself.

docs.title: Matsya developer guide
docs.text:
Summary

Matsya is a service with two modes. In architect mode it reads a paper or a typed description of a dynamic economic model, writes the model's declaration in Bellman-SYM, the project's language for staged Bellman problems, as stage files together with a prose description of the model, and checks the two against each other; in conversation mode it answers questions with passages retrieved from an index of the project's documents and literature, with one literal excerpt of a passage or, when the configuration enables the optional conversation role, with a language model's answer to a question asked in a session, each claim of which cites material supplied to the language model and quotes it. Its service and training code reside in two packages; separate operator scripts prepare the index and guides. Everything that training revises, the instruction texts, the settings and the Matsya handlers, is data in one configuration folder outside the packages; training changes nothing in the language models themselves. Section 3 lists which page of the guide answers which question.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Bellman-SYM, the language in which Matsya writes model declarations, and Matsya instructions, which defines the role texts used in each job. Used by — the Matsya user guide, which names the three parts, matsya-client, matsya-architect and matsya-master, and follows one piece of work through the command bellman-matsya; the access instructions distributed with the service give the installation, the environment variables and a Matsya token; the operator's deployment instructions describe installation on the DigitalOcean server, a rented virtual machine that runs the service. See also — the wiki pages Matsya collection, Matsya handler, Matsya instructions and Reference guides in Matsya, which define the terms this guide uses.

docs.title: 1 Program and configuration
docs.text:
Matsya consists of two kinds of thing, and the kind a change alters determines where the change is made and whether a training pass may make it. A training pass is one round in which a revised configuration is run on a set of papers, its results are measured against those of the configuration in use, and the revision is accepted or refused under the governing document's acceptance rule; the language models themselves are not changed.

The program is fixed code, tested by the packages' own tests (venv/bin/python -m pytest packages/matsya/tests, 282 tests on 9 October 2026) and changed separately from the configuration that a training pass revises. The service and training code have two packages, with resource preparation in separate operator scripts. packages/matsya is the frame: it holds the web service and the retrieval code, loads and checks the configuration, and builds for each job the job frame, the record (the class Frame of frame.py) through which a Matsya handler uses everything else. The job frame gives a Matsya handler the function that sends a message to the language model's provider, the retrieval index, the Bellman-SYM elaborator BellmanSYMDeclaration_to_ElaboratedSemanticObject (the program that checks stage files with the bellman package's functions and constructs from them the elaborated semantic object \(E\), the complete typed statement of the problem the files state: an elaborated stage for one stage file, an elaborated trellis for several), the comparator and the job's record. packages/meaning-map-training holds three programs: the comparator (compare.py), which decides whether two elaborated semantic objects have the same meaning and which a job uses as ElaboratedSemanticObject_comparator through compare_outcomes of meaning.py; the form check (form_check.py), which tests whether a description has the required headings and length; and the program that measures a training pass (round_trip.py and round_trip_eval.py). The program also fixes the slots that training fills, that is, the names under which the configuration must supply its contents and the form each content must take: the seven role keys (a role is one of the seven tasks given to a language model under an instruction text, such as SourceMaterial_to_BellmanStageProse, the Model-prose-writer, which writes the model prose from the source, or BellmanStageProse_judge, the judge), the thirteen Matsya handler names with their parameter lists, and the fifteen keys of the settings file with their types; and, for the optional conversation role, which a configuration enables by naming it among its roles, one more role key, conversation_answer, one more Matsya handler name, conversation_reply, and two more settings keys, conversation_rounds and conversation_pages, which the program requires together with the role's instruction text and refuses in a configuration that does not name the role. It answers the requests that the Model-prose-writer and Prose-to-Bellman-Sym may make for further documentation through the reading controller, which holds each role within the allowances of the settings' reading and places in a message only passages of the collections the user's grants allow, the public collections for every user and each private collection under a grant, whether or not a passage is marked model_prompt (What Matsya reads §5). It counts the language-model tokens of every message before the message is sent (a token is the unit of text, a word or part of a word, in which a provider counts and prices a message) and holds each job, and each turn of conversation mode, within the token ceilings of the settings, which a training pass does not change (What Matsya reads §4). It also fixes what a Matsya handler may report: the six kinds of event and their fields (_EVENT_FIELDS in jobs.py), the 27 validation codes, the names under which a Matsya handler reports that a language model's answer lacks the required structure or evidence (MODEL_VALIDATION_CODES in frame.py) and the fields of a request (REQUEST_FIELDS in processor.py).

The configuration, by contrast, is one folder of data supplied to the service: the service keeps every published configuration under the folder MATSYA_CONFIGURATIONS_ROOT names, each under its ID, and runs each job and turn under the one pinned to it (Updating Matsya configurations). The governing document writes it as \(\mathfrak{K} = (\mathfrak{t}, \mathfrak{s}, \mathfrak{h})\): the instruction texts \(\mathfrak{t}\), one file per role under texts/; the settings \(\mathfrak{s}\) in settings.json; and the Matsya handlers \(\mathfrak{h}\), the Python functions that run a job, in the module matsya_handler.py, the name the constant HANDLERS_FILE of the configuration loader (configuration.py) requires. A training pass revises this folder and never the packages. The folder also holds three reference guides, saved copies of published documentation pages that the Matsya handlers include in a language model's message, and manifest.json, which lists the SHA-256 digest of every other file (a digest is a 64-character code computed from a file's bytes, which changes whenever any byte changes). The program checks the folder against the manifest when the service starts and again at the start of every job, and refuses a folder that fails any check as a whole, so that no language model is called under an unchecked configuration.

Part Where Program or configuration What checks it The web service: the job routes (POST /v1/model-iterations, GET /v1/model-iterations/{job_id}, POST /v1/model-iterations/{job_id}/cancel), the search and answer routes (POST /v1/search, POST /v1/answer, GET /v1/passages/{passage_id}, GET /v1/index), the sessions (named conversations with Matsya, §2, with POST /v1/sessions/{session_id}/selected-job, which chooses the job a session's conversation discusses) and the turns of conversation mode (POST /v1/sessions/{session_id}/turns, GET /v1/sessions/{session_id}/turns/{turn_id}), the Matsya tokens, the job runner and the turn runner packages/matsya/matsya_service/: api.py (the routes and the application's start-up), auth.py (Matsya-token authentication), jobs.py (the job database with the sessions' numbered entries and the turns, and the job runner), conversation.py (the turn runner of conversation mode and the checks of a turn's answer), serve.py (the command matsya-serve), collection_access.py (the grants under which the private collections are read), answer.py (the extractive answer, a short literal excerpt from retrieved passages) program the package's tests The modules that load the configuration and build the job frame: processor, roles, source, guide pages, meaning, configuration loader packages/matsya/matsya_service/: processor.py, frame.py, roles.py, source.py, guide_pages.py, meaning.py, configuration.py program the package's tests The retrieval code: extraction, embedding, storage, search, and the reading controller through which a job reads the index and the guides' records packages/matsya/matsya_service/retrieval/ program the package's tests; the retrieval checks at every build, each a search that must return a passage of a named source The operator-run source compiler, index builder and transfer script compile_retrieval_manifest.py, build_retrieval_index.py and retrieval_bundle.py, maintained separately from the installed package program the package's tests and the retrieval checks at every build The operator-run guide builder and its construction policy, and the shared parser of links and tags matsya_guide_builder.py and guide_policy.json, maintained separately from the installed package; the page markers against guides/manifest.json and, for a manifest of the form matsya-guides/3, its records of sections, links and tag memberships The retrieval index a private folder outside every checkout, named by MATSYA_INDEX_ROOT built data, neither program nor trained its own digests; docs.title: 2 The path of one job
docs.text:
A job of architect mode starts from a request to POST /v1/model-iterations, which contains a source, either {"kind": "description", "text": ...} or a paper as its text in Markdown or LaTeX, {"kind": "paper", "text": ...}, and the job's target, the level of a declaration the job returns, stage, period, trellis or recipe, without which the request is refused; and may contain max_cycles (the cycle limit, at most cycle_maximum), starting_declaration (file names with their texts, elaborated in place of the Bellman-SYM writer's first call), model_key and source_cluster (two labels; a source whose source_cluster in the list of indexed sources equals either is left out of the job's searches and requests, so that the paper's own text is not retrieved for it, and without them every clustered source is left out), formulation (the one formulation of the model to write when the source states several), session (a named conversation with Matsya, a record of numbered entries, whose entries up to the session's revision when the job starts the job takes as its source, an answer of Matsya among them only when the user accepted it; a job of a session continues the session's earlier job, whose identity it records) and force (write even when preparation ends with open questions). The service's function for this route checks the request against the configuration's cycle_maximum, writes a job to the job database and passes it to the job runner, which runs at most two jobs at the same time. The caller receives a job identity and reads the job's state, its label (the session's name, the job's target, the version of the session's text the job was built from, the job's number in the session and its state), its progress and its result from GET /v1/model-iterations/{job_id}, and may cancel a queued or running job with POST /v1/model-iterations/{job_id}/cancel: a queued job never runs, and a running job stops before its next call of a language model, a call already sent finishing and being charged, and ends cancelled.

The job runner calls the processor, ModelProcessor.process in processor.py. The processor checks the request again, loads and checks the configuration folder, turns the source into a Source record through the Matsya handler normalize_source, builds the job's language-model token ledger, the account of the tokens charged to each call, from the settings' ceilings, takes the retrieval index once for the whole job, builds the job frame from the texts, the guides, the settings, the function that sends a message to the provider, the job's record as begun by the processor, the job runner's progress callback, the index and the source, and calls the Matsya handler cycle. From here on the configuration's code runs the job and the program only answers its calls.

The Matsya handler cycle runs preparation first: the source preparer writes the description \(M\) from the source material \(P\), and the judge compares \(M\) with \(P\). The Bellman-SYM writer then writes the initial stage files \(D\) from \(M\), and the elaborator constructs \(E\) from \(D\). Numbered iteration 1 writes \(M'\) from the dossier of \(E\), reports any difference between \(M\) and \(M'\), writes \(D'\) from \(M'\), elaborates it to \(E'\), and compares \(E\) with \(E'\). If they differ, iteration 2 begins from \(E'\) and produces \(M''\), \(D''\) and \(E''\); it compares \(E'\) with \(E''\). The cycle limit counts these numbered iterations, not the initial writing. The elaborator's refusal is sent back to the Bellman-SYM writer for repair within a writing step. A failed iteration that produces no new elaborated object has no equality verdict. For a stage target, the comparator reads one elaborated stage; for a period, trellis or recipe target, it reads the stages and their joins. The prose judges, the # from: quotations and the writer's note remain diagnostic records; none decides convergence. The job record keeps each language-model call as a digest and token counts, together with the configuration version and the identities of the pages and passages each message held. A call that would exceed a role's or job's token ceiling is refused before it is sent, and the processor ends the job not_converged with the reason token_ceiling_reached.

The source material \(P\) (SourceMaterial) is prepared into the description \(M\) (BellmanStageProse); \(M\) is declared in the stage files \(D\) (BellmanSYMDeclaration); and their elaboration is the elaborated semantic object \(E\) (ElaboratedSemanticObject). Each later prose, declaration and elaboration is one application of the same maps to the preceding elaborated object. Four roles and two programs compute these maps. A role's adopted name is its key in the program; the two programs keep their function names and state the adopted name in their docstrings.

Concept Symbol Adopted name Arrow Computed by the source preparer SourceMaterial_to_BellmanStageProse \(P \to M\) a language model under its instruction text the Bellman-SYM writer \(\Upsilon_0\) BellmanStageProse_to_BellmanSYMDeclaration \(M \to D\), \(M' \to D'\), \(M'' \to D''\) a language model under its instruction text the Bellman-SYM elaborator \(S\) BellmanSYMDeclaration_to_ElaboratedSemanticObject \(D \to E\), \(D' \to E'\), \(D'' \to E''\), or a refusal elaborate_files of meaning.py, which checks the files at the job's target and calls elaborate_text, elaborate_trellis and, for a recipe, load_recipe and specify_trellis of the bellman package the prose writer \(\Upsilon_1\) ElaboratedSemanticObject_to_BellmanStageProse \(E \to M'\), then \(E' \to M''\), from each dossier and nothing else a language model under its instruction text the judge \(J\) BellmanStageProse_judge \((M, M') \to\) a table of agreement on ten items; in preparation also \((P, M)\) a language model under its instruction text the comparator \(\cong\) ElaboratedSemanticObject_comparator \((E, E')\), then \((E', E'')\), to comparison profiles compare_outcomes of meaning.py, over the comparator of packages/meaning-map-training

The wiki pages Bellman-SYM writer, Prose writer and Judge define the three maps a language model computes in a cycle.

A turn of conversation mode. When the configuration enables the conversation role, a question asked in a session through POST /v1/sessions/{session_id}/turns is appended to the session as an entry of the user and answered in a turn, which runs on a runner of its own with two workers, so that a running job does not delay an answer. The turn runner, TurnRunner of conversation.py, loads the configuration, fixes the snapshot of the index the turn reads, binds the reading controller to it, to the collections the person asking may read and to the conversation role's allowances, elaborates a stage file the question names, and calls the Matsya handler conversation_reply, which searches once from the question, calls the role and has the controller answer its requests. The turn runner then checks the answer: every citation must name material supplied to the role in the turn and quote it. It appends the answer, or the role's questions for the user, to the session and stores the turn's record, which holds digests, identities and counts and no message text. An answer of the role enters the source material of a later job only when the user accepts it with an entry of the kind acceptance.

docs.title: The retrieval index
docs.text:
Summary

Matsya's retrieval index, in standard terms a RAG index (retrieval-augmented generation), is the store of passages from which a search returns the passages placed in a language model's message; it is built in four steps by four programs. A compiler turns the reviewed list of sources into a manifest of file digests; the operator-run script build_retrieval_index.py extracts passages from those files, embeds them, that is, computes for each passage a vector of numbers with a local embedding model so that passages of similar meaning receive similar vectors, writes a snapshot, tests it with the searches of a check file and activates it; the operator-run script retrieval_bundle.py copies the active snapshot with the embedding model into one folder for another machine; and the service opens the snapshot named by the file active.json. A search combines an exact cosine comparison of embeddings with SQLite full-text search and a count of mathematical symbols, and weights the result by collection. The snapshot also records the index's knowledge graph, each admitted document with the sections its headings open, the links its authors wrote and the tags it carries, from which a snapshot answers two operations, related and read; the search does not read these records.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Matsya collection, which defines the five groups of sources considered for the index. Used by — Collections and weights: the fields of a search request and the weights; Matsya collection: the five groups of sources. See also — What Matsya reads §5, for the reading controller that uses the index’s passages and knowledge graph.
