curl --fail-with-body -sS -X POST "$BELLMAN_MATSYA_SERVER/v1/configurations" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BELLMAN_MATSYA_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/zip" \
  --data-binary @candidate.zip

The answer, with the status 201, is {"configuration_id":"<id>","version":"<version>"}, the ID under which the service installed the folder and the version its manifest names; the same folder published again answers 200 with the same ID. The service checks every file against the manifest, then again after it has imported the Matsya handler module, and refuses an archive that escapes its folder, holds a link, a duplicate name or a file the manifest does not list, or expands beyond 24 MiB (§3). Publication changes the default not at all. bellman-matsya configuration publish <folder> sends the same request.

A job (§5) or a question (§7) selects a published configuration by its ID in the field configuration_id, and every answer on the job or the turn names the ID resolved, the default's when the request named none. An administrator changes the default with

curl --fail-with-body -sS -X PUT "$BELLMAN_MATSYA_SERVER/v1/configurations/default" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $BELLMAN_MATSYA_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{"configuration_id": "<id>"}'

The answer is {"previous_configuration_id":"<old id>","configuration_id":"<new id>","version":"<version>"}. The change takes effect for the next request, without a restart; a job or a turn already accepted keeps the ID pinned to it, as does the attempt that a reply to such a job's question starts. GET /v1/index names the current default's ID and version. bellman-matsya configuration set-default <id> sends the same request.

docs.title: The command reference
docs.text:
Summary

This page gives the commands of matsya-client, the program you run on your machine to use Matsya. It states their arguments, options, printed answers and exit statuses. It also names the fields returned by --json, so an assistant can read an answer without interpreting the printed prose.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Working with Matsya from the command line, which follows a session and a job, and Working on a project folder, which follows a model in its own folder. Continued by — The Python module and the files the client writes, which gives the corresponding Python calls. See also — Matsya in three parts, which defines a session, a job, a turn, a target and a job's label.

docs.title: 1 Reading a command's answer
docs.text:
bellman-matsya --help lists the commands. For one command's options, run its own help, for example bellman-matsya job submit --help or bellman-matsya project pull --help. In the forms below, angle brackets stand for a value you supply; square brackets enclose an optional argument. A job or session identifier is the value printed when it is created.

Every service command accepts --json except bellman-matsya configure and bellman-matsya docs. The four bellman-matsya project commands accept it too. For ordinary service commands, --json prints the service's final JSON answer unchanged. For project commands, it prints one JSON object assembled from the folder and the service's answers, and bellman-matsya job submit-prepared (§4.1) and bellman-matsya configuration effective (§9) likewise print an object that the client assembles. bellman-matsya job files --json prints the job's answer, although it also writes files. bellman-matsya ask --follow ... --json prints the turn's answer, not the followed job's answer; progress goes to standard error. bellman-matsya ask --no-wait --json prints the answer that the service gives when it accepts the question. Section 8 gives the fields.

Exit status Meaning 0 The command completed. For job wait, inspect the returned job state: needs_input, not_converged and failed are final states too. For turn wait, inspect the returned turn state: failed and interrupted are final states too. 1 The service refused a request, a local file could not be read or written, the service could not be reached, an online guide page could not be read, or the client refused a personal Anthropic key (§2.2), the address it would be sent to (§4.1), a prepared-inputs file or a service that does not name a capability the submission needs (§4.1). A command that sent the key also ends with 1 when the service accepted its work under the service's own key (§4.1). The error is printed on standard error. 2 The arguments were refused before a request, or a project command's conditions were not met, as are those of configuration effective in a project folder (§9). Argument errors include a usage line; project refusals give one sentence on standard error. 130 You interrupted a waiting command. Its message says how to inspect a job or turn that may still be running on the service.

On a machine with no saved configuration and no BELLMAN_MATSYA_TOKEN, any command other than docs or bare bellman-matsya first prints two lines directing an assistant to bellman-matsya docs --all. Those lines precede even a JSON answer. Run bellman-matsya configure first if a program needs standard output to contain JSON alone. The Matsya token itself is never printed.

docs.title: 2.1 Orientation
docs.text:
bellman-matsya with no arguments prints Markdown: what Matsya does; the installed guide's folder and the commands that print or update it; the client version; whether a token is saved or supplied by BELLMAN_MATSYA_TOKEN; and how to list the commands. In a project folder it also prints the session identifier, the latest job's label and any questions awaiting a reply. If the session cannot be read, it gives the reason. This form makes no change and has no --json option.

After the line on the Matsya token, the orientation prints one line, which never contains a key, that names the key the next job, question or reply will use; of three sentences, it prints the first whose condition holds. When BELLMAN_MATSYA_ANTHROPIC_KEY is set and not empty, the line is The environment variable `BELLMAN_MATSYA_ANTHROPIC_KEY` is set; new jobs, questions and replies that continue a job use its value in place of any saved key, and the Anthropic account of that key is charged. Otherwise, when a key is saved (§2.2), it is A personal Anthropic key is saved on this machine, in `<file>`; new jobs, questions and replies that continue a job use it, and the Anthropic account of that key is charged., with the saved file's path in place of <file>. Otherwise it is No personal Anthropic key is selected; new jobs and questions use the service's key, and a reply that would continue a job run with a personal key is refused until one is selected. When a key is selected and the service address is neither an HTTPS address nor an http address whose host is localhost, 127.0.0.1 or ::1, the line adds The service address <address> uses plain HTTP, so the client refuses to send a job, a question or a reply with this key.

docs.title: 2.2 Configuration
docs.text:
bellman-matsya configure
bellman-matsya configure --set-anthropic-key
bellman-matsya configure --clear-anthropic-key

bellman-matsya configure, without an option, asks only for a Matsya token beginning msy_. It saves the token in the user's configuration file without sending a request and retains any custom service address already saved there. Otherwise the client uses http://45.55.225.169:8710. It prints the file's path, explains that the service keeps session entries and job records, and suggests bellman-matsya index to check access. BELLMAN_MATSYA_TOKEN and BELLMAN_MATSYA_SERVER override saved values for later commands. This interactive command has no --json option; an invalid token or saved address ends with status 1.

The two options, which cannot be combined, manage the optional personal Anthropic key that a registered holder may add after the Matsya token is configured (Matsya in three parts §1); neither asks for the Matsya token, and the key is never an argument of a command. The help of configure and the set-up lines of bellman-matsya --help name them, with BELLMAN_MATSYA_ANTHROPIC_KEY, as optional additions made after the Matsya token is configured. --set-anthropic-key requires a configured Matsya token, saved by configure or set in BELLMAN_MATSYA_TOKEN. Without one it prints Error: no Matsya token is configured. A personal Anthropic key is an addition to a Matsya token, not a substitute for it: save the Matsya token the service's administrator gave you with bellman-matsya configure, or set BELLMAN_MATSYA_TOKEN. on standard error, asks for nothing, writes nothing and exits with status 1; an unreadable saved service address is reported as configure without an option reports it. With a Matsya token, it asks for the key without echoing the characters, removes the whitespace around it, and refuses a key that is then empty or contains a character other than the visible ASCII characters ! to ~ with Error: the key you entered is empty or contains a space, a line break or another character that an HTTP header does not allow; nothing was saved. and status 1. Otherwise it saves the key, followed by one line feed, in ~/.config/bellman-matsya/anthropic-key with the owner-only mode 0600, replacing a key saved before, and prints the file's path, that the jobs and questions you start are then charged to the Anthropic account of that key, and how to remove it. --clear-anthropic-key, which needs no Matsya token, deletes that file and prints whether a saved key was removed; with no key in the environment, later work then uses the service's key. configure without an option rewrites config.toml and leaves a saved key in place.

A nonempty BELLMAN_MATSYA_ANTHROPIC_KEY supplies a key without saving it, and every command uses it in place of a saved key. Every command that contacts the service removes the whitespace around the selected key and checks it in the same way before it sends a request; a key that fails the check is refused with one sentence that names its source, and the command exits with status 1 and prints no traceback. For the variable the sentence is Error: the personal Anthropic key in BELLMAN_MATSYA_ANTHROPIC_KEY is empty or contains a space, a line break or another character that an HTTP header does not allow; set the variable to the key alone, or unset it to use the service's key., and for the saved file Error: the personal Anthropic key in the saved file <path> is empty or contains a space, a line break or another character that an HTTP header does not allow; set it again with bellman-matsya configure --set-anthropic-key, or remove it with bellman-matsya configure --clear-anthropic-key., with the file's path in place of <path>. A selected key is sent, in the header Bellman-Matsya-Anthropic-Key, with a job's submission, a question and a reply named with --replies-to, and with no other request (§§4–7). No command prints it, and a message the client composes shows <Anthropic API key> in its place, as it shows <Matsya token> in place of the Matsya token. bellman-matsya configuration effective (§9) prints the address, the configuration and the session that the next job or question would use, and where the address, the Matsya token and the key come from, without either secret.

docs.title: 2.3 The guide
docs.text:
Command What it prints bellman-matsya docs Each installed page's name and title, one per line. bellman-matsya docs <page> That page in Markdown, without its front matter. The name may omit .md; dev-guide/index names a developer-guide page. bellman-matsya docs --all All installed pages in order, each preceded by a <!-- page: ... --> line naming its file. bellman-matsya docs --path The folder in which the guide is installed.

--online with a named page or --all reads its current text over HTTPS from the public Matsya client repository. The page list and titles still come from the installed client, so a newly added online page requires a client update before this command can name it. bellman-matsya docs --online without a page or --all only lists the installed pages. --path cannot be combined with --online, and a page cannot be combined with --all or --path. These argument errors end with status 2; a failure to read an online page ends with status 1 and tells you how to read the installed guide. docs has no --json option.

docs.title: 3.1 Index information
docs.text: bellman-matsya index [--json] prints Index digest, Embedding model, Configuration ID and Configuration version. The digest identifies the version of the retrieval index the service is reading. The configuration ID and version name the service's current default. Its JSON fields are index_digest, embedding_model_id, configuration_id and configuration_version and, from a service that names them, service_version and capabilities, the service's version and the features it names (§8.1), which configuration effective prints (§9).

docs.title: 3.2 Search
docs.text: bellman-matsya search <query> [--collections NAMES] [--limit N] [--json] searches for passages related to the query. --collections takes comma-separated names from repository, literature, articles, hark and buffer_stock; it may be repeated. Without it, the service searches every collection your Matsya token may read and ranks passages by their match to the query, with the collection weights applied. Use the option to restrict the search to named collections. --limit asks for 1 to 20 passages; the service's default is 8. The command prints the index digest and passage count, then each passage's path, heading and page when present, collection, score, identifier and a shortened text excerpt. The JSON answer has index_digest and passages; each passage includes its full text, passage_id, corpus, path, location and score, together with its source metadata. Collections and weights explains the collections and search weights.

docs.title: 4 Jobs that write and check a declaration
docs.text: A target is the level of declaration a job is asked to return: stage, period, trellis or recipe. A stage is one stage file; a period includes its stages and period file; a trellis includes its periods and trellis file; a recipe adds the files needed to solve it. The target is required for job submit.

docs.title: 4.1 Submit a job
docs.text:
bellman-matsya job submit <file> --target {stage,period,trellis,recipe} [--paper]
    [--name NAME | --session <session> | --no-session]
    [--max-cycles N] [--force] [--configuration-id ID]
    [--model-key KEY --source-cluster CLUSTER] [--formulation TEXT] [--json]
bellman-matsya job submit --session <session> --target {stage,period,trellis,recipe}
    [--max-cycles N] [--force] [--configuration-id ID] [--formulation TEXT] [--json]
bellman-matsya job submit-prepared <file> [--delivery-id ID] [--json]

The file of job submit must contain UTF-8 text. By default its text is a model description. --paper marks the text of a paper, whether Markdown, LaTeX or plain text; a PDF is refused before any request with the instruction to convert it first. Without --session or --no-session, the client creates a session named after the file without its extension; --name replaces that name. --session appends the file to an existing session, or, without a file, submits a job from the entries already in that session, which the job reads as they stand when it starts. --no-session sends the file directly; the job's questions then remain in its record. The three session options cannot be combined. --paper requires a file.

--max-cycles is a positive integer limiting iterations after the initial declaration; when omitted, the service uses its configured limit, subject to its maximum. --force continues to writing if preparation ends with questions and records the writer's assumptions. --configuration-id names the published configuration the job runs under, 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters (§9); without it the service's default runs the job, and either way the service's answer names the ID resolved. An ID of another form is refused with status 2 before any request, and an ID the service has not published is the service's 404. --model-key and --source-cluster, given together or not at all, name the groups of indexed sources the job must not read. --formulation names which model to write when the source states several; its text must be nonblank and at most 500 characters. With a file and a session, the command prints the session and entry numbers, the queued job identifier, the job wait line and where to see the session. Without a session it prints where to see questions in the job record. The JSON answer is the queued job object: id, state, configuration_id, credential_source and status_url. Creating a session and appending an entry are separate requests; if the later job request is refused, the error names what the session retained.

With a personal Anthropic key selected (§2.2), the job's request includes it in the header Bellman-Matsya-Anthropic-Key; the requests that create a session and append the file do not. Before its first request the command checks the address the key would be sent to. At a service address that is neither an HTTPS address nor an http address whose host is localhost, 127.0.0.1 or ::1, it creates no session, appends no entry and sends no job, prints Error: A personal Anthropic key is sent only over HTTPS or to localhost, 127.0.0.1 or ::1, and the service address is <address>; use an HTTPS address, or stop selecting the key: unset BELLMAN_MATSYA_ANTHROPIC_KEY, run bellman-matsya configure --clear-anthropic-key, or omit anthropic_api_key., and exits with status 1; it never sends the job without the key. When the service answers that the job's calls are made with that key, with credential_source client, the command prints Credential: your Anthropic API key among its lines. When the answer names service, or holds no credential_source because the service was built before personal keys and ignores the header, the command prints its usual lines, then on standard error Error: the service at <address> accepted job <id> under its own Anthropic key, not yours. and Cancel it with: bellman-matsya job cancel <id>, and exits with status 1; the job remains on the service until it ends or is cancelled.

job submit-prepared submits a job from a prepared-inputs file, a JSON object in UTF-8 that holds the exact inputs of one job as you reviewed them, and sends those inputs as the file holds them, reading no file of the model folder. The file's fields are session, required, the identifier of the session the job is submitted from, 32 lowercase hexadecimal characters; reviewed_through, required, the number of the session's last entry when you reviewed it, an integer from 1; target, required, stage, period, trellis or recipe; starting_declaration, optional, the files the job's first cycle starts from, each file's text under the name the service reads it by, such as example.bl; paths, optional and only with starting_declaration, the same names, each mapped to the file's path in the model folder, such as declaration/stages/example/example.bl, which the client prints and never sends; and configuration_id, max_cycles, force, formulation, and model_key with source_cluster, optional, sent as job submit sends the options of those names. A file that is not such an object, that lacks a required field, or that holds a malformed value or a field of another name is refused before any request with a sentence that names the field, and the command exits with status 1. With a personal Anthropic key selected, the command checks the address the key would be sent to before its first request, as job submit does.

The command first reads the service's index answer (§3.1). When that answer does not name the capability capture_at_acceptance, the service would build the job from the session as it stands when the job starts, and the command sends no job request: it prints Error: The service at <address> does not name the capability capture_at_acceptance in its index answer, so it would build the job from the session's text as it stands when the job starts, not from the history reviewed through entry <N>; the prepared inputs were not submitted. bellman-matsya job submit --session <session> --target <target> submits a job that reads the session as it stands. and exits with status 1. With --delivery-id, an answer that does not name job_delivery_id is refused in the same way, with Error: The service at <address> does not name the capability job_delivery_id in its index answer, so it would refuse a job request that names a delivery identifier; the prepared inputs were not submitted. Otherwise the job is submitted from the session with its reviewed_through, and the service fixes the job's source material when it accepts the job (Reaching the service by HTTP §6): a session that has received an entry after reviewed_through is refused by the service with 409 and a sentence that names each later entry, which the command prints before it exits with status 1, and no job is created.

The command prints Prepared inputs of <file>: session <session>, reviewed through entry <N>, target <target>; Starting declaration: with the number of files, then one line for each file, <path> as <name>, SHA-256 <digest>, with the file's path in the model folder, or its name where paths names none, the name the service reads, and the digest of the text sent; Job <job>: <state>; The service fixed session <session> through entry <N> at acceptance: version <revision> of its text, entries <numbers>.; and the job wait line; with a personal key selected, it reports the key the service used as job submit does. --delivery-id names the request, a name of at most 64 characters. When the answer to a submission is lost, as when the connection fails after the request was sent, run the same command again with the same identifier: the service returns the job it holds and creates no second one, and the command adds The service already holds delivery <ID> as this job; nothing was submitted again. A different request under the same identifier is refused by the service with 409. job status <job> reads the job at any later time (§4.2). The JSON answer is the object that the client assembles: session, reviewed_through and target, from the file; files, one object for each file sent, with name, path, which is null where paths names none, and sha256; capabilities, those the service's index answer named; and job, the service's answer to the job request (§8.2).

docs.title: 4.2 Inspect, wait for, save or cancel a job
docs.text:
Command Options and printed answer bellman-matsya job status <job> [--json] Prints the job's label, identifier and state. While it runs, it adds the current step and any cancellation request. An ended job with a record has the label and status from the first two report headings, its questions when present, the available file names and a job files command. An ended job without a record has its error and detail when present. A job whose credential_source is client adds the line Credential: your Anthropic API key; a job run under the service's key adds nothing. bellman-matsya job wait <job> [--interval SECONDS] [--json] Requests the job's state until it ends. The interval defaults to 5 seconds and cannot be negative. While waiting, it prints a time-stamped line when the state, step or cycle changes; with --json, these progress lines go to standard error. Its final answer is the same as job status. bellman-matsya job files <job> <folder> [--all-iterates] [--overwrite] [--json] Writes a new or empty model folder, then prints its file count and each relative path. It writes report.md and record.json, plus economics.md with the prose paired with the most recent available declaration files under declaration/, including for a not_converged job. The report retains that status: these files are proposals for review. --all-iterates also writes the initial declaration, then each iteration's declaration and its input prose under iterates/, with the full record. --overwrite permits a nonempty folder, replacing files of the same names while retaining others. A job without a record cannot be written. bellman-matsya job export <job> <folder> [--overwrite] [--json] Saves the job's full answer, the record as the service keeps it with every iteration and call, as job.json in the folder, which is created when it does not exist, for any state of the job: a cancelled or failed job without a record is saved with its state, its error, its configuration ID and its digests. Prints the path written, the job's state and its configuration ID. An existing job.json is refused before any request unless --overwrite is given. The file is written whole under a temporary name, then made visible as job.json in one operation. With --json, prints the full answer while still writing the file. A local comparison of two configurations reads this file, not the products-only record.json of job files. bellman-matsya job cancel <job> [--json] Cancels a queued job at once or requests cancellation of a running job, then prints its state and, if still running, the job wait line. A call already sent to the language-model provider completes before cancellation takes effect. An ended job cannot be cancelled.

For status, wait, files and cancel, --json prints the job object defined in §8.2, and for export the same object in the full view. In an ordinary model folder, an open writer note is placed beside its single stage as declaration/stages/<key>/<key>.md, or at declaration/notes.md otherwise. job files checks the folder before requesting the job, and refuses a path through a symbolic link rather than writing through it. The job state, not the command's exit status, tells you whether the writing and checking converged.

docs.title: 5 Sessions and their entries
docs.text:
A session keeps the entries written by the user and Matsya, the jobs submitted from that text, and the turns that answer questions. Its revision is the number of its latest user, paper or acceptance entry. The commands below print session and entry identifiers so the next command can name them.

Command Options and printed answer bellman-matsya session new <name> [--json] Creates an empty session. Prints its identifier and name, then the commands to add an entry and ask a question. bellman-matsya session add <session> <file> [--kind user\|paper] [--replies-to N] [--delivery-id ID] [--json] Appends the file's UTF-8 text; - reads standard input. The default kind is user; paper marks paper text. --replies-to names the numbered question this entry answers. --delivery-id is a name of at most 64 characters; a repeated delivery appends nothing. Prints the entry number and revision, or says that delivery was already held. If a reply starts the next job, it prints its identifier and the job wait line. bellman-matsya session add <session> --kind acceptance --replies-to N [--delivery-id ID] [--json] Appends an acceptance of numbered answer entry N, with no file or text. It prints the same entry and revision lines as other additions. bellman-matsya session show <session> [--json] Prints the session's identifier, name and revision; any job awaiting an answer or selected for questions; jobs by label; turn identifiers; and numbered entries with their kinds and text. bellman-matsya session select <session> <job> [--json] or bellman-matsya session select <session> --none [--json] Selects a job of this session that holds a record, or clears the selection. Prints the selected job and explains which job's outputs later questions read. The job and --none cannot be combined.

An ordinary reply is sent with session add, not with a project-specific reply command. A reply to a question of the job currently awaiting an answer starts its next job automatically, which reads the session's text as it stands when it starts, the reply included; session show or project status prints the entry number needed by --replies-to. When the answer to a reply is lost, send the reply again with the same --delivery-id: the service appends nothing and starts no second attempt, the command prints that the session already holds the delivery, and session show lists the attempt that the first delivery started among the session's jobs.

An entry of the kind user with --replies-to is sent with a selected personal Anthropic key (§2.2), since it may start a job's next attempt, and at a service address that would not receive the key it is refused before its request, as job submit is (§4.1). When the reply starts a job and the entry is not a repeated delivery, the command prints Credential: your Anthropic API key for an attempt that the service runs with that key; for an attempt that the service accepted under its own key it prints its usual lines, then the sentence of §4.1 for that job and the job cancel line, and exits with status 1. A job that ran under a personal key, with credential_source client, is continued only by a reply that includes a key. Without one the service answers 422 with The job awaiting this reply ran under a personal Anthropic key; send the reply with a personal Anthropic key, the session is left unchanged, and the command adds to that sentence Supply one with bellman-matsya configure --set-anthropic-key, BELLMAN_MATSYA_ANTHROPIC_KEY, or MatsyaClient(..., anthropic_api_key=...). The key of a reply may differ from the one the earlier job used, and a reply to a job run under the service's key may select a key for the next attempt.

docs.title: 6 Ask one question
docs.text:
bellman-matsya ask <session> <question> [--stage-file PATH] [--index-digest DIGEST]
    [--follow FOLDER | --no-wait] [--delivery-id ID] [--interval SECONDS]
    [--configuration-id ID] [--json]
bellman-matsya turn status <session> <turn> [--json]
bellman-matsya turn wait <session> <turn> [--interval SECONDS] [--json]

The question is one turn in the session. --stage-file sends a stage file whose elaborated account the answer can read. --index-digest names a stored version of the retrieval index. --configuration-id names the published configuration whose conversation role answers (§9); without it the default answers, and a job the turn starts runs under the same configuration as the turn. A configuration without the conversation role refuses the question before anything is appended. --delivery-id names the question's delivery, a name of at most 64 characters: the same question sent again under it returns the turn already asked and appends nothing, and another question under it is refused by the service with 409. --interval sets the time between requests while waiting: by default 2 seconds for the turn and 5 seconds for a job followed with --follow; it cannot be negative. Unless --no-wait is given, the command waits for the turn: while the turn runs, it prints time-stamped state and step changes, and it then prints the answer, any source quotations and their locations, questions needing your reply, or the reason an incomplete turn stopped. If the turn read a job's outputs, it names that job. If it started a job, it prints the job identifier and the command to follow it.

--follow FOLDER checks that FOLDER is new or empty before sending the question. When the turn starts a job, the command waits for it and writes its model folder there if it holds a record. If no job starts, it says so and writes nothing. With --json, the final standard output is the turn object defined in §8.4, even when a followed job has also ended and its files were written. Progress lines go to standard error. A turn that finishes with a request for input or as incomplete still completes this command with exit status 0; read record.result.status.

--no-wait prints the turn as soon as the service accepts the question, without waiting for its answer: Turn <turn>: <state>, question entry <n> of session <session>, to which a repeated delivery adds ; this delivery was received before, then Read its state with: bellman-matsya turn status <session> <turn> and Wait for its answer with: bellman-matsya turn wait <session> <turn>. It cannot be combined with --follow, and the two together are refused with status 2. turn status reads a turn once by its identifier: before the turn has finished it prints Turn <turn>: <state>, with the turn's error and its detail when the turn failed or was interrupted, and once it has finished it prints the answer as ask does. turn wait requests the turn's state every --interval seconds, 2 by default, printing a time-stamped line when its state or step changes, on standard error with --json, until the turn has finished, failed or been interrupted, and then prints it as turn status does; when you stop it, it prints how to wait again and exits with status 130. Both commands read the turn from any terminal or later process, and both print Credential: your Anthropic API key for a turn whose credential_source is client.

With a personal Anthropic key selected (§2.2), the question is sent with it, and the command checks the address it would be sent to before it sends anything, as job submit does (§4.1): at an address that would not receive the key, nothing is appended and the command exits with status 1. When the service answers that the turn's calls are made with that key, the command prints Credential: your Anthropic API key. When the answer names service, or holds no credential_source, the command prints its usual lines, then on standard error Error: the service at <address> accepted turn <id> under its own Anthropic key, not yours., and exits with status 1. A job that the turn starts uses the turn's key. A turn whose key Anthropic refuses ends incomplete with the reason provider_rejected_credential and the answer Matsya could not answer, because the language-model provider refused the Anthropic API key used for this turn. When the turn's credential_source is client, replace your key or remove it (§2.2); when it is service, tell the service's administrator.

docs.title: 7 A model's project folder
docs.text:
A project folder can hold the author's economics.md and current files under declaration/. Its .bellman-matsya/project.json remembers the session and service address. Run submit, status and pull from that folder. These commands take --json, which returns the fields in §8.5. Working on a project folder follows their use in order.

Command Options, default and printed answer bellman-matsya project init [folder] [--json] Makes folder a project; the default is the current folder, and a missing folder is created. It creates a session named after the folder, appends nonempty economics.md when present, writes .bellman-matsya/project.json and .bellman-matsya/README.md, and creates AGENTS.md with a paragraph for an assistant when no such file exists. It prints the folder and session, any entry, files written and the project submit line. If AGENTS.md exists, it leaves it unchanged and prints the paragraph for you to add. bellman-matsya project submit [--target {stage,period,trellis,recipe}] [--max-cycles N] [--configuration-id ID] [--json] Appends economics.md only if its bytes changed since the last submission. It sends recognized files under declaration/ as the starting declaration and prints which files were sent or left out, the target, the job's label and identifier, and the job wait line. Without --target, a recipe file, methods, calibration or settings selects recipe; otherwise trellis.yml selects trellis, a period file selects period, and no such file selects stage. --max-cycles is a positive integer; without it the service uses its configured limit. --configuration-id is forwarded to the job as job submit sends it. bellman-matsya project status [--json] Prints the folder's session identifier, service and revision, its entries and jobs, any selected job, questions awaiting a reply and their exact bellman-matsya session add ... --replies-to N lines, a bellman-matsya ask line and whether economics.md changed. bellman-matsya project pull [<job>] [--replace \| --into [SUBFOLDER]] [--json] By default chooses the latest ended job in the session that holds a record and writes its complete model folder to bellman-matsya-output/job-<number>/. --into selects another new or empty subfolder within the project; without a value it uses that default. This output folder holds the job's model prose as economics.md. --replace instead writes declaration files into the project folder, replacing matching files while keeping declaration files the job did not produce. When a writer leaves a question open, it writes that note to .bellman-matsya/writer-note.md, preserving an existing stage note. It writes report.md and, when model prose exists, model-prose.md; it leaves the author's economics.md unchanged and prints the paths written, replaced and kept. --replace and --into cannot be combined.

The project file contains the session identifier, service address and digest of the last submitted economics.md. The client sends a project's requests only to its configured service when that address matches the project file. A project command in a folder with no readable project file, or a pull of a job with no record, is refused with status 2. A service refusal still ends with status 1.

With a personal Anthropic key selected (§2.2), project submit sends it with the job's request and not with the entry of economics.md. At a service address that would not receive the key, the command is refused before its first request with the sentence of §4.1 and status 1, so that no entry is appended and no new digest of economics.md is recorded. Its credential line, and its error for a job that the service accepted under its own key, are those of job submit (§4.1).

docs.title: 8 Fields in JSON answers
docs.text: The client preserves the service's JSON field names. A field described as optional below is absent until the related event occurs; a value described as null is present with no value. The project commands instead compose their own objects, and so do job submit-prepared and configuration effective, whose fields §§4.1 and 9 give. configure, docs and bare bellman-matsya have no JSON form.

docs.title: 8.1 Index and search
docs.text:
index --json has index_digest (the index version), embedding_model_id (the model used to represent passages for search), configuration_id (the ID of the service's default configuration) and configuration_version (its readable version), and the printed answer has one line for each of the four. From a service that names them, it also has service_version (the service's version) and capabilities (the features the service names, capture_at_acceptance and job_delivery_id, on which job submit-prepared depends, §4.1), which the printed answer does not show. search --json has index_digest and passages, an array. A passage has these fields:

Fields Meaning passage_id, passage_sha256, text Passage identifier, digest of its full text, and that text. The printed search excerpt is shorter. corpus, source_root, source_id, path, file_sha256 Collection, root and identifier of the source, its path and file digest. access, kind, authority, version, title, source_cluster, model_prompt Source access and descriptive metadata. Some values may be null. location page, page_basis, printed_page_label, heading, line_start, line_end, char_start and char_end; when applicable, also cell_number, cell_type, stage_name, block_id, section and formula_continues. index_digest, manifest_digest, corpus_revision Versions of the index, source manifest and collection. score, raw_score, retrieval_weight, lexical_score, dense_score Weighted search score, score before weighting, weight applied, word-match score and representation-match score.

docs.title: 8.2 Jobs
docs.text:
job submit --json has id (job identifier), state (queued), configuration_id (the configuration the job runs under), credential_source (the key used for the job's language-model calls) and status_url. Under job, the answer of job submit-prepared --json (§4.1) holds the same fields with reviewed_through, revision and entry_numbers and, for a request named with --delivery-id, repeated, state then being the job's present state when repeated is true. status, wait, files, export and cancel return a job object. status, wait and files use the service's products view, the final products and report material rather than every writing cycle; cancel returns the service's job state at cancellation; export returns the full view, the record with every iteration and call. job files --all-iterates writes the full record to disk but still prints the products view with --json.

Field Meaning id, state Job identifier and current state. States are queued, running, converged, not_converged, needs_input, cancelled, failed or interrupted. label Object with model, target, revision, number, state, overtaken and the one-line text printed for a reader. A job without a session has no model, revision or number. cancel_requested, progress, events Whether cancellation was requested; current step, cycle and cycle limit when reported; and the service's call events. created_at, updated_at Times recorded by the service. result Present when the job holds a record. Its products-view fields are listed below. error, error_detail Present when a job ends with an error. The code provider_rejected_credential means that Anthropic refused the Anthropic API key that credential_source names, after its first such answer and with no request under another key. session, revision, entry_numbers, current Present for a job started from a session as each value becomes known: session identifier, version of its text, source entry numbers and whether it was current when it ended. For a job whose request named reviewed_through, the version and the entry numbers are those fixed at acceptance and are present from then on. reviewed_through For a job whose request named it, the number of the session's last entry when its user reviewed it. delivery_id The delivery identifier that the job's request named, when it named one. started_by Turn identifier when a question submitted this job. configuration_id The ID of the configuration the job runs under, fixed when the service accepted the job; null for a job recorded before the service kept it. credential_source client when the job's language-model calls are made with the personal Anthropic key sent with its request, service when they are made with the service's own key; fixed when the service accepted the job, kept when the job fails or is interrupted, and service for a job recorded before the service kept it. It names a key and never holds one, and neither configuration_id nor request_sha256 depends on it. request_sha256, source_sha256, index_digest The digest of the accepted request without its configuration_id, fixed at acceptance; the digest of the source text the job reads, a description stripped of surrounding whitespace and a paper unchanged, fixed at acceptance for a source sent with the request and for a session's text fixed then, and otherwise when the job starts; and the digest of the retrieval index the job selected when it began. Each is null until fixed.

In result, schema identifies the form of the job record; target names the requested level; structure is the form named in the model prose; status and reason state the outcome; description holds the prepared model prose; questions holds requested clarifications; and paper_source_check and paper_form_check hold checks of that prose against the source. cycles_run counts the iterations after the initial declaration. available_writing is null if no writing produced parsed files; otherwise it gives its cycle number, files, and the description from which those files were written. Cycle 0 is the initial writing from the prepared model prose. last_cycle is null if no iteration began; otherwise it describes the final iteration, with files, judging, comparison (with equal and first_difference), citations_supported and unresolved_note. last_completed_comparison gives the latest completed adjacent comparison, its left and right cycle numbers, its equal verdict and its first difference; it is null if no comparison completed. reading gives the index_digest and guides consulted. usage gives charged, calls_by_role and refusal, including any token-ceiling refusal. captured_source, present for a job whose request named reviewed_through, gives reviewed_through, revision and entries, the history the job was built from. A field the service's record does not hold is omitted from the products view. Older records keep their original field meanings and output layout.

docs.title: 8.3 Sessions
docs.text:
session new --json, session show --json and session select --json return a session object. session add --json returns that same object with three additional fields: entry (the entry appended or previously delivered), repeated (whether a delivery identifier was already used) and scheduled (null or an object with id, status_url and credential_source for the next job).

Session field Meaning id, name Session identifier and name. entries Numbered entries. Each has number, kind, text, origin, replies_to and created_at; origin names a job or turn when Matsya wrote the entry, otherwise it is null. revision Number of the latest user, paper or acceptance entry. awaiting_answer, selected_job Identifier of a job awaiting a reply, and identifier of the job selected for later questions; either may be null. jobs, turns Jobs in submission order and turn identifiers. Each listed job has id, state, revision, current and label. created_at, updated_at Times recorded by the service.

docs.title: 8.4 Turns
docs.text: ask --json and turn wait --json return the final turn object, and turn status --json the turn object as it stands; ask --no-wait --json returns instead the service's answer to the question, with id, state, question, repeated, configuration_id, credential_source and status_url. The turn object has id, session, state, question (the session entry number), configuration_id (the configuration whose conversation role answered), credential_source (client when the turn's language-model calls are made with the personal Anthropic key sent with its question, service otherwise), progress, events, created_at and updated_at; record is present when a turn has a record, while error and error_detail may be present after failure. The record has schema, turn, session, question, index_digest, versions, stage_file, fields, calls, reading, retained, decisions, dropped_decisions, usage and result. These record the source versions, any stage file supplied, material read, calls and decisions as well as the answer. In record.result, turn identifies the turn; status is answered, needs_input or incomplete; answer, citations, questions and reason give the response and any reason it stopped, the reason provider_rejected_credential when Anthropic refused the Anthropic API key that credential_source names. passages names material supplied to the turn; index_digest names the index it read; current says whether the session's text remained current; job names the job whose outputs it read, if any; and job_started names a job it submitted, if any. A citation has quote, identity, path, heading, location, authority and index_digest. Both job fields are null when no job applies, or objects with id and label when one does.

docs.title: 8.5 Project commands
docs.text:
Each project answer includes folder, the resolved project-folder path, and project, the contents of .bellman-matsya/project.json: session, server and economics_sha256 (the digest of the description at its last submission, or null). The remaining fields depend on the command:

Command Additional JSON fields project init session: the new service session; entry: the first entry or null; written: paths written; agents: created or kept for AGENTS.md; agents_paragraph: the paragraph written or offered to the user. project submit economics: appended, unchanged or absent; entry: the new entry or null; target: requested level; target_named: whether --target supplied it; starting_declaration: file names sent; left_out: paths under declaration/ not sent; job: the service's job object. project status session: current service session; awaiting: objects with number, text and the exact reply command; ask: command to ask a question; economics_changed: true, false or null if the folder has no readable nonempty description. project pull job: selected job in the products view; into: output subfolder or null with --replace; written: paths written; replaced: paths that replaced files; kept: declaration paths the job did not write.

docs.title: 9 Configurations
docs.text:
bellman-matsya configuration publish <folder> [--json]
bellman-matsya configuration set-default <id> [--json]
bellman-matsya configuration effective [--session <session>] [--configuration-id ID] [--json]

A configuration is the checked folder of instruction texts, settings, Matsya handlers and saved guides that a job or a question runs under; its configuration ID is the SHA-256 digest of its manifest.json. The service keeps every published configuration unchanged under its ID and one default, which a job or a question that names no ID runs under. configuration publish and configuration set-default are refused by the service with 403 for a Matsya token whose holder the service's operator has not named as an administrator; any Matsya token may select a published ID with --configuration-id.

configuration publish sends the folder's files, by their paths relative to the folder and without bytecode caches, as a ZIP archive, and prints the ID and the version the service answered with; the same folder published again prints the same ID. A folder that holds a symbolic link is refused with status 1 before any request. The service checks every file against the manifest before and after it imports the Matsya handler module, and refuses an archive that escapes its folder, holds a duplicate name or a file the manifest does not list, or expands beyond 24 MiB. Publication leaves the default as it is. The JSON answer has configuration_id and version.

configuration set-default makes a published ID the default and prints the new default with its version and the former default. The change takes effect for the next job or question, without a restart; a job or a question already accepted keeps the configuration pinned to it. An ID of another form than 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters is refused with status 2 before any request, and an unpublished ID is the service's 404. The JSON answer has previous_configuration_id, configuration_id and version.

configuration effective prints the settings that a new job or question sent from this terminal would use, without the Matsya token or the key: Service: <address> (from <source>), followed by , bellman-matsya <version> when the service names its version, where the source is BELLMAN_MATSYA_SERVER, the path of the configuration file or the client's built-in address; Matsya token: set (from <source>), where the source is BELLMAN_MATSYA_TOKEN or the path of the configuration file; Configuration: <id>, version <version>, the service's default, or Configuration: <id>, named with --configuration-id when that option names an ID; Session: <session> (from --session), or, in a project folder (§7) without that option, Session: <session> (from .bellman-matsya/project.json), and otherwise Session: none; Anthropic key: none; the service's own key is used, or Anthropic key: your personal key (from <source>), where the source is BELLMAN_MATSYA_ANTHROPIC_KEY or the path of the saved key file (§2.2), which at an address that would not receive the key (§4.1) reads Anthropic key: your personal key (from <source>), which the client does not send to <address>, so new work is refused before any request; and Capabilities: capture_at_acceptance, job_delivery_id, the capabilities that the service's index answer names (§3.1), or Capabilities: none named by the service. It sends one request, for the index, which carries no key. In a project folder whose project file names another service than the one the client is configured for, the command is refused with Error: This folder's session is kept by the service at <folder's address>, and the client is configured for the service at <address>; the client sends a folder's requests only to the service it is configured for. and status 2, and a configuration ID of another form than 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters is refused with status 2 before any request. The JSON answer, which the client assembles, has server and server_source; token_source; configuration_id, configuration_version, which is null for an ID named with --configuration-id, and configuration_source, named or the service's default; session and session_source; key_source and credential, which is client for a key the client sends to this address, refused for a key it does not send there and service without a key; service_version; and capabilities.

docs.title: The Python module and the files the client writes
docs.text:
Summary

The package bellman-matsya-client is also a Python module, bellman_matsya, with one function for each command that sends a request to the service, reading the same configuration and returning the service's JSON answer. This page gives the module's functions and the exact files bellman-matsya job files writes, with the report's headings, for a reader who scripts the client or reads its output by program. The commands themselves are followed in Working with Matsya from the command line and given in full in The command reference.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Matsya in three parts, which defines the session, the job, the label and the target, and The command reference, whose commands the module's functions correspond to. Continued by — Collections and weights, the collections of the retrieval index, the grants that open them and the weights of a search. See also — Reaching the service by HTTP, the requests the functions send; Working with Matsya from the command line, the commands followed through one piece of work.

docs.title: 1 The module
docs.text:
The module bellman_matsya holds the same operations as functions, which read the same configuration and return the service's JSON answer, except job_files, which returns the paths it wrote, and start_job, which returns the service's answers to its requests as {"session": ..., "entry": ..., "job": ...}, with None for a session it did not create or an entry it did not append. The functions correspond to the commands as follows: index to bellman-matsya index, search to bellman-matsya search, start_job to bellman-matsya job submit <file>, submit_job to bellman-matsya job submit --session <session> with no file, the job's request alone, or, given a description's text as source_text in place of session, to bellman-matsya job submit --no-session <file>, or, given a paper's text as source_text with paper=True, to bellman-matsya job submit --paper --no-session <file>, job to bellman-matsya job status, which takes view, products by default or full, the complete record, wait_job to bellman-matsya job wait, job_files to bellman-matsya job files, which takes overwrite and all_iterates, export_job to bellman-matsya job export, which takes overwrite and returns the job's full answer after writing job.json, cancel_job to bellman-matsya job cancel, new_session to bellman-matsya session new, add_entry to bellman-matsya session add, session to bellman-matsya session show, select_job to bellman-matsya session select, with the job None for --none, and ask to bellman-matsya ask, which returns the turn, whose turn["record"]["result"]["job_started"] names the job the turn started, or is None; publish_configuration to bellman-matsya configuration publish, which takes the folder and returns its ID and version, and set_default_configuration to bellman-matsya configuration set-default; the function passage, which returns one passage of the index by its identifier, and report_text, which composes report.md from a job as record.json holds it and sends no request, have no command. submit_job, start_job and ask take configuration_id, the ID of a published configuration, as --configuration-id names it, and submit_job and start_job take model_key and source_cluster, given together or not at all; an ID of another form than 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters raises ValueError before any request. A request the service refuses raises MatsyaError, whose status holds the HTTP status of the service's answer and detail its message: for cancel_job of a job that has ended, 409 and The job has ended. MatsyaClient(token, server_url) holds them as methods for a Matsya token and a service address given explicitly.

import bellman_matsya

started = bellman_matsya.start_job("model.md", target="stage")
job = bellman_matsya.wait_job(started["job"]["id"])
print(bellman_matsya.report_text(job))
bellman_matsya.job_files(job["id"], "proposed-model")

A personal Anthropic key (Matsya in three parts §1) is given to the client by the keyword-only argument anthropic_api_key, as in MatsyaClient(token, server_url, anthropic_api_key=key). The constructor reads neither the key saved by bellman-matsya configure --set-anthropic-key nor the environment, so a caller that omits the argument uses the service's key. It removes the whitespace around the key and raises ValueError with the sentence The personal Anthropic key is empty or contains a space, a line break or a character outside printable ASCII when the key is then empty or holds a character other than the visible ASCII characters ! to ~. The functions of the module, which read the local configuration, select the key as the command does: the value of BELLMAN_MATSYA_ANTHROPIC_KEY when it is set and not empty, otherwise the saved key, and otherwise none; a selected key with that fault raises the same ValueError. The key is sent, in the header Bellman-Matsya-Anthropic-Key, by submit_job, start_job, ask and add_entry of the kind user with replies_to, and by no other function or method. Each of these raises MatsyaError before its first request when it holds a key and the service address is neither an HTTPS address nor an http address whose host is localhost, 127.0.0.1 or ::1, with the sentence A personal Anthropic key is sent only over HTTPS or to localhost, 127.0.0.1 or ::1, and the service address is <address>; use an HTTPS address, or stop selecting the key: unset BELLMAN_MATSYA_ANTHROPIC_KEY, run bellman-matsya configure --clear-anthropic-key, or omit anthropic_api_key., so that start_job then creates no session and appends no entry. Constructing the client is not refused for that reason, and a function that sends no key, such as index, search or job, proceeds with the Matsya token alone.

The functions return the service's answer unchanged, and the caller reads there which key the service used: the credential_source of a job or a turn, client or service, and for a reply that started a job the same field under scheduled. A reply that the service refuses for want of a key raises MatsyaError, whose message adds to the service's sentence Supply one with bellman-matsya configure --set-anthropic-key, BELLMAN_MATSYA_ANTHROPIC_KEY, or MatsyaClient(..., anthropic_api_key=...). No message the module composes contains the key, which it replaces with <Anthropic API key> as it replaces the Matsya token with <Matsya token>, and the repr of a client shows only the service address.

The requests themselves, with curl examples for a user without Python, are in Reaching the service by HTTP.

docs.title: 2 The model folder and the report
docs.text:
A job returns by default its prepared model prose, the latest available declaration files and the prose from which those files were written (available_writing), its questions and the material of its report. The report includes the prose judges' findings, the latest completed comparison of adjacent elaborated semantic objects, and whether a later iteration stopped before comparison, and the language-model tokens charged. A job that ends not_converged still returns its available work; its status and reason explain why the comparison did not establish convergence. The full record also holds the initial writing, each iteration's prose, declaration and comparison, every call, and what the roles read.

bellman-matsya job files <job> <folder> writes an ended job's products into a new or empty folder, in the layout of the model folders of the project's applications:

proposed-model/
├── economics.md              the prose paired with the available declaration, after front matter naming the job, its label, the session,
│                             the version of the session's text and the date the job ended
├── report.md                 the report
├── record.json               the job as the service returned it, in the products view
└── declaration/
    ├── period.yml            a period or trellis file, when the job wrote one
    ├── trellis.yml
    ├── calibration/, settings/   calibration and settings files, when the job wrote them
    └── stages/<key>/
        ├── <key>.bl          each available stage file, <key> its name without the extension
        ├── <key>.md          the writer's note, when it leaves something open, beside a single stage
        └── methods.yml       a stage's methods file, when the job wrote one

With several stages, the writer's note stands as declaration/notes.md. A note that reads none leaves nothing open and is not written, and a record without model prose, such as that of a job that stopped in preparation with questions, writes no economics.md. A folder that holds anything is refused before any request unless --overwrite is given, which replaces the files of the same names and leaves the others. A record that names a file the client would write outside the folder is refused, and nothing is written.

report.md is composed by the client from the record, without a language model. It gives the job, its status, the number of iterations, the prose judges' findings, the latest completed comparison of adjacent elaborated semantic objects, and whether a later iteration stopped before comparison, any open writer's note or questions, and the tokens charged. A prose disagreement is reported without deciding convergence. For an older job, the report keeps its original The round-trip comparison heading and wording.

--all-iterates, which is for examining or training the procedure, adds iterates/initial/ with the first declaration and the prepared prose in model-prose.md. Each iterates/cycle-<n>/ then holds one later declaration, the prose from which it was written in model-prose.md, and the remaining iteration data in cycle.json. iterates/record-full.json holds the complete job record. Thus two iterations yield the initial declaration and two later declarations, with no additional elaboration. The files of an older job retain their original round-trip layout.

bellman-matsya job files <job> proposed-model-iterates --all-iterates

docs.title: 3 The commands in detail
docs.text:
A job of matsya-architect turns a model description into proposed stage files, the Bellman-SYM files (.bl) that declare a model's stages, and checks them. Write the description in a Markdown or text file, submit it, wait for the job to end, and write its model folder, the stage files with the model prose and the report described in §2:

bellman-matsya job submit model.md --target stage
bellman-matsya job wait <job>
bellman-matsya job files <job> proposed-model

job submit creates a session named model, after the file, appends the file's text to it as entry 1 and starts the job from that session. It prints the session's identifier and the job's, which replace <session> and <job>. --name gives the session another name, and --session <session> appends the file to a session you already have. While it waits, job wait prints the job's step and cycle whenever they change; a job may run for many minutes and ends converged, not_converged, needs_input, cancelled, failed or interrupted. A job that ends needs_input appends its questions to the session, unless you added an entry to the session while it ran; in that case they stand in its record only, and bellman-matsya job status <job> says so. bellman-matsya session show <session> prints the appended questions with their numbers, and bellman-matsya session add <session> reply.md --replies-to <number> replies to one; the first reply starts the job's next attempt, unless a later job of the session has started since. job files writes the job's model folder into a new or empty folder.

While a job is queued or runs, job status prints first the job's label (Matsya in three parts §2), such as model · stage · version 1 · job 1 · running; a queued job shows the version only when matsya-master submitted it. While it waits, job wait prints no label: each line it prints gives the time with the job's state, step and cycle, such as 14:03:05 running: step writing (Prose-to-Bellman-Sym), cycle 1 of 3. At the end of a job that holds a record, job status and job wait print the content of the first two headings of its report: the label with the identifiers of the job and of its session, such as model · stage · version 1 · job 1 · converged (<job>), session <session>, and the status and the reason in one sentence, such as The job ended converged, with the reason semantic_fixed_point.; then the job's questions, the available files and the command that writes its model folder. If those files came from an earlier cycle, the output names that cycle. A not_converged result can be saved by job files for inspection; its stage files are proposals, and the report states why the job did not converge. The label of a running job whose session's text has changed since it started ends , text changed since. The label of a job that ended converged, not_converged or needs_input after its session's text changed while it ran ends , built from an earlier version; the label of a job that ended cancelled, failed or interrupted has no such ending. The label of a job of no session is its target and its state, such as stage · running, and at its end the report's heading reads stage · converged (<job>), no session.

bellman-matsya job cancel cancels a queued or running job:

bellman-matsya job cancel <job>

The command prints the job's label and state after the request. A queued job is cancelled at once and never runs. A running job stops before its next call to the language-model provider: a call already sent finishes and is charged, and the job then ends cancelled, keeping its record with the usage of the calls it made; bellman-matsya job wait <job> waits until it has ended. A cancellation that arrives after the job's last call has finished changes nothing, and the job ends with the status it reached, such as converged. Cancelling a job that has ended is refused: the service answers 409, The job has ended, and the command exits with status 1.

A paper is submitted as its text, a Markdown or LaTeX file, with bellman-matsya job submit paper.md --paper --target stage, or from Python with bellman_matsya.start_job("paper.md", paper=True, target="stage"). The paper becomes an entry of the kind paper of a new session named after the file, or of the session that --session or session= names, and the job starts from that session, so that its questions stand in the session as any other job's do. With --no-session, or no_session=True, the paper is sent as the job's source and the job has no session, as bellman_matsya.submit_job(source_text=text, paper=True, target="stage") sends a paper's text. Without --paper, or paper=True, a file is a description. A PDF is refused before any request, the command exiting with status 2 and start_job raising ValueError, each with the sentence A paper is sent as Markdown or LaTeX text; convert the PDF first. Ask the service's administrator before you submit a paper, since its text is sent to the language-model provider.

A search returns the passages of the index, the documentation and literature the service reads, that best match a query, each with its path, its heading and its identifier:

bellman-matsya search "decision perch state and controls" --collections repository --limit 4

The collections that --collections names are listed by bellman-matsya search --help; without the option the service searches every collection your Matsya token may read. The Python function search does the same when collections is omitted. An explicit list restricts the search to those collections, and a list that names a collection your Matsya token may not read is refused with 403, Collection access is not granted.

A session serves both sides of the service: a job of matsya-architect writes the stage files of a model, and a turn of matsya-master answers one question and writes no stage file (Matsya in three parts §2 defines the three). bellman-matsya ask asks one question and prints the answer with the paths and headings of the material it cites; when the conversation role was given the outputs of the job the conversation discusses, the first line names that job by its label and identifier, as Answer from model · stage · version 1 · job 1 · converged (<job>), whether or not the answer cites those outputs:

bellman-matsya session new "a household"
bellman-matsya session add <session> notes.md
bellman-matsya ask <session> "What does the decision perch of a stage hold?"
bellman-matsya session show <session>

A question may also be asked in the session that job submit created. Once the job has ended with a record, the answer reads that job's outputs, unless you cancelled the job or added an entry to the session while it ran, a question included; in those cases select the job, as described below. bellman-matsya job submit --session <session> with no file starts a job from a session's entries as they stand.

A job may also be started by asking matsya-master for one in words, such as "Submit this as a job.": the conversation role then starts a job from the session's text as it stands, the question included, and the command prints, after the answer, the line Job <number> started from version <revision> of this session's text (<job>); follow it with: bellman-matsya job wait <job>. A question that only mentions a job starts nothing. With --follow <folder>, the command then waits for that job as bellman-matsya job wait does, printing its steps, and at its end writes the model folder into the folder as bellman-matsya job files does; the command checks before it sends the question that the folder is new or empty. The job runs on the server either way, and --follow only keeps the command attached to it:

bellman-matsya ask <session> "Submit this as a job." --follow proposed-model

A job or a question runs under one published configuration, the service's default unless --configuration-id <id> names another, and every answer on the job or the turn names the ID resolved. To compare two configurations on the same source, submit the same text directly to each, so that a session's later entries cannot change what a queued job reads, and save each job's full answer:

bellman-matsya job submit model.md --target stage --no-session --configuration-id <id A>
bellman-matsya job submit model.md --target stage --no-session --configuration-id <id B>
bellman-matsya job export <job A> records/case-1/<id A>/trial-1
bellman-matsya job export <job B> records/case-1/<id B>/trial-1

job export writes job.json, the job's full answer, for any state of the job, a failed or cancelled job among them, with its configuration ID and the digests of its accepted request, its source text and its index. The paired check meaning-map-config-pair of the package meaning-map-training reads two such files with their local configuration snapshots and reports whether the two jobs' inputs were comparable; the Matsya developer guide describes it. bellman-matsya configuration publish <folder> and bellman-matsya configuration set-default <id> are the administrator's commands that publish a configuration and make one the default.

session show lists the session's jobs by their labels and identifiers, in the order they were created, and names the selected job when one is set. A question reads the outputs of the selected job or, when none is selected, of the latest job that Matsya in three parts §3 names; any entry you add while a job runs, a description, a paper, a reply, a question or an acceptance of an answer, keeps that job from being chosen this way. To discuss another job of the session, one that holds a record, select it; --none clears the selection, and the end of a job never changes it:

bellman-matsya session select <session> <job>
bellman-matsya session select <session> --none

Service commands take --json to print the service's JSON answer unchanged; the project commands use it to print an answer assembled from the folder and the service. Bare bellman-matsya, configure and docs have no JSON form. job submit, which may send three requests, prints the answer to the job's request, ask the answer on the finished turn, also with --follow, and job files the job in the products view, the answer record.json holds. bellman-matsya <command> --help lists a command's options. When the service refuses a request, for example for a Matsya token it does not hold (401), a job or session that is not yours (404), a job that has ended for job cancel (409) or a malformed request (422), the command prints the service's message and exits with status 1. No command prints your Matsya token.

docs.title: Collections and weights
docs.text:
Summary

Matsya's retrieval index, the store of passages from which a search returns those that best match a query (Matsya in three parts §1), divides the files it indexes into five collections: this project's documentation and declarations, a private literature, journal articles, HARK and Buffer Stock Theory. This page says what each collection holds and which collections a Matsya token reads; how the options of a search, the collections, the number of passages, the named sources and the boosts, select and rank the passages; what a returned passage holds; and what Matsya itself reads when a job writes a declaration or a turn answers a question.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Matsya in three parts §1, which defines the retrieval index, its passages and its digest; Reaching the service by HTTP §4, which sends a search and reads a passage again; the command bellman-matsya search of Working with Matsya from the command line §8. Continued by — the Matsya developer guide, which begins with the program and the configuration; its page The retrieval index describes how the index is built and how a search runs. See also — the wiki page Matsya collection, with the number of sources in each collection.

docs.title: 1 The five collections
docs.text:
A source is one file admitted to the index, named by its source identifier, and a collection is a named group of sources. The index and the service's answers record a source's collection under the name corpus.

Collection What it holds repository This project's published documentation, among it the language guide, the Bellman calculus and the concept wiki, with the stage files of the applications and the notebooks of the tutorials; and a private part, development notes and presentations on the theory of the language literature A private literature: extracts and notes of books and papers on dynamic programming, category theory and computation articles Journal articles, at present all from Econometrica, gathered for the training of Matsya, the runs of a revised configuration on a set of papers: a few as the PDF files themselves, and a larger set as page-marked transcriptions and secondary readings hark The source code, documentation and examples of HARK, Econ-ARK's Heterogeneous Agents Resources and toolKit, at one fixed commit buffer_stock The LaTeX source and the PDF of the paper Theoretical Foundations of Buffer Stock Saving, at one fixed commit

The passages a search can return depend on the version of the index the service reads. Every answer of a search names that version by index_digest, its digest (Matsya in three parts §1); bellman-matsya index prints it.

docs.title: 2 Who reads each collection
docs.text:
The published part of repository, and hark and buffer_stock, are open to every Matsya token. The private part of repository, literature and articles are each read under a grant, a permission that the service's administrator records in the service's grant file for the holder of a Matsya token, under the names repository-private, literature and articles. A holder whom the grant file names holds exactly the grants named there, and every other holder receives the file's default list of grants. On the service the administrator runs, that default holds all three grants, so that every Matsya token reads all five collections unless the administrator has named its holder with fewer. A missing or malformed grant file leaves every Matsya token the published parts alone. The service reads the grant file again for every search, job and turn, so a changed grant applies from the next request.

Naming a collection in a request does not grant it. A search or an answer that names literature or articles without the grant is refused with the status 403 and the sentence Collection access is not granted, and nothing is searched. A search of repository is never refused: it returns passages of the published part, and of the private part only under its grant. A passage is returned, by a search or by GET /v1/passages/{passage_id}, only when the Matsya token may read its collection and part.

docs.title: 3 The options of a search
docs.text:
POST /v1/search and POST /v1/answer take the same JSON object, of at most 16 KiB. A field outside this table, or a value outside its range, is refused with the status 422.

Field What it sets Default Allowed values query the search text required a text of at most 1,000 characters that is not blank collections the collections searched every collection your Matsya token may read a non-empty list of the five names of §1 limit the most passages returned 8 an integer from 1 to 20 source_ids the sources the search is restricted to every source of the collections searched from 1 to 20 source identifiers, each a text of at most 240 characters that is not blank boosts a factor that multiplies the weight of a collection searched (§4) no factor an object whose names are among the collections searched, each with a number from 0 to 1000

Omit collections to search all the collections your Matsya token may read. Matsya ranks their passages by their match to the query, with the weights of §4 applied. An explicit list restricts the search to the named collections; it grants no additional access (§2).

A source identifier is copied from the source_id of a passage that an earlier search returned. A restriction to named sources keeps the selected collections and the grants: an identifier of a source outside them returns nothing. limit is an upper bound, and a search returns fewer passages when fewer match. bellman-matsya search sets query, collections with its option --collections and limit with --limit; the function search of the Python module sets all five fields.

This request searches the repository and HARK, asks for six passages and halves HARK's weight:

{
  "query": "endogenous grid method with a borrowing constraint",
  "collections": ["repository", "hark"],
  "limit": 6,
  "boosts": {"hark": 0.5}
}

docs.title: 4 How a search ranks passages
docs.text:
