A period added between two periods raises by one the index of every period on its earlier side: a repeated entry is split around the new period, and the recipe's ranges of periods and the range keys of its binding lists are raised with it and named on the status line. A calibration schedule keyed by period index, such as one that states that periods[h] is a certain age, is not read by the gesture and is yours to check. A period after the terminal one is not added from the graph, since it would change what the model ends with and move every period's index; such a period is yours to type at the head of periods, and selecting the terminal period's frame lists in Details, under moved by a period typed first, the ranges and keys of the recipe it would move. The new entry stands above the comment lines over the entry after it, so that each comment stays over the entry it describes. Where the trellis file writes one inter-period mapping for every pair, that mapping is kept where its fields leave the new period's earlier neighbor and arrive at the new period, and leave the new period and arrive at its later neighbor, as the package checks a mapping that stands for every pair; where they do not, the list is expanded to one mapping for each pair, every existing pair receiving a copy and each new pair an empty mapping, and from then on a drag between two periods fills that pair's mapping alone. answers.yml, where the folder holds it, records the expansion, and while that record stands Problems lists each mapping that differs from the others.

Removing and moving a join. A click selects a cable, a join that a connector or an inter-period mapping writes or that equal names make, and names it in Details: first its route, branch keep, periods[2]/tenure ≻ → periods[2]/keeper_cons ≺, its status in the package's words, certified or not certified with the obligations that withhold the certificate, and one row per wire with its set and its origin, a link to the entry's line where an entry writes it; then the rows of the entry, the periods and the fields as before. Backspace or Delete, while the graph holds the focus, or the button Remove in Details, takes the entry out of the file's unsaved text. A join that equal names make, which no entry writes, is selected too: Details prints joined by the names under written and offers Rename in place of Remove, and Backspace or Delete removes nothing. Rename writes the name you type in place of the arrival field you choose in the select, at every place the reading stage's file writes that field, the header that lists it and the lines that read it, and the status line names the file and the lines, allocation.bl, lines 22–23: w_c renamed to w_in. The change stands in the stage file's unsaved text; once the file is saved and the model read again, the two fields are drawn unjoined, and a drag joins them through a connector, or joins either of them to another stage. Both authored and inferred joins can be moved. A selected cable rings its plug and its socket, the two ends that move, in blue. Dragging that end to the port of another stage in the same period or the adjacent one proposes a replacement through the cable's list. Moving an inferred join writes a compact authored arrow, which takes precedence over the former inference; it does not rename a field. Undo restores the former source and selection, and saving and reopening preserves the authored replacement. Details lists the package's compatibility result and any outstanding conditions for a complete connection. Matching names alone do not establish compatibility. A join that one entry writes takes the new entry in place of the old. A join that several entries write, such as the three fields a_nxt_kp, h_nxt_kp and z_nxt_kp that keeper_cons passes to the next period's tenure in the durables model, opens the cable's list, one row for each arrival field of the stage it is dropped on with a select of the branch's continuation fields, pre-filled where the package would pair the fields on its own. Before you press join, a line names the pairs the move takes from the stage the end leaves, periods[0]/bequest_pa loses a_s: a_bq, h_s: h_bq; join takes out the entries of every pair of the cable and types the new ones. Where the joins of two stages into one stage of the next period are drawn as one line between the two periods, that line moves by its reading end alone. A removal or a move is one change of the file's text: the editor's undo reverses it where the file was open, and in a file the gesture opened, which takes the change as its text and not into its undo history, Command+Z or Ctrl+Z takes the gesture back as for a gesture of several files. The trellis left with fields that no join reaches is drawn, not refused, those fields marked on their boxes and listed under Problems.

Removing a stage from a period. A click selects a stage's card. Backspace or Delete, while the graph holds the focus, or the button Remove from periods 0–5 in Details of the selected occurrence, takes the stage's key out of the list that writes its period, in every period that list writes, and with it each entry of a connector or an inter-period mapping that joins the stage and that would name no field once the stage is gone, since no other stage of the period declares the field the entry names. The key and those entries go in one change of the file's text, so that the model is still read, and the status line names the file, the list and those periods, then each entry removed: trellis.cons-port.yml, periods[0].stages: port removed, periods 0–5; trellis.cons-port.yml, periods[0].connectors[0]: {disc.a: k} removed, periods 0–5; trellis.cons-port.yml, inter_connectors[0]: m_next: m removed, periods 0–5. An entry that another stage of the period still takes by the same field name is kept, and a join by equal names, which no entry writes, goes with the stage. Where that list is the last that holds the stage, the stage's row leaves the recipe in the same change, since the package refuses a recipe that names a stage no period holds, and one undo restores the row and the key: trellis.yml, periods[0].stages: bequest removed, periods 0; spec.yml, stages: bequest removed; trellis.yml, periods[0].connectors[0]: {a_nxt_kp: a_bq, …} removed, periods 0. The stage's files stay on disk, and the tree offers its folder for removal. Backspace removes nothing in the backward graph, and the list under the Problems button then says Backspace acts in the forward trellis view. A stage is moved to another period by removing it from one and adding it to the other with + stage; while a reading of the model stands refused, + stage and the button Stages still open the list on the last graph drawn, and a stage added there is written into the files' text as any stage added is.

Removing a stage, a period or a file from the model. For a trellis read from a recipe, the trash can in a stage's row of the Recipe tab, whose hover reads Remove tenure from this recipe, and the button Remove stage in Details of any of its stage occurrences, take the stage out of the model. Details of a selected occurrence offers its two removals in its first row, each naming its scope in its hover: Remove from periods 0–5, Takes port out of period.yml, which writes periods 0–5, and Remove stage, Removes port from spec.yml and every period; its files are deleted on save unless another recipe names them. A removal of the stage takes it out of the model: its row leaves the recipe, its key leaves every period's list that holds it, in the trellis file and the period files, each connector entry that joins it and that would name no field once it is gone leaves with it, and answers.yml loses its records of the stage where the folder holds that file. The button Remove period in Details of a selected period takes the trellis file's entry of that period out, or lowers its repeat by one where the entry writes several periods, and lowers the recipe's ranges and range keys above it, the inverse of adding a period. Each is one change of the files' unsaved text and one undo, and the status line names each file and address, as for the stage port of the portfolio model: spec.yml, stages: port removed; period.yml, stages: port removed, periods 0–5; period.yml, connectors[0]: {m_next: m} removed, periods 0–5; trellis.yml, inter_connectors[0]: disc.a: k removed, periods 0–5; deleted on save: stages/port/, settings/port.yml. Nothing is deleted from disk by the gesture: the stage's folder, stages/<key>/, the calibration, settings and methods files that no other row of any recipe of the folder names, and the period file of an entry taken out that no other entry names, are listed deleted on save and deleted when the file that named them is saved, the save's note naming them again, deleted: stages/port/; the undo of the gesture withdraws them. A file that a variant's recipe or another row still names is never listed. In the tree, a period file that no trellis file names and a stage folder within which no recipe names a file stand beside the icon button Remove, a trash can, which marks them to be deleted on the next save; a marked row is drawn dimmed with deleted on save, and its button Keep withdraws the mark. The page deletes a file that git tracks from the working tree alone, and stages nothing.

Saving. After a drag, a drop, a removal or a rename, the file the gesture edited opens in the editor at the edited line, selected, while the graph keeps the focus, and the status line names the file, the address and the periods the line reaches, trellis.yml, periods[0].connectors[0]: {m_next: m} written, flat, periods 0–5. Only a new file, a template's stage file with the files it brings or a new period file, is written to disk; every other edit stands in the file's unsaved text, which the tree marks unsaved. A drop or a form may edit several files, the recipe, a period file, the trellis file and answers.yml, and since Save writes the open file alone, you open and save each file the tree marks unsaved. Such a gesture is one undo in each file it edited, and so is a gesture that edited one file the editor did not hold open: Command+Z on macOS, Ctrl+Z elsewhere, in the tab of any of those files takes the gesture back in every one of them that still holds the text it wrote, and one undo never takes back two gestures. The status line keeps the note of the last gesture in a stage's view as in the trellis view. A line the package refuses stands in the list under the Problems button in the package's own sentence, linked to the typed line; the button take the line out at that line restores the text before the gesture while the file still holds the text the gesture made, and the last graph stays, dimmed.

docs.title: 9 What it does not do
docs.text:
It reads no model file with a parser of its own; the only parser of the language is the package's. It runs no numerical method and solves nothing. It stores no layout in the model folder, and the graph draws nothing by hand: its only edits are the gestures of §8, each of which changes the text of a file. It commits nothing on its own, resolves no conflict, holds no credential, and reformats no file.

Its editor shows one file at a time, with a tab for each file opened, and it binds a stage file that the page's recipe holds as one occurrence at a time: the occurrence you opened it as, by a double click, by Open the stage or from the head's list of positions, and otherwise, as when you click it in the tree, its first. It writes none of the following in the model folder: the trellis a stage was opened from and the places of the steps back and forward, which stay in the open page, and the sizes and folds of the regions and the choice high contrast, which stay in the browser's storage. A file a trellis reads outside the folder, as a stage file of applications/portfolio-choice/ that the trellis files of applications/cons-port/ read, opens in the editor under its path relative to the folder, ../portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl, and the tree and git's letters cover the folder alone.

docs.title: Fields, evaluation and methods
docs.text:
Summary

Every name of a stage file stands for one thing. A field is a named quantity at a perch: a state, a control, a shock or a value; a declared function and a parameter are not fields. At a policy, each field becomes a function of the state, and the policy is no argument of that function. Some fields are evaluated, which means that the stage returns their functions by name; the others are parts of a longer expression. The distinction decides where a numerical method may stand: a method that computes an operation stands on the operator, and a method that stores a function stands where a function has a name.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — The stage: perches, fields and blocks. Formal account — From source to semantics: the rule that reads fields as functions. Used by — Methodization: how a methods file names a place of the stage.

We use the consumption stage applications/portfolio-choice/declaration/stages/cons/cons.bl. The decision state \(\mathrm m_d\), cash on hand, lies in \(\mathsf X_m = \mathbb R_{++}\), and saving \(\mathrm a\) lies in \(\mathsf X_a = \mathbb R_+\). A consumption value \(\mathrm c\) is feasible at \(\mathrm m_d\) when \(\mathrm c \in \Gamma(\mathrm m_d) = (0, \mathrm m_d]\). The law of motion is \(g_\succ(\mathrm m_d, \mathrm c) = \mathrm m_d - \mathrm c\), utility is \(u\), and the continuation value function is \(V_\succ : \mathsf X_a \to [-\infty, \infty)\). A policy is a measurable function \(c : \mathsf X_m \to \mathbb R_{++}\) with \(c(\mathrm m_d) \in \Gamma(\mathrm m_d)\) for every \(\mathrm m_d\). Roman \(\mathrm c\) is a consumption value and italic \(c\) is a policy.

docs.title: 1 A value function at a policy
docs.text:
The block cntn_to_dcsn holds the line V = 𝑢(c) + V[>], an equation between fields. At a policy \(c\), consumption is \(c(\mathrm m_d)\) and saving is \(\mathrm m_d - c(\mathrm m_d)\), so the line defines the decision value function

\[V(\mathrm m_d) = u(c(\mathrm m_d)) + V_\succ(\mathrm m_d - c(\mathrm m_d)) \qquad (\mathrm m_d \in \mathsf X_m).\]

The function \(V\) has the single argument \(\mathrm m_d\), and the policy is no argument of it. The policy enters wherever the control appears, in the reward and in the law of motion alike, and we write the two at the policy as

\[G_{\succ, c}(\mathrm m_d, \mathrm w) = u(c(\mathrm m_d)) + \mathrm w, \qquad g_{\succ, c}(\mathrm m_d) = g_\succ(\mathrm m_d, c(\mathrm m_d)),\]

so that \(V(\mathrm m_d) = G_{\succ, c}\big(\mathrm m_d, (V_\succ \circ g_{\succ, c})(\mathrm m_d)\big)\). The convention follows Sargent and Stachurski, who set \(r_\sigma(x) = r(x, \sigma(x))\) and \(P_\sigma(x, x') = P(x, \sigma(x), x')\), and their policy operator is \((T_\sigma v)(x) = r(x, \sigma(x)) + \beta \sum_{x'} v(x') P(x, \sigma(x), x')\), a function of the state alone; Hernández-Lerma et al. abbreviate \(c(x, f(x))\) and \(F(x, f(x))\) to \(c(x, f)\) and \(F(x, f)\).

A function of the state and a consumption value together, \((\mathrm m_d, \mathrm c) \mapsto u(\mathrm c) + V_\succ(g_\succ(\mathrm m_d, \mathrm c))\), is needed in one place only: inside a maximization, where \(\mathrm c\) is the variable that the maximization ranges over. The line c = argmax_{cp : Γ(m_d)}(𝑢(cp) + V[>]) of the policy block is such a place. A policy found by inverting an Euler equation forms no such function.

docs.title: 2 Which fields are evaluated
docs.text:
The header of a block is its bracketed first line, which lists the block's inputs and outputs with their perches. A field is evaluated, meaning that the stage returns its function under the field's name, in two cases.

  1. The field is an output in a block's header. The header [id=cntn_to_dcsn, (V[>], c) : !cntn -> (V) : !dcsn], written here without its types, returns \(V\); a derivative line of the block, D_{m_d}V = 𝑑𝑢(c), states the derivative of that value in the decision coordinate and returns no further field. The header of the policy block returns the control \(c\). The inputs of a header are evaluated elsewhere: \(V_\succ\) by the stage that follows, and the policy by the policy block.
  2. The field is the left side of a line marked !node. In applications/smooth-ambiguity-savings/declaration/stages/sa_savings/sa_savings.bl the line CE = E_{Ψ}(V[>]^(1-γ))^(1/(1-γ)) :: [id=risk_ce, !node] returns the certainty equivalent \(CE\).

Every other field is a part of a longer expression. For an unmarked line such as W = β*V[>], the expression of \(W\) is substituted wherever \(W\) is used, and the stage returns no function under that name. A block defines a symbol once.

docs.title: 3 Evaluation
docs.text: Evaluation takes the expression on the right side of an evaluated field's line, such as \(x \mapsto f(g(h(x, l(x))))\), and returns a function \(p\) with \(p(x)\) equal to the expression at every \(x\). In the exact mathematics \(p\) is the expression computed at each \(x\), and evaluation changes nothing. Numerically, \(p\) may be an approximation, such as an interpolant of the expression's values on a grid. The approximation is a different function, with mathematics of its own, which the stage does not describe: the stage records the method, its options and what it requires.

docs.title: 4 Where a method stands
docs.text:
A methods file attaches numerical methods to places of the stage.

stage: sa_savings
methods:
  - on: E_Ψ
    method: !gauss-hermite
    settings:
      n_nodes: [n_Ψ_nodes]
  - on: cntn_to_dcsn.risk_ce
    method: !Linear
    settings:
      grid: !Cartesian
      orders: {m_d: n_m}
      bounds: {m_d: [m_min, m_max]}

A method that computes an operation stands on the operator. Gauss–Hermite quadrature is a rule for one integral against a normal or lognormal distribution, and E_Ψ names the expectation. A method that stores a function stands where a function has a name: !Linear holds \(CE\) by its values on a grid and reads it between them by linear interpolation, and cntn_to_dcsn.risk_ce names the line that returns \(CE\). The setting grid names the grid by its kind, !Cartesian, a product of one grid for each coordinate, and the grid's order and bounds stand beside it. A method of one kind is refused at a place of the other. Quadrature says how the expectation inside the line is computed and says nothing about how \(CE\) is held, so the package refuses it on the line:

!gauss-hermite does not admit target kind node; method-attachment admits operator E

An option a method requires is written beside it, and configure refuses a value outside its type.

The places a stage admits are its own answer, stage.places(), with the kind of each. A method that stores a function admits the evaluated fields, a declared function and the stored form of a builder's output, at the Evaluation that closes the builder, which the methods file names by what it stores: policy.evaluate for the policy function, and cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.value and cntn_to_dcsn.evaluate.marginal for a value function and the derivative of it that a derivative line states. A method that computes an operation admits the operator. A function that the file does not name, such as \(V_\succ \circ g_\succ\), is no place at all: an author who wants it stored writes it on a line of its own and marks the line !node.

docs.title: Abstract dynamic program (ADP)
docs.text: An abstract dynamic program (ADP), in Sargent and Stachurski's terminology, was previously called an abstract decision process in this wiki. An ADP specifies a partially ordered value space and a family of policy evaluation maps; it does not require a particular state representation or source language.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(V\) be a partially ordered set and \(\{T_\sigma:\sigma\in\Sigma\}\) a nonempty family of order-preserving self-maps on \(V\). The index \(\sigma\) names a policy. When each \(T_\sigma\) has a unique fixed point \(v_\sigma\), that point is its policy value. The optimal value is \(\sup_\sigma v_\sigma\) when this supremum exists in the specified value space.

The associated Bellman operator is

\[ Tv=\sup_{\sigma\in\Sigma}T_\sigma v, \]

where the supremum must exist in \(V\). An arbitrary partially ordered set does not ensure this. A policy is greedy for \(v\) when its update attains that supremum; existence of the supremum does not imply existence of a greedy policy.

Sargent and Stachurski's fixed-point-to-optimality result assumes well-posed policy maps, a fixed point \(\bar v\) of \(T\), a \(\bar v\)-greedy policy, and the implication \(T_\sigma v\leq v\Rightarrow v_\sigma\leq v\). These assumptions connect the operator equation to optimal policy values. They are not consequences of declaring an ADP.

docs.title: Relation to staged models
docs.text:
The recursive decision process (RDP) adds feasible actions and a choice-value aggregator that constructs the policy maps. A stationary composition of stages can define an ADP when it preserves a specified value space and order. An individual stage may instead map between the value spaces of different perches, and a finite-horizon problem requires terminal data rather than a stationary fixed point.

Value-function iteration applies \(T\) repeatedly. Policy iteration alternates policy evaluation and greedy policy selection. Their convergence requires additional assumptions; assigning a numerical method does not establish them. semiconjugacy (strong / order) describes specified relations between alternative operator forms.

Reference: Sargent and Stachurski, Dynamic Programming, Volume II: General States, 10 April 2026 edition, Definition 2.1.1, §2.1.1, and Theorem 2.1.7 and Corollary 2.1.8, pp. 66–67.

docs.title: Accretion modules
docs.text:
Accretion constructs a finite-horizon model backwards, adding one period at a time to the periods already specified. In Bellman-SYM the resulting sequence is a trellis: periods together with explicit connections between them. The reusable components are stage files, which state the equations, and period descriptions, which specify how the stage occurrences, the elaborations of a stage file at the positions of a period, are connected.

For example, we can first specify the final year of a household's life, then add the preceding retirement years, and finally the working years. Each addition supplies the equations and parameter values for that year and connects it to its successor. A longer model can reuse the same stage files while changing the income process, survival probabilities or available decisions across periods.

docs.title: Backward construction
docs.text:
We start with an empty sequence and construct the model in the following order.

  1. Specify the terminal period, including any continuation data required after its decisions, and add it to the sequence.
  2. Construct the preceding period from its stage files, with the parameter values and the numerical choices, its methods and settings, appropriate to that period.
  3. Declare the inter-period connector, which identifies compatible outgoing fields of the earlier period with incoming fields of its successor. Add the new period and its connection to the sequence.
  4. Repeat until the sequence includes every period to be modeled.

A period can contain several stages. Within-period connectors state which stage outputs supply which subsequent inputs; inter-period connectors do the same across dates. A connector identifies or renames compatible fields. Changes in resources, income or other quantities require equations in the stages, rather than an implicit transformation inside the connector.

The period records are ordinary dictionaries and lists, which can be assembled interactively or generated in a loop from a parameter schedule. A stage file need not receive the horizon or its position in the sequence: those belong to the model assembly. Each use of a file creates a separate stage occurrence with its own parameter values and numerical choices.

docs.title: Relation to backward induction
docs.text:
Accretion assembles a model; backward induction solves its successive decision problems using the solution already obtained for the next period. The two can be interleaved: after specifying and solving the terminal period, we can add and solve one earlier period at a time. Alternatively, we can assemble the finite sequence before solving it. Assembly alone produces no policy function.

Consider a final-period problem in which resources are nonnegative, any consumption between zero and available resources is feasible, utility is strictly increasing in consumption, and unspent resources have no terminal value. Its solution is to consume all resources. The preceding period's problem then uses that terminal rule to value saving. Carroll (2006, §2) describes the recursion from a final-period consumption rule to earlier rules. The choice of numerical method for each step is separate from the order of the recursion.

HARK provides a related computational arrangement: its one-period solver receives the next period's solution and the inputs for the current period. Its architecture guide documents this separation. The accretion convention of the Bellman factory uses the same backward dependence, while keeping model assembly distinct from numerical solution.

docs.title: Period indices
docs.text:
Let the nonnegative integer \(h\) count periods before the terminal period. A trellis stores its periods in accretion order: periods[0] is the terminal period, periods[1] is its predecessor, and so on. Chronological order is the reverse. If the sequence contains \(n \ge 1\) periods, its inter-period joins have indices \(0 \le h < n-1\): inter_connectors[h] joins the continuation fields of periods[h + 1] to the arrival fields of periods[h]. There is no inter-period join in a one-period model. Values used in backward induction are read in the opposite direction to the forward evolution of the state.

The terminal period can contain decisions of its own. Any continuation value supplied after those decisions is separate terminal data, rather than an additional period or an inter-period connector. The trellis guide states this convention.

Appending an earlier period does not change the indices of periods already present. If economic age is measured in one-period units and terminal age is \(T\), the age at index \(h\) is \(T-h\). Age-dependent wages or survival probabilities can therefore be supplied from a parameter schedule when each stage occurrence is constructed. Where age is itself a state of the economic model, the stage file declares it as a field.

An extensible sequence is still a finite-horizon model. An infinite-horizon problem needs its own formulation or a justified limit of finite-horizon problems; numerical solutions also require convergence and accuracy checks. A terminal decision problem and a terminal value supplied to initialize a recursion are distinct modeling choices; HARK's discussion of terminal solutions illustrates the distinction.

docs.title: Reusing model components
docs.text:
The Bellman factory organizes inputs for repeated construction. A registry stores named sources of parameter values, numerical settings and methods; a recipe selects and combines those sources for the required stage occurrences; load_recipe(directory, recipe, **fills) of bellman.trellis returns the syntactic trellis whose records hold the merged mappings, and assemble_trellis, also of bellman.trellis, elaborates and binds it in one call. A model-building loop can use the resolved inputs for an age profile without putting the entire life cycle into each stage file.

The registry and recipe are optional means of supplying these inputs. A modeler can instead construct the period records directly. The trellis guide describes those records, and the factory guide describes the factory's calls. Neither route makes a terminal condition, an equation or a numerical method unnecessary.

docs.title: Current implementation
docs.text:
Accretion is how accrete and elaborate_trellis of bellman.trellis work. A trellis is a dictionary, {"periods": [...], "inter_connectors": [...]}, each period {"stages": {key: record or stage}, "connectors": [...]}; an empty one is {"periods": [], "inter_connectors": []}. accrete(trellis, period, inter_connector) appends a period and the mapping that joins it to the period appended before it, and rewrites no existing record. elaborate_trellis(syntactic, previous=None) constructs the stage occurrences from the records, copies those that are already elaborated and, given a second argument, those whose record is unchanged, and derives each period's joins from the fields; the three trellis verbs calibrate_trellis, methodize_trellis and configure_trellis bind every stage occurrence from the mapping the syntactic trellis holds at its key.

The application supplies the sequence of periods and its connections; no function of the package appends a period of its own accord, runs backward induction or solves a life-cycle model. The trellis guide distinguishes the representation from the operations available on it.
