docs.title: Addition (methods file)
docs.text:
Summary

An addition is a methods file: a .bl file read by the stage grammar, whose first line is @methods: <stage>, and which is unioned with the stage file on the two syntax trees before elaboration. The union adds and never replaces: a block of the addition names a block of the stage by its id and adds its header entries to that block's header and its lines after that block's lines. The stage file alone states the model; the union with its additions is the stage as it is computed.

Relationship with other documents

Formal account — Methods §§8, 9: the erasure of the addition and the two levels of a stage. Builds on — Methods and Grid: the two components an addition's entries type; Settings: the declarations an addition carries. Used by — Methodization: the written form; The Bellman factory: the recipe that names the additions of each stage occurrence.

docs.title: 1 The form
docs.text:
@methods: buffer_stock

n_a : ℕ              :: ["number of points of the savings grid"]
a_min : Xa           :: ["lower bound of the savings grid"]
a_max : Xa           :: ["upper bound of the savings grid"]

[id=policy, policy.method : !egm | policy.grid : !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a))
    | evaluate.method : !Linear] {
    c[>] = 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(β*D_{a}V[>])       :: [id=InvEuler]
    m[>] = a + c[>]                 :: [id=g_cntn_to_dcsn]
    c[~] = c[>]                     :: [id=cons_choice]
}

[id=cntn_to_dcsn] {
    D_{m}V = 𝑑𝑢(c)                                  :: [id=marginal]
}

[id=dcsn_to_arvl
    | evaluate.method : !Linear(extrap=clamp)
    | evaluate.grid : !Cartesian(k=(k_min, k_max, n_k))
    | E_ψ_ξ.method : !gauss_hermite(n_ψ=n_ψ_nodes, n_ξ=n_ξ_nodes)] {
    D_{k}V[<] = E_{ψ,ξ}(R * (Γ*ψ)^(-ρ) * D_{m}V)    :: [id=marginal]
}

The file reads the buffer-stock stage, whose savings coordinate a is declared on the set Xa and whose permanent income growth factor is Γ. The first group of a bracket holds the block's own entries, its id and, where the author writes it there, the typing of the block's own method; each later group, opened by |, holds one typing entry, either of a component of the block itself by its absolute path, policy.grid, or of an operator inside the block by a path relative to the block, evaluate.method for the Evaluation that stores the builder's result and E_ψ_ξ.method for the expectation of a line. A typing entry at file level carries the full path, policy.evaluate.method : !Linear, and the union attaches it to the node the path names. A handler is written as a binding in the same way, policy.handler : "cons-port:egm", with or without a method word. The file declares each setting it reads with its domain (settings). A mark after a field names its perch: V[>] is the value at the continuation perch, V[<] at the arrival perch, and c[~] the consumption at the decision perch; a candidate the method computes, c[>], carries the mark of the perch whose coordinate it is computed at.

docs.title: 2 The rules of the union
docs.text:
The union is defined on the syntax trees and knows no word of the vocabulary: it merges structure, and the elaborator reads the merged term afterwards as if everything had been written in the stage file.

  1. Blocks by id. A block of the addition whose id equals the id of a block of the stage merges with it; a block with an id in one file only is kept. Nested blocks, the branches of a branching stage, merge by their label under their parent, and no branch is added.
  2. Entries by key. The header entries merge as a keyed collection: a typing by its subject, a key=value pair by its key, a tag by its text. A pair or a tag written in both files becomes one where the content is equal and is refused, naming both, where it differs. A component typed by both files is refused, so that each method and each grid of a block is written once.
  3. Signatures coordinate by coordinate. Within a stage the field names determine the signature: a coordinate of the addition with the name of a coordinate of the stage is that coordinate, the stage's typing is kept, and a differing type is refused. A coordinate is appended by a partial signature whose arrow says the side: () -> (h : ℝ₊ @ !ctrl) : !dcsn appends an output, a control (the role word !ctrl) chosen at the decision perch (the perch word !dcsn), and (z : ℝ) : !cntn -> () appends an input at the continuation perch. A derivative is never appended as a field: it is read by the derivative term, D_{m}V, and stated by a line. A side of a backward block's header, the inputs before the arrow or the outputs after it, admits a value field or a control and no state, since a state of a perch is a coordinate of the functions the block writes and no input of its own.
  4. Bodies appended. The lines of the addition stand after the lines of the stage's block; a line id written in both files is refused.
  5. File-level items appended. Declarations, definitions and laws of the addition are appended; a name defined in both files with different content is refused.
  6. Files in order. A stage occurrence, one use of a stage file at one position of a trellis, takes the additions its recipe names, applied in that order; the union is associative, and the stage file unioned with no addition is the stage file. A change of selection, !egm at one occurrence and !vfi at another, is written by naming another file in the recipe, never inside the union.
  7. Provenance kept. Every item keeps the file and position it was written at, so that stage.declared, the tables of parameters and settings, and the erasure are defined.

docs.title: 3 The two levels
docs.text: After the union the elaborator reads a block under the word in its method component at two levels. The declared level, stage.declared, holds the stage file's own lines. At the operative level, where the block's component holds a solution method and the addition supplies its rows, the lines by which the method computes the builder, the rows stand in place of the declared lines, so that the three lines of the endogenous grid method above stand in place of c = argmax_{cp : Γ_c(m)}(𝑢(cp) + β*V[>]), where Γ_c(m) is the feasible set of consumption at resources m. A derivative line stands at both levels; a solution method without rows, !vfi, leaves the declared lines; and where the component holds no solution method, an appended line is an authored line of the block and a second definition of a field is refused. Removing every item whose provenance is the addition returns the stage file: the erasure of the addition of Methods §8.

docs.title: Adequacy
docs.text: For this project, exact agreement means that an implementation computes the declared mathematical operation on specified inputs and observables. An approximate method instead needs a stated error or convergence result. Initiality determines how assigned operations compose; it proves neither kind of numerical claim.

docs.title: Two comparisons
docs.text:
Distinguish the exact mathematical target, a reference numerical approximation, and the package routine intended to compute that approximation. The reference approximation is defined by its method, representations and settings independently of one package implementation.

First compare the reference approximation with the target. State their domains and any maps between numerical arrays and mathematical functions, then specify the error criterion or limiting approximation family. A quadrature rule can be exact on a restricted function class while approximating a larger class. Its convergence depends on that class and the approximation assumptions.

Second compare the package computation with the reference approximation. Floating-point error and implementation error belong to this comparison; agreement to a tolerance is not exact equality. Both comparisons matter even when the same numerical routine performs several operations together.

docs.title: Composition and iteration
docs.text:
Exact agreement at compatible operation boundaries yields agreement of their composites. For approximate operations, composing individual approximations requires suitable stability or continuity estimates. Convergence of values need not imply convergence of selected policies, particularly at ties.

To study repeated Bellman updates, use a theorem suited to the declared value space. A contraction on a nonempty complete metric space has a unique fixed point and convergent exact iterates. Affine dependence on continuation value alone does not establish contraction, and nonlinear dependence does not preclude it. An order-preserving map on a complete lattice can have several fixed points. Existence, uniqueness and convergence therefore require separate hypotheses.

Lax–Richtmyer and monotone-scheme convergence results apply to their particular numerical problems and assumptions. They are not general consequences of choosing quadrature, EGM or an envelope routine. A finite collection of numerical checks also does not prove an operator identity on its entire domain.

docs.title: Terminology
docs.text:
Computational adequacy in programming-language semantics relates a stated denotational interpretation to specified operational observations. The exact-agreement convention above is the project's numerical correctness obligation; it should not be substituted for every literature definition of adequacy.

The detailed project obligations are in Initial-algebra semantics and Operator algebra. See also semantics and methodization.

docs.title: aggregation
docs.text: The value aggregator \(\mathrm G\) of a backward block, a block of a stage file whose builder carries value functions backward, is the pointwise map that combines a continuation value with the current state, the control and the shock, \(\mathrm G_\succ(v, x, a, \eta)\) on the decision edge and \(\mathrm G_\prec(v, x_\prec, \zeta)\) on the arrival edge. In expected utility \(\mathrm G_\succ(v, x, a, \eta) = \mathrm r(x, a, \eta) + \beta v\). The aggregation is the operator of the semgraph that applies it pointwise to the functions its wires carry; its kind is Aggregation (operations). A drawing labels it Value aggregation 𝐺 where it yields the value functions of a perch, and Apply 𝐺 for a map inside an expectation's brackets, whose result the expectation reads, and for a line of a policy block, which yields a candidate control or a coordinate.

docs.title: Two maps around the integral
docs.text: A statement of a backward block may apply one map to the continuation value before the shock is integrated and another to the result afterwards, so for one statement with one expectation the choice-value aggregator has the general form $$ B_\succ(x,a,\mathrm v_\succ) =\mathrm G^{\mathrm{out}}\succ\Bigl(\int}\mathrm G^{\mathrm{in}\succ\bigl(\mathrm v\succ(\mathrm g_\succ(x,a,\eta)),x,a,\eta\bigr)\,\mu_\eta(\mathrm d\eta),\,x,\,a\Bigr) $$ (Stages and perches §2.3a). The form with the aggregation inside the integral, the canonical display of §2.2, is the case \(\mathrm G^{\mathrm{out}}\) the identity. The reward-plus-discounted-expectation statement V = u(c) + β·E_η(V[>]) is the case \(\mathrm G^{\mathrm{in}}\) the identity, and there the aggregation reads the expectation's result \(w\) as its value input, \(\mathrm G(w, m, c) = \mathrm u(c) + \beta w\). An Epstein–Zin recursion has both maps nonlinear. The two placements coincide exactly when \(\mathrm G^{\mathrm{out}}\) is affine in \(w\); otherwise the placement is part of the specification.

docs.title: How the construction treats it
docs.text:
The fold follows the authored order and never moves arithmetic across an expectation. The arithmetic inside the brackets of an occurrence, an operator such as E_η(·) written inside a statement, is one aggregation box before that expectation; the arithmetic outside every occurrence is one aggregation box per maximal pointwise segment, for a block without sub-builders one box after the expectations, producing the block's output functions. Whether a box's map is affine in its value inputs is never a condition of construction: a nonlinear function of an expectation is admitted as written. Re-timing the shock to its own edge, which exposes the intermediate information set as a perch, is available and not required.

In a policy block the same kind carries the lines that define a candidate or a coordinate. A relational line, such as the candidate inequality c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(dV[>]) ⟂ a >= 0 of the consumption stage, forms one Aggregation whose rule is that relation with its clause, and a solve line one Aggregation of its residuals. The output of such a row is among the unknowns of its own rule, so the row denotes a relation, and no kind of its own (operations §4; Constraints §4).

docs.title: The kernel's domain
docs.text: Every kernel of a backward block, the builder's and every sub-builder's, is a function of the states of the perch at which the builder produces its function, the controls bound at that perch, the shocks the edge integrates, and its value inputs; the shock argument is present only before the expectation that integrates it. Monotonicity of the induced aggregator in the value follows when each map is nondecreasing in its value argument, the condition a recursive decision process requires of its aggregator (recursive decision process (RDP)).

docs.title: Representation
docs.text: The aggregation box's data is the identity of the block's G record, the block's value statements retained as immutable terms; which part of them a box applies is its position in the term. No string and no callable is stored: the printer gives the equation, and the box's compile_kernel() answers one plain Python function whose arguments are the value inputs and coordinates of the kernel and then each parameter it reads, made from the source text kernel().python, with the parameters' values passed at each call in the order kernel().parameter_values holds them. A row whose rule has no explicit side, such as a residual system, is refused under the rule kernel-target (refusals).

docs.title: Related concepts
docs.text: backward builder, sub-builder, semgraph, operator, statement.

docs.title: ASDL
docs.text:
ASDL, the Abstract Syntax Description Language, describes the structure of tree-shaped data independently of a concrete source spelling. A type lists possible constructors; each constructor has typed positions called ASDL fields. The prefix distinguishes a constructor position from an economic field.

For example, exp = Num(int value) | Add(exp left, exp right) describes two expression forms. * after a type denotes a sequence and ? an optional position. These qualifiers describe structure; they are not arithmetic. Named positions make generated representations easier to read. The original notation also supports product types, with restrictions on recursion.

docs.title: Grammar and concrete spelling
docs.text:
A concrete grammar determines how text is written. An ASDL description determines the abstract structure represented after parsing. Neither establishes name resolution, information availability or mathematical validity. Bellman-SYM parses arithmetic, function definitions and local binders in .bl; equations are not opaque terminal strings. See syntax and the abstract-grammar discussion.

A concrete encoding may identify a variant by a tag, its position or its shape. The historical name head mark refers to such an identifying tag. The ASDL paper's binary exchange format uses constructor tags and declared field order, but that does not prescribe Bellman-SYM's source format. Current period, trellis and binding YAML mappings are read according to their own contracts.

The project's generated syntax fixtures use the term JSON encoding. They are distinct from both the paper's binary format and the retained semgraph (semantic graph) of a stage.

Wang, Appel, Korn and Serra (1997), The Zephyr Abstract Syntax Description Language, §§2.2–2.7, describes constructors, fields, qualifiers and exchange. Its §3.1 illustrates that contextual restrictions can exceed what the abstract description expresses.

docs.title: Backward builder
docs.text: A backward builder is an operator that maps continuation value functions, which represent the value fields of the continuation perch, to choice values or earlier value functions using the declared transitions, payoffs and information. It is the builder of a backward block of a stage file: the decision builder, stage.dcsn.builder.bwd, of the block cntn_to_dcsn, and the arrival builder, stage.arvl.builder.bwd, of the block dcsn_to_arvl, each reached from the perch its edge leaves by a path that reads the pair of perches it joins, stage.builder["cntn", "dcsn"] for the decision builder (The builders graphs §2); the policy builder, stage.dcsn.builder.policy, stands beside them in the same graph and is read by a key of its own. Constructing a choice value, evaluating a supplied policy and optimizing that choice value are distinct operations.

docs.title: Choice values
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be the state space at the decision perch, \(\Gamma(x)\) the feasible actions, \(D=\{(x,a):a\in\Gamma(x)\}\) and \(Y\) the continuation-state space. Let \(g:D\times Z\to Y\) be a measurable law of motion, \(\kappa((x,a),dz)\) the conditional distribution of the shock, and \(G(\ell,x,a,z)\) a scalar value aggregator. For a continuation function \(v:Y\to\mathbb R\) in a specified value class, define

\[ (Bv)(x,a)=\int G(v(g(x,a,z)),x,a,z)\,\kappa((x,a),dz). \]

The chosen domain of \(B\) requires the integral to be finite on every required feasible pair, with the output in the specified choice-value class. The order of aggregation and integration follows this displayed model; a nonlinear operation authored outside expectation must not be moved inside it. Discounting appears only where the defining equations include it.

A statement may apply a second map outside the integral, \((Bv)(x,a)=G^{\mathrm{out}}\bigl(\int G^{\mathrm{in}}(v(g(x,a,z)),x,a,z)\,\kappa((x,a),dz),x,a\bigr)\), the general form of Stages and perches §2.3a; the display above is its case with \(G^{\mathrm{out}}\) the identity. In the semgraph the aggregation box that applies \(G^{\mathrm{out}}\) reads the expectation's result as its value input, and whether \(G^{\mathrm{out}}\) is affine in that input is never a condition of construction.

A trajectory conditional expectation gives an identity along the observed random state and action. Recovering a pointwise choice-value function requires sufficient state information, representative functions and conditional distributions. An almost-sure identity under one policy cannot determine payoffs for every unchosen action.

docs.title: Policy evaluation and optimization
docs.text:
For a supplied feasible measurable policy \(\pi\), define

\[ (T_\pi v)(x)=(Bv)(x,\pi(x)). \]

For optimizing evaluation, the value is \(\sup_{a\in\Gamma(x)}(Bv)(x,a)\) where that supremum belongs to the output domain. For a choice-value function \(Q\), \(\operatorname{argmax}Q\) is the maximizing set: the feasible measurable policies that attain the maximum of \(Q(x,\cdot)\) over \(\Gamma(x)\) at every state. The set may be empty, and it chooses none of its members. A selection \(s\) is a partial map that chooses one member, \(s(Q)\in\operatorname{argmax}Q\), and is defined only where that set is nonempty. With the insertion of a policy into a choice-value function, \(\iota^{*}(Q,\pi)(x)=Q(x,\pi(x))\), a named selection from the maximizing set followed by the insertion of the selected policy gives

\[ T=\iota^{*}\circ \langle B,s\circ B\rangle \quad\text{on } \{v: Bv\in\operatorname{dom}s\}, \]

and \(Tv\) is the same for every selection whose domain holds \(Bv\), since every member of the maximizing set attains the maximum (Operators §4). An operative argmax line of a stage file forms a row of kind Argmax, whose output is the maximizing set (operations); the Evaluation that follows it selects no member, and the selection belongs to the numerical method bound to the row at methodization (method types).

This is the optimizing map, not evaluation under an arbitrary supplied policy. An unattained supremum need not have this representation. An Euler equation or root relation requires feasibility and optimality conditions before its solution can supply the optimizing policy.

docs.title: Stage composition
docs.text:
The decision-to-arrival builder integrates the declared arrival aggregator and pre-decision shock using its conditional distribution. Write it as \(\mathbb T_\prec\), the decision-edge optimizing map as \(\mathbb T_\succ\), and fixed-policy evaluation as \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\). The stage maps are

\[ \mathbb T=\mathbb T_\prec\circ\mathbb T_\succ, \qquad \mathbb T_\pi=\mathbb T_\prec\circ\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}, \]

on compatible value spaces. If the arrival payoff aggregator is the identity, its builder reduces to an undiscounted transition expectation. A general reward-bearing arrival aggregator does not have that interpretation.

The entry forward builder states the probability/function pairing for transition expectations. It is not a transpose formula for the full Bellman update. See Operators and builders for the mathematical factors and Field equations and Methodization for current .bl authoring and outer YAML attachments.

docs.title: Banach contraction theorem
docs.text:
Let \((X,d)\) be a nonempty complete metric space and \(T:X\to X\) satisfy

\[ d(Tx,Ty)\leq q\,d(x,y)\quad\text{for all }x,y\in X, \qquad 0\leq q<1. \]

Then \(T\) has a unique fixed point \(x^*\) and its exact iterates satisfy

\[ d(T^n x,x^*)\leq q^n d(x,x^*). \]

Completeness, closure under \(T\) and a modulus strictly below one are essential hypotheses. Nonexpansiveness alone does not give this conclusion.

docs.title: Dynamic programming
docs.text:
A stationary Bellman operator can satisfy these conditions on a specified space of bounded functions with the supremum norm. Blackwell's sufficient conditions provides one sufficient test. Identifying the resulting fixed point with the economic value also uses the assumptions connecting the Bellman recursion to the policy problem.

For unbounded rewards, a weighted norm can be useful. Given a positive weight \(w\geq1\), define \(\|v\|_w=\sup_x|v(x)|/w(x)\) on a suitable complete function class. If a transition expectation \(P\) satisfies \(Pw\leq Cw\), constant discount \(\beta\) gives a candidate modulus \(\beta C\); the contraction argument requires \(\beta C<1\) and closure of the full value update on that class. For an optimizing update, the same bound must hold uniformly across all feasible actions or policies in its transition family. Discounting alone is insufficient.

A finite-horizon model instead uses its terminal condition and backward recursion. A geometric truncation estimate from a stationary contraction applies only with the same operator and a finite initial distance in the chosen metric. Convergence of approximate iterates or approximate fixed points needs further error and stability assumptions; see adequacy.

The theorem is used conditionally in Operator algebra. It is not a source-language validation rule.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Stokey, N. L., and Lucas, R. E., Jr., with Prescott, E. C. (1989). Recursive Methods in Economic Dynamics. Harvard University Press, §3.2, Theorem 3.2, pp. 50–52.
  • Hernández-Lerma, O., Laura-Guarachi, L. R., Mendoza-Palacios, S., and González-Sánchez, D. (2023). An Introduction to Optimal Control Theory: The Dynamic Programming Approach. Springer, §2.3.3, pp. 44–49, for the weighted-norm approach.

docs.title: Bellman algebra
docs.text: An algebra assigns mathematical sets and operations to a specified signature. In the Bellman calculus these include chosen value-function and distribution spaces, transition operations, payoff aggregation and policy evaluation or selection. This use of “operator algebra” concerns their composition, not an algebra of bounded linear operators from functional analysis.

docs.title: Terms and interpretations
docs.text:
A signature lists sorts and operation symbols with input and output types. Its term algebra \(T_\Sigma\) consists of formal expressions built from those symbols. A target algebra \(\mathcal B\) assigns a carrier set to each sort and an operation of the required type to each symbol. The interpretation \(\Upsilon\) maps terms to their mathematical meanings.

Once the target operations are fixed, ground terms have a unique homomorphic interpretation. Terms with free inputs also require an environment assigning those inputs. Initial algebra gives that result and distinguishes it from assumptions about domains, binding and software representation. If additional equations are imposed on the terms, the interpretation must satisfy them; associativity or monotonicity alone does not determine an algebra up to isomorphism.

A categorical presentation needs its own objects, morphisms and equations. A Lawvere theory model is a finite-product-preserving functor from the specified theory to sets. A many-sorted signature alone does not establish that all Bellman graph operations have this structure.

docs.title: Bellman operations
docs.text:
A backward builder can construct choice values, evaluate a supplied policy, or optimize when the appropriate selection exists. A forward builder propagates probability through transitions under a supplied policy. Both are builders, the operators the blocks of a stage file denote, and they use different domains. The probability/function pairing relates forward transport to undiscounted transition expectation, not to reward-bearing optimization.

The Bellman operator is one recursive value update. An abstract dynamic program (ADP) describes a value space and a family of policy self-maps, while a recursive decision process (RDP) additionally specifies feasible actions and an aggregator. These are useful comparisons with parts of the Bellman interpretation, not identities with the entire many-sorted algebra.

docs.title: Mathematical terms and stored graphs
docs.text:
A finite acyclic term graph can share repeated subexpressions. For pure operations with identical input assignments, evaluating a shared subterm once agrees with evaluating its copies. Sharing a random draw and independently resampling are different operations.

This mathematical account does not prescribe parser storage. Bellman-SYM parses .bl source into a temporary parsed AST (abstract syntax tree) and constructs a retained semgraph (semantic graph). Authored names and boundaries can distinguish graphs with equal mathematical denotations. Functional interpretations require the premises stated in Syntax to semantics.

See Operator algebra for the target structures and operator for the symbol/operation distinction.

docs.title: Bellman calculus
docs.text: The Bellman calculus describes how the equations of a dynamic decision problem define mathematical operations and how those operations compose. A stage records transitions, value calculations, and policy relations at three information sets. Compatible stages form periods, and period occurrences can form a finite trellis.

docs.title: The objects being related
docs.text:
A field is a quantity interpreted in its declared information context. A state vector is a chosen collection of coordinates that may summarize that information. Representing a field by a function of those coordinates requires a sufficiency assumption; a type declaration does not prove it. The entry on fields distinguishes these descriptions.

A backward builder constructs values from continuation values. A forward builder constructs a distribution of later states from a distribution of earlier states under a policy. Both are builders, the operators the blocks of a stage denote. Their relationship depends on the transition, the conditional distribution of the shocks, and the reward structure. In particular, the distribution transition is dual to the reward-free expectation operator, not to the whole reward-bearing Bellman operator.

docs.title: Composition and its limits
docs.text:
Compatible connectors, which identify the fields of adjoining stages, allow the operations of those stages to compose. Associativity permits regrouping an unchanged composition. It does not permit arbitrary changes in the order of decisions, observations, or expectations.

Initial-algebra semantics explains the unique extension of a fixed interpretation of syntax constructors. It does not establish that this interpretation describes the intended economy, that numerical approximations are exact, or that an infinite-horizon fixed point exists. Those are separate questions of adequacy, economic assumptions, and fixed-point theory.

Use the mathematical chapters for these definitions and their qualifications. Use Bellman-SYM for the modeler's syntax and workflow. Υ denotes a meaning construction within this account; it is not another name for the entire calculus.

docs.title: Bellman operator
docs.text:
A Bellman operator is an operator that updates a continuation value by evaluating current rewards and future consequences and optimizing over feasible actions. A fixed-policy operator performs the value update under a supplied policy. These are different maps even when they share transitions and rewards.

For state \(x\), feasible actions \(\Gamma(x)\) and choice-value aggregator \(B\), the optimizing update is

\[ (Tv)(x)=\sup_{a\in\Gamma(x)}B(x,a,v). \]

Its domain is a chosen class of continuation functions for which the required choice values and supremum are defined and the output belongs to the declared value space. An attained maximum and a measurable maximizing policy require additional assumptions. For a feasible measurable policy \(\pi\), fixed-policy evaluation is \((T_\pi v)(x)=B(x,\pi(x),v)\).

docs.title: Stage factorization
docs.text:
In the staged reading, write \(\mathbb T_\succ\) for optimizing continuation-to-decision evaluation and \(\mathbb T_\prec\) for decision-to-arrival aggregation; in a stage these are the decision and the arrival builders. Then

\[ \mathbb T=\mathbb T_\prec\circ\mathbb T_\succ, \qquad \mathbb T_\pi=\mathbb T_\prec\circ\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}. \]

The arrival operation integrates information revealed before the decision; the decision operation retains the choice and subsequent uncertainty in the declared order. Each map must have compatible input and output spaces. The entry backward builder defines the factors, including the distinction between constructing a choice value and selecting a policy.

A stationary Bellman operator may be a self-map whose fixed point characterizes optimal value under a verification theorem. A finite-horizon recursion can map between different time-indexed spaces and starts from specified terminal data. Neither a unique fixed point nor a convergence theorem follows from a typed stage declaration.

See abstract dynamic program (ADP) for the supremum over policy operators, Banach contraction theorem and Blackwell's sufficient conditions for conditional convergence results, and Operators and builders for the detailed stage interpretation.

docs.title: Bellman-SYM writer
docs.text:
Summary

The Bellman-SYM writer is the map \(\Upsilon_0 : M \to D\) from the description \(M\) of an economic model in prose and displayed equations, named BellmanStageProse, to the model's declaration \(D\) in Bellman-SYM, named BellmanSYMDeclaration: the stage files with the period and trellis files. A language model computes it in the role BellmanStageProse_to_BellmanSYMDeclaration, under that role's instruction text; the map is not that text. The files it returns are never read as text: they are elaborated, and what is then compared or described is the object their elaboration constructs, \(E\), named ElaboratedSemanticObject.

Relationship with other documents

Builds on — Υ: the meaning map from a stage file to the model it states, against which the Bellman-SYM writer works, and its computed part, the Bellman-SYM elaborator; Bellman-SYM: the language the declaration is written in. Used by — Prose writer: the map back from \(E\) to a description; Judge: the role BellmanStageProse_judge, which compares the description the round trip returns with the one the Bellman-SYM writer started from. See also — The factory API: the functions that elaborate the files the Bellman-SYM writer returns.

docs.title: 1 The map
docs.text:
The writer takes a description \(M\): a statement of a dynamic program in prose and displayed equations, as the model section of a paper states it, with its states and their sets, its controls and their feasible sets, each shock with its distribution and its timing, the laws of motion, the recursion, the condition that determines the policy, and the parameters. One description may state several stages and the connections between them. It returns a declaration \(D\): one stage file for each stage of the model and, for a model of several stages, the period file and the trellis file that join them, that is, the syntactic trellis and its stages. Beside the files it returns a note of what \(M\) left open and what the files therefore omit.

\(M\) is prepared from the source material \(P\), named SourceMaterial: the paper, if there is one, together with the user's prompts and the exchange with Matsya, the project's service that writes a model's description and declaration from such material. A description the user types is a \(P\) too, and it is prepared into \(M\) by the same path as a paper, by the source preparer, the role SourceMaterial_to_BellmanStageProse, the map \(P \to M\). Before it writes \(M\), the source preparer may request further pages of the calculus guide or the language guide, two of Matsya's reference guides, or passages of the retrieval index, the searchable store of passages from the documents of Matsya's collections, in the way §2 describes for the writer.

docs.title: 2 How it is computed
docs.text:
A language model computes the map. Each call sends it one message whose first part is the writer's instruction text, one of the Matsya instructions, and whose remaining parts are the pages of the language guide; the passages retrieved from the published documentation, if any; the addresses of further documentation the writer may request and, after its first request, the material its requests added; and \(M\). In place of its files the writer may answer a call with one request, a JSON object of the form its instruction text explains, to read a saved page of the language guide or a passage of the retrieval index, to list what is recorded as related to a page or passage it has been shown, or to search the index again. The program answers the request within the allowances the configuration's settings set under reading and places the result in the writer's next message, after the instruction text and the guide pages, which stay the same from call to call; the writer then writes its files or makes a further request. Such documentation explains how the language states a model and supplies no fact about the model that \(M\) describes. The instruction text says what the map does: write from \(M\) alone, name no known model, fill no gap, copy the spellings of the guide, and write under each block the sentence of \(M\) it comes from. In the configuration folder Matsya runs under the text is texts/BellmanStageProse-to-BellmanSYMDeclaration.md, and the Matsya handler write of its module matsya_handler.py builds the message and reads the answer.

The map is not its instruction text. Training the writer revises the text and the program around the call; it changes neither the map's domain nor its codomain. A revision is kept when the measures taken on a set of descriptions held out from the revision do not fall.

docs.title: 3 What follows the writer
docs.text:
Nothing reads \(D\) as text. The Bellman-SYM elaborator BellmanSYMDeclaration_to_ElaboratedSemanticObject, \(S : D \to E\), a program and not a role, elaborates every file the writer returns, with elaborate_text of bellman.factory.elaboration for one stage and elaborate_trellis for a model of several stages, and so obtains \(E\), the elaborated stage of one stage file or the elaborated trellis of several, or a refusal that names the rule, the line and the form expected (Stage functions §2). On a refusal the writer is called again with its own refused files and the refusal, up to three calls in all under the present configuration, besides the calls it answers with a request, which have an allowance of their own; a file that still does not elaborate ends the attempt, and no later step sees it.

The writer works against the meaning map Υ: it must find a file whose meaning is the model, and many files have one meaning. Two calls on one \(M\) give two files that need not agree in spelling or in the order of their blocks. They are therefore compared through their elaborations, by the comparator ElaboratedSemanticObject_comparator, \(\cong\), a program that decides whether two elaborations agree up to a renaming of their names (Judge §4), and never as text. The round trip \(M \to D \to E \to M' \to D' \to E'\) tests whether the writer and the prose writer are consistent with each other; \(D'\) is written from \(M'\) by the same role, the Bellman-SYM writer, and \(E'\) is its elaboration. Whether \(D\) is faithful to \(M\) is tested outside it: by pairs of a description and a stage file that a person or a judge has checked, by a numerical representation Ρ that reproduces a result of the paper or fails to, and by the judge, the role BellmanStageProse_judge.

For a model of several stages, elaboration selects the actual pair of stage fields at each connection. The dossier prints those resolved pairs. A connection or route that Bellman cannot certify, including one with incompatible continuation values, is returned to the writer for correction. A recipe also carries the parameter values supplied in each period, and those values enter the deterministic comparison.

docs.title: Related
docs.text: Υ · elaborated stage · prose writer · judge · Bellman-SYM · trellis

docs.title: Blackwell's sufficient conditions
docs.text:
Blackwell's conditions provide a sufficient test for a contraction. Let \(B(X)\) be the bounded real-valued functions on a nonempty set \(X\), equipped with the supremum norm, and let \(T:B(X)\to B(X)\). Assume:

  1. \(f\leq g\) implies \(Tf\leq Tg\).
  2. For some \(0\leq\beta<1\), every \(f\in B(X)\) and constant \(c\geq0\) satisfy \(T(f+c)\leq Tf+\beta c\).

To see the contraction bound, set \(d=\|f-g\|_\infty\). Since \(f\leq g+d\), the two conditions give \(Tf\leq Tg+\beta d\). Interchanging \(f\) and \(g\) gives the reverse bound, hence

\[ \|Tf-Tg\|_\infty\leq\beta\|f-g\|_\infty. \]

The same argument applies on bounded measurable functions when \(T\) maps that space into itself. Banach contraction theorem then gives a unique fixed point and convergence of exact iteration.

docs.title: Application and limits
docs.text:
An additive discounted Bellman update often has these properties when its rewards, feasibility and transitions ensure a bounded output. Positive rewards or costs alone do not establish that closure. Existence of a maximizing policy is also separate from the contraction inequality for a supremum-value update.

For a weight \(w\geq1\), an analogous argument uses \(f\leq g+dw\) and a bound \(T(f+cw)\leq Tf+qc w\) for \(c\geq0\) and \(q<1\) on a specified complete weighted function space. The model must provide the corresponding reward and transition-growth bounds. This is useful for some unbounded problems, not a theorem for every lifecycle model.

These are mathematical assumptions to check for an interpreted operator. EGM, Euler equations and a method assignment do not establish them. See Operator algebra and Bellman operator.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Stokey, N. L., and Lucas, R. E., Jr., with Prescott, E. C. (1989). Recursive Methods in Economic Dynamics. Harvard University Press, §3.2, Theorem 3.3, p. 54.
  • Hernández-Lerma, O., Laura-Guarachi, L. R., Mendoza-Palacios, S., and González-Sánchez, D. (2023). An Introduction to Optimal Control Theory: The Dynamic Programming Approach. Springer, §2.3.3, Proposition 2.36 and Theorem 2.38, pp. 47–49, for the weighted-norm argument.

docs.title: branch
docs.text: A branch is one alternative of a discrete choice, with its own continuation state and its own section of the law of motion: work or retire, adjust or keep. In a stage file the decision-to-continuation block declares the label coordinate, a control typed by the finite set of labels, d : !ctrl @ {work, retire}, and contains one labeled nested block per branch defining that branch's continuation fields; the backward block lists the per-branch continuation values as separate fields and selects among them by tuple selection indexed by the label coordinate, and the maximization line of the policy block, over the same tuple, forms a row of kind Argmax, whose output is the set of policies that choose a largest entry (Branching §§1 and 3). A stage is branching if and only if that block has labeled nested blocks; nothing else declares it.

docs.title: The mathematics
docs.text:
The continuation state space is a disjoint union of the branches' spaces, \(\mathsf X_\succ = \bigsqcup_{j \in J} \mathsf X_{\succ, j}\) (the operator algebra, Appendix F §5), one summand per label, named by the fields its branch writes: in the retirement choice the summand of work is the set of a_w and the summand of retire the set of a_r. The label adds no perch and is no state field. A function on a disjoint union is the tuple of its restrictions to the summands, and a finite measure on it the tuple of its restrictions, so a continuation value is the tuple of the branches' values, each a function on its own summand.

In the semgraph the branching block dcsn_to_cntn is one box of the forward initial diagram, whose outputs are the fields of every branch, a_w and a_r, in label order. Each branch is a bubble inside it, dcsn_to_cntn.work, holding the block's lines read at that label. The block owns one law of motion, and its section at a label, 𝑔_work≻ = 𝑔≻(·, work), is an abbreviation of the builder that reads it. Each branch value is typed on its own summand, the branch at whose position it stands in the selection tuples, and no wire carries a label in its type: the wire of a_w is ret_choice:cntn:a_w. The branches meet the rest of the builders at two operators of the existing kinds. Backward, the selection is the aggregation of the selection line, whose kernel is the tuple indexed by the label, (V_w[>] - δ, V_r[>])[d], read at the policy after one pullback per branch along its section; the maximization over the label that the choice line writes is that line's own Argmax row and not the selection. Forward, the fork is the push-forward at the policy into the disjoint union, one measure per label: the mass of the decision states the policy sends to that label, pushed along its section. Since the policy sends every decision state to one label, and where every branch line writes into its field's declared set, the masses of the branch measures sum to the mass of the decision measure; the package records this as a condition, established for ret_choice and required for tenure, whose keep line's range is not established. A branch may also be drawn by nature: the label is then a shock with its probability distribution, the value is the branch values weighted by that distribution, Σ_j p(j | x) Q_j(x), and the fork is the push-forward of the measure extended by the distribution, routed by the drawn label.

docs.title: Branch against sub-builder
docs.text: A labeled branch block is a bubble inside the forward block of the initial diagram, as a sub-builder is a bubble inside a builder, and the two are told apart by role, not by depth. A sub-builder is a factor of the builder's sequential composition on a sub-tensor of wires, so that opening it preserves the morphism. A branch bubble holds the block's lines read at its label and names one summand of the continuation space, joined to the others only by the fork or the selection; it cannot be inlined into a neighbor. No builders graph holds a bubble for a branch: there the branches are wires and boxes of the existing kinds. The name forms record the distinction: the label stands in the address, dcsn_to_cntn.work, against a statement address, policy.InvEuler. A sub-builder may sit inside one branch's slice or around the selection statement, never across part of the selection's tuple.

docs.title: Branching stages in the applications
docs.text: The finite-branch interpretation is stated in Operator algebra §5. A stage whose branches a control selects is constructed, the retirement choice ret_choice.bl and the durables model's tenure.bl among them, and so is a stage whose branches a shock selects, as the worker's aging stage worker_ageing.bl of the Cagetti–De Nardi application. The branching guide states what a branching block may contain.

docs.title: Related concepts
docs.text: semgraph, sub-builder, forward builder, backward builder, stage.

docs.title: builder
docs.text: A builder is the operator a block of a stage denotes. The block is the authored text of the .bl file; the builder is what that text means, and the two words are kept apart. The calculus defines a builder as a named composition of operators constituting a stage's input-to-output interface (Operators and builders §6). In the semgraph it is one box at the builder grain, a Builder bubble whose name is the block's identifier, and opening the bubble shows the operators it composes. A builder is reached from the stage by the ordered pair of perches it joins, the key the package resolves whatever the block's identifier, or from the perch its edge leaves; the policy builder is read by its own key, policy.

docs.title: One builder per block
docs.text:
A stage file writes one block for each edge it uses in each direction, together with a policy block, and elaboration constructs one builder for each. The buffer-stock stage has five, each reached from the perch its edge leaves (The builders graphs §2): the forward builders arvl_to_dcsn and dcsn_to_cntn, at stage.arvl.builder.fwd and stage.dcsn.builder.fwd; the backward builders cntn_to_dcsn and dcsn_to_arvl, at stage.dcsn.builder.bwd and stage.arvl.builder.bwd; and the policy builder, at stage.dcsn.builder.policy. Each path reads one key of stage.builder, the pair of perches its builder joins or, for the policy builder, the key "policy": stage.dcsn.builder.bwd is stage.builder["cntn", "dcsn"].

The two directions act on different objects. A backward builder carries value functions backward: \(\mathbb T_\succ\) on the decision edge, \(\mathbb T_\prec\) on the arrival edge, composing into the stage operator \(\mathbb T = \mathbb T_\prec \circ \mathbb T_\succ\), with \(\mathbb T_{\succ,\pi}\) the builder at a policy, one operator for each policy, whose signature is its inputs and its outputs and which is wired to the policy builder at no level. A forward builder transports probability measures along the same declared transitions, \(\mathbb M_\prec\) and \(\mathbb M_{\succ,\pi}\), composing into \(\mathbb M_\pi = \mathbb M_{\succ,\pi} \circ \mathbb M_\prec\). The policy builder is named separately from the backward builders. Its operations are those the lines of the policy block form: an Argmax row for an operative maximization line, an Aggregation for a relational line or a solve line, the Pullback of the identification where the block writes the grid line, and the Evaluation at its output (operations).

docs.title: Its signature
docs.text:
A builder signature is the builder's actual input and output wires, its dom and cod. It is derived from the operator constructed from the block; it is not a copy of the fields listed in the block header. stage.dcsn.builder.bwd.signature() answers one record with two parts, inputs and outputs, each wire with its type. On a controlled backward edge, a continuation value function is an input and the decision value function is an output. The control is the coordinate at which the operator is stated, not an input wire; the policy is an index on the operator at a policy, not an argument of its decision value function. The entry signature separates a builder signature from the signature of a many-sorted algebra.

Opening a builder preserves its signature. The boxes that replace it must keep the ordered input and output identities and types, the operation on every admissible assignment of the free inputs, the conditions under which the formulas are defined, local scope, conditional distributions and shared dependencies (semgraph).

docs.title: What a builder composes
docs.text:
The statements of a backward block fold into primitive operator boxes of three kinds, Pullback, Expectation and Aggregation, emitted in the order the terms nest them, with an Evaluation at each evaluated field, a field whose function stands on a wire under the field's name (operations).

A pullback composes a continuation function with the block's law of motion, \(K_g : v \mapsto v \circ g\); every term of function sort typed at the continuation perch receives one. An expectation integrates the shocks an occurrence \(E_S(\cdot)\) names under the conditional distribution selected from the edge's joint distribution; its output is a function of the source coordinates and the conditioning shocks that selection keeps, and a shock integrated on an earlier path is not restored. An aggregation applies a map \(G\) pointwise (aggregation): the arithmetic inside an occurrence's brackets is one aggregation box before that occurrence's expectation, and the arithmetic outside every occurrence is one box per maximal pointwise segment. For a builder at a policy, the policy indexes the pullback, aggregation or conditional distribution in which it occurs. Evaluation then returns the resulting function under the evaluated field's name and reads no policy.

Whether a statement writes its arithmetic inside or outside the occurrence decides which mathematical order it denotes, \(B_\succ = \mathbb E_\mu \circ \operatorname{lift}(G) \circ K_g\) or \(B_\succ = \operatorname{lift}(G) \circ \mathbb E_\mu \circ K_g\), and the fold never moves arithmetic across an expectation. A sub-term carrying no value input is never a box: a named function applied to fields, a parameter, an expression in fields and shocks are addends, factors and formal arguments of the aggregation's map. Evaluation at an evaluated field is the identity on a function or on a set of feasible policies into that field's declared carrier, subject to range compatibility; it makes no selection, reads no policy and inserts none. A numerical method may store an interpolant as its representation of a function without changing exact Evaluation. A statement marked !node cuts a factor out of the composition, a sub-builder.

docs.title: What a builder owns
docs.text: Each backward builder defines the aggregator \(G\) of its block. Each forward builder owns one complete law of motion \(g\), referenced by identity both by its own push-forward and by the backward pullback of the paired edge: arvl_to_dcsn supplies the map dcsn_to_arvl uses, and dcsn_to_cntn the map cntn_to_dcsn uses. Distinct forward builders own distinct maps, and no backward builder holds a \(g\) of its own. A builder's identifier is the name of its box, with no second copy of that name stored beside it.

docs.title: Grains
docs.text: A grain chooses which boxes are opened within a graph. The builder grain keeps every builder closed; the sub-builder, primitive, combined and factored grains open it further, and they need not nest. A reader reaches the two public grains by an attribute of the piece, primitives and sub_builders, on a graph and on a builder alike. The mathematics of opening is exact refinement: the builders are the symbols of a coarse signature, a derived signature morphism assigns each of them a term over the finer operations, \(\delta(\mathbb T_\succ)v = B_{\succ,s(B_\succ v)}v\), where \(s(B_\succ v)\in\operatorname{argmax}(B_\succ v)\) and the policy indexes the relevant pullback, aggregation or conditional distribution, and \(\delta(\mathbb T_\prec) = B_\prec\), and initiality makes the resulting term translation unique (Appendix B §4). A builder is primitive in one signature and composite in another, which is what operator means by the two words; semgraph owns the graphs and the grains.

docs.title: What a builder is not
docs.text: A builder is not its block, which is text; not a stage, which composes the builders of its edges; and not a numerical routine. A method attaches to a target, and a target may be a declared function, an evaluated field, a builder or an operator occurrence, but attaching one neither supplies a routine nor runs it (methodization). The Bellman operator of a stage is the composite \(\mathbb T\), not any one of its builders.

docs.title: Its kernels
docs.text: kernels() on a builder answers one record that refers to no stage: each operation in the order of application, with the plain Python function its kernel compiles to, or its printed relation where its rule is no explicit function, the names of the function's arguments and outputs, and the parameters with the values the calibration binds. A numerical operator is constructed from such records without the stage in hand (A builder §5).

docs.title: Related concepts
docs.text: backward builder and forward builder give the mathematics of the two directions; sub-builder the factor a !node cuts; operator and aggregation the boxes inside; statement the authored line; semgraph the graphs and grains; stage what the builders compose into.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
Calibration supplies values for the model's declared economic parameters. It is distinct from settings, which configure numerical approximation. Declaring risk aversion in a .bl stage file fixes its name and admissible domain; supplying a particular value calibrates that declaration.

The stage verb is stage.calibrate(calibration_source), with a source path or mapping; calibrate_trellis(elaborated, syntactic) applies it at every position of a trellis with the calibration the syntactic trellis holds there. It requires a value for every declared parameter, adds the values to the stage occurrence it is called on and returns it, with the mapping among its bindings; stage.par["ρ"] then answers the parameter's record, whose value is the number bound. Parameter names remain symbolic in retained equations. Additional shared-source keys can remain in the mapping without creating new declarations. In a trellis, a parameter name two stages of one period declare is one parameter of the period: calibrate_trellis supplies it once, from the sources of the stages that declare it, and refuses two sources that give it two values or a value outside a declaring stage's set (The trellis factory §4).

In the recommended order calibration comes first, followed by methodization and configuration. Only methodization must precede configuration, because the methods name the settings, so calibration may also be applied after either. Applying it again returns another stage version with new values; this does not prove that the binding operations commute. A failed calibration leaves the earlier stage version unchanged. A subsequent connection report on that earlier trellis reads the values it still holds, not values from the failed request. See specified stage for the complete lifecycle.

A recipe can combine baseline and overriding parameter sources before calibration: the syntactic trellis holds the merged mappings, and the stage verb binds. The merge and parent-source rules are those of the specification factory. Merging source mappings does not itself validate stage mathematics or produce a numerical solution. A calibrated stage still needs the applicable analytic assumptions, compatible methods and continuation data.

See Stage functions and Recipe functions.

docs.title: Connector
docs.text: A connector selects an outgoing continuation state field of one stage occurrence and an incoming arrival state field of another for composition. It does not rename either field. Within a period it joins stages; between periods it is an inter-period connector.

docs.title: What a pair states
docs.text:
In the period example, {k_next: k} pairs outgoing capital k_next with incoming capital k. The outgoing name is first. A bare name is admitted when exactly one eligible field of that name stands on its side of the connection; otherwise prefix that endpoint with its stage key, as in {disc.k_next: port.k}. The two endpoints must have compatible declared sets. The author remains responsible for their economic meaning, units, and information at the join; matching names or sets alone cannot establish those assumptions.

A connector performs no calculation. A change of units, return, depreciation, or other state transformation must be authored as an equation. An authored pair takes precedence over any automatic same-name matching of its endpoints. Automatic matching selects a pair only when it is uniquely compatible without conflicting with other pairs or forming a cycle. A connection report records unresolved candidates and incomplete state routes.

docs.title: Values move by composition
docs.text: More generally, for a measurable state map \(\tau:X\to Y\) and a value function \(v:Y\to\mathbb R\), the induced pullback is \(K_\tau v=v\circ\tau\). It needs no inverse of \(\tau\). A complete connector route pairs the ordered state coordinates as a permutation; partial or crossed pairs must be assessed together with the stage's joint law and backward value components. Neither matching type labels nor separate marginal laws alone establish that route.

docs.title: Between periods
docs.text: The trellis index counts backwards from terminal. An inter-period connector indexed by \(h\) joins the continuation of period \(h+1\) to the arrival of period \(h\). For the consumption–investment example, {m_next: m} belongs at this boundary. Placing this join inside the same period would instead close a cycle. See inter-period connections.

docs.title: declarative language
docs.text:
A language is declarative to the degree that a text written in it states what an object is, through its sets, probability distributions, equations and choices; takes its meaning from the meanings of its parts, with no appeal to an order of execution; and leaves the procedure that computes the object to be supplied separately. The three clauses are tested against published sources in the sections below. The phrase "to the degree" is deliberate: the modeling languages economists use occupy different positions on this scale, and the Stan and BUGS comparison below shows two of them.

Bellman-SYM is declarative in this sense. A stage file states the domains, information, choices, equations and shock probability distributions of one stage. Elaboration, the step that reads the stage files, assigns each file its meaning, the semgraph, which records the operators the stage denotes and holds no procedure for computing them. The routines that compute the stage are supplied afterwards, under methodization, and the methods file "names computations that the stage file created; it creates none" (Methodization).

docs.title: The style it is contrasted with
docs.text:
Backus (1978, §4, pp. 615–616) explains the conventional imperative style by its origin in the machine: "Von Neumann programming languages use variables to imitate the computer's storage cells; control statements elaborate its jump and test instructions; and assignment statements imitate its fetching, storing, and arithmetic." The assignment statement "is the von Neumann bottleneck of programming languages and keeps us thinking in word-at-a-time terms in much the same way the computer's bottleneck does." Of the functional program for the inner product, Backus records (§5.2, p. 617) that "It operates only on its arguments. There are no hidden states or complex transition rules" and that "It is static and nonrepetitive, in the sense that its structure is helpful in understanding it without mentally executing it."

The last property is the one an economist recognizes. The Bellman equation of the buffer-stock problem, as a paper writes it, is read without being run. A value-iteration loop that solves it must be traced, and in the project's interoperability talk the procedural approach is summarized by the observation that "the loop is the model", so that "changing the method or reusing one piece means editing the loop". A declarative text names the object; a procedure produces one approximation to it.

Bandali (2020, §1.1, p. 2) characterizes declarative modeling languages as those that "describe the transitions in a declarative manner using constraints, rather than through imperative calculations and/or statements" and "have a formal mathematical and logical foundation". The thesis's subjects are software specification languages (TLA+, Alloy, Event-B); the characterization applies equally to a model file whose equations are constraints on functions.

docs.title: What is declared, and what is supplied separately
docs.text:
Stan is the published case closest to the separation of a semgraph from its numerical realization. The Stan Reference Manual (Stan Development Team 2025, Overview, p. 1) states that "The language is responsible for defining a log density function conditioned on data", and that Stan "only requires models to be defined up to a constant that does not depend on the parameters" (§7.3, p. 77). Carpenter et al. (2017, §4, p. 16) add that the program's execution "details are the same whether a Stan program is being used by one of the built-in samplers or optimizers or being used externally by a user-defined sampler or optimizer", because other algorithms are implemented "using the log density and derivative functions supplied by a model" (§7.1, p. 26). A Stan program declares one mathematical object; the sampler is chosen separately and can be exchanged. Bandali (2020, §1.2, p. 3) states the same separation as a rule of method: "tool support and the analysis performance of those tools are subject to change, and can change much more easily than the logic and semantics of the language".

In the Bellman calculus the separation is the distinction between Υ, the mathematical interpretation of a stage file, and Ρ, its numerical realization. The entry semantics states it: "The mathematical model specifies domains, equations, shock probability distributions and feasible choices. A numerical method supplies a procedure and representations intended to approximate or compute that model." Parameters belong to Υ and define the mathematical problem; settings belong to Ρ and configure its approximation. A method tag such as !egm "selects a numerical technique for these equations; it supplies no missing condition" (Methodization).

docs.title: Meaning assigned part by part
docs.text:
A text that appeals to no order of execution must take its meaning from the mathematical objects its parts denote. Scott and Strachey (1971, p. 1) draw the founding distinction: "The numerals are expressions in a certain familiar language; while the numbers are mathematical objects (abstract objects) which provide the intended interpretations of the expressions." Schmidt (1986, Introduction, p. 1) separates syntax, "the appearance and structure of its sentences", from semantics, "the assignment of meanings to the sentences", and from pragmatics, "the usability of the language". The assignment is compositional when, in the words of Winskel (1993, §5.2, p. 60), "the denotation of a command is constructed from the denotations of its immediate subcommands", a property Winskel calls "a hallmark of denotational semantics" and one that fails for the operational semantics of a while-loop. Hutton (2023, §3, p. 3) states the consequence: "the meaning of a compound term is defined purely in terms of the meaning of its subterms. Compositionality aids understanding by ensuring that the semantics is modular and supports the use of simple equational reasoning techniques." Goguen, Thatcher, Wagner and Wright (1977, §3.2, p. 76) give the algebraic form: a grammar "yields an initial many-sorted algebra", "semantics arises from an algebra of the same type, and 'meaning' is the unique homomorphism" (see initial algebra).

None of these authors discusses declarativeness; the connection is this entry's reading, and the reader should weigh it as such. Winskel's remark supplies the connection: a compositional meaning has to be constructed from the parts of the text, and the one meaning that cannot be so constructed is the trace of a loop. In this repository Υ is the meaning map and the semgraph is its result; the fold of the statements of a block into the boxes of a builder is the construction by structural recursion.

Compositional meaning is what licenses the substitution of equals for equals, the convention Stoy (1977, §1.1, pp. 5–7) calls "one particularly important convention in mathematics" and the entry referential transparency states for this project. Backus (1978, §11.4.4, p. 624) attributes the simplicity of his systems to "the most elementary fixed naming system (naming a function in a definition) with a simple fixed rule of substituting a function for its name". A stage file follows the same discipline: a function is defined once and its name is used in the statements.

docs.title: A matter of degree
docs.text: The Stan Reference Manual shows that "declarative" names a position on a scale, by contrasting Stan with BUGS: "Unlike programs in BUGS, the declarations and statements making up a Stan program are executed in the order in which they are written" (ch. 7, p. 72); "In BUGS, for loops are declarative, defining plates in directed graphical model notation, which can be thought of as repeated substructures in the graphical model. Therefore, it is illegal in BUGS or JAGS to have a for loop that repeatedly reassigns a value to a variable" (§7.7, pp. 89–90); and "Because Stan is an imperative language, print statements can be very useful for debugging" (§7.13, p. 99). Carpenter et al. (2017, §5.2, p. 22) say the same, and add that a sampling statement "is nothing more than shorthand for incrementing the log density accumulator" (§5.1, p. 21). The object a Stan program defines, a density, is declared; the text that defines it is an ordered sequence of statements. BUGS is declarative in both respects, at the cost recorded below. Dynare's .mod file, which the project's toolkit comparison describes as "a declarative .mod language" with a separate engine, is the other declarative tool most economists have used.

docs.title: The declarative statement and its realization
docs.text:
A stage file may contain both a declaration and the lines of a method that realize it, and the mark !doc tells the two apart. The policy block of the consumption stage cons.bl states the choice as a maximization over the feasible set,

c = argmax_{cp : Γ(m_d)}(𝑢(cp) + V[>])   :: [id=optimality, !doc]

The mark !doc identifies the declarative statement of what the control is, the mathematical definition of the object; it is neither documentation to be skipped nor an implementation detail. The other lines of the block, the inverse Euler inequality with its clause, the endogenous-grid line and the identification c = c[>], are one realization of that statement by a method, the endogenous grid method. The file thus reads as the economist writes the problem, a maximization subject to a feasibility constraint, with the numerical method's lines recognizable as a realization of it. The card of the policy builder prints the !doc line under Declared and the other lines as the builder's operations (The builders graphs §3; A builder §2 for the operations): the !doc line forms no operation, and the feasible set its binder declares enters the type of the policy.

The mark draws the Stan and BUGS contrast inside one file: the statement marked !doc declares what the control is, and the other statements of the block record one way to compute it. An argmax line written without !doc is itself operative: it forms a row of kind Argmax, whose output is the set of maximizing policies, and a numerical method bound to the row makes the selection (operations).

docs.title: What declaring does not settle
docs.text:
Declaring a meaning leaves the behavior of a computation open, in two directions. First, two texts with one denotation can compute differently. The Stan Reference Manual (§6.12, pp. 70–71), on derivatives taken statement by statement through an expression of the form x − x, warns: "Rather than the x − x canceling out, it introduces a 0 into the numerator and denominator of the chain-rule evaluation. The only way to avoid this kind problem is to be careful to do the necessary algebraic reductions as part of the model". In the calculus this is a fact about Ρ, not Υ, and the entry referential transparency makes the same distinction: replacing exact expectation by a quadrature approximation "requires an error argument rather than an appeal to equality". Two realizations of one declared stage need not agree numerically, and nothing in the declaration guarantees that they do.

Second, a language that is declarative throughout forbids constructions that some computations use; the BUGS prohibition on reassignment quoted above is the example. Naish (1996, §9.3, pp. 14–15) records a related gap, between equality as written and equality in the intended interpretation: "there is nothing to prevent Prolog from attempting to unify these two terms and failing, even though they are equal in this interpretation."

docs.title: The declared artifact and its reading
docs.text: Declaring requires an artifact that can be read. Pfenning (2021, §1, p. L11.1) defines elaboration as "a translation mediating between specific forms of concrete syntax and internal representation in abstract syntax"; in this project the word names the step that reads the stage files and constructs the semgraph, and the entry syntax separates the concrete syntax a modeler writes from the abstract syntax that records its structure. Oliveira and Löh (2012, §2.1–2.2, pp. 2–3) name the price of writing a language directly as code in a host language: "shallow embeddings come at a price. We are committing to a specific semantics — in this case, evaluation." The project's review of carrier formats makes the same division, between languages with their own grammar, "Dynare .mod, dyno .dyno, Stan, Modelica, gEcon .gcn", and tools embedded in a host language, "JuMP, Pyomo/CVXPY, SSJ blocks, HARK objects, POMDPs.jl", which offer "free syntax and tooling, but no declarative artifact — nothing for Υ to read." The toolkit comparison records in the same spirit that QuantEcon "is a LIBRARY of numerical primitives, not a model-specification language". A stage file kept as abstract syntax can be read by more than one interpretation, of which the semgraph is the first.

docs.title: Where the design looks procedural
docs.text:
Three features of the design look procedural; the documents state the following about each.

  1. The order of the bindings. A stage version is the stage occurrence as it stands after elaboration or after one of its three bindings, the calibration, the methods and the settings. Methodization precedes configuration, because the methods name the settings, and calibration may come at any point; each binding adds to the stage occurrence it is called on and returns that stage (The binding verbs §§1 and 3; specified stage).
  2. Statement order within a block. The boxes of a builder are emitted in the order the terms nest them, and a builder's card lists its operations in the order of application, each after every operation whose output it reads (operations §1).
  3. Method names in outer files. A methods file names algorithms such as the endogenous grid method. It names computations that the stage file created and creates none, and a method tag supplies no missing condition (Methodization §§1 and 2), which is the declarative reading this entry gives.

docs.title: Related concepts
docs.text:
• Bellman-SYM: the language whose declarative character this entry defines.
  • semgraph and Υ — meaning construction: the meaning a stage file is assigned, and the map that assigns it.
  • Ρ — numerical representation and methodization: the numerical realization supplied separately, and the step that names it.
  • semantics: the distinction between interpretation, representation and realization.
  • syntax and statement: the concrete and abstract forms of what is declared, and the !doc mark.
  • Referential transparency and Functional programming and FFP: substitution of equals, and Backus's functional style.
  • Initial algebra: the algebraic form of compositional meaning.
  • Specified stage: the stage after methods, settings and parameter values are attached.
  • Workflow §1: the workflow in which the declaration is the first step.
