docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Summary

Settings are the values a numerical method reads: the bounds and the count of a grid, a tolerance, an iteration limit, the number of quadrature nodes, a rule chosen among finitely many labels. They configure how a computation is approximated; parameters define the economic model. A setting is declared with its domain in the methods file, the addition to the stage file, and its value, written in the settings file, is bound by configure, which refuses a value outside the declared set.

Relationship with other documents

Formal account — Methods §6: a setting as a declared name a method's label reads, with no value in the signature. Builds on — Grid: the component whose factors name settings; Methods: the words whose keyword arguments name them. Used by — Parameters and settings: the table stage.settings; Stage functions: the verb configure.

A setting is told from a parameter by the file that declares it: a parameter is declared by the stage file and defines the model, including any discrete domain that is part of the model; a setting is declared by the methods file and configures a method.

docs.title: 1 Declared with their domains
docs.text:
A methods file declares each setting it reads at file level, in the form the stage file declares a parameter, with its set and a description:

n_a : ℕ              :: ["number of points of the savings grid"]
a_min : Xa           :: ["lower bound of the savings grid"]
a_max : Xa           :: ["upper bound of the savings grid"]
n_ψ_nodes : ℕ        :: ["quadrature nodes of the permanent shock"]
tol_v : ℝ₊₊          :: ["tolerance of value function iteration"]

A bound of a grid is a point of the set the stage declares for the coordinate, Xa for the savings a or a literal set such as ℝ₊; a count is a natural number; a tolerance is a positive real; a setting valued in a finite set of labels, such as a tie-breaking rule, is declared on that set. A name is declared once in a stage, and two declarations of one name with different sets are refused. The scope of a declaration is the addition and the stage it is unioned with; where two stages of one period each declare one name, they denote one setting of that period, as a parameter name does. A grid entry names settings and holds no number: policy.grid : !Cartesian(a=(a_min, a_max, n_a)) names three. A method word's keyword argument names a declared setting where the choice is to be configured, !gauss_hermite(n_ψ=n_ψ_nodes, n_ξ=n_ξ_nodes), and may hold a number or a quoted string where the method's catalogue row admits one. An undeclared name is refused as any other is.

docs.title: 2 Bound by configure
docs.text:
The values stand in the settings file, and the stage verb stage.configure(settings_source), with a path or a mapping, binds them as calibrate, the verb of calibration, binds a parameter's value; configure_trellis(elaborated, syntactic) applies it at every position of a trellis. Configuration follows the union of the stage file with its additions and the elaboration of the unioned stage, so that the settings it binds are those the methods file declares, read against the methods and grids that name them. It refuses a value outside the declared set, naming the line of the methods file where the setting is declared, and a name with no value. A key of a shared settings file that no declaration names binds nothing and declares no new setting, so a spelling mistake in a key is found at configuration and not hidden. The bound values stand in the stage's record of bindings; no value is part of a signature.

stage.settings lists every declared setting with its value, the operator that reads it, the method there and, where the setting is a factor of that operator's grid, the grid's kind; stage.settings["n_a"] answers one setting's record, whose value is the configured value (Parameters and settings §2). stage.par lists the parameters and no setting.

An empty settings mapping is admissible for a stage whose methods declare no setting; it chooses no method. Recording a grid size demonstrates neither numerical accuracy nor adequate treatment of the bounds: at configuration the package checks each bound pair ordered and inside the coordinate's set, each count at least two and each node set strictly increasing, and nothing more. The entry specified stage states the order in which the three bindings, calibration, methodization and configuration, are made, and the specification factory states how the sources of a recipe combine. Exact configuration behavior is in Stage functions.

docs.title: Signature
docs.text:
A signature is a typed vocabulary of operation symbols. It specifies each operation's ordered input types and output type. An interpretation supplies the actual operations on objects of those types; listing a symbol is not yet giving its mathematical behavior.

In a many-sorted algebra, sorts form an index set and each sort has a carrier set of objects. For each input word of sorts and output sort, the signature provides operation symbols of that type. Their interpretations map products of the corresponding input carriers to the output carrier. Goguen, Thatcher, Wagner and Wright (1977), Initial Algebra Semantics and Continuous Algebras, §2 p. 70, gives this definition. That source uses rank for the length of the input word; a full input/output type contains more information.

docs.title: Builder signatures and mathematical signatures
docs.text:
A block header declares the input and output fields of authored text, with their sets, roles and perches. A Bellman-SYM builder signature instead gives the actual function or measure wires of the operator constructed from that block; signature() answers it as one record with two parts, inputs and outputs. On a controlled backward edge, the control is a coordinate of the functions carried by the wires and is not itself an input wire. A state of the perch at which a backward block's output stands is likewise a coordinate of the output function and is listed on no backward header (Appendix C R1). The policy is an index on the builder at a policy and is not an argument of the decision value function. A block identifier names the authored block; its statements and dependencies determine the constructed operator.

A mathematical signature for stage composition instead specifies operations such as combining compatible builders or stages. Its terms, their interpretations and the .bl constructor grammar are distinct objects. The stage term and Abstract grammar give the mathematical account.

Neither a signature nor matching inputs and outputs prove integrability, an attained maximum or admissibility of a numerical method. Methodization requires a supported existing computation and the method's contract. See sort, syntax and expression.

docs.title: Sort
docs.text:
A sort identifies a kind of object in a typed mathematical vocabulary. Its carrier is the set of objects assigned to that sort by an interpretation. The sort and its carrier are distinct: one is an index, the other a set.

An operation's type lists ordered input sorts and an output sort. Its interpretation maps the corresponding carriers. This is the many-sorted definition in Goguen, Thatcher, Wagner and Wright (1977), Initial Algebra Semantics and Continuous Algebras, §2 p. 70; see signature.

docs.title: Distinctions in a stage
docs.text:
In a stage, a grammar sort classifies a source constructor. A field domain constrains the quantity it denotes. An economic role, such as control or value, and an information context supply further meaning. A state value, a scalar payoff, a function on states and a measure over states therefore cannot be interchanged merely because a diagram connects them.

The builders graphs, the graphs of the builders, keep state-space, value and function-space types explicit: the sort of a function wire holds its coordinates and its value set. A numerical grid representation is not automatically a subsort of the exact function space: such a claim needs an embedding and its interpretation. Method labels alone do not establish carrier inclusion or derivative agreement.

See initial diagrams, parameters, settings and Fields and types.

docs.title: Source span
docs.text:
A source span identifies the interval occupied by an authored item in a .bl file. SourceSpan(file, line, column, end_line, end_column) records one-based lines and columns; columns count Unicode code points and the end position is exclusive.

bellman.syntax.lower.parse_with_spans(text, filename=None) returns the parsed AST (abstract syntax tree) and a read-only span table keyed by term address. The caller supplies both to make_stage(term, spans). Construction uses spans to locate diagnostics, then discards the table. Spans are not retained on the stage or included in the term JSON encoding. A decoded fixture supplies None instead; its construction errors still identify the item address.

Spans cover authored items such as declarations, definitions, blocks and their statements. A block's span covers its whole interval, while an error inside an expression uses its enclosing item's span. Ignored comment tokens do not receive their own item spans, although an enclosing interval may include a comment. Duplicate item addresses cannot identify two entries in one span table.

A span is an interval; a source position is a point. Neither is a symbol table, which associates names with declarations. Later method-binding diagnostics must use their own available source or provenance information; they cannot assume the discarded construction span table remains accessible.

See The stage §§1 and 6 for the distinction between source structure, construction checks and mathematical conditions.

docs.title: Specification factory
docs.text:
The specification factory merges parameter, numerical-setting and method sources according to an ordered YAML recipe, spec.yml. A recipe names every file it reads by its path from its own folder, the registry directory: the trellis file under trellis:, each stage's file under stage: in the stage's entry, and the sources of its source lists; nothing is read in place of a path it does not write. In a model folder of the repository the registry is the subfolder declaration/, which holds every file the language reads, each stage's files in a folder of their own, so that load_recipe("applications/durables/declaration", "spec.yml") reads the durables model (Model directory layout). load_recipe(directory, recipe, **fills) reads the recipe and the registry and returns the syntactic trellis; it constructs no stage and no semgraph (semantic graph), and reads the stage files' declarations only to check the names a fill gives.

Each recipe stage names its stage file and supplies all source lists for calibration, settings and methods. Resolution applies those sources in order, then any matching inclusive period-range overrides. Binding ranges do not themselves restrict stage activity; an optional stage periods interval does that separately. Ranges within one stage and binding kind must not overlap.

docs.title: Source composition
docs.text:
Mappings merge recursively. Method lists match their single on targets, merge matched entries and append new targets. Later scalars and ordinary lists replace earlier values. This preserves omitted bindings without asserting a general categorical or algebraic theorem about arbitrary merge inputs.

Source names are relative to the registry directory. A parent source is read before its child's entries; parent cycles are rejected and recursion is limited. These rules resolve data, leaving method-target and parameter and setting completeness checks to the stage operations. The current reference specifies path resolution and accepted wrappers in detail.

docs.title: Recipe slots
docs.text:
A slot is a named place in a recipe source list, such as $fill, whose value is supplied with the keyword fill= of load_recipe; the value is the fill, a mapping. A slot affects only the source lists in which it is named, so one fill can be reused at several addresses.

load_recipe is one step of the Bellman factory, the part of the package from the files to the specified trellis; a method choice is a methods mapping supplied to a methods slot, and a sweep is a family of fills, one expression over them, such as [assemble_trellis(directory, recipe, fill=f) for f in fills], with assemble_trellis of bellman.trellis.

A flat mapping supplies entries directly. A mapping whose top-level keys are all among calibration, settings and methods is interpreted by specification kind; a mixture with other keys is treated as flat. A methods slot supplies a mapping containing its methods list. The shape must match the recipe's intended use.

An unfilled slot contributes an empty mapping. A keyword naming no slot is refused with FactoryError under the rule recipe-slot-unknown. Extra keys inside a declared slot do not become model declarations. Slots are not the only source of user data: files and direct stage bindings are separate supported routes. A recipe slot is also distinct from an ASDL field, an economic field or an operation's argument.

docs.title: The syntactic trellis the recipe defines
docs.text:
syntactic["periods"][h]["stages"][key]["calibration"], and the settings and methods beside it, are the merged mappings of that stage at period h, h counting periods before the terminal one; the record holds bindings as data, not a stage, and no policy or solved stage. elaborate_trellis constructs the stage occurrences, one for each stage file at each position, from the records, and calibrate_trellis, methodize_trellis and configure_trellis bind them, completing the lifecycle of a specified stage.

Source precedence first determines each stage's record. When stages in one period declare the same parameter name, calibration then reconciles those records and binds one period value to every declaring stage; two disagreeing supplied values are refused. A value at the same name in a different period remains independent. This sharing of parameters does not identify the stages' fields.

See Recipe functions for the signatures, the merge, the slot shapes and the refusals, and The Bellman factory for the route through the calls. Calibration, settings and methodization define the three kinds of input.

docs.title: Specified stage
docs.text: A specified stage is a constructed stage with its method, numerical-setting and parameter values supplied. The name distinguishes the resulting stage occurrence from the recipe and partial source mappings used to prepare them. It is not a synonym for a solved model or a callable numerical implementation.

docs.title: Specification order
docs.text:
The recommended order of the bindings is calibrate, methodize, configure:

construction → calibration → methodization → configuration

Calibration requires values for all declared parameters. Methodization identifies the supported computations and their numerical choices. Configuration requires prior methodization and values for all referenced settings; calibration may also come after either of the others. Each binding adds to the stage occurrence it is called on and returns it; nothing is copied, and a later binding at a target replaces the earlier one (The binding verbs §1). This does not imply that the operations commute.

The four stopping points, the symbolic trellis and the trellis after each verb, are the results of the four calls: elaborate_trellis, then calibrate_trellis, methodize_trellis and configure_trellis, each reading its mapping from the syntactic trellis given as its second argument. Each binding verb with its source held fixed is a binding map, written \(\mathcal C_c\), \(M_m\) and \(K_s\) in Appendix G §7, so that a specified stage is \(K_s\,M_m\,\mathcal C_c(S)\).

docs.title: Meaning and numerical execution
docs.text:
A recognition-only method entry can leave the algorithm unspecified even when the required mappings exist. Numerical use additionally needs compatible handlers, representations, continuation or terminal data, feasible boundary treatment and accuracy checks. Analytic assumptions are not supplied by settings or calibration.

The specification factory resolves inputs to these operations; the syntactic trellis it returns is a dictionary of bindings, not the stage's mathematical graph. The entries symbolic stage, methodization, settings, calibration and parameters explain the individual concepts. Exact signatures and target behavior are in Stage functions.

docs.title: Stage
docs.text: A stage is a module of a Bellman problem with arrival, decision, and continuation information contexts. It declares the quantities relevant there and the equations for state transitions, value calculations, and policy relations. Its source is a .bl stage file in Bellman-SYM, and in Python it is the elaborated stage that elaborate_stage of bellman.stage makes of the file.

docs.title: A consumption example
docs.text:
A household begins with assets \(b\), observes income \(y\), and chooses consumption \(c\) from resources \(w=Rb+y\), leaving savings \(a=w-c\). Arrival information precedes income, decision information includes observed income, and continuation information includes the consumption choice. Assume resources suffice for the consumption decision and savings suffice for continuation value; the household's information can be richer than these scalar states.

For an admissible continuation function \(W\), the objective is \(Q(w,c)=u(c)+\beta W(w-c)\). A policy selects a feasible maximizer, and arrival value averages the resulting decision value over income. Existence of that maximizer, measurability, and finiteness of the expectation are assumptions to check. The complete walkthrough states domains, a conditional distribution of income, and sufficient conditions.

docs.title: A stage file and its stage occurrences
docs.text:
A stage occurrence is one use of the stage file in a period at a particular position in the model: the file elaborated there, with its own three bindings. Its fields, policy and numerical choices remain local to that occurrence. A parameter name declared by two stages of the same period, however, names one period parameter with one reconciled declaration and value; the same name in another period names another parameter. The construction gives each stage occurrence its own semgraph and specification, prints the file's declared name for every one, and records the position in the occurrence's provenance. Each binding adds to the elaborated object in place and returns it; a stage version is the stage occurrence as it stands after elaboration or after one of its bindings.

The stage's semgraph (semantic graph) retains its interpreted equations and definitions. Whole builders, named Bellman operations, and authored !node computations provide inspection boundaries. Scalar arithmetic inside a state transition or value aggregator is not another advertised level of that semgraph.

The field-equation tutorial develops consumption as a separate stage file, which can then be joined to discounting and portfolio choice through compatible connectors.

docs.title: statement
docs.text: A statement is one equation line of a block of a stage file, as written: V = u(c) + β*V[>] :: [id=value]. A value statement is one whose left-hand side is a value or marginal-value field; the phrase "value line" is not used for it, because the calculus's value line \(\mathsf L\) is the set in which values lie. A statement's annotation :: [...] carries its identifier and its marks, among them !node, which makes the statement a node and its result a named wire (see sub-builder), and !doc, which marks a declarative statement.

docs.title: Three readings
docs.text: In an initial diagram, a graph of the stage on its fields (semgraph), a statement is a box inside its block's box unless it is marked !doc: its input wires are the fields it reads and its output wire the field it defines, so a name a statement introduces, an intermediate field y = l + h + x or the candidate c[>] of a policy block, appears as a wire. The initial diagrams are the only graphs in which such names are recorded. In the definitions table every statement is a record of kind line, keyed by its address and holding its tags and retained term; its role, ordinal and operator occurrences are queries. In the builders graphs, the graphs of the builders, a statement is not a box: the fold replaces it by the operators it denotes, a pullback, expectations and aggregations for a value statement of a backward block, and an alias statement is substituted at its uses (Appendix C R2).

docs.title: Two kinds of statement in a backward block
docs.text: A statement whose right-hand side carries no value input, y = l + h + x, is a field equation: it extends the typing context with a derived field and belongs to the field reading. A statement whose right-hand side carries a value input, a continuation function, an expectation's result or a sub-builder's output, is folded into operators, and only such a statement may carry !node in a backward block. In a forward block every statement is a field equation and a !node marks a sub-transition.

docs.title: A property of a line
docs.text: A statement attached to an operative line by a dotted id, as the first-order condition optimality.euler is attached to the maximization line optimality, is that line's property: it forms no row, no address and no method place of its own, and it prints under the row of its line, read at the point, with its id. A dotted id whose first part names no line of its block is refused.

docs.title: A clause after a statement
docs.text: A statement may carry a clause ⟂ after it, the complementary slackness between the statement's residual and a bound, as the candidate line of the consumption stage does, c[>] <= 𝑑𝑢𝑖𝑛𝑣(dV[>]) ⟂ a >= 0. The Kuhn–Tucker condition of a policy block has three spellings, the clause on the first-order condition, a declared multiplier and the clause on the candidate line, and the three denote one relation (Constraints §§3 and 4).

docs.title: An occurrence is not a statement
docs.text: An occurrence is an operator written inside a statement, E_η(·), argmax, solve; its result is a wire the construction makes, free in the remaining coordinates, and only the operation's own method attaches to it. Marking a statement !node is the only way to make an occurrence's result a named object.

docs.title: Related concepts
docs.text: semgraph, sub-builder, aggregation, initial diagrams, expression.

docs.title: sub-builder
docs.text: A node statement is a statement of a block that the author marks !node, thereby making its left-side field an evaluated field: an expected continuation value, a post-decision value, or a candidate consumption function. An intermediate function formed by a subexpression remains unnamed. The sub-builder is the operator that statement denotes inside its backward builder. The pair follows block against builder: the block and the node are authored text, the builder and the sub-builder are what they denote. In the semgraph a sub-builder is a bubble inside the builder's bubble, named by the statement's address; in code the grain at which sub-builders are closed keeps the token node, and prose says "the sub-builder grain". Never call the operator a node, and never call a branch a node (see branch).

docs.title: The slice and the cut
docs.text: The statements a node's statement depends on, cut at earlier nodes and at the block's inputs, form its slice. Read as one operator, the slice is a factor of the builder's sequential composition on the sub-tensor of wires it reads: a cut in the sense of the calculus's Appendix B §5, and opening the bubble and composing its interior leaves the builder unchanged by the factorization theorem of Appendix B §4. The same word names the statements any wire depends on, so the slices of a builder's outputs, one for each output wire, are its parallel strands, parallel when they share no statement and meeting at a copy where they do.

docs.title: What a sub-builder contains
docs.text: Inside the bubble the same fold as for the containing builder applies to the slice: the pullback of every continuation function it reads along the block's law of motion, then its pointwise aggregations and expectations in the authored order, then identity evaluation on the resulting function into the evaluated field's declared carrier. Its G's are the maps of its aggregation boxes, one inside and one outside each expectation it contains; they are not separate authored definitions but the slice of the block's one G record that its statements form. The inputs and outputs of a sub-builder are its domain and codomain tensors, dom and cod; "boundary" is reserved for "the evaluation at a sub-builder's output".

docs.title: Its signature and kernels
docs.text:
A sub-builder's signature consists of the function wires it actually reads and writes. Its output is a function on the coordinates left after the shocks named by its expectations have been integrated, restricted to the feasible pairs when a control is among those coordinates. The control is a coordinate of that function, not a separate input wire. Its sort records the coordinates on which the function varies.

A kernel is the mathematical data an operator uses; a policy used by a builder indexes its pullback, aggregation or conditional distribution. These kernels have different domains and must not all be assigned the scalar aggregator type \(G : \mathsf L^{m} \times \mathsf X \times \mathsf A \times \mathsf Z \to \mathsf L\). The compiled callable for such data is the compiled kernel.

A value input is a value function, its derivative read by a derivative term such as D_{a}V[>], or any function formed by composing one into an expression: the pulled-back continuation function \(v \circ g\), an expectation's result, an aggregation's output, or a sub-builder's output. An unmarked line's left-side field is not evaluated; its expression is substituted where used. The !node mark instead makes the line's left-side field an evaluated output and adds its evaluation. The output is a value when every value input is a value. A line whose left side is a derivative term is a derivative line: it states a derivative of the value its builder writes and adds no output.

docs.title: Grains, parallel wires and branches
docs.text: At the sub-builder grain each sub-builder is a closed bubble and its output cuts a pointwise segment. At the primitive grain every bubble is open, only the sub-builders' identity evaluations are dropped, and adjacent pointwise aggregations merge by composing their terms, never across an expectation or two parallel paths; a merged box keeps its place after calibration. Each slice constructs its own copy of an unmarked statement it shares with another slice, and slices share only earlier sub-builder outputs and the block's inputs, a block input two slices read being substituted in each. A branch is a bubble of the forward initial diagram and no sub-builder; a sub-builder may sit inside one branch's slice or around the selection statement, never across part of the selection's tuple.

docs.title: Forward blocks
docs.text: A !node in a forward block marks a sub-transition, a factor of the law of motion \(g = g_2 \circ g_1\), which the two readings inherit as \((g_2)_\# \circ (g_1)_\#\) on measures and \(K_{g_1} \circ K_{g_2}\) on functions. Forward markers are preserved, and g is not split at them. The rule that a sub-builder maps value inputs to value inputs is a rule for backward blocks.

docs.title: Related concepts
docs.text: semgraph owns the graphs, grains and value bundles; aggregation the kernel G and its two maps; statement the authored line and its record; branch the discrete alternatives; backward builder the operator a backward block denotes.

docs.title: Bellman-SYM
docs.text: Bellman-SYM is the declarative language used to write a staged Bellman problem. A modeler states domains, information, choices, equations, and shock probability distributions in a .bl stage file. The expression syntax comes from dynspec, the host language for these declarations and equations. Outer YAML files assemble stage files into periods and a trellis, and supply methods, settings, and calibration.

docs.title: Start with an economic model
docs.text:
The stage walkthrough introduces consumption after income is observed. It explains why beginning assets, resources at the consumption decision, and savings for continuation have different information contexts. The later field-equation example separates consumption into a reusable stage file before adding discounting and investment.

A stage identifier or block name supplies an address; it does not supply an equation. A solver choice likewise cannot fill in a missing budget constraint or objective. The modeler states these relationships explicitly.

docs.title: Syntax, meaning, and computation
docs.text:
Syntax describes the written source and its parsed abstract syntax tree (AST). The meaning construction interprets that temporary AST as a semgraph (semantic graph) with retained equations and definitions. Methodization, calibration, and settings provide the numerical choices and values required for a particular calculation. Successful parsing alone establishes neither an economically admissible model nor a solved policy.

The language guide explains what to write and inspect. The Bellman calculus develops the mathematical interpretation and its assumptions in its chapters.

docs.title: Symbolic stage
docs.text:
A symbolic stage is the constructed stage before numerical methods, settings and calibration values are attached. It is what elaborate_stage(load_stage(path)) returns for one stage file, and what elaborate_trellis places at every position of a trellis. It does not mean that the stage retains a parser tree or has no interpreted mathematical equations.

load_stage(path) reads a .bl stage file into a source record, and elaborate_stage(record) parses and checks it and returns a stage containing its semgraph (semantic graph). On the symbolic stage stage.methods and stage.settings are empty, stage.par lists every parameter as unbound, and repr(stage) prints ElaboratedStage('cons', symbolic) for the consumption stage. Typed fields, equations and definitions describe the problem, with parameter names still symbolic. Further functional interpretation requires its stated assumptions; construction is not a numerical solution.

A stage file is reusable .bl source; at the elaborator boundary it is also called a stage module. A stage occurrence is that file elaborated at one position of a period, with its own three bindings; several stage occurrences of one file may sit in one period or across periods, each a separate object that shares nothing with the others, prints the file's declared name and records its position in its provenance. Each binding adds to the stage occurrence in place and returns it, and a text derived from the file is elaborated as its own stage occurrence with its origin recorded. Period and trellis assembly uses outer records; it elaborates the stage file at each position as its own stage occurrence and retains no whole-model syntax tree.

The entry specified stage describes the bindings that follow, in the recommended order calibration, methodization and configuration. Methodization supplies numerical choices without replacing missing mathematics.

See Stage functions and The stage.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Syntax specifies the forms that expressions and declarations can take. Concrete syntax is the text a modeler writes. Abstract syntax records its structure without incidental punctuation. Neither alone establishes what the model means or whether it has a solution.

Bellman-SYM stage source uses .bl stage files, including declarations, equations, function definitions, arithmetic and local binders. Supporting YAML supplies composition and binding records. Parsing constructs a temporary parsed AST (abstract syntax tree); checking and interpretation construct retained equations and diagrams. The constructed semgraph (semantic graph) retains the interpreted equations in its two initial diagrams, on the fields of the stage; it is not another name for the parsed AST.

docs.title: Grammar and contextual checks
docs.text:
A context-free grammar rule has one nonterminal on its left and alternative sequences of terminals and nonterminals on its right, conventionally written A ::= ... | .... Nonterminals name grammatical categories; terminals are source tokens. The name Pāṇini–Backus Form also refers to this production notation. ASDL instead describes abstract constructor structures.

A grammar may recognize E_{y}(V) + y as an expression while construction rejects it as arrival value when income is not yet observed. Name resolution, type agreement, binding and information availability are contextual checks, not consequences of punctuation. Integrability, sufficient states, attained optima and numerical accuracy require further conditions.

Mathematical composition terms describe specified operations on functions or measures. They are distinct from both the concrete stage grammar and a chosen runtime representation. A compositional interpretation needs specified operations and assignments to free inputs; grammar alone does not supply missing economic equations or prove equivalence of different models.

See expression, signature, The stage §1 and Abstract grammar.

docs.title: Term address
docs.text:
A term address identifies an authored item of a stage file from the parsed AST (abstract syntax tree) alone. bellman.syntax.lower.item_addresses(term) produces address–item pairs in source order. A fresh parse and its decoded term JSON encoding therefore have the same addresses without requiring source positions.

Item Address Top-level item without an authored id Its one-based position, written as a string. Named block Its header id, such as policy. Named statement Block address plus statement id, such as policy.cons_choice. Unnamed statement Block address plus one-based statement position. Labeled nested block Containing block address plus the label. Statement in that block Nested block address plus its id or position.

Explicit ids survive changes that would shift ordinal positions, but no address is invariant under arbitrary source edits. Construction diagnostics use the address to look up a source span, or report the address alone when positions are unavailable.

docs.title: Inspection and method targets
docs.text:
An address does not imply that its item is a separate graph box or an eligible numerical target. An alias can remain inspectable after substitution. Supported implicit statements and named operator occurrences can receive methods without !node; an authored node needs an explicit id for method attachment. Positional statement addresses support records and diagnostics, not stable user bindings.

The entry methodization owns the distinction between a whole builder target, a named statement, a stage-wide operator and an overriding occurrence target. These targets resolve existing computations rather than creating equations.

A decoder's path such as items[3].d.subject locates a defect inside an encoded value. It is a descriptive structural path, not a term address or a promise of JSONPath-standard conformance. See Methods and places.

docs.title: Term JSON encoding
docs.text: A Bellman-SYM syntax fixture records the parsed AST (abstract syntax tree) of a .bl stage file. bellman.syntax.lower.to_json(term) converts that tree into Python values suitable for JSON serialization. bellman.syntax.decode.from_json(data) decodes a supported encoding into a generated FILE object; it accepts already-parsed JSON values, not JSON text or a file path.

docs.title: Encoding and decoding
docs.text:
Each generated constructor becomes an object with a "__class__" tag and its declared ASDL fields, the named positions of the constructor, which are no economic fields. Absent optional positions are explicit null values; sequences become arrays. The encoder emits fields in declaration order. The serializer determines whitespace and other textual formatting, so equality of JSON values does not promise preservation of arbitrary input JSON bytes.

The decoder accepts constructors defined by the generated grammar, requires exactly their fields and checks sequence versus single-value positions. It rejects unknown constructors, missing or extra keys, arrays in single-value positions and non-FILE roots. TermDecodeError, a ValueError, identifies the defect with a descriptive path into the encoding. No data-provided name is evaluated or imported.

For supported FILE fixtures, encoding after decoding recovers the encoded values, and decoding an encoded FILE recovers the generated structure. This claim is restricted to the codec's accepted inputs: to_json can also encode subnodes that are not accepted roots of from_json. Generated single-value positions do not themselves enforce all grammar sorts or contextual rules.

docs.title: Purpose and limits
docs.text:
A parser reads concrete .bl syntax; a decoder reconstructs syntax from its saved representation. Parsing is not generally an inverse of source printing. Both routes can supply make_stage(term, spans), with None for the absent span table of a decoded fixture. Construction checks remain necessary.

Fixtures support parser and construction conformance tests. They are not persistence for the semgraph (semantic graph), and applications load .bl source rather than fixtures. After construction the stage retains interpreted equations and definitions, not this tree. See term address, ASDL and The stage §1.

docs.title: Trellis
docs.text: A trellis is a finite ordered collection of period occurrences and their inter-period connections. It records uses of stage files across dates. It is not a grid of individual state points and does not by itself assert one stored semgraph (semantic graph) for the entire horizon.

docs.title: Index and boundary data
docs.text:
The index \(h\) counts backwards from terminal: periods[0] is terminal and periods[h+1] is one period earlier than periods[h]. An inter-period connector indexed by \(h\) joins the earlier period's continuation to the later period's arrival. Backward calculation uses terminal continuation data first, then proceeds to increasing \(h\). The trellis is counted this way because it is built this way, the terminal period appended first and each earlier period after it, so that appending a period changes no index already present and the horizon is the number of periods built.

Terminal continuation data must match the terminal stage's declared inputs and domains. Calling an entry terminal does not automatically supply zero value, a terminal policy, or compatible derivatives. An infinite-horizon fixed-point condition is a different boundary problem.

docs.title: The three files and the two routes
docs.text:
A trellis is written in files or in Python. The trellis file lists the periods, the terminal period first, each written out or given as a period template repeated, together with the inter-period connectors; the period file is the template of one period; and the recipe, spec.yml, names for each stage key the stage's file and the ordered sources of its calibration, settings and methods, every path relative to the recipe's own folder. The recipe is the file of the specification factory.

The shape of a period's stages decides the route. Written as a list of keys, a period binds nothing, and load_recipe(directory, "spec.yml") reads the trellis file through the recipe, which supplies each key's file and mappings. Written as a mapping from each key to a record that names the stage file under stage and its three mappings inline or as paths, a period carries its bindings, and load_trellis(file) reads it with no recipe. The two shapes are not mixed in one file. A variant route is a second set of the three files beside the first, spec.<name>.yml, trellis.<name>.yml and period.<name>.yml. Without any file, accrete appends one period at a time to {"periods": [], "inter_connectors": []}, the terminal period first. The trellis guide §§1, 3, 5 and 6 state the three files, the two shapes, the paths and the Python route; what a recipe does with the files it names is the factory guide §3.

docs.title: Reusing stage files
docs.text: The same stage file may be parsed once and used for several stage occurrences. Each stage occurrence receives its own semgraph, methods, and settings. Stages in one period share a parameter when they declare it under the same name; the same name in another period denotes another parameter. A value that differs by period is written in the recipe, as the factory guide §3 states, or into the records by the application. The stage file itself need not encode a calendar date.

docs.title: The syntactic and the elaborated trellis
docs.text:
The syntactic trellis is the model as written: the dictionary {"periods": [{"stages": {key: record}, "connectors": [...]}], "inter_connectors": [...]}, each record holding the stage's source and its three mappings, calibration, settings and methods, as data. load_trellis(file) and load_recipe(directory, recipe, **fills) return it, and every adjustment to a model, a fill of a recipe's slot, a value that differs by period or a method choice, is made in it before elaboration and binding. The elaborated trellis is the same dictionary with an elaborated stage at every key: elaborate_trellis(syntactic) returns it symbolic, and calibrate_trellis, methodize_trellis and configure_trellis, each given the syntactic trellis as its second argument, return it specified. Neither dictionary holds a graph; the only graphs are the semgraphs inside the stages.

The trellis guide shows the files, the records and the construction sequence. Ordering conventions distinguishes this backward index from forward economic time and ordinary function-composition order.

docs.title: Υ — meaning construction
docs.text:
Summary

Υ (Upsilon) is the meaning map from a stage file to the model it states. It has two steps: the elaboration, a program of the package that constructs the elaborated stage from the file or refuses it, and the interpretation of that stage, which the Bellman calculus defines and no function computes. This page names the computed step, the elaborator \(S\), and states what it reads and what it does not.

Relationship with other documents

Formal account — Appendix A and Appendix C: the interpretation of the constructed stage and its rules. Builds on — Syntax: the parsed AST the elaboration reads and discards; The stage: how a stage is made. Used by — Elaborated stage: the object the elaborator constructs; Bellman-SYM writer and Prose writer: the two maps a language model computes around the elaborator.

Υ (Upsilon) names the interpretation that assigns mathematical meaning to a declaration. It has two steps. Elaboration, which the package performs, takes a checked phrase of a stage file to a piece of the semgraph (semantic graph): parsing first produces a temporary parsed AST, and checked construction interprets its declarations, equations, and scoped operations as the semgraph, retaining the mathematical definitions needed for subsequent inspection and calculation. Interpretation, which the Bellman calculus and Appendix C define and no function of the package computes, takes that piece to its denotation, the mathematical object it denotes.

docs.title: 1 The elaborator
docs.text:
The elaborator is the computed step of Υ, written as a map \(S : D \to E\): from a Bellman-SYM declaration \(D\), the stage files with the period and trellis files, that is, the syntactic trellis and its stages, to the elaborated stage \(E\), or to a refusal that names the rule the file does not satisfy, the line, and what to write instead. It is a deterministic program of the package and not a skill: no language model computes it, and it has no instruction text. Its functions are elaborate_text(text, origin) of bellman.factory.elaboration for one text held in memory, elaborate_stage(record) for the record load_stage returns, and elaborate_trellis(syntactic) for a trellis (The stage §1; Stage functions §2). Each parses the text into a temporary parsed AST, constructs the semgraph with its definitions, its two initial diagrams and its two builders graphs, and discards the parsed AST; the stage keeps no syntax tree.

Nothing reads \(D\) as text. A declaration is elaborated before anything reads it, and what is then inspected, compared with the result of another declaration, or described in words is \(E\): files that differ in spelling or in the order of their blocks elaborate to one stage, and the meaning of a file is read from its elaborated stage. The interpretation of \(E\), the second step of Υ, is stated by the Bellman calculus and Appendix C and computed by no function.

The word is the one of programming-language theory, where elaboration translates a surface syntax into a fully explicit, typed core form and fails where the source does not type-check. Pfenning (2021, §1, p. L11.1) introduces it as "a translation mediating between specific forms of concrete syntax and internal representation in abstract syntax", whose result is a signature of typed definitions and which produces none when an expression does not type-check (§4, p. L11.6); Ferreira and Pientka (2014, abstract) elaborate a source language in which arguments may be omitted "to a fully explicit core language" and prove that what elaborates type-checks there. The elaborator of the package is such a translation: it makes every type and every structure the stage file leaves to be inferred explicit in \(E\), or refuses the file (Elaborated stage §1).

Two maps that a language model computes stand around the elaborator. The Bellman-SYM writer \(\Upsilon_0 : M \to D\) writes a declaration from a description \(M\) of the model in prose and displayed equations, named BellmanStageProse, and the prose writer \(\Upsilon_1 : E \to M'\) writes a description from the elaborated stage's printed form. Each is a map and not the instruction text under which the model computes it, and the elaborator followed by the prose writer, \(\Upsilon_1 \circ S\), is a reading of Υ in words. The Bellman-SYM writer works against Υ: many files have one meaning, and it must find one of them.

docs.title: 2 What is interpreted
docs.text:
An equation supplies its mathematical relationship. The header of a block supplies its declared inputs, outputs, domains, and information contexts; the builder signature is derived from the operator the block denotes. Scope determines which occurrences a definition or expectation binds. A block name identifies the block; its spelling does not manufacture a transition or objective.

The resulting stage can still have free parameters and continuation inputs. Construction does not solve the stage or supply values for those free inputs. Calibration supplies parameter values; methodization attaches numerical methods to supported operations.

docs.title: 3 The mathematical contract
docs.text:
For a fixed many-sorted signature, a chosen target interpretation, and fixed free inputs, a compositional interpretation satisfies

\[ \Upsilon\bigl(\omega(t_1,\ldots,t_n)\bigr) = \omega^{\mathcal B}\bigl(\Upsilon(t_1),\ldots,\Upsilon(t_n)\bigr). \]

Here the \(t_i\) are well-sorted syntactic arguments, \(\omega\) is a constructor, and \(\omega^{\mathcal B}\) is its declared interpretation. Initial-algebra semantics states the setting in which this extension is unique. Binding and equations imposed on syntax require their own treatment; the display alone does not provide it.

Reading the stage's fields as functions of its states additionally needs conditions such as state sufficiency, integrability, and a measurable feasible policy. These obligations are distinct from grammar checks and from the correctness of a software implementation. Semantics and the construction account distinguish these responsibilities.
